units.label: Electrical Quantities, Units, and Conventions

lessons.label: Charge, Current, and What Actually Moves

sections.heading: Charge is the quantity, current is the flow
sections.body: Electric charge, measured in coulombs (C), is a property of matter the same way mass is: some fixed amount of it sits on an object. Current is a rate — how much charge crosses a cross-section of a conductor per second. One ampere (A) is defined as exactly one coulomb per second: 1 A = 1 C/s. That definition is not approximate. In the 2019 redefinition of the SI base units, the ampere was re-anchored to a fixed constant, the elementary charge e = 1.602176634e-19 C — the charge on a single electron or proton — with zero uncertainty by definition. Every coulomb is therefore an exact integer multiple of e, roughly 6.24e18 elementary charges.

sections.heading: Conventional current versus electron flow
sections.body: Benjamin Franklin, experimenting with charge in the 1750s decades before anyone knew electrons existed, arbitrarily labeled one kind of charge 'positive' and defined current as flowing from positive to negative through an external circuit. He guessed wrong about which particle actually moves in a metal wire, but the convention stuck: circuit diagrams, Kirchhoff's laws, and every textbook arrow for current still point from + to -, even though in a normal wire it is negatively charged electrons drifting the opposite way, from - to +. Both descriptions predict identical circuit behavior — power dissipation and voltage drops don't care which sign convention you use — so 'conventional current' remains standard practice in engineering.

sections.heading: Drift velocity versus signal speed
sections.body: A common misconception is that current 'travels' through a wire at nearly the speed of light. What actually moves that fast is the electric field's influence — the signal, the change in the field pattern that tells electrons everywhere in the circuit to start moving, propagates at a large fraction of light speed. The electrons themselves crawl. In a copper wire carrying a typical 1 A through a 1 mm² cross-section, the free-electron density of copper (about 8.5e28 electrons/m^3) combined with the elementary charge gives a drift velocity on the order of 0.1 mm/s — slower than a snail. A light switch flicked across a room lights the bulb almost instantly because the field signal races down the wire, not because any individual electron sprinted from the switch to the bulb.

lessons.workedExample: A 12-gauge copper wire (cross-sectional area about 3.31 mm^2) carries a steady 10 A to a space heater. Using J = I/A gives a current density of roughly 3.0e6 A/m^2. Drift velocity v_d = J / (n*e), with copper's free-electron density n ≈ 8.5e28 /m^3 and e = 1.602176634e-19 C, gives v_d ≈ 3.0e6 / (8.5e28 × 1.602e-19) ≈ 0.22 mm/s. At that crawl, an electron would take roughly an hour and a half to travel one meter — yet the heater responds to the switch in a fraction of a second, because it is the field, not the electron, that arrives fast.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'what is actually moving in your circuit?' to test whether a student memorized the current formula or understands the physical picture underneath it. A weak answer says 'electricity flows through the wire' with no distinction between charge, current, and the moving particle. A strong answer names electrons as the actual charge carriers in a metal, explains that conventional current is a historical sign convention running opposite to real electron motion, and can back up a claim about drift velocity with an order-of-magnitude number rather than a vague 'it's fast' or 'it's slow.'

questions.prompt: What does it mean that 1 ampere equals 1 coulomb per second?

options.text: Current is a measure of charge quantity, independent of time
Current is a rate: the amount of charge crossing a point per unit time
Current and charge are the same physical quantity with different names
A coulomb is a unit of current and an ampere is a unit of charge

explanations.a: Charge alone (coulombs) is the quantity; current adds the per-second rate, so this drops the time dimension entirely.
explanations.b: Correct — current is defined as charge flow per unit time, which is exactly what 1 A = 1 C/s expresses.
explanations.c: They are related but distinct: charge is measured in coulombs, current in amperes (coulombs per second); conflating them ignores the rate.
explanations.d: This reverses the units: coulombs measure charge and amperes measure current, not the other way around.

questions.prompt: Benjamin Franklin's positive-to-negative convention for current direction is now known to describe the actual motion of which particles in a typical metal wire?

options.text: Protons, which move from positive to negative
Electrons, moving in the same direction as conventional current
Electrons, moving opposite to the direction of conventional current
Neutrons, which carry no charge but still drift

explanations.a: Protons are bound in the metal's nuclei and do not drift through the wire as charge carriers.
explanations.b: Conventional current points from + to -, but the actual electrons move the opposite direction, from - to +, so this has the relationship backwards.
explanations.c: Correct — Franklin's guess about sign was wrong, so the mobile charge carriers (electrons) move opposite to the conventional current arrow.
explanations.d: Neutrons are uncharged and play no role in electrical conduction.

questions.prompt: Why does a light bulb turn on almost instantly when a switch is flipped, even though electron drift velocity is only about 0.1-0.2 mm/s?

options.text: The electrons that reach the bulb were already there before the switch was flipped, and the electric field signal that starts them all moving propagates at a large fraction of light speed
Electrons briefly accelerate to near light speed the instant the switch closes
The drift velocity figure only applies to AC circuits, not DC lighting circuits
Light bulbs do not rely on electron flow at all

explanations.a: Correct — the wire is already full of electrons everywhere along its length, and the field that tells them to start drifting propagates fast, so response is near-instant even though individual electrons crawl.
explanations.b: Electrons do not jump to relativistic speeds; their drift velocity stays on the order of fractions of a millimeter per second even under load.
explanations.c: Drift velocity is a general property of current flow in a conductor and applies to both AC and DC.
explanations.d: Incandescent and most practical bulbs do rely on current, i.e. electron flow, through a filament or circuit.

questions.prompt: Order these events from smallest to largest in terms of typical speed/magnitude, from slowest-moving physical entity to fastest-propagating effect in a household circuit.

items.text: Electron drift velocity in the copper wire (~0.1-0.2 mm/s)
Propagation of the electric field signal down the wire (large fraction of light speed)

questions.explanation: Individual electrons crawl at a fraction of a millimeter per second, while the field that coordinates their motion throughout the circuit propagates vastly faster, at a substantial fraction of the speed of light.

lessons.label: Voltage, Potential Difference, and the Meaning of Ground

sections.heading: Voltage is work per unit charge, and it is always a difference
sections.body: Voltage measures how much work is done moving a unit of charge between two points: 1 volt (V) = 1 joule per coulomb (1 V = 1 J/C). That definition already contains the key trap students fall into — voltage is inherently relational. There is no such thing as 'the voltage of a wire' in isolation, because work-per-charge only makes sense between a starting point and an ending point. Every voltage value is a potential difference between two nodes, written V_AB = V_A - V_B, and reversing the order flips the sign. A multimeter set to DC volts always has two probes for exactly this reason: it cannot report a single-node number, only the difference between wherever the two leads land.

sections.heading: Labeling nodes so the sign means something
sections.body: Because every voltage is relative, circuit analysis depends on picking one reference node and labeling every other node's voltage against it consistently. Schematics do this with a ground symbol: once a node is declared 0 V, every other labeled voltage in the diagram (5 V, -12 V, 3.3 V) is implicitly 'with respect to that ground.' Change which node you call ground and every number on the page changes, even though the physical circuit and the currents flowing through it are untouched. This is why swapping meter leads mid-measurement, or forgetting which pin was the reference, is one of the most common sources of a sign error in a student's data.

sections.heading: Signal ground, chassis ground, and earth are not the same node
sections.body: 'Ground' is used loosely for at least three distinct things. Signal ground (or circuit common) is just the 0 V reference node chosen inside a circuit — an arbitrary bookkeeping choice, often the negative battery terminal. Chassis ground is the metal enclosure of a device, tied to signal ground for shielding and safety but physically a separate conductor. Earth ground is a literal connection to a rod driven into the soil, required by electrical code on line-powered equipment so that a fault current has a low-resistance path to trip a breaker instead of electrocuting someone. A battery-powered circuit sitting on a lab bench with no earth connection is 'floating': its 0 V reference is real for internal measurements but has no defined relationship to the room's earth potential, so touching a floating circuit's ground to a grounded oscilloscope probe can create an unexpected current path or a bent measurement.

lessons.workedExample: A student measures a 'voltage' of 3.3 V at a microcontroller pin by touching only the red multimeter probe to the pin and leaving the black probe hanging in mid-air. The meter shows an unstable, drifting number instead of a clean 3.3 V, because with the black lead disconnected, there is no defined second node — the meter is picking up stray capacitive coupling from nearby AC wiring rather than measuring a real potential difference. Once the black lead is clipped to the board's ground pin (the same node the microcontroller's own 0 V reference is built from), the reading locks to a steady 3.30 V, because the measurement now has both endpoints the definition requires.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'voltage relative to what?' is checking whether a student treats voltage as a property of a single point (wrong) or a relationship between two (right). A weak answer states a bare number, '5 volts,' with no reference named. A strong answer names the reference node explicitly ('5 volts with respect to the board's ground pin, which is tied to the battery's negative terminal') and, if the circuit involves a chassis or earth connection, can say whether the circuit is floating or referenced and why that distinction mattered for a specific measurement they took.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly reflects why voltage always requires two points to be meaningful?

options.text: Voltage is defined as work done per unit charge moved between two points, so it is inherently a difference
Multimeters simply have two probes by design convention, unrelated to the physics of voltage
Voltage is a property of a single conductor, like its resistance
Two points are only needed for AC circuits, not DC

explanations.a: Correct — 1 V = 1 J/C describes work per charge moved between a start and end point, so voltage is a difference by definition, not a single-point property.
explanations.b: The two-probe design follows directly from the physics; it is not an arbitrary convention disconnected from what voltage means.
explanations.c: Resistance can be a property of one component, but voltage requires a comparison between two nodes.
explanations.d: The two-point requirement applies equally to DC and AC circuits; it comes from the definition of voltage, not the waveform type.

questions.prompt: Match each ground type to its best description.

right.text: The arbitrarily chosen 0 V reference node inside a circuit's own wiring
The metal enclosure of a device, tied to the circuit for shielding and safety
A literal connection to a rod driven into the soil, required for fault-current safety on line-powered gear

questions.explanation: Signal ground is the internal 0 V bookkeeping reference; chassis ground is the physical enclosure tied to it for shielding/safety; earth ground is the actual connection to soil that gives fault current somewhere safe to go.

questions.prompt: A battery-powered circuit on a lab bench has no connection to earth. What best describes its ground node?

options.text: It is undefined and cannot be used as a measurement reference at all
It is 'floating' — a valid internal 0 V reference, but with no defined relationship to the room's earth potential
It is automatically the same potential as earth ground because all circuits share one global ground
It is only meaningful if the circuit carries AC power

explanations.a: It is perfectly usable as an internal reference for measurements within the circuit; it simply is not tied to earth.
explanations.b: Correct — a floating circuit has a real, self-consistent 0 V node for its own measurements, but that node's relationship to earth is undefined, which is why connecting it to earth-referenced equipment can cause unexpected currents.
explanations.c: There is no single global ground shared by all circuits; a floating circuit's reference is independent of earth until a physical connection ties them together.
explanations.d: Floating vs. referenced applies to DC circuits as much as AC; it is about the presence or absence of an earth connection, not waveform type.

questions.prompt: In the worked example, why did the multimeter show an unstable reading with only the red probe connected?

options.text: The meter's battery was low
With no second node connected, there was no defined potential difference for the meter to measure, so it picked up stray coupling instead
The microcontroller pin was damaged
3.3 V circuits cannot be measured with a standard multimeter

explanations.a: A low meter battery would typically cause a low-battery indicator or general malfunction, not this specific floating-reference symptom.
explanations.b: Correct — voltage requires two defined points; with the black lead disconnected there was no second node, so the reading reflected stray environmental coupling rather than a real measurement.
explanations.c: Nothing in the scenario indicates pin damage; the instability is explained fully by the missing reference connection.
explanations.d: Standard multimeters measure 3.3 V circuits routinely; the issue was the incomplete two-probe connection, not the voltage level.

lessons.label: Resistance, Conductance, and Resistivity

sections.heading: Resistance, its reciprocal, and the material property behind both
sections.body: Resistance (R), measured in ohms (symbol Ω), is defined by Ohm's law as the ratio of voltage to current: 1 Ω = 1 V/A. Its reciprocal, conductance (G = 1/R), is measured in siemens (S) and describes how easily current flows rather than how much it is opposed. Neither number, on its own, describes a material — a fat short wire and a thin long wire of the same metal have wildly different resistances. The material property is resistivity (rho, symbol ρ), measured in ohm-meters (Ω·m), and it connects to resistance through R = ρL/A, where L is length and A is cross-sectional area. Copper's resistivity is about 1.68e-8 Ω·m at 20°C, roughly 6 times lower than iron's, which is why copper dominates wiring despite costing more per kilogram.

sections.heading: Resistance drifts with temperature
sections.body: Resistivity itself changes with temperature, and for most metals it rises as the metal heats up, because more thermal vibration in the lattice scatters the conduction electrons more often. This is captured by the linear resistance-temperature relationship R_T = R_0[1 + α(T − T0)], where R_0 is the resistance at a reference temperature T0 (usually 20°C), α is the temperature coefficient of resistance, and T is the new temperature. Copper's α is about 0.00393 per °C near 20°C, so a copper motor winding that heats up 50°C above ambient during operation has α(T − T0) = 0.00393 × 50 ≈ 0.197, meaning R_T ≈ R_0 × 1.20 — roughly 20% higher resistance than its cold, at-rest value. That formula is the tool to reach for whenever a 'hot' reading needs checking: plug in the winding's cold resistance, its temperature coefficient, and the temperature rise, and the expected resistance falls out directly — a fact motor designers and anyone measuring a hot winding must account for, since a resistance reading alone can't distinguish a damaged winding from a simply warm one without knowing the temperature.

sections.heading: Preferred values, tolerance, and reading the bands
sections.body: Resistors aren't manufactured at every possible ohm value; they're built to the E-series of preferred values, spaced logarithmically so that each step roughly covers the tolerance band of the step before it. The E12 series has 12 values per decade (10, 12, 15, 18, 22, 27, 33, 39, 47, 56, 68, 82) and is paired with ±10% tolerance parts; E24 doubles that to 24 values per decade for ±5% parts, packing values closer together because tighter tolerance means less overlap risk between adjacent nominal values. A 4-band resistor encodes two significant digits, a multiplier, and a tolerance color; a 5-band resistor swaps in three significant digits before the multiplier, giving one more digit of precision to support tighter 1-2% tolerance parts.

lessons.workedExample: A 10-meter run of 22 AWG solid copper wire (cross-sectional area about 3.26e-7 m^2, from a wire diameter of roughly 0.644 mm) is used to wire a sensor across a room. Using R = ρL/A with copper's resistivity 1.68e-8 Ω·m: R = (1.68e-8 × 10) / 3.26e-7 ≈ 0.52 Ω. That's small next to a typical kΩ sensor load, so it's usually ignored — but for a low-resistance measurement circuit or a long run carrying several amps, 0.5 Ω is enough to create a measurable voltage drop and skew a reading, which is exactly why 4-wire (Kelvin) resistance measurements exist for precision work.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing resistance basics is checking whether a student can tell a bulk material property (resistivity) apart from a per-component number (resistance) that also depends on geometry. A weak answer treats 'the wire has more resistance' and 'the wire is made of a more resistive material' as the same claim. A strong answer can say, for a specific wire, which of length, cross-section, or material changed and predict the direction of the resistance change from R = ρL/A — and, if temperature came up in their experiment, can explain why a warm component read a different resistance than expected instead of assuming the part failed.

questions.prompt: Two copper wires have the same length but wire B has twice the cross-sectional area of wire A. How does wire B's resistance compare to wire A's?

options.text: Wire B has twice the resistance of wire A
Wire B has half the resistance of wire A
Wire B has the same resistance as wire A
Wire B has four times the resistance of wire A

explanations.a: This inverts the relationship — resistance decreases, not increases, as cross-sectional area grows for a fixed length and material.
explanations.b: Correct — R = ρL/A is inversely proportional to area, so doubling A halves R when ρ and L are unchanged.
explanations.c: Resistance is directly sensitive to area through R = ρL/A; equal length and material with different areas cannot give equal resistance.
explanations.d: Resistance scales as 1/A, not 1/A^2, so a factor of two in area produces a factor of two change in resistance, not four.

questions.prompt: A copper motor winding measures 8.0 Ω cold and reads noticeably higher after running hot. What is the most likely explanation, given copper's temperature coefficient of resistance?

options.text: The winding is damaged and needs replacement
Copper's resistivity rises with temperature (about 0.393%/°C), so a hotter winding is expected to read higher resistance even with no damage
Resistance measurements are unaffected by temperature for metals
The multimeter's battery is degrading the reading

explanations.a: A resistance rise from operating temperature alone doesn't indicate damage; it's the expected behavior of copper's positive temperature coefficient.
explanations.b: Correct — copper's resistivity increases roughly 0.393% per °C near room temperature, so a winding that has heated up during operation will legitimately measure a higher resistance when hot than when cold.
explanations.c: Metals characteristically show resistivity increasing with temperature due to increased lattice vibration scattering electrons; this is a real, well-documented effect, not negligible.
explanations.d: A degrading meter battery would typically show up as a general instrument fault, not a resistance change that tracks specifically with winding temperature.

questions.prompt: Why does the E24 series pack 24 preferred values per decade while E12 packs only 12?

options.text: E24 parts are physically larger, leaving room for more markings
E24 is used for ±5% tolerance parts, which need more closely spaced nominal values than the ±10% parts E12 serves, to avoid gaps or excess overlap in coverage
E24 values are unrelated to tolerance and are just an older, obsolete standard
E12 and E24 differ only in unit prefix (ohms vs kilohms), not in value spacing

explanations.a: Series naming reflects the number of values per decade and their tolerance pairing, not physical component size.
explanations.b: Correct — tighter-tolerance parts need more closely spaced preferred values to cover the same decade without leaving unreachable resistance ranges, which is why ±5% E24 has double the steps of ±10% E12.
explanations.c: Both series remain in active production and use today, matched to different tolerance grades rather than one being obsolete.
explanations.d: Both series apply across all decades and unit prefixes; the difference is the number and spacing of significant-digit values, not the units used.

questions.prompt: Match each quantity to its correct SI unit.

right.text: Ohm (Ω)
Siemens (S)
Ohm-meter (Ω·m)

questions.explanation: Resistance is measured in ohms, its reciprocal conductance in siemens, and resistivity — the material property independent of a part's specific geometry — in ohm-meters.

lessons.label: Power, Energy, and Where the Heat Goes

sections.heading: Power is the rate, and Ohm's law gives three equivalent forms
sections.body: Electrical power is the rate at which energy is delivered or dissipated: P = IV, measured in watts, with 1 W = 1 J/s. Because voltage and current are linked through resistance by Ohm's law (V = IR), the power formula can be rewritten two more ways for the same quantity: substituting V = IR gives P = I^2*R, and substituting I = V/R gives P = V^2/R. All three describe identical physics — they just let you compute power from whichever two variables you actually measured. A resistor dissipating power does so as heat, which is why the I^2*R form is the one most often used to size a component's thermal budget: double the current through a fixed resistor and its dissipated power quadruples, not doubles.

sections.heading: Energy: joules for physics, watt-hours for everyday batteries
sections.body: Energy is power integrated over time. The SI unit is the joule (1 W for 1 s), but for anything running for hours rather than seconds, joules become an inconveniently large number, so batteries are rated in watt-hours (Wh) or, listed on the label as capacity rather than energy, milliamp-hours (mAh). Converting between them requires the battery's voltage: Wh = (mAh / 1000) * V. This is a common source of confusion because two batteries with identical mAh ratings but different voltages store different amounts of actual energy — mAh alone describes charge capacity, not energy, and only becomes an energy figure once multiplied by voltage.

sections.heading: Power ratings, derating, and where efficiency goes
sections.body: A component's power rating is the maximum it can dissipate as heat without damage, not a target to run it at continuously. A resistor rated 1/4 W (0.25 W) run at its full rating in a cramped enclosure with no airflow will run hotter than the same part on an open bench, because a resistor's rating is normally specified for still air with generous clearance; real designs commonly leave headroom, running the part at a fraction of its rating so a warmer-than-datasheet environment or a slightly wrong resistor value doesn't cook it. In a circuit made of multiple resistances in series or parallel, efficiency is simply the fraction of total power that reaches the intended load rather than being dissipated as waste heat elsewhere in the path — a number that matters whenever a circuit trades useful work for heat, from a current-limiting resistor to a voltage regulator.

lessons.workedExample: A 5 V supply drives a 100 Ω load in series with a 20 Ω current-limiting resistor, total resistance 120 Ω. Current: I = V/R = 5/120 ≈ 0.0417 A. Total power drawn from the supply: P = IV = 0.0417 × 5 ≈ 0.208 W. Power reaching the load: P_load = I^2 × 100 ≈ 0.174 W. Efficiency = P_load / P_total ≈ 83.5% — the remaining 16.5% (about 0.035 W) is wasted as heat in the series resistor. Separately, a 2000 mAh, 3.7 V lithium-ion cell stores Wh = (2000/1000) × 3.7 = 7.4 Wh of energy, meaning it could in principle deliver 7.4 W for one hour, or 1 W for 7.4 hours, before it is depleted.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about power budget because it reveals whether a student picked components by feel or by calculation. A weak answer reports a resistor's wattage rating without ever computing what the circuit actually dissipates in it, or quotes a battery's mAh as if that alone told them how long their device would run. A strong answer computes P = I^2*R (or the equivalent form) for the specific part in question, compares it against the part's rating with a stated safety margin, and — if batteries are involved — converts mAh to Wh using the battery's actual voltage before making a runtime claim.

questions.prompt: A fixed resistor has current through it doubled while its resistance stays constant. What happens to the power it dissipates?

options.text: It stays the same
It doubles
It quadruples
It is cut in half

explanations.a: Power is not independent of current in a fixed resistor; P = I^2*R means power tracks the square of current.
explanations.b: This would be true if power scaled linearly with current, but the I^2*R relationship means power scales with the square of current, not current itself.
explanations.c: Correct — P = I^2*R means doubling I multiplies power by 2^2 = 4, so the resistor's dissipation quadruples.
explanations.d: Increasing current cannot decrease power dissipation in a fixed resistor; power rises, it does not fall.

questions.prompt: Two batteries both have a 2000 mAh rating, but battery X is 3.7 V and battery Y is 12 V. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Both batteries store the same amount of energy, since mAh is an energy unit
Battery Y stores more energy, because Wh = (mAh/1000) x V and Y has the higher voltage
Battery X stores more energy because lower voltage means higher efficiency
Energy cannot be compared between batteries of different voltage

explanations.a: mAh measures charge capacity, not energy; two cells with equal mAh but different voltage store different amounts of energy.
explanations.b: Correct — energy in Wh is charge capacity multiplied by voltage, so at equal mAh the higher-voltage battery (Y, 12 V) stores more energy: 24 Wh versus X's 7.4 Wh.
explanations.c: Lower voltage does not confer higher efficiency by itself; it simply means less energy is stored per unit of charge capacity.
explanations.d: Energy can absolutely be compared once mAh is converted to Wh using each battery's voltage, which is exactly the calculation this question requires.

questions.prompt: In the worked example's 5 V, 100 Ω load with a 20 Ω series resistor, why is efficiency less than 100%?

options.text: Because the load resistor is defective
Because some of the total power drawn from the supply is dissipated as heat in the series resistor rather than reaching the load
Because 5 V supplies are inherently less efficient than higher-voltage supplies
Efficiency loss only happens in AC circuits, not this DC example

explanations.a: Nothing in the scenario indicates a defective component; the efficiency loss is an expected consequence of the series resistor's own I^2*R dissipation.
explanations.b: Correct — the series resistor dissipates its own share of the total power as heat, so only the fraction reaching the 100 Ω load counts as useful output, giving efficiency below 100%.
explanations.c: Supply voltage alone does not determine efficiency; it is the ratio of resistances (or more generally, useful output power to total input power) that sets efficiency here.
explanations.d: This kind of resistive efficiency loss applies to DC circuits just as much as AC; it is not waveform-dependent.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to determine whether a resistor is safely rated for a circuit.

items.text: Determine the current through (or voltage across) the resistor in the circuit
Compute the power it will dissipate using P = I^2*R (or P = V^2/R)
Compare the computed power against the resistor's rated power with a safety margin
Select a resistor with adequate rated power, or add cooling/derate the design

questions.explanation: You must first know the current or voltage at the resistor, then compute the actual dissipated power from it, then compare that figure to the part's rating with margin, and only then choose or adjust the component to keep it safely within budget.

lessons.label: AC vs DC, RMS, and Describing a Waveform

sections.heading: Four ways to put one number on a wiggly signal
sections.body: A DC voltage is a single number because it doesn't change. An AC voltage is a function of time, so 'the voltage' needs a qualifier before it means anything. Peak (Vp) is the maximum excursion from zero; peak-to-peak (Vpp) spans from the most negative to the most positive point, twice the peak for a symmetric wave. Average, if computed over a full cycle of a symmetric AC wave, is zero — positive and negative halves cancel — so 'average' for AC almost always means the average of the rectified (absolute-value) waveform instead. None of these numbers tell you how much heat the signal would produce in a resistor, which is the number engineers usually actually want.

sections.heading: RMS is the heating-equivalent DC value
sections.body: Root-mean-square (RMS) answers a specific, practical question: what steady DC voltage would dissipate the same average power in a resistive load as this AC waveform does? It's computed by squaring the signal (which makes negative excursions positive and weights larger swings more), averaging that squared signal, then taking the square root — undoing the square while keeping the positive-weighting effect. For a pure sine wave, this works out to Vrms = Vp / sqrt(2) ≈ 0.707 × Vp, a relationship specific to the sine shape. A square wave alternating between +Vp and -Vp is at full magnitude the entire time, so its RMS equals its peak exactly: Vrms = Vp. A triangle wave, which spends more time near zero and less time at its extremes than a sine does, has Vrms = Vp / sqrt(3) ≈ 0.577 × Vp — lower than the sine's factor because the waveform lingers less at the peak.

sections.heading: Crest factor and real-world mains numbers
sections.body: The ratio of a waveform's peak to its RMS value is its crest factor — 1.414 for a sine, 1.0 for a square wave, 1.732 for a triangle wave. A high crest factor means brief large spikes riding on a modest RMS value, which matters for sizing equipment that must survive the peak even though its heating effect tracks the RMS. Mains power is specified in RMS by convention, which is why '120 V' household power in North America (nominally 120 V RMS at 60 Hz) actually peaks near 170 V, and why the '230 V' mains common across most of the rest of the world (nominally 230 V RMS at 50 Hz) peaks near 325 V — numbers that matter directly when specifying a capacitor's or insulation's voltage rating.

lessons.workedExample: A bench function generator is set to output a 10 Vpp sine wave, so Vp = 5 V. Its RMS value is Vrms = Vp/sqrt(2) = 5/1.414 ≈ 3.54 V — this is the number a true-RMS multimeter would display, and it's the value that determines how much power the signal delivers into a resistive load. If the same generator is switched to a square wave at the same 5 V peak, the RMS jumps to the full 5 V (since the square wave sits at +5 V or -5 V the entire time), meaning the square wave delivers P = Vrms^2/R = 25/R watts into a load versus only 3.54^2/R ≈ 12.5/R watts for the sine at the identical peak voltage — exactly double the heating effect despite an identical peak.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'is that peak or RMS?' is checking whether a student can distinguish the number their oscilloscope displays from the number that determines actual power delivery, and whether they know those two numbers relate differently for different waveform shapes. A weak answer treats 'voltage' as one unambiguous quantity and can't say whether a quoted figure is peak, peak-to-peak, or RMS. A strong answer states which value they mean, can convert between peak and RMS for the specific waveform shape in their circuit (not blindly applying the sine-only /sqrt(2) factor to a square or triangle wave), and knows that mains ratings like 120 V or 230 V are RMS figures with a meaningfully higher peak.

questions.prompt: A sine wave has a peak voltage of 8 V. What is its approximate RMS value?

options.text: 8 V
4 V

explanations.a: 8 V would be the RMS value for a square wave at that peak, not a sine wave; a sine's RMS is lower than its peak.
explanations.b: Correct — for a sine wave, Vrms = Vp/sqrt(2) = 8/1.414 ≈ 5.66 V.
explanations.c: 4 V would be exactly half the peak, but the sine RMS factor is 1/sqrt(2) ≈ 0.707, not 0.5.
explanations.d: 11.3 V exceeds the peak voltage, which is impossible — RMS can never be larger than peak for any waveform.

questions.prompt: Why does a square wave's RMS value equal its peak value exactly, unlike a sine wave's?

options.text: Square waves have no negative portion
A square wave sits at its full positive or negative magnitude for the entire cycle, with no time spent at intermediate values, so squaring and averaging returns the same magnitude
RMS only applies to sine waves, so the square wave figure is undefined and coincidentally reported as equal to peak
Square waves have a crest factor of 1.414, same as a sine wave

explanations.a: A symmetric square wave does have a negative portion, alternating between +Vp and -Vp; that is not what makes its RMS equal its peak.
explanations.b: Correct — because the square wave is always at full magnitude (never partway between), the mean of its squared value equals Vp^2 exactly, so the square root returns Vp itself.
explanations.c: RMS is well-defined for any periodic waveform, including square waves; it is not a sine-only concept.
explanations.d: A square wave's crest factor is 1.0 (peak equals RMS), not 1.414, which is the sine wave's crest factor.

questions.prompt: North American mains power is rated 120 V RMS at 60 Hz. Approximately what is its peak voltage?

options.text: About 85 V
About 120 V, same as RMS
About 170 V
About 240 V

explanations.a: 85 V would result from multiplying by 0.707 rather than dividing by it — this is roughly the RMS value if 120 V were mistaken for peak, not the actual peak.
explanations.b: Peak equals RMS only for a square wave; mains power is sinusoidal, so its peak exceeds its RMS value.
explanations.c: Correct — for a sine wave, Vp = Vrms x sqrt(2) = 120 x 1.414 ≈ 170 V.
explanations.d: 240 V would be roughly double the RMS value, which overshoots the sine wave's actual peak-to-RMS relationship.

questions.prompt: Order these three sine-wave-relevant voltage figures for a signal with Vp = 10 V, from smallest to largest.

items.text: RMS value (Vp/sqrt(2) ≈ 7.07 V)
Peak value (10 V)
Peak-to-peak value (20 V)

questions.explanation: For this 10 V peak sine wave, RMS (≈7.07 V) is smaller than the peak (10 V), which in turn is smaller than the peak-to-peak span (20 V, twice the peak for a symmetric wave).

lessons.label: SI Prefixes, Significant Figures, and Unit Discipline

sections.heading: Engineering notation and the prefix ladder
sections.body: Electronics quantities span an enormous range — a femtofarad of stray capacitance next to a kilofarad supercapacitor — so SI prefixes exist to keep numbers in a readable band. Moving from small to large: pico- (p, 10^-12), nano- (n, 10^-9), micro- (μ, 10^-6), milli- (m, 10^-3), the base unit, kilo- (k, 10^3), mega- (M, 10^6), and giga- (G, 10^9) cover nearly everything a student circuit will touch, from picofarad capacitors to gigahertz clock signals. Engineering notation, a variant of scientific notation restricted to exponents that are multiples of three, is used specifically so the exponent always lines up with one of these named prefixes — 4.7e-9 F is more usefully written 4.7 nF than as 0.0000000047 F or even 4.7 x 10^-9 F.

sections.heading: Dimensional analysis as a free error check
sections.body: Every equation in electronics carries units, and tracking them through a calculation catches mistakes before they become a burned-out part. If a calculation for current comes out in volt-ohms instead of amperes, the error is caught immediately, without needing to know whether the numeric answer 'looks right.' This habit costs nothing and catches a specific, common failure mode: mixing a value in one prefix with a formula that expects the base unit, such as plugging milliohms into a formula written for ohms. Since the 2019 SI redefinition, the base units themselves are anchored to fixed constants of nature rather than to physical artefacts or experiments: the elementary charge e is now DEFINED as exactly 1.602176634e-19 C, with zero uncertainty. Because 1 A = 1 C/s and the second is itself defined from a fixed caesium transition frequency, the ampere inherits that exactness — it is no longer realised by measuring the force between two current-carrying wires. The practical consequence for a bench measurement is that the unit is not what limits you; your instrument is.

sections.heading: One prefix slip destroys credibility — and sometimes the part
sections.body: The single most common unit error in student electronics work is confusing milli- (10^-3) and micro- (10^-6), a factor-of-1000 mistake that a quick glance at a schematic or datasheet won't always catch, because 'mA' and 'μA' look nearly identical on a page. Applying a current meant to be 2.3 mA as 2.3 A instead — a different, more dramatic slip, but the same category of error — is enough to instantly destroy components rated for tens of milliamps, like a standard LED with a typical forward current around 20 mA. The fix is procedural, not clever: write out the full prefix name when it matters, double-check the exponent before plugging a number into a formula, and treat a suspiciously round or suspiciously extreme result as a signal to re-check units rather than to write it down. The same discipline extends to reporting a measurement itself — a resistance measured on a multimeter should be written with a number of significant figures that matches the instrument's actual precision and an explicit uncertainty, such as 4.70 Ω ± 0.05 Ω, rather than a string of digits the instrument never actually resolved.

lessons.workedExample: A datasheet lists an LED's maximum forward current as 20 mA and a lab power supply is set to source what the student intends to be 2.3 mA of test current through it via a current-limiting resistor calculation. If the student's spreadsheet cell is accidentally left in amps rather than milliamps, the supply is set to 2.3 A — a thousand-fold overcurrent well past the LED's 20 mA rating — and the LED fails instantly. A dimensional-analysis check before touching the supply would have caught it: computing R = V/I with I entered as 2.3 (intending mA but with no unit label attached) gives a resistor value 1000x too small to limit current to a safe level, a mismatch that becomes obvious the moment units are tracked explicitly through the formula instead of trusted by eye.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks a student to state a result's precision, or to double check a suspiciously large or small number, is testing unit discipline rather than the underlying circuit theory. A weak answer reports a number with far more digits than the instrument could have measured, or can't explain what would happen if a decimal or prefix were off by one step. A strong answer states a measured quantity with an explicit uncertainty matched to the instrument's actual resolution, and can walk through a dimensional-analysis check showing why a stated result's units and order of magnitude make sense for the circuit at hand.

questions.prompt: Order these SI prefixes from smallest to largest multiplier.

items.text: pico (p)
micro (μ)
milli (m)
kilo (k)
giga (G)

questions.explanation: In order of increasing multiplier: pico is 10^-12, micro is 10^-6, milli is 10^-3, kilo is 10^3, and giga is 10^9.

questions.prompt: A student intends to set a current source to 2.3 mA but accidentally enters 2.3 A. Roughly how large is this error?

options.text: About 10 times too large
About 1000 times too large
About 100 times too large
Negligibly small, since both are 'current' units

explanations.a: A factor-of-10 error would correspond to confusing adjacent decade steps, not the milli-to-base-unit gap, which is a factor of 1000.
explanations.b: Correct — milli- is 10^-3, so going from mA to A (the base unit) without dividing by 1000 inflates the value by exactly that factor.
explanations.c: A factor of 100 doesn't correspond to any standard SI prefix gap; milli-to-base is specifically a factor of 1000.
explanations.d: Units of the same physical quantity (current) can still differ by orders of magnitude; 'both are current' does not make the numeric error negligible.

questions.prompt: The 2019 SI redefinition fixed the elementary charge e at an exact numerical value with zero uncertainty. Why does that give the ampere zero uncertainty too?

options.text: Because a coulomb is defined as an exact integer multiple of e, and an ampere is exactly one coulomb per second — so once e has no uncertainty, neither does the ampere built from it
It changed the ampere's symbol from A to amp
It redefined the ampere as exactly equal to one volt divided by one ohm
It abolished the ampere as a base unit entirely

explanations.a: Correct — with e fixed at an exact value by definition, every coulomb is an exact integer multiple of e, and since 1 A = 1 C/s, the ampere inherits that same exactness with no measurement uncertainty.
explanations.b: The redefinition changed the underlying definition, not the unit's symbol, which remains A.
explanations.c: V = IR (Ohm's law) is a circuit relationship between existing units, not the formal SI definition basis chosen for the ampere.
explanations.d: The ampere remains one of the seven SI base units; the redefinition changed its definition's foundation, not its status as a base unit.

questions.prompt: A multimeter with limited resolution measures a resistor's value. Which reporting choice best matches good unit/precision discipline?

options.text: 4.70 Ω ± 0.05 Ω, matching the instrument's actual resolution and stating uncertainty explicitly
4.700000 Ω, reporting every digit the calculator display showed
About 5 Ω, since exact values don't matter much
4700 mΩ, with no uncertainty stated

explanations.a: Correct — stating a value to the precision the instrument can actually resolve, with an explicit uncertainty, is the standard for honest measurement reporting.
explanations.b: Reporting far more digits than the instrument resolved implies false precision the measurement doesn't actually have.
explanations.c: Rounding away real, obtainable precision throws away information the instrument did provide, which is its own form of poor discipline.
explanations.d: Changing prefixes to milliohms doesn't fix the underlying issue: uncertainty still needs to be stated regardless of which unit prefix is used.

units.label: Circuit Fundamentals and Laws

lessons.label: Ohm's Law and Where It Stops Working

sections.heading: V = IR, and what 'ohmic' actually promises
sections.body: Georg Ohm published the relation V = IR in 1827, but the law is really an empirical claim about a material, not a universal fact about circuits: for a conductor held at constant temperature, current is directly proportional to applied voltage, so the V-I plot is a straight line through the origin and R is a single constant slope. Metal resistors, copper wire, and carbon-film resistors are ohmic across a huge working range because their charge-carrier density barely changes with the field applied. That constancy is the whole point: it is what lets you swap R = V/I into KVL and KCL equations and solve a linear system. The moment a component's internal physics depends on V or I itself, the line stops being straight, and 'the resistance' stops being one number.

sections.heading: Three benchtop components that break the line
sections.body: A silicon diode's current follows the Shockley equation, I = I_S(e^(V/nV_T) - 1), where V_T (the thermal voltage) is about 26 mV at room temperature and n is an ideality factor near 1-2. The curve is flat near zero then rises exponentially past roughly 0.6-0.7 V forward bias — nothing like a line through the origin. An incandescent tungsten filament is ohmic in the sense that it obeys V = IR at any instant, but R itself climbs as the filament heats: tungsten's resistivity rises with temperature, so a filament's hot resistance at full brightness runs on the order of ten to fifteen times its cold, room-temperature resistance, which is exactly why a bulb draws a large inrush current the instant it is switched on. An NTC (negative-temperature-coefficient) thermistor goes the opposite way: its resistance falls as it self-heats or as ambient temperature rises, often following an exponential beta-parameter model, which is why NTC thermistors are used as inrush limiters and temperature sensors rather than as fixed resistors.

sections.heading: Static resistance vs. small-signal resistance
sections.body: For any component, static (DC) resistance is just R = V/I at one operating point — the slope of the line from the origin to that point on the curve. Small-signal (dynamic, or incremental) resistance is r = dV/dI, the slope of the tangent line at that point. On a straight ohmic line these two are identical everywhere. On a curved characteristic like a diode's, they diverge: a diode biased at 0.65 V and 10 mA has a static resistance of 65 ohms, but its dynamic resistance — what matters for how it responds to a small AC ripple riding on that bias — is closer to n V_T / I, only a few ohms. Confusing the two is a common circuit-analysis error whenever a nonlinear device sits in an AC small-signal path.

lessons.workedExample: A diode is biased at 0.65 V, 10 mA (static R = 65 ohms) and, at a nearby point, 0.68 V, 22 mA. Dynamic resistance from those two points: r = ΔV/ΔI = (0.68 - 0.65) / (0.022 - 0.010) = 0.03 V / 0.012 A = 2.5 ohms. Using the formula r ≈ nV_T/I with n = 1 at I = 10 mA gives 26 mV / 10 mA = 2.6 ohms, matching closely. A student who plugs the diode's static 65-ohm value into an AC gain formula instead of the ~2.5-ohm dynamic value will be off by more than 25x.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who sees a V-I plot with a resistor and a diode or LED asks 'is this thing ohmic?' to check whether the student understands that R = V/I is a description of a straight-line special case, not a law every component obeys. A weak answer says 'no, Ohm's law doesn't apply to diodes' and stops there. A strong answer names the static-vs-dynamic-resistance distinction, explains why the tangent slope is what matters for small-signal behavior, and can compute both numbers from two nearby points on the curve — showing the concept was used, not just recited.

questions.prompt: A component is called 'ohmic' over some range if, in that range,

options.text: its resistance is always exactly 1 ohm
current is proportional to voltage, giving a straight V-I line through the origin with constant slope
it draws no current at low voltage
its resistance decreases as temperature rises

explanations.a: Ohmic just means constant proportionality, not any particular resistance value.
explanations.b: Correct — ohmic means V = IR holds with R constant, so the V-I plot is a straight line through the origin.
explanations.c: Many non-ohmic devices, like diodes, also draw negligible current at low voltage; that alone doesn't make something ohmic.
explanations.d: That describes an NTC thermistor specifically, which is a non-ohmic example, not the general definition of ohmic.

questions.prompt: Match each component to how its resistance behaves as it operates.

right.text: Stays essentially constant (ohmic)
Follows an exponential I-V curve, not a fixed R
Rises several-fold as it self-heats
Falls as temperature rises

questions.explanation: A metal resistor is ohmic; a diode's current rises exponentially with forward voltage; a tungsten filament's resistance climbs several-fold as it heats to incandescence; an NTC thermistor's resistance falls as it warms.

questions.prompt: A diode operating at 0.65 V and 10 mA has static resistance V/I = 65 ohms. Its dynamic resistance dV/dI at that same point is about 2.5 ohms. Why are these so different?

options.text: One of the two measurements must be a mistake, since a device can only have one resistance
Static resistance is the slope from the origin to the point; dynamic resistance is the slope of the tangent line, and on a curved characteristic those slopes differ
Dynamic resistance only applies to resistors, not diodes
The diode must be defective

explanations.a: Both numbers are correct simultaneously; a nonlinear device legitimately has two different resistance values depending on which slope you mean.
explanations.b: Correct — static resistance is V/I (chord slope from the origin), dynamic resistance is dV/dI (tangent slope); on a curved I-V plot like a diode's these are generally not equal.
explanations.c: Dynamic resistance is defined for any device with a V-I curve, and it is most useful precisely for nonlinear devices like diodes.
explanations.d: This is normal diode behavior, not a defect — every forward-biased diode shows this static/dynamic split.

questions.prompt: Why does a tungsten filament bulb draw a large inrush current the instant it is switched on?

options.text: Because the filament's resistance is at its lowest (cold) value before it heats up, so the initial current is much higher than the steady operating current
Because the power supply voltage spikes momentarily
Because tungsten is not a conductor at room temperature
Because the filament resistance is highest when cold

explanations.a: Correct — cold tungsten resistance is roughly ten to fifteen times lower than hot operating resistance, so at switch-on the low resistance draws a much larger current until the filament heats up.
explanations.b: The inrush is a property of the filament's own resistance change, not a supply voltage spike.
explanations.c: Tungsten conducts fine at room temperature; it is a metal, just at lower resistance than when hot.
explanations.d: This has the direction backwards — cold resistance is lower, not higher, than hot resistance.

lessons.label: Kirchhoff's Current and Voltage Laws

sections.heading: KCL: charge cannot pile up at a node
sections.body: Gustav Kirchhoff published both circuit laws in 1845 while still a student, and each one is a conservation law wearing circuit clothes rather than a consequence of Ohm's law. Kirchhoff's Current Law says the sum of currents entering any node equals the sum leaving it — equivalently, the algebraic sum of all currents at a node, with entering currents positive and leaving currents negative, is zero. The physical reason is charge conservation: a node is an idealized point with no capacity to store charge, so if 3 A flows in from one branch and 1 A flows out through a second, the remaining 2 A must leave through whatever branches are left. KCL holds regardless of what the branches contain — resistors, sources, diodes — because it says nothing about V-I relationships at all, only about current bookkeeping.

sections.heading: KVL: energy conservation around a loop
sections.body: Kirchhoff's Voltage Law says the algebraic sum of voltage rises and drops around any closed loop is zero. This is energy conservation: a unit of charge that leaves a point, travels around a closed path through sources and resistors, and returns to the same point must return with the same potential energy it left with, so every rise (crossing a source from - to +) must be matched by drops (crossing resistors in the direction of current flow, or crossing a source from + to -). The sign convention that trips students up: pick a loop direction, and as you traverse each element, a voltage drop in your direction of travel is added as a positive term and a rise is added as a negative term, with the total set to zero. Crucially, KVL applies to any closed path you can draw in a network, even a path with no source in it at all — parallel branches sharing two nodes form such a loop, and KVL then just says the two branches have equal voltage.

sections.heading: A two-loop worked check, and where KVL breaks
sections.body: A genuine two-loop network needs two independent equations. Take a single source feeding a series resistor into a node from which two more resistors run in parallel back to the source's return rail: one loop is source-series resistor-first parallel branch; the second loop is the two parallel branches by themselves, with no source. KVL on the source loop gives the total current; KVL on the source-free loop is exactly the statement that the two parallel resistors share the same voltage, which is what justifies combining them by the parallel formula in the first place. KVL, however, assumes the electric field is conservative (path-independent), which fails when a changing magnetic flux threads the loop: Faraday's law then adds an EMF equal to -dΦ/dt around that path, so summing static IR drops no longer gives zero. Real inductors and transformers rely on exactly this loophole, and it is why KVL is stated for static, non-time-varying magnetic conditions, or applied loop-by-loop with the induced EMF added explicitly as its own term.

lessons.workedExample: A 12 V source in series with R1 = 2 ohm feeds node A, from which R2 = 6 ohm and R3 = 3 ohm both return to the common ground rail (R2 and R3 in parallel). This is a two-loop network: loop 1 runs source-R1-R2-back to the source, loop 2 runs R2-R3, a source-free loop whose KVL statement is simply that R2 and R3 share the same voltage. Combine them: R2‖R3 = (6×3)/(6+3) = 2 ohm, so the source sees R1 + 2 = 4 ohm total, drawing I = 12/4 = 3 A, and node A sits at V_A = 3 A × 2 ohm = 6 V. That gives I(R2) = 6/6 = 1 A and I(R3) = 6/3 = 2 A. KCL at node A then checks the whole solution: 1 A + 2 A = 3 A, exactly matching the current the source supplies.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask 'why does KVL work?' specifically to catch students who memorized 'sum of drops equals sum of rises' without knowing it's energy conservation, not an algebra rule. A weak answer recites the sign convention. A strong answer says a charge returning to its start must have the same potential energy, so drops must balance rises — and, if pushed further, can say the law assumes no changing magnetic flux through the loop, which is the one place it needs an explicit EMF correction term. That last point separates a student who has only used KVL from one who understands its domain of validity.

questions.prompt: KCL (sum of currents at a node is zero) is a direct consequence of which physical principle?

options.text: Ohm's law
Conservation of charge
Conservation of energy
Faraday's law of induction

explanations.a: Ohm's law relates V, I, and R for a single element; it says nothing about how current splits at a node.
explanations.b: Correct — a node cannot accumulate charge, so current in must equal current out at every instant.
explanations.c: Conservation of energy is what underlies KVL, not KCL.
explanations.d: Faraday's law concerns induced EMF from changing flux, which is a complication for KVL, not the basis of KCL.

questions.prompt: Under what condition does simple KVL (sum of IR drops equals sum of source voltages) fail to hold exactly?

options.text: When any resistor in the loop is non-ohmic
When there is more than one resistor in the loop
When a changing magnetic flux threads the loop, inducing an EMF not accounted for by static IR drops
When the loop contains a node with three or more branches

explanations.a: KVL still holds with non-ohmic elements; you just can't replace their V-I relation with a simple R.
explanations.b: Multiple resistors are exactly what ordinary KVL is built to handle; this doesn't break the law.
explanations.c: Correct — Faraday's law adds an EMF of -dΦ/dt around a loop with changing flux, so the static IR-drop sum alone no longer equals zero.
explanations.d: Node branching is a KCL consideration and does not by itself invalidate KVL around a loop.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for solving the two-loop network (12 V source, R1 = 2 ohm in series, then R2 = 6 ohm and R3 = 3 ohm in parallel to the return rail).

items.text: Recognize that the source-free loop formed by R2 and R3 means, by KVL, they share the same voltage
Combine R2 and R3 by the parallel formula to get a single equivalent resistance
Apply KVL to the source loop (source, R1, and the R2‖R3 equivalent) to find the total source current and node voltage
Use the node voltage to find the individual currents through R2 and R3, then check them against the source current with KCL

questions.explanation: The source-free loop's KVL statement (equal voltage across the parallel pair) is what justifies combining them into one equivalent resistance; only then can KVL on the source loop yield total current and node voltage, after which KCL checks that the individual branch currents recombine correctly.

questions.prompt: In the worked example, I(R2) = 1 A and I(R3) = 2 A, and the source supplies I = 3 A. What does checking 1 A + 2 A = 3 A confirm?

options.text: That R2 and R3 are ohmic
That KCL holds at node A: the current the source delivers into the node equals the sum of currents leaving through the two parallel branches
That the source voltage was measured correctly
That R1 has no effect on the circuit

explanations.a: Both resistors were assumed ohmic from the start; this check doesn't test that assumption.
explanations.b: Correct — this is exactly KCL at node A, confirming the branch currents found from the node voltage are self-consistent with the total current the source supplies.
explanations.c: Source voltage was a given, not something this current check verifies.
explanations.d: R1 sets the total current (via the 4-ohm total loop resistance) and clearly does affect the circuit; this check doesn't suggest otherwise.

lessons.label: Series and Parallel Networks

sections.heading: Why series adds and parallel adds by reciprocals
sections.body: Two resistors in series share the same current by KCL (there is nowhere else for charge to go along a single path), so the total voltage across both is I*R1 + I*R2 = I*(R1+R2), meaning series resistances simply add: R_eq = R1 + R2 + ... Two resistors in parallel share the same voltage by KVL (they connect the same two nodes, so the loop between them has no source and must have zero net drop), so the total current is V/R1 + V/R2 = V*(1/R1 + 1/R2), meaning parallel resistances combine by adding reciprocals: 1/R_eq = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + ..., which for exactly two resistors simplifies to the product-over-sum shortcut R_eq = (R1*R2)/(R1+R2). Both rules are just KCL or KVL applied to the simplest possible sub-network, not separate laws — which is why they generalize cleanly to any number of resistors and to more complex ladder and bridge networks by repeated reduction.

sections.heading: Reducing a ladder network step by step
sections.body: A ladder network — a chain of series elements feeding successive parallel branches — is reduced from the far end inward: combine the innermost parallel or series group into one equivalent resistor, then that equivalent becomes part of the next group out, and repeat until a single R_eq remains at the source terminals. This lets you find total source current immediately, and then work backward: the node voltage nearest the source sets the current split into the next parallel pair, which sets the next node voltage, and so on down the ladder. Each step is nothing more than the series or parallel rule applied locally, but doing it in the right order — inside out — is what makes an otherwise complicated network tractable by hand.

sections.heading: A fault changes every current and voltage, not just its own branch
sections.body: Because a ladder network's branches all share the same source and the same equivalent-resistance chain, a fault in one branch propagates everywhere. An open circuit in a parallel branch removes that branch's conductance entirely, so the parallel combination's equivalent resistance rises (toward the value of whichever branch remains), the total resistance the source sees rises, and total source current falls — but the voltage at the node in front of the fault actually rises, since the remaining current is now forced entirely through the surviving branch. A short circuit does the opposite: it drives that parallel section's equivalent resistance toward zero, so total resistance falls, total source current rises, and the shared node's voltage collapses toward zero, starving every other branch fed from that node. Predicting the direction of these swings — not just recomputing the numbers — is the skill a fault question is really testing.

lessons.workedExample: A 24 V source feeds R1 = 4 ohm in series to node A. From node A, R2 = 12 ohm runs directly back to the source, in parallel with a second branch of R3 = 6 ohm in series with R4 = 6 ohm (also 12 ohm total). Reducing inside out: the two 12-ohm branches in parallel give R_eq = (12×12)/(12+12) = 6 ohm, so total resistance is R1 + 6 = 10 ohm, source current is 24/10 = 2.4 A, and V_A = 2.4 × 6 = 14.4 V, splitting evenly into 1.2 A per branch. Now open R4: the R3-R4 branch carries zero current, so the parallel section is just R2 = 12 ohm, total resistance becomes 4 + 12 = 16 ohm, source current drops to 24/16 = 1.5 A, but V_A rises to 1.5 × 12 = 18 V — higher than before the fault, even though total current fell.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'what happens if this resistor fails open?' is testing whether a student can reason about a network qualitatively, not just recompute a formula. A weak answer just re-solves the whole circuit with no intuition about direction. A strong answer predicts before calculating: removing a parallel branch raises that section's resistance, so total current falls but the shared node voltage rises because the remaining current is forced through fewer paths — and can explain why a short does the opposite. That directional reasoning is what separates a student who understands the network from one who only plugged into formulas.

questions.prompt: Why do resistances add directly in series but combine by reciprocals in parallel?

options.text: It is an arbitrary convention with no physical basis
Series resistors share the same current (KCL), so voltages add directly; parallel resistors share the same voltage (KVL), so currents add, which means conductances (reciprocals of resistance) add
Because series circuits are always larger than parallel circuits
Because parallel resistors always have equal resistance values

explanations.a: Both rules follow directly from KCL and KVL applied to the simplest sub-networks; they are not arbitrary.
explanations.b: Correct — same-current elements add their voltage drops (series sum), and same-voltage elements add their currents, which is equivalent to adding conductances (parallel reciprocal rule).
explanations.c: Physical size of the resulting equivalent resistance depends on the specific values, not on which topology is used.
explanations.d: Parallel resistors can have any values; equal values are just a special case.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to reduce the ladder network (R1 in series to node A, then R2 in parallel with the R3-R4 series branch) to a single equivalent resistance.

items.text: Combine R3 and R4 in series, since they carry the same current along their shared branch
Combine that R3+R4 result with R2 in parallel, since both branches share node A's voltage
Add R1 in series with the parallel result, since R1 carries the full source current
Divide the source voltage by the final equivalent resistance to get total source current

questions.explanation: Ladder reduction works from the innermost group outward: first collapse the series R3-R4 branch, then combine that with the parallel R2 branch, then add the series R1, and only then compute total current from the fully reduced equivalent resistance.

questions.prompt: In the worked example, before any fault, the source draws 2.4 A and node A sits at 14.4 V. After R4 opens, source current drops to 1.5 A but node A's voltage rises to 18 V. Why does the node voltage rise even though total current fell?

options.text: Because the source voltage increased when R4 opened
Because with the R3-R4 branch gone, all remaining current is forced through R2 alone, and the total resistance seen by the source rose enough that less of the 24 V is dropped across R1
Because opening R4 has no real effect on node A
Because R2's resistance value changed when R4 opened

explanations.a: The source voltage is fixed at 24 V throughout; it does not change due to a branch fault.
explanations.b: Correct — losing the parallel branch raises the parallel section's equivalent resistance from 6 ohm to 12 ohm, so a larger share of the fixed 24 V appears across that section (node A) and less across R1.
explanations.c: Node A's voltage changes substantially (14.4 V to 18 V), so the fault clearly does affect it.
explanations.d: R2's own resistance value (12 ohm) never changes; only the combination it participates in changes when R4 opens.

questions.prompt: If instead R4 were shorted (0 ohm) rather than opened, what would happen to node A's voltage compared to the normal 14.4 V case?

options.text: It would rise further above 14.4 V
It would fall below 14.4 V, since the shorted branch drives that parallel section's resistance toward zero, pulling more of the source voltage across R1 instead
It would stay exactly at 14.4 V
The source would stop supplying any current

explanations.a: A short lowers the parallel section's resistance, which pulls node A's voltage down, not up — the opposite of what an open circuit does.
explanations.b: Correct — a short circuit in one branch drags the parallel equivalent resistance toward zero, so total resistance falls, more voltage is dropped across R1, and node A's voltage collapses toward zero relative to its normal value.
explanations.c: A short changes the parallel section's resistance substantially, so node A's voltage must change too.
explanations.d: A short circuit increases source current (lower total resistance), it does not stop current flow.

lessons.label: Dividers and the Loading Problem

sections.heading: The voltage divider ratio, and its current dual
sections.body: Two resistors R1 and R2 in series across a source Vin carry the same current I = Vin/(R1+R2) by KCL, so the voltage across R2 is Vout = I*R2 = Vin*R2/(R1+R2) — the voltage-divider equation. It is nothing more than Ohm's law applied to a series pair, but it is the single most-used relation in analog circuit design: it sets bias points, scales sensor signals down to an ADC's input range, and forms the reference in countless feedback networks. The current divider is its dual: for two resistors R1 and R2 in parallel carrying a total current Itotal, current splits inversely with resistance, I(R1) = Itotal*R2/(R1+R2) and I(R2) = Itotal*R1/(R1+R2) — the smaller resistor takes the larger share of current, because it is easier to push charge through.

sections.heading: A divider is only ideal if nothing else is attached
sections.body: The voltage-divider formula assumes Vout is measured by something that draws no current — an ideal, infinite-impedance voltmeter. Any real next stage (an op-amp input, an ADC pin, a multimeter) has a finite input resistance, and that resistance appears electrically in parallel with R2 the instant it is connected. The divider no longer sees R2 alone; it sees R2‖RL, a smaller resistance, which pulls Vout below the value the ideal formula predicts. This is the loading problem: the act of measuring or using the divider's output changes the very quantity being measured, and the error grows larger as RL gets closer to R2 in size.

sections.heading: Sizing the error, and the 10x rule
sections.body: For a 100 kΩ / 100 kΩ divider read by a load with RL = 1 MΩ input resistance — exactly ten times R2 — the loaded R2‖RL combination is (100k×1M)/(100k+1M) ≈ 90.9 kΩ instead of 100 kΩ. The output ratio drops from the ideal 50% to 90.9/(100+90.9) ≈ 47.6%, meaning the reading comes in about 4.8% low. That specific case is where the common '10x rule' comes from: keeping a downstream input impedance at ten times or more the divider's relevant output resistance keeps loading error in the low single digits — good enough for most bench measurements — while getting only 2-3x separation can push the error into double digits. Designers who need better than that either push the ratio further (100x) or buffer the divider's output with an op-amp follower, whose high input impedance and low output impedance sidestep the loading problem entirely.

lessons.workedExample: A 100 kΩ / 100 kΩ divider runs off a 10 V ideal source, so the unloaded output is Vin*R2/(R1+R2) = 10*100k/200k = 5.0 V. A multimeter with 1 MΩ input resistance is connected to read it. The multimeter's 1 MΩ now sits in parallel with the divider's 100 kΩ R2: R2‖RL = (100k×1M)/(1.1M) ≈ 90.9 kΩ. Recomputing with this loaded value: Vout = 10*90.9k/(100k+90.9k) ≈ 4.76 V. The meter reads 4.76 V instead of the true 5.0 V — a 4.8% low reading, purely from the meter's own finite input resistance, with no fault in the divider itself.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'did you account for your meter's loading?' is testing whether a student understands that measurement is not passive — connecting an instrument changes the circuit. A weak answer insists the divider math is correct and doesn't consider the meter at all. A strong answer names the specific mechanism (the meter's input resistance parallels R2, pulling the node down), can estimate the size of the error from the two resistance values, and explains the fix — either a much higher-impedance meter or a buffer stage — rather than just flagging that an error exists.

questions.prompt: In a voltage divider Vout = Vin*R2/(R1+R2), what assumption does this formula make about whatever is connected to read Vout?

options.text: That it has zero resistance
That it draws no current, i.e., has infinite input resistance
That it is a current source
That it matches R2 exactly

explanations.a: Zero resistance would short R2 to ground, collapsing Vout to zero — the opposite of the ideal assumption.
explanations.b: Correct — the formula assumes the measuring device draws no current, so it doesn't change the current flowing through R1 and R2.
explanations.c: A current source connected at the output would inject or draw current in a way the simple divider formula doesn't account for at all.
explanations.d: Matching R2 exactly would cause severe loading (halving the effective R2‖RL), not eliminate the loading problem.

questions.prompt: A 100 kΩ / 100 kΩ divider off a 10 V source is read by a 1 MΩ meter. About what does the meter read, compared to the ideal 5.0 V?

options.text: Exactly 5.0 V, since 1 MΩ is a large resistance
About 4.76 V, roughly 4.8% low
About 2.5 V, half the ideal value
About 5.5 V, higher than the ideal value

explanations.a: 1 MΩ is only ten times R2, not large enough relative to R2 to make the loading error negligible.
explanations.b: Correct — the meter's 1 MΩ in parallel with R2's 100 kΩ gives about 90.9 kΩ, dropping the reading to roughly 4.76 V, about 4.8% low.
explanations.c: Halving would require the load resistance to equal R2 exactly, not be ten times larger.
explanations.d: Loading always pulls Vout below the ideal value in this configuration; it cannot push it higher.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to calculate the loading error when a divider's output is read by a finite-impedance meter.

items.text: Compute the ideal (unloaded) Vout using Vin*R2/(R1+R2)
Combine R2 with the meter's input resistance in parallel to get the loaded effective resistance
Recompute Vout using the loaded effective resistance in place of R2
Compare the loaded and ideal Vout values to find the percent error

questions.explanation: You need the ideal baseline first, then combine the meter's input resistance with R2 in parallel, then recompute the actual output with that loaded value, and only then compare the two results to quantify the error.

questions.prompt: What does the '10x rule' recommend, and what does it trade off?

options.text: Keep the downstream input impedance at least ten times the divider's relevant output resistance, accepting a low-single-digit loading error rather than the larger error from a closer impedance match
Always use exactly ten resistors in a divider network
Keep R1 exactly ten times R2 for best accuracy
Multiply the final reading by ten to correct for loading

explanations.a: Correct — a roughly 10:1 impedance separation, as in the worked example, keeps loading error in the low single digits; smaller separations push the error higher, and a designer needing even less error goes to 100x or buffers the output.
explanations.b: The rule concerns impedance ratios, not resistor count.
explanations.c: The R1:R2 ratio sets the division ratio, not the loading error, which instead depends on the load's impedance relative to R2.
explanations.d: There is no fixed multiplier correction; the actual error depends on the specific resistance values involved.

lessons.label: Thevenin and Norton Equivalents

sections.heading: Any linear two-terminal network is just two numbers
sections.body: Léon Charles Thévenin published the theorem in 1883: from the outside, any network of linear resistors and independent sources, viewed through just two terminals, behaves exactly like a single ideal voltage source Vth in series with a single resistor Rth, no matter how many components are hidden inside. Vth is the open-circuit voltage — what a high-impedance meter reads across the terminals with nothing else attached — and Rth is the resistance the network presents looking into those terminals with every independent source zeroed (voltage sources shorted, current sources opened). This is a genuinely useful compression: a battery pack, a sensor with its bias network, or an entire amplifier's output stage can each be swapped for two numbers when you only care about how they drive an external load, not what happens inside.

sections.heading: Norton's dual, and converting between them
sections.body: Edward Norton, working at Bell Labs, described the current-source dual in an internal 1926 technical report: the same network can equally be modeled as an ideal current source Isc (the short-circuit current the terminals would deliver) in parallel with a resistance Rn. The two models are interchangeable because Rn always equals Rth, and the source values are linked by Ohm's law: Vth = Isc * Rth, or equivalently Isc = Vth / Rth. Whichever form is more convenient for the next calculation — Thevenin for a network feeding a load in series, Norton for one feeding a current-summing node — can be produced from the other with one division or multiplication, so there is never a reason to solve the same network twice.

sections.heading: Finding Vth and Rth from the bench, not the schematic
sections.body: The power of the theorem is that Vth and Rth can be measured on a sealed black box with no knowledge of what's inside. First, measure the open-circuit voltage with a high-impedance meter — that reading is Vth directly. Second, attach a known test resistor R_test as a load and measure the terminal voltage under load, V_load; since V_load = Vth * R_test/(Rth + R_test) is exactly a voltage-divider relation with Rth playing the role of R1, solving for the one unknown gives Rth = R_test * (Vth/V_load - 1). With Vth and Rth in hand, the box's behavior under any other load can be predicted with the same divider formula, without ever opening it or measuring its internal current.

lessons.workedExample: A sealed black box's terminals read 9 V open-circuit, so Vth = 9 V. Loading it with a known R_test = 100 ohm resistor drops the terminal voltage to V_load = 6 V. Solving Rth = R_test*(Vth/V_load - 1) = 100*(9/6 - 1) = 100*0.5 = 50 ohm. The Norton equivalent follows immediately: Isc = Vth/Rth = 9/50 = 0.18 A, Rn = 50 ohm. To predict behavior under a new 200 ohm load without touching the box again: V = Vth*RL/(Rth+RL) = 9*200/(50+200) = 1800/250 = 7.2 V.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe Thevenin equivalents because reducing a black box to two numbers and predicting new behavior from them is exactly the skill needed to characterize a real sensor, battery, or signal source without redesigning the whole test each time a load changes. A weak answer re-measures every new load from scratch or can't explain why only two measurements (open-circuit and one loaded reading) fully pin down the model. A strong answer states plainly that any linear two-terminal network has exactly two independent parameters, shows the algebra that extracts Rth from one loaded reading, and then uses the resulting model to predict — not re-measure — a different load's behavior.

questions.prompt: What does Rth represent in a Thevenin equivalent?

options.text: The resistance of the load that will eventually be connected
The resistance seen looking into the network's terminals with all independent sources zeroed (voltage sources shorted, current sources opened)
The total resistance of every resistor in the network added together
The resistance of the wire connecting the two terminals

explanations.a: Rth is a property of the source network alone, independent of whatever load will later be attached.
explanations.b: Correct — Rth is defined as the equivalent resistance at the terminals once every independent source inside is zeroed, leaving only the passive network.
