explanations.c: Simply summing every resistor ignores how they're actually connected (series/parallel/bridge), which changes the equivalent resistance.
explanations.d: There is no assumption of a connecting wire; Rth is a property of the open network.

questions.prompt: Match each Thevenin/Norton quantity to how it is obtained.

right.text: Open-circuit voltage measured with a high-impedance meter
Short-circuit current the terminals would deliver
Solved from a known test resistor's loaded voltage reading
Divide by Rth

questions.explanation: Vth is the open-circuit voltage; Isc is the short-circuit current; Rth is found from a known test load's loaded-voltage reading using the divider relation; and Vth converts to Isc by dividing by Rth.

questions.prompt: A black box reads 9 V open-circuit and 6 V when loaded with a known 100 ohm resistor. What is Rth?

options.text: 100 ohm
50 ohm
150 ohm
9 ohm

explanations.a: 100 ohm is the test resistor's own value, not the solved Rth.
explanations.b: Correct — Rth = R_test*(Vth/V_load - 1) = 100*(9/6 - 1) = 100*0.5 = 50 ohm.
explanations.c: 150 ohm would be R_test + Rth added incorrectly rather than solved from the divider equation.
explanations.d: 9 ohm mistakes Vth's numeric value for a resistance; Vth is a voltage, not a resistance.

questions.prompt: Using Vth = 9 V and Rth = 50 ohm from the black box, what voltage would appear across a new 200 ohm load, without any further measurement of the box itself?

options.text: 9 V, since Vth never changes
7.2 V, from V = Vth*RL/(Rth+RL) = 9*200/250
4.5 V, half of Vth regardless of the load
1.8 V, from Isc times the new load resistance

explanations.a: 9 V is only the open-circuit value; any finite load draws current through Rth and drops some voltage, so the terminal voltage under load is always less than Vth.
explanations.b: Correct — the Thevenin model predicts terminal voltage under any load with the same divider formula: 9*200/(50+200) = 7.2 V.
explanations.c: A 50/50 split only occurs when RL happens to equal Rth, which is not the case here (RL = 200, Rth = 50).
explanations.d: Isc times RL is not the right relation here; Isc is the current if the terminals were shorted (RL = 0), not a general formula for other loads.

lessons.label: Maximum Power Transfer vs Efficiency

sections.heading: Why RL = Rth maximizes power, and caps efficiency at 50%
sections.body: Model any source as its Thevenin equivalent, Vth in series with Rth, driving a load RL. The load current is I = Vth/(Rth+RL), so the power delivered to the load is P = I^2*RL = Vth^2*RL/(Rth+RL)^2. Taking dP/dRL and setting it to zero shows the maximum occurs exactly at RL = Rth — the maximum power transfer theorem. At that point the same current flows through Rth and RL, and since they're equal in value, they dissipate equal power: half the total power the source generates is lost inside the source itself, capping efficiency at 50% at the very operating point where delivered power peaks. Pushing RL higher than Rth lowers the power delivered but raises efficiency, since a shrinking fraction of the (also-shrinking) total power is lost in Rth.

sections.heading: Two different goals, two different design rules
sections.body: This is why RF systems, where getting the most signal power out of a fixed source matters more than wasting some of it, deliberately match RL to Rth: antenna and transmission-line impedance matching is the classic case, since a mismatched RF line reflects power back toward the source instead of radiating it. Legacy tube audio amplifiers did the same thing, using an output transformer whose turns ratio matched the tube's high Rth to an 8-ohm speaker. Modern solid-state audio amplifiers deliberately do the opposite: heavy negative feedback drives their output impedance down to a small fraction of an ohm, far below RL, trading away maximum power transfer for a high damping factor and flat frequency response. Power distribution has the opposite goal: a wall socket or a long transmission line is modeled as a small Rth feeding a load RL that is normally many times larger, so the vast majority of the power lands in the load and only a small fraction is wasted as I^2*Rth heating in the source and wiring. Deliberately running RL >> Rs is what keeps a power grid's transmission losses in the single-digit percent range instead of the 50% ceiling that maximum-power matching would force.

sections.heading: A battery's internal resistance, and why it grows with use
sections.body: A real battery is exactly this Thevenin picture: an EMF source E in series with an internal resistance r that rises as the cell's chemistry depletes. A two-load test finds both: attach a known resistor R_a, measure the terminal voltage V1 (giving current I1 = V1/R_a), then repeat with a different known resistor R_b to get V2 and I2 = V2/R_b. Two linear equations, V = E - I*r, in two unknowns solve directly: r = (V1-V2)/(I2-I1), then E = V1 + I1*r. A fresh AA cell typically has r on the order of a few tenths of an ohm, so it barely sags under a normal load. A nearly depleted AA can have r rise to several ohms or more — its open-circuit voltage may look almost normal, but under any real load nearly all of the sagging voltage drop happens inside the battery itself, which is why a 'dead' battery can still read close to 1.5 V on a voltmeter yet fail to drive a motor.

lessons.workedExample: A battery under test is loaded first with R_a = 9 ohm, giving a measured terminal voltage V1 = 1.35 V, so I1 = 1.35/9 = 0.15 A. Loaded next with R_b = 4 ohm, the terminal voltage is V2 = 1.20 V, so I2 = 1.20/4 = 0.30 A. Solving the two-load equations: r = (V1-V2)/(I2-I1) = (1.35-1.20)/(0.30-0.15) = 0.15/0.15 = 1.0 ohm, and E = V1 + I1*r = 1.35 + 0.15*1.0 = 1.5 V. This battery's 1.0-ohm internal resistance is already well above a fresh cell's, so under the 4-ohm load it loses 0.30 V (20%) inside itself before any of it reaches the load — a fresh cell with a much smaller r would lose only a few percent under the same load.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe maximum power transfer because it is a favorite place for students to overgeneralize a rule from one domain (audio matching) into another where it is actively wrong (efficient power delivery). A weak answer states 'match the load to the source' as a universal rule. A strong answer names the actual trade-off — matched impedance gives maximum power at only 50% efficiency, while an efficiency-focused system deliberately mismatches with RL >> Rs — and can connect it to a concrete case like battery internal resistance, showing they understand it as a design choice driven by the goal, not a fixed law.

questions.prompt: At the maximum-power-transfer condition RL = Rth, what is the efficiency of power delivery to the load?

options.text: 100%, since this is the optimal operating point
50%, since Rth and RL are equal and carry the same current, so they dissipate equal power
0%, since all power is lost in Rth
It depends on Vth

explanations.a: Maximum delivered power and maximum efficiency occur at different operating points; RL = Rth maximizes power, not efficiency.
explanations.b: Correct — with RL = Rth, equal current flows through equal resistances, so exactly half the total power is dissipated in each, capping efficiency at 50%.
explanations.c: Half the power reaches the load at this condition, not zero.
explanations.d: The 50% split is a ratio between two equal resistances carrying the same current; it holds regardless of the specific Vth value.

questions.prompt: Why does a power distribution system deliberately use RL much greater than the source's internal resistance, rather than matching them?

options.text: Because matching would deliver too much power to the load
Because the goal is high efficiency (minimizing the fraction of power wasted as heat in the source/wiring), and RL >> Rs achieves that even though it delivers less than the theoretical maximum power
Because RL must always be at least ten times Rth by regulation
Because matched impedance would cause the source to short-circuit

explanations.a: Matching does not deliver 'too much' power; it delivers the maximum possible power, just at poor efficiency, which is a different objective than distribution systems have.
explanations.b: Correct — distribution systems prioritize efficiency, and RL >> Rs pushes most of the (smaller total) power into the load rather than wasting half of it in the source, unlike the matched case.
explanations.c: There's no such fixed regulatory ratio; the RL >> Rs practice follows from the physics of efficiency, not a rule number.
explanations.d: Matched impedance (RL = Rth) is a normal, stable operating condition, not a short circuit (which would be RL = 0).

questions.prompt: In the two-load battery test, loading with 9 ohm gives V1 = 1.35 V and loading with 4 ohm gives V2 = 1.20 V. What is the internal resistance r?

options.text: 0.15 ohm
1.0 ohm
9.0 ohm
4.0 ohm

explanations.a: 0.15 A is I1 in this problem, not the internal resistance.
explanations.c: 9.0 ohm is R_a, one of the known test load resistors, not the solved internal resistance.
explanations.d: 4.0 ohm is R_b, the other known test load resistor, not the solved internal resistance.

questions.prompt: A 'dead' AA battery can still read close to 1.5 V open-circuit on a voltmeter but fails to spin a motor. What does the internal-resistance model say is happening?

options.text: The battery's EMF E has dropped to near zero, even though the meter somehow still reads 1.5 V
The battery's internal resistance r has risen substantially, so under a real (low-resistance) load most of the voltage drops across r inside the battery rather than reaching the load
The voltmeter itself is malfunctioning
The motor's resistance has increased to match the battery's

explanations.a: If E had actually dropped near zero, the open-circuit voltmeter reading (which draws negligible current) would show that drop directly; the scenario states it still reads close to 1.5 V.
explanations.b: Correct — a voltmeter draws almost no current, so it barely samples r's voltage drop and reads close to E; a motor draws real current, and with a large r most of E is lost inside the battery before reaching the motor.
explanations.c: Nothing in the scenario suggests meter malfunction; the behavior is fully explained by a depleted cell's rising internal resistance.
explanations.d: The motor's resistance is a separate, roughly fixed property of the motor; it doesn't change to 'match' the battery.

lessons.label: Nodal Analysis, Mesh Analysis, and Superposition

sections.heading: Node-voltage and mesh-current: two systematic bookkeeping schemes
sections.body: Both methods exist so a circuit with several unknowns can be solved as one linear system instead of by ad-hoc series/parallel reduction. Node-voltage analysis: pick one node as ground (0 V reference), then for every other node write a KCL equation expressing currents leaving that node through each resistor as (V_node - V_neighbor)/R, and set the sum equal to any current sources feeding that node directly. A circuit with three non-reference nodes gives three equations in three unknown node voltages, solved simultaneously. Mesh-current analysis is the dual: assign a circulating current to each independent loop, write one KVL equation per loop summing IR drops (with shared branches carrying the difference of the two adjacent loop currents), and solve the resulting system for the loop currents. Mesh analysis only applies cleanly to planar circuits (ones that can be drawn with no crossing wires); node-voltage analysis has no such restriction, which is why it generalizes better to circuit-simulator software.

sections.heading: Superposition: solve for one source at a time
sections.body: For a linear circuit with multiple independent sources, superposition says the total response (any current or voltage) equals the sum of the responses to each source acting alone, with every other independent source zeroed. Zeroing a voltage source means replacing it with a short (0 V, since an ideal voltage source's internal resistance is zero); zeroing a current source means replacing it with an open circuit (0 A, since an ideal current source's internal resistance is infinite). Solve the simplified single-source circuit, record the contribution (with its sign/direction), restore that source, zero the next one, and repeat. The technique trades one complicated multi-source circuit for several simpler single-source ones — but it only works for currents and voltages, which add linearly; power does not superpose, because power is proportional to current squared, so power contributions from separate sources cannot simply be added.

sections.heading: Power balance as the final sanity check
sections.body: However a circuit was solved, the answer must satisfy one more conservation law: total power delivered by all sources must equal total power dissipated by all resistors, since a circuit can neither create nor destroy energy. Computing this balance after solving is a nearly free check — a sign error in a KVL equation or a mixed-up node index tends to survive the algebra but shows up as an imbalance here, because the error usually breaks the delicate cancellations that made the original equations consistent. A source can also come out delivering zero or even negative power (absorbing power) in a solved circuit; that isn't a mistake by itself, but it is exactly the kind of result worth checking against the power balance before trusting it.

lessons.workedExample: A 10 V source in series with R1 = 5 ohm feeds node A; a 1 A current source also injects directly into node A; from node A, R2 = 10 ohm returns to ground. Superposition, source by source: with the current source opened, the circuit is just the 10 V source driving R1 and R2 in series, giving I(R2) = 10/(5+10) = 0.667 A. With the voltage source shorted, the 1 A splits between R1 and R2 as a current divider, giving I(R2) = 1*5/(5+10) = 0.333 A. Summing: I(R2) = 0.667 + 0.333 = 1.0 A. A direct node-voltage solve confirms it: KCL at node A gives (10-V_A)/5 + 1 = V_A/10, solving to V_A = 10 V, so I(R2) = 1.0 A and, notably, I(R1) = (10-10)/5 = 0 A — the two superposition contributions to R1's current turn out equal and opposite, canceling exactly. Power balance: the voltage source delivers 10*0 = 0 W, the current source delivers 10*1 = 10 W, and R2 dissipates 1.0^2*10 = 10 W while R1 dissipates 0 W — 10 W in, 10 W out, confirming the solution.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges push on nodal/mesh setup and superposition because they reveal whether a student has a repeatable method or is pattern-matching from memorized simple circuits. A weak answer can solve a textbook series-parallel circuit but stalls the moment a circuit has a genuine loop structure or two independent sources. A strong answer sets up the node or mesh equations systematically, applies superposition correctly (including getting the zeroing rule right for each source type), and — the real tell — checks the final answer with a power balance rather than just trusting the algebra, catching the sign errors that are otherwise invisible until a downstream calculation quietly comes out wrong.

questions.prompt: When applying superposition, how should a current source be treated while solving for the contribution of a different source in the same circuit?

options.text: Replace it with a short circuit
Replace it with an open circuit
Leave it exactly as it is
Replace it with a resistor equal to the load resistance

explanations.a: Shorting is the correct treatment for a zeroed voltage source, not a current source.
explanations.b: Correct — an ideal current source has infinite internal resistance, so zeroing it (setting its current to 0 A) means opening that branch entirely.
explanations.c: Leaving every source active defeats the purpose of superposition, which isolates one source's contribution at a time.
explanations.d: There is no rule to replace a zeroed source with an arbitrary resistor; the correct substitution is a specific open or short depending on source type.

questions.prompt: In the worked example, superposition gives I(R1) contributions of +0.667 A (from the voltage source alone) and -0.667 A (from the current source alone), summing to 0 A. Why can't the same additive logic be used to superpose the power dissipated in R1 from each source?

options.text: Power can be superposed the same way; the 0 W result for R1 is found by adding the two sources' individual power contributions directly
Because power is proportional to current squared, so it is a nonlinear function of the sources; power contributions from separate sources cannot simply be added together
Because R1 is not an ohmic resistor
Because superposition only applies to voltage, never to current

explanations.a: This is exactly the mistake superposition invites for power; squaring breaks the linear additivity that makes superposition valid for currents and voltages.
explanations.b: Correct — since P = I^2*R, power is a nonlinear (quadratic) function of current, so the total power must be computed from the final combined current, not by summing each source's individual power contribution.
explanations.c: R1's ohmic or non-ohmic nature is irrelevant here; the issue is the mathematical form of the power formula itself.
explanations.d: Superposition applies to both voltage and current (and to any quantity that's a linear function of the sources); it simply fails for power specifically.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of the superposition method for a circuit with a voltage source and a current source.

items.text: Zero the current source (open it) and solve the circuit with only the voltage source active, recording the quantity of interest
Restore the current source, then zero the voltage source (short it), and solve the circuit with only the current source active
Algebraically sum the two individual-source contributions, respecting sign and direction, to get the total response
Check the final combined solution against a power balance, computed from the true combined currents and voltages, not from summed individual powers

questions.explanation: Superposition solves each source's contribution in turn with the others zeroed, sums the linear quantities (current or voltage) with correct signs, and only then checks the final combined result with a power balance, since power itself must be computed from the combined solution rather than summed source by source.

questions.prompt: In the worked example's power balance, the voltage source delivers 0 W, the current source delivers 10 W, and the resistors dissipate a total of 10 W. What does this check confirm?

options.text: That the voltage source is broken
That the solved node voltage and branch currents are self-consistent, since total power delivered by all sources equals total power dissipated by all resistors
That R1 and R2 have equal resistance
That superposition cannot be trusted for this circuit

explanations.a: A source delivering 0 W in a solved circuit isn't necessarily broken — here it's simply because I(R1) came out to exactly 0 A, so the voltage source happens to carry no current in this particular combined solution.
explanations.b: Correct — energy conservation requires total delivered power to equal total dissipated power; getting 10 W = 10 W confirms the node-voltage solution is internally consistent.
explanations.c: R1 = 5 ohm and R2 = 10 ohm are explicitly unequal in this circuit; the power balance doesn't imply anything about their relative sizes.
explanations.d: The power balance checking out is evidence the superposition-derived answer (I(R2) = 1.0 A) is correct, not a reason to distrust the method.

units.label: Passive Components: Resistors, Capacitors, Inductors

lessons.label: Resistors in the Real World

sections.heading: Four families, four tradeoffs
sections.body: A resistor's construction decides what it is good for. Carbon film resistors are a carbon layer laser-cut into a helical track on a ceramic rod; they are cheap and common but sit around 5% tolerance with a temperature coefficient (TCR) of -200 to -500 ppm/degC, meaning resistance drifts noticeably with heat. Metal film resistors sputter a nickel-chromium alloy instead of carbon, cutting TCR to roughly 50-100 ppm/degC and tolerance to 1%, with far less electrical noise, which is why they dominate signal paths. The noise gap has a mechanism: carbon film's granular carbon-particle contacts generate excess 1/f (current) noise that grows with applied voltage and DC current, stacked on top of the Johnson-Nyquist thermal noise every resistor has, while metal film's continuous sputtered NiCr layer has far less granular contact noise to add. That is why precision signal-chain designs specify a metal film part's noise index (in dB) as a real selection criterion, not just its tolerance and TCR. Wirewound resistors coil resistance wire around a ceramic core for high power handling (tens of watts), but a coil is an inductor: an ordinary wirewound part looks inductive above a few kHz. William Ayrton and John Perry solved this in the 1880s with a bifilar winding, now called an Ayrton-Perry winding, that folds the wire back on itself so the magnetic fields cancel. Thin-film precision resistors, laser-trimmed after deposition, reach 0.1% tolerance and TCR as low as 5-25 ppm/degC, used in voltage references and precision dividers.

sections.heading: Tolerance and TCR compound in a real circuit
sections.body: Tolerance is the manufacturing spread at room temperature; TCR is how much resistance moves per degree after that. A 1% resistor can still be a poor choice if its TCR is 200 ppm/degC and the circuit spans 50 degC of self-heating or ambient swing, because that adds another 1% of drift on top of the initial tolerance. Precision dividers (ADC reference ladders, current-sense scaling) usually spend the money on 0.1%/25 ppm parts specifically to keep that combined error under control.

sections.heading: Power rating, derating, and shunt sensing
sections.body: A resistor's printed wattage (e.g., 0.25 W) is only guaranteed up to a rated ambient, commonly 70 degC for standard through-hole parts, above which the manufacturer's derating curve cuts allowable power linearly to zero at the maximum body temperature, often around 155 degC. Run that same 0.25 W resistor in a 100 degC enclosure and it may only tolerate a fraction of its rated power before it drifts or fails. Current-sensing shunts push resistance deliberately low - milliohms - so that I squared R self-heating and TCR-driven drift stay small, and they use four-terminal Kelvin connections so the measurement leads sit inside the current-carrying leads, removing lead and contact resistance from the reading entirely.

lessons.workedExample: A student builds a battery current monitor with a 10 milliohm shunt rated 1%, TCR 100 ppm/degC, sensing up to 5 A. At 5 A the shunt dissipates I squared R = 25 * 0.01 = 0.25 W, enough self-heating to raise its body temperature 20-30 degC above ambient in a small enclosure. That temperature rise alone shifts resistance by roughly 100 ppm/degC * 25 degC = 0.25%, on top of the 1% tolerance - a nearly 1.25% worst-case error on the current reading. Wiring the shunt with four-terminal Kelvin sense leads removes connector resistance from the picture, but does nothing for the thermal drift; only a lower-TCR shunt or active temperature compensation fixes that part.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who sees 'we used a 1% resistor' wants to know if the student understands that 1% is a room-temperature snapshot, not a guarantee under load. The strong answer names the resistor family used, states its TCR, and shows a back-of-envelope calculation of drift from self-heating or ambient swing, then explains why that mattered (or didn't) for the measurement's required precision. The weak answer treats 'precision resistor' as a purchased property rather than an interacting set of specs - tolerance, TCR, and power rating - that has to be checked against the specific operating temperature the circuit will actually see.

questions.prompt: Why is a wirewound resistor a poor choice for a signal path above a few kHz unless it uses a special winding?

options.text: Its carbon film degrades at high frequency
The coiled wire geometry adds parasitic inductance that behaves like an inductor
Wirewound resistors always exceed 5% tolerance
Wirewound resistors cannot dissipate more than 0.1 W

explanations.a: Wirewound resistors use resistance wire, not carbon film - that failure mode does not apply.
explanations.b: Correct - winding wire into a coil creates parasitic inductance, so the part's impedance rises with frequency unless the winding cancels the field, as an Ayrton-Perry winding does.
explanations.c: Tolerance is independent of the inductance problem; wirewound parts are made to a range of tolerances.
explanations.d: Wirewound resistors are typically chosen for HIGH power handling, tens of watts, not low power.

questions.prompt: Match each resistor family to its defining property.

right.text: Cheap, ~5% tolerance, high TCR
1% tolerance, low noise, ~50-100 ppm/degC TCR
High power handling, coil geometry adds inductance
Laser-trimmed to 0.1% tolerance, TCR as low as 5-25 ppm/degC

questions.explanation: Carbon film is the cheap, higher-drift default; metal film trades cost for lower noise and tighter TCR; wirewound trades frequency response for power handling; thin-film precision parts are laser-trimmed for the tightest tolerance and TCR.

questions.prompt: A 0.25 W through-hole resistor is rated for full power up to 70 degC ambient. What happens if it is operated at 100 degC ambient?

options.text: Nothing changes; the rating is independent of ambient temperature
Its allowable power is derated below 0.25 W, following the manufacturer's derating curve toward zero at the max body temperature
Its tolerance improves because heat anneals the film
Its power rating increases to compensate for the higher ambient

explanations.a: The rated wattage is only valid up to the rated ambient; above it, allowable power drops.
explanations.b: Correct - datasheets specify a derating curve from the rated ambient (often 70 degC) down to zero allowable power at the maximum body temperature (often around 155 degC).
explanations.c: Heat does not improve tolerance; it typically increases resistance drift via TCR.
explanations.d: Power rating decreases, not increases, as ambient temperature rises.

questions.prompt: Why do current-sensing shunt resistors use four-terminal Kelvin connections?

options.text: To double the effective resistance value
To remove lead and contact resistance from the voltage measurement across the shunt
To allow the shunt to be used at higher voltages
To reduce the shunt's TCR to zero

explanations.a: Kelvin sensing does not change the resistance value; it changes how it is measured.
explanations.b: Correct - separate sense leads placed inside the current-carrying leads mean the measured voltage reflects only the shunt element, not connector or wire resistance.
explanations.c: Kelvin sensing addresses measurement accuracy, not voltage rating.
explanations.d: TCR is a material property of the shunt element and is unaffected by how it is wired for measurement.

lessons.label: Capacitors: Charge Storage and Dielectric Reality

sections.heading: Q = CV and the energy it stores
sections.body: A capacitor stores charge Q proportional to applied voltage V through its capacitance C: Q = CV. Because voltage across the capacitor changes as charge accumulates, the stored energy is not simply Q times V but the integral of that relationship, giving E = 0.5 * C * V^2. This is why a capacitor bank charged to a higher voltage stores dramatically more energy than one charged to a modest voltage at the same capacitance - doubling voltage quadruples stored energy, which matters directly for flash capacitors and defibrillator design, and is exactly why a charged high-voltage capacitor is dangerous even after its circuit is powered off.

sections.heading: Ceramic dielectrics are not one part
sections.body: The EIA classifies ceramic capacitors by dielectric stability. Class I dielectrics, most commonly C0G/NP0, use a paraelectric formulation that barely shifts with temperature or voltage - capacitance stays within about 30 ppm/degC and is essentially bias-independent, but the material only supports small capacitance values in a small case. Class II dielectrics, X7R and the much less stable Y5V, use ferroelectric formulations that pack far more capacitance into the same volume, at a cost: X7R can lose roughly 30-70% of its rated capacitance as DC bias approaches the part's rated voltage, and Y5V can lose even more, plus both age (capacitance slowly decays after each solder reflow). A student who reads '10 microfarad X7R' off a datasheet and assumes 10 microfarad in circuit is very often wrong.

sections.heading: Electrolytics, film, and the specs that decide survival
sections.body: Aluminum electrolytic capacitors use an oxide layer as the dielectric and a wet or solid electrolyte as one plate; this gives huge capacitance per volume but comes with polarity (reverse voltage can rupture the part) and a finite life set by electrolyte evaporation, roughly halving with every 10 degC of operating temperature rise. Film capacitors (polyester, polypropylene) are non-polar, stable, and low-loss, but bulkier per microfarad. Across all types, three specs decide whether a capacitor survives its job: equivalent series resistance (ESR), which sets how much it self-heats under AC ripple; ripple-current rating, the maximum AC current it can dissipate that heat from; and leakage current, the small DC current that bleeds through the dielectric over time. A capacitor picked purely by capacitance value and voltage rating, ignoring ESR and ripple current, is a common cause of premature failure in switching power supplies.

lessons.workedExample: A 100 microfarad, 16 V aluminum electrolytic is placed on a buck converter's output, carrying 500 mA RMS of switching ripple current. Its datasheet lists ESR = 0.2 ohm and a ripple-current rating of 400 mA at 105 degC. Power dissipated inside the capacitor is I^2 * ESR = 0.5^2 * 0.2 = 0.05 W, which does not sound large, but it is concentrated in a small volume and the part is already over its 400 mA ripple rating, so it runs hotter than rated - the manufacturer's rule of thumb (life halves every 10 degC above rated temperature) means a capacitor rated for 5,000 hours at 105 degC could fail in well under a year of continuous operation. Swapping to a capacitor rated for 700 mA ripple, or paralleling two smaller ones to split the current, solves it without changing the nominal capacitance.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe capacitor choice because 'I used a 10 microfarad capacitor' sounds precise but is frequently a lie in practice, especially with X7R or Y5V parts under DC bias. A strong answer distinguishes the dielectric family used, states whether bias derating was checked against the datasheet's capacitance-vs-voltage curve, and for electrolytics in a power path, cites ESR or ripple-current rating rather than just capacitance and voltage. A weak answer treats capacitance as a fixed number stamped on the part, with no acknowledgment that the number on the case is a rated value under specific conditions the actual circuit may not meet.

questions.prompt: A capacitor is charged from 5 V to 10 V (same capacitance). By what factor does its stored energy increase?

options.text: 2x
4x
It stays the same, since Q = CV is linear

explanations.a: Energy scales with V squared, not V, so doubling voltage is not a doubling of energy.
explanations.b: Correct - E = 0.5*C*V^2, so doubling V quadruples E (2^2 = 4).
explanations.c: 10x would require a much larger voltage change than doubling.
explanations.d: Charge Q does scale linearly with V, but stored energy does not - it depends on V squared.

questions.prompt: Match each capacitor type or class to its defining behavior.

right.text: Very stable, bias-independent, low capacitance per volume
Can lose 30-70% of rated capacitance under DC bias
Polarized, finite life tied to electrolyte evaporation
Non-polar, low-loss, bulkier per microfarad

questions.explanation: C0G/NP0 is the stable, low-capacitance-density Class I option; X7R is a Class II dielectric that trades stability for density and loses significant capacitance under bias; aluminum electrolytics are polarized with a finite, temperature-dependent life; film capacitors are non-polar and stable but physically larger per microfarad.

questions.prompt: Which two specs, beyond capacitance and voltage rating, determine whether an electrolytic capacitor survives sustained AC ripple current in a power supply?

options.text: Case color and lead spacing
ESR and ripple-current rating
Dielectric class letter and package height
Tolerance percentage and case material

explanations.a: Case color and lead spacing have no bearing on thermal survival under ripple.
explanations.b: Correct - ESR sets how much internal heating occurs per amp of ripple current, and the ripple-current rating is the maximum the part can dissipate that heat from at its rated temperature.
explanations.c: Dielectric class letters (C0G, X7R) apply to ceramic capacitors, not electrolytics.
explanations.d: Tolerance affects nominal accuracy, not thermal survival under ripple current.

questions.prompt: A datasheet lists a 10 microfarad X7R ceramic capacitor rated for 25 V. At its actual operating bias of 20 V, the effective capacitance is best described as:

options.text: Exactly 10 microfarad, since X7R is a stable Class I dielectric
Likely well below 10 microfarad, since X7R capacitance drops significantly as DC bias approaches rated voltage
Higher than 10 microfarad, since bias increases ferroelectric polarization
Undefined, because X7R capacitors cannot be used with DC bias at all

explanations.a: X7R is a Class II, not Class I, dielectric - it is not bias-stable the way C0G/NP0 is.
explanations.b: Correct - X7R is a ferroelectric Class II dielectric that can lose roughly 30-70% of its rated capacitance as bias approaches the rated voltage, so 20 V on a 25 V-rated part is well into significant derating territory.
explanations.c: Capacitance decreases, not increases, under DC bias for ferroelectric dielectrics.
explanations.d: X7R capacitors are routinely used with DC bias; the issue is that the effective capacitance is lower than the label suggests, not that it cannot be used.

lessons.label: Inductors and Magnetic Energy Storage

sections.heading: v = L di/dt and stored magnetic energy
sections.body: An inductor opposes changes in current, not current itself: the voltage across it is v = L * di/dt, proportional to how fast current is changing rather than to current directly. That is the mirror image of a capacitor, where current depends on dv/dt. Energy is stored in the magnetic field the current creates, E = 0.5 * L * I^2, released back into the circuit as current decreases. This symmetry with capacitor energy (0.5*C*V^2) is why inductors and capacitors together form resonant tanks and filters: one stores energy in an electric field, the other in a magnetic field, and energy sloshes between them.

sections.heading: Core material sets the saturation ceiling
sections.body: An air-core inductor has no magnetic material to concentrate flux, so it needs many turns for modest inductance but never saturates - inductance stays constant regardless of current. Ferrite cores (sintered iron-oxide ceramics) concentrate flux enormously, giving high inductance in a small package, but the core has a saturation flux density: past a certain current, the core's magnetic domains stop aligning further, permeability collapses, and inductance drops sharply - a inductor that reads 100 microhenries at low current can effectively vanish at its saturation current, undermining any circuit that assumed constant inductance. Powdered iron cores saturate more gradually (a 'soft' saturation knee) at the cost of higher core loss, making them a common compromise in power-supply inductors where a hard collapse is dangerous.

sections.heading: Kickback, flyback diodes, and the limits of a real part
sections.body: Because v = L*di/dt, interrupting current through an inductor abruptly (di/dt approaching infinity, as when a switch opens) produces a voltage spike large enough to arc across a switch or destroy a transistor - inductive kickback, the same effect used deliberately in ignition coils and flyback converters. A flyback diode placed across an inductive load (a relay coil, a motor) gives that current a path to keep flowing after the switch opens, clamping the spike to roughly one diode drop instead of hundreds of volts. Real inductors also have DC resistance (DCR) from the wire itself, causing resistive loss and a voltage drop under load, and a self-resonant frequency (SRF) where the winding's parasitic capacitance resonates with the inductance - above SRF the part behaves capacitively instead of inductively, which is why an inductor chosen for a high-frequency filter must have its SRF checked, not just its inductance value.

lessons.workedExample: A relay coil (10 mH, 100 ohm DC resistance) is switched by a transistor from a 12 V supply, drawing 120 mA. Without a flyback diode, opening the switch tries to force di/dt to be enormous in a very short time; since v = L*di/dt, the coil's voltage swings hugely negative for an instant - easily hundreds of volts - which can punch through a transistor rated for 40 V. Adding a diode across the coil, cathode to the supply side, gives the 120 mA a decaying path through the diode and coil resistance instead: the voltage spike clamps to about 12.7 V (supply plus one diode drop) instead of an uncontrolled several hundred, and the transistor survives switching cycle after switching cycle.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe inductor questions because a wrong answer here usually means a fried transistor in the actual build, not just an inaccurate reading. A strong answer names the mechanism (v = L*di/dt spikes when current is interrupted quickly) and the specific fix (a flyback diode, sized for the coil's current), and separately recognizes that a real inductor is not just an L value - it has a saturation current above which inductance collapses and a self-resonant frequency above which it stops behaving like an inductor at all. A weak answer treats 'inductor' as an ideal component with one number on it and cannot explain why the relay driver circuit needed a diode in the first place.

questions.prompt: Why does abruptly interrupting current through an inductor produce a large voltage spike?

options.text: Because v = L*di/dt, and a fast current change (large di/dt) produces a large voltage
Because the inductor's resistance increases sharply when switched off
Because stored charge on the inductor's plates is suddenly released
Because the core material becomes magnetized in reverse

explanations.a: Correct - the inductor's voltage is proportional to the rate of change of current, so forcing current to stop nearly instantly demands a very large (in principle infinite) voltage.
explanations.b: Inductor resistance (DCR) does not change sharply on switch-off; it is a separate, roughly constant property of the winding.
explanations.c: Inductors store energy in a magnetic field, not as charge on plates - that description applies to capacitors.
explanations.d: Kickback is a voltage response to di/dt, not a description of core magnetization reversing.

questions.prompt: Order the events when a switch driving an unprotected relay coil is opened, from first to last.

items.text: Switch opens, forcing current through the coil toward zero very quickly
v = L*di/dt produces a large voltage spike across the coil
The spike appears across the switch/transistor, which may exceed its voltage rating
Without a flyback diode, the transistor can be damaged or destroyed

questions.explanation: Opening the switch forces a rapid current change, which by v = L*di/dt produces a large induced voltage; that voltage appears across the open switch, and if it exceeds the switch's rating, damage follows - which is exactly what a flyback diode is added to prevent.

questions.prompt: An inductor rated 100 microhenries is driven well past its saturation current in a power converter. What happens to its inductance?

options.text: It stays at 100 microhenries regardless of current
It increases, since more current means a stronger field
It drops sharply, since the core material can no longer concentrate additional flux
It becomes negative

explanations.a: Constant inductance regardless of current is true only for air-core inductors, not core materials with a saturation limit.
explanations.b: Saturation is the opposite effect - inductance falls, not rises, as the core stops responding to more current.
explanations.c: Correct - past saturation, the core's domains stop aligning further, permeability collapses, and inductance drops sharply, undermining the assumption of constant L.
explanations.d: Inductance does not go negative from saturation; it falls toward a much smaller effective value.

questions.prompt: Above an inductor's self-resonant frequency (SRF), the part behaves:

options.text: As an ideal inductor with reduced inductance
Capacitively, because the winding's parasitic capacitance dominates
As a pure resistor
Identically to below SRF, since SRF only affects DC behavior

explanations.a: Above SRF the part is no longer acting like an inductor at all, reduced or otherwise.
explanations.b: Correct - above SRF, the parasitic winding capacitance resonates with the inductance and then dominates, so the part's impedance behaves capacitively rather than inductively.
explanations.c: DC resistance (DCR) is present at all frequencies but does not become the dominant behavior above SRF - capacitive behavior does.
explanations.d: SRF is specifically a frequency-domain effect and has no meaning at DC; behavior clearly changes above it.

lessons.label: Reading a Datasheet Without Being Fooled

sections.heading: Absolute maximum vs recommended operating conditions
sections.body: Every component datasheet carries two very different tables that beginners routinely conflate. Absolute maximum ratings define the edge past which the part is not guaranteed to survive at all - a voltage or current the manufacturer tested to failure, with no promise of correct behavior anywhere near it, and often no promise the part isn't damaged from a single brief excursion. Recommended operating conditions are the range the part is actually specified to work correctly within, usually with real margin below the absolute maximums. Designing a circuit that pins a component near its absolute maximum rating - reasoning 'the datasheet says it can handle this' - is a common student mistake; the professional habit is to design to the recommended operating range and treat the absolute maximum as a never-touch line, not a target.

sections.heading: Typical is not guaranteed
sections.body: Electrical characteristics tables list typical, minimum, and maximum columns for the same parameter. 'Typical' describes the center of the distribution across a batch of parts under specific test conditions - it is a marketing-adjacent number, not something any individual unit is contractually guaranteed to hit. A robust design uses the min/max columns (whichever bounds the failure mode that matters) because that is the range the manufacturer will actually stand behind across process variation, temperature, and aging. A headline 'typical' figure on the first page of a datasheet is frequently reachable only under a narrow footnoted condition - a specific supply voltage, a specific temperature, a specific test frequency - that a real circuit will not always meet.

sections.heading: Footnotes and thermal resistance
sections.body: Conditions footnotes are where a headline number becomes honest or misleading. A capacitor's 'low ESR' figure might be measured only at 100 kHz and 25 degC, useless for predicting behavior at the actual switching frequency and ambient temperature of a design. Thermal resistance, theta-JA (junction-to-ambient, in degC/W), is the number that converts a part's internal power dissipation into a real temperature rise: temperature rise = power dissipated * theta-JA, so a part dissipating 0.5 W with theta-JA = 100 degC/W will run 50 degC above ambient - potentially enough to hit thermal shutdown or a derating knee in a warm enclosure, even though the part's dissipation alone looked modest on paper. Theta-JA is only ever measured on a specific reference PCB - a copper area and layer count stated in a footnote - so a real board with less copper pour can run hotter than theta-JA predicts. Theta-JC (junction-to-case) is the number that matters once a heatsink is added, since it bypasses the PCB's often-dominant thermal path entirely and characterizes heat flow straight into the case instead.

lessons.workedExample: A student is choosing a linear regulator that datasheet lists as dropping 'typically 0.3 V' with an absolute maximum input voltage of 40 V, and theta-JA = 65 degC/W in a small SOT-23 package. They plan to feed it from a 24 V supply to produce 5 V output at 100 mA, reasoning the 40 V max gives plenty of margin. The actual power dissipated in the regulator is (24V - 5V) * 0.1A = 1.9 W, and temperature rise = 1.9 W * 65 degC/W = about 124 degC above ambient - the regulator will hit thermal shutdown almost immediately, despite operating nowhere near its 40 V absolute maximum. The number that mattered was theta-JA times dissipated power, not the input voltage headroom the student focused on.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask 'how did you choose that part?' specifically to catch students who picked a component off a single headline spec. A strong answer names which number actually constrained the design - often a min/max guaranteed value or a thermal-resistance calculation - and explicitly distinguishes it from the absolute maximum rating and from any typical-only figure. A weak answer cites a number pulled straight from a datasheet's front page ('it's rated for 40 volts, so we're fine') without checking whether that number was the relevant one, under the relevant conditions, guaranteed rather than typical.

questions.prompt: What is the key difference between a part's absolute maximum rating and its recommended operating conditions?

options.text: They are two names for the same specification
Absolute maximum is the edge with no guarantee of survival past it; recommended operating conditions are the range the part is specified to actually work correctly within
Recommended operating conditions are always higher than absolute maximum ratings
Absolute maximum ratings only apply to voltage, never current or temperature

explanations.a: They describe fundamentally different things: survival limits versus a guaranteed-correct-operation range.
explanations.b: Correct - absolute maximum is a destruction/no-guarantee boundary; recommended operating conditions is the range within which correct, specified behavior is promised.
explanations.c: It is the opposite - recommended operating conditions sit below the absolute maximum with margin.
explanations.d: Absolute maximum ratings commonly cover voltage, current, and temperature, among other parameters.

questions.prompt: A datasheet's electrical characteristics table lists a 'typical' value for a parameter. What does that number represent?

options.text: The guaranteed worst-case value across all manufactured units
The absolute maximum the part can withstand
An approximate center of the distribution across a batch under specific test conditions, not a guarantee for any individual part
The value measured at the part's absolute maximum temperature

explanations.a: Worst-case guaranteed values are given by the min/max columns, not the typical column.
explanations.b: Typical values are far from the absolute maximum rating; they describe expected normal behavior.
explanations.c: Correct - typical is a central-tendency figure under specific test conditions, useful for estimation but not a per-unit guarantee.
explanations.d: Typical values are usually measured at standard test conditions (often 25 degC), not extreme temperature.

questions.prompt: A part dissipates 0.8 W and has theta-JA = 80 degC/W. If ambient temperature is 25 degC, roughly what temperature does the part reach?

options.text: About 25 degC (theta-JA does not affect temperature)
About 64 degC
About 89 degC
About 130 degC

explanations.a: Theta-JA converts dissipated power directly into a temperature rise above ambient; it is central to the calculation, not something to ignore.
explanations.b: 64 degC is just the temperature rise itself (0.8 W * 80 degC/W); it still needs to be added to the 25 degC ambient.
explanations.c: Correct - temperature rise = 0.8 W * 80 degC/W = 64 degC; added to 25 degC ambient gives about 89 degC.
explanations.d: This overshoots the correct total; it does not match 0.8 W * 80 degC/W + 25 degC ambient.

questions.prompt: Why might a headline 'low ESR' or 'low dropout' number on a datasheet's front page be misleading for a specific design?

options.text: Front-page numbers are always guaranteed minimums, so they cannot be misleading
The headline figure is often measured only under a specific footnoted condition (frequency, voltage, temperature) that the real circuit may not match
Datasheets are legally required to list only worst-case numbers on the front page
Headline numbers apply only to the absolute maximum rating table

explanations.a: Front-page headline numbers are frequently typical values under narrow test conditions, not guaranteed minimums.
explanations.b: Correct - a conditions footnote (e.g., measured at 100 kHz and 25 degC) can make an otherwise impressive number irrelevant to a design operating outside those conditions.
explanations.c: There is no such requirement; manufacturers choose which flattering number to headline.
explanations.d: Headline specs typically come from the electrical characteristics table, not the absolute maximum ratings table.

lessons.label: Parasitics: Every Component Is an RLC

sections.heading: No component is pure
sections.body: Every real passive part is, underneath its schematic symbol, a small network of all three basic elements. A capacitor has equivalent series resistance (ESR, from the electrode material and electrolyte or dielectric losses) and equivalent series inductance (ESL, from the leads and internal plate geometry) in series with its intended capacitance. A resistor has lead inductance from its physical length and shunt capacitance between its ends. A wire is itself an inductor, roughly 1 nH per millimeter for typical hookup wire geometry - small, but not zero, and it adds up over the length of a PCB trace or a lead.

sections.heading: Self-resonance flips a capacitor into an inductor
sections.body: A capacitor's ESL forms a series LC circuit with its own capacitance. Below the resulting self-resonant frequency (SRF), the part behaves as expected: impedance falls as frequency rises, the way an ideal capacitor should. At SRF, the capacitive and inductive reactances cancel and impedance hits a minimum, set mostly by ESR. Above SRF, ESL dominates and the part's impedance starts rising with frequency - it is now acting like an inductor, not a capacitor. A 100 nF ceramic capacitor in a small package might have an SRF in the tens of MHz; used well above that frequency, it no longer filters the way its printed value suggests, and a designer needing high-frequency filtering has to check SRF, not just capacitance.

sections.heading: Why decoupling capacitor placement is not cosmetic
sections.body: This is exactly why a 100 nF decoupling capacitor must sit physically at the chip's power pin rather than a centimeter away on the board. The trace connecting a capacitor to the chip acts as an inductor (about 1 nH/mm), and that trace inductance is in series with the capacitor's own ESL - both work against the capacitor's job of supplying a fast, low-impedance current pulse the instant a digital chip switches. A capacitor placed a few centimeters away can have enough added trace inductance to raise the effective impedance at the switching frequency well above what the decoupling was supposed to achieve, leaving the chip to draw current through comparatively slow, inductive supply traces instead of the nearby low-impedance capacitor. This is also the core reason a circuit that behaves perfectly at 1 kHz can misbehave at 10 MHz: at 1 kHz, nanohenries of trace or lead inductance are negligible (reactance = 2*pi*f*L is tiny), but at 10 MHz the same inductance has ten thousand times the reactance, comparable to or larger than the resistances and capacitive reactances the circuit was designed around, so parasitics that were invisible at low frequency start dominating the circuit's actual behavior.

lessons.workedExample: A designer places a 100 nF ceramic decoupling capacitor 15 mm away from a microcontroller's power pin instead of directly adjacent. The trace contributes roughly 15 mm * 1 nH/mm = 15 nH of added series inductance. At the microcontroller's fast digital switching edges (effective frequencies in the tens of MHz), the reactance of just that trace inductance, X = 2*pi*f*L, at 30 MHz works out to roughly 2*pi*30e6*15e-9 = about 2.8 ohms - comparable to or larger than the capacitor's own ESR, and enough to blunt the capacitor's ability to supply a clean current pulse. The chip sees voltage sag on its supply pin during switching, sometimes enough to cause glitches or resets, even though the '100 nF should be plenty' reasoning was correct at DC and low frequency.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing PCB layout or 'why did you put the capacitor right next to the chip?' is testing whether the student understands parasitics as physical, not abstract - that a millimeter of copper is a real inductor with a real reactance at the frequencies that matter. A strong answer explains that trace and lead inductance (roughly 1 nH/mm) combines with a capacitor's own ESL, and that this combination only matters once reactance (2*pi*f*L) becomes comparable to the circuit's other impedances - which happens at MHz-scale switching edges, not at DC. A weak answer says 'it's just good practice' without being able to explain what would actually go wrong if the capacitor were moved away.

questions.prompt: Above a capacitor's self-resonant frequency (SRF), how does its impedance behave as frequency increases further?

options.text: It keeps falling, exactly as an ideal capacitor's would
It rises, because equivalent series inductance (ESL) now dominates the part's behavior
It stays flat at the SRF minimum indefinitely
It becomes purely resistive and stays fixed at the ESR value

explanations.a: That describes behavior below SRF; above SRF the part no longer behaves like an ideal capacitor.
explanations.b: Correct - above SRF, ESL dominates the impedance and it rises with frequency, meaning the part now behaves inductively.
explanations.c: Impedance is at a minimum near SRF but does not stay flat above it; it rises.
explanations.d: ESR sets the impedance minimum near SRF but does not describe behavior well above it, where inductive reactance grows.

questions.prompt: Roughly how much series inductance does 15 mm of ordinary PCB trace or wire add, using the approximation given?

options.text: About 0.15 nH
About 1.5 nH
About 15 nH
About 150 nH

explanations.a: This is off by two orders of magnitude from the 1 nH/mm approximation.
explanations.b: This is off by one order of magnitude from the 1 nH/mm approximation.
explanations.c: Correct - using roughly 1 nH per millimeter, 15 mm gives about 15 nH.
explanations.d: This is ten times larger than the 1 nH/mm approximation gives for 15 mm.

questions.prompt: Why can a circuit that works fine at 1 kHz misbehave at 10 MHz, even with the same components and layout?

options.text: Component values change with frequency in a way datasheets never document
Parasitic reactances (from lead/trace inductance, ESL, ESR) are negligible at 1 kHz but become comparable to the circuit's intended impedances at 10 MHz
Resistors stop conducting above 1 MHz
Capacitors physically discharge on their own above audio frequencies

explanations.a: Datasheets do document frequency-dependent behavior (SRF, ESR curves); the issue is designers not checking it, not that it is undocumented.
explanations.b: Correct - inductive reactance (2*pi*f*L) and other parasitic effects scale with frequency, so nanohenries that are irrelevant at 1 kHz can dominate at 10 MHz.
explanations.c: Resistors continue conducting at high frequency; their lead inductance and shunt capacitance become significant, but conduction itself does not stop.
explanations.d: Capacitors do not spontaneously discharge from frequency alone; the issue is impedance behavior, not charge loss.

questions.prompt: Match each real component to a parasitic element it actually carries, as described in this lesson.

right.text: ESL and ESR in series with its capacitance
Lead inductance and shunt capacitance between its ends
Roughly 1 nH per millimeter of series inductance

questions.explanation: A capacitor's real-world model adds ESL and ESR in series with the ideal capacitance; a resistor adds lead inductance and end-to-end shunt capacitance; a wire or trace behaves as an inductor of roughly 1 nH per millimeter.

lessons.label: Choosing and Combining Passives for a Build

sections.heading: Why you can't just buy any resistance value
sections.body: Resistors and capacitors are not sold in every possible value; they are stocked in preferred-number series - E12 (12 values per decade, for 10% or 5% parts), E24 (24 values, common for 5% and 1%), and E96 (96 values, for 1% and tighter) - standardized in IEC 60063. These series trace back to French engineer Charles Renard, who in 1877 devised a logarithmically spaced set of preferred numbers to standardize cordage and cable sizes for military balloons; the same logarithmic spacing logic (each step roughly a constant percentage larger than the last) carries directly into how component values are stocked today. When a design needs a value the series does not offer - say, exactly 4.7 kilohms plus a trim to 4.85 kilohms - the fix is combining stock values, not special-ordering a part.

sections.heading: Series and parallel combination to hit a target
sections.body: Resistors in series simply add: R_total = R1 + R2. Resistors in parallel combine as R_total = (R1*R2)/(R1+R2), always less than the smallest individual value. Capacitors do the opposite - they add in parallel (C_total = C1 + C2) and combine reciprocally in series, which is why capacitor combination is used less often for fine-tuning a value and resistors dominate that role. A common pattern is a large resistor in series with a small trim resistor to land close to an oddball target value that no single E96 part provides, or two same-value resistors in parallel to halve a value while also halving the effective power rating burden per part.

sections.heading: Building a tolerance error budget
sections.body: Combining parts also combines their tolerances, but not by simple addition when the errors are independent and random - worst-case errors from independent 5% parts combine in quadrature (the square root of the sum of squares), not by adding directly. Two independent 5% resistors in a voltage divider give a worst-case ratio error of roughly sqrt(5%^2 + 5%^2), about 7%, not 10%. Whether that 7% is acceptable depends entirely on what the circuit needs: a ratio driving an LED's rough brightness has huge margin for 7% error, but a ratio setting an ADC's reference divider or a precision timing RC constant may need to stay within 1% or better, which is exactly when it becomes worth paying for 1% or 0.1% precision parts instead of parts pulled from the cheap bin. Precision is a design decision made per-node, not a blanket policy applied to every resistor in a schematic.

lessons.workedExample: A student needs a voltage divider that outputs exactly 2.50 V from a 5.00 V rail (ratio 0.500) to feed a microcontroller's ADC reference check. Using two 5% E24 resistors of equal value (each contributing independent 5% tolerance) gives a worst-case ratio error of about sqrt(5%^2+5%^2) = 7.07%, meaning the actual divided voltage could land anywhere from about 2.32 V to 2.68 V - unacceptable if the ADC comparison needs better than 1% accuracy. Switching both resistors to 0.1% thin-film precision parts drops the worst-case ratio error to about sqrt(0.1%^2+0.1%^2) = 0.14%, comfortably inside spec, at a few times the per-resistor cost - money well spent on this one node, while every other 5% resistor in the same design (an LED current-limiter, a pull-up) stays exactly as it was.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask 'why did you use a precision resistor here but a regular one there?' to test whether tolerance choice was deliberate or accidental. A strong answer identifies the specific node where error matters (a reference divider, a timing constant) and shows the quadrature-combined tolerance math that justified paying for precision parts there, while explaining why cheap 5% parts were fine everywhere else. A weak answer either uses 5% everywhere and cannot explain the resulting error on a sensitive node, or uses expensive precision parts everywhere out of caution, unable to say why the cost was justified on parts where it clearly was not needed.

questions.prompt: Two independent 5% tolerance resistors set a voltage divider ratio. What is the approximate worst-case combined ratio error, using quadrature combination?

options.text: 5%, since only one resistor's error matters
10%, since the two 5% errors add directly
About 7%, since independent errors combine as the square root of the sum of squares
0%, since the two errors cancel out

explanations.a: Both resistors' tolerances contribute to the ratio error, not just one.
explanations.b: Direct addition overstates the worst-case error for independent random tolerances; quadrature combination is the correct approach.
explanations.c: Correct - sqrt(5%^2 + 5%^2) is about 7.07%, the standard way to combine independent tolerance sources.
explanations.d: Independent tolerances do not reliably cancel; quadrature combination assumes they could align unfavorably in the worst case.

questions.prompt: What are the E12, E24, and E96 series, and where do they trace from historically?

options.text: Arbitrary numbers chosen independently by each manufacturer, with no shared history
Preferred-number series standardized in IEC 60063, tracing back to Charles Renard's 1877 logarithmic preferred-number system
A numbering scheme invented by capacitor manufacturers in the 1990s
A binary encoding scheme unrelated to resistor or capacitor values

explanations.a: These series are standardized (IEC 60063) precisely so manufacturers share a common set of stocked values.
explanations.b: Correct - E12/E24/E96 are logarithmically spaced preferred-number series standardized in IEC 60063, tracing back to Charles Renard's 1877 preferred-number system originally devised for military balloon cordage.
explanations.c: The underlying preferred-number logic long predates the 1990s and is not capacitor-specific.
explanations.d: These are decimal, logarithmically spaced value series, not a binary encoding.

questions.prompt: Two 100-ohm resistors are combined in parallel. What is the resulting resistance?

options.text: 200 ohm
100 ohm
50 ohm
0 ohm

explanations.a: 200 ohm is what you get from combining the two resistors in series, not parallel.
explanations.b: 100 ohm would be the value of a single resistor alone, not the parallel combination of two.
explanations.d: Parallel combination of two nonzero resistors never produces zero resistance.

questions.prompt: A design has one node (an ADC reference divider) needing tight tolerance and ten other nodes (LED current limiters, pull-ups) where 5% is fine. What is the lazy-but-correct approach to component selection?

options.text: Use 0.1% precision resistors everywhere, since more precision is never wrong
Use 5% resistors everywhere, since a divider is just a divider
Use precision resistors only at the ADC reference divider, and cheap 5% parts everywhere else
Randomly mix precision and standard parts across all nodes

explanations.a: This wastes money on nodes where 5% error has no functional consequence, like an LED current limiter.
explanations.b: This ignores that the ADC reference divider specifically needs tighter accuracy than 5% parts can reliably provide.
explanations.c: Correct - precision tolerance should be spent where the error budget actually requires it, and skipped where it doesn't matter functionally.
explanations.d: Component selection should be deliberate per-node based on what accuracy each node needs, not random.

units.label: Semiconductor Devices: Diodes, BJTs, MOSFETs

lessons.label: Doping, the PN Junction, and the Diode

sections.heading: Adding impurities on purpose
sections.body: Pure silicon is a poor conductor: each atom has four valence electrons, all locked into covalent bonds with its neighbors, leaving almost no free carriers. Doping deliberately breaks that symmetry by replacing roughly one silicon atom in a million with an impurity — a typical doping level runs around 10^15 to 10^18 dopant atoms per cm^3, against silicon's own atomic density of about 5x10^22 atoms per cm^3, which is where that 'one in a million' ratio comes from. Phosphorus or arsenic has five valence electrons, so four bond normally and the fifth is loosely held, free to conduct as a negative carrier — this is n-type material. Boron has three valence electrons, leaving one bond incomplete, a 'hole' that behaves like a mobile positive charge — this is p-type. Neither material alone does anything interesting; the physics starts when the two are grown together in a single crystal.

sections.heading: The depletion region and built-in potential
sections.body: Where n-type meets p-type, free electrons near the boundary diffuse into the p-side and holes diffuse into the n-side, and the pair recombine. This leaves behind fixed, immobile dopant ions — positive on the n-side, negative on the p-side — with no free carriers between them, called the depletion region. Those exposed ions set up an internal electric field that opposes further diffusion, and equilibrium is reached at a built-in potential of about 0.6-0.7 V for silicon. Forward bias (positive terminal to the p-side) fights this field, narrows the depletion region, and lets current flow once the applied voltage approaches that built-in potential; reverse bias widens the depletion region and current stays near zero until breakdown. Breakdown itself is usually avalanche multiplication: a high enough reverse field accelerates the few free carriers crossing the depletion region to enough kinetic energy that a collision with the lattice knocks loose a new electron-hole pair, and each of those carriers can do the same, so the carrier population cascades and reverse current rises sharply at a fairly well-defined breakdown voltage.

sections.heading: The Shockley equation and real forward drops
sections.body: The ideal diode law is I = Is(exp(V/(n*Vt)) - 1), where Is is the tiny reverse saturation current, n is the ideality factor (close to 1 for good diodes), and Vt = kT/q is the thermal voltage — about 25.85 mV at 300 K (room temperature). Because current depends exponentially on voltage, the forward drop looks almost fixed in practice: roughly 0.7 V for silicon, 0.3 V for germanium (a smaller bandgap gives a smaller built-in potential), and 1.8-3.4 V for LEDs, which need enough energy per electron to emit a photon — red LEDs sit near 1.8-2.2 V, blue and white nearer 3.0-3.4 V. That forward drop is not perfectly constant with temperature: it falls by about -2 mV per degree C as the device warms, because Is grows with temperature.

lessons.workedExample: A student wires a red LED (rated Vf approx 2.0 V) directly across two AA batteries (3.0 V) with no resistor and it dies instantly. Using the Shockley relationship qualitatively: the LED's current rises exponentially once V approaches its forward drop, so the 'extra' 1.0 V above 2.0 V demands enormous current that only the battery's internal resistance limits — likely hundreds of mA, well past the LED's 20 mA rating. Adding a 47 ohm series resistor forces the drop to split: about 2.0 V across the LED and 1.0 V across the resistor, giving I = 1.0 V / 47 ohm approx 21 mA, matching the datasheet.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'why does your diode have a fixed voltage drop instead of behaving like a resistor?' to check whether a student understands that the drop comes from an exponential current-voltage law, not an ohmic one. A weak answer says 'diodes just drop 0.7 volts.' A strong answer explains that current depends exponentially on voltage past the built-in potential, so a small voltage window covers a huge current range — which is exactly why diodes always need a current-limiting resistor and why the drop shifts slightly with temperature and LED color.

questions.prompt: What is the thermal voltage Vt used in the Shockley diode equation at 300 K?

options.text: About 25.85 mV
About 0.7 V
About 2.585 V
About 300 mV

explanations.a: Correct — Vt = kT/q evaluates to about 25.85 mV at 300 K, the value that scales the exponential term in I = Is(exp(V/(n*Vt)) - 1).
explanations.b: 0.7 V is the approximate forward voltage drop of a silicon diode, not the thermal voltage.
explanations.c: This is off by a factor of 100 from the correct thermal voltage.
explanations.d: 300 mV is not the thermal voltage; it is close to the temperature in Kelvin divided by 1, which is not how Vt is computed.

questions.prompt: Match each material or device to its approximate forward voltage drop.

right.text: About 0.7 V
About 0.3 V
About 1.8-2.2 V
About 3.0-3.4 V

questions.explanation: Silicon's built-in potential gives roughly 0.7 V; germanium's smaller bandgap gives roughly 0.3 V; LED forward voltage tracks photon energy, so red LEDs sit near 1.8-2.2 V and blue/white LEDs near 3.0-3.4 V.

questions.prompt: A silicon diode's forward voltage drop at a fixed current is measured warm and cold. What happens as the diode heats up?

options.text: The forward drop rises by about 2 mV per degree C
The forward drop falls by about 2 mV per degree C
The forward drop stays exactly constant with temperature
The forward drop doubles for every 10 degree C rise

explanations.a: The drop falls, not rises, with increasing temperature.
explanations.b: Correct — the reverse saturation current Is grows with temperature, so at fixed forward current the diode needs less voltage to sustain it, giving a drift of roughly -2 mV/degC.
explanations.c: The Shockley equation's Is term is temperature-dependent, so the drop is not constant.
explanations.d: That description matches a different physical rule (rough doubling of reaction rates) and is not the diode's temperature coefficient.

questions.prompt: Order these events as a PN junction is formed and reaches equilibrium, starting from separate n-type and p-type crystals.

items.text: N-type and p-type silicon are grown together in one crystal
Free electrons near the boundary diffuse into the p-side and holes diffuse into the n-side
Diffusing carriers recombine, leaving fixed dopant ions exposed near the junction
The exposed ions create a built-in electric field that halts further net diffusion

questions.explanation: The junction must exist before carriers can diffuse across it; diffusion causes recombination that exposes fixed ions; those ions then generate the field that establishes the depletion region and built-in potential at equilibrium.

questions.prompt: Why does phosphorus-doped silicon (n-type) conduct via free electrons rather than holes?

options.text: Phosphorus has three valence electrons, leaving an incomplete bond
Phosphorus has five valence electrons, so one electron per atom is not needed for bonding and is free to conduct
Phosphorus atoms are physically larger than silicon atoms
Phosphorus does not bond with silicon at all

explanations.a: Three valence electrons describes boron, which produces p-type material with holes, not n-type.
explanations.b: Correct — phosphorus's fifth valence electron has no bonding role in the silicon lattice, so it is loosely bound and free to act as a negative charge carrier.
explanations.c: Atomic size affects lattice strain, not the electron-donating behavior that defines n-type doping.
explanations.d: Phosphorus does substitute into the silicon lattice and bond with neighboring atoms; only one electron is left over.

lessons.label: Diode Families and Their I-V Curves

sections.heading: Rectifiers and Schottky diodes: two ways to pass current one way
sections.body: The 1N400x family (1N4001 through 1N4007) are general-purpose silicon rectifier diodes, differing mainly in peak inverse voltage (PIV) — the maximum reverse voltage they can block without breaking down — from 50 V for the 1N4001 up to 1000 V for the 1N4007, all rated around 1 A forward current with a roughly 0.7-1.0 V forward drop. A Schottky diode replaces the PN junction with a metal-to-semiconductor junction, which drops less energy per carrier and gives a forward voltage of only about 0.2-0.4 V — useful anywhere that wasted power matters, like a reverse-polarity-protection diode in a battery-powered device. The tradeoff is a much lower PIV and higher reverse leakage current than an equivalent silicon rectifier.

sections.heading: Reverse recovery time: how fast a diode actually turns off
sections.body: A diode does not stop conducting the instant the current reverses; carriers stored in the junction during forward conduction must first sweep out or recombine, and during that interval the diode briefly conducts backward. This reverse recovery time (trr) is read directly off a datasheet's switching characteristics table or test curve. A small-signal switching diode like the 1N4148 has trr around 4 ns, fast enough for RF and digital clamping. A general-purpose 1N4007 rectifier, by contrast, has trr in the microsecond range — around 1000x slower — because its junction is built for high voltage blocking, not speed. A Schottky diode has essentially no minority-carrier storage at all, so its reverse recovery is negligible, which is why Schottky diodes dominate high-frequency switching supplies.

sections.heading: Zener diodes: breakdown as a feature, and reading the reverse curve
sections.body: Every diode eventually breaks down in reverse if pushed hard enough, but a Zener diode is manufactured to break down at a specific, well-controlled voltage (its Zener voltage, Vz) and survive there indefinitely as long as its power rating is respected. Below Vz it behaves like an ordinary reverse-biased diode with tiny reverse leakage current; at Vz the reverse curve turns almost vertical, so current can swing over a wide range while voltage stays nearly pinned. That flat, vertical segment is what makes Zeners useful as voltage references — a series resistor sets the current, and the Zener clamps the voltage. Reading a real datasheet's reverse I-V curve means locating three landmarks: the leakage current just below breakdown, the knee where the curve turns vertical at Vz, and the PIV or maximum reverse voltage the part can survive without exceeding its power dissipation.

lessons.workedExample: A designer needs a 5 V reference from a 12 V supply using a 1N4733A Zener (Vz = 5.1 V, rated 1 W). They pick a series resistor to set Zener current around 20 mA: R = (12 V - 5.1 V) / 0.02 A = 345 ohm, so they use a standard 330 ohm resistor, giving about 20.9 mA through the Zener and roughly 107 mW dissipated in it — well under the 1 W limit. If the load pulls no current, all 20.9 mA flows through the Zener; if the load pulls 10 mA, the Zener current drops to about 10.9 mA and the output voltage barely moves, because the reverse curve is nearly vertical at that current.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'why did you choose a Schottky diode there instead of a regular rectifier?' or 'how do you know your Zener won't overheat?' to see if the student picked a part from a datasheet feature, not a part bin. A weak answer says 'it's a diode, it blocks reverse current.' A strong answer names the specific tradeoff — lower forward drop but lower PIV and higher leakage for the Schottky, or the wattage math for the Zener's bias current — showing the student read the curve, not just the part number.

questions.prompt: Match each diode type to the property that best distinguishes it.

right.text: Wide range of peak inverse voltage ratings (50-1000 V) for general rectification
Low forward drop (0.2-0.4 V) from a metal-semiconductor junction
Deliberately operated in reverse breakdown as a voltage reference
Very fast reverse recovery (about 4 ns) for digital/RF switching

questions.explanation: The 1N400x series is defined by its PIV range for rectification; Schottky diodes are defined by their low forward drop; Zener diodes are used deliberately in reverse breakdown; the 1N4148 is defined by its fast (about 4 ns) reverse recovery time.

questions.prompt: Approximately how does the 1N4148's reverse recovery time compare to a 1N4007's?

options.text: The 1N4148 is about 1000x faster (around 4 ns vs microseconds)
The 1N4148 is about 1000x slower
They are essentially identical, both in the microsecond range
The 1N4007 has no measurable reverse recovery time

explanations.a: Correct — the 1N4148 switches in about 4 ns while the 1N4007, built for high-voltage blocking rather than speed, recovers in the microsecond range, roughly a thousandfold difference.
explanations.b: This reverses the comparison; the small-signal switching diode is the faster of the two.
explanations.c: Their recovery times differ by roughly three orders of magnitude, not negligibly.
explanations.d: Every PN-junction rectifier has nonzero reverse recovery from stored minority carriers; only a true Schottky junction approaches negligible recovery.

questions.prompt: On a Zener diode's reverse I-V curve, what does the nearly vertical segment at the breakdown voltage represent?

options.text: A region where voltage changes drastically for almost no change in current
A region where current changes drastically for almost no change in voltage
The diode's forward conduction region
A malfunction indicating the part has failed

explanations.a: This describes the opposite behavior; the vertical segment means voltage stays nearly fixed while current varies.
explanations.b: Correct — the nearly vertical breakdown segment means the Zener holds voltage almost constant across a wide current range, which is exactly the property that makes it useful as a reference.
explanations.c: Forward conduction is a separate region on the positive-voltage side of the curve, not the reverse breakdown knee.
explanations.d: Reverse breakdown at the rated Zener voltage is the diode's normal, designed-for operating mode, not a failure.

questions.prompt: Why is a Schottky diode often chosen for a reverse-polarity-protection application in a battery-powered device over a standard silicon rectifier?

options.text: It has a higher peak inverse voltage rating
It has a lower forward voltage drop, wasting less power
It has slower reverse recovery, which improves protection
