That last piece is often the single biggest tell: a student who can point to a timestamped supply-voltage sag as the reason for an outlier has run a real, defensible experiment; a student who says they "threw out the weird ones" has not.

questions.prompt: In a test of whether decoupling capacitor value affects switching-regulator ripple, what should the control condition be?

options.text: The same board and load with no capacitor installed, to establish the baseline noise floor
A completely different board design as a point of comparison
The largest capacitor value tested, run twice
A theoretical calculation with no physical measurement

explanations.a: Correct — the control isolates the variable under test by holding everything else identical and removing only the capacitor, showing what ripple exists before any capacitor gets credit for reducing it.
explanations.b: A different board introduces many uncontrolled differences beyond just the capacitor, defeating the purpose of a control.
explanations.c: Repeating the largest value is a repeat measurement, not a control condition that isolates the variable's absence.
explanations.d: A control must be measured under the same real conditions as the test trials, not merely calculated.

questions.prompt: Why should a circuit be allowed to thermally settle for a few minutes after power-up before the first logged measurement?

options.text: Because component values and offsets drift as the circuit warms up, and that drift could be mistaken for the effect under test
Because oscilloscopes require a warm-up period to display any trace at all
Because capacitors are illegal to measure while cold
It is unnecessary; readings are equally valid at any time after power-up

explanations.a: Correct — resistor temperature coefficients, op-amp offset drift, and similar effects mean early readings can reflect warm-up transients rather than the variable being tested.
explanations.b: Modern scopes display a trace immediately; the settling concern is about the circuit under test, not the scope itself.
explanations.c: There is no such restriction; this distractor is not a real constraint.
explanations.d: Thermal drift is a real, documented confound, which is exactly why settling time matters.

questions.prompt: A student sees one data point that looks far off from its neighbors in a repeated-measures run. What is the defensible response?

options.text: Delete it immediately since it clearly doesn't fit the trend
Investigate the logged conditions at that timestamp for a specific documented cause before deciding whether to exclude or re-measure it
Average it in without comment, since all data must be kept no matter what
Replace it with the average of the other readings

explanations.a: Deleting a point simply because it disagrees with expectation is expectation bias, not a defensible experimental decision.
explanations.b: Correct — checking the logged supply voltage, timestamp, or notes for a specific cause (a probe slip, a voltage sag) before excluding or re-measuring the point keeps the decision evidence-based rather than expectation-driven.
explanations.c: Genuine equipment faults (a slipped probe, a tripped current limit) are legitimate reasons to exclude a reading once documented; "never exclude anything" is not the rule either.
explanations.d: Silently substituting a fabricated value for a real measurement misrepresents the data and is worse than either keeping or documented exclusion.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for designing and running a controlled bench sweep, from first to last.

items.text: Identify the one independent variable to sweep and list every variable to hold fixed
Decide the number of repeats per condition and the acceptance criteria for a valid reading, before starting
Power on the circuit and allow it to thermally settle before the first logged reading
Run the control condition and each swept condition, logging timestamp, supply voltage, and ambient temperature with every reading
Investigate any anomalous readings against the logged conditions before excluding or re-measuring them

questions.explanation: The variable and fixed conditions must be defined first; repeat count and acceptance criteria are set next, before any bias from seeing results can creep in; thermal settling happens after power-on but before real data collection; the control and swept conditions are then run with full logging; anomalies are investigated against that log only after the run, never simply discarded on sight.

units.label: AC Circuits, Transients, and the Frequency Domain

lessons.label: RC and RL Transients

sections.heading: An exponential chase toward equilibrium
sections.body: Close a switch connecting a battery, resistor, and capacitor in series and the capacitor voltage does not jump to the supply voltage — it chases it exponentially. Kirchhoff's voltage law around the loop gives a first-order linear differential equation, V(t) = Vfinal + (Vinitial - Vfinal)e^(-t/tau), whose solution's rate is set by a single quantity: the time constant tau = RC, in seconds when R is in ohms and C in farads. Physically, tau is how long the resistor takes to move roughly two-thirds of the remaining charge onto the capacitor's plates. A bigger R throttles the charging current; a bigger C demands more charge to reach the same voltage, so both stretch tau.

sections.heading: Landmarks that make an exponential readable
sections.body: Because the curve never mathematically finishes, engineers use fixed checkpoints instead of 'done.' After one tau the gap between the signal and its final value has closed by a factor of e (~2.718): the rising curve reaches 63.2% of its final value, and the falling curve has decayed to 36.8% of its starting value. After two tau, 86.5%; after three, 95.0%; after five tau, 1 - e^-5 = 99.3%, which is why '5 tau' is the standard rule of thumb for calling a transient settled — a defibrillator's discharge or a camera flash's recharge is engineered around exactly this figure.

sections.heading: RL circuits: same math, a different bottleneck
sections.body: An inductor enforces the mirror-image rule: current, not voltage, cannot jump instantaneously, because di/dt through L induces a back-EMF that opposes the change. Solving the loop equation for a series R-L circuit gives an identical exponential form with tau = L/R (henries over ohms, also seconds). Doubling R now shortens tau, the opposite dependence from an RC circuit, because a larger resistance drains stored magnetic energy faster. The same exponential form applies to current: i(t) = Ifinal + (Iinitial - Ifinal)e^(-t/tau). This tau governs relay coil turn-off spikes and the ramp-up of current in a motor winding or an inductive ballast. Break a relay coil's current abruptly (an open switch presents a near-infinite R, so tau collapses toward zero) and V = -L(di/dt) spikes to hundreds of volts in an instant, which is why a flyback diode is needed to give that current a path to decay through instead of arcing across the switch contacts.

lessons.workedExample: A student steps a 5 V square wave into an unknown capacitor through a measured 10 kOhm resistor and captures the response on an oscilloscope. The trace crosses 3.16 V (63.2% of 5 V) at t = 2.2 ms after the step. Setting tau = RC: 2.2 ms = (10,000 ohm)(C), so C = 2.2 ms / 10,000 ohm = 220 nF — a value they can now cross-check against the capacitor's printed code. They confirm by checking that the trace is within 0.7% of 5 V (99.3%) at 5 tau = 11 ms, matching the scope readout.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'how did you find that capacitance?' to see whether a student understands the exponential or just eyeballed a curve. A strong answer names the 63.2% landmark, reads a specific time off the scope at that voltage, and shows the algebra tau = RC -> C = tau/R with units carried through. A weak answer says 'we watched until it looked flat' — that has no defined endpoint, since an exponential is never exactly flat, and it reveals the student doesn't know why 5 tau (99.3%) is the conventional stopping point rather than some arbitrary visual judgment.

questions.prompt: In an RC charging circuit, what fraction of the final voltage has the capacitor reached after exactly one time constant?

explanations.a: 50% is the half-life figure used for radioactive decay curves, not the RC time constant's landmark — it would correspond to about 0.69 tau, not 1 tau.
explanations.b: Correct — V(tau) = Vfinal(1 - e^-1) = Vfinal(0.632), so a rising exponential reaches 63.2% of its final value after one tau.
explanations.c: 36.8% (e^-1) is the remaining fraction on a decaying/discharging curve after one tau, not the fraction gained on a charging curve.
explanations.d: 99.3% is the settled fraction after five time constants, not one.

questions.prompt: For a series RL circuit, what happens to the time constant tau = L/R if R is doubled while L stays fixed?

options.text: tau doubles
tau is halved
tau is unchanged
tau becomes zero

explanations.a: Doubling R does not lengthen tau in an RL circuit; that dependence describes RC, where tau = RC scales up with R.
explanations.b: Correct — tau = L/R, so doubling R halves tau: a larger resistance drains the inductor's stored magnetic energy faster, the opposite of the RC case.
explanations.c: R appears directly in the RL time constant, so changing it does change tau.
explanations.d: tau only reaches zero if R becomes infinite; doubling a finite R just halves a finite tau.

questions.prompt: Order these charging-curve checkpoints from least time elapsed to most, as a capacitor charges toward its final voltage.

items.text: One time constant elapsed (63.2% reached)
Circuit switch is closed at t = 0
Three time constants elapsed (95.0% reached)
Five time constants elapsed (99.3% reached, 'settled')

questions.explanation: The transient begins when the switch closes (t = 0), then passes through one tau at 63.2%, three tau at 95.0%, and five tau at 99.3%, which is the conventional threshold for calling the transient complete.

questions.prompt: Match each time-constant formula to the circuit and physical quantity it governs.

right.text: Series resistor-capacitor circuit; capacitor voltage cannot jump instantaneously
Series resistor-inductor circuit; inductor current cannot jump instantaneously

questions.explanation: An RC circuit's time constant is RC because the resistor limits the charging current onto the capacitor, whose voltage is the state variable that cannot change instantaneously; an RL circuit's time constant is L/R because the inductor's back-EMF opposes changes in its current, the state variable that cannot jump.

lessons.label: Phasors, Impedance, and Reactance

sections.heading: Why AC needs a new kind of resistance
sections.body: A resistor's voltage and current stay in lockstep — V = IR at every instant, no matter the frequency. A capacitor and inductor do not: they store energy rather than dissipate it, so their opposition to current depends on how fast the voltage is changing. That opposition is reactance. Capacitive reactance is Xc = 1/(2*pi*f*C); it falls as frequency rises because a capacitor's displacement current grows with dV/dt. Inductive reactance is Xl = 2*pi*f*L; it rises with frequency because a faster-changing current induces a larger opposing back-EMF. Both are measured in ohms, but neither dissipates power the way R does.

sections.heading: Phasors: collapsing sine waves into rotating vectors
sections.body: Tracking sin(2*pi*f*t + phi) terms through a circuit by hand is unworkable, so engineers since Charles Proteus Steinmetz's 1893 phasor method represent each sinusoid as a complex number (a phasor) whose magnitude is the amplitude and whose angle is the phase, all rotating together at the circuit's single frequency. Impedance Z = R + jX packages resistance and reactance into one complex quantity, with capacitive reactance entering as -j/(2*pi*f*C) and inductive reactance as +j*2*pi*f*L. Ohm's law becomes V = IZ using phasor algebra, and |Z| = sqrt(R^2 + X^2) with phase angle theta = arctan(X/R) recovers the familiar magnitude and lag/lead between voltage and current.

sections.heading: The 90-degree rule and where the power goes
sections.body: In a pure capacitor, current leads voltage by 90 degrees ('ICE': in a capacitor, I leads E); in a pure inductor, current lags voltage by 90 degrees ('ELI': in an inductor, E leads I). Because power is the product of voltage and current, and a 90-degree-shifted sine and cosine average to zero over a cycle, an ideal reactance dissipates no net energy — it just trades energy back and forth with the source, quantified as reactive power in volt-amperes-reactive (VAR). Real power in watts is delivered only by the in-phase (resistive) component: P = VrmsIrmscos(theta), where cos(theta) is the power factor. Reactive power is quantified the same way with the shifted component: Q = VrmsIrmssin(theta), giving VAR the same rigor as watts. A load with a large reactive component draws more current than its real power alone would suggest, which is why utilities penalize industrial customers for a low power factor.

lessons.workedExample: A 100 Hz signal drives a 47 nF capacitor in series with a 2 kOhm resistor. Xc = 1/(2*pi*100*47e-9) = 33.9 kOhm, far larger than R, so Z = 2000 - j33,868 ohm, |Z| = 33,927 ohm, and theta = arctan(-33,868/2000) = -86.6 degrees. The current phasor leads the source voltage by 86.6 degrees, almost the full 90 degrees expected of a nearly pure capacitor, confirming that at 100 Hz this small capacitor's reactance swamps the resistor and the circuit behaves almost like an open capacitor with a whisper of resistive damping.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks a student to explain why their circuit's current 'leads' or 'lags' the voltage to test whether reactance is understood as an energy-storage phase shift, not just a formula to plug into. A strong answer connects the shift to the physical mechanism — a capacitor's current is largest when voltage is changing fastest (at the zero crossing), which is why it leads — and can compute Xc or Xl at the operating frequency from measured R, C, or L. A weak answer recites 'ICE' and 'ELI' without being able to say why the phase shift is exactly 90 degrees or what happens to the reactive power physically.

questions.prompt: As frequency increases, what happens to capacitive reactance Xc and inductive reactance Xl?

options.text: Both increase
Xc increases, Xl decreases
Xc decreases, Xl increases
Both stay constant, since reactance depends only on component value

explanations.a: Xc = 1/(2*pi*f*C) has frequency in the denominator, so it falls, not rises, as frequency increases.
explanations.b: This reverses both relationships: Xc actually falls with frequency and Xl actually rises with frequency.
explanations.c: Correct — Xc = 1/(2*pi*f*C) falls as f rises because a capacitor passes fast-changing signals more easily, while Xl = 2*pi*f*L rises as f rises because a faster-changing current induces a larger opposing back-EMF.
explanations.d: Reactance is explicitly frequency-dependent for both components; only resistance R is frequency-independent.

questions.prompt: In an ideal inductor driven by a sinusoidal source, how does the current phasor relate to the voltage phasor?

options.text: Current leads voltage by 90 degrees
Current lags voltage by 90 degrees
Current and voltage are in phase
Current lags voltage by 180 degrees

explanations.a: A 90-degree current lead describes a capacitor, not an inductor — that is the 'ICE' relationship.
explanations.b: Correct — the mnemonic 'ELI' captures it: in an inductor (L), voltage (E) leads current (I) by 90 degrees, equivalently current lags voltage by 90 degrees, because the inductor's back-EMF opposes the change in current.
explanations.c: In-phase voltage and current describes a pure resistor, where there is no energy storage to introduce a phase shift.
explanations.d: A 180-degree shift would mean the current is fully inverted relative to voltage, which does not occur in a passive L, R, or C element.

questions.prompt: Match each quantity to its correct description.

right.text: Complex quantity combining resistance and reactance, magnitude in ohms
Energy actually dissipated, delivered by the in-phase component, in watts
Energy traded back and forth with no net dissipation, in VAR
Fraction of apparent power that is real power, ranges from 0 to 1

questions.explanation: Impedance packages R and X into one complex ohm value; real power (watts) comes only from the in-phase voltage-current product; reactive power (VAR) is the non-dissipative energy exchange from the 90-degree-shifted component; power factor is cos(theta), the ratio describing how much of the apparent power is actually real power.

lessons.label: Passive Filters: First and Second Order

sections.heading: The RC divider as a frequency-selective circuit
sections.body: An RC low-pass filter is just a voltage divider where one leg's 'resistance' (the capacitor's reactance) changes with frequency. At low frequency Xc is huge, so almost all the input voltage appears across the capacitor (the output); at high frequency Xc collapses toward zero, shorting the output to ground. The cutoff frequency, where output power drops to half (voltage to 1/sqrt(2) = 0.707 of input, the -3 dB point), occurs where R and Xc are equal in magnitude: f_c = 1/(2*pi*R*C). Swap the resistor and capacitor's positions and the same math produces a high-pass filter with an identical cutoff formula but the opposite passband.

sections.heading: Roll-off: what happens past cutoff
sections.body: Past cutoff, a single-pole RC filter's response falls at a fixed rate of 20 dB per decade (a factor of 10 in frequency) — equivalently about 6 dB per octave (a factor of 2). This is a straight line on log-log axes because each additional decade compounds the same 1/10 reduction in reactance ratio. A single RC stage is a first-order filter with exactly one pole; cascading stages, or moving to a genuinely second-order LC topology, doubles the roll-off to 40 dB/decade, at the cost of a resonant peak or dip near cutoff rather than the flat, gentle knee of a first-order stage.

sections.heading: LC and RLC: band-pass and band-stop
sections.body: A series inductor and capacitor form a network whose combined reactance is zero at one specific resonant frequency and large everywhere else, letting a designer pick off (band-pass) or reject (band-stop, or 'notch') a narrow range of frequencies rather than just everything above or below a single cutoff. Placing an LC series branch in shunt to ground creates a band-stop notch (it shorts the target frequency to ground while passing others); placing it in the signal path creates a band-pass (it passes the target frequency and blocks others). Adding the resistor's damping (making it a true RLC network) sets how narrow that passband or notch is — a topic developed further under resonance and Q. The '-3 dB' label itself comes straight from the 0.707 voltage ratio: dB = 20*log10(Vout/Vin) = 20*log10(1/sqrt(2)) = -3.01 dB, rounded to -3 dB. Active op-amp filters, which add gain and sharper roll-offs without bulky inductors, are deliberately left to the analog-electronics branch; this lesson stays with what R, L, and C alone can do.

lessons.workedExample: A student needs a low-pass filter with a 1 kHz cutoff from a parts bin holding a 10 kOhm resistor and a box of standard capacitors. Solving f_c = 1/(2*pi*R*C) for C: C = 1/(2*pi*1000*10,000) = 15.9 nF. The nearest stock value is 15 nF, giving an actual cutoff of f_c = 1/(2*pi*10,000*15e-9) = 1061 Hz, a 6% shift they note in their write-up. On the bench, they confirm by sweeping a function generator and measuring the output amplitude drop to 0.707 of the input (roughly -3 dB) right around 1060 Hz, and they check the roll-off by measuring the output at 10 kHz, which should sit about 20 dB below the passband level.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'why did you pick those component values?' to check whether the cutoff formula was actually used, or values were just copied from a datasheet example. A strong answer works f_c = 1/(2*pi*R*C) in both directions — choosing C from a target f_c and a stock R, then recomputing the real cutoff from the actual stock value used — and can say what -3 dB means physically (output power halved, voltage at 0.707). A weak answer cannot explain why -3 dB rather than some other number marks 'cutoff,' or confuses the roll-off rate of a single RC stage with that of a second-order network.

questions.prompt: At the -3 dB cutoff frequency of an RC low-pass filter, what is true about the output voltage relative to the input?

options.text: It is 50% of the input voltage
It is 70.7% of the input voltage
It is equal to the input voltage
It is zero

explanations.a: 50% is the half-power point stated in terms of power, but 50% of input voltage is not the -3 dB voltage figure — that confuses power ratio with voltage ratio.
explanations.b: Correct — -3 dB corresponds to half the output power, and since power scales with voltage squared, the voltage ratio at that point is 1/sqrt(2) = 0.707, or 70.7% of the input.
explanations.c: Equal input and output voltage would be 0 dB, the passband condition, not the cutoff point.
explanations.d: Zero output would only occur at frequencies far past cutoff, not at the cutoff frequency itself.

questions.prompt: A single-pole RC filter has a roll-off of 20 dB per decade past cutoff. What roll-off would a genuine second-order (two-pole) filter have?

options.text: 10 dB per decade
20 dB per decade, the same, because roll-off does not depend on order
40 dB per decade
60 dB per decade

explanations.a: 10 dB per decade is slower than even a single pole provides; it does not correspond to any standard filter order.
explanations.b: Roll-off does scale with the number of poles; a second-order filter is steeper than a first-order one, not equal to it.
explanations.c: Correct — each pole contributes 20 dB/decade, so a second-order (two-pole) filter rolls off at 40 dB/decade, twice the rate of a single RC stage.
explanations.d: 60 dB/decade would require a third-order (three-pole) filter, not a second-order one.

questions.prompt: Order these steps for designing an RC low-pass filter to a target cutoff frequency and verifying it on the bench.

items.text: Pick a target cutoff frequency f_c for the application
Choose a stock resistor value and solve C = 1/(2*pi*f_c*R)
Select the nearest available stock capacitor and recompute the actual f_c it produces
Sweep a function generator and measure where the output drops to 0.707 of input to confirm the actual cutoff

questions.explanation: Design starts from the target cutoff, works backward through the formula to a component value, accounts for the nearest real stock part by recomputing the true cutoff, and finally verifies that real-world cutoff on the bench by measuring the -3 dB (0.707) point.

questions.prompt: Match each passive filter topology to what it does to a narrow target frequency band.

left.text: LC series branch placed in the signal path
LC series branch placed in shunt to ground

right.text: Passes frequencies below cutoff, attenuates above
Passes frequencies above cutoff, attenuates below
Passes a narrow band around resonance (band-pass)
Rejects a narrow band around resonance, shorting it to ground (band-stop/notch)

questions.explanation: An RC low-pass keeps low frequencies and cuts high; an RC high-pass does the reverse; an LC series branch in the signal path passes its resonant frequency (band-pass) because its impedance drops to near zero there; the same branch in shunt to ground instead shorts that resonant frequency to ground while passing others (band-stop).

lessons.label: Resonance and Q

sections.heading: The frequency where L and C cancel
sections.body: An inductor's reactance rises with frequency while a capacitor's falls; at exactly one frequency the two are equal in magnitude and, being opposite in sign, cancel completely. For a series LC branch this makes the total reactance zero, so impedance collapses to just the parasitic resistance and current peaks sharply. For a parallel LC tank the same cancellation makes impedance peak instead, since the two branches' currents cancel and almost none flows from the source. Either way, the resonant frequency is f0 = 1/(2*pi*sqrt(L*C)) — set only by the L and C values, independent of any resistance in the circuit.

sections.heading: Quality factor: how sharp is the peak
sections.body: Resonance by itself only says where the peak sits; the quality factor Q says how narrow and tall it is. Q compares energy stored per cycle to energy dissipated per cycle, and for a series RLC circuit Q = (1/R)*sqrt(L/C), or equivalently Q = f0/BW, where BW is the -3 dB bandwidth around f0. For a parallel RLC tank the formula flips to its dual, Q = R*sqrt(C/L): now a larger R means less current shunted away from the tank, so higher parallel resistance gives a higher, sharper Q — the opposite dependence from the series case, where a larger R dissipates more and lowers Q. A high-Q circuit — a crystal oscillator's resonator can reach Q in the tens of thousands — has very low resistive loss relative to its stored energy, giving a razor-narrow passband useful for tuning one radio station out of a crowded band. A low-Q circuit, dominated by resistance, gives a broad, gentle hump instead.

sections.heading: Q also predicts ringing in the time domain
sections.body: The same Q that sets frequency-domain sharpness also governs how a circuit responds to a step or impulse in time. A second-order RLC step response is classified by its damping ratio zeta = 1/(2Q): overdamped (zeta > 1, Q < 0.5) settles sluggishly with no overshoot; critically damped (zeta = 1, Q = 0.5) reaches final value fastest without any overshoot, the design target for instruments like an analog panel meter; underdamped (zeta < 1, Q > 0.5) overshoots and rings, oscillating at nearly f0 while decaying, with more ringing cycles visible the higher the Q. A student who sees a step response ring for many cycles before settling is looking at the time-domain signature of a high-Q resonance — the same physical property that makes a bell 'ring' rather than 'thud.'

lessons.workedExample: A student builds a series RLC circuit with L = 10 mH, C = 100 nF, and a measured series resistance of 15 ohm (including the inductor's winding resistance). Resonant frequency: f0 = 1/(2*pi*sqrt(0.01*100e-9)) = 1/(2*pi*sqrt(1e-9)) = 5033 Hz. Quality factor: Q = (1/15)*sqrt(0.01/100e-9) = (1/15)*sqrt(100,000) = (1/15)(316.2) = 21.1. Predicted bandwidth: BW = f0/Q = 5033/21.1 = 238 Hz. On the bench they sweep the generator, find the current peaks at 5.0 kHz, and measure the two -3 dB frequencies at about 4.88 kHz and 5.12 kHz — a 240 Hz spread, matching the prediction and confirming a moderately high-Q, underdamped circuit.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who sees a resonant circuit in a project usually asks 'what is your Q and how do you know?' to separate a student who found a peak by trial and error from one who can predict circuit behavior. A strong answer computes Q from component values (Q = (1/R)*sqrt(L/C)) beforehand, predicts the -3 dB bandwidth, and connects it to whatever ringing or sharpness was observed on the bench. A weak answer can locate the resonant peak experimentally but cannot say whether the circuit is under- or overdamped, or why a narrower peak (higher Q) also means more ringing cycles in a step response — treating the frequency- and time-domain views as unrelated facts rather than two faces of the same Q.

questions.prompt: What determines the resonant frequency f0 of a series LC circuit?

options.text: Only the resistance R
Only the inductance L and capacitance C, via f0 = 1/(2*pi*sqrt(L*C))
The applied voltage amplitude
The quality factor Q alone

explanations.a: Resistance does not set the resonant frequency; it only affects the sharpness (Q) of the response around that frequency.
explanations.b: Correct — resonance occurs where inductive and capacitive reactance cancel, which depends only on L and C: f0 = 1/(2*pi*sqrt(L*C)), independent of R.
explanations.c: The resonant frequency is a property of the circuit's L and C, not of the signal driving it; changing voltage amplitude does not shift where the peak occurs.
explanations.d: Q depends on R, L, and C together and describes sharpness, not the location of the peak, which is f0.

questions.prompt: A step response that overshoots and rings for several cycles before settling indicates which damping condition?

options.text: Overdamped (Q < 0.5)
Critically damped (Q = 0.5)
Underdamped (Q > 0.5)
No resonance is present

explanations.a: An overdamped response settles sluggishly toward its final value with no overshoot or ringing at all — the opposite of what is described.
explanations.b: A critically damped response reaches its final value as fast as possible without overshooting or ringing — it would show at most one smooth approach, not multiple cycles.
explanations.c: Correct — ringing that overshoots and oscillates near f0 while decaying is the signature of an underdamped (Q > 0.5) response; more visible ring cycles indicate a higher Q.
explanations.d: Ringing at a characteristic frequency is direct evidence of resonance in the circuit, not its absence.

questions.prompt: Match each Q-related quantity to what it describes.

right.text: Ratio of energy stored per cycle to energy dissipated per cycle
The -3 dB frequency spread around resonance
Classifies the step response as over-, critically, or underdamped

questions.explanation: Q itself is defined as the ratio of stored to dissipated energy per cycle; dividing f0 by Q gives the -3 dB bandwidth of the resonant peak; and the damping ratio zeta, derived from Q, classifies whether the time-domain step response overshoots and rings (underdamped), settles fastest with no overshoot (critically damped), or settles sluggishly (overdamped).

questions.prompt: Order these damping conditions from least ringing/overshoot to most, as Q increases from a low value.

items.text: Overdamped (Q < 0.5): sluggish, no overshoot
Critically damped (Q = 0.5): fastest settling, no overshoot
Underdamped, moderate Q: some overshoot, a few ring cycles
Underdamped, high Q: many visible ring cycles before settling

questions.explanation: As Q rises from below 0.5 through 0.5 and beyond, the step response moves from sluggish non-oscillatory settling, to the fastest possible non-oscillatory settling at critical damping, to increasingly pronounced ringing as Q climbs further into the underdamped regime.

lessons.label: Reading a Bode Plot

sections.heading: Two log axes and a straight-line shortcut
sections.body: Hendrik Bode developed this plotting method at Bell Labs in the 1930s to make frequency response tractable by hand. A Bode magnitude plot puts frequency on a logarithmic horizontal axis and gain in decibels (20*log10(Vout/Vin)) on the vertical axis. Plotting both this way turns a curved, hard-to-read response into straight-line segments: a flat passband at 0 dB, then a line falling at a fixed slope past cutoff. The real curve rounds off near the corner, but the straight-line 'asymptotic' approximation — flat, then a sloped line, meeting exactly at f_c — is accurate to within about 3 dB at the corner itself and gets tighter a decade away, which is why engineers sketch Bode plots by hand using only two rulers and a few landmark frequencies. That 3 dB gap is not a rule of thumb but a direct consequence of the real curve sitting at 1/sqrt(2) of the asymptote's value there: 20*log10(sqrt(2)) = 3.01 dB, rounded to 3 dB.

sections.heading: Reading order and slope by inspection
sections.body: A decade is a 10x frequency change; an octave is a 2x change (used more in audio). On the magnitude plot, the passband is wherever the line sits flat near 0 dB; the cutoff or corner frequency is where the flat line meets the sloped line, which is also where the real (rounded) curve crosses -3 dB; and the roll-off slope past that corner reveals the filter's order directly — 20 dB/decade per pole. A two-pole (second-order) filter's asymptote falls at 40 dB/decade, distinguishable from a single pole's 20 dB/decade by comparing the drop over any measured decade of frequency, no fitting required.

sections.heading: The paired phase plot
sections.body: Every magnitude plot has a companion phase plot, frequency on the same log axis against phase shift in degrees. Each pole contributes a phase shift that transitions smoothly from 0 to -90 degrees, centered exactly at that pole's corner frequency, where the phase has swung through -45 degrees; a zero contributes the mirror-image +90-degree swing. A two-pole low-pass filter's phase therefore approaches -180 degrees at high frequency, not -90, because the shifts from both poles add. Reading the phase plot alongside the magnitude plot lets a student confirm a filter's order independently of the slope measurement — count how many 90-degree phase swings appear, and that count matches the number of poles.

lessons.workedExample: A student measures an unknown black-box filter's output amplitude at several frequencies and plots gain in dB against log frequency. The trace is flat near 0 dB below 500 Hz, crosses -3 dB right at 500 Hz, and by 5 kHz (one decade up) has fallen to -20 dB, indicating a single-pole low-pass with f_c = 500 Hz and a 20 dB/decade roll-off. Assuming the internal topology is a simple RC stage and reading a 4.7 kOhm resistor value off the board, they solve f_c = 1/(2*pi*R*C) for C: C = 1/(2*pi*500*4700) = 67.7 nF, matching the nearest stock value of 68 nF printed on the extracted capacitor.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge hands a student an unlabeled Bode magnitude plot and asks what circuit produced it, to test whether they can read slope and corner frequency as physical information rather than just decoration. A strong answer identifies the corner from where the flat line meets the sloped line (or the -3 dB crossing), measures the roll-off in dB per decade to state the filter order, and can back-calculate a component value if one part of the circuit is known. A weak answer can say 'it's a low-pass filter' from the general downward shape but cannot extract a numeric cutoff or distinguish a 20 dB/decade single-pole roll-off from a 40 dB/decade two-pole roll-off on the same axes.

questions.prompt: On a Bode magnitude plot, a filter's response falls from 0 dB to -40 dB over exactly one decade of frequency past cutoff. What roll-off rate and filter order does this indicate?

options.text: 20 dB/decade, first order (one pole)
40 dB/decade, second order (two poles)
6 dB/decade, a fractional-order filter
40 dB/octave, second order

explanations.a: A first-order filter falls only 20 dB over one decade; a 40 dB drop over one decade is twice that rate.
explanations.b: Correct — a 40 dB drop over one decade of frequency is a 40 dB/decade roll-off, contributed by two poles (20 dB/decade each), so the filter is second order.
explanations.c: 6 dB/decade is far slower than what a 40 dB drop over a decade represents, and passive RLC filters have integer pole counts, not fractional order.
explanations.d: The measurement given (40 dB over one decade) is stated per decade, not per octave; converting to per-octave would give roughly 12 dB/octave, not 40.

questions.prompt: On the paired phase plot of a single-pole low-pass filter, what is the phase shift exactly at the pole's corner frequency?

options.text: 0 degrees
-45 degrees
-90 degrees
-180 degrees

explanations.a: 0 degrees is the phase shift far below the corner frequency, in the passband, not at the corner itself.
explanations.b: Correct — a single pole's phase transitions smoothly from 0 to -90 degrees, passing through exactly -45 degrees at its own corner frequency.
explanations.c: -90 degrees is the phase shift reached only well above the corner frequency (roughly a decade or more past it), not at the corner.
explanations.d: -180 degrees would require two poles' worth of phase shift; a single pole alone approaches only -90 degrees at high frequency.

questions.prompt: Order these steps for reading an unknown circuit's cutoff frequency and component value off a measured Bode magnitude plot.

items.text: Plot measured gain in dB against log frequency
Locate where the flat passband line meets the sloped line, or the -3 dB crossing
Measure the roll-off slope in dB per decade past that corner to confirm filter order
Use the known R (or C) and the identified cutoff frequency to solve for the unknown component

questions.explanation: Reading a Bode plot starts with the raw log-log gain data, then locates the corner frequency from the -3 dB point, then checks the roll-off slope to confirm how many poles are present, and only then plugs the identified cutoff into the known formula to solve for a missing component value.

lessons.label: Time Domain to Frequency Domain

sections.heading: A square wave is secretly a sum of sines
sections.body: Joseph Fourier's early-1800s claim that any periodic waveform can be built from sine waves at integer multiples of its fundamental frequency seemed radical enough that Lagrange reportedly objected to it at the time; it is now the basis of all spectrum analysis. A square wave of fundamental frequency f decomposes into only the odd harmonics — f, 3f, 5f, 7f — with amplitudes falling as 1/n: the third harmonic is 1/3 the fundamental's amplitude, the fifth is 1/5, and so on, all added with the right phase to build the flat tops and sharp edges. Summing just the fundamental and third harmonic already produces a rough square-ish shape; summing dozens of terms sharpens the corners toward the ideal, infinitely fast transition.

sections.heading: Why real circuits round the edges (and overshoot)
sections.body: No physical path has infinite bandwidth, so once a signal travels through any real filter, cable, or amplifier, the highest harmonics needed for those sharp corners get attenuated first — a low-pass characteristic is unavoidable in any real conductor. The result is visibly rounded edges and slower rise times on a scope, even when no filter was deliberately added. Truncating the Fourier series at a finite number of harmonics also produces the Gibbs phenomenon, described by Josiah Willard Gibbs in 1899: a fixed roughly 9% overshoot that appears right at the discontinuity no matter how many additional harmonics are included, only narrowing in width, never shrinking in height — a fingerprint of bandwidth-limiting that a student can recognize on any square-wave step edge.

sections.heading: Seeing the spectrum: the scope's FFT mode
sections.body: A modern oscilloscope's FFT mode converts a captured time-domain trace into this same frequency-domain picture instantly, but three settings shape what it shows. The window function (Hann, flat-top, rectangular) trades frequency resolution against amplitude accuracy — a mismatch between the capture length and the signal's period otherwise leaks energy into neighboring bins, called spectral leakage. The resolution bandwidth, set by the capture's record length and sample rate, determines how close two tones can sit before merging into one peak. And the noise floor sets the smallest signal the FFT can distinguish from random noise. Together these let a student spot a mains hum spike at 60 Hz (or 50 Hz) buried under a signal that looks clean in the time domain, or measure harmonic distortion by comparing a fundamental's peak height to its harmonics' peak heights directly.

lessons.workedExample: A student captures a 1 kHz square wave on a scope after it passes through an audio amplifier and switches to FFT mode. The spectrum shows sharp peaks at 1 kHz, 3 kHz, 5 kHz, and 7 kHz with amplitudes roughly following the predicted 1, 1/3, 1/5, 1/7 ratios, confirming the Fourier decomposition — but the 7 kHz peak is noticeably lower than 1/7 predicts, and a faint unexpected spike appears at 60 Hz that was invisible on the time-domain trace. They conclude the amplifier's limited bandwidth is attenuating the higher harmonics (explaining the rounded corners they see in the time domain) and that a 60 Hz mains hum is coupling into the circuit, something only the FFT view made visible.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who sees rounded edges or ringing on a supposedly 'square' wave asks the student to explain it in the frequency domain, not just say 'the scope was bad.' A strong answer names the missing high harmonics as the cause of rounding, can point to Gibbs overshoot if ringing appears at the edges, and knows that an FFT of the same trace would show those harmonics falling off faster than the ideal 1/n prediction. A weak answer treats the rounded corners as measurement noise or a probe problem, missing that it is a real, predictable consequence of any bandwidth-limited path acting on a harmonic-rich waveform.

questions.prompt: According to the Fourier series for an ideal square wave, which harmonics are present, and how does their amplitude scale?

options.text: All integer harmonics, amplitude falling as 1/n
Only odd harmonics, amplitude falling as 1/n
Only even harmonics, amplitude falling as 1/n^2
Only the fundamental, with no harmonics

explanations.a: A square wave's Fourier series excludes the even harmonics entirely; only odd multiples of the fundamental appear.
explanations.b: Correct — an ideal square wave is built from odd harmonics only (f, 3f, 5f, 7f...), with each harmonic's amplitude falling as 1/n relative to the fundamental.
explanations.c: Even harmonics are absent from a symmetric square wave's spectrum, and the odd harmonics present fall as 1/n, not 1/n^2.
explanations.d: A square wave requires infinitely many harmonics to build its sharp corners; the fundamental alone produces only a smooth sine wave, not a square shape.

questions.prompt: A truncated Fourier series reconstruction of a square wave shows a persistent overshoot right at each edge, about 9% of the step height, that does not shrink even as more harmonics are added. What is this phenomenon called?

options.text: Aliasing
The Gibbs phenomenon
Spectral leakage
Harmonic distortion

explanations.a: Aliasing is a sampling artifact where signals above the Nyquist frequency fold back into the measured spectrum, unrelated to Fourier series truncation.
explanations.b: Correct — this is the Gibbs phenomenon, described by Gibbs in 1899: truncating a Fourier series at a discontinuity always leaves a roughly 9% overshoot that narrows in width but never shrinks in height as more terms are added.
explanations.c: Spectral leakage is an FFT windowing artifact where energy smears into neighboring frequency bins, a different effect from the fixed-height edge overshoot described here.
explanations.d: Harmonic distortion refers to a circuit generating unwanted harmonics of its own, not the mathematical overshoot inherent to a truncated Fourier reconstruction.

questions.prompt: Match each scope FFT setting or concept to what it controls.

right.text: Trade-off between frequency resolution and amplitude accuracy; reduces spectral leakage
How close two tones can sit in frequency before merging into one peak
The smallest signal level distinguishable from random background

questions.explanation: The window function shapes the trade-off between frequency resolution and amplitude accuracy and controls spectral leakage; resolution bandwidth, set by record length and sample rate, determines how close two tones can be before their peaks merge; the noise floor sets the smallest signal the FFT display can distinguish from random noise.

questions.prompt: Order these Fourier-series partial sums for a square wave from fewest harmonics included to most, as the reconstruction becomes progressively sharper-cornered.

items.text: Fundamental only (f)
Fundamental plus third harmonic (f, 3f)
Fundamental through seventh harmonic (f, 3f, 5f, 7f)
Fundamental through many dozens of harmonics

questions.explanation: Starting from just the fundamental (a plain sine wave), each added odd harmonic sharpens the corners of the reconstruction further toward the ideal square wave, with the fixed-height Gibbs overshoot persisting even as the number of included harmonics grows into the dozens.

units.label: Landmark Work and Open Debates

lessons.label: The Transistor: Bell Labs, December 1947

sections.heading: A circuit that shouldn't have worked, and did
sections.body: On 16 December 1947, John Bardeen and Walter Brattain at Bell Labs pressed two gold contacts, separated by a sliver of plastic, onto a slab of germanium and watched a weak input signal come out amplified. On 23 December they demonstrated it to Bell Labs management: the point-contact transistor, the first solid-state amplifier. It replaced a function vacuum tubes had owned for four decades, using a fraction of the power and none of the filament heat or fragility. Bardeen and Brattain worked inside a solid-state physics group led by William Shockley, who had assigned them to find a semiconductor alternative to the tube after his own field-effect ideas failed to produce a working device. Shockley's field-effect amplifier tried to modulate current by applying an external electric field across a slab of semiconductor, but the field never reached the bulk material: unanticipated electronic states trapped right at the semiconductor's surface, later named surface states, absorbed and screened out the applied field before it could penetrate deep enough to control the current flowing underneath. Bardeen worked out this screening mechanism, and that diagnosis is what pushed the group away from Shockley's field-geometry and toward a point-contact design, where two metal contacts pressed directly onto the germanium could sidestep the surface-state barrier rather than try to punch through it.

sections.heading: Shockley's junction transistor and the patent snub
sections.body: Shockley was reportedly furious that the breakthrough came from his subordinates' point-contact design rather than his own field-effect approach, and over the 1947 Christmas holiday he worked out a more robust, theoretically cleaner alternative: the bipolar junction transistor (BJT), with current flowing through the bulk of a semiconductor sandwich rather than a fragile surface contact. Bell Labs' patent attorneys left Shockley off the original point-contact patent application, partly because his field-effect concept overlapped with a 1926 patent Julius Lilienfeld had already filed, and partly because he had not built the working device himself. Shockley's junction transistor, published theoretically in 1949, was not physically realized in workable form until 1951, and it became the design that dominated manufacturing.

sections.heading: The 1956 Nobel and the walkout that seeded Silicon Valley
sections.body: In 1956, Bardeen, Brattain, and Shockley shared the Nobel Prize in Physics for the transistor effect, but the personal rift never healed. Shockley left Bell Labs in 1955 to found Shockley Semiconductor Laboratory near his mother's home in Mountain View, California, hoping to commercialize silicon transistors himself. His management was abrasive and secretive enough that in 1957 eight of his key researchers, including Robert Noyce and Gordon Moore, resigned together. Shockley branded them the 'traitorous eight.' They founded Fairchild Semiconductor with financing from Fairchild Camera and Instrument, and Fairchild's alumni went on to found Intel, AMD, and dozens of other firms, seeding the industry cluster that became Silicon Valley.

lessons.workedExample: A student explaining 'why does everyone call it the Bell Labs transistor and not the Shockley transistor?' should trace two separate inventions under one roof: Bardeen and Brattain's point-contact device, physically demonstrated 23 December 1947, versus Shockley's bipolar junction design, only a paper concept at that point and not built until 1951. The patent record backs this up — the original filing lists Bardeen and Brattain, not Shockley — even though all three later shared the Nobel. A judge asking 'who invented the transistor' is really testing whether the student can separate demonstration date, patent authorship, and Nobel credit, which do not all point to the same person.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe this history because 'the transistor was invented in 1947' is the kind of fact students memorize without knowing it hides a three-way credit dispute with real consequences: Shockley's exclusion from the original patent, his resentment, and the 1957 walkout that founded Fairchild. A strong answer names Bardeen and Brattain's point-contact device as the physically demonstrated first, distinguishes it from Shockley's later BJT, and connects the personal rift to the founding of Fairchild Semiconductor. A weak answer says only 'Shockley invented the transistor at Bell Labs,' collapsing three people and two device types into one name and missing the causal chain to Silicon Valley itself.

questions.prompt: Which device did Bardeen and Brattain physically demonstrate to Bell Labs management on 23 December 1947?

options.text: The bipolar junction transistor
The point-contact transistor
The field-effect transistor
The integrated circuit

explanations.a: The bipolar junction transistor was Shockley's design, worked out theoretically over the following weeks and not physically realized until 1951.
explanations.b: Correct — the point-contact transistor, using two gold contacts pressed onto germanium, was what Bardeen and Brattain built and demonstrated in December 1947.
explanations.c: A field-effect device was Shockley's original target, but his attempts failed to produce a working amplifier before Bardeen and Brattain's design succeeded.
explanations.d: The integrated circuit came over a decade later, from Jack Kilby and Robert Noyce in 1958-1959.

questions.prompt: Why was Shockley's name left off the original point-contact transistor patent application?

options.text: He had resigned from Bell Labs before the patent was filed
He had not built the working device, and his field-effect concept overlapped with Lilienfeld's earlier patent
He asked to be excluded to avoid controversy
Patent law at the time barred group supervisors from being named

explanations.a: Shockley did not leave Bell Labs until 1955, years after the 1947 patent filing.
explanations.b: Correct — Bell's attorneys excluded him because he had not physically built the point-contact device and because his field-effect idea risked being invalidated by Lilienfeld's earlier patent claims.
explanations.c: There is no record of Shockley requesting exclusion; by most accounts he was angered by it.
explanations.d: No such general rule existed; supervisors are commonly listed as inventors when they contribute to the claimed invention.

questions.prompt: Order these events chronologically.

items.text: Bardeen and Brattain demonstrate the point-contact transistor
Bardeen, Brattain, and Shockley share the Nobel Prize in Physics
Shockley founds Shockley Semiconductor Laboratory
The 'traitorous eight' resign to found Fairchild Semiconductor

questions.explanation: The transistor was demonstrated in December 1947; the Nobel Prize came in 1956; Shockley founded his own company in 1955 before the Nobel was announced, but the walkout that founded Fairchild happened in 1957, after both the Nobel and the founding of Shockley Semiconductor.

questions.prompt: Match each person to their specific contribution.

right.text: Built and demonstrated the point-contact transistor
Conceived the bipolar junction transistor after the 1947 demonstration
Left Shockley Semiconductor in 1957 to found Fairchild
Held an earlier field-effect patent that complicated Shockley's patent claim

questions.explanation: Bardeen and Brattain built the physical point-contact device; Shockley worked out the junction transistor theory afterward; the traitorous eight left Shockley's company to found Fairchild in 1957; Lilienfeld's 1920s field-effect patent was the prior art that kept Shockley off the original transistor patent.

lessons.label: Before Silicon: Tubes, Lilienfeld, and the Move to Si

sections.heading: The vacuum-tube ceiling
sections.body: Before the transistor, every amplifying or switching circuit ran through a vacuum tube: a glass envelope with a heated filament boiling off electrons that a grid voltage could throttle. Tubes worked, but they consumed real power just to keep the filament glowing, generated heat that damaged nearby components, and burned out on a schedule measured in months. ENIAC, the 1945 general-purpose electronic computer built at the University of Pennsylvania, ran roughly 17,000 vacuum tubes and needed a dedicated tube-replacement crew, because on average a tube failed every couple of days, each failure capable of halting the whole machine. Reliability, not raw function, was the wall the field needed to break through.

sections.heading: Lilienfeld's patents, decades ahead of a working device
sections.body: The field-effect idea that would eventually displace the tube was not new in 1947. Julius Lilienfeld, an Austrian-Hungarian physicist working in the United States, filed a Canadian patent in October 1925 and a US patent in October 1926 (granted 1930) describing a method of controlling current through a semiconductor using an external electric field, essentially a conceptual field-effect transistor. He filed further related patents around 1928. No working device or publication accompanied these filings, and the materials science of the era could not produce sufficiently pure semiconductor crystals, so Lilienfeld's ideas sat dormant. Decades later, when Bell Labs sought its own field-effect patents, Lilienfeld's prior art was cited against them, which is part of why Shockley's name was kept off the 1947 point-contact patent.

sections.heading: Wartime silicon and the move away from germanium
sections.body: A second thread ran through Bell Labs' own wartime radar work. Silicon point-contact rectifiers, simple crystal detectors used to demodulate radar signals, were manufactured in bulk during World War II, and Russell Ohl's 1940 discovery of the silicon p-n junction (found accidentally in a cracked, impure silicon sample) planted the germ of solid-state rectification years before the transistor existed. The 1947 transistor itself used germanium, which was easier to purify and had higher electron mobility, but germanium's narrow band gap made it leak current badly above about 75 degrees Celsius, an unacceptable limit for real equipment. Gordon Teal, who had pushed for silicon research at Bell Labs, moved to Texas Instruments and in May 1954 announced the first commercially produced silicon transistor. Silicon's wider band gap tolerated far higher temperatures, and, critically, silicon forms a stable native oxide (silicon dioxide) that germanium does not, which became the foundation of the planar and MOS processes that would soon dominate.

lessons.workedExample: A student comparing 'why silicon and not germanium?' should cite three concrete facts, not a vague appeal to silicon being 'better': germanium transistors degrade badly above roughly 75 degrees C due to their narrow band gap, silicon tolerates much higher temperatures, and silicon's native oxide layer enabled the planar manufacturing process that germanium's oxide chemistry could not support. A fair-quality answer might add Gordon Teal's May 1954 Texas Instruments silicon transistor as the concrete turning point, showing the switch was not instantaneous in 1947 but took roughly seven more years of engineering.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask about the pre-transistor and pre-silicon history because it tests whether a student understands invention as a process with false starts, not a single eureka moment. The trap is treating 1947 as the whole story: a strong answer explains why Lilienfeld's 1925-1928 patents did not produce a real device (no purified-crystal manufacturing yet), quantifies the vacuum tube's reliability problem with a real number like ENIAC's roughly 17,000 tubes, and can state the specific material reason silicon replaced germanium rather than just saying 'it was better.' A weak answer treats the transistor as materializing from nothing in 1947 and cannot say why silicon eventually won.

questions.prompt: Approximately how many vacuum tubes did ENIAC (1945) use, and what was the practical consequence?

options.text: About 1,700 tubes; the machine rarely failed
About 17,000 tubes; tubes failed often enough to need a dedicated replacement crew
About 170,000 tubes; the machine was too large to fit in one building
About 170 tubes; reliability was not a concern

explanations.a: 1,700 undercounts ENIAC's tube total by roughly a factor of ten.
explanations.b: Correct — ENIAC used roughly 17,000 vacuum tubes, and tube failures were frequent enough to require dedicated maintenance, illustrating the reliability wall tubes hit.
explanations.c: 170,000 overstates the real figure by roughly a factor of ten.
explanations.d: Reliability was a major practical constraint on tube-based computers, not a non-issue.

questions.prompt: Why did Lilienfeld's 1925-1928 field-effect patents not lead to a working transistor at the time?

options.text: He never filed for patent protection
The materials science to produce sufficiently pure semiconductor crystals did not yet exist
Bell Labs blocked him from publishing
His patents were rejected as invalid at the time

explanations.a: Lilienfeld did file patents, in Canada in 1925 and the US in 1926, plus further ones around 1928.
explanations.b: Correct — the conceptual field-effect idea existed on paper, but the crystal-purification techniques needed to build a working device would not exist for another two decades.
explanations.c: Bell Labs had no involvement with Lilienfeld's independent, decades-earlier patent filings.
explanations.d: The patents were granted (the main one in 1930); the problem was building a working device, not patent validity at the time of filing.

questions.prompt: What specific material property of silicon, compared to germanium, made it the eventual winner for transistors?

options.text: Silicon is a better electrical insulator overall
Silicon tolerates much higher temperatures and forms a stable native oxide useful for manufacturing
Silicon is a heavier element, making devices more durable
Silicon has higher electron mobility than germanium

explanations.a: Both are semiconductors, not insulators; that framing misidentifies the relevant property.
explanations.b: Correct — silicon's wider band gap resists the high-temperature current leakage that limits germanium to roughly 75 degrees C, and its native oxide layer enabled the planar process.
explanations.c: Physical weight is irrelevant to transistor performance.
explanations.d: Germanium actually has higher electron mobility than silicon; silicon won for thermal stability and oxide chemistry, not mobility.

questions.prompt: Order these events chronologically.

items.text: Lilienfeld files his Canadian field-effect patent
Ohl discovers the silicon p-n junction
ENIAC is completed with roughly 17,000 vacuum tubes
Texas Instruments announces the first commercial silicon transistor

questions.explanation: Lilienfeld's Canadian patent was filed in 1925, Ohl's p-n junction discovery came in 1940, ENIAC was completed in 1945, and Texas Instruments announced its silicon transistor in May 1954.

lessons.label: The Integrated Circuit and the Kilby-Noyce Dispute

sections.heading: Kilby's hybrid proof of concept
sections.body: By the late 1950s, engineers faced the 'tyranny of numbers': building complex circuits meant hand-wiring hundreds of discrete transistors, resistors, and capacitors, and every extra connection was a new point of failure. Jack Kilby, new to Texas Instruments and without seniority to take summer vacation, spent the summer of 1958 working alone on the problem. On 12 September 1958 he demonstrated a phase-shift oscillator built from every component carved out of a single sliver of germanium, with fine gold wires bonded by hand to connect them. It was a real integrated circuit, but a hybrid one: the components were monolithic, while the interconnects were still individually wired, which made it impractical to manufacture at scale.

sections.heading: Noyce's monolithic silicon answer
sections.body: At Fairchild Semiconductor, Robert Noyce reached a related but more manufacturable answer a few months later. Noyce's design, patent filed in 1959, built on Jean Hoerni's planar process, developed at Fairchild that same year, which used a flat layer of silicon dioxide grown directly on the silicon surface to protect and isolate the junctions. Because that oxide layer was already there, Noyce could deposit a pattern of metal film directly on top of it to wire the components together, eliminating Kilby's hand-bonded wires entirely. This monolithic approach, all components and all interconnects on one silicon chip made with repeatable photolithographic steps, was what let integrated circuits scale into mass production.

sections.heading: A decade of litigation, a shared legacy
sections.body: Both Texas Instruments and Fairchild filed competing patent claims, and the US Patent Office declared a formal interference proceeding to decide who had priority. Kilby's patent application was filed first, in February 1959, months ahead of Noyce's July 1959 filing, and initial rulings favored Kilby. Texas Instruments and Fairchild fought this through the courts for roughly a decade before settling in 1966 with a cross-licensing agreement, letting both companies build on each other's patents rather than have one side win outright. History has generally credited Kilby with the first working integrated circuit and Noyce with the first commercially practical one, a distinction reflected in the fact that Kilby won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2000, specifically 'for his part in the invention of the integrated circuit,' while Noyce, who had died in 1990, was ineligible since the Nobel is never awarded posthumously.

lessons.workedExample: A student asked 'who invented the integrated circuit' should resist a single-name answer. Kilby's 12 September 1958 germanium device proved the concept first and filed for patent first (February 1959), but its hand-wired gold interconnects made it a lab curiosity, not a product. Noyce's July 1959 monolithic silicon design, built on Hoerni's planar process, replaced those wires with a photolithographically deposited metal layer, which is the specific innovation that let ICs be mass-manufactured instead of hand-assembled one at a time. The honest answer: Kilby proved it could be done, Noyce showed how to make it manufacturable, and the decade of litigation between their employers ended in cross-licensing rather than a clean winner.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe this dispute because 'Kilby and Noyce invented the IC' is often recited without any grasp of what each man actually contributed, or that the case went to formal patent litigation rather than settling immediately. A strong answer names the specific technical difference, hand-bonded wires on germanium versus a photolithographic metal layer on planar silicon, and can explain why that difference mattered for manufacturing at scale, not just as a trivia date. A weak answer either credits only one man or cannot say what separates a hybrid from a monolithic integrated circuit, which is the whole substance of the dispute.

questions.prompt: What made Kilby's September 1958 device a 'hybrid' rather than a fully monolithic integrated circuit?

options.text: It used silicon instead of germanium
Its components were built into one piece of germanium, but its interconnects were individually hand-wired
It had no working components at all, only a design sketch
It used the planar process, which Kilby had invented

explanations.a: Kilby's device used germanium, not silicon; the germanium-versus-silicon choice is unrelated to the hybrid-versus-monolithic distinction.
explanations.b: Correct — Kilby's components were fabricated on one piece of germanium, but the wiring between them still required individually bonded gold wires, unlike Noyce's later fully monolithic approach.
explanations.c: Kilby's device was a working, demonstrated phase-shift oscillator, not merely a sketch.
explanations.d: The planar process was developed by Jean Hoerni at Fairchild in 1959, after Kilby's demonstration, and was used in Noyce's design, not Kilby's.

questions.prompt: What specific innovation let Noyce's design eliminate Kilby's hand-bonded wires?

options.text: Using germanium instead of silicon
A metal interconnect layer deposited directly on the planar process's silicon-dioxide surface
Replacing wires with a second layer of transistors
Using a larger chip so wires could be spaced farther apart

explanations.a: Noyce's approach used silicon, and the material switch itself did not eliminate the wiring problem; the planar oxide layer did.
explanations.b: Correct — because Hoerni's planar process left a protective oxide layer on the silicon surface, Noyce could deposit a patterned metal film on top of it to connect components, replacing hand-bonded wires.
explanations.c: Stacking a second transistor layer was not the mechanism; the fix was the metal interconnect layer on the oxide.
explanations.d: Wider spacing does not eliminate the need for individually bonded wires; the innovation was the deposited metal layer itself.

questions.prompt: Why did Jack Kilby, not Robert Noyce, receive the Nobel Prize for the integrated circuit in 2000?

options.text: Noyce's contribution was later found to be plagiarized
Noyce had died in 1990, and the Nobel Prize is never awarded posthumously
Only Kilby's patent survived the litigation
Noyce declined the nomination

explanations.a: There is no finding of plagiarism; Noyce's monolithic design was an independent, genuine innovation.
explanations.b: Correct — Robert Noyce died in 1990, and Nobel Prizes are not awarded posthumously, leaving Kilby as the eligible recipient in 2000.
explanations.c: The litigation ended in a 1966 cross-licensing settlement, not a sole surviving patent.
explanations.d: There is no record of a declined nomination; the reason was Noyce's death, not a personal choice.

questions.prompt: Order these events chronologically.

items.text: Kilby demonstrates his hybrid integrated circuit at Texas Instruments
Kilby files his integrated-circuit patent application
Noyce files his monolithic integrated-circuit patent application
Texas Instruments and Fairchild settle with a cross-licensing agreement

questions.explanation: Kilby demonstrated his device in September 1958, filed his patent in February 1959, Noyce filed his competing patent in July 1959, and the two companies settled the resulting litigation with cross-licensing in 1966.

lessons.label: Moore's Law: Observation, Roadmap, or Self-Fulfilling Prophecy

sections.heading: A magazine prediction, not a law of physics
sections.body: In April 1965, Gordon Moore, then research director at Fairchild Semiconductor, wrote an article for Electronics magazine titled 'Cramming More Components onto Integrated Circuits.' Asked to predict the next decade, Moore observed that the number of components economically fabricated on a single chip had been doubling roughly every year since 1959, and projected that trend would continue for at least ten more years. It was an extrapolation from a handful of data points, not a physical law, and Moore himself revised it in 1975: watching the doubling rate slow as chips grew more complex, he updated his forecast to a doubling roughly every two years, the version that stuck in popular use, though it is commonly and incorrectly quoted as 'eighteen months.'

sections.heading: Dennard scaling supplied the power story
sections.body: Moore's projection explained how many transistors could fit on a chip, but not why smaller transistors could also run faster without melting. That came from Robert Dennard and colleagues at IBM, whose 1974 paper on ion-implanted MOSFETs described scaling rules: shrink every linear dimension of a transistor by a factor, drop the operating voltage by the same factor, and power density stays roughly constant even as the chip does more work per unit area. Dennard scaling is what let each new process generation deliver both more transistors and higher clock speeds at manageable power, and for three decades the two trends together made 'Moore's law' feel like an inevitable performance curve rather than just a transistor count.

sections.heading: The 2005 break, and what 'Moore's law' means today
sections.body: Dennard's model ignored subthreshold leakage current, negligible in 1970s transistors but exponentially larger as gate oxides thinned. By around 2005 to 2007, leakage had grown large enough that shrinking a transistor no longer let engineers drop the voltage proportionally, and clock speeds stalled near 3 to 4 gigahertz even as transistor counts kept climbing. The industry's answer was multicore processors, spreading work across several slower, cooler cores instead of pushing one core faster. Today the debate is live and unresolved: skeptics point out that process 'node names' like 3 nanometers no longer describe any single physical transistor dimension, that transistor cost per function has stopped falling as fast as it once did, and that leading fabs now need years, not one, to double density. Optimists counter that 3D stacking, chiplets, and new transistor geometries keep effective computing power climbing by other means, so whether Moore's law is dead, merely slowing, or continuing in a different form remains a genuinely open question among engineers, not a settled fact.

lessons.workedExample: A student claiming 'Moore's law says computers get twice as fast every 18 months' should be corrected on two counts using this lesson's own numbers: Moore's actual 1965 doubling period was one year, revised by Moore himself in 1975 to two years, and the law describes transistor count, not speed, which is a separate story supplied by Dennard scaling until that broke down around 2005-2007. A stronger framing: from 1965 to about 2005, transistor doubling (Moore) and power-constant scaling (Dennard) reinforced each other, but after Dennard scaling failed the industry shifted to multicore chips, so raw clock speed has been roughly flat for two decades even while transistor counts kept rising.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe Moore's law because the popular version has drifted so far from the 1965 text that most students cannot state what Moore actually predicted, when he revised it, or why the trend eventually broke. A strong answer distinguishes the 1965 one-year doubling from the 1975 two-year revision, names Dennard scaling as the separate mechanism that made transistor count translate into speed, and can explain the leakage-current reason it broke down around 2005 rather than treating that break as unexplained. A weak answer recites '18 months' as an eternal physical law and cannot say what actually stopped scaling or how the industry adapted.

questions.prompt: In his original 1965 Electronics article, what doubling period did Gordon Moore project, and what did he revise it to in 1975?

options.text: 18 months in 1965, revised to 12 months in 1975
1 year in 1965, revised to 2 years in 1975
2 years in 1965, revised to 18 months in 1975
5 years in 1965, never revised

explanations.a: Moore's original figure was one year, not 18 months, and his revision lengthened the period rather than shortening it.
explanations.b: Correct — Moore's 1965 article projected doubling roughly every year, and his 1975 revision, as the rate slowed, lengthened that to roughly every two years.
explanations.c: This reverses the actual direction; Moore's revision lengthened the doubling period, and '18 months' was never his own published figure.
explanations.d: Moore's original period was one year, and he did revise it in 1975.

questions.prompt: What did Robert Dennard's 1974 scaling rules add on top of Moore's transistor-count observation?

options.text: A method for hand-wiring integrated circuits
A rule showing power density stays roughly constant as transistors shrink and voltage drops proportionally
The invention of the silicon planar process
A prediction of exactly when Moore's law would end

explanations.a: Hand-wiring interconnects was Kilby's 1958 hybrid IC approach, unrelated to Dennard's later scaling theory.
explanations.b: Correct — Dennard's 1974 paper showed that scaling down transistor dimensions while proportionally dropping voltage kept power density roughly constant, which is what let smaller transistors also run faster without overheating.
explanations.c: The planar process was Jean Hoerni's 1959 contribution at Fairchild, a different innovation from Dennard's scaling rules.
explanations.d: Dennard's paper described a scaling relationship; it did not forecast a specific end date, which only became apparent decades later as leakage current grew.

questions.prompt: What specifically caused Dennard scaling to break down around 2005-2007?

options.text: A shortage of silicon wafers
Subthreshold leakage current grew large enough that voltage could no longer be dropped proportionally with size
Patent litigation between chip makers halted further shrinking
Multicore processors made single-transistor scaling unnecessary

explanations.a: Wafer supply was not the limiting factor; the issue was a physical effect inside the transistors themselves.
explanations.b: Correct — Dennard's original model ignored subthreshold leakage, which was negligible in the 1970s but grew exponentially as transistors shrank, eventually preventing further proportional voltage reduction.
explanations.c: Litigation is not documented as a cause of the Dennard scaling breakdown; the cause was a physical effect, leakage current.
explanations.d: Multicore processors were the industry's response to the breakdown, not its cause.

questions.prompt: Order these developments chronologically.

items.text: Moore publishes his original doubling prediction in Electronics
Dennard and colleagues publish their MOSFET scaling rules
Moore revises his doubling period to roughly two years
Dennard scaling breaks down and the industry shifts to multicore designs

questions.explanation: Moore's original article was published in 1965, Dennard's scaling paper came in 1974, Moore revised his projection in 1975, and Dennard scaling broke down around 2005-2007, prompting the shift to multicore processors.

lessons.label: The Current War and the Standards We Inherited

sections.heading: Edison's DC network and its distance limit
sections.body: Thomas Edison's Pearl Street Station, opened in 1882, distributed direct current at about 110 volts to nearby customers in Manhattan. DC at that voltage could not travel far: resistive losses in the copper wire meant a generating station had to sit within roughly a mile or two of every customer, so cities needed a power plant every few blocks. Edison, heavily invested in DC equipment patents, resisted alternating current and ran a public campaign through the late 1880s emphasizing AC's higher voltages as a safety hazard, including staged demonstrations electrocuting animals to argue AC was too dangerous for public use.

sections.heading: Westinghouse, Tesla, and the transformer's economics
sections.body: George Westinghouse licensed Nikola Tesla's AC induction motor and polyphase system patents in 1888, betting that AC's real advantage, the transformer, would win commercially. A transformer can step voltage up for transmission (cutting resistive losses over long lines) and step it back down for safe local use, something DC systems of that era had no equivalent way to do. This let a single AC plant serve a whole region instead of a plant every few blocks. Westinghouse underbid Edison's General Electric for the contract to light the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago, a high-visibility public demonstration of AC's reliability, and in 1893 also won the contract to harness Niagara Falls.

sections.heading: Niagara Falls, frozen standards, and DC's modern return
sections.body: The Adams Power Plant at Niagara Falls, financed partly by J.P. Morgan and using Westinghouse and Tesla's polyphase AC system, began operating on 26 August 1895 as the first large-scale AC generating plant in the world, and by 1896 was transmitting power to Buffalo, roughly 20 miles away, a distance no contemporary DC system could match. AC's practical victory settled the technical debate but left a historical accident baked into today's grid: American engineers standardized on 60 hertz and roughly 120 volts, while European engineers, developing their own equipment independently, settled on 50 hertz and roughly 230 volts, a split with no deep physical necessity behind it, just incompatible early choices that became too expensive to unify once millions of devices depended on them. Modern high-voltage DC (HVDC) transmission lines, used for very long undersea or cross-country links, partially vindicate Edison's original instinct: at extreme distances DC avoids AC's inductive and capacitive losses, though only because modern solid-state power electronics can now do the voltage conversion that 1880s DC technology could not.

lessons.workedExample: A student asked 'didn't Edison just lose the current war?' should complicate that with the HVDC point: Edison's argument that DC has no waste, no inductive losses over a line, was correct in principle, but 1880s DC had no analog of the transformer to change voltage cheaply, so it lost on the economics of that era. Modern HVDC links, such as those connecting offshore wind farms to the mainland grid, use solid-state converters to step DC voltage up and down, something unavailable to Edison, and they now beat AC for very long-distance or undersea transmission specifically because they avoid AC's reactive power losses over great distances. The 'winner' of the 1880s-90s was AC for distribution; the story is more nuanced for today's longest transmission links.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe the current war because the popular story, 'Edison was wrong, Westinghouse and Tesla were right,' erases both the specific mechanism (the transformer) that decided the 1880s-90s contest and the modern HVDC nuance that Edison's instinct was not simply mistaken. A strong answer names the transformer as the concrete technical reason AC won distribution, cites a real event like the 1895 Niagara Adams plant or the 1893 Chicago exposition contract rather than a vague 'AC was better,' and can explain why 60 Hz versus 50 Hz persists as pure historical accident rather than physics. A weak answer treats the outcome as inevitable and cannot explain why DC is now used at all in modern grids.

questions.prompt: What specific piece of equipment gave AC its decisive economic advantage over Edison's DC system?

options.text: The vacuum tube
The transformer, which could step voltage up for transmission and down for local use
The induction motor alone, regardless of voltage
The storage battery

explanations.a: The vacuum tube postdates the current war by decades and played no role in it.
explanations.b: Correct — the transformer let AC be transmitted at high voltage (low resistive loss) and then stepped down for safe local delivery, something 1880s DC equipment could not do.
