explanations.a: hFE sets which I_B curve the Q-point lands on, not the load line's own endpoints.
explanations.b: Correct — setting I_C = 0 gives V_CE = V_CC, and setting V_CE = 0 gives I_C = V_CC/R_C, the two endpoints of the straight line imposed by KVL on the collector loop.
explanations.c: The I_B curves are a separate family; the load line comes from the external resistor and supply, independent of any one I_B curve.
explanations.d: Coupling capacitors affect the AC load line, not the DC one.

questions.prompt: In the worked example, why does the AC load line reach zero current at a lower V_CE (11.25 V) than the DC load line (15 V)?

options.text: Because the coupling capacitor blocks all AC current
Because the AC load resistance (750 Ω, the parallel combination) is smaller than R_C alone, giving the AC line a steeper slope through the same Q-point
Because V_CC dropped when the load was connected
Because the Q-point moved to a different I_B curve

explanations.a: A coupling capacitor passes AC while blocking DC; it does not block the signal current itself.
explanations.b: Correct — R_C || R_load = 750 Ω is smaller than the 1.5 kΩ DC path, so the AC line is steeper and reaches zero current sooner, at a lower voltage, for the same Q-point.
explanations.c: V_CC is unaffected by adding an AC-coupled load; only the AC resistance the signal sees changes.
explanations.d: Both lines pass through the same DC Q-point; only their slope away from that point differs.

questions.prompt: Match each load-line feature to what it tells you.

left.text: Load line crossing a specific I_B curve
Distance from Q-point to the V_CE-axis intercept
I_C times V_CE at a point on the line

right.text: Locates the actual DC operating point (Q-point)
Available upward (toward cutoff) voltage swing before clipping
Instantaneous power dissipation at that point
Inverse of the effective resistance (DC or AC) the transistor sees

questions.explanation: The Q-point is where the load line meets the chosen I_B curve; distance to the cutoff-side intercept sets available upward swing; I_C*V_CE at any point is instantaneous power; and the line's slope is set by -1/R, so steeper lines correspond to smaller effective resistances.

questions.prompt: Order these steps for finding maximum undistorted swing using a load line.

items.text: Plot the DC load line from (V_CC, 0) to (0, V_CC/R_C)
Mark the Q-point at its intersection with the bias-set I_B curve
Measure the shorter of the two distances from Q to each axis intercept
Double that shorter distance to state the maximum symmetric peak-to-peak swing

questions.explanation: The load line must exist before a Q-point can be placed on it; once placed, the limiting (shorter) side sets how far the signal can swing symmetrically in both directions, and that value doubled gives peak-to-peak swing.

lessons.label: BJT Bias Networks and Bias Stability

sections.heading: Fixed-base bias: simple and unreliable
sections.body: The simplest way to bias a BJT is a single resistor from V_CC to the base, setting I_B = (V_CC - V_BE)/R_B and relying on I_C = hFE * I_B. The flaw is that hFE is not a fixed number: the onsemi datasheet for the 2N3904 lists hFE from 100 to 300 at I_C = 10 mA, a 3:1 spread between the guaranteed minimum and maximum for the very same part number, before accounting for unit-to-unit variation or temperature. A fixed-base design calculated for hFE = 200 could land I_C anywhere from roughly half to one-and-a-half times the intended value depending on which actual transistor gets soldered in. Temperature makes it worse: V_BE drifts by about -2 mV per degree Celsius, so as a transistor self-heats, V_BE effectively drops, I_B rises for a fixed R_B, I_C rises further, the transistor dissipates more power, and it can heat further still — a feedback loop that fixed-base bias does nothing to resist.

sections.heading: The stability factor and emitter degeneration
sections.body: Bias stability is quantified by the stability factor S = dI_C/dI_CO, describing how much a change in the transistor's leakage/thermal current I_CO translates into a change in I_C; fixed-base bias has S close to its worst-case value of (1 + hFE), meaning leakage and hFE variation pass through almost unattenuated. Adding a resistor R_E in the emitter path creates negative feedback: if I_C rises, more current flows through R_E, raising the emitter voltage, which reduces V_BE (since the base voltage is held roughly fixed by the bias network) and throttles I_B back down. This single resistor can pull S down by a factor of ten or more depending on how large R_E is relative to R_B/hFE, directly fighting both the hFE spread and the thermal runaway loop.

sections.heading: Four-resistor voltage-divider bias: the practical standard
sections.body: The most common real-world topology adds a second base resistor to ground, forming a voltage divider (R1, R2) that sets a base voltage largely independent of hFE, combined with an emitter resistor R_E for the degeneration described above. Choosing the divider current several times larger than the expected base current makes the base voltage stiff — insensitive to hFE — while R_E does the thermal stabilizing work. This four-resistor network is why almost every discrete BJT amplifier you see in a real schematic has that same recognizable shape: two resistors from V_CC and ground to the base, one from emitter to ground, and R_C to the collector.

lessons.workedExample: A fixed-base design targets I_C = 1 mA using R_B = (V_CC - V_BE)/I_B with hFE assumed at 200, giving I_B = 5 µA and R_B ≈ 2.28 MΩ for V_CC = 12 V. Swap in a 2N3904 with hFE = 100 (within its own datasheet's guaranteed range) and I_C drops to about 0.5 mA; swap in one with hFE = 300 and I_C rises to about 1.5 mA — a 3:1 spread in the actual operating current from parts that are all nominally the same transistor. Redesigning with voltage-divider bias — R1 = 47 kΩ, R2 = 10 kΩ, R_E = 1 kΩ, same V_CC = 12 V — sets a base voltage near 2.1 V regardless of hFE, so I_C stays within a few percent of 1.4 mA across the same hFE = 100-300 range.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe bias-network choice because it is the cleanest test of whether a student understands manufacturing variation as a real engineering constraint, not just an abstraction. A weak answer picks a single resistor value from a simulation with one assumed hFE and never mentions that real transistors vary. A strong answer names the datasheet hFE spread for the actual part used, explains why voltage-divider bias with an emitter resistor makes the Q-point insensitive to that spread, and can say what happens to the Q-point if the ambient temperature rises 20 degrees.

questions.prompt: Why does fixed-base bias (single resistor from V_CC to the base) make I_C unpredictable across a batch of nominally identical transistors?

options.text: Because I_C = hFE * I_B, and hFE varies unit-to-unit and with temperature, while I_B is fixed by R_B alone
Because V_CC itself varies randomly between builds
Because R_B changes value when current flows through it
Because fixed-base bias has no base resistor at all

explanations.a: Correct — with I_B set only by R_B and V_CC, any spread in hFE (like the 2N3904's datasheet range of 100-300) multiplies directly into I_C.
explanations.b: The instability comes from hFE variation in the transistor, not from the supply voltage.
explanations.c: Resistors are treated as fixed values; they do not change with current in this analysis.
explanations.d: Fixed-base bias does use one resistor from V_CC to the base — that is exactly what makes I_B fixed and I_C hFE-dependent.

questions.prompt: How does an emitter resistor R_E stabilize I_C against a rise in temperature?

options.text: It absorbs excess heat directly, cooling the transistor
If I_C rises, more voltage drops across R_E, which lowers V_BE and throttles I_B back down — negative feedback
It increases hFE to compensate for V_BE drift
It has no effect on temperature stability, only on gain

explanations.a: R_E provides electrical feedback, not thermal heat dissipation, in this role.
explanations.b: Correct — rising I_C raises the emitter voltage across R_E, which (with base voltage held roughly fixed by the divider) reduces the effective V_BE and pulls I_B, and therefore I_C, back down.
explanations.c: R_E does not change hFE; it counteracts the effect of hFE and V_BE variation on I_C.
explanations.d: R_E does reduce AC gain somewhat, but its primary bias-stability role is thermal/hFE stabilization via negative feedback.

questions.prompt: Match each bias topology to its characteristic stability behavior.

right.text: Stability factor near its worst case, hFE spread passes through almost fully
Improved stability via negative feedback, but base voltage still shifts somewhat with hFE
Base voltage held stiff by low divider impedance, plus emitter feedback — best practical stability

questions.explanation: Fixed-base bias has no feedback and the worst stability factor; adding just an emitter resistor without a stiff base voltage still helps but is limited; the full four-resistor divider-plus-emitter network combines a hFE-independent base voltage with emitter feedback for the best practical stability.

questions.prompt: Order the events in the thermal-runaway feedback loop that fixed-base bias fails to resist.

items.text: Transistor self-heats from power dissipation
V_BE drops by about -2 mV per degree Celsius of temperature rise
For a fixed R_B, the lower effective V_BE lets I_B (and thus I_C) rise further
Higher I_C increases power dissipation, driving temperature up again

questions.explanation: Self-heating lowers V_BE, which (with no emitter-degeneration feedback to oppose it) allows I_C to rise, which increases dissipation and drives temperature up further, closing a positive-feedback loop that unchecked fixed-base bias cannot break.

lessons.label: MOSFET Biasing and the Square-Law Region

sections.heading: The square law and overdrive voltage
sections.body: In saturation, a MOSFET's drain current follows I_D = 0.5 * k' * (W/L) * (V_GS - V_th)^2, where k' is the process transconductance parameter and W/L is the transistor's width-to-length ratio. The quantity (V_GS - V_th) is the overdrive voltage, V_OV, and it is the real design knob: for a given device geometry, choosing V_OV directly sets I_D, and it also sets transconductance, since g_m = 2*I_D/V_OV in this square-law model. A small V_OV (a few hundred millivolts) gives high g_m per unit current — efficient for low-power analog stages — but pushes the device closer to the threshold, where the square-law approximation itself grows less accurate and process variation in V_th has a proportionally larger effect. A larger V_OV trades some of that efficiency for a Q-point that is more robust to threshold shifts.

sections.heading: Self-bias and current-mirror tails
sections.body: Because a MOSFET's gate draws essentially no DC current, the bias problem is entirely different from a BJT: there is no base-current loading to account for, and a gate can be biased through a resistor of any size, even megohms, without disturbing the Q-point. The common self-biasing approach places a source resistor R_S between the source and ground, with the gate referenced to ground (or a fixed divider): as I_D tends to rise, the voltage across R_S rises, which reduces V_GS and throttles I_D back down — the same negative-feedback principle as BJT emitter degeneration. In IC design, self-bias is more often replaced by a current-mirror tail: a reference branch sets a known current, and a mirrored transistor forces that same current into the amplifying device regardless of its own V_th, sidestepping threshold spread almost entirely.

sections.heading: Contrast with BJT bias: what gets easier, what gets harder
sections.body: The absence of base current removes one entire failure mode that plagues BJT bias networks — no divider current needs to dominate a base-current draw, and no hFE spread multiplies through the design. But MOSFETs bring their own variation: V_th spread between nominally identical parts can run several hundred millivolts even within one manufacturing lot, directly on top of the (V_GS - V_th) term the current depends on quadratically. The body effect adds another wrinkle — when the source is not tied directly to the bulk/substrate, a reverse source-bulk voltage raises the effective V_th, shifting the Q-point in multi-stage stacks where lower devices' sources sit above ground. And for the same bias current, a MOSFET's g_m is typically several times lower than a BJT's g_m = I_C/V_T, since the BJT's exponential relationship gives more transconductance per milliamp than the MOSFET's square law does.

lessons.workedExample: A design targets I_D = 2 mA using a MOSFET with k'*(W/L) = 4 mA/V^2 and V_th = 0.8 V (nominal). Solving I_D = 0.5*4*(V_OV)^2 for V_OV gives V_OV = 1 V, so V_GS = 1.8 V. Adding a source resistor R_S = 500 Ω for self-bias, and setting the gate at a fixed 3 V through a resistor divider (drawing negligible gate current), gives V_S = 3 - 1.8 = 1.2 V, so I_D through R_S should be 1.2 V / 500 Ω = 2.4 mA — close to but not exactly the 2 mA target because V_GS and I_D are coupled through R_S and must be solved together. If the actual part's V_th is 1.0 V instead of 0.8 V (a plausible lot-to-lot shift), I_D drops measurably, and R_S's feedback pulls the Q-point only partway back toward the target.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask about MOSFET biasing to see whether a student understands that removing one variable (base current) does not mean removing all variability — it swaps hFE spread for V_th spread and the body effect. A weak answer says "MOSFETs are easier to bias because there's no gate current," full stop. A strong answer adds that V_th still varies significantly between parts, that overdrive voltage is the actual design lever, and that self-bias or a current mirror is what actually protects the Q-point from that variation, not the absence of gate current alone.

questions.prompt: In the square-law model I_D = 0.5*k'*(W/L)*(V_GS - V_th)^2, what is the 'overdrive voltage' V_OV?

options.text: V_GS itself
V_th itself
The quantity (V_GS - V_th), the gate voltage in excess of threshold
The drain-source voltage V_DS

explanations.a: V_GS alone does not account for how far above threshold the device is biased.
explanations.b: V_th is the threshold itself, not the margin above it.
explanations.c: Correct — V_OV = V_GS - V_th is the excess gate drive above threshold, and it is the quantity that is squared to set I_D.
explanations.d: V_DS determines whether the device is in saturation at all, but is not the overdrive voltage.

questions.prompt: Why does a MOSFET gate biased through a very large resistor (even megohms) not disturb the DC Q-point, unlike a BJT base?

options.text: Because the gate draws essentially no DC current, so no significant voltage drops across the resistor
Because MOSFET gates are always grounded
Because large resistors have no resistance at DC
Because V_th is zero for all MOSFETs

explanations.a: Correct — with negligible gate current, even a very large gate resistor drops almost no DC voltage, so the gate sits at essentially the voltage set by the rest of the bias network.
explanations.b: Gates are biased to whatever voltage the circuit requires, not always to ground.
explanations.c: Resistors retain their resistance at DC; the point is that near-zero current flows through it.
explanations.d: V_th is a nonzero device parameter (often several hundred millivolts to a volt or more) for real MOSFETs.

questions.prompt: Match each BJT bias concept to its MOSFET analog or contrast.

left.text: Base current loading the bias divider (BJT)

right.text: V_th spread between parts (MOSFET)
Overdrive voltage V_OV as the design knob (MOSFET)
Source resistor R_S for self-bias (MOSFET)
Essentially absent — gate draws no DC current (MOSFET)

questions.explanation: hFE spread maps to V_th spread as the main part-to-part variation; V_BE's turn-on role maps to V_OV as the voltage-above-threshold design variable; R_E's negative-feedback role maps directly to R_S; and base-current loading has no real MOSFET counterpart since gate current is negligible.

questions.prompt: For the same bias current, how does a MOSFET's transconductance g_m typically compare to a BJT's?

options.text: Much higher, because the square law grows faster than the BJT's exponential relationship
Roughly identical, since both depend only on current
Lower, because the BJT's exponential I_C-V_BE relationship gives more transconductance per unit current than the MOSFET's square law
Undefined, since MOSFETs have no transconductance

explanations.a: The exponential BJT relationship, not the square law, is the steeper one near a given operating current.
explanations.b: g_m = I_C/V_T for a BJT versus g_m = 2*I_D/V_OV for a MOSFET — these differ in general, especially since V_OV is typically much larger than the thermal voltage V_T (~26 mV).
explanations.c: Correct — because V_OV is usually several hundred millivolts or more, well above the ~26 mV thermal voltage that sets the BJT's g_m, the MOSFET delivers less transconductance per milliamp of bias current.
explanations.d: MOSFETs do have a well-defined transconductance; it is simply smaller per unit current than a BJT's.

lessons.label: Current Mirrors and Active Loads

sections.heading: The basic two-transistor mirror and its errors
sections.body: A current mirror uses one diode-connected transistor (base tied to collector) carrying a known reference current I_REF, and a second matched transistor sharing the same V_BE, forcing it to conduct a copy of that current. In an ideal world the mirrored current equals I_REF exactly. Two real effects break that ideal. First, base current: both transistors draw base current from the reference branch, so the diode-connected device's collector current is I_REF minus two base currents, introducing an error on the order of 2/hFE — a few percent for a typical hFE around 100-200. Second, the Early effect: if the mirrored transistor's V_CE differs from the reference transistor's V_CE (which it usually does, since it feeds a different part of the circuit), its collector current shifts slightly with V_CE due to base-width modulation, described by the transistor's finite output resistance r_o = V_A/I_C, where V_A is the Early voltage.

sections.heading: Widlar and Wilson refinements
sections.body: Widlar (1965), in a paper on IC circuit techniques written while he was at Fairchild, showed that adding an emitter resistor to only the output transistor of a mirror lets a small, precise current be generated using resistor values that are far more practical to fabricate on a chip than the huge resistors a plain design would need — this Widlar current source became a staple for generating microamp-level bias currents, and appeared in influential designs like the 741 op-amp. Wilson (1967), working at Tektronix, found a three-transistor mirror — the Wilson mirror — that adds a feedback transistor holding both mirror transistors at nearly the same V_CE, which cancels most of the Early-effect mismatch and gives a very high output resistance and wide voltage compliance. A cascode current mirror achieves a similar high-output-resistance result by stacking a common-base transistor on top of the mirror output.

sections.heading: From resistor loads to active loads
sections.body: A common-emitter or common-source stage's voltage gain is approximately -g_m * R_C when a resistor sets the DC operating point. But R_C is doing double duty — setting both the DC bias and the AC load — and a large R_C needed for high gain also eats supply headroom and chip area. Replacing R_C with a current-mirror active load (a current source built from a matched PNP or PMOS mirror, biasing the stage at a fixed current while presenting a very high AC resistance r_o) lets gain approach -g_m * (r_o(NPN) || r_o(PNP)), often one to two orders of magnitude larger than a practical resistor value would allow, since r_o for a real transistor is commonly hundreds of kilohms to megohms. This substitution — a current source in place of a passive resistor — is the single idea that let differential pairs and op-amp gain stages reach the gains needed for negative-feedback circuits on a chip, without R_C ever fitting on practical silicon area.

lessons.workedExample: A gain stage biased at I_C = 100 µA has g_m = I_C/V_T ≈ 100 µA / 26 mV ≈ 3.85 mA/V. With a resistor load R_C = 50 kΩ, gain magnitude is g_m*R_C ≈ 3.85 mA/V * 50 kΩ ≈ 193 — respectable, but R_C = 50 kΩ at that bias current also drops 5 V across itself, eating into headroom on anything but a high supply rail. Replacing R_C with a PNP current-mirror active load whose r_o ≈ 500 kΩ (Early voltage around 50 V at 100 µA), combined with the NPN's own r_o ≈ 500 kΩ, gives a parallel resistance of 250 kΩ and a gain magnitude of 3.85 mA/V * 250 kΩ ≈ 963 — roughly five times higher, from the same bias current, without a 5 V resistor drop.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges push on current mirrors and active loads because the topic separates students who can name a component from students who understand what the component buys. A weak answer says "I used a current mirror to bias it" with no sense of the error sources or why it beats a resistor. A strong answer names the specific error term the chosen mirror topology addresses — base-current error for a plain mirror, Early-effect mismatch for a Wilson or cascode mirror — and can explain, with the r_o-versus-R_C comparison, why an active load raises gain rather than just saving board space.

questions.prompt: In a plain two-transistor current mirror, what causes the mirrored current to differ slightly from I_REF even before any Early-effect mismatch?

options.text: The two transistors drawing base current from the reference branch, roughly a 2/hFE error
The supply voltage being unregulated
The transistors being different types (NPN vs PNP)
The mirror having no error at all under any condition

explanations.a: Correct — both transistors' base currents are drawn from the reference branch, so the diode-connected transistor's own collector current (and hence the mirrored copy) is reduced by roughly 2/hFE relative to I_REF.
explanations.b: Supply regulation affects overall bias levels but is not the specific mechanism behind the base-current mirror error.
explanations.c: A basic mirror uses two matched transistors of the same type; mixing types is not the source of this particular error.
explanations.d: Even a well-matched plain mirror has the base-current error described, before Early effect is considered.

questions.prompt: What specific problem does the Wilson mirror's extra feedback transistor solve compared to a plain two-transistor mirror?

options.text: It eliminates the need for a reference current entirely
It holds both mirror transistors at nearly equal V_CE, canceling most of the Early-effect mismatch and raising output resistance
It doubles the mirrored current automatically
It removes the requirement that the two transistors be matched

explanations.a: A Wilson mirror still requires a reference current branch; it does not eliminate that requirement.
explanations.b: Correct — by forcing near-equal V_CE on the two current-setting transistors, the Wilson topology (Wilson, 1967) cancels most of the Early-effect current mismatch and gives high output resistance.
explanations.c: The Wilson mirror still targets a 1:1 (or ratioed) copy of I_REF, not an automatic doubling.
explanations.d: Matching between the mirror transistors is still important for accuracy; the Wilson topology does not remove that requirement.

questions.prompt: Why does replacing a resistor collector load R_C with a current-mirror active load typically increase a gain stage's voltage gain?

options.text: Because the active load's AC resistance (r_o, often hundreds of kΩ or more) is usually much larger than a practical R_C, and gain scales with load resistance
Because active loads increase g_m of the amplifying transistor
Because active loads eliminate the need for any bias current
Because resistors always have negative resistance at high frequency

explanations.a: Correct — gain magnitude is g_m times the effective load resistance; an active load's high r_o (versus a practical resistor value limited by headroom and area) directly raises that effective load resistance and thus gain.
explanations.b: g_m is set by the amplifying transistor's own bias current, not by the load device.
explanations.c: An active load still carries a well-defined bias current; it replaces the resistor's role, not the current itself.
explanations.d: Resistors do not exhibit negative resistance in this context; the comparison is simply r_o versus a practical R_C value.

questions.prompt: Order these current-mirror developments from the basic topology to progressively more refined ones, based on what each one primarily fixes.

items.text: Plain two-transistor mirror (base-current and Early-effect error present)
Widlar mirror (adds emitter resistor for low, practical-resistor-value output currents)
Wilson mirror (adds feedback transistor to equalize V_CE and cancel Early-effect mismatch)

questions.explanation: The plain mirror is the baseline with both error sources present; the Widlar mirror addresses generating small currents practically without removing Early-effect mismatch; the Wilson mirror specifically targets and largely cancels the Early-effect mismatch via V_CE equalization.

lessons.label: Coupling, Bypassing, and the Low-Frequency Edge

sections.heading: AC coupling caps and the high-pass pole they create
sections.body: A coupling capacitor sits in series between stages (or between a source and the input, or the output and a load) so that each stage's DC bias point stays isolated from the next — the capacitor blocks DC entirely while passing AC. But a capacitor in series with a resistance forms a high-pass filter, with a -3 dB corner frequency at f = 1/(2*pi*R*C), below which gain rolls off at 20 dB per decade. The resistance R in that formula is whatever the capacitor sees looking both directions — typically the source's output resistance in series with the next stage's input resistance. Choosing too small a coupling capacitor pushes this pole up into the frequency range the circuit is meant to amplify, quietly attenuating bass content in an audio stage or slow-changing signals in an instrumentation stage, without any obvious sign in a DC bias check.

sections.heading: The bypass capacitor trade-off
sections.body: An emitter (or source) resistor used for bias stability, as covered in BJT bias networks, also reduces AC gain, because that same negative feedback that stabilizes the DC operating point also opposes AC signal swings. A bypass capacitor placed across the emitter resistor shorts it to AC ground above its own corner frequency, restoring full AC gain (gain rises toward -g_m*R_C) while leaving the DC bias-stabilizing role of R_E untouched, since the capacitor is an open circuit at DC. This is a genuine trade-off, not a free lunch: below the bypass capacitor's corner frequency the stage reverts to the lower, degenerated gain, so the bypass cap itself introduces another low-frequency pole (and, in some layouts, a nearby zero) that shapes the roll-off alongside the coupling capacitors.

sections.heading: Stacking poles versus going fully DC-coupled
sections.body: A multi-stage amplifier typically has one coupling capacitor at the input, one between each pair of stages, one at the output, and possibly a bypass capacitor per stage — each contributes its own high-pass corner. Where these poles land relative to each other determines the overall low-frequency roll-off shape: poles spaced well apart give a gentler transition, while poles clustered near the same frequency compound into a steeper roll-off and more phase shift near the bottom of the passband. The alternative is DC coupling — connecting stages directly, with no series capacitor — which removes the low-frequency limit entirely (gain extends to DC) but forces every stage's small DC offset and bias imperfection to add up and amplify through every subsequent stage, since there is no capacitor to block that drift from propagating. DC-coupled designs need deliberate offset-cancellation or level-shifting to stay usable, which AC-coupled designs get for free from the capacitors themselves.

lessons.workedExample: A two-stage audio amplifier uses a 1 µF input coupling capacitor into a stage whose input resistance is 10 kΩ, giving a corner at f = 1/(2*pi*10 kΩ*1 µF) ≈ 15.9 Hz — comfortably below the 20 Hz low end of the audio band, a reasonable choice. Its emitter bypass capacitor is 47 µF across a 220 Ω emitter resistor (in parallel with the source resistance the emitter sees, effectively lower), giving a corner well below 100 Hz as intended so the midband gain boost applies across most of the audio range. But the output coupling capacitor, sized at only 0.1 µF into a 1 kΩ load, gives f = 1/(2*pi*1 kΩ*0.1 µF) ≈ 1.6 kHz — a pole that lands squarely inside the audio band, audibly thinning out bass and lower midrange despite the input stage being sized correctly.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask about coupling and bypass capacitors because sizing them correctly requires connecting a formula to a real engineering consequence a listener or instrument would notice, not just picking round capacitor values. A weak answer picks 0.1 µF or 1 µF everywhere because that is what a tutorial showed. A strong answer computes the actual R the capacitor sees at each location, states the resulting corner frequency, and explains — as in the worked example — how one undersized capacitor buried in an otherwise correct design can still roll off the very frequencies the circuit was built to pass.

questions.prompt: A coupling capacitor sees a total resistance of 2 kΩ looking both directions. What capacitance places the -3 dB corner at approximately 20 Hz?

options.text: About 4 µF
About 0.04 µF
About 40 µF
About 400 pF

explanations.a: Correct — C = 1/(2*pi*f*R) = 1/(2*pi*20*2000) ≈ 3.98 µF, so roughly 4 µF places the corner near 20 Hz.
explanations.b: 0.04 µF into 2 kΩ gives a corner in the low kHz range, far above 20 Hz.
explanations.c: 40 µF into 2 kΩ would place the corner well below 20 Hz (around 2 Hz), lower than required, not matching the 20 Hz target.
explanations.d: 400 pF is far too small; into 2 kΩ that gives a corner in the hundreds-of-kHz range.

questions.prompt: Why does a bypass capacitor across the emitter resistor increase AC gain without disturbing the DC Q-point?

options.text: It removes the emitter resistor from the circuit permanently
It is an open circuit at DC (leaving R_E's bias-stabilizing role intact) but a short at AC frequencies above its corner (removing R_E's gain-reducing feedback)
It increases hFE at AC frequencies
It only works if R_E is removed from the circuit first

explanations.a: The capacitor is placed in parallel with R_E, not in place of it; R_E remains in the DC path.
explanations.b: Correct — a capacitor blocks DC entirely, so R_E still sets the DC bias, but above the bypass corner frequency the capacitor shorts R_E for AC signals, removing the gain-reducing negative feedback and restoring higher AC gain.
explanations.c: hFE is a transistor property and is not altered by a bypass capacitor.
explanations.d: The bypass capacitor is added in parallel with R_E specifically so both roles (DC stability and AC gain) can coexist, without removing R_E.

questions.prompt: What is the main practical drawback of a fully DC-coupled (no series capacitors) multi-stage amplifier compared to an AC-coupled one?

options.text: It cannot amplify low frequencies at all
Each stage's small DC offset and bias imperfection propagates and amplifies through every subsequent stage, requiring deliberate offset handling
It requires more coupling capacitors than an AC-coupled design
It cannot be built with BJTs, only MOSFETs

explanations.a: DC coupling actually extends gain down to DC (0 Hz) since there is no high-pass pole from a series capacitor.
explanations.b: Correct — with no capacitor blocking DC between stages, any offset or bias error at one stage passes straight into the next stage's input and gets amplified again, compounding through the chain.
explanations.c: DC coupling uses fewer or no coupling capacitors between stages, not more.
explanations.d: DC coupling is a topology choice independent of whether BJTs or MOSFETs are used.

questions.prompt: Order these steps for diagnosing which capacitor is causing unwanted low-frequency roll-off in a multi-stage amplifier.

items.text: List every coupling and bypass capacitor in the signal path along with the resistance each one sees
Compute f = 1/(2*pi*R*C) for each capacitor individually
Identify which computed corner frequency lands closest to (or inside) the desired passband
Increase that specific capacitor's value to push its corner below the passband

questions.explanation: You must first know every capacitor and its associated resistance, then compute each corner frequency, identify the offending (highest, in-band) corner, and only then resize that specific capacitor rather than guessing across the whole circuit.

lessons.label: Thermal Effects, Drift, and Safe Operating Area

sections.heading: Thermal runaway in class-AB output stages
sections.body: A class-AB output stage biases a complementary pair of transistors to conduct a small quiescent current through both devices simultaneously, avoiding the crossover distortion of class-B while keeping dissipation far below class-A. That quiescent current is set by holding a small V_BE-equivalent voltage across the base-emitter junctions of both output devices. Because V_BE drops by roughly 2 mV per degree Celsius as a junction warms, and because the output transistors themselves are the heat source, a fixed bias voltage becomes dangerous: as the output devices warm from carrying their quiescent current, their effective V_BE requirement drops, which — if the bias voltage across them is truly fixed — lets quiescent current rise, which raises dissipation, which raises temperature further. This is thermal runaway, a positive-feedback loop that can destroy output transistors within seconds if nothing tracks the temperature.

sections.heading: V_BE-multiplier compensation
sections.body: The standard fix is to make the bias voltage itself track temperature the same way the output junctions do, so the loop gets negative feedback instead of positive. A V_BE multiplier — a transistor with a resistor divider across its base-emitter junction and collector-emitter path — produces a voltage that is a fixed multiple of one V_BE drop, and if that multiplier transistor is thermally coupled to the output devices' heatsink, its own V_BE falls with temperature at the same rate, pulling the bias voltage down just enough to hold quiescent current roughly constant as everything heats up. A simpler alternative uses a string of ordinary diodes in the bias path instead of a multiplier transistor, relying on the diodes' own -2 mV/°C drift and mounting them against the same heatsink.

sections.heading: Safe operating area and watching drift directly
sections.body: Beyond bias-point drift, every power transistor has a safe operating area (SOA) — a boundary on the I_C-V_CE plane, published on the datasheet, combining the maximum current rating, maximum voltage rating, a maximum power (I*V = constant) curve, and (for pulsed or DC operation at high voltage) a secondary-breakdown limit that curves the boundary in further than a simple power hyperbola would suggest. A load line that pokes outside the SOA at any point means the device can fail under that condition even if the average dissipation looks acceptable, which is why the DC or AC load line from earlier in this unit should always be checked against the manufacturer's SOA graph, not just against a single P_D(max) number. Thermal resistance from junction to ambient, θ_JA, is what converts a given dissipation into a temperature rise (ΔT = P_D * θ_JA); a heat gun aimed at a biased transistor, or freeze spray to cool it, is a simple bench way to watch a Q-point (measured V_CE or I_C) visibly drift in real time, making the abstract θ_JA and V_BE-tempco numbers into something you can see move on a meter.

lessons.workedExample: A class-AB output stage biases its complementary pair with a fixed 1.2 V from a simple resistor divider instead of a V_BE multiplier, targeting 20 mA of quiescent current at 25°C. After ten minutes of idling, the heatsink reaches 45°C, a 20°C rise. With V_BE dropping about 2 mV/°C per junction, and two junctions in series in the pair (each ~0.6 V nominally), the combined effective turn-on voltage has fallen by roughly 80 mV out of the original ~1.2 V budget for a 20°C rise. Because the divider voltage did not follow that drop, quiescent current creeps up sharply — a bench measurement might show I_Q rising from 20 mA well past 100 mA over the same ten minutes, with no change in the input signal, visible directly as a rising DC reading on a multimeter across a small series sense resistor.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges bring up thermal drift and SOA because it is the one topic where "my simulation matched my calculation" is not enough — real transistors get warm, and a design that only exists on paper or in an ideal SPICE model has never been tested against that. A weak answer has never measured a Q-point before and after the circuit has been running for several minutes. A strong answer describes an actual bench observation — a rising quiescent current, a warm heatsink, a V_CE reading that shifted — and can explain it with the V_BE tempco and thermal-resistance numbers rather than just saying "it got warm."

questions.prompt: What is the core positive-feedback mechanism behind thermal runaway in a class-AB output stage with fixed bias voltage?

options.text: Rising temperature raises V_BE requirement, which lowers I_C, which cools the device
Rising temperature lowers the effective V_BE requirement, which (with fixed bias voltage) raises I_C, which raises dissipation and temperature further
Rising temperature has no effect on V_BE or I_C in silicon transistors
Rising temperature increases the transistor's SOA rating, allowing more current safely

explanations.a: This describes negative feedback (self-correcting), which is the opposite of what happens with a fixed, non-tracking bias voltage.
explanations.b: Correct — V_BE falls about -2 mV/°C, so a fixed bias voltage allows more current as the junction warms, raising dissipation and temperature in a loop that reinforces itself.
explanations.c: V_BE's dependence on temperature (~-2 mV/°C) is a well-established real effect in silicon BJTs, central to this failure mode.
explanations.d: A device's SOA rating is a fixed datasheet limit; it does not increase with the device's own temperature — if anything, thermal limits tighten as a device runs hotter.

questions.prompt: How does a V_BE multiplier, thermally coupled to the output transistors' heatsink, prevent thermal runaway?

options.text: It provides a fixed bias voltage that never changes with temperature
Its own V_BE falls with temperature at the same rate as the output junctions, so the bias voltage it produces tracks downward, holding quiescent current roughly constant rather than letting it climb
It disconnects the output transistors once a temperature threshold is reached
It increases the output transistors' hFE to compensate for heat

explanations.a: A fixed, non-tracking bias voltage is exactly the condition that causes runaway; the multiplier's value is deliberately temperature-dependent, not fixed.
explanations.b: Correct — because the multiplier transistor sits on the same heatsink and shares the -2 mV/°C V_BE drift, its output bias voltage falls in step with what the output junctions need, converting the loop from positive to (approximately) neutral or negative feedback.
explanations.c: A V_BE multiplier provides continuous compensation, not a hard disconnect at a threshold.
explanations.d: hFE is a separate device parameter; the multiplier's compensation works through bias voltage, not through altering the output transistors' current gain.

questions.prompt: Why must a load line be checked against a transistor's safe operating area (SOA) graph, not just against a single maximum power number?

options.text: Because SOA includes a secondary-breakdown limit that curves the boundary in tighter than a simple constant-power hyperbola at high voltage
Because SOA and maximum power dissipation are always numerically identical
Because SOA only applies to MOSFETs, not BJTs
Because a single P_D(max) number is always more conservative than the SOA graph

explanations.a: Correct — especially at higher voltages, secondary breakdown pulls the real safe boundary in below what a pure I*V = constant power curve would allow, so a load line can be under the power limit yet still outside the true SOA.
explanations.b: They coincide only over part of the graph (the constant-power region); at higher voltages the SOA is tighter due to secondary breakdown.
explanations.c: SOA graphs are published for BJTs as well as MOSFETs; secondary breakdown is a BJT-specific mechanism, but SOA as a concept applies broadly.
explanations.d: The SOA graph, not a single P_D(max) figure, is the more conservative (tighter) constraint at higher voltages, which is exactly why relying on P_D(max) alone can be misleading.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of the thermal-runaway loop as it plays out in a fixed-bias class-AB output stage.

items.text: Output junctions carry quiescent current and dissipate power, warming the heatsink
Junction V_BE requirement falls by about -2 mV per degree Celsius of warming
Fixed bias voltage now exceeds what is needed, so quiescent current rises
Higher quiescent current increases dissipation, raising temperature further

questions.explanation: Dissipation warms the junctions first; that warming lowers the V_BE they need to conduct; against an unchanging fixed bias voltage that lets current rise; and the higher current dissipates more power, closing the loop back to further heating.

questions.prompt: Match each thermal quantity or tool to its role in this lesson.

left.text: Heat gun or freeze spray on a biased transistor

right.text: Converts a given power dissipation into a temperature rise, ΔT = P_D * θ_JA
Bench method to watch Q-point drift in real time
Datasheet boundary combining current, voltage, power, and secondary-breakdown limits
Tracks temperature to hold class-AB quiescent current roughly constant

questions.explanation: θ_JA is the conversion factor from dissipated power to temperature rise; a heat gun or freeze spray is a hands-on way to observe Q-point drift; the SOA graph is the full safe-operation boundary; and a heatsink-mounted V_BE multiplier is the temperature-tracking compensation element.

units.label: Small-Signal Models and Single-Stage Amplifiers

lessons.label: From Large Signal to Small Signal

sections.heading: Why linearize a curved device at all
sections.body: A transistor's true I-V relationship is exponential (BJT) or square-law (MOSFET), not a line. Solving a whole amplifier stage with that nonlinear equation every time would be miserable, so analog designers use a two-step trick: first find the DC bias point Q (the fixed I_C and V_CE, or I_D and V_DS, set by resistors and supply voltages with no signal applied), then treat any AC input as a tiny wiggle around Q. Over a small enough excursion, the curve looks like its own tangent line at Q — a first-order Taylor expansion. That tangent line is the small-signal model, and it turns a transcendental device equation into linear circuit elements a student can solve with Ohm's law and superposition.

sections.heading: The hybrid-pi parameters
sections.body: For a BJT, the tangent slope of I_C versus V_BE at Q is the transconductance gm = I_C / V_T, where V_T = kT/q is about 25.85 mV at 300 K (room temperature), so gm is roughly 38.6 mA per volt for every 1 mA of collector current. The base still draws some current, modeled as an input resistance r_pi = beta / gm between base and emitter. The collector current is not perfectly independent of V_CE either — early voltage V_A captures that slope as an output resistance ro = V_A / I_C, typically tens to hundreds of kilo-ohms. A MOSFET's tangent slope is different in form because I_D is square-law in overdrive: gm = 2*I_D / V_OV, where V_OV = V_GS - V_th. Same idea, different algebra, because the underlying physics (exponential diffusion current vs. square-law channel current) differs.

sections.heading: Where the tangent line stops matching the curve
sections.body: The small-signal model is only as good as the assumption that the signal is small relative to the curvature of the device equation. Three failure modes matter for a science-fair project. First, large swing: if V_be swings tens of millivolts, the exponential BJT relationship visibly bends away from its tangent, producing harmonic distortion the linear model cannot predict. Second, slew limiting: at high frequency and large amplitude, the maximum rate of change the circuit can deliver (set by bias current charging a capacitance) is exceeded, and the output becomes a straight ramp instead of tracking the input — a nonlinear, large-signal phenomenon entirely outside hybrid-pi. Third, leaving the active (BJT) or saturation (MOSFET) region entirely — clipping into cutoff or into the triode/saturation boundary — breaks the model's core assumption that Q stays fixed.

lessons.workedExample: A BJT is biased at I_C = 1 mA with beta = 100 and Early voltage V_A = 100 V. At 300 K, gm = 1 mA / 25.85 mV = 38.7 mA/V. Then r_pi = beta/gm = 100 / 0.0387 A/V = 2.59 kOhm, and ro = V_A/I_C = 100 V / 1 mA = 100 kOhm. Compare a MOSFET biased at I_D = 1 mA with V_OV = 0.2 V: gm = 2(1 mA)/0.2 V = 10 mA/V — noticeably lower transconductance per milliamp than the BJT, which is the classic BJT-vs-MOSFET gm trade a judge expects a student to know cold.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'what happens to your gain if the signal gets bigger?' to find out whether a student memorized a gain formula or understands that the formula is a local approximation. A weak answer treats gm, r_pi, and ro as fixed device constants. A strong answer says the model is a tangent line at the bias point, names the specific number V_T ≈ 25.85 mV or V_OV, and can predict qualitatively that a large swing produces distortion because the real exponential or square-law curve bends away from that tangent — which is exactly the kind of failure a science-fair oscilloscope trace would show as flattened or asymmetric peaks.

questions.prompt: A BJT is biased at I_C = 2 mA at 300 K. Approximately what is gm?

options.text: About 0.077 A/V (77 mA/V)
About 2 A/V
About 0.0026 A/V (2.6 mA/V)
It cannot be found without knowing beta

explanations.a: Correct — gm = I_C/V_T = 2 mA / 25.85 mV ≈ 0.0774 A/V, about 77 mA/V, consistent with ~38.6 mA/V per mA of I_C.
explanations.b: This overstates gm by roughly two orders of magnitude; it does not correspond to the I_C/V_T relationship.
explanations.c: This is the inverse of the right magnitude — it looks like V_T/I_C rather than I_C/V_T.
explanations.d: gm depends only on I_C and V_T for a BJT, not on beta; beta instead sets r_pi = beta/gm.

questions.prompt: Why does a MOSFET's gm formula (gm = 2*I_D/V_OV) look different from a BJT's (gm = I_C/V_T)?

options.text: MOSFETs do not have a small-signal model
The underlying large-signal I-V law differs — square-law channel current versus exponential diffusion current — so the tangent slope at Q takes a different algebraic form
MOSFETs are only used at high frequency, so the formula includes frequency terms
V_OV and V_T are the same physical quantity written differently

explanations.a: MOSFETs have a hybrid-pi-style small-signal model too; gm = 2*I_D/V_OV is exactly that model's transconductance.
explanations.b: Correct — the small-signal parameter is the tangent slope of the device's own large-signal law, and BJT (exponential) and MOSFET (square-law) devices have different laws.
explanations.c: Neither formula contains a frequency term; both are DC/low-frequency tangent slopes.
explanations.d: V_OV = V_GS - V_th is an overdrive voltage set by bias; V_T = kT/q is the thermal voltage, a physical constant at a given temperature. They are unrelated quantities that happen to share the letter V.

questions.prompt: Match each small-signal parameter to its defining formula.

right.text: I_C / V_T
beta / gm
V_A / I_C
2 * I_D / V_OV

questions.explanation: gm for a BJT is I_C/V_T (thermal-voltage-based); r_pi is beta/gm; ro is the Early-voltage-based V_A/I_C; MOSFET gm is 2*I_D/V_OV, reflecting the square-law device equation.

questions.prompt: A student drives a small-signal amplifier with an input large enough that the output waveform on an oscilloscope shows visibly flattened, asymmetric peaks compared to the input sine wave. What does this most directly indicate?

options.text: The signal has exceeded the small-signal regime, so the device's tangent-line approximation no longer matches its true curved I-V law
r_pi has become negative
The Early voltage has changed
gm is now frequency-dependent

explanations.a: Correct — flattened, asymmetric output is the classic signature of the real exponential/square-law curve bending away from the tangent line the small-signal model assumes, i.e., a large-signal effect.
explanations.b: r_pi is a resistance derived from device physics and bias current; it does not go negative from large swing.
explanations.c: V_A is a device parameter that does not change with signal amplitude; distortion here is not an Early-voltage effect.
explanations.d: gm itself is a DC/low-frequency tangent slope; the described symptom is amplitude-dependent distortion, not a frequency-dependent effect.

lessons.label: Common Emitter and Common Source

sections.heading: The workhorse inverting stage
sections.body: The common-emitter (CE) and common-source (CS) stages are the default choice whenever a circuit needs real voltage gain from a single transistor. The signal enters at the base or gate, the emitter or source is held at AC ground (directly or through a bypassed resistor), and the output is taken off the collector or drain through a load resistor R_C or R_D. Because the transistor's controlled current flows from supply through that load resistor, and an increasing input turns the device on harder — pulling more current through R_C and dropping the output voltage lower — the stage inverts: output swings opposite to input, a 180-degree phase shift. The core small-signal result is gain Av = -gm * R_C (BJT) or Av = -gm * R_D (MOSFET): the resistor converts the transistor's controlled current back into a voltage, and gm sets how much current a given input volt produces.

sections.heading: Impedance looking in and looking out
sections.body: The input impedance differs sharply between the two devices. A BJT's base draws real current, so the CE stage presents r_pi (typically a few kilo-ohms) to whatever is driving it — a real loading effect on the source. A MOSFET's gate is insulated, so the CS stage's DC input impedance is enormous (set only by bias resistors, not by gm or r_pi), which is one of the two big reasons designers reach for MOSFETs at a sensitive input node. Looking out from the output, both stages present R_C || ro (or R_D || ro) — the load resistor in parallel with the transistor's own finite output resistance — so a very large R_C does not buy unlimited gain once ro becomes the dominant term.

sections.heading: Degeneration: trading gain for everything else
sections.body: Adding a resistor R_E (or R_S) between the emitter/source and AC ground, left unbypassed, is called degeneration. It introduces negative feedback: as output current tries to rise, the voltage dropped across R_E rises too, reducing the effective V_be or V_gs driving the device and throttling the current back down. The gain becomes approximately Av ≈ -R_C/R_E, largely independent of gm — which is exactly the point, because gm depends on bias current and temperature, both of which drift. Degeneration linearizes the stage (a wider input range stays proportional), raises input impedance (roughly by a factor of (1+beta) for a BJT), and stabilizes bias against beta and temperature variation. The explicit cost is gain: an undegenerated CE stage might have Av of -200 or more, while a heavily degenerated one trades that down to single digits in exchange for predictability.

lessons.workedExample: A CE stage has I_C = 1 mA (gm ≈ 38.7 mA/V at 300 K), R_C = 5 kOhm, ro = 100 kOhm, and no degeneration. Output resistance is R_C || ro = 5k || 100k ≈ 4.76 kOhm, and Av = -gm*R_C = -38.7 mA/V * 5 kOhm ≈ -193, a large inverting gain. Now add R_E = 200 Ohm unbypassed: Av ≈ -R_C/R_E = -5000/200 = -25. Gain drops by a factor of about 8, but the stage now tolerates a beta variation from 100 to 300 (common between transistor batches) with the gain barely moving, whereas the undegenerated version's gain would have shifted noticeably with beta-driven changes to the bias point.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'why did you add that extra resistor at the emitter, and why is your gain so much lower now?' is testing whether a student understands degeneration as a deliberate trade rather than a mistake. A weak answer treats the lower gain as an unexplained side effect or a design error. A strong answer names the trade directly: R_E buys linearity, higher input impedance, and bias stability against beta and temperature spread, at the explicit cost of gain — and can state the approximate formula Av ≈ -R_C/R_E to show the trade is quantified, not just described.

questions.prompt: Why does a common-emitter stage invert its input signal?

options.text: Because BJTs are inherently AC-coupled devices
Because a rising input turns the transistor on harder, pulling more current through R_C and dropping the output voltage lower
Because r_pi has a negative sign in the small-signal model
Inversion only happens if the stage is degenerated

explanations.a: AC coupling (via a capacitor) is a separate biasing technique unrelated to why the stage inverts.
explanations.b: Correct — more input drive means more collector current pulled through R_C, so V_out = V_CC - I_C*R_C falls as V_in rises, giving the 180-degree phase shift.
explanations.c: r_pi is a positive resistance in the small-signal model; it has nothing to do with sign inversion.
explanations.d: The CE/CS stage inverts whether or not it is degenerated; degeneration changes the gain magnitude, not the sign.

questions.prompt: A CS stage and a CE stage are both driven from a source with significant output resistance. Which statement about DC input loading is correct?

options.text: The CE stage loads the source less because r_pi is always larger than a MOSFET's gate impedance
The CS stage loads the source negligibly at DC because the gate is insulated, while the CE stage presents a finite r_pi that does load the source
Both stages load the source identically because both use gm in their gain formula
Neither stage loads the source; loading only matters for follower stages

explanations.a: This reverses the real relationship — a MOSFET's insulated gate presents essentially infinite DC input impedance, far higher than any r_pi.
explanations.b: Correct — an insulated gate draws no DC current, so CS input impedance is set only by bias resistors, while a BJT's base current makes r_pi (a few kilo-ohms typically) a real loading term.
explanations.c: Both stages use gm in the gain formula, but input impedance is a separate property governed by r_pi (BJT) versus the insulated gate (MOSFET).
explanations.d: Input loading matters for any stage, including CE/CS; it is not unique to followers, though followers are prized for minimizing it on the output side.

questions.prompt: In a degenerated CE stage with Av ≈ -R_C/R_E, why is this gain expression preferred over -gm*R_C for a production design?

options.text: It is larger in magnitude, giving more gain
It depends mainly on two resistor values rather than on gm, which drifts with bias current and temperature
It eliminates the need for a collector resistor entirely
It removes the phase inversion

explanations.a: Degeneration reduces gain magnitude relative to -gm*R_C; that is the cost being paid, not a benefit.
explanations.b: Correct — resistor ratios are far more stable and predictable across units and temperature than gm, which depends on bias current and V_T.
explanations.c: R_C is still required in this formula and in the physical circuit; degeneration adds R_E, it does not remove R_C.
explanations.d: The stage still inverts; degeneration affects gain magnitude and stability, not the sign of the transfer function.

questions.prompt: Match each CE/CS stage property to what determines it.

right.text: -gm * R_C (or R_D)
r_pi
R_C parallel with ro
approximately -R_C / R_E

questions.explanation: Undegenerated gain is -gm*R_C; BJT input impedance is r_pi; output impedance is R_C in parallel with the transistor's own ro; degenerated gain becomes approximately -R_C/R_E, largely independent of gm.

lessons.label: Followers: Common Collector and Common Drain

sections.heading: A stage that gives up voltage gain on purpose
sections.body: The common-collector (emitter follower) and common-drain (source follower) stages take the signal in at the base or gate and out at the emitter or source, with the collector or drain tied directly to a supply rail. The output tracks the input almost exactly, offset by a fixed V_BE drop (about 0.6-0.7 V for a BJT) or by the MOSFET's V_GS, giving a voltage gain just under 1 rather than greater than 1. That sounds like a step backward after the CE/CS stage's job of amplifying voltage, but voltage gain was never the point here: these stages exist to move current, not to amplify voltage, and they do that job extremely well — the emitter current is (1+beta) times the base current, so a follower delivers a current gain of roughly (1+beta) into its load, letting a weak, high-impedance signal drive a much heavier one.

sections.heading: Impedance transformation is the actual product
sections.body: The follower's real function is transforming impedance. Looking into the base, a load resistance R_E appears magnified by (1+beta): R_in ≈ (1+beta) * R_E, so a follower presents a large, gentle load to whatever drives it. Looking out from the emitter, the story reverses — a source impedance driving the base gets divided down by roughly the same factor, giving R_out ≈ 1/gm + R_S/(1+beta), a small output impedance capable of driving a stiff, low-impedance load without sagging. The MOSFET source follower does the same job with an important caveat: because the gate draws no current, there is no (1+beta) current gain to speak of, but the impedance-lowering role at the output is preserved through gm.

sections.heading: The classic buffer role, and where it fails
sections.body: This combination — high R_in, low R_out, gain near unity — is exactly what a buffer needs: insert a follower between a delicate, high-impedance source (a sensor, a filter's output node) and a demanding, low-impedance load (a speaker, a long cable, a low-value potentiometer), and the source barely notices the load is there. Two failure modes are worth knowing. First, the fixed V_BE (or V_GS) offset means a follower cannot swing its output all the way to the supply rails or reproduce DC-precise levels without extra compensation. Second, a single-transistor follower is asymmetric: it can source current easily through the transistor but can only sink current through its bias resistor, so driving a capacitive load — which demands a fast sinking current to slew the output down quickly — can produce visibly slower falling edges than rising edges, sometimes even distortion, unless the design adds a class-AB-style pull-down path.

lessons.workedExample: An emitter follower has I_C = 2 mA (gm ≈ 77.3 mA/V), beta = 150, and R_E = 1 kOhm, driven from a source with R_S = 10 kOhm. R_in ≈ (1+150)*1 kOhm ≈ 151 kOhm — the follower barely loads a source expecting to drive into hundreds of kilo-ohms. R_out ≈ 1/gm + R_S/(1+beta) = 1/0.0773 A/V + 10 kOhm/151 ≈ 12.9 Ohm + 66.2 Ohm ≈ 79 Ohm — low enough to comfortably drive an 8 Ohm-to-a-few-hundred-Ohm load without significant signal sag, even though the source itself was a stiff 10 kOhm.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes followers by asking 'your gain is basically 1 — why bother with this stage at all?' A weak answer has no response beyond 'it's a buffer' with no mechanism. A strong answer explains the actual product being sold: impedance transformation, quantified with R_in ≈ (1+beta)*R_E and R_out ≈ 1/gm + R_S/(1+beta), and connects it to a concrete need in the student's own circuit — for instance, isolating a high-impedance sensor from a load that would otherwise pull its output voltage down. Bonus credit for naming the asymmetric-drive limitation if the project drives anything capacitive, like an LED string or a long cable.

questions.prompt: Why is an emitter follower's voltage gain close to but just under 1, rather than much greater than 1 like a CE stage?

options.text: The output is taken at the emitter, which tracks the base input directly, offset only by the fixed V_BE drop — there is no R_C converting current into an amplified voltage swing
Followers use a different, weaker transistor than CE stages
beta is always less than 1 in a follower configuration
The collector resistor is too small in follower designs

explanations.a: Correct — the emitter voltage simply follows the base voltage minus V_BE; there is no collector-resistor voltage-amplifying mechanism in this topology.
explanations.b: The same transistor type is used; the topology, not the device, determines the gain.
explanations.c: beta is a current gain (typically 50-300), unrelated to why voltage gain is near 1.
explanations.d: The collector is tied directly to the supply rail in a follower, with no collector resistor at all — that is the defining feature of the topology.

questions.prompt: What is the primary functional purpose of a common-collector/common-drain stage in a real circuit?

options.text: To provide large voltage gain
To transform impedance — presenting a large R_in to the source and a small R_out to the load — while passing the signal through at near-unity voltage gain
To invert the signal phase
To filter out high frequencies

explanations.a: Voltage gain is deliberately near 1, not large; that is not the stage's job.
explanations.b: Correct — the follower's value is in R_in ≈ (1+beta)*R_E and R_out ≈ 1/gm + R_S/(1+beta), letting it buffer a delicate source from a demanding load.
explanations.c: Followers do not invert; output tracks input in phase (with a fixed DC offset), unlike the CE/CS stage.
explanations.d: A follower is not inherently a filter; its bandwidth is set by other circuit elements, not by its core function.

questions.prompt: A single-transistor emitter follower drives a capacitive load and shows a fast rising edge but a noticeably slower falling edge on an oscilloscope. What explains this?

options.text: The transistor's beta increases at high frequency

The follower can actively source current through the transistor to pull the output up quickly, but can only sink current through its bias resistor to pull the output down, which is slower into a capacitive load
V_BE decreases as the signal rises
The output impedance becomes negative during the falling edge

explanations.a: beta does not systematically increase with frequency in a way that explains this asymmetry; the effect is about current-sourcing versus current-sinking paths.
explanations.b: Correct — this is the classic asymmetric-drive limitation of a single-transistor follower: sourcing is active (through the transistor) while sinking is passive (through a resistor), which is slow against a capacitive load's demand for sinking current.
explanations.c: V_BE is roughly constant (about 0.6-0.7 V) across normal operation; it is not the cause of edge-rate asymmetry.
explanations.d: Output impedance does not go negative; the asymmetry comes from having only one active current-delivery direction, not from a sign change in impedance.

questions.prompt: Order the reasoning steps for deciding to insert an emitter follower between a high-impedance sensor and a low-impedance load.

items.text: Notice the sensor's output sags when connected directly to the low-impedance load
Recognize the sensor is a high-impedance source that needs to be isolated from loading effects
Insert a follower so R_in ≈ (1+beta)*R_E presents a light load to the sensor
Confirm the follower's R_out ≈ 1/gm + R_S/(1+beta) is low enough to drive the load without sagging

questions.explanation: The design process starts with observing the loading symptom (sag), diagnosing the cause (impedance mismatch), applying the fix (a follower's high input impedance protects the source), and finally verifying the follower's low output impedance can actually drive the target load.

lessons.label: Common Base, Common Gate, and the Cascode

sections.heading: The third configuration: signal in at the emitter or source
sections.body: Common base (CB) and common gate (CG) complete the set of three single-transistor configurations: the base or gate is held at AC ground, the signal drives in at the emitter or source, and the output comes off the collector or drain — the mirror image of a follower's input/output assignment. Driving in at the emitter means the source sees a very low input impedance, approximately 1/gm (a few tens of ohms at typical bias currents), because a small emitter voltage change produces a large change in the exponential BJT current. The current gain from input to output is essentially unity — whatever current is pushed in at the emitter comes back out at the collector, since almost none of it is diverted into the base. On its own, a CB/CG stage is an awkward amplifier (low input impedance is rarely what a source wants to see), but it has one property that makes it indispensable: the output current is nearly independent of collector/drain voltage, which is the seed of a much more useful compound stage.

sections.heading: Why CB/CG stages resist the Miller effect
sections.body: A CE/CS stage's grave weakness at high frequency is the Miller effect: its inverting, high-gain nature multiplies the small base-collector (or gate-drain) capacitance into an enormous apparent input capacitance. A CB/CG stage sidesteps this entirely. Because its base/gate terminal is grounded, there is no signal voltage swing across that same feedback capacitance from input to output — the capacitance simply doesn't see a gain-multiplied voltage difference across it, so there is no Miller multiplication. Combined with the low input impedance (which itself keeps any RC time constant at that node small), CB/CG stages are inherently fast, which is why they show up in RF front ends and in the second half of the next section's compound stage.

sections.heading: The cascode: cascading a CE into a CB
sections.body: The cascode stacks a CE (or CS) stage directly into a CB (or CG) stage: the first transistor converts input voltage into a signal current exactly as it would alone, but instead of dropping that current across a resistor at high impedance (which would create Miller-multiplied capacitance at its collector), it hands the current to a CB stage's low-impedance emitter input. The first transistor's collector barely moves in voltage — CB's input impedance is only ~1/gm — so the Miller effect at the first transistor's base-collector capacitance is nearly eliminated even though the whole stage still delivers CE-like transconductance gain. The second benefit is output resistance: stacking transistors this way raises the output resistance looking into the cascode's drain/collector to roughly gm*ro*ro (the second stage's ro multiplied up by its own gm*ro), far higher than a single stage's ro alone — valuable for building high-gain amplifier stages or accurate current sources. The cost is headroom: two transistors stacked between the rails eat into the available output voltage swing, which can matter in a low-supply-voltage design.

lessons.workedExample: A cascode uses two identical transistors each with gm = 38.7 mA/V (I_C = 1 mA) and ro = 100 kOhm. A single CE stage alone would offer output resistance of just ro = 100 kOhm. The cascode's output resistance is approximately gm*ro*ro = 0.0387 A/V * 100 kOhm * 100 kOhm ≈ 387 MOhm — roughly 3,870 times higher than the single stage. That massive output resistance is exactly what a current-source-loaded high-gain amplifier needs, since gain in that topology is set by gm times the total output resistance at the node; a judge would expect a student building a precision current mirror or a high-gain op-amp-like stage to name the cascode as the tool for exactly this reason.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'why did you stack two transistors instead of using one bigger one?' to check whether a student understands the cascode as solving two named problems at once — Miller capacitance and low output resistance — rather than copying a textbook circuit without knowing why. A weak answer says 'it gives more gain' with no mechanism. A strong answer explains that the top CB/CG transistor holds the bottom transistor's collector/drain nearly constant in voltage (eliminating Miller multiplication of C_mu or C_gd) while simultaneously boosting output resistance to roughly gm*ro*ro, and can name the trade-off: reduced output voltage swing from stacking two devices between the supply rails.

questions.prompt: Approximately what is the input impedance looking into the emitter of a common-base stage?

options.text: r_pi, the same as a common-emitter stage
Approximately 1/gm, typically tens of ohms
Infinite, because the base is grounded
Approximately gm*ro

explanations.a: r_pi is the base input impedance of a CE stage; the emitter input impedance of a CB stage is a different, much smaller quantity.
explanations.b: Correct — a small emitter voltage change drives a large exponential current change, so the emitter looks like a low impedance of about 1/gm.
explanations.c: Grounding the base sets the reference node for the input signal; it does not make the emitter impedance infinite — quite the opposite, it makes it low.
explanations.d: gm*ro is on the order of a stage's intrinsic voltage gain magnitude, not an impedance value in ohms at this node.

questions.prompt: Why does a common-base/common-gate stage avoid the Miller effect that plagues a CE/CS stage?

options.text: CB/CG stages have no base-collector or gate-drain capacitance at all
The base/gate is held at AC ground, so there is no gain-multiplied voltage swing across the feedback capacitance from input to output
CB/CG stages operate only at DC
Miller effect only applies to MOSFETs, not BJTs

explanations.a: The physical capacitance (C_mu or C_gd) is still present in the device; the stage's topology is what prevents it from being multiplied.
explanations.b: Correct — Miller multiplication requires a voltage swing across the feedback capacitance driven by the stage's own gain; grounding the base/gate removes that swing at this node.
explanations.c: CB/CG stages are prized specifically for good high-frequency (AC) behavior, not for DC-only operation.
explanations.d: The Miller effect is a general phenomenon that applies to both BJT (C_mu) and MOSFET (C_gd) inverting/high-impedance stages.

questions.prompt: In a cascode built from two matched transistors each with gm and ro, what is the approximate output resistance looking into the top transistor's collector/drain?

options.text: ro
2*ro
gm*ro*ro
1/gm

explanations.a: ro is the output resistance of a single stage alone; the cascode's whole point is to exceed this.
explanations.b: Simple series combination is not how cascoding raises resistance; the boost is multiplicative through gm, not additive.
explanations.c: Correct — the top CB/CG stage multiplies the bottom stage's ro by its own gm*ro, giving roughly gm*ro*ro, far above a single stage's ro.
explanations.d: 1/gm is the order of magnitude of the CB/CG stage's input impedance at its emitter/source, not the output resistance at its collector/drain.

questions.prompt: Match each property to the stage it primarily describes.

left.text: Unity current gain, low input impedance
Output resistance boosted to roughly gm*ro*ro
Reduced output voltage swing from stacking devices

right.text: Common base / common gate (unity current gain)
Common base / common gate (no Miller multiplication)
Cascode (boosted output resistance)
Cascode (reduced voltage headroom)

questions.explanation: A standalone CB/CG stage has unity current gain, low input impedance, and no Miller multiplication of its own feedback capacitance; the cascode compound stage built from CE-into-CB inherits the anti-Miller property, additionally boosts output resistance to roughly gm*ro*ro, and pays for it with reduced headroom from stacking two devices.

lessons.label: The Miller Effect and Bandwidth

sections.heading: How a few picofarads become hundreds
sections.body: Every BJT has a small base-collector capacitance C_mu (and every MOSFET a gate-drain capacitance C_gd), often just a few picofarads on a datasheet — easy to dismiss as negligible. In a common-emitter or common-source stage, though, that capacitance bridges the input node to an output node swinging with gain -Av in the opposite direction. From the input's point of view, charging that capacitor by one volt requires supplying not just its own charge but also fighting the much larger opposing swing at the other end, because the voltage across the capacitor is changing by (1+|Av|) volts for every one volt at the input. John Miller described this effect in 1920, and the result carries his name: the capacitance appears at the input multiplied by roughly (1+|Av|), so C_in ≈ C_mu * (1 + |Av|). A modest 2 pF junction capacitance in a stage with gain of 100 looks like roughly 200 pF sitting on the input node — enough to dominate the circuit's bandwidth.

sections.heading: Gain, f_T, and the bandwidth you actually get
sections.body: This creates a direct tension: the same gain that makes a CE/CS stage useful also multiplies the input capacitance that limits how fast it can respond. A transistor's own intrinsic speed limit is its transition frequency f_T — the frequency at which its short-circuit current gain falls to 1 — and no amount of circuit cleverness raises a device past that ceiling. But well below f_T, a single high-gain CE/CS stage's usable bandwidth is set primarily by the Miller-inflated input capacitance interacting with the driving source's impedance, not by f_T itself. This is why designers trade gain for bandwidth deliberately: lowering the stage's gain (through degeneration, or by using a cascode to remove Miller multiplication entirely) can push the achievable bandwidth up by roughly the same factor the gain came down — a gain-bandwidth trade a student should expect to measure directly on a scope or Bode plot.

sections.heading: Finding the dominant pole without full algebra
sections.body: A full transfer-function derivation of a multi-node amplifier is painful by hand. Open-circuit time-constant (OCTC) analysis is the back-of-envelope shortcut: for each capacitor in the circuit, find the resistance it sees with every other capacitor open-circuited (removed), multiply resistance by capacitance to get a time constant, and sum all these time constants. The sum approximates 1/omega_(-3dB), the reciprocal of the dominant pole frequency. In practice one term usually dwarfs the others — the Miller-multiplied C_mu sitting on a high-impedance input node is the classic case — and that single R*C product tells you which node to redesign if bandwidth is the bottleneck, without solving the full circuit.

lessons.workedExample: A CE stage has C_mu = 2 pF, gain magnitude |Av| = 80, and is driven from a source with output resistance R_S = 10 kOhm. Miller-multiplied input capacitance is C_in ≈ 2 pF * (1 + 80) = 162 pF. Using OCTC with just this dominant term, the time constant at the input node is R_S * C_in = 10 kOhm * 162 pF ≈ 1.62 microseconds, giving an estimated bandwidth of about 1/(2*pi*1.62 microseconds) ≈ 98 kHz. Swapping the CE stage for a cascode (which removes the Miller multiplication almost entirely, leaving only the unmultiplied C_mu ≈ 2 pF) drops the input time constant to R_S * 2 pF = 20 nanoseconds, pushing the estimated bandwidth up to roughly 8 MHz — an ~80x bandwidth improvement, matching the ~80x gain that was Miller-multiplying the capacitance in the first place.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'why did your high-gain stage roll off in bandwidth so much earlier than the transistor's datasheet f_T?' to separate a student who blames a vague 'parasitic capacitance' from one who can name the actual mechanism. A weak answer shrugs at unexplained frequency roll-off. A strong answer names the Miller effect specifically, states C_in ≈ C_mu*(1+|Av|), and can walk through an OCTC estimate showing which single node's R*C time constant dominates — ideally connecting it to a design fix they actually tried, such as adding a cascode or accepting lower gain for more bandwidth.

questions.prompt: A CE stage has C_mu = 3 pF and voltage gain magnitude |Av| = 50. Approximately what Miller-multiplied capacitance appears at the input?

options.text: 3 pF
50 pF
153 pF

explanations.a: 3 pF is the unmultiplied device capacitance; it ignores the Miller multiplication entirely.
explanations.b: 50 pF would result from multiplying by |Av| alone, but the correct factor is (1+|Av|), not |Av|.
explanations.c: Correct — C_in ≈ C_mu * (1+|Av|) = 3 pF * 51 = 153 pF.
explanations.d: This is the inverse relationship; Miller multiplication increases, not decreases, the apparent input capacitance.

questions.prompt: Why does the Miller effect specifically hit inverting, high-gain stages like CE/CS, but not a follower or a common-base stage nearly as hard?

options.text: Followers and CB/CG stages have no base-collector or gate-drain capacitance

Miller multiplication scales with (1+|Av|); followers have |Av| near 0 (gain just under 1 in the same direction) and CB/CG stages hold the base/gate at AC ground, so neither produces a large opposing voltage swing across the feedback capacitance
Miller effect only occurs above f_T
Followers and CB/CG stages use physically different transistors without C_mu

explanations.a: The physical capacitance exists in any BJT/MOSFET regardless of circuit configuration; what differs is whether the topology multiplies it.
explanations.b: Correct — the multiplication factor (1+|Av|) is small for a near-unity-gain follower and the CB/CG configuration removes the opposing swing at the grounded terminal entirely, so neither multiplies its feedback capacitance the way an inverting high-gain CE/CS stage does.
explanations.c: The Miller effect operates well below f_T; it is a mid-band bandwidth-limiting mechanism, not an above-f_T phenomenon.
explanations.d: The same class of transistor is typically used in all these configurations; the difference is circuit topology, not device type.

questions.prompt: What does open-circuit time-constant (OCTC) analysis approximate, and how is each term computed?
