options.text: The exact transfer function; each term is found by full nodal analysis with all capacitors present simultaneously
The reciprocal of the dominant pole frequency; each term is the resistance a given capacitor sees with all other capacitors open-circuited, multiplied by that capacitance, then summed
The device's f_T; each term is a ratio of transconductances
The exact phase response; each term requires solving a full differential equation

explanations.a: OCTC is explicitly an approximation shortcut, not a full nodal solution with all capacitors active at once — that would require solving the complete transfer function.
explanations.b: Correct — sum each capacitor's R*C time constant, computed with every other capacitor open-circuited, to approximate 1/omega_(-3dB).
explanations.c: f_T is a separate device parameter (unity current-gain frequency); OCTC does not compute it.
explanations.d: OCTC avoids a full differential-equation solution; that is precisely why it is used as a back-of-envelope estimate.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of estimating a CE stage's bandwidth using the Miller effect and OCTC.

items.text: Find the stage's voltage gain magnitude |Av|
Compute the Miller-multiplied input capacitance C_in ≈ C_mu*(1+|Av|)
Find the resistance the input node sees (e.g., the driving source's R_S)
Multiply R_S by C_in to get the dominant time constant, then estimate bandwidth as 1/(2*pi*R*C)

questions.explanation: You need the gain first to compute the Miller multiplication factor, then apply it to C_mu to get C_in, then pair that capacitance with the resistance at its node to form the dominant RC time constant that sets the estimated -3dB bandwidth.

lessons.label: The Differential Pair

sections.heading: One tail current, split two ways
sections.body: A differential pair takes two matched transistors, ties their emitters (or sources) together to a single tail current source, and drives each base (or gate) with one half of a differential input. With no input difference, the fixed tail current I_TAIL splits evenly, I_TAIL/2 down each side. As the input difference V_id grows, one transistor is driven harder and steals a larger share of the fixed tail current from its partner — the pair does not create more current from nothing, it only redistributes what the tail source already supplies. This built-in current-conservation property is what makes the differential pair the near-universal front end of op-amps and comparators: it responds to the difference between two signals while, to first order, ignoring whatever the two inputs do in common.

sections.heading: The transfer curve and its linear range
sections.body: For a BJT pair, the exponential device law makes the split follow a hyperbolic tangent: I_C1 - I_C2 = I_TAIL * tanh(V_id / 2V_T). Near V_id = 0 this curve is nearly straight, giving a differential gain of gm*R_C per side (the same gm*R_C from the single-stage CE result, since each transistor locally behaves like a degenerated CE stage around the shared tail node) — but the tanh function bends noticeably once V_id approaches roughly 2*V_T, or about 50 mV at 300 K, and by around 100 mV (4*V_T) the pair is essentially fully switched, with nearly all the tail current diverted to one side. A MOSFET pair follows a square-law curve instead of tanh, giving a wider linear range that scales with the devices' overdrive voltage V_OV rather than being pinned to the fixed ~50 mV of a BJT pair — one of the real trade-offs between bipolar and MOS front ends.

sections.heading: Common mode, CMRR, and offset from real-world mismatch
sections.body: If both inputs move together (a common-mode signal) rather than differentially, an ideal tail current source holds I_TAIL fixed, so the split stays even and the differential output does not move at all — common-mode gain would be zero. A real tail source has finite output resistance R_tail, not infinite, so a common-mode input does slightly modulate the total tail current, producing a small but nonzero common-mode gain. The ratio of differential gain to this residual common-mode gain is the common-mode rejection ratio (CMRR), and it improves directly with a larger R_tail — which is exactly why real tail current sources are built from cascoded current mirrors rather than a plain resistor. Finally, no two transistors or resistors are perfectly identical: a mismatch in V_BE (or V_th for MOSFETs) between the two sides, or a mismatch between the two R_C/R_D loads, shows up as an input offset voltage — the differential input required to force the output back to its nominal zero-difference point even with V_id truly at zero. This offset, typically a few millivolts for a discrete BJT pair, is a direct, measurable fingerprint of manufacturing mismatch.

lessons.workedExample: A BJT differential pair is biased with I_TAIL = 2 mA (I_C = 1 mA per side at balance), R_C = 5 kOhm each, and R_tail = 500 kOhm. Differential gain per side is gm*R_C = 38.7 mA/V * 5 kOhm ≈ 193 (matching the single CE-stage result). Near V_id = 0 the curve tracks this gain closely, but as V_id approaches 50 mV (about 2*V_T at 300 K), the tanh curve visibly bends and the incremental gain drops well below 193 — a student sweeping V_id on a curve tracer would see the output clearly flattening out beyond this point, well before the pair fully switches around 100 mV. If the two R_C resistors differ by just 1% (5000 Ohm vs 5050 Ohm), the resulting output imbalance at V_id = 0 corresponds to an input-referred offset voltage on the order of a few hundred microvolts to low millivolts, depending on the exact mismatch and gm.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'why does your differential pair's output flatten out at larger input differences, and what determines exactly where it flattens?' to test whether a student can connect a curve-tracer observation to the underlying math. A weak answer says the amplifier 'saturates' with no further detail. A strong answer names the tanh transfer function, states that the roughly linear region extends to about ±50 mV (±2*V_T) at 300 K for a BJT pair, and can explain that CMRR and offset trace back to two distinct physical causes — finite tail resistance for CMRR, and device/resistor mismatch for offset — rather than treating both as the same vague 'imperfection'.

questions.prompt: In a balanced BJT differential pair with I_TAIL = 2 mA and no input difference, what is I_C in each transistor?

options.text: 2 mA in each
1 mA in each
0 mA in each, until a differential input is applied
It depends on beta, not on I_TAIL

explanations.a: This would double the tail current; the tail source supplies a fixed total that is split, not duplicated, between the two sides.
explanations.b: Correct — with a balanced pair and zero input difference, I_TAIL splits evenly, giving I_TAIL/2 = 1 mA per side.
explanations.c: The tail current flows continuously through whichever combination of the two transistors is conducting; it does not sit at zero absent an input difference.
explanations.d: The split at balance is set by the fixed I_TAIL and the pair's symmetry, not directly by beta.

questions.prompt: Approximately over what input-difference range does a BJT differential pair's transfer curve stay close to linear, at 300 K?

options.text: About ±5 mV
About ±50 mV
About ±500 mV
About ±5 V

explanations.a: This underestimates the linear range; ±5 mV is far tighter than the tanh curve's actual near-linear region.
explanations.b: Correct — the tanh transfer curve I_TAIL*tanh(V_id/2V_T) stays reasonably linear out to roughly ±2*V_T, about ±50 mV at 300 K, before visibly bending.
explanations.c: By ±500 mV the pair is already fully switched (essentially all tail current on one side), far past the linear region.
explanations.d: ±5 V is wildly beyond any meaningful part of the transfer curve for a typical differential pair supply range.

questions.prompt: Why does increasing the tail current source's output resistance R_tail improve CMRR?

options.text: It increases the differential gain directly
A higher R_tail holds the total tail current more constant when both inputs move together, suppressing common-mode gain while leaving differential gain unaffected
It reduces V_BE mismatch between the two transistors
It has no effect on CMRR, only on offset voltage

explanations.a: Differential gain (gm*R_C per side) does not depend on R_tail; R_tail's role is specifically about common-mode behavior.
explanations.b: Correct — a higher-impedance tail source better approximates an ideal fixed current, so a common-mode input signal produces less change in total tail current and thus less common-mode output swing, raising CMRR = differential gain / common-mode gain.
explanations.c: V_BE mismatch is a separate physical effect (device-to-device variation), unrelated to the tail source's output resistance.
explanations.d: R_tail specifically affects common-mode gain and therefore CMRR; offset voltage instead comes from device and resistor mismatch.

questions.prompt: Match each differential-pair non-ideality to its physical origin.

left.text: Gain compression beyond ~50 mV input difference

right.text: Finite tail current source output resistance
V_BE (or V_th) or load-resistor mismatch between the two sides
The tanh (or square-law) shape of the transfer curve bending away from its linear tangent

questions.explanation: Common-mode gain traces to the tail source's finite output resistance; input offset voltage traces to real device and resistor mismatch; gain compression at larger input differences traces to the transfer curve's inherent nonlinearity away from V_id = 0.

lessons.label: Cascading Stages and Output Stages

sections.heading: Why cascaded gain never quite reaches the product of open-circuit gains
sections.body: Chaining two amplifier stages promises multiplied gain — stage one's Av1 times stage two's Av2 — but that product only holds if stage two presents an infinite load to stage one, which real stages never do. Every stage has some finite output resistance R_out1, and the next stage has some finite input resistance R_in2, and those two form a voltage divider: the signal that actually reaches stage two is attenuated by a factor of R_in2/(R_in2+R_out1) before stage two even sees it. So the real cascaded gain is Av1 * [R_in2/(R_in2+R_out1)] * Av2, always somewhat below the naive open-circuit product. This is exactly why the follower stages from earlier in this unit matter here: inserting a follower between a high-output-impedance CE stage and a low-input-impedance next stage recovers most of the lost gain, because the follower's whole job is making that voltage-divider penalty small.

sections.heading: Output stages: the last link before the real-world load
sections.body: The final stage of an amplifier chain has a different job than internal gain stages — it must deliver real current into a low-impedance load like a speaker without wasting excessive power as heat. Class A biases the output transistor to conduct continuously through the entire signal cycle, which gives excellent linearity (no discontinuity where a device switches off) but is inherently wasteful: with a resistive load, the theoretical maximum efficiency is only 25%, meaning at least three-quarters of the delivered power is dissipated as heat in the transistor and bias resistor even in the best case. Class B instead uses two complementary transistors, each conducting for only half the cycle (one for positive swings, one for negative), which raises the theoretical maximum efficiency to about 78.5% — a large practical win for anything battery-powered or heat-constrained.

sections.heading: Crossover distortion and the class-AB compromise
sections.body: Class B's efficiency comes at a cost: near the zero crossing, where the signal hands off from one transistor to the other, both devices are near cutoff and each needs roughly a diode-drop of input voltage before it starts conducting again, producing a small dead zone in the output near zero — crossover distortion, audible as a rough, buzzy quality on quiet passages. Class AB fixes this by adding a small quiescent bias current, just enough to keep both output transistors slightly on even at the zero crossing, so there is no dead zone to cross. This sacrifices a little of Class B's efficiency (the quiescent current itself dissipates some power even at idle) in exchange for eliminating the audible crossover artifact, which is why nearly every real push-pull audio output stage runs class AB rather than pure class B, trading a few points of efficiency for linearity exactly the way single-stage degeneration traded gain for linearity earlier in this unit.

lessons.workedExample: A CE first stage has open-circuit gain Av1 = -150 and output resistance R_out1 = 4 kOhm. It drives a second CE stage with input resistance R_in2 = 2 kOhm (r_pi) and open-circuit gain Av2 = -80. The naive product Av1*Av2 = 12,000. The real loading divider is R_in2/(R_in2+R_out1) = 2k/6k = 0.333, so actual cascaded gain is -150 * 0.333 * -80 ≈ 4,000 — only a third of the naive estimate. Inserting an emitter follower with R_in ≈ 150 kOhm between the two stages changes the divider to roughly 150k/154k ≈ 0.974, recovering the cascaded gain to about -150 * 0.974 * -80 ≈ 11,700, close to the full open-circuit product.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'you measured less gain from your two-stage amplifier than Av1 times Av2 predicted — why?' to see whether a student understands interstage loading as a real, quantifiable effect rather than dismissing the gap as 'component tolerance.' A weak answer has no model for the discrepancy. A strong answer names the voltage-divider loading term R_in2/(R_in2+R_out1) explicitly and, for an audio-output question, can distinguish class A, B, and AB by their efficiency numbers (25% and 78.5% being the two textbook ceilings) and explain crossover distortion as the physical reason class AB exists as a compromise rather than always running pure class B.

questions.prompt: Why is real cascaded gain (Av1 followed by Av2) always less than or equal to the simple product Av1*Av2?

options.text: Transistors lose gain with age
The finite R_out1 of the first stage and finite R_in2 of the second stage form a voltage divider that attenuates the signal handed between stages
Av1*Av2 is only a rough guess with no physical basis
Cascading always inverts the signal an extra time, canceling some gain

explanations.a: Device aging is unrelated to this gap; the effect is present even with brand-new, ideal-tolerance transistors.
explanations.b: Correct — the loading divider R_in2/(R_in2+R_out1) is the specific, quantifiable mechanism, and it is always less than or equal to 1.
explanations.c: Av1*Av2 is the correct open-circuit (unloaded) prediction; it has a real physical basis, it simply assumes an infinite-impedance connection between stages that never exists in practice.
explanations.d: Extra inversions change the sign of the gain, not its magnitude; they do not explain the reduced magnitude from loading.

questions.prompt: What is the theoretical maximum efficiency of a class A output stage with a resistive load, and why is it so much lower than class B?

options.text: 25%, because the output transistor conducts continuously through the whole cycle, dissipating significant power even when delivering little signal
78.5%, the same as class B
100%, because class A has no crossover distortion
0%, because class A never delivers usable output power

explanations.a: Correct — continuous conduction through the full cycle, even during low-signal or zero-signal portions, caps resistive-load class A efficiency at 25%, versus 78.5% for class B's two-transistor half-cycle-each scheme.
explanations.b: Class A and class B have different theoretical ceilings precisely because of their different conduction patterns; they are not the same number.
explanations.c: Class A's efficiency limitation is unrelated to crossover distortion, which is a class B/AB phenomenon; class A's ceiling is capped well below 100% by continuous conduction.
explanations.d: Class A stages do deliver real output power; the issue is how much power is wasted as heat relative to what is delivered, not that no output power is produced.

questions.prompt: What causes crossover distortion in a pure class B output stage, and how does class AB address it?

options.text: Both output transistors are near cutoff at the zero crossing, needing a diode-drop of input before conducting again, leaving a small dead zone; class AB adds a small quiescent bias current so both transistors stay slightly on through the crossing
The load impedance changes sign at zero crossing; class AB adds a capacitor to compensate
Crossover distortion is caused by Miller capacitance; class AB removes it with a cascode
Class B has no crossover distortion; class AB was invented purely to save power

explanations.a: Correct — the two complementary transistors handing off near zero output each need to overcome their own turn-on voltage, producing a dead zone that a small class-AB quiescent bias current eliminates by keeping both slightly conducting.
explanations.b: Load impedance does not change sign at the zero crossing in this way; the distortion is a transistor turn-on effect, not a load-impedance effect.
explanations.c: Miller capacitance and cascoding are separate topics (interstage/high-frequency behavior), unrelated to the output-stage crossover mechanism.
explanations.d: Class B does exhibit crossover distortion; class AB exists specifically to reduce it, trading away some efficiency rather than gaining it.

questions.prompt: Order these output-stage design considerations from most linear/least efficient to least linear/most efficient.

items.text: Class A (continuous conduction, resistive-load max efficiency 25%)
Class AB (small quiescent bias, no dead zone, efficiency between the two)
Class B (half-cycle conduction each device, max efficiency 78.5%, crossover distortion present)

questions.explanation: Class A is the most linear (no conduction dead zone) but least efficient at 25% maximum; class AB sits in between by adding just enough quiescent bias to avoid crossover distortion; class B is the most efficient at up to 78.5% but suffers crossover distortion from its dead zone at the zero crossing.

units.label: Op-Amp Circuits and Real Device Limits

lessons.label: The Ideal Op-Amp and the Virtual Short

sections.heading: Two rules that fall out of a limit, not out of magic
sections.body: The two golden rules of ideal op-amp analysis (no current flows into either input, and negative feedback forces the two inputs to the same voltage) are usually handed to students as axioms. They are not axioms; they are the limiting case of a real amplifier as its open-loop gain A_OL goes to infinity. A real op-amp is a differential amplifier: Vout = A_OL(V+ - V-), with A_OL commonly 10^5 to 10^6 (the classic uA741 specifies roughly 200,000, about 106 dB). Close a negative-feedback loop around that amplifier and something forces V+ - V- to shrink: if V- ever drifted even a millivolt away from V+, a gain of 200,000 would try to swing the output by 200 V, which the supply rails cannot do, so the loop reacts by adjusting the output until the error is driven back down to microvolts. As A_OL goes to infinity, that residual error goes to zero, and V+ = V- becomes exact: the virtual short.

sections.heading: Why the inputs draw (almost) no current
sections.body: The second rule comes from input impedance, not gain. A bipolar-input op-amp like the 741 draws tens to hundreds of nanoamps of base current at each input; a JFET or CMOS input op-amp draws picoamps to femtoamps. Because that current is orders of magnitude below the milliamp-scale currents flowing in typical feedback resistors, treating it as zero introduces negligible error in a first-pass hand analysis, even though it becomes the dominant DC error source once you scale resistors up into the megohm range.

sections.heading: Where the virtual short quietly stops being true
sections.body: Students misdiagnose circuits in three recurring situations. First, open loop: with no feedback path from output to the inverting input, there is nothing to force V+ = V-; any tiny input difference gets multiplied by A_OL and slams the output against a supply rail. Second, saturation: even with feedback present, if the required output voltage exceeds what the supply rails allow, the op-amp cannot produce it, the loop breaks, and V- stops tracking V+. Third, positive feedback: comparators and Schmitt triggers deliberately feed the output back to the non-inverting input, which is regenerative rather than corrective, so any imbalance grows instead of shrinking and the output is driven to whichever rail the imbalance favors. In all three cases, writing V+ = V- and solving a linear equation gives a wrong answer, because the assumption that created that equation, negative feedback holding the error near zero, no longer holds.

lessons.workedExample: A student builds a non-inverting amplifier with Rf = 100 k and Rin = 1 k, expecting gain 101, but wires the feedback resistor from the output to the non-inverting input instead of the inverting input by mistake. The circuit now has positive feedback: any noise pushes V+ away from V-, the loop amplifies that difference instead of canceling it, and the output rails to +Vcc or -Vcc almost immediately. Probing the output with a scope shows a clean DC level pinned near a supply rail rather than an amplified sine wave. Recognizing this as a broken virtual-short assumption (positive feedback, not negative) is the fast diagnostic; tracing wires pin-by-pin is the slow one.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about the virtual short because it is the single assumption underlying every op-amp gain equation in the project, and misapplying it in one of the three failure modes (open loop, saturation, positive feedback) is the most common silent error in student circuits. A weak answer recites V+ = V- as a rule of thumb and cannot say when it fails. A strong answer explains that it is a consequence of high open-loop gain plus negative feedback, and can immediately diagnose a rail-stuck output as either saturation or a positive-feedback wiring mistake rather than treating both as the same kind of failure.

questions.prompt: Why does negative feedback force V+ approximately equal to V- in a real op-amp circuit?

options.text: Because the op-amp's inputs are physically wired together
Because the very high open-loop gain amplifies any input difference into an output swing the feedback network uses to cancel that difference
Because op-amps contain a comparator that forces the two inputs to match
Because the input bias current is exactly zero

explanations.a: The inputs are separate, high-impedance terminals; they are not physically connected.
explanations.b: Correct — with A_OL on the order of 10^5-10^6, even a microvolt input difference would demand an output swing the supply rails cannot deliver, so the feedback loop settles until the input difference is negligible.
explanations.c: The virtual short is a consequence of linear negative feedback around a high-gain amplifier, not a separate comparator function.
explanations.d: Bias current being small explains why no current flows into the inputs (the other golden rule), not why the input voltages match.

questions.prompt: An op-amp circuit's output is measured pinned at +Vcc regardless of the input signal. Which of the three virtual-short failure modes could explain this WITHOUT any wiring mistake?

options.text: Bias current cancellation
Output saturation because the demanded output exceeds the supply rail
A slightly high gain-bandwidth product
Input offset voltage of exactly zero

explanations.a: Bias current cancellation is a DC error-reduction technique, not a cause of rail-stuck output.
explanations.b: Correct — if the required output voltage exceeds the rails, the op-amp cannot produce it, the feedback loop breaks, and the output sits at the rail regardless of correctly-wired negative feedback.
explanations.c: Gain-bandwidth product affects AC bandwidth, not whether the output can physically exceed the supply rails.
explanations.d: Zero offset voltage would make the circuit behave more ideally, not push the output to a rail.

questions.prompt: Match each situation to why the virtual short fails there.

right.text: No feedback path exists to correct any input difference
The feedback loop is physically unable to reach the voltage it needs to
Feedback reinforces rather than cancels the input difference

questions.explanation: Open-loop has no correcting path at all; saturation has a correcting path that cannot reach the required output voltage; positive feedback has a path that amplifies the error instead of canceling it.

questions.prompt: Why is it reasonable to treat op-amp input current as zero in a first-pass hand analysis?

options.text: Because input current is genuinely always zero
Because nanoamp-to-femtoamp input currents are negligible next to the milliamp-scale currents typical feedback resistors carry
Because feedback forces input current to zero, just like it forces voltage to match
Because only inverting-input current matters

explanations.a: Real op-amps draw measurable bias current (nA for bipolar inputs, pA-fA for FET/CMOS inputs); it is only approximately zero.
explanations.b: Correct — the approximation is good because of the scale mismatch between input current and the currents flowing through typical resistor values, not because the current is truly zero.
explanations.c: Input current is set by the input transistor's biasing, independent of the feedback network; feedback controls voltage, not input current.
explanations.d: Both inputs draw a comparably small current in a well-matched op-amp; it is not exclusive to one input.

lessons.label: The Core Configurations

sections.heading: Inverting and non-inverting: same golden rules, opposite input impedance
sections.body: The inverting amplifier grounds the non-inverting input, so the virtual short pins the inverting input at 0 V (virtual ground). Kirchhoff's current law at that node gives Vin/Rin = -Vout/Rf, so gain = -Rf/Rin. Because the inverting input sits at a fixed virtual ground, the input impedance the source sees is simply Rin, no more. The non-inverting amplifier instead applies Vin directly to the non-inverting input; the virtual short makes the inverting-input node track Vin, and the same feedback divider gives gain = 1 + Rf/Rin. Here the source drives the op-amp's actual input terminal, so it sees the op-amp's own enormous input impedance (megohms to teraohms), not a resistor. This impedance contrast is the practical reason designers pick one topology over the other: inverting amps are easy to sum and offer a fixed, known load; non-inverting amps preserve a high-impedance source.

sections.heading: Buffers and summing amplifiers as special cases
sections.body: Set Rf = 0 and Rin = infinity in the non-inverting formula and gain collapses to exactly 1: the voltage follower, or buffer, whose entire purpose is impedance transformation rather than voltage gain, isolating a high-impedance source from a low-impedance load. The summing amplifier extends the inverting topology by feeding multiple input resistors into the same virtual-ground node; superposition at that node gives Vout = -Rf(V1/R1 + V2/R2 + ...), so each channel is weighted independently by its own resistor, a technique that predates digital mixing and was standard in analog audio consoles and analog computers.

sections.heading: The difference amplifier: correct on paper, limited by resistors in practice
sections.body: A four-resistor difference amplifier subtracts two inputs with gain R2/R1, provided the two resistor ratios on each input leg are matched exactly. Real resistors are not exact: even 1% tolerance parts can sit anywhere within that 1% band, and a mismatch between the two ratio pairs directly degrades common-mode rejection ratio (CMRR), the amplifier's ability to reject a signal common to both inputs while passing the difference. The op-amp itself may be specified with CMRR above 100 dB, but the discrete difference amplifier built around it inherits the resistor network's precision, not the chip's: worst-case CMRR follows CMRR ≈ (1+Av)/(4·tolerance), and for a unity-gain stage built from ordinary 1% resistors that works out to roughly 34 dB, a 65-70 dB shortfall from what the silicon could deliver. Reaching higher CMRR demands 0.1% or laser-trimmed resistor networks, or abandoning the discrete topology altogether for an integrated instrumentation amplifier.

lessons.workedExample: A student builds a difference amplifier to reject 60 Hz common-mode hum picked up by long sensor leads, using an op-amp datasheet-specified at 100 dB CMRR and four 10 k, 1% resistors (R1=R3=10k, R2=R4=10k, unity gain). On the bench, injecting a 1 Vpp common-mode signal into both inputs simultaneously, they measure roughly 15-20 mVpp leaking through to the output, corresponding to a CMRR near 34 dB rather than the chip's 100 dB. Swapping in 0.1% resistors on the same op-amp drops the leakage by roughly a factor of ten, confirming the resistor network, not the amplifier, was the bottleneck.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing CMRR in a difference-amp project is checking whether the student understands that a datasheet spec describes the chip in isolation, not the circuit as built. A weak answer quotes the op-amp's 100 dB CMRR as if it applies to the whole board. A strong answer identifies the resistor-matching mechanism, estimates the achievable CMRR from the resistor tolerance actually used, and explains the fix (tighter-tolerance resistors, trimming, or switching to an instrumentation amplifier) rather than blaming the chip for noise the resistors let through.

questions.prompt: Why does the inverting amplifier present an input impedance of exactly Rin to the source, while the non-inverting amplifier presents the op-amp's own (much higher) input impedance?

options.text: Because the inverting configuration always uses larger resistors
Because the inverting input sits at virtual ground, so the source only ever drives current into Rin; the non-inverting input connects the source straight to the op-amp's high-impedance terminal
Because non-inverting amplifiers do not obey the virtual-short rule
Because inverting amplifiers have no feedback resistor

explanations.a: Resistor size is a design choice, not the reason for the impedance difference.
explanations.b: Correct — the virtual ground in the inverting case fixes the node the source drives into, so Rin alone sets the impedance; the non-inverting case has the source driving the op-amp input terminal directly.
explanations.c: Both configurations rely on the virtual short; the impedance difference comes from where the source connects, not from which rule applies.
explanations.d: The inverting amplifier requires a feedback resistor (Rf) to set its gain; it just is not what determines input impedance.

questions.prompt: A difference amplifier uses an op-amp specified at 100+ dB CMRR but ordinary 1% resistors. What CMRR should the student realistically expect from the built circuit?

options.text: Still above 100 dB, since the chip sets the ceiling
Near 34 dB, because resistor mismatch, not the chip, becomes the limiting factor
0 dB, because 1% resistors make CMRR undefined
Exactly the resistor tolerance percentage expressed in dB

explanations.a: The chip's CMRR is a ceiling only if the surrounding resistor network is at least as precise; 1% resistors fall far short of that.
explanations.b: Correct — worst-case mismatch between the two resistor ratio legs with 1% parts typically caps CMRR near 34 dB (CMRR ≈ (1+Av)/(4·tolerance)) regardless of the op-amp's own spec.
explanations.c: CMRR is degraded, not undefined; the circuit still rejects most, just not nearly all, of the common-mode signal.
explanations.d: CMRR in dB is not a direct percentage conversion of resistor tolerance; it comes from the ratio-mismatch analysis, landing near 34 dB for 1% parts, close to (not far below) what a naive tolerance-derived guess of 40 dB would suggest.

questions.prompt: Match each op-amp configuration to its output equation.

right.text: Vout = -Rf/Rin * Vin
Vout = (1 + Rf/Rin) * Vin
Vout = Vin
Vout = -Rf(V1/R1 + V2/R2)

questions.explanation: Inverting gain is -Rf/Rin from virtual-ground KCL; non-inverting gain is 1+Rf/Rin; a buffer is the non-inverting case with Rf=0 giving unity gain; a summing amplifier weights each input independently at the shared virtual-ground node.

questions.prompt: What is the primary purpose of a unity-gain voltage follower (buffer)?

options.text: To amplify the input signal by a large factor
To invert the input signal without changing its magnitude
To isolate a high-impedance source from a low-impedance load without adding voltage gain
To sum multiple input signals together

explanations.a: A follower has gain of exactly 1; it provides no voltage amplification.
explanations.b: A follower is non-inverting; the output tracks the input in phase, not inverted.
explanations.c: Correct — with Rf=0 and Rin=infinity, gain collapses to 1, and the circuit's value is presenting a high input impedance to the source while driving a low-impedance load from the op-amp's low output impedance.
explanations.d: Summing multiple inputs is the job of a summing amplifier, a different topology built from the inverting configuration.

lessons.label: Integrators, Differentiators, and Nonlinear Blocks

sections.heading: Swapping a resistor for a capacitor changes algebra into calculus
sections.body: Replace the feedback resistor of an inverting amplifier with a capacitor and the virtual-ground KCL equation becomes Vout = -(1/RC) times the time-integral of Vin: an integrator. Replace the input resistor with a capacitor instead and you get Vout = -RC times the time-derivative of Vin: a differentiator. In the frequency domain, the integrator's transfer function is -1/(sRC), which on a Bode plot is a straight line falling at -20 dB/decade through all frequencies, crossing 0 dB at f = 1/(2*pi*RC), with gain formally infinite at DC. The differentiator is the mirror image, -sRC, rising at +20 dB/decade without limit as frequency increases.

sections.heading: Why a bare integrator ramps away and a bare differentiator screams
sections.body: Infinite DC gain is not a theoretical curiosity, it is a circuit that will not stay put. Any real op-amp has a nonzero input offset voltage, typically low millivolts for a general-purpose part; the integrator treats that offset exactly as it treats a real input signal and integrates it continuously, so the output ramps steadily toward a supply rail and sticks there, even with the input grounded. The standard fix is a resistor Rf placed in parallel with the integrating capacitor, which caps the DC gain at -Rf/Rin instead of infinity (the circuit still integrates well above the corner frequency set by Rf and C, but no longer accumulates offset without bound). The differentiator's problem is the opposite extreme: +20 dB/decade gain with no ceiling means any high-frequency noise on the input, far more of it exists than most students expect, gets amplified more than the signal itself, often enough to make the circuit oscillate. The fix is a small resistor in series with the input capacitor, which flattens the response above a chosen frequency and turns an unbounded differentiator into a stable one that still differentiates the frequencies that matter.

sections.heading: Log and antilog amplifiers exploit a diode's exponential curve
sections.body: A diode's current-voltage relationship is exponential, I = Is(e^(V/Vt) - 1), where Vt = kT/q is about 26 mV at room temperature. Placing a diode or diode-connected transistor in the feedback path of an inverting amplifier makes Vout proportional to the logarithm of Iin; placing it in the input path instead produces an antilog (exponential) amplifier. Both circuits are directly useful for compressing wide-dynamic-range signals, but both inherit the diode's strong temperature dependence through Vt and the saturation current Is, so precision log/antilog ICs add temperature-compensating networks or matched transistor pairs rather than relying on a single bare diode.

lessons.workedExample: A student builds a bare integrator with R = 10 k and C = 100 nF, expecting a clean triangle wave from a square-wave input, and grounds the input to test the baseline first. Instead of sitting at 0 V, the output creeps upward over a few seconds and pins at the positive rail. The op-amp's few-millivolt input offset voltage, divided by RC = 1 ms, is being integrated continuously: even 2 mV of offset produces a ramp rate of roughly 2 mV / 1 ms = 2 V/s, enough to hit a 12 V rail in about 6 seconds. Adding a 1 M feedback resistor across the capacitor caps the DC gain at -100 (Rf/Rin), which holds the output near zero at DC while leaving the integration behavior intact for frequencies well above 1/(2*pi*Rf*C).
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks why a bare integrator drifts because it tests whether the student actually built and debugged the circuit rather than simulating an idealized version. A weak answer treats the ramp as a mystery or a broken part. A strong answer names input offset voltage as the cause, explains why infinite DC gain amplifies it without bound, and describes the shunt-resistor fix in terms of the corner frequency it sets, showing they diagnosed a real bench symptom rather than reciting the ideal transfer function.

questions.prompt: Why does a bare op-amp integrator's output ramp toward a supply rail even with the input grounded?

options.text: Because the capacitor is charged from the factory
Because the op-amp's input offset voltage is continuously integrated by the circuit's infinite DC gain
Because grounding the input creates a short circuit that damages the op-amp
Because integrators only work with AC signals

explanations.a: Capacitors are not pre-charged; the ramp is generated by the circuit's own operation.
explanations.b: Correct — the integrator's transfer function -1/(sRC) has infinite gain at DC, so even a few millivolts of input offset voltage gets integrated continuously, producing a steadily rising output.
explanations.c: Grounding the input is a normal test condition and does not short or damage the op-amp.
explanations.d: Integrators respond to DC as well as AC; the infinite DC gain is precisely the problem here.

questions.prompt: What is the standard fix for a bare differentiator's tendency to amplify high-frequency noise and oscillate?

options.text: Add a resistor in parallel with the feedback capacitor
Add a resistor in series with the input capacitor to cap the high-frequency gain
Remove the feedback resistor entirely
Increase the input capacitor's value

explanations.a: A parallel resistor across the feedback capacitor is the integrator's fix (capping DC gain), not the differentiator's.
explanations.b: Correct — a series input resistor introduces a pole that flattens the +20 dB/decade rise above a chosen frequency, taming high-frequency noise gain while preserving differentiation at lower frequencies.
explanations.c: The differentiator has no separate feedback resistor in its bare form (feedback is through the resistor, input is through the capacitor); removing components does not address unbounded gain.
explanations.d: Increasing the input capacitor increases differentiator gain further, worsening the noise problem rather than fixing it.

questions.prompt: Match each circuit to its ideal transfer function.

right.text: -1/(sRC), falling at -20 dB/decade
-sRC, rising at +20 dB/decade

questions.explanation: The integrator's capacitor in the feedback path yields -1/(sRC); the differentiator's capacitor in the input path yields -sRC, the mirror-image slope.

questions.prompt: Why are precision log and antilog amplifiers sensitive to temperature?

options.text: Because op-amps only work correctly at room temperature
Because the diode's exponential I-V relationship depends on the thermal voltage Vt = kT/q and on a temperature-dependent saturation current
Because logarithmic circuits require liquid cooling to function
Because feedback capacitors change value sharply with temperature

explanations.a: Op-amps have a wide operating temperature range; the sensitivity here is specific to the diode's exponential relationship, not the op-amp generally.
explanations.b: Correct — Vt is directly proportional to absolute temperature, and the diode's saturation current Is is also strongly temperature-dependent, so both terms of the exponential relationship drift with temperature.
explanations.c: No cooling is required; the issue is a design/compensation concern, not a thermal-management one.
explanations.d: The temperature sensitivity comes from the diode's exponential curve used to create the log/antilog function, not from capacitor drift.

lessons.label: Instrumentation Amplifiers and Precision Front Ends

sections.heading: Three op-amps, one gain resistor
sections.body: The classic instrumentation amplifier (in-amp) topology uses three op-amps arranged in two stages. The first stage is a pair of non-inverting buffer amplifiers, one per input, cross-coupled through a single external resistor R_G that ties their two inverting inputs together through two fixed internal resistors R. Because each input drives a non-inverting op-amp terminal directly, the in-amp presents very high input impedance at both inputs, unlike a plain four-resistor difference amplifier whose input impedance depends on the divider resistors themselves. The second stage is an ordinary difference amplifier that subtracts the two buffered outputs. The overall differential gain works out to G = 1 + 2R/R_G: a single external resistor sets the gain of the entire circuit, which is why commercial in-amps like the Analog Devices AD620 or the Texas Instruments (Burr-Brown) INA128 expose just one gain-setting pin.

sections.heading: Why the common-mode rejection does not depend on resistors the user picks
sections.body: In a discrete difference amplifier, CMRR is capped by how well the user's four external resistors match, and 1% parts leave real dynamic-range loss on the table. The three-op-amp in-amp sidesteps that dependency by construction: the first stage passes common-mode signals through both buffers at unity gain (common-mode is present identically at both buffer outputs, differential signal is what gets amplified by 1 + 2R/R_G), so R_G's exact value affects gain but not common-mode behavior. The critical matching that determines CMRR happens in the second-stage difference amplifier's four resistors, and in an integrated in-amp those resistors are fabricated and laser-trimmed on the same die at the factory, achieving matching far tighter than any 1% or even 0.1% external resistor network a student could assemble on a breadboard. This is why parts in the AD620/INA128 class specify CMRR above 100 dB at a gain of 100, a figure a hand-built difference amplifier with external resistors essentially cannot reach.

sections.heading: Scope of the topology
sections.body: This lesson covers the amplifier topology itself, the buffer-plus-difference-amp architecture and why its CMRR mechanism is structurally different from a discrete difference amp's. The sensor-side circuitry that typically feeds an in-amp, a resistive bridge, its excitation source, and any additional signal conditioning, is a separate concern that belongs with sensor and instrumentation topics rather than with amplifier design; a project that pairs an in-amp with a bridge sensor is combining two distinct subsystems, each with its own error budget.

lessons.workedExample: A student needs a gain of 100 to amplify a small differential sensor signal riding on several volts of common-mode noise. Using an AD620-class in-amp, the datasheet gain equation G = 1 + 49.4 k/R_G solved for G = 100 gives R_G approximately 499 ohms, a single resistor to select. On the bench, injecting a shared 2 Vpp common-mode signal into both inputs while looking at the output shows only a few hundred microvolts of feedthrough, consistent with the datasheet's CMRR spec well above 100 dB at that gain, a result the student could not have reached with a discrete four-resistor difference amplifier and standard-tolerance parts.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks why the project used an instrumentation amplifier instead of a plain op-amp difference amplifier to test whether the student understands the actual mechanism, not just that in-amps are the fancier part. A weak answer says the in-amp is more accurate because it is a specialized chip. A strong answer explains that the difference amplifier's CMRR is capped by external resistor matching while the in-amp's critical matching is trimmed on-die at manufacture, so the gain-setting resistor the student chooses affects gain but not the CMRR ceiling.

questions.prompt: In the three-op-amp instrumentation amplifier, what does the single external resistor R_G primarily set?

options.text: The overall differential gain of the circuit
The common-mode rejection ratio
The output offset voltage
The input bias current

explanations.a: Correct — G = 1 + 2R/R_G, so a single external resistor directly sets the differential gain of the whole in-amp.
explanations.b: CMRR is determined mainly by the second-stage difference amplifier's on-die resistor matching, not by R_G.
explanations.c: Output offset voltage is a DC error spec of the amplifier stages, not something R_G is used to set.
explanations.d: Input bias current is set by the input transistor type and biasing inside the chip, unrelated to R_G.

questions.prompt: Why can an integrated in-amp achieve CMRR above 100 dB at gain 100 when a discrete four-resistor difference amplifier with 1% resistors cannot?

options.text: The in-amp uses a completely different, non-resistive subtraction method
The in-amp's critical resistors are matched and laser-trimmed on the same die at the factory, far exceeding what external 1% resistors achieve
The in-amp does not use negative feedback
The in-amp operates only at DC, avoiding CMRR degradation

explanations.a: The in-amp's second stage is still a resistor-based difference amplifier; the difference is manufacturing precision, not the underlying method.
explanations.b: Correct — on-die resistor networks can be matched and trimmed to a precision no external discrete resistor selection realistically matches, which is the structural reason for the CMRR gap.
explanations.c: In-amps use negative feedback throughout, just like discrete op-amp circuits.
explanations.d: In-amps are used across a frequency range, not restricted to DC; CMRR does vary with frequency but that is not the reason for the gap described here.

questions.prompt: Order the signal path through a three-op-amp instrumentation amplifier from input to output.

items.text: Differential input signal (plus common-mode) arrives at the two non-inverting buffer inputs
Each buffer amplifies the differential component via the shared R_G path while passing common-mode at unity
The two buffer outputs feed a second-stage difference amplifier
The difference amplifier subtracts the two buffered signals to produce the final single-ended output

questions.explanation: Signals enter the two input buffers, the first stage amplifies the differential component while leaving common-mode signals unaffected in relative terms, and the second-stage difference amplifier performs the final subtraction to produce a clean single-ended output.

questions.prompt: Which subsystem is explicitly OUT OF SCOPE for a lesson on the in-amp topology itself, belonging instead to sensor/instrumentation coverage?

options.text: The gain-setting resistor R_G
The second-stage difference amplifier
A resistive bridge sensor and its excitation source feeding the in-amp
The first-stage input buffers

explanations.a: R_G is part of the in-amp topology itself, directly setting its gain.
explanations.b: The second-stage difference amplifier is a core structural part of the in-amp topology.
explanations.c: Correct — the bridge sensor and its excitation/conditioning chain are separate sensor-side subsystems, covered elsewhere, not part of the amplifier topology itself.
explanations.d: The first-stage buffers are a core structural part of the in-amp topology.

lessons.label: DC Errors: Offset, Bias Current, and Drift

sections.heading: Offset voltage: the mismatch built into every real input pair
sections.body: An ideal op-amp outputs zero volts when both inputs are tied together. A real one does not, because its input differential pair is never perfectly matched; the small internal mismatch shows up as an equivalent input offset voltage (Vos), a fictitious DC voltage that, if inserted in series with one input, reproduces the observed output error. Part grade matters enormously here: a general-purpose bipolar part like the uA741 specifies Vos around 5 mV typical, while a precision part like the OP07, designed specifically to minimize this error, specifies Vos down around 25 uV typical, roughly a 200x improvement. Vos also drifts with temperature (its tempco, typically a few uV/degC on precision parts, worse on general-purpose ones), so a circuit calibrated at room temperature can accumulate additional error as ambient temperature shifts.

sections.heading: Bias current and offset current: two related but distinct numbers
sections.body: Both op-amp inputs draw a small current into (or out of) the chip; the average of the two is the input bias current (Ib), and the difference between them is the input offset current (Ios), always smaller than Ib because it reflects only the mismatch between two otherwise-similar currents. Both currents flow through whatever resistance sits at each input, producing a voltage error (I times R) that the amplifier treats as a real signal. The standard mitigation is to add a resistor at the non-inverting input equal to the inverting input's effective source resistance (Rin parallel with Rf), so that equal bias currents flowing through matched resistances create equal, and therefore canceling, voltage errors at both inputs. This cancels Ib's contribution but not Ios's, since Ios is by definition the part of the bias current that does not match between the two inputs.

sections.heading: Building an actual referred-to-input error budget
sections.body: A rigorous error estimate does not stop at Vos alone. Total input-referred DC error is approximately Vos plus (Ios times the effective source resistance), and this input-referred error is then multiplied by the noise gain (1 + Rf/Rin, the same expression regardless of whether the amplifier is wired inverting or non-inverting) to predict the resulting output error. Skipping the noise-gain multiplication is the single most common mistake in a student error budget: a 25 uV input offset in a gain-of-1000 stage does not produce 25 uV at the output, it produces 25 mV, a difference large enough to matter in a precision measurement.

lessons.workedExample: A student designs an inverting amplifier with Rin = 1 k and Rf = 100 k (noise gain = 101) using a uA741, which specifies Vos around 5 mV typical and Ib around 80 nA typical. Without bias-current compensation, the input-referred error from Ios alone (roughly 20 nA typical times the 1 k parallel 100 k source resistance, about 990 ohms) contributes under 20 uV, negligible next to the 5 mV Vos. The dominant term is Vos itself: multiplied by the noise gain of 101, it predicts roughly 505 mV of DC error at the output, comparable to a real signal in a low-level measurement, and a strong argument for switching to an OP07-class part where the same calculation yields roughly 2.5 mV instead.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks for an error budget because it is the clearest test of whether a student can move from a datasheet number to a predicted output error rather than just quoting the datasheet. A weak answer states Vos or Ib in isolation and stops. A strong answer multiplies input-referred error by the correct noise gain, names which term (offset voltage or bias current) dominates for their specific resistor values, and can say why a precision part like the OP07 would change the outcome by orders of magnitude rather than a small percentage.

questions.prompt: Roughly how much better is the OP07's typical input offset voltage compared to the uA741's?

options.text: About 2x better (25 mV vs 5 mV)
About 200x better (25 uV vs 5 mV)
They are essentially the same
The uA741 is actually better

explanations.a: This misreads the units; the OP07's spec is in microvolts, not millivolts.
explanations.b: Correct — 5 mV (741) versus 25 uV (OP07) is roughly a 200x reduction, reflecting the OP07's design focus on minimizing input offset.
explanations.c: The two parts differ by roughly two orders of magnitude in this specification, not a negligible amount.
explanations.d: The OP07 is the precision part here; its offset voltage is far lower than the 741's.

questions.prompt: What does adding a resistor at the non-inverting input, sized to match the inverting input's effective source resistance, accomplish?

options.text: It eliminates all input offset voltage
It cancels the voltage error caused by input bias current, since equal currents through matched resistances cancel
It doubles the amplifier's gain
It increases the amplifier's bandwidth

explanations.a: Offset voltage arises from internal transistor mismatch, a separate error source this resistor does not address.
explanations.b: Correct — matching the resistance at both inputs means the (nearly equal) bias currents produce matched voltage drops that cancel in the differential result, leaving only the smaller offset-current-driven residual error.
explanations.c: This resistor is for DC error cancellation, not gain setting, which is controlled by the feedback network.
explanations.d: This has no direct effect on bandwidth.

questions.prompt: A circuit has an input-referred DC error of 25 uV and a noise gain of 1000. What output DC error should be predicted, and why is skipping this step a common mistake?

options.text: 25 uV at the output, because errors don't scale with gain
25 mV at the output, because input-referred error must be multiplied by the noise gain to predict output error
25 V at the output, because gain always applies twice
0 V, because offset voltage cancels at high gain

explanations.a: Input-referred error is amplified along with the signal by the noise gain; it does not stay fixed at the input's value once referred to the output.
explanations.b: Correct — 25 uV times 1000 = 25 mV; skipping this multiplication is the most common student mistake because it makes a real error look negligible when it is not.
explanations.c: Noise gain is applied once to convert an input-referred error to an output error, not twice.
explanations.d: Offset voltage does not cancel with gain; higher gain makes its output effect larger, not smaller.

questions.prompt: Match each DC error term to its definition.

right.text: Equivalent input voltage that reproduces the output error caused by internal input-pair mismatch
Average of the two input currents
Difference between the two input currents

questions.explanation: Vos models transistor mismatch as an equivalent input voltage; Ib is the average of the two input currents; Ios is the difference between them, always smaller than Ib since it reflects only the mismatch.

lessons.label: AC Limits: GBW, Slew Rate, and Full-Power Bandwidth

sections.heading: Gain-bandwidth product: a fixed budget you spend on gain or on speed
sections.body: A compensated op-amp's open-loop gain rolls off at -20 dB/decade above a low corner frequency, and across that rolloff the product of gain and frequency is approximately constant, the gain-bandwidth product (GBW). The classic uA741 specifies a GBW around 1 MHz. Because closed-loop bandwidth is set by where the noise gain curve crosses the open-loop gain curve, closed-loop bandwidth is approximately GBW divided by noise gain (1 + Rf/Rin). A 741 configured for a noise gain of 100 therefore has a closed-loop small-signal bandwidth around 10 kHz; configured as a unity-gain buffer, it can use nearly the full 1 MHz. This is a real tradeoff, not a rule of thumb to memorize: every dB of gain a circuit demands is a dB of bandwidth it gives up, and choosing a higher-GBW part is the only way to buy back both at once.

sections.heading: Slew rate is a completely separate speed limit
sections.body: GBW describes small-signal behavior, how fast the amplifier responds to a tiny change. Slew rate (SR) describes the amplifier's absolute maximum rate of output voltage change, set by how fast internal compensation capacitance can be charged by the limited bias current available inside the chip; it is expressed in V/us and does not depend on signal amplitude. The 741 specifies SR around 0.5 V/us, meaning its output cannot swing faster than half a volt every microsecond no matter how large a step is demanded. Slew rate limiting produces a large-signal distortion mechanism entirely distinct from bandwidth rolloff.

sections.heading: Full-power bandwidth and telling the two limits apart on a scope
sections.body: Full-power bandwidth (FPBW) is the frequency above which a full-amplitude sine wave can no longer be reproduced without slew-rate distortion: FPBW = SR / (2*pi*Vpeak). Because Vpeak appears in the denominator, FPBW shrinks as the demanded output swing grows, so a circuit can look perfectly fine at low amplitude at a given frequency and visibly distort once the amplitude is turned up, even though the frequency never changed. On a scope, the two limits look different: bandwidth limiting (an amplitude that is too high for the closed-loop gain to sustain, but still below the slew limit) rounds off the sine wave's peaks while its shape stays sinusoidal, its slope varying smoothly like a true sine derivative; slew limiting instead produces a triangular wave with a constant-slope ramp on both edges, because the output is climbing or falling at the fixed maximum rate (SR) regardless of what the ideal sinusoid's instantaneous slope should be.

lessons.workedExample: A 741 wired for a small-signal closed-loop bandwidth of 500 kHz (noise gain 2, since GBW/2 = 500 kHz) is asked to output a 10 Vpp sine wave at 20 kHz, well inside that small-signal bandwidth. Computing full-power bandwidth with SR = 0.5 V/us and Vpeak = 5 V: FPBW = 0.5e6 / (2*pi*5) is approximately 15,900 Hz, meaning 20 kHz is already above FPBW at this amplitude. On the scope the output is not a clipped-but-rounded sine; it is a clean triangle wave with a slope of 0.5 V/us on both the rising and falling edges, the signature of slew limiting rather than bandwidth limiting, even though the requested frequency sits comfortably inside the amplifier's small-signal bandwidth.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks a student to explain a distorted waveform on their scope because it is a fast test of whether they understand two genuinely different failure mechanisms or have memorized one vague idea of an amplifier being too slow. A weak answer says the signal is too fast for the op-amp and stops there. A strong answer identifies the waveform shape (rounded-but-sinusoidal versus triangular with constant slope), names the correct limit (bandwidth versus slew rate), and can compute full-power bandwidth to show the amplitude, not just the frequency, is what pushed the circuit past its slew limit.

questions.prompt: A 741 (GBW approximately 1 MHz) is configured for a noise gain of 100. What is its approximate closed-loop small-signal bandwidth?

options.text: 1 MHz, unaffected by gain
100 kHz
10 kHz
1 kHz

explanations.a: Closed-loop bandwidth is not fixed; it falls as noise gain rises because GBW is approximately constant.
explanations.b: This would require a noise gain of 10, not 100.
explanations.c: Correct — closed-loop bandwidth is approximately GBW / noise gain = 1 MHz / 100 = 10 kHz.
explanations.d: This would require a noise gain of 1000, not 100.

questions.prompt: Why does full-power bandwidth shrink as the required output amplitude increases, even though the op-amp's slew rate spec does not change?

options.text: Because slew rate itself decreases at higher amplitudes
Because a larger sine wave requires a faster peak rate of change to complete the same cycle in the same time, and FPBW = SR/(2*pi*Vpeak) has Vpeak in the denominator
Because GBW decreases at higher amplitudes
Because higher amplitude signals have lower frequency content

explanations.a: Slew rate is a fixed internal-circuit limit; it does not itself vary with the signal being reproduced.
explanations.b: Correct — a sine wave's peak slope scales with both frequency and amplitude, so a larger required amplitude reaches the fixed slew-rate ceiling at a lower frequency, which is exactly what the inverse relationship to Vpeak in the FPBW formula captures.
explanations.c: GBW is a small-signal open-loop parameter and is not what full-power bandwidth is derived from.
explanations.d: Amplitude and frequency are independent signal parameters; higher amplitude does not imply lower frequency content.

questions.prompt: On an oscilloscope, how does slew-rate-limited distortion typically look different from bandwidth-limited distortion?

options.text: Slew limiting produces a triangular wave with constant-slope edges; bandwidth limiting produces a rounded but still sinusoidal shape
They look identical and cannot be distinguished visually
Slew limiting produces a square wave; bandwidth limiting produces a triangle wave
Bandwidth limiting always produces a flat, clipped line at the rails

explanations.a: Correct — slew limiting forces a fixed maximum rate of change on both edges (a triangle), while bandwidth limiting rounds off peak amplitude but preserves a smoothly varying, still-sinusoidal shape.
explanations.b: The two mechanisms produce visually distinct waveform shapes, which is exactly how a student can diagnose which limit they have hit.
explanations.c: Slew limiting produces a triangle wave, not a square wave; a square wave would suggest hard rail-to-rail clipping, a different failure mode entirely.
explanations.d: Rail clipping is a third, distinct failure mode; bandwidth limiting rounds and reduces amplitude but does not flat-line at the rails.

lessons.label: Supplies, Ranges, and Choosing the Part

sections.heading: Rail-to-rail versus classic headroom
sections.body: A classic op-amp topology like the 741 needs its input common-mode voltage to stay roughly 1.5-2 V away from each supply rail, and its output cannot swing all the way to the rails either, typically stopping a volt or more short. A rail-to-rail input/output (RRIO) part uses different internal input-stage and output-stage topologies specifically designed to operate with the common-mode range and output swing extending to, or very near, the supply rails themselves. On a dual +/-15 V supply the classic part's lost headroom barely matters; on a single 3.3 V or 5 V supply, where the entire usable range might be a few volts, that same 1.5-2 V loss on each end can consume most of the available range, which is why RRIO parts are the default choice for low-voltage, single-supply designs.

sections.heading: Common-mode violations and phase reversal
sections.body: Driving a non-RRIO op-amp's input outside its specified common-mode range does not just cause ordinary clipping. Many classic bipolar-input parts exhibit phase reversal: instead of the output simply saturating at a rail, internal input-stage transistors fall out of their normal active region and the output can snap to the opposite rail from what the input polarity would suggest, an especially dangerous failure in a feedback or comparator-like circuit because the polarity flip can turn negative feedback into positive feedback for as long as the violation lasts. Staying within the datasheet's specified common-mode range, or choosing an RRI part when the input signal is expected to approach a rail, avoids the problem entirely.

sections.heading: Single-supply operation and PSRR at frequency
sections.body: Without a negative rail, an AC signal that swings both positive and negative needs to be biased around a mid-supply reference (commonly Vcc/2, generated with a resistor divider and often buffered) so the whole waveform sits within the single positive supply's range rather than trying to go negative into a rail that does not exist. Power supply rejection ratio (PSRR), the op-amp's ability to keep noise on its supply rail from reaching the output, is typically excellent at DC (often 90 dB or more on general-purpose parts) but degrades steeply with frequency in the same way open-loop gain does, so supply noise in the tens or hundreds of kHz couples through far more than the DC spec would suggest, which is why decoupling capacitors close to the supply pins matter even when the DC PSRR spec looks reassuring.

sections.heading: Choosing an input stage by source impedance
sections.body: The three common input-stage families trade off differently. Bipolar input stages offer the lowest voltage noise but draw bias current in the nanoamp-to-microamp range, making them best suited to low source impedances where that current does not create a large voltage error. JFET input stages cut bias current to the picoamp range at some cost in voltage noise, suiting higher-impedance sources like photodiodes. CMOS input stages push bias current down further still, into the femtoamp range, and commonly pair with rail-to-rail operation and low supply voltages, at the cost of higher offset drift and 1/f noise compared to the best bipolar parts. Matching input-stage type to source impedance is a selection decision as consequential as gain or bandwidth.

lessons.workedExample: A student builds a photodiode transimpedance amplifier, a very high source impedance application, using a classic bipolar-input op-amp because it happened to be in the parts bin. The bipolar part's nanoamp-scale bias current, flowing through the large feedback resistor typical of a transimpedance stage, produces a DC output offset large enough to swamp the small photocurrent signal they are trying to measure. Swapping to a JFET-input op-amp with picoamp-scale bias current reduces that same error by roughly three orders of magnitude, without changing anything else in the circuit, because the input-stage choice, not the circuit topology, was the actual bottleneck.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks why a particular op-amp was chosen because part selection reveals whether a student treated the op-amp as an interchangeable black box or actually reasoned about source impedance, supply voltage, and signal swing. A weak answer says they used the part that was available or that seemed popular. A strong answer connects a specific spec (bias current type for a high-impedance sensor, rail-to-rail range for a low-voltage single supply, common-mode range for an input that approaches a rail) to a specific requirement of their circuit.

questions.prompt: Why do rail-to-rail input/output (RRIO) op-amps matter more on a single 3.3 V supply than on a dual +/-15 V supply?

options.text: RRIO parts are only manufactured for low-voltage supplies
The 1.5-2 V of headroom a classic topology loses at each rail consumes a much larger fraction of a few-volt total range than of a 30 V range
Classic op-amps cannot function at all below 5 V
RRIO parts have higher open-loop gain than classic parts

explanations.a: RRIO and classic topologies both exist across a range of supply voltages; the distinction is about headroom, not manufacturing restriction.
explanations.b: Correct — a fixed 1.5-2 V loss at each rail is nearly the entire usable range at 3.3 V but is a small fraction of a 30 V total range, which is why RRIO matters far more at low supply voltages.
explanations.c: Many classic op-amps do function below 5 V; the issue is reduced usable signal range, not total failure.
explanations.d: Open-loop gain is not the distinguishing factor between RRIO and classic topologies; input/output headroom is.

questions.prompt: What makes phase reversal a particularly dangerous failure mode compared to ordinary output clipping?

options.text: It permanently destroys the op-amp
The output can snap to the opposite rail from what the input polarity suggests, which can turn negative feedback into positive feedback while the violation persists
It only happens with rail-to-rail parts
It causes the supply voltage to reverse polarity

explanations.a: Phase reversal is a functional misbehavior during a common-mode violation, not typically permanent physical damage.
explanations.b: Correct — the polarity-flipped output can effectively convert a negative-feedback circuit's behavior into a positive-feedback one for the duration of the violation, an unexpected and destabilizing failure mode.
explanations.c: Phase reversal is a classic-topology (often bipolar-input) issue; RRIO parts are specifically designed to avoid common-mode range violations that trigger it.
explanations.d: Supply voltage itself is unaffected; only the op-amp's output behavior is disrupted.

questions.prompt: Match each op-amp input-stage type to its typical bias-current characteristic.

right.text: Nanoamp-to-microamp bias current, lowest voltage noise, best for low source impedance
Picoamp-scale bias current, suited to higher-impedance sources like photodiodes
Femtoamp-scale bias current, often paired with rail-to-rail and low-voltage operation

questions.explanation: Bipolar stages trade higher bias current for the lowest voltage noise; JFET stages cut bias current to the picoamp range for higher-impedance sources; CMOS stages push bias current lowest still and commonly pair with rail-to-rail, low-voltage designs.

questions.prompt: Why does PSRR being excellent at DC (for example 90+ dB) not guarantee good rejection of supply noise at 100 kHz?

options.text: PSRR is constant across all frequencies by definition
PSRR degrades with frequency in a manner similar to open-loop gain rolloff, so high-frequency supply noise couples through far more than the DC spec suggests
PSRR only applies to negative supply rails, not positive ones
100 kHz supply noise cannot physically reach the op-amp's output

explanations.a: PSRR is frequency-dependent; treating it as a single constant number ignores the rolloff that matters in practice.
explanations.b: Correct — PSRR falls off with frequency much like open-loop gain does, so a good DC spec does not protect against higher-frequency supply noise, which is why decoupling capacitors remain necessary.
explanations.c: PSRR is generally specified and relevant for both supply rails, not restricted to one.
explanations.d: Supply noise absolutely can couple through to the output; that coupling is exactly what a degraded high-frequency PSRR describes.

units.label: Feedback, Stability, and Reading Bode and Nyquist

lessons.label: The Feedback Equation and What It Buys

sections.heading: Black's trade: giving up gain to buy control
sections.body: In 1927, Bell Labs engineer Harold Black sketched the negative-feedback amplifier on a ferry commute, aiming to tame the drift and distortion of the vacuum-tube repeaters strung along transcontinental phone lines (his patent was filed in 1928, granted in 1937 after a long fight to convince skeptical reviewers a stable amplifier could deliberately throw away gain). The core relation is deceptively simple: if a forward amplifier has open-loop gain A and a feedback network returns a fraction beta of the output to subtract from the input, the closed-loop gain is A_cl = A / (1 + A*beta). Define the loop gain T = A*beta, the single number that governs everything feedback does. When T is large, A_cl approaches 1/beta -- the closed-loop gain is set almost entirely by a passive, stable feedback network rather than by the messy, temperature- and part-dependent forward amplifier.

sections.heading: Desensitivity: how (1+T) flattens gain drift and distortion
sections.body: Differentiating the closed-loop equation gives dA_cl/A_cl = [1/(1+T)] * dA/A: a fractional change in raw gain A is suppressed by the desensitivity factor 1/(1+T) at the output. A 50% swing in A from transistor beta spread or thermal drift becomes only 50%/(1+T) at A_cl. The same mechanism attacks harmonic distortion, because a distortion product generated inside the loop is, from the loop's point of view, just another unwanted gain error, so it too shrinks by 1/(1+T). What feedback does not buy is any reduction in input-referred noise or DC offset voltage: those errors originate at or ahead of the summing node, so the loop amplifies them by the same gain it amplifies the wanted signal by, and they come out the far side undiminished relative to the signal -- unlike a gain error or distortion product generated inside the loop, which the loop can see and suppress.

sections.heading: Bandwidth for gain, at constant gain-bandwidth product
sections.body: A dominant-pole amplifier holds gain-bandwidth product GBW roughly constant: open-loop gain rolls off at -20 dB/decade past the dominant pole, so gain times frequency stays fixed. Closing the loop trades that same GBW differently: closed-loop bandwidth extends by the factor (1+T) relative to where the forward amplifier alone would have -3 dB'd, because the loop keeps output error small until the loop gain itself has fallen to unity. Every one of these benefits -- flat gain, low distortion, wide bandwidth -- is purchased with the same currency: raw open-loop gain A surrendered to build up loop gain T. There is no free lunch; a designer who wants more desensitization must start with more A to spend.

lessons.workedExample: An op-amp has open-loop DC gain A0 = 100,000 (100 dB) and unity-gain bandwidth GBW = 1 MHz. Wired for a closed-loop gain of 1/beta = 100 (beta = 0.01), the loop gain at DC is T = 100,000 * 0.01 = 1,000 (60 dB). Actual A_cl = 100,000/1,001 = 99.9, essentially the ideal 100. Closed-loop bandwidth extends to roughly GBW/(1/beta) = 1 MHz/100 = 10 kHz. Now suppose temperature drift cuts A0 in half, to 50,000: T drops to 500, and A_cl shifts by only 0.5/(1+500) = 0.0998% -- a 50% raw gain collapse becomes a rounding error at the output.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'what does feedback actually cost you?' to separate a student who memorized 'feedback is good' from one who can quantify the trade. A strong answer names the loop gain T for their specific circuit, states the desensitivity factor 1/(1+T) with a real number, and connects it to the bandwidth they measured falling short of the open-loop GBW. A weak answer says feedback 'reduces distortion and stabilizes gain' with no T, no formula, and no acknowledgment that the closed-loop gain itself is bounded by how much A they started with.

questions.prompt: An amplifier has open-loop gain A = 10,000 and feedback fraction beta = 0.01. Using A_cl = A/(1+A*beta), what is the closed-loop gain?

options.text: About 99
Exactly 100

explanations.a: Correct: T = A*beta = 100, so A_cl = 10,000/101 approx 99.0 -- close to but slightly under the ideal 1/beta.
explanations.b: 100 is the ideal 1/beta limit as T approaches infinity, but with T only 100 the actual value is measurably below it.
explanations.c: 10,000 is the raw open-loop gain A, ignoring the feedback loop entirely.
explanations.d: 0.01 is beta itself, not the closed-loop gain.

questions.prompt: In a loop with T = 99, the open-loop gain A drifts by 20% due to temperature. Roughly how much does the closed-loop gain A_cl shift?

options.text: 20%, the same as A
10%, half of A's drift
0.2%, suppressed by 1/(1+T)
0%, feedback eliminates all drift

explanations.a: This ignores the desensitivity factor entirely -- it is the drift of A, not A_cl.
explanations.b: There is no factor-of-two rule here; the suppression is 1/(1+T), not 1/2.
explanations.c: Correct: dA_cl/A_cl = dA/A / (1+T) = 20%/100 = 0.2%.
explanations.d: Feedback suppresses drift, but T is finite, so some residual drift always remains.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to predict a closed-loop amplifier's -3 dB bandwidth starting from open-loop op-amp specs.

items.text: Read the open-loop unity-gain bandwidth (GBW) off the datasheet
Pick the desired closed-loop gain, 1/beta
Compute the loop gain T = A*beta at the frequency of interest
Estimate closed-loop bandwidth as roughly GBW divided by 1/beta

questions.explanation: You start from the amplifier's fixed GBW, choose the gain you want to close the loop at (which sets beta), use that to find the loop gain T, and only then can you estimate how far the (1+T) bandwidth extension pushes the -3 dB point -- which for a dominant-pole amp reduces to GBW/(1/beta).

questions.prompt: Match each feedback quantity to what it represents.

right.text: Closed-loop gain A_cl
Loop gain T
Desensitivity / distortion-reduction factor
Bandwidth extension factor

questions.explanation: A_cl = A/(1+T) is the closed-loop gain; T = A*beta is the loop gain that everything else is expressed in terms of; 1/(1+T) shrinks gain drift and distortion; (1+T) is the same factor working in the opposite direction to stretch bandwidth, since it multiplies the frequency where loop gain falls to unity.

lessons.label: The Four Feedback Topologies

sections.heading: Two independent choices name the topology
sections.body: Every feedback amplifier makes two independent choices, and their combination gives the topology its name. First: how does the feedback signal mix with the input? Series mixing subtracts a feedback voltage in series with the source, like a battery fighting the input voltage. Shunt mixing subtracts a feedback current at a shared node, like a tap draining current away from the input. Second: what does the feedback network sample at the output? Shunt sampling taps the output voltage in parallel, the way a voltmeter would. Series sampling senses the output current by sitting in series with the load path, the way an ammeter would. Naming convention lists mixing first, sampling second: series-shunt, shunt-shunt, series-series, shunt-series. All four of these ideal (1+T) impedance rules assume the feedback network itself is ideal and non-loading; a real resistive feedback network -- Rf in a transimpedance stage, for instance -- does load the forward amplifier, and the standard way to account for that is to fold the feedback network into an equivalent two-port model (h-, y-, z-, or g-parameters, chosen to match the topology) before applying the ideal Rin/Rout rules to the loaded forward amplifier.

sections.heading: Each combination builds a different ideal amplifier and impedance
sections.body: Series-shunt (voltage feedback) builds a voltage amplifier: series mixing raises input resistance by the factor (1+T), and shunt sampling lowers output resistance by (1+T) -- exactly what a voltage amp wants, high Rin so it doesn't load the source, low Rout so it doesn't sag under the load. Shunt-shunt builds a transresistance amplifier (current in, voltage out): both Rin and Rout drop by (1+T), useful because you want the input to absorb current without building voltage. Series-series builds a transconductance amplifier (voltage in, current out): both Rin and Rout rise by (1+T), so the stage looks like a near-ideal current source. Shunt-series builds a current amplifier: Rin drops, Rout rises by (1+T), matching a current-in/current-out ideal.

sections.heading: Reading the topology off a real schematic
