Fairchild releases the uA702, the first monolithic operational amplifier
Monolithic op-amp unit costs fall toward well under a dollar in volume production

questions.explanation: The term and concept came from Ragazzini's 1947 analog-computer work, GAP/R commercialized a vacuum-tube version with the K2-W in 1952, Fairchild introduced the first monolithic version in 1963 with the uA702, and mass production later drove monolithic unit costs down dramatically.

lessons.label: Live Debates: Feedback, TIM, and Audio Distortion

sections.heading: Otala's claim: feedback can create the distortion it's supposed to remove
sections.body: By the 1960s, transistor power amplifiers commonly used large amounts of global negative feedback to drive measured harmonic distortion down to very low steady-state levels. Finnish engineer Matti Otala challenged the assumption that more feedback was simply better, publishing 'Transient Distortion in Transistorized Audio Power Amplifiers' in 1970. Otala argued that fast, complex transients, the kind real music produces, could momentarily overwhelm an amplifier's input stage: if the output could not slew fast enough to keep up with a sudden input step, the error signal fed back to the input would overshoot, driving that first stage into brief nonlinear clipping. He named this transient intermodulation distortion, or TIM, sometimes framed as slew-induced distortion, and argued that heavy global feedback, by widening the gap between an amplifier's fast raw input and its slower corrected output during a transient, could make TIM worse rather than better.

sections.heading: The counterargument: a compensation problem, not a feedback problem
sections.body: Audio engineers Bob Cordell and Douglas Self pushed back over the following decades, arguing TIM is not an inherent cost of negative feedback itself but a symptom of an amplifier whose slew rate and open-loop bandwidth are too low for the compensation scheme and feedback factor applied to it. Their position: design the input stage and compensation network so open-loop bandwidth and slew rate comfortably exceed what audio transients demand, and TIM effectively disappears, while the feedback continues to measurably lower steady-state harmonic and intermodulation distortion, treated as real, audible improvement rather than a self-defeating trade. In this framing, blaming feedback itself for TIM misidentifies which stage of the design actually needs fixing.

sections.heading: Why this stayed a live dispute rather than settling
sections.body: The disagreement never fully resolved, and that is worth stating plainly rather than papering over. Otala's camp pointed to listener reports of harshness in heavily fed-back amplifiers that bench measurements of steady-state distortion did not capture, arguing standard test signals (steady sine waves) simply miss transient behavior. Cordell and Self countered that once slew rate and bandwidth are properly engineered, careful transient measurements show no residual TIM penalty from feedback, and that many claimed audible differences fail to survive controlled listening tests. The dispute sits at the boundary between two kinds of evidence, engineering measurement and subjective listening, that audio design has never fully reconciled, which is exactly why it remains a fair question for a judge rather than a settled textbook fact.

lessons.workedExample: Consider an amplifier with open-loop bandwidth of only 20 kHz and a modest slew rate, wrapped in heavy global feedback to push steady-state total harmonic distortion down to 0.001% on a sine-wave test. Feed it a fast musical transient, like a snare drum's leading edge, and by Otala's argument the output cannot keep pace with the sudden input step; the feedback network sees a large momentary error and drives the input stage into brief clipping, producing TIM that a steady-state sine-wave THD test never exercises and therefore never reports. Cordell and Self's rebuttal: redesign that same amplifier with wider open-loop bandwidth and adequate slew rate for the compensation network in use, and the same heavy feedback now has no transient error large enough to clip the input stage, so the sine-wave THD figure and the transient behavior both improve together rather than trading off.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who raises TIM is testing whether a student can hold a genuinely unresolved engineering dispute honestly, rather than declaring a false winner. A weak answer picks a side and states it as settled fact, either 'feedback is bad for audio' or 'TIM was debunked.' A strong answer names both positions accurately, Otala's transient-distortion mechanism tied to slew-rate limits and Cordell/Self's rebuttal that adequate bandwidth and slew rate remove the effect, states what kind of evidence each side leans on (transient measurement and listening versus steady-state measurement and controlled listening tests), and is willing to say the dispute has never been cleanly settled rather than forcing a tidy conclusion the science does not support.

questions.prompt: According to Matti Otala's 1970 argument, what specifically causes transient intermodulation distortion (TIM)?

options.text: A fast input transient outrunning the amplifier's slew rate, causing the fed-back error signal to overshoot and briefly drive the input stage into nonlinear clipping
Vacuum tubes overheating during long listening sessions
A mismatch between speaker impedance and amplifier output impedance
Power supply ripple at the mains frequency

explanations.a: Correct — Otala argued that when a transient input changes faster than the amplifier's output can slew, the resulting large error signal fed back to the input can momentarily clip that stage, producing TIM.
explanations.b: Otala's mechanism concerns transistor amplifiers and slew-rate limits, not vacuum-tube thermal behavior.
explanations.c: Speaker-amplifier impedance matching is a separate issue from the slew-rate-driven mechanism Otala described.
explanations.d: Power supply ripple produces a different, well-understood hum-related distortion, not the transient mechanism Otala named.

questions.prompt: What is the core of Bob Cordell and Douglas Self's counterargument to Otala's TIM claim?

options.text: That negative feedback should never be used in audio amplifiers under any circumstances

That TIM results from inadequate slew rate and open-loop bandwidth relative to the compensation and feedback applied, not from feedback itself, and that properly designed amplifiers show no such penalty
That distortion measurements are meaningless and only listening tests matter
That Otala's 1970 paper contained a mathematical error in his feedback equations

explanations.a: Cordell and Self did not argue against feedback in general; they argued the problem lay in inadequate slew rate and bandwidth, not in feedback itself.
explanations.b: Correct — their position is that adequate open-loop bandwidth and slew rate eliminate TIM, and that feedback, properly implemented, still measurably reduces distortion without the trade-off Otala described.
explanations.c: Cordell and Self relied heavily on careful measurement, including transient measurement, rather than dismissing measurement altogether.
explanations.d: The dispute is about design trade-offs and mechanisms, not a claimed arithmetic error in Otala's paper.

questions.prompt: Why does this lesson describe the feedback-and-TIM dispute as genuinely unresolved rather than settled?

options.text: Because no one has ever built an amplifier with adequate slew rate to test the claim

Because the two sides lean on different kinds of evidence, transient behavior and listener reports versus steady-state and controlled listening measurement, and the disagreement has persisted across decades without a clean resolution
Because Otala later retracted his 1970 paper entirely
Because modern amplifiers no longer use any negative feedback

explanations.a: Amplifiers with high slew rate and bandwidth have been built and tested extensively; that is not why the dispute persists.
explanations.b: Correct — the sides draw on different evidentiary approaches and the underlying disagreement about subjective audibility versus engineering measurement has never been cleanly closed.
explanations.c: There is no record of Otala retracting his transient-distortion work; the dispute continued with Cordell and Self responding to it rather than a retraction ending it.
explanations.d: Global negative feedback remains standard in most modern audio power amplifier designs.

questions.prompt: Match each position in the TIM debate to the person or people who held it.

left.text: Heavy global feedback can worsen distortion during fast transients via slew-rate limiting
TIM is a compensation/bandwidth design flaw, not an inherent cost of feedback

right.text: Matti Otala
Bob Cordell and Douglas Self

questions.explanation: Otala originated the transient-intermodulation-distortion argument in 1970, tying it to feedback amplified error signals overshooting during transients; Cordell and Self argued the real fix is adequate slew rate and open-loop bandwidth, not less feedback.

questions.prompt: Why did standard steady-state total harmonic distortion (THD) sine-wave testing fail to capture the effect Otala described?

options.text: Because sine-wave THD testing measures power supply voltage, not distortion
Because a steady sine wave does not present the amplifier with the fast, complex transient that Otala argued was needed to exceed the slew-rate limit and trigger input-stage clipping
Because THD testing only works on vacuum-tube amplifiers
Because THD testing had not been invented until after Otala's 1970 paper

explanations.a: Steady-state THD testing measures harmonic distortion in the output signal, not supply voltage.
explanations.b: Correct — a steady sine wave changes too slowly to trigger the slew-rate-limited overshoot Otala's TIM mechanism depends on, so standard THD tests could report excellent numbers while missing transient-driven distortion.
explanations.c: THD testing applies to both tube and transistor amplifiers; that is not the limitation at issue.
explanations.d: THD testing predates Otala's 1970 paper; his argument was precisely that this established test missed a real effect.

lessons.label: Open Questions and the Analog/Digital Boundary

sections.heading: The 'digitize early' trend and the counter-trend
sections.body: For decades the dominant strategy in signal processing has been to convert a signal to digital as close to the sensor as possible, then do everything else, filtering, mixing, correction, in software with a DSP or general-purpose processor, because digital processing is cheap, reprogrammable, and insensitive to component tolerance in a way analog circuits are not. That trend genuinely shrank how much analog circuitry ships in a typical product. But it did not eliminate analog design, because every system still needs a real analog front end: an amplifier and filter to condition the signal before the analog-to-digital converter, and the converter itself is fundamentally an analog circuit. A counter-trend, digitally assisted analog, has grown alongside this: chips that use an on-board digital core to calibrate and trim an analog circuit's imperfections in real time, self-correcting offset, gain, and mismatch that a pure analog design would otherwise need expensive precision components to control.

sections.heading: A genuine analog revival: in-memory compute for AI inference
sections.body: A newer counter-current is analog in-memory computing for AI inference, where a memory array itself, often built from resistive elements like memristors or ReRAM cells, performs the multiply-accumulate arithmetic of a neural network directly as an analog physical process (current summing on a wire), rather than shuttling data back and forth to a separate digital arithmetic unit. The appeal is real: it can cut the energy spent moving data, which dominates the power budget of digital neural-network accelerators. The ceiling is also real: analog compute is limited by device-to-device variation, drift over time and temperature, and noise, so it tends to suit lower-precision inference tasks that can tolerate some error, not the exact, reproducible arithmetic that training or high-precision inference requires.

sections.heading: The talent and automation question
sections.body: A separate, ongoing argument concerns whether analog IC design can be automated the way digital design was, and it stays unresolved because analog design resists it. Digital synthesis tools let an engineer describe intended behavior in a hardware description language and let software generate a working gate-level circuit, largely because digital circuits reduce to well-defined logical correctness. Analog circuits do not reduce that cleanly: a workable analog design has to simultaneously satisfy noise, bandwidth, power, layout parasitics, process variation, and stability margins, tightly coupled trade-offs that current electronic design automation tools can assist with but not fully replace expert judgment for. That gap feeds a widely discussed shortage of experienced analog designers, since the discipline still depends on intuition built over years in a way digital design increasingly does not, and how far automation can close that gap remains genuinely open.

lessons.workedExample: A student proposing a science-fair project on 'AI chips' who says only 'AI runs on digital processors' is half right and dated: consider a company building an edge-AI sensor for always-on keyword detection, where battery life matters more than exact accuracy. An analog in-memory compute design, using a resistive memory array to perform the neural network's multiply-accumulate step as physical current summation, can cut the energy per inference dramatically compared to moving every value through a digital multiplier-accumulator. But the same designer would not use that approach for the cloud server training the network, where reproducible, high-precision arithmetic matters more than energy per operation, and drift or device mismatch in an analog array would corrupt training. The honest framing: analog in-memory compute is displacing digital in specific, error-tolerant, power-constrained niches, not everywhere.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge raising this topic wants to see whether a student can resist a simple 'analog is dying' or 'analog is having a comeback' narrative and instead name where each trend actually applies. A weak answer picks one trend, digitization or analog revival, and generalizes it to the whole field. A strong answer names both directions honestly: signal processing has moved heavily toward digitize-early-then-DSP, digitally assisted self-calibrating analog is compensating for the analog front end that never went away, and analog in-memory compute is a real but precision-limited niche for AI inference, and can explain why analog design resists full EDA automation in a way digital synthesis does not, tying it to the coupled, non-reducible trade-offs analog circuits carry.

questions.prompt: What is 'digitally assisted analog,' and why has it grown alongside the digitize-early trend?

options.text: Analog circuits that use an on-board digital core to calibrate and trim imperfections like offset and gain mismatch in real time, reducing the need for expensive precision analog components
A method of replacing all analog circuits with pure digital logic
A type of vacuum tube used only in legacy equipment
A protocol for converting analog signals into digital audio files

explanations.a: Correct — digitally assisted analog uses embedded digital calibration to correct analog imperfections in real time, letting cheaper analog components achieve precision that would otherwise require costly matched parts.
explanations.b: It augments analog circuits with digital calibration rather than eliminating the analog portion entirely; an analog front end is still required.
explanations.c: This is a modern mixed-signal IC technique, unrelated to vacuum tubes.
explanations.d: This is a circuit design technique, not a file-format conversion protocol.

questions.prompt: What is the fundamental ceiling limiting analog in-memory compute for AI inference?

options.text: It cannot run any neural network arithmetic at all
Device-to-device variation, drift, and noise in the analog elements, which makes it better suited to lower-precision, error-tolerant inference than to exact, reproducible arithmetic
It only works when connected to a vacuum-tube amplifier
It requires more energy than digital multiply-accumulate units in every case

explanations.a: Analog in-memory arrays do perform multiply-accumulate arithmetic directly, via physical current summation; the limitation is precision, not capability.
explanations.b: Correct — variation, drift, and noise in the analog memory elements limit how precisely and reproducibly the array can compute, making it suited to error-tolerant inference rather than exact arithmetic like training.
explanations.c: Analog in-memory compute uses resistive memory elements such as memristors or ReRAM, not vacuum tubes.
explanations.d: The appeal of analog in-memory compute is specifically that it can reduce energy versus digital data movement in appropriate tasks, not that it always uses more.

questions.prompt: Why has electronic design automation (EDA) been far more successful at automating digital circuit design than analog circuit design?

options.text: Because analog circuits are simpler and require no automation

Because digital circuits reduce to well-defined logical correctness that synthesis tools can generate directly, while analog circuits must simultaneously satisfy tightly coupled trade-offs like noise, bandwidth, power, and stability that resist that kind of reduction
Because no analog design automation tools exist at all
Because digital circuits use fewer transistors than analog circuits

explanations.a: Analog circuits are not simpler; their design space is arguably harder to automate precisely because it is less reducible than digital logic.
explanations.b: Correct — digital synthesis works because correctness reduces to logical behavior, while analog design must jointly satisfy interacting physical trade-offs that current EDA tools can assist with but not fully automate.
explanations.c: Analog EDA tools do exist and assist designers; the claim in this lesson is that they cannot fully replace expert judgment, not that no tools exist.
explanations.d: Transistor count is not the reason automation succeeds for digital and struggles for analog; it is the nature of the design trade-offs.

questions.prompt: Why would a company choose analog in-memory compute for an always-on, battery-powered keyword-detection sensor but not for training the neural network in the cloud?

options.text: Because analog in-memory compute cannot be manufactured at all

Because the edge sensor task tolerates some inference error in exchange for lower energy per operation, while training requires reproducible, high-precision arithmetic that analog drift and device variation would corrupt
Because cloud servers do not use any electricity
Because training requires more memory capacity than any analog array can physically provide

explanations.a: Analog in-memory compute chips are real, manufactured products used in specific inference applications.
explanations.b: Correct — the energy-per-inference savings suit an error-tolerant, power-constrained edge task, while training needs the reproducible precision that analog drift and mismatch would undermine.
explanations.c: Cloud servers consume substantial electricity; that is not the distinguishing factor here.
explanations.d: Memory capacity is not the core reason; the distinguishing factor is precision and reproducibility, not raw storage size.

questions.prompt: Order these developments in the analog/digital boundary discussion from earliest emphasis to most recent.

items.text: Digitize-early-then-DSP becomes the dominant signal-processing strategy
Digitally assisted, self-calibrating analog circuits emerge to correct analog imperfections that the analog front end still requires
Analog in-memory compute using resistive memory elements is explored for energy-efficient AI inference

questions.explanation: Digitize-early-then-DSP became the long-standing dominant strategy first; digitally assisted analog calibration grew as a response to the analog front end that digitization never eliminated; analog in-memory compute for AI inference is the more recent counter-current explored for its energy advantages in error-tolerant tasks.

units.label: Active Filters, Noise, and Precision Design

lessons.label: Filter Approximations and Their Trade-offs

sections.heading: No filter is free: picking what to sacrifice
sections.body: An ideal low-pass filter passes everything below its cutoff and blocks everything above it with a vertical wall. Real filters cannot do that, so filter design is a menu of named approximations, each trading one property for another. Stephen Butterworth described the first of these in his 1930 Wireless Engineer paper 'On the Theory of Filter Amplifiers': a response with no ripple anywhere in the passband, achieved by setting as many derivatives of the magnitude response to zero at DC as the order allows. This 'maximally flat' shape is the default choice when passband amplitude accuracy matters more than a sharp transition.

sections.heading: Chebyshev, Bessel, and elliptic: what each one buys
sections.body: The Chebyshev approximation, built on Pafnuty Chebyshev's equal-ripple polynomials, allows a controlled ripple (commonly 0.1 dB to 3 dB) across the passband in exchange for a steeper roll-off than a Butterworth of the same order — the ripple energy is spent buying transition sharpness. The Bessel filter, derived from Bessel polynomials, gives up roll-off steepness entirely to make the group delay nearly constant across the passband, so a step or pulse passes through with minimal overshoot and ringing; it is the choice for pulse and oscilloscope-trigger circuits, not for tight frequency selectivity. The elliptic (Cauer) filter accepts ripple in both the passband and the stopband and in return delivers the steepest possible roll-off for a given order — it reaches a target attenuation in the fewest poles, at the cost of a non-monotonic stopband and the worst phase behavior of the four.

sections.heading: Comparing on shared axes and the universal roll-off rate
sections.body: Plotted on the same Bode magnitude axes at the same order and cutoff, a 4th-order Butterworth, Chebyshev, Bessel, and elliptic filter overlay near the cutoff but diverge sharply past it: the elliptic drops fastest right after cutoff, Chebyshev next, Butterworth next, and Bessel last, while the Bessel's phase (and hence group delay) stays flattest through the passband where the others bend. The true all-pole families — Butterworth, Chebyshev, and Bessel — share the same asymptotic far-stopband slope: an nth-order filter's magnitude eventually falls at -20n dB/decade, because each pole contributes one factor of 1/f to the asymptotic response. A 2nd-order Butterworth, Chebyshev, or Bessel filter rolls off at -40 dB/decade far from cutoff no matter which of those three approximations shaped its near-cutoff behavior. Elliptic is the exception: its finite stopband transmission zeros mean it is not all-pole, and far out those zeros flatten its asymptotic slope to only -20 dB/decade (odd order) or -40 dB/decade (even order) regardless of n — the price it pays for the steepest possible roll-off right at cutoff.

lessons.workedExample: A student needs to reject 60 Hz noise on an ECG-like signal above a 40 Hz cutoff without distorting the shape of the QRS pulse. A 4th-order Chebyshev with 1 dB ripple would hit -60 dB by about 120 Hz, but its ringing would smear the pulse edges. A 4th-order Bessel instead reaches only about -20 dB by 120 Hz — much gentler — but preserves pulse shape because its group delay is flat, so all frequency components in the pulse arrive together. The student picks Bessel and compensates the weaker 60 Hz rejection with a separate notch filter, rather than asking one low-pass to do both jobs.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who sees 'I used a 4th-order Butterworth low-pass' wants to hear why that family was chosen over the alternatives, because the choice reveals whether the student understood the trade-off or just copied a filter-design calculator's default. A strong answer names the competing requirement (flat passband gain, steep roll-off, or clean pulse response) and explains which approximation serves it and why the others would have cost something the project needed — for example, rejecting Chebyshev because its ripple would have corrupted an amplitude measurement. A weak answer cannot say what would go wrong with a different family, which signals the filter was selected by trial and error in software, not by understanding the response it produces.

questions.prompt: Which filter approximation gives up steep roll-off in exchange for nearly constant group delay across the passband?

options.text: Butterworth
Chebyshev
Bessel
Elliptic

explanations.a: Butterworth optimizes for a maximally flat passband magnitude, not flat group delay.
explanations.b: Chebyshev trades passband ripple for steeper roll-off than Butterworth; it does not prioritize flat delay.
explanations.c: Correct — the Bessel filter is derived from Bessel polynomials specifically to keep group delay nearly constant, minimizing pulse overshoot and ringing at the cost of a gentle roll-off.
explanations.d: Elliptic filters maximize roll-off steepness per order and have the worst phase behavior of the four, the opposite of flat delay.

questions.prompt: A 3rd-order all-pole low-pass filter, far above its cutoff frequency, will asymptotically roll off at approximately what rate?

options.text: -20 dB/decade
-40 dB/decade
-60 dB/decade
-80 dB/decade

explanations.a: -20 dB/decade is the rate for a 1st-order filter, not 3rd-order.
explanations.b: -40 dB/decade corresponds to a 2nd-order filter.
explanations.c: Correct — for the true all-pole families (Butterworth, Chebyshev, Bessel) the asymptotic roll-off is -20n dB/decade for order n, so a 3rd-order all-pole filter rolls off at -60 dB/decade; elliptic filters are the exception, since their finite stopband zeros cap the far-out slope at -20 or -40 dB/decade regardless of order.
explanations.d: -80 dB/decade would require a 4th-order filter.

questions.prompt: Match each filter approximation to the property it prioritizes.

right.text: Maximally flat passband magnitude, no ripple
Steepest roll-off for a given order, ripple in both bands
Controlled passband ripple traded for steeper roll-off than Butterworth

questions.explanation: Butterworth is defined by zero passband ripple (maximally flat); Chebyshev accepts passband ripple to steepen the transition beyond Butterworth; elliptic accepts ripple in both passband and stopband to achieve the steepest possible roll-off of the three.

questions.prompt: Order these four 4th-order filters (same cutoff) from steepest to gentlest roll-off just past the cutoff.

items.text: Elliptic
Chebyshev
Butterworth
Bessel

questions.explanation: Elliptic spends ripple in both bands to roll off fastest; Chebyshev spends passband ripple alone to roll off faster than Butterworth's ripple-free response; Bessel sacrifices roll-off steepness entirely for flat group delay, making it the gentlest of the four.

lessons.label: Sallen-Key and Multiple-Feedback Topologies

sections.heading: Sallen-Key: a second-order section from two resistors and two capacitors
sections.body: R.P. Sallen and E.L. Key published their voltage-controlled voltage-source (VCVS) filter topology out of MIT Lincoln Laboratory in 1955, and the circuit that bears their names is still the most common way to build an active second-order low-pass or high-pass section. A single op-amp, two resistors, and two capacitors set both the corner frequency f0 and the quality factor Q; for the equal-component low-pass case (R1=R2=R, C1=C2=C), f0 = 1/(2*pi*R*C) and Q is fixed by the op-amp's noninverting gain K through Q = 1/(3-K). Because the op-amp is wired for noninverting gain rather than as an integrator, the Sallen-Key needs no resistor matching for unity gain and is easy to cascade stage by stage.

sections.heading: Unity-gain versus equal-component design, and the Q sensitivity trap
sections.body: Designers choose between two conventions: the unity-gain version fixes K=1 (Q=1/(3-1)=0.5 for equal components, so Q is instead set by unequal R or C ratios) which avoids gain error from resistor tolerance, or the equal-component version which sets R1=R2 and C1=C2 and instead tunes Q entirely through the feedback gain K. The equal-component approach is popular because identical parts are cheap and easy to source, but it hides a serious problem: as the target Q rises, K must approach 3, and the sensitivity of Q to K becomes proportional to Q itself. A 1% error in the gain-setting resistors can shift a Q of 10 by roughly 10%, visibly reshaping the passband peak or even pushing the poles unstable. This is why Sallen-Key sections are rarely pushed past Q of about 5-10 in practice.

sections.heading: Multiple feedback: the inverting alternative for demanding Q
sections.body: The multiple-feedback (MFB) topology replaces the Sallen-Key's noninverting VCVS with the op-amp used as an inverting amplifier, with two feedback paths (hence the name) setting f0 and Q through resistor and capacitor ratios rather than through a critical gain term. Because MFB does not rely on a gain approaching a limiting value to hit high Q, its component sensitivities stay much better behaved as Q increases, making it the preferred topology for high-Q bandpass sections and for filters that must maintain good response well above their nominal passband, where the Sallen-Key's finite op-amp bandwidth and gain-dependent Q start to degrade performance. The cost is an inverted output and a design that is somewhat less intuitive to hand-tune than the Sallen-Key's directly-readable f0/Q formulas.

lessons.workedExample: A student builds a Sallen-Key low-pass with equal 10 kOhm resistors and equal 10 nF capacitors, giving f0 = 1/(2*pi*10k*10nF) = 1.59 kHz. To get Q = 8 for a peaky test filter, they solve Q=1/(3-K) for K = 3 - 1/8 = 2.875, set with a noninverting gain network of 18.75 kOhm over 10 kOhm. Using 5%-tolerance resistors, worst-case opposing tolerance (Rf 5% low, Rg 5% high) drops the realized gain to K=2.70, dropping Q to about 3.3 — a roughly 59% Q error from a 5% component error. Switching to 1% resistors improves things but does not tame them: worst-case K=2.84 still gives Q of about 6.2, a roughly 23% Q error. This is the Q-sensitivity trap made concrete: at Q=8 the circuit is so sensitive that even 1% resistors leave a large Q error, and resistor grade alone cannot fully fix it.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'why did you pick Sallen-Key over multiple feedback?' to see whether the student chose a topology for a reason or because it was the first circuit a tutorial showed. A strong answer connects the choice to the target Q and frequency range — Sallen-Key for a low-Q, low-frequency, easy-to-cascade stage, or MFB for a high-Q bandpass where gain-dependent sensitivity would have made Sallen-Key unstable to component tolerance. Naming the specific failure mode (K approaching 3, Q sensitivity scaling with Q) is the signal of real understanding; a student who cannot say what breaks at high Q likely picked the topology from a calculator without knowing its limits.

questions.prompt: In an equal-component Sallen-Key low-pass filter, what happens to Q sensitivity as the target Q increases?

options.text: Sensitivity stays constant regardless of Q
Sensitivity to component tolerance grows roughly proportional to Q itself
Sensitivity decreases because higher gain overrides tolerance error
Sensitivity only affects f0, never Q

explanations.a: Sensitivity is not constant — it grows as the noninverting gain K approaches the limiting value of 3.
explanations.b: Correct — because Q = 1/(3-K), as Q rises K approaches 3 and small errors in K produce increasingly large swings in Q, so sensitivity scales with Q.
explanations.c: Higher gain does not cancel tolerance error; it is precisely the mechanism that amplifies it near K=3.
explanations.d: The sensitivity problem is specifically a Q sensitivity issue arising from the gain term; f0 in the equal-component design depends only on R and C, not K.

questions.prompt: Why is the multiple-feedback (MFB) topology generally preferred over Sallen-Key for high-Q bandpass filters?

options.text: MFB uses fewer components than Sallen-Key
MFB sets Q through resistor/capacitor ratios rather than a gain term approaching a critical limit
MFB does not require an op-amp
MFB has a noninverting output, which is easier to cascade

explanations.a: Both topologies use a single op-amp with a similar component count; that is not the distinguishing factor.
explanations.b: Correct — MFB derives Q from ratios of passive components rather than requiring a gain that approaches a limiting value, so it stays better-behaved as Q rises.
explanations.c: MFB still requires an op-amp, used in an inverting configuration.
explanations.d: MFB produces an inverted output, which is actually a minor drawback, not an advantage.

questions.prompt: Match each design choice to its consequence in a Sallen-Key filter.

right.text: Q set by unequal resistor/capacitor ratios instead of gain
Q set entirely by the noninverting gain K
Component tolerance can destabilize the filter's response

questions.explanation: Unity-gain designs avoid a critical gain term by using unequal R/C ratios to set Q; equal-component designs use identical R and C but set Q via the gain K; pushing Q high in the equal-component design drives K toward 3, where ordinary component tolerance can visibly distort or destabilize the response.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for designing an equal-component Sallen-Key low-pass filter for a target f0 and Q.

items.text: Choose equal R and C values to set f0 = 1/(2*pi*R*C)
Solve Q = 1/(3-K) for the required noninverting gain K
Select feedback resistors to realize gain K
Check whether resistor tolerance produces acceptable Q error at that K

questions.explanation: f0 is fixed first by the equal R and C values, then the required K is derived from the target Q, then physical resistors are chosen to realize K, and finally the design must be checked for Q sensitivity to tolerance since that sensitivity grows as K approaches 3.

lessons.label: State-Variable, Biquad, and Switched-Capacitor Filters

sections.heading: Three outputs from one circuit: the state-variable filter
sections.body: The state-variable filter (a specific biquad realization) uses two integrators and a summing amplifier — typically three or four op-amps total — to solve the second-order filter differential equation directly, producing simultaneous low-pass, high-pass, and band-pass outputs from the same set of components. Because f0 is set by the integrator time constants (R and C) and Q is set independently by the summing/gain stage, a designer can tune corner frequency and Q without the two interacting, unlike the Sallen-Key where component choices couple both parameters together. This independence also means component sensitivity is low: a given percentage error in a resistor produces roughly the same percentage error in f0 or Q, not an amplified error the way a high-Q Sallen-Key's gain term can.

sections.heading: The trade: more op-amps for tunability and multiple responses
sections.body: The state-variable topology's price is component count — three or four op-amps and typically six to eight resistors versus the Sallen-Key's one op-amp — plus correspondingly higher power draw and board area. For a project needing only a single fixed low-pass response, that cost is not worth paying. But when a design needs to sweep f0 and Q independently (an audio equalizer stage, a tunable test filter), or needs low-pass, band-pass, and high-pass outputs simultaneously from one signal (a state-variable filter can also sum the three outputs with weighted gains to synthesize a notch or an all-pass response), the extra op-amps buy real flexibility and low sensitivity that a single-op-amp topology cannot match.

sections.heading: Switched-capacitor filters: trading a resistor for a clock
sections.body: A switched-capacitor filter replaces each resistor in an active-filter topology with a capacitor rapidly switched between two nodes; the average current delivered by a capacitor C switched at clock frequency fclk mimics a resistor of value R = 1/(fclk * C). Because the corner frequency of the resulting filter is then set by a ratio of a clock frequency to an on-chip capacitor ratio rather than by absolute RC values, the corner tracks the clock precisely and can be retuned in software just by changing fclk — this is how integrated parts like the MF10 or LTC1060 offer a programmable corner with no external resistor trimming. The trade-offs are real: the switching action itself injects clock-frequency noise (clock feedthrough) onto the output, and because the filter samples its input at fclk it is subject to aliasing exactly like any sampled system, so a switched-capacitor filter still needs a simple external RC or single-pole anti-alias filter ahead of it to remove input energy near and above the Nyquist frequency of its own switching clock.

lessons.workedExample: A student needs a 1 kHz low-pass with independently adjustable Q for a lab demo showing resonance peaking. A single-op-amp Sallen-Key would couple f0 and Q through shared components, making 'sweep Q while holding f0 fixed' awkward to wire with potentiometers. A state-variable filter built from three op-amps solves this: one potentiometer in the summing stage sweeps Q from 0.5 to 20 while the two integrator RC pairs stay untouched, holding f0 at 1 kHz throughout the sweep. For a second demo needing a filter whose corner retunes from 500 Hz to 5 kHz on command, the student instead reaches for an LTC1060 switched-capacitor filter driven by a variable clock, changing the corner by changing clock frequency alone — but adds a simple RC anti-alias filter ahead of it, since the switched-capacitor stage samples its input at the clock frequency fclk itself, which for a part like the LTC1060 in 50:1 mode is set to about 50 times the desired corner frequency, and would otherwise alias high-frequency noise into the passband.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing filter topology choice wants to know whether the student picked a state-variable or switched-capacitor filter because the project genuinely needed independent tuning or clock-programmable corners, or because they copied a reference design without understanding its cost. A strong answer names the specific need — simultaneous outputs, independent f0/Q tuning, or software-retunable corner — and can also name the specific cost paid for it: more op-amps and power, or clock feedthrough and the need for an anti-alias stage. A weak answer treats 'more op-amps' as unconditionally better or does not know that a switched-capacitor filter still needs an anti-alias filter in front of it, which suggests the aliasing behavior was never actually understood.

questions.prompt: What is the main advantage of a state-variable filter over a single-op-amp Sallen-Key section?

options.text: It uses fewer components
f0 and Q can be tuned independently, and it produces low-pass, high-pass, and band-pass outputs simultaneously
It requires no op-amps at all
It eliminates the need for capacitors

explanations.a: The state-variable filter uses more components (three or four op-amps) than a Sallen-Key, not fewer.
explanations.b: Correct — the two-integrator-plus-summer structure lets f0 (set by the integrators) and Q (set by the summing stage) be adjusted independently, and it naturally provides three simultaneous filter responses.
explanations.c: State-variable filters require multiple op-amps to implement the integrators and summer.
explanations.d: Capacitors are still required in the integrator stages that set f0.

questions.prompt: Why does a switched-capacitor filter still need an anti-alias filter ahead of it, even though it is itself a filter?

options.text: Because it amplifies the input signal too much
Because it samples its input at the switching clock rate and is therefore subject to aliasing like any sampled system
Because switched-capacitor filters cannot pass DC
Because the clock frequency is always lower than the filter's own corner frequency

explanations.a: Gain is unrelated to the aliasing issue; the concern is sampling, not amplification.
explanations.b: Correct — because a switched-capacitor filter operates by sampling its input at fclk, energy near or above its effective Nyquist frequency can fold down into the passband, so an external anti-alias filter is still required.
explanations.c: DC handling is not the reason; the issue is specifically about sampled-system aliasing.
explanations.d: The clock frequency is set well above the filter's corner (commonly tens to a hundred times higher), not below it.

questions.prompt: Match each filter type to its defining trade-off.

right.text: Low sensitivity and independent tuning, at the cost of extra op-amps
Clock-programmable corner, at the cost of clock feedthrough and required anti-alias filtering
Single op-amp simplicity, at the cost of coupled f0/Q and Q sensitivity at high Q

questions.explanation: The state-variable filter buys independent tuning and low sensitivity with extra op-amps; the switched-capacitor filter buys a clock-programmable corner at the cost of clock feedthrough and a required anti-alias filter; the Sallen-Key buys single-op-amp simplicity but couples f0 and Q and suffers Q sensitivity at high Q.

questions.prompt: Order these stages as signal flows through a switched-capacitor low-pass filter system.

items.text: External anti-alias RC filter removes energy near the switching Nyquist frequency
Switched-capacitor stage samples the input at the clock frequency
Switched capacitors emulate resistors whose value depends on clock frequency
Filtered output emerges with a corner set by the clock-to-capacitor ratio

questions.explanation: The anti-alias filter must condition the signal before it reaches the sampled switched-capacitor stage; the stage then samples the input at the clock rate, using switched capacitors that behave as clock-dependent resistors, ultimately producing an output whose corner frequency tracks the clock-to-capacitor ratio.

lessons.label: Noise in Analog Circuits

sections.heading: Thermal noise: the floor set by physics, not design error
sections.body: John B. Johnson measured a random voltage fluctuation present in every resistor even with no current flowing, and Harry Nyquist gave it a theoretical derivation the same year, both published in 1928 (Physical Review); the effect is now called Johnson-Nyquist or simply thermal noise. It arises from the random thermal motion of charge carriers and its mean-square voltage density is 4kTR, where k is Boltzmann's constant, T is absolute temperature, and R is resistance — meaning a 1 kOhm resistor at room temperature (300 K) produces about 4 nV/rtHz of noise voltage density, a number worth memorizing as a reference point since it scales as the square root of R. This noise cannot be designed away; it is a floor set by resistance and temperature, not a flaw in a particular part.

sections.heading: Shot noise and flicker (1/f) noise: two other fundamental sources
sections.body: Shot noise arises because current is not a smooth fluid but a stream of discrete electron charges crossing a barrier (a p-n junction, for instance) at random times; its current-noise density is sqrt(2qI), where q is the electron charge and I is the DC current, and unlike thermal noise it requires current flow to exist at all — a reverse-biased junction with zero current has no shot noise. Flicker noise, universally called 1/f noise, has a power spectral density that rises as frequency falls, dominating at low frequencies in nearly every active device (op-amps, transistors, even some resistors) for reasons tied to trapping and release of carriers at material defects. Most precision op-amp datasheets report a 1/f corner frequency — the point below which flicker noise exceeds the device's flat thermal/shot noise floor — and precision instrumentation is designed to either operate above that corner or use chopping to remove it (a technique covered in a later lesson).

sections.heading: Combining sources in quadrature and the noise-bandwidth correction
sections.body: Because independent noise sources are uncorrelated, their voltage or current contributions do not add directly — they add in quadrature (as the square root of the sum of squares). A practical amplifier noise budget therefore combines the op-amp's input voltage-noise density, its input current-noise density multiplied by the source impedance (since current noise only becomes a voltage problem across an impedance), and the thermal noise of any resistors in the signal path, each converted to the same units and summed as sqrt(v1^2 + v2^2 + ... ). This combined density must then be integrated over the circuit's actual bandwidth to get a total RMS noise voltage, and for the common case of a single-pole low-pass response with -3 dB frequency f_3dB, the equivalent noise bandwidth is not f_3dB itself but 1.57*f_3dB, because the filter's gentle roll-off lets in extra noise energy beyond the -3 dB point that a brick-wall filter of the same cutoff would have excluded.

lessons.workedExample: A student builds a photodiode amplifier with a 1 MOhm feedback resistor and a single-pole response with f_3dB = 10 kHz. The resistor's thermal noise density is sqrt(4kTR) = sqrt(4 * 1.38e-23 * 300 * 1e6) which is about 129 nV/rtHz. The op-amp contributes a comparatively small 10 nV/rtHz voltage noise. Combined in quadrature: sqrt(129^2 + 10^2) which is about 129 nV/rtHz (the resistor dominates completely). Applying the noise bandwidth correction, the equivalent noise bandwidth is 1.57 * 10 kHz = 15.7 kHz, so total RMS output noise is roughly 129 nV/rtHz * sqrt(15.7 kHz) which is about 16 microvolts RMS. The student learns the feedback resistor, not the op-amp, sets the noise floor here — reducing it would mean lowering that resistor value, not buying a lower-noise op-amp.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'what sets your circuit's noise floor?' to find out whether a student can trace a measured noise number back to a physical source rather than treating noise as an unexplained fuzziness on the scope. A strong answer identifies the dominant contributor by comparing actual densities (as in the worked example, where a large feedback resistor swamps the op-amp's own noise) and can state why swapping to a 'better' op-amp would not have helped. A weak answer says only 'there was noise so I added a capacitor,' without knowing whether the source was thermal, shot, or flicker, or whether the fix addressed the actual dominant term.

questions.prompt: Approximately what is the thermal noise voltage density of a 1 kOhm resistor at 300 K?

options.text: 0.4 nV/rtHz
4 nV/rtHz
40 nV/rtHz
400 nV/rtHz

explanations.a: This is too low by a factor of 10 for a 1 kOhm resistor at room temperature.
explanations.b: Correct — sqrt(4kTR) for R=1 kOhm at T=300 K works out to about 4 nV/rtHz, a standard reference figure.
explanations.c: This value is closer to what a 100 kOhm resistor would produce, not 1 kOhm.
explanations.d: This value is off by roughly two orders of magnitude for a 1 kOhm resistor.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes how to combine independent noise sources such as op-amp voltage noise and resistor thermal noise?

options.text: Add the noise voltages directly (arithmetic sum)
Add the noise voltages in quadrature (square root of the sum of squares)
Use only the largest single source and ignore the rest
Multiply the noise voltages together

explanations.a: Direct arithmetic addition overstates total noise because it assumes the sources are perfectly correlated, which independent noise sources are not.
explanations.b: Correct — independent (uncorrelated) noise sources combine as the square root of the sum of their squares, i.e. in quadrature.
explanations.c: While a dominant source can approximate the total when it is much larger than the others, correct practice is still to combine all sources in quadrature, not to discard them outright.
explanations.d: Multiplying noise voltages has no physical basis; power spectral densities add, and voltage densities combine in quadrature.

questions.prompt: Match each noise source to its defining characteristic.

right.text: Present in any resistor even with zero current flowing, density 4kTR
Requires DC current flow across a barrier, density sqrt(2qI)
Power spectral density rises as frequency falls, dominates below a device's corner frequency

questions.explanation: Thermal noise exists in any resistor from carrier motion alone, independent of current; shot noise arises from discreteness of charge crossing a barrier and requires current flow; flicker (1/f) noise rises at low frequency and dominates below each device's characteristic corner frequency.

questions.prompt: For a single-pole low-pass amplifier with f_3dB = 10 kHz, what is the equivalent noise bandwidth used to compute total RMS output noise?

options.text: 10 kHz
6.28 kHz
15.7 kHz
20 kHz

explanations.a: Using f_3dB directly underestimates the total noise because the single-pole roll-off lets in extra noise energy beyond the -3 dB point.
explanations.b: 6.28 kHz would come from confusing f_3dB with an angular-frequency conversion; it is not the noise bandwidth factor.
explanations.c: Correct — the noise bandwidth of a single-pole response is 1.57*f_3dB, so 1.57 * 10 kHz = 15.7 kHz.
explanations.d: 20 kHz overstates the correction; the actual factor is 1.57, not 2.

lessons.label: Distortion, Dynamic Range, and How They Are Measured

sections.heading: Where harmonics come from: curved transfer functions
sections.body: Total harmonic distortion (THD) measures how much energy a nonlinear circuit adds at integer multiples of an input sine wave's frequency, expressed as the ratio of the RMS sum of harmonic amplitudes to the fundamental's amplitude. The distortion originates in the device physics: a bipolar junction transistor's collector current follows an exponential relationship with base-emitter voltage (the Ebers-Moll/Shockley diode-law dependence), so even a small-signal sine input rides on a curved exponential and comes out with added second- and third-harmonic content; a MOSFET's drain current instead follows a square law in the saturation region, which by itself generates predominantly second-harmonic distortion for a single-ended stage. THD+N extends the same measurement to include all non-fundamental energy — harmonics plus broadband noise — making it the more honest number for comparing real amplifiers, since a circuit can have excellent THD but poor THD+N if its noise floor is high.

sections.heading: Intermodulation distortion and feedback's role in suppressing it
sections.body: Intermodulation distortion (IMD) is what the same nonlinearity produces when two tones at different frequencies are present simultaneously: the curved transfer function generates sum and difference products (f1+f2, f1-f2, and higher-order combinations like 2f1-f2) that fall at frequencies neither input tone occupies, which is a more realistic test for real signals than a single sine tone and a standard measurement for RF and audio power stages. Negative feedback suppresses both THD and IMD by the same factor: for an amplifier with open-loop gain A and feedback factor beta, the loop gain T = A*beta reduces distortion (and gain error, and output impedance) by 1/(1+T), so doubling the loop gain roughly halves the distortion — a direct, quantifiable payoff for adding feedback, which is why precision analog stages are built with as much loop gain as stability allows.

sections.heading: Measuring distortion: FFT, dBc, and the noise-floor ceiling
sections.body: The direct way to measure THD is to drive the circuit with a clean sine wave, capture the output, and run an FFT; each harmonic's level is read off relative to the fundamental in dBc (decibels relative to the carrier), and THD is computed from the ratio of harmonic RMS sum to fundamental amplitude. A classic alternative for very low distortion measurements is the notch-and-residual method: a sharp notch filter (historically a Wien-bridge null network) removes the fundamental from the output, and everything left over — the residual — is amplified and measured directly as the distortion-plus-noise content, which avoids needing enormous dynamic range in a single FFT capture. Either way, the measurement is only as good as the analyzer: if the test instrument's own noise floor or its own residual distortion sits within a few dB of the distortion being measured, the reported number describes the instrument, not the circuit under test, which is why serious THD measurements state the analyzer's floor alongside the result.

lessons.workedExample: A student measures a preamp's THD+N at -80 dBc (0.01%) using an audio analyzer rated for a -100 dBc noise floor, comfortably 20 dB below the reading, so the number is trustworthy. Encouraged, they then test a second, better-designed preamp and get a reading of -98 dBc — suspiciously close to the analyzer's own -100 dBc floor. Rather than reporting '-98 dBc THD+N,' they recognize the measurement is now floor-limited: the true distortion could be anywhere well below -98 dBc, and the analyzer cannot resolve it. They report the result as '<-98 dBc, limited by analyzer noise floor' rather than treating -98 dBc as a precise circuit specification.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'how do you know your distortion number is real and not just your test equipment?' is checking whether the student understands that every distortion measurement is bounded by the analyzer's own floor. A strong answer states the analyzer's noise floor or residual distortion spec and shows the measured value sits comfortably above it (or, if not, says so explicitly rather than reporting a floor-limited number as a clean spec). A weak answer reports a distortion figure with no reference to what the measurement instrument itself could resolve, which is the same error as reporting a scale's reading without knowing the scale's own uncertainty.

questions.prompt: A MOSFET's drain current follows a square-law dependence on gate-source voltage in saturation. What distortion signature does this predominantly produce for a single-ended stage with a single sine input?

options.text: Primarily third-harmonic distortion
Primarily second-harmonic distortion
Only intermodulation products, no harmonics
Only shot noise, no distortion

explanations.a: A square-law nonlinearity (an x^2 term) generates a second-harmonic term from a sine input, not primarily third-harmonic.
explanations.b: Correct — squaring a sine wave produces a DC term and a term at twice the input frequency, so a MOSFET's square-law transfer curve predominantly generates second-harmonic distortion in a single-ended stage.
explanations.c: Intermodulation products require two or more input tones; a single sine tone into a nonlinearity produces harmonics, not IMD.
explanations.d: Shot noise is a separate, unrelated noise mechanism; the square-law curve is a distortion (nonlinearity) mechanism, not a noise source.

questions.prompt: How does negative feedback with loop gain T = A*beta affect an amplifier's distortion?

options.text: It has no effect on distortion, only on gain
It reduces distortion by a factor of 1/(1+T)
It increases distortion by a factor of (1+T)
It eliminates distortion entirely regardless of T

explanations.a: Feedback affects far more than gain — it also reduces distortion, gain error, and output impedance by the same 1/(1+T) factor.
explanations.b: Correct — distortion (like gain error) is suppressed by the factor 1/(1+T), so more loop gain directly and predictably reduces distortion.
explanations.c: This reverses the direction of the effect; feedback reduces distortion, it does not amplify it.
explanations.d: Feedback reduces distortion by a finite factor set by T; it does not eliminate it entirely except in the unreachable limit of infinite loop gain.

questions.prompt: Match each measurement concept to its description.

right.text: Ratio of harmonic energy to fundamental, from a single input tone
Sum and difference products generated when two input tones are present
Harmonics plus broadband noise, all non-fundamental energy included

questions.explanation: THD measures only harmonic energy relative to the fundamental from a single tone; THD+N adds in all broadband noise as well; intermodulation distortion is specifically the sum-and-difference products that appear when two or more tones drive a nonlinearity simultaneously.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of the notch-and-residual method for measuring low-level distortion.

items.text: Drive the circuit under test with a clean sine wave
Pass the output through a sharp notch filter tuned to the fundamental
Amplify the remaining residual signal
Measure the residual as the distortion-plus-noise content

questions.explanation: A clean sine drives the circuit first; the notch filter then removes the large fundamental from the output, leaving only distortion products and noise; that small residual is amplified since it is otherwise too small to measure directly; the amplified residual is then measured as the distortion-plus-noise figure.

lessons.label: Precision Techniques: Chopper, Auto-Zero, Guarding, and Layout

sections.heading: Moving DC error out of the noisy 1/f region
sections.body: An op-amp's input offset voltage and its slow thermal drift both live at DC and low frequency — exactly where 1/f noise is largest. Chopper-stabilized and auto-zero amplifiers exploit that by modulating the signal path so DC error is shifted up to a chopping frequency where the amplifier's noise floor is flat and low, then demodulated back down after amplification; the chopper amplifier alternately reverses the input connection at a clock rate (commonly tens of kHz) and synchronously un-reverses the output, which converts the amplifier's DC offset into an AC signal at the chop frequency that later filtering removes, while auto-zero amplifiers instead periodically sample and null their own offset in a separate phase, storing a correction on a capacitor. Commercial parts using these techniques (Analog Devices' and Texas Instruments' zero-drift op-amp families are common examples) routinely reach offset voltages below 1 microvolt and drift under roughly 0.05 microvolt per degree C, one to two orders of magnitude better than a good ordinary bipolar op-amp.

sections.heading: What chopping costs
sections.body: The correction is not free. The switching action itself injects charge and produces output spikes at the chop or auto-zero clock frequency and its harmonics — visible on a scope as small periodic glitches riding on the output — so a chopper amplifier's own datasheet noise spectrum typically shows a bump right at the clock frequency even though the 1/f floor below it is excellent. A design that needs the amplifier's full bandwidth near the chop frequency, or that cannot tolerate any output artifact at that frequency (an audio path, for instance, if the chop clock happens to land in the audible band), may need to filter the output or choose a chop frequency deliberately placed outside the signal band of interest.

sections.heading: Layout and grounding: the physical half of precision design
sections.body: A precision circuit with a theoretically perfect amplifier still fails if the board around it leaks current or picks up interference. A guard ring — a trace carried at the same potential as a sensitive high-impedance node and routed to encircle it — intercepts surface leakage current across the PCB substrate that would otherwise flow into that node through the board's finite surface resistance, redirecting the leakage into the guard trace instead of the signal path; this matters most at a femtoamp-to-picoamp input like a photodiode or electrometer front end, where leakage of even a few picoamps can swamp the signal. Keeping the summing node (the op-amp's inverting input in a transimpedance or inverting stage) physically small and its trace short limits both stray capacitance, which would otherwise form an unwanted pole or invite noise pickup, and the surface area exposed to leakage. Star grounding — routing every ground return to a single common point rather than daisy-chaining grounds through a shared trace — prevents return currents from one stage developing a voltage drop that couples into another stage's reference. Supply decoupling with a capacitor placed close to each op-amp's power pins suppresses high-frequency supply noise and prevents one stage's transient current demand from disturbing another stage sharing the same rail.

lessons.workedExample: A student builds a photodiode transimpedance amplifier with a 100 megaohm feedback resistor to detect very low light levels, expecting picoamp-level signal currents. On first test, the output sits at an unexpected DC offset that drifts with room temperature and does not match the calculation from the op-amp's offset spec alone. Investigating the board, they find the summing node trace runs directly alongside a 5V supply trace with no guard ring, and surface leakage across the FR4 substrate between the two is on the order of a few picoamps — comparable to the signal itself. Adding a guard ring at the same potential as the summing node, driven from a low-impedance buffer, intercepts that leakage before it reaches the sensitive node, and the drift drops to match the op-amp's own datasheet offset drift.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing 'why does your circuit have unexplained offset or drift?' is testing whether the student can separate an electrical noise-floor problem from a physical layout problem, since precision failures are just as often board leakage or ground coupling as they are amplifier noise. A strong answer diagnoses the source with a concrete number — comparing expected leakage current across the board's surface resistance to the signal current, or naming a specific ground loop — and describes the physical fix (guard ring, star ground, decoupling) rather than reaching for a 'better' op-amp. A weak answer blames a vague 'noise' without distinguishing whether the culprit is the amplifier's own noise floor, board leakage, or ground coupling, since each has a different fix.

questions.prompt: How does a chopper-stabilized amplifier reduce DC offset and drift?

options.text: It uses a larger feedback resistor to swamp the offset
It modulates the DC offset up to a chop clock frequency, away from the noisy 1/f region, then demodulates it back down for removal
It physically cools the amplifier die to reduce thermal noise
It increases the amplifier's open-loop gain to cancel offset

explanations.a: A larger feedback resistor changes gain and noise contribution but does not address offset modulation.
explanations.b: Correct — by periodically reversing the input connection at a clock rate and un-reversing the output synchronously, the DC offset is converted to an AC signal at the chop frequency where the noise floor is flat, and can then be filtered out.
explanations.c: Chopper stabilization is a signal-processing technique, not a thermal management technique; it does not rely on cooling the die.
explanations.d: Open-loop gain affects overall amplifier gain accuracy but is not the mechanism chopper stabilization uses to remove offset.

questions.prompt: What is the primary purpose of a guard ring around a high-impedance summing node on a PCB?

options.text: To shield the node from electromagnetic radiation only
To intercept surface leakage current across the board substrate before it reaches the sensitive node
To increase the trace's current-carrying capacity
To reduce the resistance of the signal trace itself

explanations.a: EMI shielding is a different concern; a guard ring specifically addresses conductive surface leakage, not radiated interference.
explanations.b: Correct — a guard ring held at the same potential as the sensitive node intercepts leakage current flowing across the board's finite surface resistance, diverting it away from the high-impedance node.
explanations.c: Current-carrying capacity is unrelated; guard rings deal with leakage current at high-impedance nodes, not power delivery.
explanations.d: A guard ring does not lower trace resistance; it redirects leakage current via a nearby trace held at matching potential.

questions.prompt: Match each precision-design technique to the problem it addresses.

right.text: DC offset and 1/f drift in the amplifier itself
Surface leakage current into a high-impedance node
Return-current coupling between stages sharing a ground path
High-frequency noise and transient demand on the power rail

questions.explanation: Chopper stabilization removes DC offset and drift; a guard ring intercepts surface leakage current into a sensitive node; star grounding prevents return-current coupling between stages; supply decoupling suppresses high-frequency rail noise and transient loading.

questions.prompt: What is a known downside of chopper-stabilized amplifiers compared to ordinary op-amps?

options.text: They cannot achieve sub-microvolt offset
They inject switching artifacts (spikes/glitches) at the chop clock frequency and its harmonics
They have no 1/f noise reduction benefit at all
They require a negative supply rail that ordinary op-amps do not

explanations.a: Chopper-stabilized parts routinely achieve well below 1 microvolt offset; this is their main strength, not a limitation.
explanations.b: Correct — the switching action needed to modulate out DC offset injects charge and produces output artifacts at the chop frequency and its harmonics, visible as periodic glitches on the output.
explanations.c: 1/f noise reduction is precisely the benefit chopper stabilization provides; the trade-off is the switching artifact it introduces in exchange.
explanations.d: Supply rail requirements are not the defining trade-off of chopper stabilization; the relevant cost is the clock-related switching artifact.

units.label: Designing, Tuning, and Defending an Analog Project

lessons.label: From Specification to Topology

sections.heading: Spec Numbers Choose the Topology
sections.body: A project spec is a set of constraints, not a suggestion: source impedance, required gain, bandwidth, noise floor, output swing, and supply rail all point toward a topology before a single part number is picked. A bridge sensor with a differential, low-impedance output and a common-mode voltage sitting near mid-supply calls for an instrumentation amplifier, chosen for its high common-mode rejection ratio (CMRR), rather than a plain op-amp difference-amp configuration that needs precisely matched resistors to reject common-mode noise. A photodiode or other current-output sensor calls for a transimpedance stage, not a voltage amplifier, because the sensor's output impedance is enormous and a voltage divider would swamp the signal. Bandwidth and gain are not independent choices either: every op-amp has a gain-bandwidth product (GBW), the frequency at which open-loop gain falls to unity, and a stage's closed-loop bandwidth is approximately GBW divided by closed-loop gain.

sections.heading: Why Gain Gets Distributed, Not Dumped
sections.body: A single op-amp with GBW = 1 MHz set to a closed-loop gain of 100 has a closed-loop bandwidth of roughly 10 kHz — workable for a spec needing 1 kHz, but with no margin left for component tolerance or an extra pole from load capacitance. Splitting gain across two stages (10x and 10x, say) gives each stage far more bandwidth margin, since each stage's own gain, and hence its GBW penalty, is lower even though total gain is unchanged. Distributing gain also matters for precision: an error at the first stage — input offset voltage, or bias current times source resistance — gets multiplied by every gain stage that follows it once referred to the output. The first stage should therefore be the highest-precision device in the chain; later stages can be cheaper parts, since their own errors are diluted by less remaining downstream gain.

sections.heading: The Written Error Budget
sections.body: A defensible design turns 'it works' into a table: input offset voltage, offset drift over the expected temperature range, input-referred noise integrated over the closed-loop bandwidth, gain error from resistor tolerance and finite loop gain, and bandwidth margin (closed-loop bandwidth versus spec, as a ratio, not just 'wide enough'). Each term is converted to an output-referred value in the signal's own units, then summed — worst-case addition for a conservative bound, or root-sum-square (RSS) if the sources are statistically independent, the more realistic bound for uncorrelated noise and drift. That total is compared against what the downstream ADC resolution or the judge's stated accuracy requirement actually needs; if the budget exceeds it, the fix is a lower-offset part, more averaging, or a narrower bandwidth, not hope.

lessons.workedExample: A student needs to condition a strain-gauge half-bridge that outputs ±5 mV full-scale from a 350 Ω source, driving a 3.3 V single-supply ADC that expects 0-3.3 V centered at 1.65 V, with 1 kHz bandwidth for vibration testing. A single-stage instrumentation amp at gain 330 (INA333, unity-gain bandwidth ~350 kHz) would land closed-loop bandwidth near 1 kHz — no margin. Instead: stage 1 is an INA333 at gain 100 (RG ≈ 1 kΩ, per G = 1 + 100 kΩ/RG), giving ~3.5 kHz bandwidth and rejecting bridge common-mode noise via >100 dB CMRR; stage 2 is an OPA2333 op-amp at gain 3.3 that also sums in a 1.65 V reference to re-center the signal for the single-supply ADC. Total gain is 330, split so neither stage is bandwidth-starved.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask 'why this op-amp, why this gain split' because the answer separates a part picked off a datasheet cover page from one chosen against the spec. A weak answer says 'I used an op-amp with high gain and it worked in simulation.' A strong answer names the actual constraint that drove the choice — 'a single gain-of-330 stage only gave me 1 kHz of closed-loop bandwidth with zero margin, so I split it 100x/3.3x' — and can produce the written error budget: offset, drift, gain error, and noise, all summed and compared to the ADC's least-significant bit. That budget is the evidence a judge is actually looking for.

questions.prompt: An op-amp with a gain-bandwidth product of 1 MHz is configured for a closed-loop gain of 100. What is its approximate closed-loop bandwidth?

options.text: 1 MHz
100 kHz
10 kHz
1 kHz

explanations.a: 1 MHz is the GBW itself (the open-loop unity-gain frequency), not the bandwidth after closed-loop gain is applied.
explanations.b: 100 kHz would hold at a gain of 10, not 100.
explanations.c: Correct — closed-loop bandwidth is approximately GBW divided by closed-loop gain: 1 MHz / 100 = 10 kHz.
explanations.d: 1 kHz would require a gain of 1000, ten times higher than the stated gain.

questions.prompt: Why should the highest-precision (lowest offset, lowest drift) device in a multi-stage chain go first, closest to the source?

options.text: Because it's cheaper to buy one precision part than several
Because the first stage handles the most current
Because errors introduced at the first stage are multiplied by all the gain that follows, so they dominate the total output-referred error
Because the first stage sets the supply voltage for the rest of the chain

explanations.a: Cost isn't the reason — the placement is about where an error gets amplified most, not about part price.
explanations.b: Amplifier stages set voltage gain, not current handling; that's not why placement matters here.
explanations.c: Correct — an offset or noise term introduced at the input is referred to the output multiplied by every downstream gain stage, so it dominates the error budget; a later stage's own error is diluted by less remaining gain.
explanations.d: Supply voltage is a system-wide choice, not something the first stage determines for later stages.

questions.prompt: Match each error-budget term to what it represents.

right.text: DC error present at zero input signal
Change in offset voltage as temperature changes
Deviation from nominal gain, from resistor tolerance and finite loop gain
Headroom between a stage's closed-loop bandwidth and the spec's required bandwidth

questions.explanation: Offset voltage is the DC error at zero input; drift is how that offset changes with temperature; gain error is the deviation from the nominal designed gain caused by resistor tolerance and finite loop gain; bandwidth margin is the ratio between a stage's actual closed-loop bandwidth and what the spec requires.

questions.prompt: Order the steps in turning a project spec into a chosen topology and parts.

items.text: Identify the source's signal type and impedance (differential bridge, current-output sensor, single-ended voltage)
Compute the total gain needed to map the signal range to the required output swing
Check candidate stages' gain-bandwidth product against the bandwidth spec, splitting gain across stages if margin is thin
Select specific parts meeting the offset, noise, and supply requirements
Build the written error budget and confirm the total is within the needed accuracy

questions.explanation: You must first know what kind of source you have and its impedance, then compute how much total gain is needed, then check whether that gain fits in a bandwidth-limited stage or must be split, then pick real parts against those constraints, and finally verify the whole chain's errors on paper before building.

lessons.label: SPICE Simulation and Where It Misleads

sections.heading: Five Analyses, Five Different Questions
sections.body: SPICE offers several distinct analyses, and each answers a question the others can't. A .op analysis finds the DC operating point — the bias voltages and currents every other analysis linearizes around, so it should be checked first. A .ac analysis sweeps frequency and reports the small-signal (Bode) response around that operating point; it is fast but assumes linearity, so it cannot show clipping or slew-rate limiting. A .tran analysis simulates the actual time-domain waveform, capturing nonlinear effects like slew-rate limiting and output clipping that .ac cannot, at the cost of speed and a dependence on correct initial conditions. A .noise analysis computes output- and input-referred noise density from each device's noise model, integrable into a total rms figure. A .step sweep varies one parameter — temperature, a resistor value, a supply voltage — across a run, and Monte Carlo draws many randomized runs from each toleranced component's distribution, revealing yield and spread rather than a single nominal answer.

sections.heading: Macromodels vs. an Ideal Block
sections.body: A vendor SPICE macromodel for a real part reproduces finite GBW, input offset, slew rate, and output swing near the rails — unlike a generic ideal op-amp (VCVS) block with infinite everything, which will pass a design that a real part cannot meet. But even a good macromodel can hide things: some bipolar-input parts exhibit phase reversal, where the output snaps to the wrong rail if input common-mode is exceeded, a behavior simplified models sometimes omit; output current limiting and thermal shutdown are often approximated; and the 1/f noise corner is sometimes flattened out entirely. Matching a macromodel's simulated curves against the datasheet's typical curves before trusting it is a real check, not a formality.

sections.heading: Convergence Errors and What the Netlist Never Saw
sections.body: Convergence errors — SPICE's Newton-Raphson solver failing to find a self-consistent operating point — usually trace to a floating node, such as an AC-coupling capacitor with no DC bias path to ground, or a feedback loop starting a .tran run from an undefined state; the fix is an .ic statement setting initial node voltages, or a bleed resistor providing a DC path. Even a simulation that converges cleanly is blind to layout: trace inductance, ground-plane impedance, and stray capacitance at a high-impedance node exist nowhere in the netlist unless explicitly added as estimated parasitic elements. A schematic that is rock-stable in SPICE can still oscillate on the bench because of a few nanohenries of trace inductance sitting inside the feedback path.

lessons.workedExample: A student simulates a non-inverting amplifier at gain 10, first with an ideal op-amp block: .ac shows a flat 20 dB response out past 10 MHz. Swapping in an LM358 SPICE macromodel and rerunning .ac shows the response actually rolls off near 100 kHz, consistent with the LM358's roughly 1 MHz gain-bandwidth product divided by a gain of 10. A .tran run driving a 1 kHz, 2 V square wave then reveals slanted, not square, edges — the LM358's ~0.3 V/µs slew rate limits how fast the output can move, an effect .ac cannot show since it only models small-signal behavior. A .noise sweep from 1 Hz to 100 kHz integrates to a few µV rms at the output, a figure the ideal block reports as exactly zero.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe simulation choices because 'I simulated it in SPICE' means nothing if the simulation used an ideal op-amp block — that only proves the topology's algebra, not that the chosen real part meets spec. A strong answer names the specific macromodel used (the LM358 model from the manufacturer, not an ideal block), states which analysis caught which limitation (.tran caught slew-rate-limited edges that .ac could not show), and says plainly what SPICE could not tell them — usually layout parasitics or the exact 1/f noise corner. A weak answer treats 'it simulated fine' as equivalent to 'it will work on the bench.'

questions.prompt: Which analysis must be run and check out before an .ac or .tran simulation's results are meaningful, since it establishes the DC bias point the small-signal model is linearized around?

options.text: .op
.noise
.step
Monte Carlo

explanations.a: Correct — .op finds the DC operating point, the bias condition every AC or transient analysis linearizes or integrates around.
explanations.b: .noise reports noise density given an already-established operating point; it doesn't establish that point itself.
explanations.c: .step re-runs another analysis across a swept parameter; it depends on that analysis, not the other way around.
explanations.d: Monte Carlo re-runs another analysis across randomized component values; it doesn't establish the DC bias point on its own.

questions.prompt: Why does simulating with an ideal op-amp block risk misleading a student compared to a real vendor macromodel?

options.text: Ideal blocks run slower in simulation
An ideal block has infinite GBW, slew rate, and output swing, so it never shows the bandwidth roll-off, slew limiting, or clipping that a real part will exhibit
