explanations.a: Correct — the clock is a shared, timing-critical signal; inserting extra gating logic directly into its path can create glitches or added skew that propagate to every flip-flop it drives, which is why a dedicated clock-enable input on the flip-flop itself is preferred.
explanations.b: AND gates can switch at clock frequencies; the concern is about glitches and skew, not raw switching capability.
explanations.c: Clock-enable is a standard, common flip-flop feature; it is not impossible, just implemented via a dedicated input rather than by gating the clock line.
explanations.d: Gating the clock does not zero out setup time; it is unrelated to the setup-time specification.

lessons.label: Synchronous Design: Setup, Hold, and the State Machine

sections.heading: Three timing numbers that bound every clock period
sections.body: Every flip-flop datasheet specifies setup time (tsu), the minimum time data must be stable before the clock edge; hold time (th), the minimum time it must stay stable after the edge; and clock-to-Q delay (tcq), how long after the clock edge the new output actually appears. Between two flip-flops connected by combinational logic with worst-case delay tlogic, and accounting for clock skew tskew (the difference in arrival time of the same clock edge at the two flops), the maximum usable clock frequency is bounded by fmax = 1 / (tcq + tlogic + tsu + tskew) — every term in that sum eats into the clock period, so speeding up a design means attacking whichever term dominates, usually tlogic through fewer gate levels or a faster technology. This is the same propagation-delay accounting from gate-level timing, now applied end-to-end between two clocked storage elements instead of through a single gate.

sections.heading: Hold violations don't care about clock speed
sections.body: A setup violation happens when data arrives too close to the clock edge to be captured reliably, and it can always be fixed by slowing the clock down, giving tlogic more time to settle before the next edge. A hold violation is fundamentally different: it happens when data changes too soon after the clock edge, racing ahead of the previous value the flip-flop was supposed to still be capturing, and it depends only on the fastest path delay and clock skew, not on the clock period at all — slowing the clock down changes nothing, because both the edge and the fast-arriving new data are still separated by the same short interval. Hold violations are fixed by adding delay to the offending fast path (deliberately inserting buffers) or by controlling skew, which is exactly why clock skew is treated as a first-class timing term rather than an afterthought: excessive skew can turn an otherwise-safe design into one with a hold violation on real silicon.

sections.heading: One clock, and the Moore/Mealy choice
sections.body: The standard discipline for a synchronous design is to use a single clock (or a small number of clearly related clock domains with disciplined crossing logic) driving every flip-flop, so that the fmax analysis above applies uniformly and no ad hoc timing relationships need separate verification. A finite state machine (FSM) built this way is either Moore, where outputs depend only on the current state, or Mealy, where outputs depend on the current state and the current inputs; Mealy machines can react within the same clock cycle an input changes (often using fewer states) while Moore machines are glitch-safer on outputs since they never respond mid-cycle to input noise. State encoding is binary (using log2(N) flip-flops for N states, minimizing flip-flop count) or one-hot (using N flip-flops, one per state, trading flip-flops for simpler, often faster next-state logic since only one bit is ever 1). Any real state register has unused encoded values if N is not a power of two (binary) or if more than one bit could spuriously be set (one-hot); a robust design adds explicit default-case logic routing every unused state back to a safe known state, since without it a corrupted state register (from a glitch or a power-up race) can lock the FSM into a dead state forever.

lessons.workedExample: A design has tcq=0.5 ns, tsu=0.3 ns, worst-case combinational tlogic=4.2 ns, and tskew=0.2 ns. fmax = 1/(0.5+4.2+0.3+0.2) = 1/5.2 ns ≈ 192 MHz. The design is currently clocked at 250 MHz (4 ns period), which is below its safe fmax requirement — a setup violation, since 4 ns < 5.2 ns needed. A student 'fixes' the failing timing by slowing the clock to 150 MHz (6.67 ns period), which does resolve the setup violation since now 6.67 ns > 5.2 ns. But if a separate fast path in the same design (say tcq=0.5 ns plus a 0.1 ns pass-through, well under any clock period) also has a hold violation because its data changes too soon after the same clock edge, slowing the clock to 150 MHz does nothing for that path — the hold check compares only fast-path delay plus skew against tsu/th, entirely independent of clock period, so the hold violation persists at any clock speed until a delay buffer is added to that specific fast path.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who hears a student say 'I fixed the timing failure by slowing the clock' will immediately ask whether the failure was setup or hold, because that single follow-up question separates real understanding from pattern-matched vocabulary. A strong answer explains that slowing the clock only ever helps a setup violation, and that a hold violation needs a structurally different fix — added delay on the fast path — because hold checks don't reference the clock period at all. On FSM design, a judge probing 'what happens if your state register glitches into an unused encoding' wants to hear about explicit default-state recovery logic, not silence, since an FSM with no default case can lock up permanently on real hardware even though it worked perfectly in simulation.

questions.prompt: Given tcq=0.5 ns, tlogic=4.2 ns, tsu=0.3 ns, and tskew=0.2 ns, what is fmax?

options.text: ≈192 MHz
≈500 MHz
≈50 MHz

explanations.a: Correct — summing all four terms gives 5.2 ns, and 1/5.2 ns ≈ 192 MHz.
explanations.b: This would require a period near 2 ns, far shorter than the 5.2 ns the summed terms actually require.
explanations.c: This corresponds to a 20 ns period, much longer than necessary given the stated delays.
explanations.d: This would require a sub-nanosecond period, physically inconsistent with the 5.2 ns budget from the given terms.

questions.prompt: Why does slowing the clock down fail to fix a hold violation?

options.text: Because the hold check compares fast-path delay and skew against hold time, independent of the clock period
Because hold violations only occur at clock frequencies above 1 GHz
Because slowing the clock always makes hold violations worse, never better or neutral
Because hold time only applies to Mealy machines, not Moore machines

explanations.a: Correct — a hold violation is a race between the same clock edge's effect on two flops via a very fast path, and that race's outcome does not depend on how far apart clock edges are, so period-related fixes are structurally powerless against it.
explanations.b: Hold violations can occur at any clock frequency; they are not tied to a particular frequency range.
explanations.c: Hold violations are simply unaffected by clock period — neither better nor worse — not specifically worsened.
explanations.d: Hold time is a property of the flip-flop hardware itself and applies equally regardless of Moore/Mealy output style.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes a Mealy FSM's outputs from a Moore FSM's outputs?

options.text: Mealy outputs depend on current state and current inputs; Moore outputs depend only on current state
Mealy machines cannot have more than 4 states; Moore machines have no state limit
Moore machines require two clocks; Mealy machines require only one
Mealy and Moore machines are identical in output behavior but differ only in encoding style

explanations.a: Correct — this dependency difference is exactly why Mealy outputs can change mid-cycle in response to input changes (reacting faster, often with fewer states) while Moore outputs only change at the clock edge (glitch-safer).
explanations.b: State count is unrelated to the Moore/Mealy distinction; both can have arbitrarily many states.
explanations.c: Both are standard single-clock synchronous designs; the distinction is about output dependency, not clock count.
explanations.d: Their output timing behavior differs meaningfully, which is the entire reason the distinction is made.

questions.prompt: Match each state-encoding style to its trade-off.

right.text: Uses log2(N) flip-flops for N states, minimizing flip-flop count
Uses N flip-flops (one per state), often giving simpler and faster next-state logic

questions.explanation: Binary encoding is compact in flip-flop count but its next-state logic can be more complex; one-hot spends more flip-flops but typically simplifies and speeds up the next-state decode since only one bit is ever active.

questions.prompt: Order the diagnostic steps for a synchronous design that fails timing.

items.text: Determine whether the failure is a setup violation or a hold violation
If setup: compute fmax from tcq, tlogic, tsu, tskew and check the clock period against it
If setup-limited, slow the clock or reduce tlogic (fewer logic levels)
If hold-limited instead, add delay to the fast path or reduce skew, since clock period is irrelevant

questions.explanation: The fix depends entirely on which violation type occurred, so classifying setup versus hold must come first; setup violations are addressed through the period/fmax relationship, while hold violations require path-delay or skew fixes regardless of clock period.

units.label: Microcontrollers: Architecture, GPIO, ADC, and PWM

lessons.label: Inside a Microcontroller

sections.heading: One chip, one memory map, or two memories entirely
sections.body: A microcontroller (MCU) packs a CPU core, program memory (Flash), working memory (SRAM), often a slice of EEPROM, and a set of peripherals — timers, ADC, UART — onto one die. The organizing question is whether instructions and data share a memory space. Von Neumann architecture (named for John von Neumann's 1945 EDVAC report) uses one address space and one bus for both, which is simple but means fetching an instruction and fetching data can collide. Harvard architecture, named after the Harvard Mark I relay computer (1944), keeps program and data memory on separate buses so the CPU can fetch the next instruction while reading or writing data in the same cycle. Most MCUs are 'modified Harvard': separate physical Flash and SRAM, but instructions can still read constants out of Flash. Atmel's AVR core is a clean example — one clock cycle fetches an instruction from Flash while the previous instruction's data access happens on the SRAM bus.

sections.heading: The whole program model is memory-mapped registers
sections.body: Peripherals are not separate chips you wire up — they are hardware blocks whose control and status live at fixed addresses in the CPU's address space. Setting a GPIO pin high is not a function call into an operating system; it is a single store instruction writing a bit into a port register at, say, address 0x25 on an AVR or a peripheral-bus address on a Cortex-M. This is why 'bare metal' firmware is really just reading and writing memory: the datasheet's register map is the entire programming interface.

sections.heading: Clocks, resets, and the 8-bit vs 32-bit trade
sections.body: An MCU's internal RC oscillator is cheap and needs no external parts, but drifts roughly 1-10% with temperature and supply voltage — fine for blinking an LED, unusable for precise UART timing over a long cable. An external crystal, by contrast, holds around 20 parts per million (ppm), and a PLL can multiply a slow reference up to the core's run speed. Reset sources multiply too: power-on reset, an external reset pin, a watchdog timeout, and brown-out detection, which forces reset if supply voltage sags below a threshold rather than let the core execute garbage on flaky power. Fuses (AVR) or option bytes (STM32) are one-time or rarely-changed configuration bits set outside normal firmware — they pick the clock source, enable brown-out detection, or lock the Flash from readout. Choosing a core is a real trade: an 8-bit AVR like the ATmega328P runs its instruction set at up to 20 MHz with a handful of KB of Flash and SRAM and dirt-cheap peripherals, while a 32-bit Cortex-M0+ or M4 runs 48 MHz to 180+ MHz, addresses far more memory linearly, and — on the M4 — adds a hardware floating-point unit and DSP instructions, at higher cost and power.

lessons.workedExample: A student's ATmega328P (Arduino Uno) project needs to log sensor readings with timestamps accurate to within a few milliseconds over a 20-minute run. Running on the internal 8 MHz RC oscillator, the clock can drift 1-2%, which is 12-24 seconds over 20 minutes — enough to visibly desync the log from a stopwatch. Switching the fuse bits to select the external 16 MHz crystal (already on the Uno board) drops that error to roughly 20 ppm, under 0.03 seconds over the same run — a change made entirely in fuse configuration, not code.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'why does your board need a crystal, and what happens if you skip it?' to check whether the student understands the MCU is not a black box that magically keeps time. A strong answer names the internal RC oscillator's percent-level drift versus the crystal's ppm-level stability and connects it to a concrete failure (timestamps drifting, UART bytes garbling because both ends assume a slightly different bit rate). A weak answer says 'the crystal makes it more accurate' with no mechanism or number — that is a memorized fact, not an understood trade-off.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes Harvard architecture from Von Neumann architecture?

options.text: Harvard uses separate buses for program and data memory; Von Neumann shares one bus for both
Harvard has no RAM at all
Von Neumann architecture is only used in 8-bit chips
Harvard architecture cannot execute instructions from Flash

explanations.a: Correct — Harvard keeps program and data memory on separate buses so instruction fetch and data access can happen in the same cycle; Von Neumann shares one address space and bus for both.
explanations.b: Harvard architectures still have RAM for data; they simply separate it from program memory.
explanations.c: Von Neumann-style single-bus designs appear across both 8-bit and larger CPUs; it is not tied to word width.
explanations.d: Modified Harvard MCUs like AVR execute instructions from Flash constantly — that is the entire point of program memory.

questions.prompt: Why would a project needing accurate UART timing over a long run switch from the internal RC oscillator to an external crystal?

options.text: The RC oscillator cannot run above 1 MHz
The RC oscillator drifts roughly 1-10% while a crystal holds around 20 ppm, and UART framing depends on both ends agreeing on bit rate
Crystals are required by law for any UART communication
The RC oscillator only works when the chip is not sourcing current

explanations.a: Internal RC oscillators on AVR parts typically run near 8 MHz or faster, well above 1 MHz; speed is not the limiting factor here.
explanations.b: Correct — a percent-level drift on RC vs. a ppm-level crystal directly threatens UART, which has no separate clock line and relies on both sides sampling at nearly the same rate.
explanations.c: There is no such requirement; plenty of low-precision applications run fine on RC oscillators.
explanations.d: Oscillator choice has nothing to do with whether the chip is sourcing current on its pins.

questions.prompt: Match each reset/configuration mechanism to what it does.

right.text: Forces reset if supply voltage sags below a safe threshold
Forces reset if firmware fails to periodically 'kick' a hardware timer, catching a hung program
Selects rarely-changed chip configuration such as clock source, outside normal firmware execution
Holds the core in reset until supply voltage stabilizes at startup

questions.explanation: Brown-out detection guards against sagging supply voltage; a watchdog timer catches a hung program; fuses/option bytes configure the chip outside normal firmware; power-on reset holds the core until startup voltage is stable.

questions.prompt: A student picks an 8-bit ATmega328P over a 32-bit Cortex-M4 for a simple LED-blinking and button-reading project. What is the most accurate justification?

options.text: The ATmega328P is cheaper and its peripheral set is sufficient; the Cortex-M4's higher clock speed and floating-point unit add cost and complexity the task does not need
8-bit chips cannot drive GPIO pins
32-bit cores cannot run below 100 MHz
The Cortex-M4 has no memory-mapped registers

explanations.a: Correct — matching core capability to task need (avoiding an unnecessary FPU and higher power/cost) is exactly the kind of trade-off named in the lesson.
explanations.b: 8-bit MCUs drive GPIO routinely; that is one of their most basic functions.
explanations.c: Cortex-M cores can be clocked well below 100 MHz; clock speed is configurable, not a floor.
explanations.d: Every MCU core, 8-bit or 32-bit, exposes peripherals through memory-mapped registers — that is the universal programming model described in the lesson.

lessons.label: GPIO, Electrically

sections.heading: Push-pull vs. open-drain: two ways to drive a wire
sections.body: A GPIO pin configured push-pull has two active transistors: one pulls the pin to the supply rail for a logic high, the other pulls it to ground for a logic low, so the pin actively drives both states. Most MCU outputs default to push-pull. An open-drain (or open-collector) output only has the pull-down transistor — driving low is active, but 'high' just means the transistor turns off and the pin floats, relying on an external or internal pull-up resistor to actually pull it to the rail. Open-drain matters whenever multiple devices need to share one line without fighting: I2C's SDA/SCL lines are open-drain specifically so any device can pull the line low without risking two chips shorting rail-to-ground against each other.

sections.heading: Floating inputs, pull-ups, and hysteresis
sections.body: An MCU input pin left unconnected — floating — has no defined voltage; it picks up stray capacitive coupling from nearby switching signals and can read random highs and lows, flipping a button-read routine unpredictably. The fix is a pull-up or pull-down resistor that fixes the idle voltage. Most MCUs, including AVR, include a configurable internal pull-up, typically 20-50 kilohm, enabled with a single register bit — convenient for a button to ground without adding an external resistor, though too weak to sink much current if misused as an output load. Digital inputs also use a Schmitt-trigger comparator with hysteresis: instead of one threshold voltage, it has a higher trip point going low-to-high and a lower one going high-to-low, so a slow or noisy edge does not chatter the input rapidly between states as it crosses a single fixed threshold.

sections.heading: Current limits and driving real loads
sections.body: A GPIO pin can sink or source current directly — sourcing means the pin supplies current out through the load to ground (LED anode to pin, cathode to a series resistor to ground... more commonly, pin through resistor to LED to ground); sinking means the load's current flows into the pin to ground, with the LED's supply-side resistor tying to the rail. Either way a series resistor sets the current, since an LED's forward voltage drop is roughly fixed and the pin otherwise has no other current limit but the resistor and its own internal output impedance. A typical AVR pin is rated around 20-40 mA absolute maximum, and the whole port or chip has a combined current budget — sinking 20 mA on every pin of an 8-pin port simultaneously can exceed the chip's total rating even if each pin is individually within spec. For a relay coil, DC motor, or anything drawing more than a few tens of milliamps, a pin should never drive the load directly; instead it switches a MOSFET's gate, and the MOSFET switches the load's higher current, with a flyback (freewheeling) diode across an inductive load like a relay coil or motor to clamp the voltage spike generated when the field collapses at turn-off — without it, that spike can exceed the MOSFET's breakdown voltage and destroy it.

lessons.workedExample: A student wires a push-button between a GPIO pin and ground, with the internal pull-up disabled and no external resistor. The pin reads randomly between HIGH and LOW even with the button untouched, and the Serial Monitor prints spurious button presses. Enabling the AVR's internal ~30 kohm pull-up (pinMode(pin, INPUT_PULLUP) on Arduino) fixes it instantly: the pin now idles firmly at 5V through the pull-up, and pressing the button pulls it solidly to ground, giving a clean, repeatable digital signal without adding a single external part.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe GPIO wiring because it is where a project's electrical understanding either shows or does not — a student who says 'I put a resistor on it' without saying why reveals they copied a tutorial. A strong answer explains what a floating input does electrically (picks up noise, no defined voltage) and why a pull-up fixes it, and separately explains why a relay or motor needs a MOSFET and flyback diode rather than a direct pin connection — naming the inductive kick specifically. A weak answer treats 'add a resistor' or 'add a transistor' as ritual rather than a consequence of a specific electrical failure mode.

questions.prompt: Why does I2C use open-drain outputs on SDA and SCL instead of push-pull?

options.text: Open-drain pins use less power than push-pull pins in all cases
It lets multiple devices share the same line and pull it low without any two devices actively driving opposite states and shorting against each other
Open-drain is required by law for any multi-device serial bus
Push-pull outputs cannot be used for clock signals

explanations.a: Power draw is not the reason; the safety of a shared bus with multiple drivers is.
explanations.b: Correct — open-drain means every device can only actively pull low or release the line, so no device ever fights another by driving the opposite active state simultaneously.
explanations.c: There is no such law; the choice is an electrical engineering necessity for a shared bus, not a regulatory one.
explanations.d: Push-pull outputs drive clock signals constantly in other contexts (e.g. SPI's SCK); the issue is specific to shared, multi-master lines.

questions.prompt: A floating (unconnected) digital input pin reads randomly between HIGH and LOW. What is the root cause?

options.text: The pin has no defined voltage and picks up stray capacitive coupling from nearby signals
The MCU's internal clock is malfunctioning
The pin is permanently damaged
The pin is drawing too much current

explanations.a: Correct — with no pull-up, pull-down, or driven source, the pin's voltage is undefined and easily swayed by nearby switching noise.
explanations.b: Clock malfunction would affect timing broadly, not cause this specific floating-input symptom.
explanations.c: Floating behavior is normal and expected for any unconnected digital input; it does not indicate damage.
explanations.d: An input pin (not driving a load) does not source or sink significant current; current draw is irrelevant here.

questions.prompt: Why must a flyback diode be placed across a relay coil or motor driven by a MOSFET switched from a GPIO pin?

options.text: It reduces the coil's resistance
It clamps the voltage spike generated when the coil's magnetic field collapses at turn-off, protecting the MOSFET from breakdown
It increases the current the coil can draw
It converts the coil's AC signal to DC

explanations.a: A flyback diode has no effect on the coil's DC resistance.
explanations.b: Correct — an inductor resists sudden current change, so at turn-off it generates a large reverse voltage spike; the diode gives that current a path to circulate safely instead of overvolting the switching MOSFET.
explanations.c: The diode does not increase current draw; it only provides a path for the collapsing field's current after turn-off.
explanations.d: Relay coils and DC motors driven this way run on DC, not AC; there is no AC-to-DC conversion involved.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of correctly switching a relay coil from an MCU GPIO pin, from first design decision to last physical connection.

items.text: Recognize the relay coil draws more current than the pin can safely source or sink
Choose a MOSFET rated for the coil's voltage and current, with its gate driven by the GPIO pin
Add a flyback diode across the coil to clamp the turn-off voltage spike
Connect the coil, MOSFET, and diode into the switched circuit and test

questions.explanation: Design starts from recognizing the pin cannot drive the load directly, then selecting a MOSFET to do the switching, then adding the flyback diode for protection, and finally wiring and testing the assembled circuit.

lessons.label: Digitizing a Signal: the ADC

sections.heading: Successive approximation: a binary search on voltage
sections.body: Most MCU analog-to-digital converters use successive-approximation (SAR) conversion. A sample-and-hold circuit first freezes the input voltage; then a comparator runs a binary search against an internal DAC. Step one, the DAC outputs half the reference voltage; if the held input is above that, bit is set to 1 and the search continues in the upper half, otherwise 0 and it continues in the lower half. Step two halves the remaining range again, and so on for as many bits as the ADC's resolution — a 10-bit SAR ADC takes 10 comparison steps to resolve one sample, each step narrowing the bracket by half, converging exactly like a guess-the-number binary search.

sections.heading: Resolution, reference voltage, and the size of one step
sections.body: Resolution sets how many discrete codes span the reference range: a 10-bit ADC has 1024 codes (0-1023). With a 5V reference, one least-significant-bit (LSB) step is 5V / 1024 ≈ 4.88 mV — any two input voltages closer together than that are indistinguishable to the ADC. The reference voltage itself is a direct error source: if it is meant to be exactly 5.00V but is actually 4.95V, every conversion is off by that same 1% multiplicatively, even though the ADC's internal comparisons were perfect. That is why precision projects use a dedicated voltage reference chip rather than the MCU's regulated supply rail, which can sag under load. Acquisition also takes real time: the sample-and-hold capacitor must charge to the input voltage during a short acquisition window, and if the signal source has high output impedance — a rule of thumb is above roughly 10 kilohm — the capacitor cannot charge fully in that window, and the reading reads systematically low or noisy. A simple op-amp buffer between a high-impedance sensor and the ADC input fixes this by presenting a near-zero source impedance.

sections.heading: Quantization noise, oversampling, and ENOB
sections.body: Even a perfect ADC has quantization error: rounding a continuous voltage to the nearest code introduces noise with an RMS value of q/√12, where q is the LSB step size — for the 4.88 mV example, that noise floor is about 1.4 mV. Oversampling trades speed for resolution: taking 4 times as many samples and averaging (with proper decimation/filtering) statistically gains one additional effective bit of resolution, so 16x oversampling can turn a 10-bit ADC into an effective 12-bit one. This connects to ENOB (effective number of bits), the datasheet spec that says how many bits are actually usable once real-world noise, non-linearity, and reference error are accounted for — an ADC nominally '12-bit' might only deliver 10.5 ENOB, meaning the bottom bit and a half are noise, not signal.

lessons.workedExample: A student measures a thermistor voltage divider with a 10-bit AVR ADC and a 5V reference, expecting to distinguish 0.1°C changes. Each ADC code covers about 4.88 mV; if the divider's sensitivity near room temperature is only 2 mV per 0.1°C, two adjacent temperature readings a tenth of a degree apart often produce the identical ADC code — the resolution is not fine enough. Oversampling 16 samples per reading and averaging gains roughly 2 extra effective bits (to about 12-bit resolution, 1.2 mV per code), enough to reliably separate 0.1°C steps, at the cost of taking 16x longer per reading.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'what's your ADC's actual resolution in your units, not just in bits?' because converting bits to volts-per-code (or degrees-per-code) is the step that reveals whether a student can connect a datasheet number to their physical measurement. A strong answer computes the LSB size from the reference voltage and bit count, and if precision was an issue, names oversampling and the roughly-4x-samples-per-extra-bit trade-off as the fix. A weak answer says '10-bit is very precise' without ever computing what one bit is worth in the units that matter for the experiment.

questions.prompt: A 10-bit ADC uses a 5V reference. What is the size of one LSB step?

options.text: About 4.88 mV
About 48.8 mV
5 mV exactly
About 0.49 mV

explanations.a: Correct — 5V / 1024 codes ≈ 4.88 mV per code, exactly as computed in the lesson.
explanations.b: This is off by a factor of 10; it would correspond to dividing by roughly 102 codes, not 1024.
explanations.c: 5V divided evenly is not how ADC resolution works; the reference must be divided by the number of codes (1024), not treated as one step.
explanations.d: This is off by a factor of 10 in the other direction — it would be the LSB of a 13-bit ADC on the same reference, not a 10-bit one.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of a successive-approximation ADC conversion, from first to last.

items.text: Sample-and-hold freezes the input voltage
Internal DAC outputs half the reference voltage and the comparator checks if the held input is above or below it, setting the top bit
The search narrows to the remaining half-range and repeats the compare-and-set step for each lower bit
After all bits are resolved, the final digital code is output as the conversion result

questions.explanation: SAR conversion first freezes the input, then performs a binary search one bit at a time from most significant to least significant, and finally outputs the assembled code.

questions.prompt: Why does a high-impedance signal source (well above ~10 kohm) cause inaccurate ADC readings even if the ADC itself is functioning correctly?

options.text: High source impedance changes the reference voltage
The sample-and-hold capacitor cannot fully charge to the input voltage within the short acquisition window, so the reading is systematically off
High impedance sources always produce negative voltages
The ADC's resolution decreases when source impedance rises

explanations.a: Source impedance and reference voltage are separate parts of the circuit; one does not directly change the other.
explanations.b: Correct — charging the hold capacitor through a large source resistance in a short acquisition window is an RC charging problem, and if the time constant is too large relative to the window, the capacitor undercharges.
explanations.c: There is no such rule connecting source impedance to voltage sign.
explanations.d: The ADC's bit resolution (number of codes) is fixed by hardware; source impedance affects accuracy of the sampled value, not the resolution spec itself.

questions.prompt: A datasheet lists an ADC as '12-bit' but its ENOB (effective number of bits) is 10.5. What does that gap mean?

options.text: The ADC actually has 10.5 physical bits of hardware
Real-world noise and non-linearity make roughly the bottom 1.5 bits of the nominal 12-bit output unreliable as signal
The ADC needs a firmware update to reach 12 bits
ENOB only applies to ADCs with an external reference

explanations.a: The physical bit count (12) is fixed by the hardware's code count; ENOB is a separate, empirically measured effective performance figure.
explanations.b: Correct — ENOB captures how many bits are actually usable once quantization noise, reference error, and non-linearity are included, which can be less than the nominal resolution.
explanations.c: ENOB reflects physical/electrical limitations, not something firmware can raise.
explanations.d: ENOB applies to any ADC, internal or external reference; it is a general accuracy metric.

lessons.label: Timers and PWM

sections.heading: A counter and a compare register are the whole engine
sections.body: An MCU hardware timer is a register that increments once per clock tick (or once per N ticks, if a prescaler divides the clock down first). Everything else — PWM, precise delays, frequency measurement — is built from comparing that counter against one or more compare registers. In fast PWM mode, the counter counts up from 0 to a maximum (TOP), the output pin is set high at 0 and driven low the instant the counter matches the compare value, then the counter resets to 0 and repeats — producing one sawtooth-shaped counting cycle per PWM period. Phase-correct PWM instead counts up to TOP and back down to 0, comparing on both the up and down slopes, which makes the pulse symmetric around the cycle's center; this is more expensive (roughly half the maximum frequency for the same TOP) but avoids introducing DC-average glitches, which matters for motor control and some phase-sensitive applications.

sections.heading: The frequency/resolution trade is arithmetic, not a mystery
sections.body: PWM frequency for fast mode is fPWM = fclk / (N × prescaler), where N is the counter's range (256 for an 8-bit timer, 65536 for 16-bit, or a custom TOP value) and prescaler divides the source clock. On a 16 MHz AVR with no prescaling and an 8-bit timer, fPWM = 16,000,000 / 256 ≈ 62.5 kHz, with only 256 discrete duty-cycle steps. Raising TOP to get finer duty-cycle resolution (say, 4096 steps using a 16-bit timer) proportionally lowers the achievable frequency for the same clock and prescaler — the same divide-down math applies, so a 12-bit-resolution PWM on that clock runs closer to 3.9 kHz. There is no way to get both high frequency and high resolution from the same clock without raising the underlying timer clock itself.

sections.heading: The same hardware measures signals and makes a DAC
sections.body: Input capture mode runs the counter free and, on an external edge (rising, falling, or both), latches the current counter value into a capture register and can fire an interrupt — subtracting two successive captured values gives a period or pulse width directly in clock ticks, which is how a timer measures an ultrasonic sensor's echo pulse or an incoming signal's frequency without any software polling loop. Output compare mode is the mirror image: set a compare value once, and the pin toggles or a flag fires at exactly that count, useful for a single precisely-timed pulse rather than a repeating PWM waveform. PWM itself, run through a simple RC low-pass filter, becomes a crude digital-to-analog converter — the filter averages the high-frequency pulse train into a DC-ish level proportional to duty cycle, cheap but with ripple and a settling-time trade-off against the filter's cutoff. Hobby servos use a fixed convention rather than variable-duty PWM: a pulse repeated every 20 ms (50 Hz) whose width, not duty cycle, encodes position — typically 1 ms for one end of travel and 2 ms for the other, with 1.5 ms at center.

lessons.workedExample: A student wants to dim an LED array smoothly using PWM plus an RC filter as a mini-DAC, targeting a filtered ripple under 50 mV. At the AVR's default 490 Hz PWM frequency (Arduino's analogWrite on most pins), a simple single-pole RC filter needs a fairly low cutoff to knock down that much ripple, which also makes the filter slow to settle when the duty cycle changes — a visible lag when fading. Switching the timer's prescaler to run PWM at 62.5 kHz instead lets the filter use a much higher cutoff (since the ripple frequency is over 100x higher) while still meeting the same 50 mV ripple target, and the filter now settles fast enough that fades look instantaneous — the same RC filter values behave completely differently once the underlying PWM frequency changes.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who sees PWM in a project asks for the actual frequency and duty-cycle resolution being used, because 'I used PWM to control it' says nothing about whether the student understands the fPWM = fclk/(N×prescaler) trade-off they made, often invisibly, by calling a default library function. A strong answer states the frequency, explains why that frequency was chosen (motor whine above/below audible range, filter ripple, servo timing compatibility), and can compute what changing the prescaler would do. A weak answer cannot say what frequency their PWM actually runs at.

questions.prompt: On a 16 MHz clock with no prescaling, what is the fast-PWM frequency using an 8-bit timer (TOP = 256)?

options.text: About 62.5 kHz
About 625 kHz
16 MHz
About 6.25 kHz

explanations.a: Correct — fPWM = fclk / (N × prescaler) = 16,000,000 / (256 × 1) ≈ 62.5 kHz, exactly as derived in the lesson.
explanations.b: This is off by a factor of 10 from the correct division of clock by counter range.
explanations.c: 16 MHz is the raw clock rate, not the PWM frequency after dividing by the 256-count timer range.
explanations.d: This is off by a factor of 10 in the other direction from the correct result.

questions.prompt: A project needs finer PWM duty-cycle resolution at the same clock and prescaler. What is the direct consequence of raising TOP to get that resolution?

options.text: The PWM frequency drops proportionally, since fPWM = fclk / (N × prescaler)
Nothing changes except resolution; frequency stays fixed
The clock speed automatically increases to compensate
Resolution and frequency are unrelated on hardware timers

explanations.a: Correct — since N appears in the denominator of the frequency formula, a larger TOP (finer resolution) directly and proportionally lowers frequency for a fixed clock and prescaler.
explanations.b: Frequency is coupled to N through the formula; it cannot stay fixed if N changes with clock and prescaler held constant.
explanations.c: The hardware clock source does not adjust itself based on timer configuration; it must be changed independently.
explanations.d: They are directly coupled through fPWM = fclk / (N × prescaler), which is the core trade-off in this lesson.

questions.prompt: Match each timer-based technique to what it accomplishes.

right.text: Latches the counter value on an external edge, letting software compute a period or pulse width from clock ticks
Fires a flag or toggles a pin at one precisely timed count, for a single precise pulse
Produces a crude analog voltage proportional to duty cycle by averaging the pulse train
The hobby-servo convention encoding shaft position by pulse width, not duty cycle

questions.explanation: Input capture measures external edges via the counter; output compare produces one precisely timed event; PWM through an RC filter approximates a DAC; and hobby servos use pulse width, not duty cycle, at a fixed 50 Hz repetition rate.

questions.prompt: Why does phase-correct PWM run at roughly half the maximum frequency of fast PWM for the same TOP value?

options.text: It compares on both the up-count and down-count slopes of a full up-down cycle instead of one up-count sawtooth per period
Phase-correct PWM uses a slower internal clock automatically
It requires two separate timers running simultaneously
Phase-correct PWM has no relationship between frequency and TOP

explanations.a: Correct — counting all the way up and back down doubles the ticks per PWM period compared to fast PWM's single up-count sawtooth, halving the achievable frequency for the same TOP.
explanations.b: The clock source itself is unchanged; only the counting pattern (up-down vs. up-reset) differs.
explanations.c: Phase-correct PWM runs on the same single timer hardware as fast PWM; it does not require a second timer.
explanations.d: The same fPWM = fclk/(N×prescaler)-style relationship holds, just with an effectively doubled period for the same TOP.

lessons.label: Interrupts and Real Time

sections.heading: The vector table and the cost of responding
sections.body: Every interrupt source — a timer overflow, a pin change, a UART byte arriving — has a fixed slot in the vector table, a list of addresses the CPU jumps to automatically when that interrupt fires. Responding is not free: entry latency is the delay between the electrical event and the first instruction of the interrupt service routine (ISR) executing, and it is not perfectly constant. On an AVR it typically takes a handful of clock cycles just to finish the current instruction and push the return address, but if interrupts happen to be globally disabled (inside another ISR, or inside a critical section) at that moment, latency jumps by however long that disabled window lasts. That variability is jitter, and for time-critical work — sampling audio at a fixed rate, generating a precise pulse — jitter matters as much as average latency, because it is the worst case, not the average, that determines whether a real-time deadline is met.

sections.heading: Priorities, nesting, and races with the main loop
sections.body: Cortex-M cores support prioritized, nestable interrupts: a higher-priority ISR can interrupt a lower-priority one already running, while AVR's simpler model runs one ISR at a time with interrupts disabled by default during it (nesting requires explicitly re-enabling them mid-ISR, which is done rarely and carefully). Either way, any variable an ISR writes and the main loop also reads (or vice versa) must be declared volatile — without it, the compiler is free to assume the variable never changes outside code it can see, and can cache a stale copy in a register, silently ignoring updates the ISR makes. Even volatile is not enough for multi-byte variables like a 16-bit or 32-bit counter: on an 8-bit AVR, reading or writing such a variable takes multiple instructions, and if an interrupt fires mid-access, the main loop can read half-old, half-new bytes — a non-atomic read-modify-write race producing a corrupted value that neither the old nor new one. The fix is a critical section: briefly disabling interrupts around the multi-byte access.

sections.heading: Polling vs. interrupts is a latency budget question
sections.body: Polling — checking a flag or pin in a loop — is simpler and avoids interrupt overhead entirely, but its response latency is bounded by however long the rest of the loop body takes to get back around to checking again; if that loop body sometimes takes 5 ms, an event needing a response within 1 ms will sometimes be missed no matter how fast the polling check itself is. A hardware timer ISR (or any interrupt) decouples response time from the main loop's workload, which is exactly why a delay loop like Arduino's delay() — which blocks the entire CPU, unable to respond to anything, for the specified duration — must be replaced by a timer interrupt (or non-blocking millis()-based timing) the moment a program needs to do more than one time-sensitive thing at once.

lessons.workedExample: A student's project reads a rotary encoder with a polling loop that also updates an LCD display; the LCD write occasionally takes 3 ms. The encoder can produce pulses faster than that during a fast spin, and pulses arriving during the 3 ms LCD write are missed entirely, causing the counted position to drift from the physical dial. Moving the encoder read into a pin-change interrupt fixes it: the ISR fires and increments the count within a few clock cycles of the actual edge regardless of what the main loop is doing, and the shared count variable is declared volatile and, since it is a 16-bit value on an 8-bit AVR, read inside a short critical section in the main loop to avoid a torn read.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about missed events or glitchy counts specifically to see whether the student can diagnose a timing bug rather than just patch symptoms — 'sometimes it skips counts' is a symptom; 'my polling loop was blocked by a 3ms LCD write' is a root cause. A strong answer names the specific blocking operation, explains why an interrupt decouples response time from main-loop workload, and can explain why the shared variable needed both volatile and a critical section. A weak answer adds a delay or a retry without ever identifying why events were being lost in the first place.

questions.prompt: Why must a variable written by an ISR and read by the main loop be declared volatile?

options.text: Without it, the compiler may cache the variable in a register and never notice updates the ISR makes elsewhere
volatile makes the variable update faster
volatile is required by the C standard for all interrupt-related code, regardless of sharing
volatile prevents the ISR from ever being interrupted

explanations.a: Correct — without volatile, the compiler can legally assume the variable is unchanged by anything it cannot see executing (like an ISR) and optimize away re-reads, reading a stale cached value.
explanations.b: volatile has no effect on speed; if anything it can slightly slow access by forcing memory reads instead of using a cached register value.
explanations.c: volatile is only needed for variables actually shared between contexts (ISR and main loop, or between ISRs); it is not a blanket requirement for all interrupt code.
explanations.d: volatile only affects how the compiler treats memory access ordering/caching; it says nothing about interrupt nesting or priority.

questions.prompt: Why can reading a 16-bit counter shared with an ISR on an 8-bit AVR produce a corrupted value even if the variable is declared volatile?

options.text: The 8-bit CPU reads a 16-bit value in two separate instructions, and an interrupt firing between them can leave the read half-old, half-new
volatile only works for 8-bit variables
16-bit variables cannot be used in interrupt-driven code at all
The ISR always corrupts any variable it touches

explanations.a: Correct — this is the non-atomic read-modify-write race described in the lesson: a multi-byte access takes multiple instructions on an 8-bit core, and an interrupt mid-access can tear the read.
explanations.b: volatile applies to any size variable; the atomicity problem is separate from what volatile does.
explanations.c: 16-bit shared variables are used constantly in embedded code; they simply need a critical section around multi-byte access, not avoidance.
explanations.d: The ISR itself does not corrupt the variable directly; the corruption comes from an interleaved, non-atomic access from the main loop.

questions.prompt: Order the diagnostic steps for the encoder-plus-LCD example, from noticing the symptom to the final fix.

items.text: Notice the counted encoder position drifts from the physical dial during fast spins
Trace the polling loop and find the LCD write occasionally blocks for 3 ms
Recognize encoder pulses arriving during that blocked window are missed by polling
Move the encoder read into a pin-change interrupt with a volatile, critical-section-protected shared count

questions.explanation: Diagnosis starts from the observed symptom, traces it to the specific blocking operation, identifies the mechanism of the missed events, and ends with the interrupt-based fix that decouples response time from the main loop.

questions.prompt: Why must Arduino's blocking delay() be replaced with a timer interrupt (or non-blocking millis()-based timing) once a program needs to do more than one time-sensitive thing at once?

options.text: delay() halts the entire CPU for its duration, so the program cannot respond to any other event while it runs
delay() only works for durations under 1 ms
delay() disables all GPIO pins permanently
delay() and interrupts cannot coexist in the same program at all

explanations.a: Correct — delay() blocks the whole CPU, so any other event needing timely handling during that window is delayed or missed entirely.
explanations.b: delay() can block for arbitrarily long durations; the problem is not a duration limit but the blocking behavior itself.
explanations.c: delay() does not disable GPIO; pins keep their configured state, they simply cannot be responded to by new code during the block.
explanations.d: Interrupts can still fire during delay() on most platforms (delay() does not disable interrupts globally); the issue is that the main-loop code cannot react to their flags until delay() returns.

lessons.label: Serial Buses: UART, I2C, and SPI

sections.heading: UART: no clock line, so framing has to do all the work
sections.body: UART (Universal Asynchronous Receiver-Transmitter) sends bytes with no shared clock signal between devices — each side must independently time its bits at the agreed baud rate. A frame starts with a start bit (line pulled low), then typically 8 data bits, then one or more stop bits (line returns high) marking the frame's end; the receiver resynchronizes to the start bit's falling edge each frame, so timing error cannot accumulate across an entire message, only across one byte. Because of that per-byte resync, UART tolerates a baud-rate mismatch of roughly 2-3% between transmitter and receiver before bits start landing far enough from center to misread — which is exactly why the earlier lesson's internal-RC-oscillator drift of 1-10% is a real risk for UART: two boards each individually off by a couple percent in opposite directions can combine past that tolerance.

sections.heading: I2C: two wires, open-drain, addresses, and clock stretching
sections.body: I2C (Inter-Integrated Circuit) uses two open-drain lines, SDA (data) and SCL (clock), both pulled high externally by pull-up resistors, letting many devices share the bus since any device can only pull a line low, never actively drive it high. A controller (historically called 'master') addresses one of up to 127 devices with a 7-bit address sent at the start of each transaction, and every byte, including the address, is followed by a single ACK/NACK bit from the receiver confirming it was received. A slower peripheral can perform clock stretching — holding SCL low itself to pause the controller until it is ready for the next bit, a built-in flow-control mechanism unique to I2C among these three buses. Pull-up resistor sizing is a real constraint, not an afterthought: the bus capacitance and pull-up value set an RC rise time, and the I2C specification caps that rise time at 1000 ns for standard mode (100 kHz) and 300 ns for fast mode (400 kHz) — too large a pull-up (too slow) corrupts fast-mode timing, too small wastes power and can violate the drive-low current limits of the weakest device on the bus.

sections.heading: SPI: fast and simple, at the cost of more pins
sections.body: SPI (Serial Peripheral Interface) uses a shared clock (SCK) driven by the controller, separate data lines for each direction (MOSI, MISO), and a dedicated chip-select (CS) line per peripheral rather than an address scheme — the controller selects exactly one device at a time by pulling its CS line low. Because SPI has an explicit clock, there is no baud-rate-matching problem like UART's, and it typically runs several times faster than I2C. Its one subtlety is CPOL/CPHA mode: CPOL sets whether the clock idles high or low, and CPHA sets whether data is sampled on the clock's first or second edge after CS goes active — the transmitter and receiver must agree on both, giving four standard SPI modes, and picking the wrong one produces bytes that are shifted by exactly one bit and look like noise. Choosing a bus for a multi-sensor board is a real trade: I2C's two shared wires scale to many devices cheaply but slower and with more protocol overhead; SPI is faster and simpler in software but needs one extra CS pin per device, quickly running out of GPIO on a board with many peripherals (longer, noisier links move to CAN; higher bandwidth moves to USB).

lessons.workedExample: A student wiring five I2C sensors to one MCU picks a 10 kohm pull-up on each of SDA and SCL for a bus with roughly 100 pF of combined trace and pin capacitance, running at fast-mode 400 kHz. The RC rise time works out to about 1000 ns (10 kohm x 100 pF), which exceeds the fast-mode 300 ns limit, so the topmost sensor's data bits are corrupted and its readings intermittently fail. Dropping to 2.2 kohm pull-ups cuts the rise time to about 220 ns, under the fast-mode limit, and all five sensors read reliably — the same wiring, the same code, the only change is the resistor value chosen against the bus's actual capacitance.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who sees a multi-sensor board with I2C asks why that bus was chosen over SPI, because the answer reveals whether the student understands the trade-off (pin count vs. speed) or just copied whichever bus the first sensor library happened to use. A strong answer names the pin savings of I2C's shared two wires against SPI's per-device chip-select requirement, and if the student changed a pull-up value or picked a CPOL/CPHA mode, can explain why in terms of rise time or clock-edge sampling. A weak answer cannot say what the pull-up resistors are for or what would happen if SPI's clock polarity were wrong.

questions.prompt: Why does UART tolerate roughly 2-3% baud-rate mismatch between transmitter and receiver but not much more?

options.text: The receiver resynchronizes to the start bit each frame, so timing error only accumulates across one byte before the next frame resets it, but too much per-byte drift still misreads bits
UART has a shared clock line that corrects timing automatically
Baud rate mismatch never actually causes errors in UART
UART uses I2C-style clock stretching to compensate

explanations.a: Correct — the per-frame resync bounds how much timing error can build up, giving UART its characteristic few-percent tolerance rather than needing exact clock matching.
explanations.b: UART is specifically asynchronous — it has no shared clock line; that is exactly why baud-rate matching matters in the first place.
explanations.c: Mismatch beyond the tolerance does cause bit errors, as stated in the lesson; it is not harmless at any level.
explanations.d: Clock stretching is an I2C-specific mechanism; UART has no clock line to stretch.

questions.prompt: What does I2C clock stretching allow a peripheral to do?

options.text: Hold SCL low to pause the controller until the peripheral is ready for the next bit
Change its own 7-bit address mid-transaction
Broadcast data to all devices on the bus simultaneously without addressing
Increase the bus's maximum clock frequency beyond its rated mode

explanations.a: Correct — clock stretching is a peripheral holding SCL low as a flow-control mechanism, pausing the controller until it is ready to continue.
explanations.b: Clock stretching has nothing to do with address assignment; addresses are fixed or set independently of this mechanism.
explanations.c: I2C transactions are still addressed to a specific device; clock stretching does not create a broadcast mode.
explanations.d: Clock stretching slows the effective transaction rate by pausing, it does not raise the bus's maximum rated frequency.

questions.prompt: Two SPI devices are configured with mismatched CPOL/CPHA settings. What is the resulting symptom?

options.text: Received bytes appear shifted by a bit and look like noise, because the two sides disagree on which clock edge to sample data
The bus automatically renegotiates to a matching mode
Chip-select stops working entirely
The clock frequency doubles unexpectedly

explanations.a: Correct — CPOL/CPHA mismatch means sampling happens on the wrong clock edge relative to when data changes, producing bit-shifted, garbled bytes.
explanations.b: SPI has no auto-negotiation; both sides must be configured to agree on mode in advance.
explanations.c: Chip-select operates independently of CPOL/CPHA; it still selects the device even if the data comes out garbled.
explanations.d: CPOL/CPHA settings affect clock polarity and sampling edge, not the clock's frequency.

questions.prompt: Match each bus feature to the bus it belongs to.

left.text: Start bit and stop bit framing, no shared clock line

right.text: SPI
I2C
UART

questions.explanation: SPI selects devices with dedicated chip-select lines; I2C addresses devices over a shared bus with ACK/NACK and supports clock stretching; UART frames bytes with start/stop bits and has no shared clock line at all.

lessons.label: A Short History of the Microcontroller

sections.heading: From the 4004 to the first single-chip computer
sections.body: The Intel 4004 (1971), designed by Federico Faggin, Ted Hoff, Stanley Mazor, and Masatoshi Shima for a Japanese calculator company, was the first commercial single-chip microprocessor — a CPU alone, still needing separate memory and I/O chips around it to do anything. The leap to a true microcontroller — CPU, ROM, RAM, and I/O all on one die — came from Texas Instruments engineers Gary Boone and Michael Cochran, whose 1971 single-chip calculator design became the foundation for the TMS1000 family, announced in 1974 as the first high-volume, general-purpose commercial microcontroller. The distinction mattered enough to become a patent fight: engineer Gilbert Hyatt claimed priority based on 1970s patent filings, but after decades of litigation the U.S. Patent Office found Hyatt's earliest filing actually describing the invention dated to 1977 — six years after TI had already shipped it — and granted TI's request to officially recognize Boone as the inventor of the single-chip microcontroller.

sections.heading: 8-bit families that defined a generation of embedded design
sections.body: Intel's 8051, released in 1980, became one of history's most cloned architectures — decades later, dozens of vendors still sold pin-compatible or instruction-compatible 8051 variants, because so much embedded firmware and engineer training had accumulated around it. Microchip's PIC line, and Atmel's AVR, arrived to compete on similar territory: AVR in particular came from two students, Alf-Egil Bogen and Vegard Wollan, at the Norwegian Institute of Technology in Trondheim, who designed the core in 1996 at a local chip house, Nordic VLSI (today Nordic Semiconductor), before Atmel commercialized it — the name AVR is often expanded as a nod to the two designers' initials. AVR's single-cycle instruction execution and orthogonal instruction set made it a favorite for compiler-generated C code rather than hand-written assembly, a real shift in how embedded firmware got written.

sections.heading: 32-bit cores and the hobbyist explosion
sections.body: ARM's Cortex-M series, launched starting in 2004 with the Cortex-M3, brought a 32-bit RISC core with built-in interrupt hardware (the NVIC) and a standardized instruction set to low-cost microcontrollers, letting chip vendors license one proven core instead of designing their own — a business model that made 32-bit power available at 8-bit-era prices within a few years. The Arduino project, started in 2005 by Massimo Banzi and collaborators at the Interaction Design Institute Ivrea in Italy, did not invent any new silicon; its contribution was wrapping an existing AVR chip in an open-source board design, a simplified C++ library, and a free IDE, collapsing the time from unboxing to a blinking LED from days of datasheet-reading to minutes — which is arguably why microcontrollers reached hobbyists and students at all. That trajectory continued into Espressif's ESP32 (2016), which folded Wi-Fi and Bluetooth radios directly onto an MCU die, and the Raspberry Pi Foundation's RP2040 (2021), a dual-core Cortex-M0+ chip designed in-house specifically to be cheap and easy to program — each shift is the same story as Arduino's: what used to require a specialist's board and toolchain became something a student project could suddenly attempt over a weekend.

lessons.workedExample: A student researching why their $4 Arduino-compatible board can run a full TCP/IP stack over Wi-Fi, something unthinkable on an 8-bit MCU a decade earlier, traces the chain: the ESP32 (2016) integrates a 32-bit dual-core processor and radio silicon that would have been multiple separate, expensive chips in the 1990s AVR era; ARM's Cortex-M licensing model (from 2004) let a chip vendor like Espressif buy a proven 32-bit core instead of designing one from scratch, dropping both cost and development time; and Arduino's 2005 tooling legacy means the same simplified programming environment still works on this vastly more powerful chip. None of these three facts alone explains the $4 price tag — it is the licensing-model shift plus the tooling continuity together.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'why did you pick this chip, and what changed to make it possible for a student project?' to test whether the student sees microcontrollers as a technology with a history and trade-offs, not an interchangeable commodity. A strong answer can place their chip in the lineage — an ARM-licensed 32-bit core, or an AVR descendant — and name what specific capability that lineage unlocked for their project (radios on-die, cheaper 32-bit math, better tooling). A weak answer cannot say whether their chip is 8-bit or 32-bit, or what company designed the core silicon versus the board around it.

questions.prompt: What was the key difference between the Intel 4004 (1971) and the TMS1000 family (1974)?

options.text: The 4004 was a CPU alone needing separate memory/IO chips, while the TMS1000 put CPU, ROM, RAM, and IO on one die as a true single-chip microcontroller
The 4004 was 32-bit and the TMS1000 was 8-bit
The TMS1000 came before the 4004
There was no meaningful difference between them

explanations.a: Correct — the 4004 was the first commercial microprocessor but needed external memory and I/O chips, while the TMS1000 family integrated everything onto a single chip, the defining feature of a microcontroller.
explanations.b: Both were far narrower than 32-bit; the 4004 was a 4-bit processor, and the distinction between them is integration, not bit width.
explanations.c: The 4004 (1971) predates the TMS1000 family's 1974 announcement.
explanations.d: The single-chip integration is exactly the meaningful difference described in the lesson.

questions.prompt: How was the TI vs. Gilbert Hyatt microcontroller-invention patent dispute ultimately resolved?

options.text: The Patent Office found Hyatt's earliest filing describing the invention dated to 1977, six years after TI had shipped it, and recognized TI's Gary Boone as the inventor
Hyatt was awarded the patent because he filed first
The dispute is still unresolved today
TI and Hyatt were declared co-inventors

explanations.a: Correct — despite Hyatt's claim based on 1970s filings, the Patent Office traced his earliest filing actually describing the invention to 1977, well after TI's 1971 design and 1974 product, and recognized Boone.
explanations.b: Hyatt did not file first in a way that actually described the invention; his qualifying filing came years after TI's product existed.
explanations.c: The Patent Office did reach a resolution recognizing TI and Boone, as described in the lesson.
explanations.d: The outcome recognized Boone and TI specifically, not a co-invention split.

questions.prompt: Match each microcontroller or platform to its origin.

right.text: Designed by two students at the Norwegian Institute of Technology in 1996
Started in 2005 by Massimo Banzi and collaborators at Interaction Design Institute Ivrea
Launched in 2004 as a licensable 32-bit core for chip vendors
Released by Intel in 1980 and became one of the most cloned architectures in history

questions.explanation: AVR came from Bogen and Wollan at NTH in 1996; Arduino was started by Banzi and collaborators in 2005; the Cortex-M3 launched in 2004 as a licensable core; and the Intel 8051 (1980) became extremely widely cloned.

questions.prompt: Order these microcontroller milestones chronologically, earliest first.

items.text: Intel 4004, the first commercial single-chip microprocessor
TI TMS1000 family, the first high-volume single-chip microcontroller
AVR core designed at the Norwegian Institute of Technology
ARM Cortex-M3 launched as a licensable 32-bit core
Arduino project started, wrapping AVR in an open-source board and IDE

questions.explanation: The 4004 (1971) preceded the TMS1000 family (1974); AVR followed in 1996; Cortex-M3 launched in 2004; and Arduino started in 2005, after all four of the preceding technologies existed.

units.label: Firmware Engineering and the Embedded Bench

lessons.label: From C to a Running Chip: the Embedded Toolchain

sections.heading: Cross-compiling and two output files
sections.body: Firmware is built with a cross-compiler: a toolchain like arm-none-eabi-gcc that runs on your laptop but emits machine code for a different CPU, an ARM Cortex-M rather than an x86. The compiler and linker produce an ELF file (Executable and Linkable Format, the same container Linux uses) carrying code, data, and debug symbols together. A programmer rarely wants the whole ELF; arm-none-eabi-objcopy strips it down to an Intel HEX or raw binary image — Intel's 1973 HEX format encodes each line as an ASCII record: a leading colon, a 2-hex-digit byte count, a 4-hex-digit load address, a record-type byte (00 for a data record, 01 for end-of-file, others for extended addressing), the data payload itself, and a trailing checksum byte computed as the two's-complement of the sum of every preceding byte in the record. A flash tool re-sums each incoming line and rejects it if the checksum doesn't match, catching a corrupted transfer before it writes bytes to exact memory addresses — all without any symbol information.

sections.heading: The linker script: where .text, .data, .bss, stack, and heap live
sections.body: A linker script maps the compiled sections onto physical memory. .text (compiled instructions) and rodata (constants) sit in flash, which survives power loss. .data (initialized global variables) also has a copy stored in flash but must live in RAM at runtime, so startup code copies it from flash to RAM before main() runs. .bss (uninitialized/zero globals) needs no flash copy at all — startup code just zeroes that RAM range. The stack grows downward from the top of RAM and the heap grows upward from the end of .bss; on a chip like the STM32F103 with 20 KB of RAM, a stack collision with a growing heap is a real and common bug.

sections.heading: Vector table, registers, and getting code onto silicon
sections.body: On an ARM Cortex-M, address 0x00000000 (remapped from flash, e.g. 0x08000000 on STM32) holds the vector table: word 0 is the initial stack pointer value, word 1 is the reset handler address — hardware loads both directly on power-up, before any instruction executes. Peripheral registers are accessed through volatile pointers (GPIOC->ODR |= (1<<13)) because the compiler must not cache a value that hardware can change asynchronously; bitmasks let one bit toggle without disturbing its neighbors. Vendor HALs (ST's HAL_GPIO_WritePin, Arduino's digitalWrite) trade a few extra cycles of function-call overhead for portability over direct register writes. Getting code onto the chip uses a UART/USB bootloader, an SPI-based ISP programmer (AVR's 6-pin ICSP), or SWD/JTAG (2-wire vs 4-wire debug interfaces); AVR fuse bytes and STM32 option bytes configure clock source and protection outside normal flash and can brick a board if misprogrammed.

lessons.workedExample: A student targets an STM32F103C8 (64 KB flash at 0x08000000, 20 KB RAM at 0x20000000). arm-none-eabi-gcc compiles main.c to an object file; the linker script places .text/.rodata in flash and reserves .data/.bss/stack/heap in RAM, producing blink.elf. arm-none-eabi-objcopy -O ihex converts it to blink.hex. At reset, the CPU reads the vector table's word 0 (stack pointer) and word 1 (reset handler), startup code copies .data from flash to RAM, zeroes .bss, then calls main(), which executes GPIOC->ODR ^= (1 << 13) to toggle the onboard LED on pin PC13. An ST-Link probe flashes the image over the two-wire SWD interface.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask 'what happens between writing your code and the LED turning on?' because it separates students who used a library as a black box from those who can trace their own program's execution. A weak answer stalls at 'I wrote code and uploaded it.' A strong answer names the specific steps — compilation to an ELF, the linker script deciding where .data and .bss live, startup code initializing RAM before main() runs, and the vector table telling the CPU where to start — because that student can actually debug a hard fault or a corrupted global instead of guessing.

questions.prompt: Why does startup code need to copy the .data section from flash to RAM before main() runs?

options.text: Because .data holds compiled instructions that the CPU can only execute from RAM
Because .data holds initialized global variables, which must be writable at runtime, but flash only stores their initial values
Because the linker script requires all sections to be duplicated for error correction
Because .data is only used during debugging and is discarded afterward

explanations.a: Instructions live in .text and execute directly from flash on most microcontrollers; that is not why .data is copied.
explanations.b: Correct — global variables with nonzero initial values must be modifiable in RAM at runtime, so flash stores only their starting values and startup code copies them into RAM before main() runs.
explanations.c: There is no such duplication-for-error-correction requirement in a standard linker script.
explanations.d: This is backwards: .data is essential at runtime, not a debug-only artifact.

questions.prompt: A peripheral register pointer is declared volatile in firmware. What problem does this specifically prevent?

options.text: The compiler caching the register's value in a CPU register and skipping a fresh read/write, missing hardware-driven changes
The linker placing the variable in the wrong memory section
The stack overflowing into the heap
The vector table pointing to the wrong reset handler

explanations.a: Correct — without volatile, the compiler may assume a memory location cannot change on its own and optimize away repeated reads or writes, which is fatal when hardware updates that address asynchronously.
explanations.b: volatile is a correctness qualifier for access behavior, not a section-placement directive.
explanations.c: Stack/heap collisions are a memory-layout issue unrelated to the volatile qualifier.
explanations.d: The vector table is set by the linker script and startup code, not affected by volatile on a peripheral pointer.

questions.prompt: Order the steps from source code to a running LED-blink program on an STM32 board flashed over SWD.

items.text: arm-none-eabi-gcc compiles main.c into an object file
The linker script places .text/.rodata in flash and reserves .data/.bss/stack/heap in RAM, producing an ELF
objcopy converts the ELF to an Intel HEX or binary image
An SWD probe (e.g. ST-Link) writes the image into flash
At reset, hardware loads the initial stack pointer and reset handler from the vector table, startup code initializes RAM, then main() runs

questions.explanation: Compilation produces object code, linking places sections into memory regions and yields an ELF, objcopy extracts a flashable image, the probe writes it into the chip's flash, and only then does reset-time hardware behavior (vector table, RAM init) hand control to main().

questions.prompt: Match each programming/configuration mechanism to its description.

left.text: AVR fuse bytes / STM32 option bytes

right.text: 2-wire ARM debug interface used by probes like ST-Link/J-Link
SPI-based 6-pin programming interface used with tools like avrdude
Firmware already resident on-chip that receives a new image over serial without a dedicated programmer
Configuration bits outside normal flash controlling clock source, brown-out, or protection level; misprogramming can brick the chip

questions.explanation: SWD is ARM's 2-wire debug/programming interface; ISP is AVR's SPI-based in-circuit programming; a resident bootloader reprograms flash over a serial link without external hardware; fuse/option bytes configure low-level chip behavior and are risky to misprogram.

lessons.label: Program Structure: Superloop, Cooperative Scheduling, and RTOS

sections.heading: Why delay() breaks everything else
sections.body: The default beginner pattern is a superloop that calls delay(1000) to blink an LED once a second. delay() works by busy-waiting: the CPU does nothing else for that entire second, so a button press, an incoming UART byte, or a second timed task is simply invisible until the delay returns. The standard fix is non-blocking timing built on millis(), a free-running counter of elapsed milliseconds since boot: each loop pass checks if (millis() - lastTime >= interval) and, if true, does the work and resets lastTime, instead of stopping the CPU. Every task keeps its own lastTime and interval variables, so the superloop can service an LED, a button debounce, and a telemetry send in the same pass without any of them blocking the others.

sections.heading: Cooperative scheduling as explicit state machines
sections.body: Scaling this pattern past two or three tasks means writing each task as a finite state machine that does a small bounded slice of work per call and returns control voluntarily — this is cooperative round-robin scheduling: the programmer, not an OS, decides when each task yields. A task that reads a sensor over I2C, for example, is written as states (START, WAIT_FOR_DATA, PROCESS) rather than a blocking read, so a slow bus transaction never stalls the LED or the button. The cost is discipline: if one task's state machine forgets to bound its work and loops internally, it silently starves every other task, since there is no scheduler forcing it to give up the CPU.

sections.heading: FreeRTOS: tasks, priorities, queues, and their price
sections.body: FreeRTOS, started by Richard Barry around 2003 and now maintained by Amazon Web Services, replaces the hand-written state machines with real preemption: each task gets its own stack and priority, and a higher-priority task interrupts a lower one automatically via a timer-tick scheduler, rather than relying on every task to yield politely. Tasks communicate safely through queues instead of shared globals, avoiding the race conditions that plague hand-rolled cooperative code. That safety costs RAM: each task needs its own stack, commonly a few hundred bytes to a couple of kilobytes depending on call depth, plus a Task Control Block of roughly 100 bytes, so a modest three-to-five-task system typically consumes on the order of 1-10 kB of RAM — a meaningful fraction of a small MCU's 20-64 kB total. The decision rule: reach for an RTOS when you have multiple genuinely independent timing domains with hard deadlines that must preempt each other (a motor-control loop that cannot wait on a Wi-Fi stack), not for a single blink-and-button project where a superloop with millis() timing does the same job with none of the RAM cost or debugging complexity.

lessons.workedExample: A science-fair data logger needs to blink a status LED every 500 ms, debounce a button, and send a telemetry line over UART every 2 s. Version one is a superloop: three sets of (lastTime, interval) pairs are checked each pass with millis()-based non-blocking timing, and the whole system fits in under 2 KB of RAM. Version two adds a Wi-Fi module whose connect routine can block for seconds and a PID loop stabilizing a fan speed at a fixed 1 kHz deadline; here the student switches to FreeRTOS with three tasks (control at high priority, telemetry at low priority, Wi-Fi at low priority) connected by a queue, because a blocked Wi-Fi call must never delay the control task, and cooperative code cannot guarantee that.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask why a project uses (or doesn't use) an RTOS because it is a decision that should be justified by the timing requirements of the specific project, not by what sounded advanced on a datasheet. A weak answer says 'FreeRTOS is more professional.' A strong answer names the actual competing timing domains — for instance, a hard 1 kHz control deadline next to a Wi-Fi call that can block for seconds — and explains that preemption, not habit, is what an RTOS buys you, while also being honest that a superloop with millis() would have been simpler and sufficient for a project without a genuine preemption need.

questions.prompt: Why does calling delay(1000) inside a superloop break a project that also needs to respond to a button press?

options.text: delay() consumes too much flash memory to leave room for button-handling code
delay() busy-waits, so the CPU cannot check the button (or do anything else) until the delay finishes
delay() disables the microcontroller's GPIO pins while it runs
delay() requires an RTOS to function correctly

explanations.a: delay() is a tiny function; flash usage is not the problem.
explanations.b: Correct — delay() blocks execution entirely for its duration, so no other code, including a button check, runs until it returns.
explanations.c: GPIO pins remain electrically active during delay(); it is CPU execution, not the pins, that is blocked.
explanations.d: delay() is a basic library function that works standalone; it has nothing to do with requiring an RTOS.

questions.prompt: In a millis()-based non-blocking timing pattern, what does each independent task need to track on its own?

options.text: A shared global lastTime variable used by every task in the program
Its own lastTime and interval, so it can independently check elapsed time each loop pass
A dedicated hardware timer peripheral per task
Nothing; millis() timing does not require any per-task state

explanations.a: A single shared lastTime cannot represent multiple tasks running on different intervals at once.
explanations.b: Correct — each task compares millis() against its own lastTime and interval so tasks run independently without blocking each other.
explanations.c: The pattern's whole appeal is that it needs no dedicated hardware timer per task, just software bookkeeping against the shared millis() counter.
explanations.d: Per-task state (lastTime, interval) is exactly what makes the pattern work; without it tasks cannot track their own schedules.

questions.prompt: Match each FreeRTOS concept to its role.

right.text: An independent unit of code with its own stack, scheduled by the OS
A ranking that determines which ready task the scheduler runs first
A structure for safely passing data between tasks without shared-variable race conditions
The scheduler forcibly interrupting a lower-priority task to run a higher-priority one

questions.explanation: A task is a schedulable unit with its own stack; priority ranks tasks for scheduling; queues move data between tasks safely; preemption is the scheduler interrupting a lower-priority task so a higher-priority one can run immediately.
