questions.prompt: Order these systems from least to most capable of guaranteeing a hard real-time deadline is met even when another part of the program is busy.

items.text: A single superloop using blocking delay() calls
A superloop using non-blocking millis()-based timing for each task
Hand-written cooperative round-robin scheduling with explicit task state machines
FreeRTOS with priority-based preemptive scheduling

questions.explanation: Blocking delay() offers no deadline guarantee at all; millis()-based timing improves responsiveness but still depends on every task finishing its slice promptly; cooperative state machines add structure but still rely on every task yielding voluntarily; only preemptive scheduling can guarantee a high-priority deadline is met regardless of what a lower-priority task is doing.

lessons.label: Concurrency Bugs and Defensive Firmware

sections.heading: Torn reads between an ISR and the main loop
sections.body: An interrupt service routine (ISR) can preempt the main loop at any instruction boundary, which makes ordinary multi-byte variables dangerous. On an 8-bit AVR core, Arduino's own millis() counter (timer0_millis, a 32-bit unsigned long) is updated by the Timer0 overflow ISR one byte at a time, since the 8-bit core can only move a single byte per instruction; if the main loop reads the low bytes, gets interrupted mid-read while the ISR rolls part of the counter over, and then reads now-stale high bytes, it assembles a torn value that never existed at any real instant — sometimes wildly wrong. The real millis() implementation avoids exactly this by wrapping the multi-byte read in a critical section (interrupts briefly disabled with cli(), then restored with sei()) so the read is atomic from the main loop's point of view. The same hazard applies to any shared variable wider than the CPU can access in one instruction, including flags checked in one place and set in another.

sections.heading: Priority inversion: Mars Pathfinder, 1997
sections.body: A subtler race is priority inversion: a low-priority task grabs a shared resource (a mutex), a high-priority task blocks waiting for it, and a medium-priority task — unrelated to the resource — preempts the low-priority task and runs indefinitely, indirectly starving the high-priority task. This is not hypothetical: NASA's Mars Pathfinder lander began resetting itself sporadically after landing in 1997 because a low-priority meteorological data-collection task held a mutex that a high-priority bus-management task needed, while a medium-priority communications task kept preempting the low-priority one; the watchdog then reset the system, thinking it had hung. The fix, priority inheritance (temporarily boosting the low-priority task's priority while it holds the contested resource), was already built into the VxWorks RTOS but had not been enabled, and NASA engineers uplinked the fix remotely.

sections.heading: Watchdogs, brown-outs, and Cortex-M fault triage
sections.body: A watchdog timer resets the MCU unless firmware periodically 'kicks' it, but the classic misuse is kicking it unconditionally from a fast periodic ISR regardless of whether the main loop is actually making progress — a main loop stuck in an infinite state still gets fed by the ISR and the watchdog never fires, defeating its entire purpose; the kick belongs in the main loop, after real work completes. Brown-out detection resets the chip when supply voltage sags below threshold, a common symptom during motor inrush current. On a Cortex-M hard fault, the CPU automatically pushes R0-R3, R12, the link register, the program counter, and xPSR onto the stack before entering the fault handler; reading the stacked PC out of that frame identifies the exact faulting instruction. assert() macros and a small fault-logging buffer (kept in a RAM region the linker script excludes from startup zeroing) that records the stacked PC before reset turn a mystery reboot into a traceable one.

lessons.workedExample: A student's motor controller resets itself every few minutes. They add a watchdog and feed it from a 1 ms timer ISR to 'be safe' — but the main loop occasionally gets stuck in a blocking I2C wait, and because the ISR keeps kicking the watchdog regardless, the hang is never caught and the board just becomes unresponsive until manual power-cycling. Moving the kick into the main loop, right after the I2C transaction completes each pass, means a genuine hang now stops feeding the watchdog and the chip resets itself within the configured timeout (e.g. 500 ms) instead of hanging silently, restoring the watchdog's actual purpose: catching software lockups, not masking them.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe watchdog and interrupt-safety questions because a project that resets randomly under load usually has one of these bugs, and 'I added a watchdog to fix crashes' is a red flag if the student cannot say where the kick lives. A weak answer treats the watchdog as a magic crash-preventer. A strong answer explains that kicking from an ISR unconditionally defeats the watchdog because it feeds regardless of whether the code it's meant to protect is actually alive, and can further describe how they diagnosed a specific reset (brown-out during motor start vs. a genuine main-loop hang) rather than just observing that resets happen.

questions.prompt: A student's ISR kicks the watchdog every 1 ms regardless of what the main loop is doing. What problem does this create?

options.text: The watchdog resets the chip too frequently, causing constant reboots
The watchdog never fires even if the main loop hangs, because the ISR keeps feeding it independent of main-loop progress
The ISR consumes too much flash memory to run reliably
The watchdog timer's clock source becomes inaccurate

explanations.a: The opposite is true: unconditional kicking suppresses resets, it does not cause extra ones.
explanations.b: Correct — the watchdog is meant to catch a hung main loop, but if an unrelated ISR keeps feeding it, a genuinely stuck main loop is never detected.
explanations.c: This is not a flash-usage issue; it is a logic issue about what condition triggers the kick.
explanations.d: The clock source is unaffected by where in the code the kick is called.

questions.prompt: In the 1997 Mars Pathfinder priority-inversion incident, what actually caused the spacecraft's system resets?

options.text: A hardware brown-out from insufficient solar power
A low-priority task holding a mutex a high-priority task needed, while a medium-priority task kept preempting the low-priority one, so the watchdog reset the system thinking it had hung
A torn 16-bit read of a shared timer variable
A stack overflow caused by unbounded recursion

explanations.a: The resets were a software scheduling issue (priority inversion), not a power-supply fault.
explanations.b: Correct — this is the textbook priority-inversion case: a medium-priority task starved a low-priority mutex holder, indirectly blocking a high-priority task, and the watchdog reset the system, which was resolved by enabling priority inheritance.
explanations.c: Torn reads are a real concurrency bug but were not the documented cause of the Pathfinder resets.
explanations.d: Stack overflow was not the reported mechanism; the issue was priority scheduling around a shared mutex.

questions.prompt: Match each symptom to its most likely cause.

left.text: MCU resets repeatedly when a motor starts
A shared multi-byte counter occasionally reads a wildly wrong value
The system resets on a schedule even though the main loop is not actually hung
A hard fault handler fires with a captured PC pointing into an unrelated function

right.text: Brown-out reset from supply voltage sagging under motor inrush current
A torn (non-atomic) read racing against an ISR update
Watchdog kicked unconditionally from an ISR rather than gated on real main-loop progress
Stack overflow corrupting memory near the faulting call, making the fault appear in unrelated code

questions.explanation: Motor inrush sagging supply voltage triggers brown-out resets; racing ISR/main-loop access to a multi-byte variable produces torn reads; an ISR-fed watchdog masks real hangs and can still reset on unrelated timing; stack overflow corrupting nearby memory makes faults appear to originate in unrelated code.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of triaging a Cortex-M hard fault using the automatically stacked registers.

items.text: The CPU hits a fault condition (e.g. invalid memory access)
Hardware automatically pushes R0-R3, R12, LR, PC, and xPSR onto the stack
The fault handler executes and reads the stacked frame from the stack pointer
The engineer reads the stacked PC to identify the exact faulting instruction

questions.explanation: A fault condition triggers exception entry, hardware automatically stacks the register frame before the handler runs, the handler then reads that frame off the stack, and the stacked program counter reveals which instruction actually faulted.

lessons.label: The Logic Analyzer and the Mixed-Signal Scope

sections.heading: Sample rate must chase the edge, not the bit rate
sections.body: A common mistake is choosing a sample rate close to a protocol's bit rate, as if capturing a digital signal were like capturing a sine wave under the Nyquist criterion (2x the signal frequency). Digital edges are not sine waves: a real transition on a bus like I2C Fast Mode (400 kHz, so a nominal bit period of 2.5 microseconds) still has a finite rise time shaped by bus capacitance and pull-up resistance, and placing that transition accurately in time requires sampling well faster than the bit period itself. The working rule of thumb is 4-10x the fastest actual edge rate, not the nominal bit rate — for a bus with edges on the order of 100 ns, that argues for a sample rate in the tens of megasamples per second, even though the bit rate itself is only 400 kHz. Undersampling relative to the edge does not produce an obvious error; the decoder still emits a fully formed, plausible-looking byte stream, just with edges placed at the wrong instant, so timing measurements (setup time, ACK position) read as valid numbers that are simply incorrect.

sections.heading: Thresholds, ground reference, and protocol decoders
sections.body: Every logic analyzer channel classifies a voltage as high or low against a threshold, typically set near the midpoint of the logic family in use — about 1.65 V for a 3.3 V system, following the VIL/VIH bands in the target chip's datasheet. A threshold set for 5 V logic on a 3.3 V bus, or a noisy or floating ground reference between the probe and the board, shifts the apparent crossing point and can flip bits near the threshold, especially on a signal with slow edges. Protocol decoders are a software layer built on top of the raw sampled bits: a UART decoder reconstructs start bit, data bits, parity, and stop bit from the timing between edges; an I2C decoder recognizes start/stop conditions and ACK/NACK bits; an SPI decoder frames bytes by chip-select and honors clock polarity and phase (CPOL/CPHA). All of them trust that the raw samples were captured correctly — a decoder cannot tell you your sample rate was too low.

sections.heading: Triggers and the memory-depth tradeoff
sections.body: Trigger types let you capture the moment that matters instead of hours of idle bus traffic: edge (rising/falling on one channel), pulse-width (catches a runt pulse shorter, or a stuck pulse longer, than expected), glitch (catches a sub-normal anomaly narrower than any valid bit), and protocol triggers (fire on a specific I2C address or SPI byte pattern). Capture window is bounded by memory depth divided by sample rate: 10,000 samples at 4 megasamples/second buys only 2.5 milliseconds of window, so a bug that occurs sporadically over seconds forces a choice between a lower sample rate (losing edge accuracy) or more memory depth, which is exactly why analyzers advertise memory in the millions of samples.

lessons.workedExample: A student debugging an I2C sensor at 400 kHz sets a $10 logic analyzer to 1 MS/s, reasoning that this is over twice the bit rate. The decoder happily displays a full transaction with an address, a write bit, and what looks like a valid ACK — but the ACK bit position is wrong because the actual bus edges (rounded by bus capacitance) fall between sample points at that rate, and the decoder just picks the nearest sample without any warning. Reconfiguring the same analyzer to 24 MS/s (roughly 60x the bit rate and well above the 4-10x edge-rate rule for ~100 ns edges) resolves the same transaction with the ACK correctly placed, revealing the actual bug: the sensor was NACK-ing, not ACK-ing, the first attempt.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask about sample-rate choice because a student who names a specific number and justifies it against the signal's edge rate, not its nominal bit rate, has clearly captured real data rather than copied a screenshot. A weak answer says 'I set it as high as it would go' or cites the bit rate as if it were the deciding factor. A strong answer explains that edges, not bit periods, set the required sample rate, and can describe a specific case where an undersampled capture looked plausible but was later shown to be wrong — because that is the actual failure mode of this tool, and judges want to know the student has been burned by it once.

questions.prompt: What is the right basis for choosing a logic analyzer's sample rate for a digital bus?

options.text: Twice the protocol's nominal bit rate, following the Nyquist criterion for sine waves
Roughly 4-10x the fastest actual edge rate on the bus, since edges (not the bit period) determine timing accuracy
Whatever the analyzer's maximum sample rate is, regardless of the signal
The same rate as the target microcontroller's CPU clock

explanations.a: The Nyquist criterion applies to reconstructing sine waves; digital edges need much higher oversampling relative to their actual (often much faster than bit-rate-implied) transition speed.
explanations.b: Correct — accurately placing an edge in time requires sampling several times faster than the edge itself transitions, which is usually much faster than the nominal bit rate suggests.
explanations.c: Maximizing rate blindly may be wasteful or reduce available capture window; the target should be tied to the actual edge rate.
explanations.d: The CPU clock rate is unrelated to the bus signal's own edge speed.

questions.prompt: A logic analyzer's voltage threshold is set for 5 V logic while probing a 3.3 V bus with a noisy ground connection. What is the likely result?

options.text: The capture will be perfectly accurate since threshold only affects analog scope channels
Some transitions near the threshold may be misclassified as the wrong logic level, corrupting the decoded data
The sample rate will automatically adjust to compensate
The protocol decoder will detect the mismatch and refuse to decode

explanations.a: Threshold classification applies directly to logic-analyzer channels, not just analog scope channels.
explanations.b: Correct — a mismatched threshold combined with a noisy ground shifts the apparent crossing point, which can flip the classification of bits near that threshold.
explanations.c: Sample rate and threshold are independent settings; one does not compensate for the other.
explanations.d: Decoders trust the sampled bits and have no way to detect a threshold or ground-reference problem; they will happily decode corrupted data.

questions.prompt: Match each trigger type to what it is designed to catch.

right.text: A rising or falling transition on a specified channel
A pulse that is shorter or longer than an expected duration
An anomalous, sub-normal-width transition narrower than any valid bit
A specific pattern such as an I2C address or SPI byte value

questions.explanation: Edge triggers fire on rising/falling transitions; pulse-width triggers catch runt or oversized pulses; glitch triggers catch anomalies narrower than any valid signal; protocol triggers fire on a decoded pattern like an address or byte value.

questions.prompt: Order the setup steps for capturing an I2C transaction that only happens sporadically over several seconds.

items.text: Set the voltage threshold to match the bus's logic-level standard (e.g. ~1.65 V for 3.3 V logic)
Choose a sample rate at least 4-10x the bus's actual edge rate
Check that memory depth divided by sample rate covers the multi-second window the sporadic event needs
Arm a protocol or edge trigger on the condition of interest and start the capture

questions.explanation: Threshold must be set correctly before any capture is meaningful, sample rate must be chosen relative to the actual edge rate, memory depth must be checked against the required window given that rate, and only then does arming the trigger make sense.

lessons.label: Debugging: SWD/JTAG, printf, and GPIO Instrumentation

sections.heading: Why halting the core can break the very thing you're debugging
sections.body: A breakpoint set through SWD or JTAG halts the CPU completely at a chosen instruction, letting you inspect registers and memory at leisure. A watchpoint does the same but triggers on a memory access or value change rather than an instruction address. Both are ideal for a logic bug in code that has no relationship to physical time — but a control loop is exactly the opposite case. If a breakpoint fires inside a PID loop driving a motor, the CPU freezes with whatever PWM duty cycle was last written still physically applied to the driver, the physical system (a spinning wheel, a moving arm) keeps evolving in the real world while the code that was supposed to be correcting it is frozen, and the integral term stops accumulating. Resuming execution afterward hands the loop a huge, artificial discontinuity between what it last computed and what the world has become, which can look exactly like a code bug that isn't there. For anything with real-time physical stakes, halting the core is not a neutral observation — it changes the experiment.

sections.heading: Real-time instrumentation: GPIO toggling and SWO/ITM trace
sections.body: The cheapest way to measure real execution time without stopping anything is to toggle a spare GPIO pin high at the start of a code section and low at the end, then read the pulse width on an oscilloscope — a technique sometimes called the poor man's profiler, adding only a few instructions of overhead (tens of nanoseconds) rather than halting execution. ARM Cortex-M parts go further with SWO (Serial Wire Output) and the Instrumentation Trace Macrocell (ITM): a single trace pin can carry printf-style messages or raw data words out of the chip at full speed, viewable in an SWV console on tools like an ST-Link, without stopping the CPU and without consuming a UART peripheral or its baud-rate-limited bandwidth.

sections.heading: The Heisenbug cost of blocking printf, and systematic bisection
sections.body: A blocking UART printf() call can take hundreds of microseconds to several milliseconds per line, depending on baud rate and string length, because the CPU waits for each byte to physically shift out. Sprinkling these into a timing-sensitive section is a classic way to create a Heisenbug: adding the print statement delays execution just enough to dodge a race condition, so the bug vanishes while the debug code is present and reappears the moment it's removed. When a fault could be hardware (a bad connection, a marginal component) or firmware (a logic error), the systematic approach is bisection: swap in a known-good component or board to see if the fault follows the hardware, and separately run a minimal known-good firmware image to see if the fault follows the code, narrowing the search by half with each substitution instead of guessing.

lessons.workedExample: A student's balancing robot falls over the instant they set a breakpoint inside the PID update function to inspect a variable — the motors freeze at their last commanded duty cycle while the robot's own inertia keeps tipping it, so the breakpoint itself causes the exact failure they were trying to diagnose. Switching approach, they toggle a spare GPIO high at loop entry and low at loop exit, and a scope shows the loop typically completes in 210 microseconds but occasionally spikes to 340 microseconds when a sensor read stalls — a fact a breakpoint could never reveal because it would have frozen the very loop being measured. They confirm the spike is firmware, not a flaky I2C connection, by swapping in a second known-good sensor board and seeing the spike persist.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask 'how did you debug the timing of your control loop?' because setting a breakpoint on a live motor system is a rookie mistake that reveals a student hasn't thought about what debugging tools actually do to a running system. A weak answer describes stepping through code with breakpoints on a system that has real-time physical stakes, unaware that this changes the very behavior being measured. A strong answer describes a non-invasive method — a GPIO toggle read on a scope, or SWO trace — and explains specifically why a breakpoint would have been the wrong tool for that particular measurement, showing they understand the difference between observing and disturbing a system.

questions.prompt: Why is setting a breakpoint inside a live motor-control PID loop risky, beyond just being inconvenient?

options.text: Breakpoints only work on code that has already finished executing
Halting the CPU freezes the last commanded output while the physical system keeps moving, creating a discontinuity that can masquerade as a code bug
Breakpoints permanently erase the value of any variable they are set on
SWD and JTAG cannot be used on any system with a motor attached

explanations.a: Breakpoints halt execution at a chosen point during a run, not after it finishes.
explanations.b: Correct — the physical world (motor, wheels, inertia) does not pause when the CPU does, so resuming after a halt hands the control loop a state that no longer matches what it last computed.
explanations.c: Breakpoints do not erase variable values; they simply pause execution so values can be inspected.
explanations.d: SWD/JTAG work fine on motor-driven systems; the issue is what halting does to a live control loop, not a hardware incompatibility.

questions.prompt: What is the main advantage of SWO/ITM trace output over a blocking UART printf() call for debugging timing-sensitive code?

options.text: SWO/ITM requires no debug probe at all
SWO/ITM can send trace data out without halting the CPU or blocking on slow byte-by-byte UART transmission, so it disturbs timing far less
SWO/ITM automatically fixes any race condition it detects
SWO/ITM works only when the CPU is halted at a breakpoint

explanations.a: SWO/ITM trace still requires a debug probe (e.g. an ST-Link) capturing the trace pin.
explanations.b: Correct — ITM writes go out over a dedicated trace pin at speed without the CPU blocking on UART byte transmission, which is exactly why it introduces far less timing disturbance than printf.
explanations.c: Trace tools observe behavior; they do not automatically fix logic bugs.
explanations.d: SWO/ITM is meant for use while the CPU is running, not while halted; that is the whole point of using it over a breakpoint.

questions.prompt: Match each debugging technique to its defining characteristic.

right.text: Halts the CPU entirely, ideal for state inspection but disruptive to real-time control
Near-zero overhead, non-invasive real execution-time measurement on an external instrument
Sends trace data out a dedicated pin without halting the CPU or consuming a UART
Can take hundreds of microseconds or more per call, risking a Heisenbug that disappears when the print is added

questions.explanation: Breakpoints halt the core entirely; GPIO toggling gives a near-zero-overhead external timing measurement; SWO/ITM streams trace data without halting or using a UART; blocking printf is slow enough to itself change timing-sensitive behavior.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of a systematic bisection to determine whether an intermittent fault is hardware or firmware.

items.text: Observe the intermittent fault and note the conditions under which it occurs
Swap in a known-good hardware component (e.g. a second sensor board) with the same firmware
Check whether the fault persists (implicating firmware) or disappears (implicating the original hardware)
If firmware is implicated, run a minimal known-good firmware image on the original hardware to isolate the specific code path

questions.explanation: Bisection starts from an observed symptom, substitutes one variable (hardware) at a time while holding the other constant, checks whether the fault follows the substitution, and then further narrows within whichever half (hardware or firmware) still shows the fault.

lessons.label: Measuring Firmware Timing and Resources

sections.heading: Worst case, not average, is what breaks a control loop
sections.body: A control loop that averages 210 microseconds against a 500-microsecond deadline sounds comfortable, but the average hides whatever the code does on its rare slow path: a branch into error handling, a loop whose iteration count depends on input data, or an occasional blocking flash write triggered by a logging routine. If that slow path takes 480 microseconds once every few thousand iterations, the average barely moves, but the one iteration that actually matters — the one that determines whether the loop meets its 500-microsecond deadline — is the worst case, not the mean. A real-time system must be budgeted and reported against worst-case execution time (WCET), because a control loop does not fail gracefully on its average performance; it fails on the single iteration where it runs too slowly and the physical system it's driving overshoots or oscillates.

sections.heading: Finding the worst case: latency histograms and idle-pin duty cycle
sections.body: ISR latency is the time from an interrupt request to the first instruction of its handler executing; jitter is how much that latency varies across triggers, driven by critical sections that briefly disable interrupts or by a higher-priority ISR getting in first. A single average latency number is nearly useless here — what matters is the tail, so the standard technique is to toggle a GPIO pin at ISR entry, capture thousands of triggers on a scope or logic analyzer, and build a histogram: a tight cluster with a long thin tail reveals the rare worst case that an average would erase. CPU load can be measured the same non-invasive way: a GPIO pin held high only while an explicit idle loop is running and low whenever real work executes gives a duty cycle that is directly the CPU load percentage, without any software profiling code skewing the very number it's measuring.

sections.heading: Stack high-water marks and the linker map
sections.body: To find how close a task's stack ever came to overflowing, firmware fills unused stack RAM at boot with a known pattern (commonly 0xA5A5) and later scans how far that pattern has been overwritten by real stack usage — FreeRTOS exposes this directly as uxTaskGetStackHighWaterMark(), reporting the deepest point a task's stack ever reached across its whole run, not just its usage at the moment you happened to check. Flash and RAM budgets come straight out of the linker's map file, which lists the exact byte size of .text, .data, .bss, and the free space remaining in each memory region; checking that file catches a budget overrun — for instance a debug build that no longer fits in a 64 KB flash part — before it becomes a runtime crash.

lessons.workedExample: A team's 2 kHz control loop (500 microsecond period) is timed by toggling a spare GPIO pin at loop start and stop, then viewed on a scope with persistence mode over several minutes. The average pulse width is 210 microseconds, comfortably under budget — but persistence mode reveals a faint second cluster of pulses near 480 microseconds, caused by an occasional SD-card log write that blocks briefly. The team reports the honest number to judges: 'worst case 480 microseconds against a 500-microsecond deadline,' not the flattering 210-microsecond average, and separately confirms via uxTaskGetStackHighWaterMark() that the logging task's stack peaked at 340 of its allocated 512 bytes, leaving headroom rather than silently corrupting adjacent memory.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask for worst-case numbers, not averages, because a control system that is reported only by its mean performance is exactly the kind of report that hides the one failure mode that actually matters. A weak answer proudly states an average loop time with no mention of variability. A strong answer reports a worst-case figure measured against the actual deadline, explains what specific rare event produces that worst case (a blocking write, an occasional longer branch), and shows the reasoning connects to why a control loop's stability depends on its slowest iteration, not its typical one.

questions.prompt: Why should a 2 kHz control loop be judged against its worst-case execution time rather than its average?

options.text: Because average execution time is impossible to measure on embedded hardware
Because the loop only needs to meet its deadline on any single iteration to cause instability if it misses that one time, so a rare slow iteration matters more than the typical case
Because worst-case numbers are always required by regulation for student science-fair projects
Because average execution time is always higher than worst-case execution time

explanations.a: Average execution time is straightforward to measure; that is not the reason worst case matters more.
explanations.b: Correct — a control loop's stability can be broken by a single missed deadline, so the rare slow iteration, not the typical one, determines whether the system actually works.
explanations.c: There is no such regulatory requirement; the reason is purely about what determines real-time correctness.
explanations.d: This is backwards by definition: worst case is always greater than or equal to average execution time.

questions.prompt: A GPIO pin is held high only while an explicit idle loop runs, and low whenever real work executes. What does the resulting duty cycle on a scope directly represent?

options.text: The CPU's clock frequency
The percentage of time the CPU spends doing real work versus idling, i.e. CPU load
The worst-case ISR latency
The amount of free RAM remaining

explanations.a: Clock frequency is a fixed hardware property; the duty cycle instead reflects how busy the CPU is relative to that clock.
explanations.b: Correct — the fraction of time the pin is low (real work) versus high (idle) is, by construction, the CPU load percentage, measured non-invasively.
explanations.c: ISR latency requires timing from an interrupt request to handler entry, a different measurement than an idle-vs-busy duty cycle.
explanations.d: Free RAM is a static memory-budget quantity, unrelated to this timing-based measurement.

questions.prompt: Match each measurement technique to what it reveals.

left.text: ISR latency histogram from thousands of triggers
Idle-pin duty cycle on a scope
Stack fill pattern (e.g. 0xA5A5) scanned after a run

right.text: The tail behavior and jitter of interrupt response time, not just its average
Overall CPU load as a percentage of busy vs idle time
The deepest point a task's stack ever reached across its whole run
Exact byte sizes of .text/.data/.bss and remaining free flash/RAM

questions.explanation: A latency histogram exposes tail/jitter behavior an average hides; idle-pin duty cycle gives CPU load directly; a stack fill pattern reveals the historical high-water mark of stack usage; the linker map reports exact memory-region byte budgets.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of measuring a task's stack high-water mark using a fill-pattern technique.

items.text: At boot, before the task runs, fill its unused stack region with a known pattern (e.g. 0xA5A5)
Let the system run normally so the task's real stack usage overwrites part of the pattern during its worst moments
Scan the stack region to find how far the known pattern has been overwritten
Report the deepest overwritten point as the historical worst-case stack usage

questions.explanation: The pattern must be written before the task ever runs so any overwrite is attributable to real usage, the system must run long enough to hit its worst moments, the scan finds how far the pattern was disturbed, and that boundary is reported as the true historical high-water mark.

lessons.label: Power Measurement and Low-Power Firmware

sections.heading: Sleep modes, wake sources, and the duty-cycled pattern
sections.body: Most microcontrollers offer graded sleep modes. Idle mode stops the CPU core but leaves peripherals and clocks running, so it wakes on almost any interrupt with negligible latency and only a modest current savings. Power-down (or stop) mode shuts off most clocks including the main oscillator, dropping current draw by orders of magnitude — an ATmega328P, for example, falls from several milliamps active at 16 MHz to roughly a microamp in power-down — but only a small set of wake sources still work, typically an external pin interrupt or a real-time-clock alarm, and waking costs extra latency because a crystal oscillator can take several milliseconds to restart and stabilize. Low-power firmware exploits this by duty-cycling: sleeping in power-down mode for long stretches and waking briefly to sample a sensor and transmit, so the system spends the overwhelming majority of its time at microamp-level current and only a small fraction at milliamp-level active current.

sections.heading: Average current is an integral, not the sleep current alone
sections.body: The number that determines battery life is the average current over one full duty cycle, I_avg = (1/T) times the integral of instantaneous current i(t) over the period T — in practice, the area under a measured current-vs-time curve for one complete active-plus-sleep cycle, divided by that cycle's length. A design can have an excellent microamp-level sleep current and still drain a battery quickly if the active burst is long, frequent, or drags in a slow oscillator startup on every wake; conversely, a modest active current is fine if it is brief and rare. Reporting only the datasheet's power-down current, without measuring the actual duty-cycled average, is a common and misleading shortcut.

sections.heading: Measuring the profile, and where the mAh math goes wrong
sections.body: A shunt resistor (commonly 1-10 ohms) in series with the supply, read on an oscilloscope, is the cheap way to convert current into a measurable voltage, but it struggles with dynamic range: a shunt sized to read a milliamp active burst produces a voltage from a microamp sleep current too small to resolve above scope noise, so one shunt value rarely covers both ends of a 1000x current swing. Dedicated auto-ranging current-measurement instruments (such as a Qoitech Otii or a Joulescope) are built specifically to track current across that full range in one capture. Once average current is known, naive battery-life math (rated capacity in mAh divided by average current in mA) overstates real life, because it ignores self-discharge (a battery loses charge sitting unused even with zero load), the regulator's own quiescent current (an LDO can draw single-digit to double-digit microamps with no load at all, sometimes rivaling the MCU's own sleep current), and reduced usable capacity at low temperature, especially in coin-cell and alkaline chemistries.

lessons.workedExample: A sensor node sleeps in power-down mode at 2 uA and wakes every 10 seconds for a 50 ms burst averaging 8 mA to sample and transmit. Average current = (8 mA x 0.05 s + 0.002 mA x 9.95 s) / 10 s = (0.400 + 0.0199) mA*s / 10 s ~= 42 uA. Against a 220 mAh coin cell, naive life = 220 mAh / 0.042 mA ~= 5,238 hours (~218 days). Adding a 3 uA LDO quiescent current the student initially forgot raises the sleep baseline to 5 uA, average current to ~45 uA, and life to ~203 days — a real 15-day loss from a component that never shows up on a datasheet's 'active current' line.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask for a measured average current, not a quoted sleep-mode datasheet number, because the datasheet number describes an idealized single state while the real device spends most of its life in a duty cycle between two very different currents. A weak answer cites the power-down current as if it were the whole story. A strong answer presents an actual measured or calculated average current as an integral over one duty cycle, and can name at least one concrete error source — quiescent regulator current, self-discharge, or temperature — that makes their naive mAh-divided-by-current estimate an upper bound rather than a promise.

questions.prompt: Compared to idle mode, what is the main tradeoff of putting an MCU into power-down (stop) mode?

options.text: Power-down mode draws more current but wakes instantly on any interrupt
Power-down mode draws far less current, but only a limited set of wake sources work and waking takes longer due to oscillator restart
Power-down mode and idle mode have identical current draw and wake behavior
Power-down mode disables all wake sources permanently until manual reset

explanations.a: This reverses the tradeoff: power-down draws less current, not more, and has slower, not instant, wake response.
explanations.b: Correct — power-down mode stops most clocks for a large current reduction, but wake sources are limited to things like pin interrupts or an RTC alarm, and restarting the oscillator adds wake latency.
explanations.c: Idle mode keeps peripherals and clocks running for fast wake at modest savings; power-down is a much deeper, slower-to-wake state, so the two are not equivalent.
explanations.d: Power-down still supports specific wake sources (e.g. pin interrupt, RTC alarm); it does not disable waking entirely.

questions.prompt: Why is the average current over a full duty cycle, rather than the power-down current alone, the number that should be used to estimate battery life?

options.text: Because the power-down current is always higher than the active current
Because the active bursts, even though brief, can contribute significantly to total charge drawn, so ignoring them understates real consumption
Because battery capacity is only specified for average current, never for peak current
Because power-down current cannot be measured with standard instruments

explanations.a: This is backwards; power-down current is dramatically lower than active current, not higher.
explanations.b: Correct — average current integrates both the long low-current sleep periods and the brief high-current active bursts, and a frequent or long active burst can dominate the total even if sleep current is tiny.
explanations.c: Battery capacity ratings (mAh) are used against whatever current is drawn, average or otherwise; this is not a labeling restriction.
explanations.d: Power-down current can be measured, though it requires an instrument with enough dynamic range or sensitivity, which is a separate issue from why average current matters.

questions.prompt: Match each factor to its effect on real-world battery life versus the naive mAh-divided-by-current estimate.

left.text: Undersized shunt resistor for dynamic range

right.text: Drains the battery even with zero load from the circuit itself
Adds a constant baseline current that can rival the MCU's own sleep current, often missed if only MCU current is measured
Reduces usable battery capacity, especially in coin-cell and alkaline chemistries
Not a battery-life factor itself, but a measurement error source that can misreport the current values feeding the calculation

questions.explanation: Self-discharge drains a battery independent of the load; regulator quiescent current adds a hidden baseline draw; low temperature reduces usable capacity; an undersized shunt is a measurement-technique error, not a battery chemistry or load effect.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of estimating battery life for a duty-cycled sensor node.

items.text: Measure the current profile across one full active-plus-sleep cycle with an appropriate instrument
Compute the average current as the area under that profile divided by the cycle period
Divide the battery's rated mAh capacity by the average current to get a naive life estimate
Adjust that estimate downward for self-discharge, regulator quiescent current, and temperature effects

questions.explanation: Battery-life estimation starts from a real measured current profile, reduces it to a single average current via the integral, applies the naive mAh/current division, and then corrects that optimistic number for real-world losses the naive calculation ignores.

units.label: Reading Digital Traces: Timing, Duty Cycle, and Eye Diagrams

lessons.label: Reading a Digital Timing Diagram

sections.heading: Lanes, levels, and decoded buses
sections.body: A timing diagram is a set of parallel time axes, one per signal, each drawn as a stepped high/low trace rather than a continuous curve, because a digital line is only ever supposed to sit at one of two logic levels. A single-bit lane (a clock, a chip-select) shows raw highs and lows. A bus lane groups several related wires (an 8-bit data bus, a decoded SPI or I2C stream) into one collapsed track drawn as alternating high-low blocks labeled with the value they carry in hex, with a crosshatched or 'X' region marking an undefined or don't-care interval. Modern logic analyzers (Saleae Logic, a scope's built-in I2C/SPI/UART decoder) overlay a decoded protocol lane directly beneath the raw electrical trace, turning bit patterns into annotated packets (address, R/W bit, ACK/NAK, data byte) so a student can read a transaction like a sentence instead of counting pulses.

sections.heading: Setup and hold: the window a flip-flop actually samples in
sections.body: A clocked register (a D flip-flop, a microcontroller's input latch) does not sample data continuously; it only cares about the data's value in a narrow window around the active clock edge. Setup time (t_su) is the minimum interval data must already be stable before that edge; hold time (t_h) is the minimum interval it must stay stable after it. A 74AHC74-class flip-flop typically specifies t_su around 3 ns and t_h around 0.5 ns. On a real capture, annotating these windows means drawing a small bracket around the clock edge on the data lane and checking the data line does not transition inside it — a violation there is the doorway to the metastability failures covered later in this unit.

sections.heading: Propagation delay versus the skew trap
sections.body: Propagation delay is measured cause-edge to effect-edge: find the edge that causes a change (a clock rising, an input toggling) and the edge it causes downstream (data becoming valid, a gate's output switching), then read the time between them with cursors. The trap is that two channels probed with mismatched lead or cable lengths accumulate different signal-path delays before the signal even reaches the instrument, and that channel skew reads on-screen exactly like extra logic delay. Coax with a velocity factor near 0.66c propagates roughly 5 ns per meter, so a 1-meter cable-length mismatch between two channels can silently add several nanoseconds nowhere near the device under test. Multi-channel scopes address this with a deskew calibration routine: feeding the same fast edge into every channel simultaneously (a shared reference square wave) and adjusting each channel's internal time offset until all the displayed edges line up removes cable and probe-tip skew from every later measurement, rather than leaving a student to catch it by accident.

lessons.workedExample: A student captures a 74HC04 inverter's input and output using two logic-analyzer channels wired with a 1-meter lead on the input and a 10-cm lead on the output. They measure 14 ns from input edge to output edge and conclude the gate is running about 50% slower than its 9 ns typical t_pd (rated at VCC = 4.5 V, C_L = 15 pF, per the datasheet). Re-wiring both channels with matched 10-cm leads drops the measured delay to 8.7 ns, matching the datasheet almost exactly — the extra ~5 ns in the first measurement was cable skew from the mismatched lead lengths, not logic delay at all.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe timing-diagram reading because it separates a student who treats every number on the screen as ground truth from one who understands the instrument's own wiring is part of the measurement. A weak answer reports the raw cursor delta as 'the propagation delay' and stops. A strong answer names the specific cause-and-effect edge pair being measured, checks whether the channels were length-matched, and can say by how much a mismatch could have skewed the reading — ideally citing the datasheet value the measurement should land near.

questions.prompt: A student measures 14 ns of propagation delay across a 74HC04 inverter (9 ns typical per datasheet) using leads of 1 m and 10 cm on the two channels. Matching both leads to 10 cm drops the reading to 8.7 ns. What explains the original 14 ns reading?

options.text: The inverter was genuinely running 50% slower under the first setup
Channel skew from the mismatched cable lengths added extra apparent delay
The datasheet value of 9 ns was wrong
Setup time was violated on the input channel

explanations.a: A gate's propagation delay doesn't change based on how it's probed; the device itself was unaffected.
explanations.b: Correct — the 1 m vs 10 cm lead mismatch added several nanoseconds of cable propagation delay that had nothing to do with the gate, which is why matching the leads recovered the datasheet-consistent value.
explanations.c: The datasheet value was confirmed correct once skew was removed from the measurement.
explanations.d: Setup/hold time applies to clocked registers sampling data, not to measuring a combinational gate's propagation delay.

questions.prompt: What does setup time (t_su) specify for a clocked flip-flop?

options.text: The minimum time data must be stable before the active clock edge
The maximum time the output can take to change after the clock edge
The minimum time data must remain stable after the active clock edge
The total width of the clock pulse

explanations.a: Correct — setup time is the required stable window immediately before the sampling edge.
explanations.b: That describes clock-to-output propagation delay, a separate parameter.
explanations.c: That describes hold time, the window required after the edge, not before it.
explanations.d: Clock pulse width is a separate timing spec from setup/hold.

questions.prompt: Match each timing-diagram term to its definition.

right.text: Minimum time data must be stable before the clock edge
Minimum time data must remain stable after the clock edge
Time from a cause edge to the effect edge it produces
Timing offset added by mismatched probe or cable lengths, not by the device

questions.explanation: Setup and hold define the stable window around a clock edge; propagation delay is the true cause-to-effect device delay; skew is an artifact of the measurement setup that can be mistaken for propagation delay.

questions.prompt: Order the events of a decoded I2C write transaction as they appear left to right on a captured bus-lane trace.

items.text: START condition (SDA falls while SCL is high)
7-bit address plus R/W bit clocked out
ACK bit from the addressed slave
Data byte clocked out
ACK/NAK bit for the data byte
STOP condition (SDA rises while SCL is high)

questions.explanation: An I2C write begins with START, then the address+R/W byte, an ACK from the slave, the data byte, another ACK/NAK, and finally STOP — the order a decoder overlays on a captured bus lane.

lessons.label: Duty Cycle, Period, and What They Encode

sections.heading: Reading period and duty cycle off a trace
sections.body: Period (T) is the time from one rising edge to the next equivalent rising edge; duty cycle (D) is the fraction of that period the signal spends high, D = t_high / T, usually read with a scope's or logic analyzer's cursors placed at the two crossings that bound one high pulse. Duty cycle is how a PWM (pulse-width-modulated) signal encodes an analog quantity in a purely digital line: a switching regulator, an LED dimmer, or a motor driver varies D while holding T fixed, and a downstream low-pass filter (or the physical inertia of an LED or motor) averages the pulses into a continuous value. The relation is Vavg = D x VDD — an 8-bit PWM channel driving a 5 V LED at 50% duty averages to 2.5 V at the load, even though the pin itself is only ever at 0 V or 5 V.

sections.heading: Quantization steps and the aliasing trap
sections.body: Because most microcontroller PWM peripherals set duty from an integer compare register, duty cycle is quantized. The Arduino Uno's default analogWrite() uses an 8-bit register (0-255) at roughly 490 Hz, so one LSB changes duty by only 1/255 = 0.39%. Stepping the register by a single count and watching a filtered, averaged trace shows Vavg move in discrete stair-steps rather than a smooth ramp — the quantization is visible, not just theoretical. A separate artifact shows up on the scope screen itself: if the record length or trigger repeats at nearly (but not exactly) an integer multiple of the PWM period, successive acquisitions sample the duty envelope at a slightly different phase each sweep, and the displayed waveform appears to slowly drift sideways — a beat between the acquisition interval and the PWM period, not a real change in the signal.

sections.heading: Duty cycle versus absolute pulse width
sections.body: Not every PWM-like signal is decoded by its duty percentage. A hobby servo or ESC (electronic speed controller) reads a control signal at a fixed 50 Hz frame (20 ms period) and decodes the absolute pulse width in microseconds, typically 1.0-2.0 ms, with 1.5 ms as center/neutral — the firmware inside the servo ignores duty cycle as a percentage entirely. Reporting a 1.5 ms pulse as '7.5% duty cycle' is arithmetically correct but conceptually backwards for that application: changing the 20 ms frame period without touching the 1.5 ms pulse width still centers the servo, while changing duty cycle without preserving the pulse width in microseconds would not.

lessons.workedExample: A student PWMs a 5 V LED from an Arduino Uno pin 9 using analogWrite(9, 128), giving D = 128/255 = 50.2% at ~490 Hz. A DMM behind an RC low-pass reads 2.52 V, matching Vavg = D x VDD = 0.502 x 5 V = 2.51 V. Stepping the register from 1 to 2 changes duty by only 0.39%, and on a fine-vertical-scale scope trace the averaged output visibly steps rather than ramping. Separately, driving a hobby servo with a 1.5 ms pulse inside a fixed 20 ms frame centers it; describing that as 'duty cycle 7.5%' is true but useless to the servo, which decodes pulse width in microseconds, not duty percentage.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe duty cycle to see whether a student treats it as an abstract percentage or as a physical quantity being encoded. A weak answer reports a duty-cycle number with no reference to what it drives. A strong answer connects the number to Vavg = D x VDD for a PWM-dimmed load, recognizes when a system (a servo, an ESC) actually decodes absolute pulse width instead of duty percentage, and can explain a sideways-drifting scope trace as an acquisition-timebase beat rather than a real signal change.

questions.prompt: A 5 V PWM signal is measured at 60% duty cycle. What is the expected average (filtered) voltage?

explanations.a: 5.0 V would only occur at 100% duty cycle (constant high), not 60%.
explanations.b: Correct — Vavg = D x VDD = 0.60 x 5 V = 3.0 V.
explanations.c: 2.5 V corresponds to 50% duty cycle, not 60%.
explanations.d: 0.6 V mistakes the duty fraction itself for the averaged voltage instead of scaling it by VDD.

questions.prompt: Why is it misleading to describe a hobby servo's 1.5 ms control pulse (inside a 20 ms frame) primarily as '7.5% duty cycle'?

options.text: Because the math is wrong — 1.5 ms out of 20 ms is not 7.5%
Because the servo's firmware decodes absolute pulse width in microseconds, not duty percentage, so preserving duty while changing the frame period would not center it the same way
Because servos do not use PWM-style signals at all
Because duty cycle only applies to signals faster than 1 kHz

explanations.a: 1.5 ms / 20 ms = 7.5%, so the arithmetic itself is correct.
explanations.b: Correct — servo/ESC firmware reads pulse width in microseconds against a fixed frame; duty percentage is the wrong abstraction even though the number is arithmetically valid.
explanations.c: Servo control signals are pulse-based and often described alongside PWM, so the issue isn't that PWM concepts don't apply at all.
explanations.d: Duty cycle is a general ratio and applies at any frequency; the issue here is which quantity the receiver actually decodes.

questions.prompt: Match each term to what it describes.

right.text: Time from one rising edge to the next equivalent rising edge
Fraction of the period spent high, t_high / T
Smallest change in duty possible given an N-bit compare register (1/2^N)
Apparent sideways drift when acquisition interval and PWM period are nearly, but not exactly, integer multiples

questions.explanation: Period and duty cycle define the raw waveform; quantization step reflects finite PWM register resolution; the beat effect is a display artifact from acquisition timing, not a real signal change.

questions.prompt: An Arduino Uno's 8-bit analogWrite() register is stepped from 1 to 2 (out of 255). What does this do to the measured average output voltage?

options.text: Nothing measurable — 8-bit resolution is too coarse to see any change
It changes Vavg by one quantization step, about 1/255 (0.39%) of VDD
It doubles Vavg
It changes the PWM period, not the duty cycle

explanations.a: The change is small but real and visible as a discrete step on a fine-scale averaged trace.
explanations.b: Correct — one LSB of an 8-bit compare register moves duty by 1/255, so Vavg moves by that same fraction of VDD.
explanations.c: Vavg scales with duty cycle, not with the register value in isolation; a one-count step near the bottom of the range moves Vavg by only one small quantization step, not by a factor of two of VDD.
explanations.d: PWM frequency/period is set by the timer configuration, not by the compare register that sets duty.

lessons.label: Edges, Rise Time, and Signal Integrity on a Breadboard

sections.heading: Rise time and the knee frequency it implies
sections.body: Rise time (t_r) is conventionally measured 10-90%: the time for an edge to travel from 10% to 90% of its final voltage swing, read with two horizontal cursors on a scope. A fast edge is not a single frequency — it is a sum of many harmonics, and a widely used rule of thumb (from signal-integrity engineer Howard Johnson) says the edge's meaningful spectral content extends up to a knee frequency f_knee = 0.5 / t_r. A CMOS output with a 2 ns rise time has f_knee = 0.5 / 2 ns = 250 MHz, so even if that pin is toggling at only 1 MHz, the physical wire carrying it must behave well up to 250 MHz or the edge itself gets distorted.

sections.heading: Ringing, overshoot, and ground bounce
sections.body: A length of wire is not just a resistor; it has self-inductance, roughly 1 nH per millimeter for a straight lead in free air. That inductance forms an underdamped LC resonance with the input capacitance of whatever it drives (a few pF to ~10 pF for a CMOS gate), and a fast edge exciting that resonance produces overshoot above the rail and ringing that decays over several nanoseconds before settling. When several outputs on a shared ground return switch simultaneously, the shared lead inductance causes the local ground reference to bounce upward for the switching instant — ground bounce — which can corrupt a neighboring low-level signal referenced to that same ground.

sections.heading: Decoupling, unterminated jumpers, and why shortening a wire is a real fix
sections.body: A 100 nF ceramic capacitor placed within a few millimeters of an IC's VCC pin, with a short via to the ground plane, supplies the instantaneous switching current locally instead of forcing it through several centimeters of supply-trace inductance; placement close to the pin matters because even a few millimeters of extra lead reintroduces the inductance the cap was meant to remove. On a breadboard, long unterminated jumpers (tens of centimeters) act as unmatched transmission lines for fast edges, reflecting energy back and forth until it damps out. A rough rule of thumb: a line behaves like a lumped connection rather than a transmission line only while its electrical length stays under about one-sixth of the edge's effective wavelength, and FR4-style propagation runs near 15 cm per nanosecond, so a sub-nanosecond edge can already start reflecting on a breadboard jumper only a few centimeters long. Shortening a jumper reduces both its loop inductance and its electrical length relative to the edge's rise time, which is why cutting a wire from 20 cm to 3 cm genuinely removes the physical cause of an intermittent glitch rather than just moving the probe somewhere the glitch happens not to show.

lessons.workedExample: A student drives a 74HC595 shift register's clock input from an Arduino (t_r about 5 ns, VDD = 5 V) over a 20 cm breadboard jumper. The scope shows the clock edge overshooting to 6.3 V (26% overshoot) and ringing for roughly 20 ns before settling — underdamped ringing from the jumper's loop inductance (roughly 200 nH for a straight 20 cm wire) resonating with the shift register's input capacitance. Each edge also drags the local ground up by about 300 mV, corrupting a nearby analog sensor reading (ground bounce). Shortening the jumper to under 3 cm and adding a 100 nF ceramic capacitor within 5 mm of the 74HC595's VCC pin drops the overshoot below 5% and eliminates the sensor glitches.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe rise time and signal integrity because a breadboard fix that 'just worked' is easy to stumble into and hard to explain — the giveaway of real understanding is naming the physical mechanism (loop inductance resonating with input capacitance, or shared ground return) rather than describing the fix as trial and error. A strong answer says shortening the wire lowered its inductance and shortened its electrical length relative to the edge's rise time; a weak answer says 'moving the wire fixed it' with no causal chain.

questions.prompt: A CMOS gate has a 10-90% rise time of 2 ns. Using f_knee = 0.5 / t_r, what is the approximate knee frequency of that edge?

options.text: 25 MHz
250 MHz
500 MHz
2.5 GHz

explanations.a: This is off by a factor of 10 from the correct calculation.
explanations.b: Correct — f_knee = 0.5 / 2 ns = 250 MHz.
explanations.c: This would result from omitting the factor of 0.5 in the formula.
explanations.d: This overstates the result by roughly a factor of 10.

questions.prompt: On a breadboard, a 20 cm jumper carrying a fast clock edge shows 26% overshoot and about 20 ns of ringing before settling. What is the physical cause?

options.text: The Arduino's output driver is defective
The jumper's loop inductance resonating (underdamped) with the input capacitance of the driven gate
The clock frequency is too low for the wire to carry
Static discharge from handling the breadboard

explanations.a: The driver is producing a normal edge; the ringing is added by the external wiring, not the chip's output stage.
explanations.b: Correct — the wire's self-inductance and the gate's input capacitance form an LC circuit that a fast edge excites into underdamped ringing.
explanations.c: A lower clock frequency does not prevent ringing on a single fast edge; ringing is a property of the edge's rise time and the wire's inductance, not the repetition rate.
explanations.d: Static discharge would appear as a single random spike, not a repeatable, edge-triggered ringing pattern.

questions.prompt: Match each signal-integrity phenomenon to its physical cause.

left.text: Reflections on a long unterminated jumper
Purpose of a 100 nF cap next to VCC

right.text: Wire loop inductance resonating with the driven gate's input capacitance
Shared return-path inductance carrying current from multiple simultaneously switching outputs
Impedance mismatch on a line long relative to the edge's rise time, bouncing energy back and forth
Supplying instantaneous switching current locally so it doesn't have to travel through inductive supply traces

questions.explanation: Ringing comes from lead inductance resonating with load capacitance; ground bounce comes from shared return-path inductance under simultaneous switching; reflections come from an unterminated line long relative to the edge; a nearby decoupling cap shortens the path the switching current has to travel.

questions.prompt: Order the steps a student should take to diagnose and fix ringing observed on a breadboarded clock line.

items.text: Observe overshoot and ringing on the scope trace at the driven gate's input
Hypothesize lead inductance resonating with input capacitance as the cause
Shorten the jumper and add a decoupling capacitor near the load's VCC pin
Re-probe the same node to confirm overshoot and ringing are reduced

questions.explanation: A sound diagnostic process observes the artifact first, forms a physical hypothesis for its cause, makes a targeted change, and then re-measures to confirm the change actually addressed the mechanism rather than just moving the probe.

lessons.label: Glitches, Bounce, and Metastability in a Capture

sections.heading: Real glitch, probe artifact, or invisible entirely?
sections.body: A narrow, unexpected pulse in a capture has three possible explanations, and telling them apart is the actual skill. It might be a genuine logic glitch (a real, brief transition caused by the circuit, such as an XOR hazard or a bus contention moment). It might be a probe artifact — a poor ground-clip connection or nearby EMI coupling into a long, unshielded probe lead, which usually disappears or changes shape if the ground connection is redone or a shorter ground spring is substituted for the alligator-clip lead. Or it might be a runt pulse the capture never actually recorded correctly: a sample rate must be several times faster than a pulse's width to resolve it, so a 200 microsecond glitch is safely visible at 100 MSa/s but can fall entirely between samples at 1 kSa/s (1 ms per sample) — not attenuated, simply absent from the data. A quick way to rule out an artifact is to repeat the capture: a probing artifact tends to change character or vanish when the ground path or lead position changes, while a genuine circuit glitch reproduces at the same relative time in the sequence.

sections.heading: Contact bounce: milliseconds of mechanical mess
sections.body: A mechanical switch or pushbutton does not transition cleanly; the metal contacts physically bounce apart and together several times before settling, typically producing on the order of 1-10 ms of chatter with several distinct short pulses inside that window. A slow capture (sampling on the order of milliseconds) can miss the individual bounces and show one clean edge, while firmware polling fast enough to catch a bounce as a second press causes real bugs like double-counted button presses. Standard fixes are an RC filter feeding a Schmitt-trigger input (which converts the slow chatter into one clean digital edge) or a firmware debounce window that ignores further edges for a fixed dead time after the first one.

sections.heading: Metastability and catching a fault that happens once an hour
sections.body: When an asynchronous signal is clocked directly into a flip-flop without a synchronizer, occasionally the setup/hold window from the prior lesson is violated and the flip-flop enters a metastable state: its output hovers near the midpoint between logic levels — around half of VDD — for an unpredictable duration, sometimes tens of nanoseconds, before resolving (usually, but not always correctly) to one valid rail. Catching this on a scope requires two features working together: a glitch or runt trigger armed on any excursion that stays between the valid logic thresholds longer than expected, and infinite (or very long) persistence, which overlays every acquisition from a long capture window onto one display so a fault that occurs once an hour still leaves a visible trace.

lessons.workedExample: A student's pushbutton-driven counter sometimes increments by 2 instead of 1. A 1 kSa/s capture of the button pin shows one clean edge, yet the bug persists. Switching to a 100 MSa/s logic analyzer reveals the contact chattering between 0 V and 3.3 V for about 6 ms after the initial press, with several bounces each only 50-200 microseconds wide — individually invisible at 1 kSa/s, since each 1 ms sample interval is longer than a single bounce. The firmware's interrupt handler was fast enough to register two of the bounces as separate presses. Adding a 10 ms software debounce window in the interrupt handler fixes the double-count.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe this because a raw description of 'it glitched sometimes' says nothing, while a systematic elimination process says everything: checking the probe ground, raising the sample rate to see if a suspected pulse survives, and quantifying bounce duration or metastable settling time rather than eyeballing a single screenshot. A strong answer names which of the three explanations (real glitch, probe artifact, missed runt pulse) applies and the specific capture setting — sample rate, trigger type, persistence — that confirmed it; a weak answer treats every anomaly on screen as automatically real.

questions.prompt: Roughly how long does mechanical contact bounce typically last on a pushbutton or switch?

options.text: 1-10 nanoseconds
1-10 microseconds
1-10 milliseconds
1-10 seconds

explanations.a: Nanosecond-scale events are far faster than mechanical contact motion.
explanations.b: Microsecond-scale bounce is too short for typical mechanical switch chatter, which is dominated by the physical mass of the contacts.
explanations.c: Correct — mechanical bounce typically chatters for about 1-10 ms as the contacts physically settle.
explanations.d: Second-scale chatter would make ordinary buttons unusable; real bounce settles far faster than that.

questions.prompt: A logic analyzer capturing at 1 kSa/s (1 ms per sample) is used to look for a 200 microsecond glitch. What happens?

options.text: The glitch is captured but shown at reduced amplitude
The glitch can fall entirely between samples and simply not appear in the data
The glitch is captured but stretched to look wider than it is
The sample rate has no effect on whether a glitch is captured

explanations.a: A digital logic analyzer records logic levels, not amplitude, so a missed sample isn't shown as attenuated — it's simply not recorded.
explanations.b: Correct — since 200 microseconds is far shorter than the 1 ms sample interval, the glitch can occur and fully resolve between two consecutive samples, leaving no trace in the capture.
explanations.c: Digital sampling doesn't stretch missed events; it either catches an edge on a sample or it doesn't record it at all.
explanations.d: Sample rate directly determines the shortest pulse a capture can reliably resolve, so it matters a great deal here.

questions.prompt: What does a metastable flip-flop output typically look like on a fast oscilloscope capture?

options.text: A clean, fast transition directly between the two valid logic rails
The output hovering near the midpoint between logic levels for an unpredictable duration before resolving to a rail
A perfectly periodic oscillation at the clock frequency
The output permanently stuck at 0 V

explanations.a: A clean transition is the normal, non-metastable case; metastability is defined by the absence of a clean transition.
explanations.b: Correct — metastability shows up as the output lingering near mid-supply for an unpredictable interval before settling to a valid level.
explanations.c: Metastable events are irregular and setup/hold-violation-triggered, not periodic.
explanations.d: A permanently stuck output points to a hardware fault, not a metastable event, which always eventually resolves.

questions.prompt: Match each capture technique or fix to its purpose.

right.text: Arms the scope to capture pulses narrower than, or excursions shorter than, a set threshold
Overlays every acquisition from a long capture window, so a rare event still leaves a visible mark
Analog smoothing plus a hysteresis input that turns slow mechanical chatter into one clean digital edge
Software dead time after the first detected edge that ignores further bounces

questions.explanation: Glitch/runt triggers catch narrow or out-of-spec pulses; infinite persistence accumulates rare events over time; RC+Schmitt debounces in hardware; a firmware dead-time window debounces in software.

lessons.label: Eye Diagrams: How They Are Built and What Closes Them

sections.heading: Building an eye from thousands of overlapping bits
sections.body: An eye diagram is built by taking a long serial data capture, recovering (or already knowing) the bit clock, slicing the waveform into segments exactly one unit interval (UI) long, and overlaying all of those segments on a single time axis with a persistence display so thousands of bit transitions stack on top of one another. Where most transitions agree, the overlaid traces form dense bands; where timing or amplitude varies bit to bit, the traces spread out. The resulting shape resembles an open human eye, with the open region in the middle representing every combination of bit-to-bit variation the link actually produced. Because each new UI-length segment starts wherever the previous one ended, a single long capture of ordinary traffic can populate the eye with every possible bit-transition pattern (0-to-1, 1-to-0, 1-to-1 held, and so on) without needing a special test pattern, though standards labs often use a dedicated pseudo-random bit sequence (PRBS) generator to guarantee even coverage of transition types.

sections.heading: Eye height, eye width, and the sampling point
sections.body: Eye height is the vertical opening measured at the center of the unit interval — it quantifies voltage margin, i.e. how much noise or attenuation the signal can tolerate before a receiver misreads a 1 as a 0 or vice versa. Eye width is the horizontal opening measured at the decision voltage — it quantifies timing margin, i.e. how much a receiver's sampling instant can drift (from jitter, clock error) before it samples during a transition instead of a stable bit. The optimal sampling point is the location inside the eye where it is both tallest and widest, ideally near the 50% point of the UI; a nearly closed eye at that point predicts bit errors even if the raw waveform still looks like a recognizable digital signal at a glance.

sections.heading: Four eye killers, mask testing, and where eyes show up for students
sections.body: Four mechanisms close an eye. Intersymbol interference (ISI) comes from a bandwidth-limited channel spreading each bit's energy into its neighbors, rounding edges and narrowing the eye both vertically and horizontally. Jitter moves edges in time, narrowing eye width. Attenuation reduces signal amplitude uniformly, shrinking eye height. Crosstalk and noise add unwanted voltage at every point in the eye, blurring its edges. Compliance testing overlays a keep-out mask — a hexagonal forbidden region in the eye's center defined by a standard (USB, PCI Express, Ethernet) — and the waveform must never enter it. Students encounter closing eyes most often on USB and Ethernet links, on LVDS pairs, and, less formally, on I2C or SPI buses stretched over long or high-capacitance wiring, where edges round enough that the signal itself starts to look eye-shaped even though those buses are not normally eye-tested.

lessons.workedExample: A student builds a compliance-style eye for a USB 2.0 full-speed link (12 Mb/s, unit interval about 83.3 ns) by triggering on the recovered clock and overlaying about 2,000 consecutive bit periods with infinite persistence. A short, well-terminated cable gives a wide-open eye; swapping in a 3-meter unshielded cable visibly shortens eye height near mid-UI (ISI attenuating high-frequency content more than low-frequency content) and narrows eye width from accumulated jitter. Separately, probing a 400 kHz Fast-mode I2C bus stretched across a 2-meter ribbon (roughly 300 pF of parasitic capacitance, close to the I2C spec's 400 pF bus-capacitance limit) shows edges rounding past the spec's 300 ns maximum rise time, visible directly as a partially closed eye shape on the SDA line.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask about eye diagrams because the picture compresses thousands of individual bit measurements into one glance, and asking a student to point at eye height versus eye width tests a common confusion: which axis is voltage margin and which is timing margin. A weak answer describes the eye shape without connecting either axis to a physical cause. A strong answer says eye height at the sampling instant reflects noise/amplitude margin, eye width reflects jitter/timing margin, and names which of the four eye-closing mechanisms was dominant in their own data — ISI from a long cable, or crosstalk from a nearby switching line.

questions.prompt: Swapping a short USB cable for a 3-meter unshielded one visibly reduces eye height near the center of the unit interval. What is the primary mechanism?

options.text: Crosstalk from an adjacent unrelated signal
Intersymbol interference from the longer, more bandwidth-limited channel attenuating high-frequency content more than low-frequency content
The unit interval getting longer
A change in the transmitter's clock frequency

explanations.a: Crosstalk requires coupling from another nearby signal, which isn't implicated by simply lengthening the same cable.
explanations.b: Correct — a longer cable is a more bandwidth-limited channel, so ISI spreads each bit's energy into its neighbors, closing the eye vertically and horizontally.
explanations.c: The unit interval is set by the data rate, which is unchanged by cable length.
explanations.d: Cable length does not alter the transmitter's clock frequency.

questions.prompt: Match each eye-closing mechanism to its effect on the eye diagram.

right.text: Bandwidth-limited channel spreads each bit's energy into neighboring bits, closing the eye in both axes
Moves edge timing bit to bit, narrowing eye width
Reduces signal amplitude uniformly, shrinking eye height
Adds unwanted voltage at every point in the waveform, blurring the eye's edges

questions.explanation: ISI closes the eye in both dimensions by smearing bits together; jitter closes it horizontally by moving edges in time; attenuation closes it vertically by shrinking amplitude; crosstalk/noise blurs the whole trace.

questions.prompt: Eye width, measured at the decision voltage, primarily quantifies what?

options.text: Timing margin — how much a receiver's sampling instant can drift before hitting a transition
Voltage margin — how much noise the signal can tolerate
The absolute data rate of the link
The number of bits captured to build the eye

explanations.a: Correct — eye width is a horizontal (time-axis) measurement, so it reflects how much timing jitter or sampling-clock drift the link can tolerate before misreading a bit.
explanations.b: Voltage margin is what eye height, a vertical measurement, quantifies instead.
explanations.c: Data rate sets the unit interval that the eye is normalized to, but eye width itself measures margin within that interval, not the rate.
explanations.d: The number of overlaid bits affects how well-populated the eye picture is, not what eye width measures.

questions.prompt: Order the steps used to build an eye diagram from a captured serial bitstream.

items.text: Recover or otherwise determine the bit clock
Slice the waveform into segments exactly one unit interval long
Align every segment to a common time reference
Overlay all segments on one plot using a persistence display

questions.explanation: The clock must be known before the waveform can be sliced into unit-interval segments; those segments must share a common time reference before they can be meaningfully overlaid into the final eye picture.

lessons.label: Jitter Decomposition and the Bathtub Curve

sections.heading: Random versus deterministic jitter, and three ways to measure the same wobble
sections.body: Jitter is the deviation of a signal's edges from their ideal, evenly spaced positions in time, and it splits into two families with different statistics. Random jitter (RJ) comes from thermal and other noise sources, is modeled as Gaussian, and has an unbounded tail — in principle an arbitrarily large deviation is possible, just increasingly unlikely. Deterministic jitter (DJ) is bounded and repeatable, coming from causes like periodic coupling (power-supply ripple riding onto a clock) or duty-cycle distortion. The same underlying wobble can be reported three different ways: period jitter (how much each individual cycle's period deviates from the average period), cycle-to-cycle jitter (the difference between two adjacent periods), and time interval error, TIE (how far each edge has drifted from where an ideal, jitter-free reference clock would place it) — TIE accumulates over time in a way the other two do not, since it is measured against a fixed reference rather than the signal's own neighboring edges.

sections.heading: Why peak-to-peak grows with time while RMS does not, and the dual-Dirac model
sections.body: Because RJ is Gaussian and unbounded, observing more cycles increases the chance of catching an unusually extreme one, so a peak-to-peak jitter number quoted without an observation time or bit count is close to meaningless — it keeps growing the longer you watch. RMS jitter (the standard deviation, sigma, of that same Gaussian) is a population-level statistic and converges to a stable value regardless of how long you observe. The dual-Dirac model turns this into something usable for a target bit-error rate: total peak-to-peak jitter TJ = DJ_pp + n x RJ_rms, where n is the number of standard deviations corresponding to the target BER. At BER = 1e-12, that multiplier works out to n approximately 14.07, because the Gaussian tail probability of exceeding roughly 7.03 sigma on each side of the distribution equals 1e-12.

sections.heading: The bathtub curve and the aperture-jitter limit on ADC performance
sections.body: Plotting measured or extrapolated bit-error rate against sampling position across one unit interval produces the bathtub curve: BER is near zero across most of the eye's center and rises steeply near the edges, shaped like a bathtub's cross-section. Because directly counting errors down to BER = 1e-12 would require collecting over a trillion bits, the dual-Dirac model is used instead to extrapolate the curve's steep flanks from a much shorter, statistically well-behaved measurement.
