explanations.d: Q15 is signed and centered on zero, not restricted to 0 to 1.

questions.prompt: Why is saturating arithmetic generally preferred over ordinary wraparound overflow in a signal-processing chain?

options.text: Saturation uses fewer CPU cycles than wraparound in all cases
Wraparound can flip an out-of-range positive sample into a large negative one, producing a much worse artifact than a clipped peak
Saturation increases the effective bit resolution of the signal
Wraparound is not supported by two's-complement arithmetic

explanations.a: Saturation typically costs extra cycles (or dedicated hardware instructions) compared to letting overflow wrap freely.
explanations.b: Correct — silent wraparound can turn a large positive value into the most negative representable value, a sign-flip artifact far worse than the gentle flattening saturation produces.
explanations.c: Saturation changes overflow behavior, not the number of bits available for resolution.
explanations.d: Wraparound is exactly the native behavior of two's-complement overflow; that is why it needs an explicit saturation step to avoid.

questions.prompt: Match each filter to the description of how it is computed in integer math.

right.text: Running sum updated with one add and one subtract per new sample
Single subtract, shift, and add per sample; no multiply needed
Eight multiply-accumulates per output sample

questions.explanation: A moving average only needs a running sum (add new, subtract oldest), an EMA implemented as y += (x - y) >> k needs no multiply at all, and an 8-tap FIR needs eight multiply-accumulates per sample, trading more cycles for sharper frequency response.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of one EMA filter update using the shift-based form `y += (x - y) >> k`.

items.text: Compute the difference between the new sample x and the current output y
Right-shift that difference by k bits
Add the shifted result to the current output y
Store the updated y as the new filter output

questions.explanation: The EMA update first finds how far the new sample is from the current output, scales that gap down by the shift amount (setting the filter's time constant), adds the scaled gap back onto the output, and stores the result as the new running output for the next sample.

lessons.label: Precision Mixed-Signal Design

sections.heading: Where the return current actually goes
sections.body: A ground pour is not one uniform node; it carries real return current, and that current physically follows the path of least inductance — which, on a solid plane, means directly underneath the signal trace it belongs to. Digital switching (clock edges, SPI/I2C toggling, and especially a switching regulator's inductor current) injects sharp current pulses into whatever ground it shares. Separating analog and digital ground pours and joining them at a single star point, placed right at the sensitive component (typically the ADC's ground pin), keeps those digital return-current pulses from crossing through the analog section on their way back to source. Splitting the plane itself is riskier than it sounds: if a trace crosses a slot in the ground plane, its return current is forced to detour around the slot, and that detour is exactly the kind of loop that couples noise into a nearby analog signal.

sections.heading: Driving the ADC input and keeping noise out of band
sections.body: An ADC's sample-and-hold capacitor must charge to the input voltage within a short acquisition window; a high-impedance sensor source often cannot supply that charge fast enough on its own, which shows up not as random noise but as a systematic gain or offset error, so a low-impedance buffer op-amp is usually placed ahead of the ADC input. Separately, per the Nyquist–Shannon sampling theorem, any signal energy above half the sampling rate (fs/2) folds back — aliases — into the signal band once sampled, indistinguishable from real in-band signal. An anti-alias filter, often a simple passive RC or an active low-pass ahead of the ADC, bandlimits the input below fs/2 before the ADC ever samples it; skipping this step is invisible on a clean bench signal but shows up as unexplained noise the moment any real-world interference is present.

sections.heading: Reference noise, self-heating, and timing the conversion
sections.body: The ADC's voltage reference sets the size of one least-significant bit, so reference noise subtracts directly from usable resolution — a noisy 3.3 V regulator used as reference can cost several effective bits compared to a low-noise reference with strong power-supply rejection ratio (PSRR), the metric for how well a regulator attenuates ripple reaching its output. Precision resistors and sensors also drift with self-heating: a resistor dissipating even modest power warms over seconds to minutes and its value creeps with temperature, a slow error a single calibration cannot catch. Finally, timing matters: triggering a conversion right as a nearby switching regulator's inductor current transitions injects a noise burst into that exact sample; deliberately timing conversions to a quiet point in the switcher's cycle, or switching to a low-noise LDO during the critical measurement, avoids it. Applied together, these fixes are why boards routinely climb from around 8 effective bits on a nominal 12-bit ADC up to 11 or 12 once grounding, anti-aliasing, and reference noise are all addressed.

lessons.workedExample: A student's board uses a 12-bit ADC sampling at 100 kHz but measures only about 8 effective bits by comparing a clean sine-wave input to the recorded output and computing the noise floor. The digital ground and analog ground share one pour with a switching regulator routed straight through the middle, there is no anti-alias filter, and the ADC reference is tapped directly off the noisy 3.3 V rail. The student separates the pours to a star point at the ADC, adds a passive RC anti-alias filter with a cutoff a decade below the 50 kHz Nyquist limit, and swaps the reference to a dedicated low-noise LDO with high PSRR. Re-running the same sine-wave test afterward shows the noise floor dropping enough to recover effective resolution close to the ADC's full 12 bits.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges push on this because "we used a 12-bit ADC" is a datasheet number, not a measurement, and any student who ran a real sine-wave or histogram test to find their actual effective number of bits (ENOB) has done something most fair projects skip entirely. A weak answer quotes the ADC's rated resolution as if it were achieved. A strong answer reports a measured ENOB, names the specific fix that moved it (star grounding, an anti-alias filter, a cleaner reference), and can explain in physical terms — return-current path, aliasing, reference noise — why that fix mattered rather than just that it did.

questions.prompt: Why does joining separate analog and digital ground pours at a single star point near the ADC help precision, compared to letting both share one uniform plane everywhere?

options.text: It reduces the total resistance of the ground network
It keeps sharp digital return-current pulses from routing through the sensitive analog section
It increases the ADC's rated bit resolution
It has no electrical effect, only a cosmetic layout benefit

explanations.a: Star grounding is about controlling current path, not primarily about minimizing total resistance.
explanations.b: Correct — return current follows the path of least inductance, and a star point at the ADC keeps digital switching current from detouring through the analog return path.
explanations.c: A part's rated resolution is fixed by its silicon; grounding affects how much of that resolution is usable (effective bits), not the datasheet spec.
explanations.d: The effect is a real reduction in coupled noise, not merely cosmetic.

questions.prompt: An ADC samples at 100 kHz with no anti-alias filter ahead of it, and a stray 80 kHz interference signal is present at the input. What happens?

options.text: The ADC automatically rejects any signal above its sample rate
The 80 kHz interference aliases down into the signal band, indistinguishable from a real low-frequency signal
The interference is stored correctly at 80 kHz in the digital output with no distortion
The ADC's reference voltage shifts to compensate

explanations.a: An ADC has no inherent frequency rejection; anything present at the input gets sampled, filter or not.
explanations.b: Correct — 80 kHz is above the 50 kHz Nyquist limit (half the 100 kHz sample rate), so per the sampling theorem it folds back into the observable band as a false low-frequency component.
explanations.c: Digital sampling cannot represent a frequency above fs/2 as itself; it appears folded (aliased), not faithfully reproduced.
explanations.d: Aliasing is a sampling-theorem effect unrelated to the reference voltage.

questions.prompt: Match each mixed-signal issue to its cause or fix.

right.text: Measures how well a regulator/reference attenuates supply ripple
Bandlimits the signal below fs/2 before sampling
A resistor or sensor's value creeping as it warms from dissipated power
Supplies charge fast enough to the sample-and-hold capacitor from a high-impedance source

questions.explanation: PSRR quantifies supply-ripple rejection, an anti-alias filter prevents out-of-band energy from folding into the signal band, self-heating drift is a slow thermal error from power dissipation, and an input buffer solves the charge-delivery problem of a high-impedance source driving a sample-and-hold input.

questions.prompt: Order the fixes as the student in the worked example applied them to move the board from about 8 effective bits toward 12.

items.text: Separate analog and digital ground pours to a single star point at the ADC
Add a passive RC anti-alias filter ahead of the ADC input
Replace the noisy shared-rail reference with a dedicated low-noise LDO
Re-run the sine-wave ENOB test to confirm the improvement

questions.explanation: The student addressed grounding, then bandlimited the input, then cleaned up the reference, and only afterward re-measured effective bits to confirm the combined fixes actually worked, rather than assuming they did.

lessons.label: EMC, ESD, and Field Reliability

sections.heading: Fast edges and loop area are what radiate
sections.body: A circuit radiates electromagnetic interference in rough proportion to the current in a loop, the area that loop encloses, and how fast the current changes (di/dt for magnetic/radiated emissions, dv/dt for electric-field coupling). A slow analog signal is a poor antenna; a MOSFET gate driven with a fast edge, or a digital clock with sharp transitions, is rich in high-frequency harmonics and radiates efficiently even at modest current. Two cheap fixes attack the edge rate directly rather than the layout: a series termination resistor placed at the driver end of a trace forms an RC with the trace and driver output impedance, deliberately slowing the edge, and a slew-rate-limited gate driver does the same thing at the source, tamping down di/dt before it ever reaches a loop that could radiate it.

sections.heading: Return-path discipline is a layout decision
sections.body: Just as in mixed-signal grounding, return current in a fast-switching loop wants the path of least inductance — directly beneath the trace, on a continuous plane. Any high-di/dt loop, such as a motor driver's power stage or a switching regulator's inductor loop, should be laid out with its outbound and return paths as physically close together as the components allow, minimizing enclosed area, and never routed across a slot or split in the return plane, which would force a detour and enlarge the effective loop.

sections.heading: ESD, latch-up, and the environment between bench and field
sections.body: Exposed connectors need protection from electrostatic discharge: IEC 61000-4-2 defines standard test levels, including 8 kV contact discharge and 15 kV air discharge, and a TVS (transient-voltage-suppression) diode or clamp diode on each exposed pin gives a fast, low-impedance path to shunt that energy away from the chip. CMOS devices carry an inherent risk called latch-up: the chip's well structure forms a parasitic PNPN (silicon-controlled-rectifier-like) path that, if triggered by a voltage transient beyond the supply rails, can snap into a low-impedance short from VDD to ground that persists until power is cycled — and can destroy the part if the resulting current is not limited quickly. Cable shields need their own discipline too: a shield is typically grounded at one end for low-frequency noise or both ends for high-frequency EMI, with drain wires kept as short as possible, since a long drain wire itself becomes an antenna. Beyond the circuit, three environmental factors quietly kill projects between the workbench and the fair table: thermal cycling that fatigues solder joints and connectors, vibration that loosens a header or connector over repeated handling, and condensation from humidity that corrodes exposed traces or bridges pins with a barely-conductive film — none of which show up in a clean, dry, temperature-stable lab test.

lessons.workedExample: A student's motor driver board resets a nearby MCU whenever the motor starts. Probing near the MOSFET's gate-drive trace with a near-field probe and spectrum analyzer shows a broadband emissions spike coinciding with each switching edge. The gate trace runs a 5 V/ns edge through a loop between the MOSFET and its gate-drive source that measures roughly 2 cm² in enclosed area. Adding a 33-ohm series resistor at the driver output slows the edge, and re-routing the trace to hug the return plane shrinks the loop to under 0.5 cm². Re-measuring with the same near-field probe shows the emissions spike reduced enough that the nearby MCU stops resetting when the motor starts.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe EMC and reliability because most fair-day failures are not core electronics bugs, they are field effects that never appeared on the bench: an unrelated board resetting near a motor, a connector working loose after transport, or a board fogging up outdoors. A weak answer blames a mystery failure on "bad luck" or a vaguely "faulty" component. A strong answer names a specific mechanism and mitigation tied to an observed symptom — a series resistor added after tracing an MCU reset to switching noise, or a TVS diode added after an exposed input pin failed an ESD test — showing the student diagnosed the failure rather than just patched around it.

questions.prompt: Two circuits carry the same fast-switching current, but one has a much larger current-loop area than the other. What does that difference mainly affect?

options.text: The DC resistance of the loop
How efficiently the loop radiates electromagnetic interference
The total power consumed by the circuit
The circuit's tolerance to temperature drift

explanations.a: Loop area and DC resistance are largely independent properties of a trace layout.
explanations.b: Correct — radiated emissions scale with loop area (along with current magnitude and edge rate), so a larger loop with the same fast-switching current radiates more efficiently.
explanations.c: Power consumption depends on voltage and current draw, not primarily on the geometric loop area.
explanations.d: Loop area is an EMC layout property, not a thermal one.

questions.prompt: What is CMOS latch-up?

options.text: A normal low-power sleep state the chip enters when idle
A parasitic PNPN structure triggering a persistent low-impedance short from VDD to ground
A software condition where an interrupt handler never returns
The intended behavior of a TVS diode when clamping a transient

explanations.a: Latch-up is a destructive fault condition, not an intended low-power state.
explanations.b: Correct — a transient beyond the supply rails can trigger a parasitic PNPN path inherent to CMOS wells, creating a persistent low-impedance short that can destroy the part if current is not limited quickly.
explanations.c: That describes a software hang, an unrelated failure mode at a different layer of the system.
explanations.d: A TVS diode's intended job is to shunt a transient safely; latch-up is the chip failure mode a designer is trying to avoid, not a protection mechanism.

questions.prompt: Match each practice or component to its purpose.

left.text: TVS diode on an exposed pin
Routing return current directly beneath a signal trace

right.text: Slows a fast edge to reduce radiated emissions
Shunts an ESD transient away from sensitive circuitry
Avoids turning the drain wire itself into a radiating antenna
Minimizes loop area to reduce coupled and radiated noise

questions.explanation: A series resistor tames edge rate at the source, a TVS diode clamps ESD energy at an exposed pin, a short drain wire avoids adding its own antenna, and hugging the return path to the signal trace minimizes the enclosed loop area that drives emissions.

questions.prompt: Order the diagnostic steps the student in the worked example took to fix the motor-driver EMI problem.

items.text: Notice the nearby MCU resets whenever the motor starts
Probe the gate-drive trace with a near-field probe and spectrum analyzer
Add a series resistor and shrink the gate-drive loop area
Re-measure emissions and confirm the MCU no longer resets

questions.explanation: The student first observed the symptom, then localized the source with a near-field probe before changing anything, then applied a targeted fix to the identified edge and loop, and only then confirmed the fix worked by re-measuring rather than assuming it did.

units.label: Applications and Case Studies: Sensor-Driven Embedded Projects

lessons.label: Designing a Sensor-Driven Experiment End to End

sections.heading: Requirement to block diagram
sections.body: A sensor project starts as a measurement requirement, not a parts list: what physical quantity, over what range, with what accuracy, and how fast does it change? That requirement drives a block diagram — transducer, signal conditioning, ADC, microcontroller, storage — before any part number is chosen. Sensor selection then follows three specs from the datasheet: range (does it cover the expected values without clipping), resolution (the smallest change it can distinguish, often set by the ADC bit depth sharing that range), and response time (how fast the sensor's output tracks a step change, usually given as a thermal or mechanical time constant). Picking a sensor with a 10-second response time to catch an event that happens in 200 ms is a design failure no amount of clever firmware can fix.

sections.heading: Sampling rate and the error budget
sections.body: Sampling rate is not arbitrary. The Nyquist–Shannon sampling theorem (Harry Nyquist's 1928 telegraphy work, formalized by Claude Shannon in 1949) says you must sample at least twice the highest frequency present in the signal or you alias it into false low-frequency noise. In practice, engineers sample 5–10x the signal bandwidth so filters and derivative terms stay clean. Accuracy is likewise not one number but a budget: transducer accuracy, conditioning-circuit error (op-amp offset voltage, gain tolerance), and ADC quantization error (one LSB = full-scale range / 2^bits) each contribute, and independent errors combine as a root-sum-square, not a simple sum — so a 0.2 degree sensor feeding a 12-bit ADC over a 100-degree span (LSB ≈ 0.024 degrees) is still sensor-limited, and improving the ADC alone buys nothing.

sections.heading: Timestamps, drift, and surviving a power loss
sections.body: Every logged sample needs a trustworthy timestamp, usually from a real-time clock (RTC) chip with its own crystal. A typical ±20 ppm crystal accumulates error at 20 microseconds per second, which works out to roughly 50–60 seconds — about a minute — per month; a multi-week deployment can drift by several minutes unless resynced against a reference clock. Finally, a logger that writes to SD card or flash must survive power loss mid-write: naive logging can corrupt the whole file if power drops while a block is being written. The fix is append-only writes with periodic flush/fsync calls, so at worst you lose the last unflushed sample instead of the entire dataset.

lessons.workedExample: A student logging fermentation temperature picks a thermistor with a 10-minute thermal time constant, so they sample once every 30 seconds (well above 2x, comfortably resolving the slow curve). Their error budget: thermistor ±0.2°C, conditioning op-amp offset contributing ≈50mV → ≈0.05°C, and a 12-bit ADC over a 0–100°C range giving an LSB of ≈0.024°C — root-sum-square total ≈ 0.21°C, dominated by the thermistor. Their RTC's ±20ppm crystal drifts about a minute a month, so they resync it against a phone's NTP time weekly. Data is appended as CSV lines to the SD card with an fsync after each write, so a dead battery mid-experiment loses at most one row.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'how did you pick your sampling rate and how accurate is this number really?' because most fair projects default to whatever delay(1000) felt convenient and never touch the question again. A weak answer says 'I sampled every second because that seemed reasonable.' A strong answer names the phenomenon's time constant, states the sampling rate as a multiple of it, and can decompose the final error into sensor, conditioning, and quantization pieces — showing the student understands their number is a budget, not a guess, and knows which term dominates.

questions.prompt: Why do embedded projects typically sample at 5-10x the signal bandwidth instead of exactly 2x (the Nyquist minimum)?

options.text: Sampling exactly at 2x is mathematically impossible on a microcontroller
The margin leaves room for filtering, derivative terms, and imperfect anti-aliasing to still work cleanly
Microcontroller ADCs cannot sample slower than 10x any signal
It has no real benefit; 2x is always sufficient in practice

explanations.a: 2x sampling is achievable in theory and practice; it is the theoretical minimum, not an impossibility.
explanations.b: Correct — exactly 2x sampling requires a perfect signal and a perfect anti-alias filter, neither of which exists; extra margin keeps downstream filtering and derivative calculations well-behaved.
explanations.c: ADC sample rates are a hardware limit unrelated to this margin convention; many ADCs sample far faster than 10x any given signal.
explanations.d: 2x is the bare theoretical floor; running that close in a real system risks aliasing from any imperfection in filtering.

questions.prompt: A crystal used in an RTC has a ±20 ppm tolerance. Roughly how much timestamp drift accumulates over one month of continuous operation?

options.text: About 1 second
About 1 minute
About 1 hour
About 1 day

explanations.a: 20 ppm over a full month (about 2.6 million seconds) accumulates far more than a single second of drift.
explanations.b: Correct — 20 ppm means 20 microseconds of error per second; over roughly 2.6 million seconds in a month that totals about 50-60 seconds, roughly a minute.
explanations.c: An hour of drift from 20 ppm would require a much longer elapsed time than one month.
explanations.d: A full day of drift is two orders of magnitude too large for a 20 ppm crystal over one month.

questions.prompt: Match each stage of the sensor error budget to what determines its contribution.

right.text: The sensor's own datasheet accuracy spec
Op-amp offset voltage and gain tolerance in the front-end circuit
Full-scale range divided by 2^(bit depth)

questions.explanation: Transducer error comes from the sensor's own rated accuracy; conditioning error comes from the amplifier/filter stage's offset and gain imperfections; ADC quantization error is fixed by the converter's resolution (LSB size) over the chosen full-scale range.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of designing a sensor-driven experiment, from first to last.

items.text: State the measurement requirement (quantity, range, accuracy, speed)
Sketch the block diagram (transducer, conditioning, ADC, MCU, storage)
Select the sensor by range, resolution, and response time
Choose sampling rate from the phenomenon's bandwidth
Compute the end-to-end error budget and plan power-loss-safe logging

questions.explanation: The requirement defines the block diagram, which frames what kind of sensor is needed; only once a candidate sensor's response time is known can a sampling rate be justified, and only then can the error budget and logging plan be finalized around the chosen chain.

lessons.label: Case Study: Low-Cost Air-Quality Monitors vs Reference Instruments

sections.heading: How a $20 particle sensor actually works
sections.body: Sensors like the Plantower PMS5003 and Nova SDS011 measure PM2.5 with a laser diode, a fan or heater that draws air across the beam, and a photodetector that counts light-scattering pulses as particles cross it. Firmware inside the sensor converts scatter counts into a particle-count-per-bin histogram and then into an estimated mass concentration, assuming a particle density and size distribution. That assumption is the sensor's weak point: it is calibrated against a specific reference aerosol, so any real-world plume with a different particle composition (wildfire smoke, road dust, sea salt) will scatter light differently than the calibration aerosol did, biasing the mass estimate. An MCU reads the result over UART as a serial data frame at a fixed interval — no analog conditioning needed, but the digital number it hands you already carries the sensor's calibration assumptions baked in.

sections.heading: The humidity problem and the Barkjohn correction
sections.body: Optical PM sensors have a well-documented positive bias at high relative humidity: airborne particles absorb water and swell (hygroscopic growth), scattering more light per unit of actual dry mass, so the raw reading overstates PM2.5 as humidity climbs — often severely above 70-80% RH. Barkjohn, Gantt, and Clements (2021, Atmospheric Measurement Techniques) developed the correction the US EPA now applies nationally to PurpleAir data: a multilinear regression using the PurpleAir's own onboard relative-humidity sensor as a predictor alongside the raw PM2.5 reading, trained against 39 collocated reference sites across 16 states. Adding the humidity term measurably reduced bias and improved agreement with reference monitors compared to using the raw reading alone — a textbook case of a known physical mechanism (hygroscopic growth) becoming a correctable term rather than an excuse to distrust the sensor.

sections.heading: Colocation and reporting agreement honestly
sections.body: The only credible way to validate a low-cost sensor is colocation: running it side-by-side with a reference-grade instrument (a Federal Reference Method or Federal Equivalent Method monitor) over the same air for days to weeks, then comparing the paired readings. The right report is a linear regression of low-cost vs reference readings, giving slope (does the sensor read proportionally right), intercept/bias (does it read high or low at zero), and R-squared (how tightly the two track together) — never a bare claim like 'accurate to within 10%' without showing the regression and the conditions it was run under. A slope near 1.0 with a small intercept and high R-squared under the tested humidity range is a real, bounded validation claim; anything less should be reported as exactly that, not smoothed over.

lessons.workedExample: A student colocates an SDS011 sensor next to a nearby EPA reference monitor's public hourly PM2.5 feed for two weeks. Plotting raw SDS011 readings against reference values gives slope 1.4, intercept +3 micrograms/m3, R-squared 0.81 — the sensor overreads, especially on humid afternoons. They add relative humidity (from the SDS011's own housing sensor) as a second regressor following the Barkjohn approach: PM2.5_corrected = a + b*(raw PM2.5) + c*(RH). Refitting drops the slope to 1.05, intercept to +1 microgram/m3, and R-squared rises to 0.93. The student reports both the raw and RH-corrected fits with the humidity range they were tested over (35-85% RH), rather than claiming the sensor is simply 'accurate.'
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'how do you know your air-quality readings are correct?' because low-cost PM sensors are notorious for confidently wrong numbers, and a project that just plots the raw serial output hasn't grappled with that. A weak answer says the sensor's datasheet claims high accuracy. A strong answer describes a colocation run against a reference instrument, reports slope/bias/R-squared rather than a vague accuracy percentage, and names humidity as the dominant known bias — ideally showing they tried or at least understand the Barkjohn-style RH correction rather than treating the raw number as ground truth.

questions.prompt: Why does relative humidity cause low-cost optical PM2.5 sensors like the PMS5003 to overread?

options.text: High humidity damages the laser diode, making it scatter light randomly
Water absorbed by airborne particles makes them swell, so they scatter more light per unit of actual dry particle mass
Humidity increases the fan speed, drawing in more particles than normal
The UART communication becomes unreliable in humid air, corrupting the data frame

explanations.a: Humidity does not damage the laser diode; the bias is a measurement artifact from particle physics, not sensor damage.
explanations.b: Correct — hygroscopic growth means particles absorb water and swell in humid air, scattering more light for the same underlying dry mass, which the sensor's algorithm converts into an inflated mass reading.
explanations.c: Fan speed in these sensors is fixed by design and is not modulated by ambient humidity.
explanations.d: The UART link itself is a digital interface unaffected by humidity in this way; the bias is physical, at the sensing stage, not a communication error.

questions.prompt: What did Barkjohn, Gantt, and Clements (2021) add to the raw PurpleAir PM2.5 reading to build the EPA's national correction?

options.text: Temperature only, ignoring humidity entirely
The sensor's onboard relative-humidity reading, in a multilinear regression against reference monitors
A fixed multiplier of 2x applied to every raw reading regardless of conditions
GPS location data to identify which city the sensor was in

explanations.a: The Barkjohn correction is built around relative humidity as the key added predictor, not temperature alone.
explanations.b: Correct — the correction regresses reference-monitor PM2.5 against the raw sensor reading plus the sensor's own relative-humidity measurement, trained across 39 collocated reference sites.
explanations.c: A single fixed multiplier would not account for how bias varies with humidity conditions, which is exactly what the regression approach captures.
explanations.d: Location was used to select diverse collocation sites for training the model, but is not itself a term applied in the correction equation.

questions.prompt: Match each colocation validation metric to what it tells you.

right.text: Whether the sensor reads proportionally correct as concentration rises
Whether the sensor reads systematically high or low even near zero
How tightly the sensor's readings track the reference instrument overall

questions.explanation: Slope captures proportional scaling error, intercept captures a constant offset/bias, and R-squared captures how well the two data series correlate overall — reporting all three (rather than one vague accuracy claim) is what an honest colocation validation looks like.

lessons.label: Case Study: Open-Source Scientific Instruments

sections.heading: A published instrument, not just a hobby build
sections.body: A growing body of peer-reviewed work turns Arduino and Raspberry Pi projects into real scientific instruments. Open-source colorimeters and photometers built from an LED, a photodiode, and a microcontroller replicate benchtop spectrophotometer measurements at a fraction of the cost. Public Lab's community-developed spectrometer kits pair a webcam or Pi camera with a diffraction grating and open firmware to produce absorbance and emission spectra for citizen science, from oil-spill monitoring to water quality. The OpenFlexure microscope, described by Collins et al. (2020, Biomedical Optics Express), is a 3D-printed, motorized, fully automated microscope stage that achieves robotic sample positioning and autofocus using a Raspberry Pi and stepper motors instead of the precision machined parts of a commercial stand — bringing a feature normally reserved for instruments costing tens of thousands of dollars into a build costing a few hundred.

sections.heading: How these instruments prove they work
sections.body: What separates a real instrument from a demo is a validation section: the design paper runs the device against a reference method and reports the agreement quantitatively. Common tools are a regression R-squared against a certified reference, a Bland-Altman analysis (Bland & Altman, 1986) plotting the difference between the two instruments against their mean to show the limits of agreement rather than a single misleading correlation number, and a limit of detection — the smallest signal reliably distinguishable from a blank, typically defined as roughly three times the standard deviation of blank measurements divided by the calibration slope. A paper that skips this step and shows only a pretty photo of the device has not demonstrated it measures anything correctly.

sections.heading: Reproducibility, and the library-depth debate
sections.body: Because these are meant to be rebuilt by other labs and classrooms, a credible open instrument publishes a full bill of materials with part numbers and costs, and pins the exact firmware version used to generate the paper's results (a git commit hash or tagged release) — without that, another group's rebuild is a different instrument. There is a live debate in this community over whether high-level libraries (Arduino's `Wire.h`, CircuitPython drivers) help or hurt learning: proponents say they let students focus on experimental design instead of I2C timing; critics argue that hiding register-level control means a student can build a working sensor node without ever understanding what their code is actually telling the hardware to do, leaving a gap that surfaces the first time a library abstraction breaks.

lessons.workedExample: A team rebuilds an open-source colorimeter design to measure chlorophyll concentration in pond water samples. They publish their BOM (LED, photodiode, op-amp, Arduino Nano, total under $30) and pin the exact firmware commit they used. To validate it, they run 20 samples of known chlorophyll concentration through both their device and a lab spectrophotometer: the regression against the reference gives R-squared 0.97, and a Bland-Altman plot shows the two instruments agree within ±0.8 micrograms/L across the tested range with no trend at high concentrations. They determine limit of detection from 10 blank readings: 3 times the blank standard deviation divided by their calibration slope gives roughly 0.3 micrograms/L, below which they do not trust a reading.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'how do you know your open-source build actually works, not just that it turns on?' because a 3D-printed instrument that looks impressive can still be scientifically worthless without validation. A weak answer points to the device lighting up or producing a plausible-looking number. A strong answer describes running known samples or a reference instrument alongside it, reports a real agreement statistic like R-squared or Bland-Altman limits of agreement rather than 'it matched pretty well,' and states a limit of detection so it is clear what range of results can actually be trusted.

questions.prompt: What does a Bland-Altman analysis show that a simple R-squared correlation does not?

options.text: Whether the two instruments' readings are correlated at all
The actual difference between the two instruments across their measurement range, revealing biases a correlation can hide
The exact firmware version used to collect the data
The bill of materials cost of each instrument

explanations.a: Correlation is what R-squared already measures; Bland-Altman goes further by examining the actual differences.
explanations.b: Correct — Bland-Altman plots the difference between paired measurements against their mean, which can reveal a bias that grows or shrinks across the range even when R-squared looks high, since strong correlation does not guarantee good agreement.
explanations.c: Firmware versioning is a reproducibility practice, unrelated to what a Bland-Altman statistical plot shows.
explanations.d: Bill of materials cost is documentation for rebuilding the device, not a statistical agreement measure.

questions.prompt: Why does a validation paper for an open-source instrument need to pin the exact firmware version used to produce its results?

options.text: Because firmware version numbers are required by journal formatting rules
Because a different firmware build could change measurement behavior, so an unpinned version makes another lab's rebuild a different, unverified instrument
Because firmware cannot be open-sourced without a version number
Because it has no real effect on reproducibility, it is purely a courtesy

explanations.a: This is not a formatting convention; it directly affects whether results can be trusted as reproducible.
explanations.b: Correct — firmware controls timing, calibration constants, and processing logic; without pinning the exact version, a rebuild running different code is not truly the same validated instrument.
explanations.c: Open-sourcing and versioning are separate concerns; code can be open without being version-pinned, which is exactly the reproducibility gap this practice closes.
explanations.d: It has a direct, not cosmetic, effect: differing firmware can silently change calibration or timing behavior.

questions.prompt: Match each open-source instrument to what it primarily measures or does.

right.text: Absorbance/concentration from an LED and photodiode pair
Automated, motorized sample positioning and focus for microscopy
Emission/absorbance spectra from a webcam and diffraction grating

questions.explanation: A colorimeter/photometer measures light absorbance with an LED-photodiode pair; the OpenFlexure microscope (Collins et al., 2020) provides robotic, motorized sample positioning and autofocus; Public Lab's spectrometer kits use a webcam and diffraction grating to capture spectra for citizen science.

questions.prompt: Order these steps in validating a homemade colorimeter against a reference spectrophotometer.

items.text: Prepare samples of known concentration
Measure each sample on both the homemade device and the reference instrument
Compute regression R-squared and a Bland-Altman limits-of-agreement plot
Determine limit of detection from repeated blank measurements

questions.explanation: You first need known samples to measure, then paired readings from both instruments to compare, then statistical agreement analysis on those paired readings, and finally a separate blank-measurement step to establish the smallest reliably detectable signal.

lessons.label: Closed-Loop Control on a Microcontroller

sections.heading: PID on a fixed sample interval
sections.body: A microcontroller implements PID control in discrete time: at each fixed sample interval it reads the sensor, computes error e[n] = setpoint minus measurement, and outputs u[n] = Kp*e[n] + Ki*sum(e)*dt + Kd*(e[n]-e[n-1])/dt. Unlike an analog PID circuit, this loop only runs as often as the timer interrupt fires, so the sample interval itself is a design choice — too slow and the controller cannot react to fast disturbances; too fast and the derivative term amplifies sensor noise into jittery output. The integral term is a running sum, which creates a specific failure mode: if the actuator saturates (a heater already at 100% duty, unable to add more heat) while error is still positive, the integral keeps accumulating — integral windup — and the controller overshoots badly once it finally starts responding. The fix is anti-windup clamping: freeze or clamp the integral accumulator whenever the output is already saturated.

sections.heading: Derivative filtering and actuator saturation
sections.body: The derivative term is the most fragile part of a digital PID loop because it amplifies whatever noise rides on the sensor signal — a thermistor reading with 0.1 degree of ADC quantization noise, differenced sample to sample, can dominate the output. The standard fix is a low-pass filter on the derivative term (or on the measurement itself before differencing), trading a small amount of responsiveness for a controller that does not chatter. On the output side, real actuators saturate: a heater's PWM duty cycle cannot exceed 100%, a motor driver cannot exceed its supply voltage. The controller output must be clamped to the actuator's real range before it is applied, and that same clamp state is exactly what the anti-windup logic needs to watch.

sections.heading: Tuning, jitter, and where control theory hands off
sections.body: Ziegler and Nichols (1942) published the classic tuning method still taught today: push the loop to sustained oscillation with proportional-only control to find the ultimate gain and oscillation period, then apply published ratios to get starting Kp, Ki, Kd values. It is fast but often produces an aggressive, overshoot-prone loop, which is why many practicing engineers instead hand-tune from those starting values by watching the step response and adjusting one term at a time. A subtlety specific to embedded systems: loop jitter — the sample interval varying because of interrupts, other tasks, or a non-real-time scheduler — corrupts the derivative term specifically, since it divides by dt; an inconsistent dt turns a stable derivative gain into an unpredictable one, even though Kp and the integral sum are far less sensitive to the same jitter. Beyond a single-actuator loop like this, multi-axis, multi-loop, and model-based control belongs to the deeper robotics-control-systems material.

lessons.workedExample: A student builds a PID temperature controller for an incubator: a thermistor feeds a 10-bit ADC, a resistive heater is driven by PWM, and the control loop runs on a 500ms timer interrupt. Using Ziegler-Nichols, they find the ultimate gain Ku=8 and oscillation period Tu=40s with proportional-only control, giving starting values Kp=4.8, Ki=0.24, Kd=24 from the standard PID ratios. The raw derivative term chatters because of ADC noise, so they add a single-pole low-pass filter on the temperature reading before differencing. When the heater saturates at 100% duty during warm-up, they clamp the integral accumulator to stop windup, cutting overshoot from 4°C to under 1°C. They log the actual loop interval and find it varies by ±15ms due to an SD-card write blocking the main loop — enough jitter to visibly roughen the derivative term until they move logging off the control task.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes PID tuning because 'I used a PID library' is not an answer, and a controller that oscillates or overshoots in the demo gives away that the student never diagnosed why. A weak answer cannot explain what each of Kp, Ki, Kd does or why their loop overshoots. A strong answer names their tuning method (even simple Ziegler-Nichols starting values), explains a windup or noise problem they actually hit and how they fixed it (clamping, filtering), and — if their control loop shares a processor with logging or networking — can say whether they checked for loop jitter and what it did to their derivative term.

questions.prompt: Why does integral windup occur, and what is the standard fix?

options.text: It occurs because the derivative term divides by a very small dt; fixed by increasing the sample interval
It occurs because the integral term keeps accumulating error while the actuator is saturated and cannot respond further; fixed by clamping the integral accumulator when the output is saturated
It occurs because Kp is set too low; fixed by raising Kp
It occurs only in analog PID circuits, not digital ones

explanations.a: That describes the derivative-noise problem, not integral windup, which is a separate failure mode tied to the integral term and actuator saturation.
explanations.b: Correct — while the actuator is pinned at its limit, remaining error keeps adding to the integral sum, so once the actuator can respond again the controller badly overshoots; anti-windup clamping halts accumulation during saturation.
explanations.c: Raising Kp does not address the accumulation happening in the integral term during saturation; it can make overshoot worse.
explanations.d: Integral windup is a general PID phenomenon; discrete digital implementations are if anything more prone to it because the integral is an explicit running sum.

questions.prompt: Why does loop jitter (a varying sample interval) corrupt the derivative term more than the proportional or integral terms?

options.text: The derivative calculation divides the error change by dt, so an inconsistent dt directly distorts the computed rate of change
The proportional term also divides by dt, so all three terms are equally affected
Loop jitter only affects the actuator's PWM output, not any PID term
The integral term is the most sensitive to jitter because it is a running sum

explanations.a: Correct — the derivative term is (e[n]-e[n-1])/dt; if dt varies unpredictably from one sample to the next, the same error change produces a different, noisy derivative estimate.
explanations.b: The proportional term Kp*e[n] does not involve dt at all, so jitter does not directly distort it.
explanations.c: Jitter's direct mathematical effect is on the derivative calculation itself, before it ever reaches the actuator.
explanations.d: The integral term does use dt (multiplying the running sum by dt), but a varying dt changes its accumulation only gradually, not the sharp per-sample distortion the derivative suffers.

questions.prompt: Order the Ziegler-Nichols (1942) closed-loop tuning procedure.

items.text: Run the loop with proportional-only control (Ki=Kd=0)
Increase Kp until the output sustains steady oscillation
Record the ultimate gain Ku and oscillation period Tu
Apply the published Ziegler-Nichols ratios to compute starting Kp, Ki, Kd

questions.explanation: The method starts proportional-only, raises gain until sustained oscillation appears, records the gain and period at that oscillation point, and only then converts those two numbers into starting PID gains via the published ratio table.

questions.prompt: Why must a controller's computed output be clamped to the actuator's real range (for example, 0-100% PWM duty) before it is applied?

options.text: Because the PID math can compute an output beyond what the actuator can physically produce, and applying an unclamped value risks both incorrect behavior and windup
Because clamping improves the derivative term's noise filtering
Because Ziegler-Nichols tuning requires clamped output by definition
It is unnecessary; PID output is always naturally within the actuator's range

explanations.a: Correct — nothing in the PID formula inherently limits u[n] to 0-100%; a large error can compute a duty cycle far outside what the actuator can do, and that saturation state is exactly what anti-windup logic needs to detect.
explanations.b: Clamping the output range and filtering the derivative term address two different problems: actuator limits versus sensor noise.
explanations.c: Ziegler-Nichols tuning determines gains; it says nothing about output clamping, which is a separate implementation necessity.
explanations.d: PID output can easily exceed actuator limits, especially right after a large setpoint change, which is precisely why saturation and windup are real concerns.

lessons.label: Wireless Sensor Nodes and the Energy Budget

sections.heading: BLE, LoRa, and Wi-Fi are different trades, not tiers
sections.body: The three common radios for a battery-powered sensor node trade range, throughput, and current draw against each other in opposite directions. Bluetooth Low Energy covers tens of meters at hundreds of kbps and draws roughly single-digit to low-teens milliamps during a short transmit burst, then drops to microamp-level sleep current between connections — built for frequent, nearby, low-latency exchanges like a phone syncing a sensor reading. LoRa trades throughput for range: a few hundred bits per second up to tens of kbps, but kilometers of range in open terrain using chirp spread-spectrum modulation, at the cost of a transmit burst that can pull tens to over a hundred milliamps for a longer time-on-air. Wi-Fi is the throughput winner (megabits per second) but the power hog: joining a network and holding a TCP/IP stack open commonly draws well over a hundred milliamps during transmission, which makes it a poor default for a node that has to survive weeks on a coin cell or small LiPo.

sections.heading: Duty cycling and the mAh arithmetic
sections.body: None of these radios matter as much as how often the node wakes up. A node that samples and transmits once every 10 minutes but sleeps at a few microamps in between spends the overwhelming majority of its energy budget asleep, so average current is dominated by (duty fraction) times (active current) plus the sleep floor. The arithmetic that decides whether a deployment survives: battery capacity in mAh divided by average current in mA gives runtime in hours. A 2000mAh battery drawing an average of 0.5mA (mostly sleep, with brief LoRa bursts) lasts roughly 4000 hours, about 5-6 months; the same battery averaging 5mA from a chattier Wi-Fi duty cycle lasts roughly 400 hours, barely more than two weeks — a 10x difference driven entirely by how the radio and sleep schedule were chosen, not by battery size.

sections.heading: Packet loss and integrity for a node nobody can reach
sections.body: A remote node will lose packets to interference, range, or a receiver briefly offline, so a naive fire-and-forget send silently drops data. Store-and-forward buffering — logging each reading locally and only clearing it from the buffer once the gateway acknowledges receipt — trades a small amount of flash for guaranteed eventual delivery, and is standard practice for any unattended deployment. The same physical inaccessibility raises a security requirement: a node buried in a field or bolted to a pole cannot be walked back to a bench if its firmware is compromised, so over-the-air firmware updates need cryptographic signature verification before the new image is accepted, and ideally a secure-boot chain that refuses to run unsigned code at all — without it, a single malicious or corrupted OTA update can permanently brick or hijack every unreachable node in the field.

lessons.workedExample: A student deploys a soil-moisture node in a school garden, transmitting once every 15 minutes over LoRa to a receiver 400m away. Active current during the ~200ms transmit burst is 90mA; sleep current between bursts is 2 microamps. Average current works out to roughly (90mA * 0.2s + 0.002mA * 899.8s) / 900s, dominated by the tiny sleep term plus a small transmit contribution, landing near 0.022mA. On a 2000mAh battery that predicts over 90,000 hours — clearly bottlenecked by battery self-discharge, not the radio, so the design easily covers a multi-week science-fair deployment. The student adds a 200-reading local flash buffer so a missed gateway acknowledgment doesn't lose data, and confirms the node's OTA update path rejects an unsigned firmware image before accepting it.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'how long does your node actually run on that battery, and how do you know?' because 'we used a big battery' is not an energy budget. A weak answer has no current measurements and guesses at battery life. A strong answer states measured (not just datasheet) active and sleep currents, shows the duty-cycle arithmetic converting those into an average current and then a runtime estimate, and can explain what happens to a reading if a transmission is lost mid-deployment — showing they engineered for the radio being unreachable, not just for it working in the demo.

questions.prompt: A remote sensor node's average current is dominated by which factor in a well-designed duty-cycled deployment?

options.text: The peak transmit current of the radio, since it is the largest single number
The sleep current and how large a fraction of time the node spends asleep
The battery's rated capacity in mAh alone
The microcontroller's clock speed while asleep

explanations.a: Peak transmit current is large but brief; over a long duty cycle it contributes only a small fraction of the total energy compared to how long the node sleeps.
explanations.b: Correct — because the node spends the overwhelming majority of time asleep at microamp-level current, that sleep current and the duty fraction dominate the average current calculation, not the brief active bursts.
explanations.c: Battery capacity sets how long a given average current can be sustained, but it does not itself determine what that average current is.
explanations.d: A sleeping microcontroller is not running at its clock speed; sleep current is largely independent of the active clock speed.

questions.prompt: Why is Wi-Fi generally a poor choice for a sensor node that must run unattended for weeks on a small battery?

options.text: Wi-Fi cannot transmit sensor data, only large files
Wi-Fi's transmit current draw is typically well over a hundred milliamps, far higher than BLE or LoRa bursts, draining a small battery much faster
Wi-Fi has no range limitations, so it wastes power reaching unnecessary distances
Wi-Fi cannot be duty-cycled at all

explanations.a: Wi-Fi transmits any data type, including small sensor payloads; the issue is power, not data type.
explanations.b: Correct — joining a network and holding a TCP/IP stack open during transmission draws well over a hundred milliamps for Wi-Fi radios, several times higher than a BLE or LoRa transmit burst, which shortens battery life dramatically at the same duty cycle.
explanations.c: Wi-Fi in fact has a shorter typical range (tens of meters) than LoRa, not an unlimited one; that is not the reason it drains batteries faster.
explanations.d: Wi-Fi radios can be duty-cycled, but even duty-cycled, their active-current cost per transmission is much higher than BLE or LoRa.

questions.prompt: Match each radio technology to its defining tradeoff for a battery-powered sensor node.

right.text: Tens of meters range, hundreds of kbps, low active current for frequent nearby exchanges
Kilometers of range, low throughput, longer transmit bursts drawing tens to over a hundred milliamps
Highest throughput, short indoor range comparable to BLE (shorter than LoRa), highest transmit current draw

questions.explanation: BLE favors frequent, nearby, low-power exchanges; LoRa trades throughput for long range with a higher but time-limited transmit current; Wi-Fi offers the most bandwidth but at the highest transmit current and a range shorter than LoRa's, making it the most power-hungry option of the three for an unattended node.

questions.prompt: Why does an unreachable field-deployed node need secure-boot verification for firmware updates?

options.text: Because it improves the radio's transmit range
Because a corrupted or malicious OTA update cannot be fixed by physically walking to the node and reflashing it by hand
Because secure boot reduces the node's average current draw
It is only needed for Wi-Fi nodes, not LoRa or BLE nodes

explanations.a: Secure boot is a firmware-integrity mechanism with no effect on radio range or RF performance.
explanations.b: Correct — since the node is physically inaccessible, an unsigned or corrupted firmware update accepted over the air could permanently disable or compromise it, with no easy way to recover by hand; verifying signatures before accepting new firmware prevents that.
explanations.c: Secure boot checks firmware authenticity; it does not directly affect sleep or transmit current.
explanations.d: The physical-inaccessibility risk applies regardless of which radio the node uses; any unattended node accepting OTA updates needs this protection.

lessons.label: Presenting an Embedded Project to Judges

sections.heading: Bring evidence, not just the working device
sections.body: A demo that runs on the table proves the project works right now, in that room, for that one run — it proves almost nothing about how it was engineered. Judges are trained to look past the demo for evidence of a real process: a schematic showing the actual circuit (not a photo of a breadboard), a logic-analyzer or oscilloscope capture showing what the signals actually looked like on real hardware (an I2C bus trace, a PWM duty cycle, a UART frame), and — for any measurement claim — a calibration curve plotting the device's output against a reference instrument across the tested range, with error bars from multiple repeated runs rather than a single number presented as fact. A single run tells you nothing about the device's repeatability; three to five repeated trials with visible spread is the minimum that lets anyone judge whether a result is real or noise.

sections.heading: Document conditions, and defend timing claims with data
sections.body: Every result needs its conditions attached: which firmware version produced it (a commit hash or tagged release, matching the reproducibility standard used by published open instruments), what the test setup was, and under what environmental conditions (temperature, humidity, battery state) it was collected. Timing claims are a specific trap: a datasheet number like '2ms conversion time' describes the part under ideal conditions, not your system with interrupts, other tasks, and bus contention competing for the same processor. A credible timing claim is measured — a logic analyzer or a toggled GPIO pin captured on a scope showing the actual worst-case latency observed across many trials — not copied from a datasheet and presented as what the finished system does.

sections.heading: Safety, and the questions judges reliably ask
sections.body: Any project with a battery or mains-adjacent circuit should be able to state basic safety practice: correct battery chemistry handling (no puncturing or shorting LiPo cells), fusing or current limiting on anything driving a heater or motor, and isolation from mains voltage if any part of the build goes near it. Judges consistently return to three questions regardless of project topic: why this sensor and not an alternative (forcing the student to justify range, resolution, and cost tradeoffs rather than 'it's what we had'), what is your uncertainty (forcing a real error-budget or calibration-curve answer, not a vague 'pretty accurate'), and what fails first (forcing the student to have actually stress-tested the system rather than only ever run it under ideal conditions).

lessons.workedExample: A student presenting a heater-control project brings: a hand-drawn schematic of the thermistor divider and MOSFET driver stage, a scope capture showing the PWM output at 1kHz with measured rise time, a calibration curve of their thermistor reading against a lab thermometer across 20-80°C (slope 0.98, R-squared 0.995, from five repeated runs with visible error bars), and a note pinning the firmware to a specific git commit. When a judge asks about their control loop's timing, instead of quoting the microcontroller's datasheet interrupt latency, they show a logic-analyzer capture of 200 loop iterations with the measured worst-case jitter (18ms) and explain that an SD-card write occasionally blocked the control loop, which they identified from that exact data.
lessons.judgeFraming: This lesson describes the standard the rest of the unit builds toward, which is why judges probe it directly rather than accepting a working demo at face value: a project that only demonstrates behavior, without a schematic, calibration data, or measured (not datasheet) timing, cannot be distinguished from one that got lucky once. A weak presentation has a working device and confident verbal claims with no data behind them. A strong presentation has a small stack of evidence — schematic, a scope or logic-analyzer capture, a calibration curve with error bars, and a documented firmware version — and can answer 'what fails first' with a specific, tested failure mode rather than 'I don't know, it hasn't failed yet.'

questions.prompt: Why is a datasheet timing number (e.g., a sensor's rated conversion time) not sufficient evidence for a timing claim about a finished embedded system?

options.text: Datasheet numbers are always wrong and should never be cited
The datasheet describes the part under ideal conditions, while the real system has interrupts, other tasks, and bus contention that can add latency the datasheet does not capture
Datasheets do not contain any timing information
Judges are not allowed to ask about timing

explanations.a: Datasheet numbers are accurate for the part in isolation; the issue is that they do not reflect the full system's behavior, not that they are wrong.
explanations.b: Correct — a real embedded system shares its processor and buses with other tasks, so the worst-case latency actually observed in the finished system can differ substantially from an isolated-part datasheet figure, which is why a measured capture is the credible evidence.
explanations.c: Datasheets commonly do contain timing specs; the problem is what those specs do and do not represent about the assembled system.
explanations.d: Timing questions are one of the standard categories judges are described as probing in this lesson.

questions.prompt: Why should a measurement claim be backed by error bars from multiple repeated trials rather than a single run?

options.text: A single run cannot reveal whether a result is repeatable or was just noise that time
Repeated trials are only needed if the first run looked wrong
Error bars are a formatting convention with no scientific purpose
A single clean-looking run is always more trustworthy than an average of several runs

explanations.a: Correct — one run cannot distinguish a genuine, repeatable result from a lucky or unlucky single measurement; repeated trials with visible spread let a judge assess actual repeatability.
explanations.b: Repeated trials matter regardless of whether the first run looks correct, since a single good-looking result can still be an outlier.
explanations.c: Error bars convey run-to-run variability, a real property of the measurement process, not just a presentation style.
explanations.d: A single run, however clean-looking, provides no information about variability and is less trustworthy than an averaged, repeated measurement.

questions.prompt: Match each type of evidence a project should bring to what it demonstrates.

right.text: The actual designed circuit, not a photo of wiring
What signals actually looked like on real hardware, not an assumed value
How well the device's output agrees with a reference instrument, across repeated runs

questions.explanation: A schematic documents the intended circuit design, a logic-analyzer or scope capture documents observed real-hardware signal behavior, and a calibration curve with error bars documents measured agreement with a reference across repeated trials.

questions.prompt: Order these steps for building a measured (not datasheet-based) timing claim about a control loop.

items.text: Instrument the loop (e.g., toggle a GPIO pin or use a logic analyzer)
Run many loop iterations under realistic operating conditions
Capture and record the actual timing across all iterations
Report the measured worst-case jitter or latency, not the datasheet figure

questions.explanation: You first add a way to observe timing, then run enough iterations under real conditions to expose actual behavior, then capture that timing data, and only then can you report a measured worst-case figure instead of an idealized datasheet number.

units.label: Power Conversion Foundations

lessons.label: What Power Electronics Actually Converts

sections.heading: Four classes, one job: reshaping electrical power
sections.body: Power electronics converts electrical power from one form to another using switching devices rather than continuous linear control. Four canonical classes cover essentially all conversions: AC-DC (rectifiers, from a wall adapter's bridge rectifier to a utility-scale HVDC converter station), DC-DC (buck, boost, buck-boost, and resonant converters that step a battery or bus voltage up or down), DC-AC (inverters, from a solar microinverter's grid-tied output to a motor drive's variable-frequency output), and AC-AC (cycloconverters and AC voltage controllers, like a triac lamp dimmer or a soft-starter that chops the mains waveform directly). Real systems chain several of these stages together.

sections.heading: The switch-inductor-capacitor triad
sections.body: All four classes are built from the same three components used differently: a switch (MOSFET, IGBT, diode, or thyristor) that connects or disconnects energy flow in microseconds, an inductor that stores energy in its magnetic field and enforces continuous current, and a capacitor that stores energy in its electric field and enforces continuous voltage. A buck converter's switch chops a DC bus; the inductor and capacitor low-pass filter the chopped waveform into a smooth lower DC voltage. An inverter's switches synthesize an AC waveform from a DC bus using pulse-width modulation, with an output LC filter smoothing the switched edges toward a sine wave. Swap which quantity you hold constant and which you chop, and the same triad produces any of the four conversions.

sections.heading: Why switching beats dissipating
sections.body: A closed ideal switch has zero voltage across it; an open ideal switch has zero current through it. In both states the instantaneous power V times I is zero, so an ideal switch dissipates nothing regardless of how much power flows through it. A linear regulator, by contrast, holds its pass transistor partially on, dropping real voltage while carrying real current continuously -- that product is heat. Real switches have finite on-resistance and finite switching time, so they do dissipate some power, but far less than a device forced to linger in its lossy middle region.

sections.heading: Newell's 1973 cube
sections.body: In "Power Electronics -- Emerging from Limbo," presented at the IEEE Power Electronics Specialists Conference in 1973, William E. Newell proposed the field's founding definition: power electronics sits at the intersection of three older disciplines -- power (energy, machines), electronics (semiconductor devices), and control (feedback, stability) -- visualized as three axes meeting at a cube. The framing stuck because it explains why the field needs all three: a converter is simultaneously a power-handling system, a semiconductor circuit, and a closed-loop regulator.

lessons.workedExample: A 65 W USB-C laptop charger illustrates the whole chain end to end. Mains power (100-240 Vac) first passes through an AC-DC stage: a diode bridge rectifier plus a power-factor-correction boost converter produces a roughly 380 V DC bus. That bus feeds a DC-DC stage -- commonly an LLC resonant half-bridge switching around 100 kHz -- whose MOSFETs chop the 380 V into a high-frequency AC waveform for a small ferrite transformer, which is then rectified and filtered down to the regulated 20 V, 3.25 A output the laptop expects. Every stage uses the switch-inductor-capacitor triad. Notice there's no dropper resistor anywhere -- a resistive 380 V-to-20 V drop at 3.25 A would need to dissipate over 1 kW.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask 'which conversion class is this, and why not just use a resistor or a pot?' because it tests whether a student understands mechanism or is pattern-matching a datasheet. A strong answer names the correct class (DC-DC, AC-DC, and so on), points to the actual switch-inductor-capacitor elements in their schematic, and explains that the switch's near-zero V-times-I product in both states is what keeps efficiency high -- not 'because it's digital.' A weak answer says a chip 'regulates the voltage' without naming what element stores energy between switching events, or claims switching is efficient because it's newer technology rather than because of the V-times-I argument.

questions.prompt: Why does an ideal switch dissipate essentially no power in either of its two states?

options.text: Because it switches too fast for heat to build up
Because voltage across it is zero when closed and current through it is zero when open, so V times I is zero both ways
Because switches are made of semiconductor rather than resistive material
Because it only handles AC, not DC, power

explanations.a: Speed doesn't eliminate dissipation by itself; real switches do have finite switching-transition losses precisely because they aren't instantaneous.
explanations.b: Correct -- with zero voltage across the closed switch and zero current through the open switch, the instantaneous power product V times I is zero in both operating states.
explanations.c: Material alone doesn't explain it; a resistor is also semiconductor-adjacent in some forms but still dissipates power continuously under load.
explanations.d: Switches handle both AC and DC power flow; the dissipation argument is about voltage/current states, not waveform type.

questions.prompt: In William E. Newell's 1973 framing, power electronics sits at the intersection of which three domains?

options.text: Power, electronics, and control
Power, thermal, and mechanical design
Electronics, software, and control
Power, electronics, and economics

explanations.a: Correct -- Newell's cube places power electronics at the intersection of power (energy/machines), electronics (semiconductor devices), and control (feedback/stability).
explanations.b: Thermal and mechanical design are real engineering concerns for converters but are not the three axes Newell named.
explanations.c: Software wasn't one of Newell's three axes; control (feedback and stability) was, which predates the software-control framing.
explanations.d: Economics is a project constraint, not one of the three founding disciplines Newell identified.

questions.prompt: Match each conversion class to a real example device.

right.text: Bridge rectifier plus PFC boost stage in a wall charger
LLC resonant half-bridge stepping down a 380 V bus
Solar microinverter producing grid-tied output
Triac lamp dimmer chopping the mains waveform

questions.explanation: AC-DC conversion is exemplified by a bridge rectifier plus PFC boost; DC-DC by an LLC resonant stage stepping a DC bus down; DC-AC by a solar microinverter; and AC-AC by a triac dimmer that chops the mains waveform directly without an intermediate DC bus.

questions.prompt: Order the energy-flow stages in the 65 W laptop charger worked example, from mains input to regulated output.

items.text: AC mains input (100-240 Vac)
Bridge rectifier plus PFC boost produces a roughly 380 V DC bus
LLC resonant half-bridge chops the bus into high-frequency AC for a ferrite transformer
Output rectifier and filter produce the regulated 20 V DC output

questions.explanation: Energy flows from raw mains through rectification and power-factor correction to a DC bus, then through a resonant DC-DC stage that chops the bus for the transformer, and finally through an output rectifier and filter to reach the regulated low-voltage DC the laptop expects.

lessons.label: Power, Energy, and the Efficiency Budget

sections.heading: Instantaneous power vs average power
sections.body: Instantaneous power is p(t) = v(t) times i(t) at a single moment; it swings wildly in a switching converter because the switch current is a train of pulses, not a smooth trickle. What actually matters for heat, battery drain, and thermal design is average power, P = the integral of p(t) over one period divided by the period T. A switch might carry 5 A peak current for only 20% of each cycle and 0 A the rest of the time -- the average delivered current is nowhere near the peak, and confusing the two is a common source of undersized or wildly oversized component choices.

sections.heading: RMS: why the mean isn't enough for heating
sections.body: Resistive heating and current ratings depend on I squared R, not on I itself, so a pulsed waveform's heating effect is captured by its RMS (root-mean-square) value, not its arithmetic mean. A capacitor's ripple-current rating, a wire's ampacity, and a diode's power dissipation are all specified against RMS current precisely because a narrow, tall current pulse can have a modest mean but a much larger RMS -- and it's the RMS value that predicts the temperature rise. Datasheets that quote 'ripple current (RMS)' are telling you which number to actually use.

sections.heading: The efficiency budget
sections.body: Efficiency is defined as eta = Pout / Pin, and the power lost to heat is Ploss = Pin - Pout. Rearranging, Ploss = Pout times (1 - eta) / eta, which shows the loss grows nonlinearly as eta drops -- near 100% efficiency, small percentage-point changes swing the absolute heat dissipated by a large relative amount, which is why converter designers chase the last few points of efficiency so aggressively even when the percentage gain looks small on paper.

sections.heading: Power density: the second axis
sections.body: Efficiency alone doesn't judge a converter -- power density, measured in watts per cubic inch, is the other axis every real design trades against. The Little Box Challenge, run by Google and the IEEE Power Electronics Society from 2014 to 2016, offered a $1 million prize to entrants who could build a 2 kW, 120/240 Vac split-phase inverter at 50 W/in^3 -- roughly ten times denser than commercial inverters of that era -- which forced competitors toward wide-bandgap devices and aggressive thermal design. Density and efficiency often pull against each other: shrinking passives usually means raising switching frequency, which raises switching loss.

lessons.workedExample: A 50 W DC-DC converter is redesigned to raise efficiency from 90% to 95%. At 90%, Pin = Pout / eta = 50 / 0.90 = 55.6 W, so Ploss = 55.6 - 50 = 5.6 W. At 95%, Pin = 50 / 0.95 = 52.6 W, so Ploss = 52.6 - 50 = 2.6 W. A five-point efficiency gain that looks small on a datasheet more than halves the dissipated heat, from 5.6 W to 2.6 W. That difference can be the gap between needing a heatsink and not, or between hitting a target power density and missing it, because the smaller heat load lets the enclosure shrink.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe efficiency because 'my converter is efficient' is a claim anyone can make, but 'at 50 W out, raising eta from 90% to 95% cuts my dissipation from 5.6 W to 2.6 W, which is why I could drop the heatsink' is a claim only someone who did the arithmetic can make. A strong answer produces the eta = Pout/Pin relationship from memory and applies it to their own numbers; a weak answer cites a headline efficiency percentage from a datasheet without connecting it to the actual heat their enclosure has to shed or the power density they were chasing.

questions.prompt: A converter delivers 50 W of output at 95% efficiency. Approximately how much power is dissipated as loss?

explanations.a: This understates the loss; Pin = 50/0.95 = 52.6 W, so Ploss = 2.6 W, not 0.5 W.
explanations.b: Correct -- Pin = Pout/eta = 50/0.95 = 52.6 W, so Ploss = Pin - Pout = 2.6 W.
explanations.c: 5.6 W is the loss at 90% efficiency for the same 50 W output, not at 95%.
explanations.d: That would mean zero output power delivered, which contradicts the given 50 W output.

questions.prompt: Why do capacitor ripple-current ratings and wire ampacity specs use RMS current rather than average current?

options.text: RMS is always numerically larger, so it's a safety margin convention
Resistive heating depends on I squared R, and RMS is the current value that correctly predicts that heating for a pulsed waveform
Average current is harder to measure with standard instruments
RMS and average are identical for any waveform, so it doesn't matter which is used

explanations.a: RMS isn't just a padded average -- it's the specific quantity that maps directly to I-squared-R heating, not an arbitrary margin.
explanations.b: Correct -- heating follows I squared R, and only the RMS value of a pulsed current correctly represents its heating effect, which can be much larger than the arithmetic mean for narrow pulses.
explanations.c: Both average and RMS current are readily measurable with standard meters; measurement difficulty isn't the reason for the convention.
explanations.d: RMS and average are only equal for a constant (DC) waveform; for pulsed or AC waveforms they differ substantially, which is exactly why the distinction matters.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

right.text: v(t) times i(t) evaluated at a single moment in time
The integral of instantaneous power over one period, divided by the period
The current value that correctly predicts I-squared-R heating for a pulsed or AC waveform
Delivered power divided by converter volume, in watts per cubic inch

questions.explanation: Instantaneous power is the single-moment V-times-I product; average power integrates that over a full period; RMS current is the value that correctly predicts heating for non-constant waveforms; power density expresses output power per unit converter volume.

questions.prompt: The Little Box Challenge (Google/IEEE, 2014-2016) targeted what power density for its 2 kW inverter?

options.text: 5 W/in^3

explanations.a: 5 W/in^3 was closer to typical commercial inverter density at the time, not the challenge's target.
explanations.b: Correct -- the Little Box Challenge target was 50 W/in^3, roughly ten times denser than commercial inverters of that era.
explanations.c: 500 W/in^3 overstates the target by a full order of magnitude.
explanations.d: 0.5 W/in^3 is far too low to have been a stretch target for the competition.

lessons.label: Linear Regulators and Their Hard Ceiling

sections.heading: Series-pass regulation: a variable resistor in the path
sections.body: A linear regulator holds a pass transistor between input and output, with an error amplifier comparing a sampled fraction of Vout to a reference and adjusting the transistor's conduction to hold Vout constant as load or Vin changes. Robert Widlar's uA723, introduced at Fairchild in 1967, was one of the first widely used integrated regulators built on exactly this principle, and the topology hasn't fundamentally changed since: the pass device behaves like a voltage-controlled resistor, continuously absorbing whatever voltage the load doesn't need.

sections.heading: Dropout, quiescent current, and PSRR
sections.body: Three numbers define a regulator's real-world behavior. Dropout voltage is the minimum Vin-Vout headroom the pass device needs before it can no longer regulate; a standard bipolar regulator might need 2 V of headroom, while a low-dropout (LDO) part built around a PMOS or PNP pass device can regulate with as little as 0.1-0.3 V.
