Quiescent current, Iq, is what the regulator itself consumes regardless of load -- critical in battery-powered designs, where modern LDOs draw only microamps. PSRR (power supply rejection ratio) measures, in decibels, how well the regulator suppresses ripple or noise arriving on Vin before it reaches Vout; a good LDO might offer 60-70 dB of rejection at low frequency.

sections.heading: The unavoidable ceiling: eta approximately equals Vout/Vin
sections.body: Because the pass device carries the full load current while dropping the full Vin-Vout difference, Pin = Vin times I and Pout = Vout times I share the same current, so eta = Pout/Pin = Vout/Vin -- a hard ceiling no amount of clever design can raise. Stepping 12 V to 5 V can never exceed about 42% efficiency, no matter how well the regulator IC is built; the missing energy becomes heat in the pass device, full stop.

sections.heading: Where linear still wins
sections.body: Despite the ceiling, linear regulation is the right choice in specific cases: when Vin-Vout headroom is small (post-regulating a switcher's output by only a volt or two costs little), when the load needs an ultra-quiet, ripple-free rail (analog references, RF local oscillators, high-resolution ADC supplies), or when switching-frequency EMI is unacceptable near sensitive analog or RF circuitry. The noise numbers make the case concrete: a well-filtered buck converter typically still leaves 10-30 mV of switching ripple on its output, while a low-noise LDO such as Analog Devices' LT3045 holds output noise under 1 uVrms and delivers roughly 60 dB of PSRR out past several hundred kilohertz -- exactly the margin a 16-bit ADC reference or an RF local oscillator needs to hit its own noise floor. Quiescent current tells a similar story for battery gear: a modern nanopower LDO drawing under 1 uA leaves a coin-cell sensor's shelf-life budget almost untouched, while the switching losses and gate-drive overhead of even an efficient buck converter can dominate a design's sleep-mode current draw at that scale. A linear regulator has no switching harmonics to filter or shield against, which is often worth its efficiency penalty on a small, low-power rail.

lessons.workedExample: A student needs a clean 5 V, 1.2 A rail from a 12 V battery to feed an ADC reference. Using a linear regulator, eta = Vout/Vin = 5/12 = 41.7%, so Pout = 5 V times 1.2 A = 6 W and Pin = Pout/eta = 14.4 W, giving Ploss = 14.4 - 6 = 8.4 W dissipated in the regulator. A TO-220 package with no heatsink typically has a junction-to-ambient thermal resistance around 60-65 degC/W, which would push the junction temperature over 500 degC above ambient -- clearly impossible, meaning the design needs either a real heatsink capable of holding that resistance under roughly 10 degC/W, or a switching pre-regulator to knock 12 V down to, say, 6 V before the LDO takes over the last, cleaner volt of drop.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe the efficiency ceiling because it separates a student who chose a linear regulator for a defensible reason from one who grabbed whatever chip was in the parts bin. A strong answer computes eta = Vout/Vin for their own rail, states the resulting heat in watts, and explains the actual thermal plan (heatsink sizing or a pre-regulator) -- or argues the low-noise/no-EMI benefit justified the loss on a specific sensitive rail. A weak answer says 'the regulator gets warm' without a number, or claims linear regulators are simply less efficient without being able to say why the ceiling is Vout/Vin specifically.

questions.prompt: A linear regulator steps 9 V down to 5 V at 1 A. What is its theoretical maximum efficiency?

options.text: About 56%
About 90%
About 44%
100%, since linear regulators have no switching losses

explanations.a: Correct -- eta = Vout/Vin = 5/9 = 55.6%, roughly 56%, since Pout and Pin share the same load current.
explanations.b: 90% would require Vin far closer to Vout than 9 V is to 5 V; it isn't achievable by a series-pass linear regulator at this ratio.
explanations.c: 44% understates it; that figure is close to the 5V-from-12V case from the lesson, not the 9V-to-5V case asked here.
explanations.d: Linear regulators have no switching losses, but they still dissipate (Vin-Vout) times I continuously in the pass device, so 100% is never reached.

questions.prompt: What does PSRR (power supply rejection ratio) measure on a linear regulator?

options.text: How much current the regulator itself consumes with no load
The minimum input-to-output headroom required to stay in regulation
How well the regulator suppresses ripple or noise on Vin before it reaches Vout
The maximum output current the pass device can supply

explanations.a: That describes quiescent current (Iq), a separate specification from PSRR.
explanations.b: That describes dropout voltage, not PSRR.
explanations.c: Correct -- PSRR, in decibels, quantifies how much input ripple or noise is attenuated before appearing on the output.
explanations.d: That describes the regulator's current rating, not its ripple-rejection performance.

questions.prompt: Match each linear-regulator term to its meaning.

right.text: Minimum Vin-Vout headroom needed to stay in regulation
Current the regulator consumes regardless of load
Decibel measure of input-ripple rejection
The theoretical maximum efficiency of a series-pass regulator

questions.explanation: Dropout voltage is the minimum required headroom, quiescent current is the regulator's own no-load draw, PSRR quantifies ripple rejection in decibels, and Vout/Vin sets the hard efficiency ceiling of any series-pass linear regulator.

questions.prompt: Which scenario is the strongest justification for choosing a linear regulator over a switching converter?

options.text: Stepping a 24 V bus down to 3.3 V at 5 A
Supplying a low-noise analog reference just 1 V below an already-regulated rail
Maximizing battery runtime in a large voltage step-down
Minimizing enclosure heat in a high-current design

explanations.a: A large step-down at high current is exactly where the Vout/Vin ceiling makes a linear regulator wasteful and thermally impractical.
explanations.b: Correct -- a small headroom keeps Ploss = (Vin-Vout) times I small, and the linear regulator's lack of switching noise suits a sensitive analog reference.
explanations.c: Battery runtime favors high efficiency, which a large-ratio linear regulator cannot provide.
explanations.d: Minimizing heat in a high-current design favors switching conversion, not a linear regulator's continuous dissipation.

lessons.label: Rectifiers: Half-Wave, Full-Wave, and Bridge

sections.heading: Half-wave: one diode, half the waveform
sections.body: A half-wave rectifier passes only the half-cycle where the diode is forward biased, blocking the other half entirely. Into a resistive load with no filtering, the average (DC) output is Vavg = Vpk / pi (about 0.318 times Vpk), and the RMS output is Vrms = Vpk / 2. Because the diode conducts for only 180 degrees of every 360-degree cycle, the load current is idle half the time, which is why half-wave circuits are rare in real power supplies except for very light, cost-sensitive loads.

sections.heading: Full-wave center-tap and bridge: same average, different diode drop
sections.body: A center-tapped full-wave rectifier or a four-diode bridge rectifier both use the negative half-cycle instead of wasting it, doubling the average output to Vavg = 2 Vpk / pi (about 0.637 times Vpk), with Vrms = Vpk / sqrt(2) (about 0.707 times Vpk) -- the same RMS as the original sine wave, since every part of the waveform is now used. The difference between the two topologies is the diode drop: a center-tapped design routes current through only one diode at a time, while a bridge always routes current through two diodes in series, subtracting roughly 1.4 V (two silicon drops) from the output instead of 0.7 V, in exchange for not needing a center-tapped transformer.

sections.heading: Capacitor filtering narrows the conduction angle
sections.body: Adding a filter capacitor changes the picture: the diodes now conduct only in short bursts near each waveform peak, just long enough to recharge the capacitor before the next peak arrives, then stay off while the capacitor alone supplies the load. This narrow conduction angle means the diodes carry brief, high-amplitude current pulses to deliver the same average current a continuously conducting diode would. The peak-to-peak ripple can be estimated as Vpp is approximately I load times T divided by C, where T is the recharge interval (about 1/(2 f_line) for full-wave, 1/f_line for half-wave).

sections.heading: Crest factor and poor power factor
sections.body: Because the AC line current is drawn only in short pulses near the voltage peaks, its ratio of peak to RMS value -- the crest factor -- runs high, often 3 or more, and the resulting true power factor of an unimproved capacitor-input rectifier front end is typically only 0.5-0.65 even into a purely resistive-looking DC load, because power factor accounts for both phase displacement and harmonic distortion of the current. Standards such as IEC 61000-3-2 cap the harmonic current equipment above 75 W can draw from the mains, which is exactly why offline power supplies above that threshold are required to add an active power-factor-correction stage.

lessons.workedExample: A 12 V RMS transformer secondary feeds a full-wave bridge rectifier into a 1000 uF capacitor supplying a 15 ohm, roughly 1 A load at 60 Hz. Peak secondary voltage is 12 times 1.414 = 16.97 V; subtracting the bridge's two diode drops (about 1.4 V) gives a peak capacitor voltage near 15.6 V. With full-wave recharging every T = 1/(2 times 60) = 8.33 ms, the ripple estimate is Vpp = I times T / C = 1 A times 0.00833 s / 0.001 F = 8.3 V peak-to-peak -- more than half the peak voltage. Increasing the capacitor roughly 4.7x to 4700 uF drops that to about 1.8 V, showing why 1000 uF is undersized for this load and a much larger bulk capacitor is needed to hold ripple to a reasonable level.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe rectifier ripple and crest factor because the naive assumption -- 'a 12 Vac transformer feeds a 12 V supply' -- is wrong on two counts: the DC output is actually closer to Vpk (about 17 V before diode drops), and the diode current isn't a smooth trickle but a narrow, high-amplitude pulse near each peak. A strong answer computes an actual ripple estimate from Vpp = I T / C and can explain why the AC-side current is peaky (poor crest factor, poor power factor) rather than sinusoidal. A weak answer assumes the rectified DC voltage equals the AC RMS rating and has no ripple estimate at all.

questions.prompt: For an unfiltered full-wave rectified sine wave with peak voltage Vpk, what is the average (DC) output voltage?

options.text: Vpk / pi
2 Vpk / pi
Vpk / sqrt(2)
Vpk

explanations.a: Vpk/pi is the average for an unfiltered half-wave rectifier, which only uses one half-cycle, not full-wave.
explanations.b: Correct -- full-wave rectification uses both half-cycles, doubling the half-wave average to 2 Vpk/pi, about 0.637 times Vpk.
explanations.c: Vpk/sqrt(2) is the RMS value of the full-wave rectified output (and of the original sine wave), not its average.
explanations.d: Vpk is the peak value only, reached momentarily at each waveform crest, not the average over a full cycle.

questions.prompt: Why does a four-diode bridge rectifier drop more voltage than a center-tapped full-wave rectifier for the same peak input?

options.text: Bridge diodes are always a different, lossier diode type
The bridge routes load current through two diodes in series at any instant, while the center-tapped design uses only one
The bridge rectifies only half the waveform
The center-tapped design uses a larger filter capacitor by convention

explanations.a: Diode type isn't dictated by the topology; the same diodes could be used in either circuit.
explanations.b: Correct -- current always flows through two series diodes in a bridge, roughly doubling the diode drop to about 1.4 V versus 0.7 V for the single-diode path in a center-tapped design.
explanations.c: Both bridge and center-tapped topologies are full-wave; that isn't the source of the extra drop.
explanations.d: Filter capacitor sizing is an independent design choice, not a defining feature of either rectifier topology.

questions.prompt: Why is the true power factor of an unimproved capacitor-input rectifier front end typically only 0.5-0.65, even feeding a purely resistive DC load?

options.text: The transformer itself has poor magnetic coupling
The AC-side current is drawn in narrow, high-crest-factor pulses near the voltage peaks, which distorts it away from a sinusoid
Silicon diodes inherently shift current 90 degrees out of phase with voltage
Power factor only applies to inductive loads, so this figure must be a measurement error

explanations.a: Transformer coupling efficiency is a separate issue from the harmonic-distortion cause of poor power factor here.
explanations.b: Correct -- the capacitor only recharges near each peak, so line current is a narrow pulse train rather than a sinusoid, and that harmonic distortion drags power factor down even with no phase-shifting reactive load.
explanations.c: Diodes don't introduce a 90-degree phase shift; the poor power factor here comes from harmonic distortion, not reactive phase displacement.
explanations.d: Power factor accounts for harmonic distortion as well as phase displacement, so a distorted resistive-load current still produces a low power factor.

questions.prompt: Order the events of one AC line cycle for a capacitor-input bridge rectifier feeding a DC load.

items.text: Capacitor voltage exceeds the rectified AC input voltage, so both bridge diodes in that half-cycle's path are reverse biased and off
The capacitor alone supplies the load, discharging and its voltage slowly falling
The rising AC input voltage exceeds the falling capacitor voltage plus two diode drops, turning the conducting diode pair back on
A brief high-current pulse recharges the capacitor back up to near the new peak

questions.explanation: After the capacitor is charged near a peak, the diodes turn off while the capacitor alone feeds the load and its voltage sags; once the rising AC input again exceeds the sagging capacitor voltage by enough to forward-bias the diode pair, they conduct again in a short, high-amplitude pulse that recharges the capacitor toward the next peak.

lessons.label: Filtering, Ripple, and Hold-Up

sections.heading: C, LC, and pi filters
sections.body: A single bulk capacitor across a rectifier's output is the simplest filter -- it charges near each peak and coasts the load through the gap, as described in the previous lesson. An LC filter adds a series inductor before the capacitor, forming a second-order low-pass that attenuates ripple far more steeply for the same capacitance, because the inductor resists the rapid current changes the ripple represents. A pi filter (capacitor-inductor-capacitor) adds a second capacitor ahead of the inductor, giving an even steeper roll-off at the cost of an extra bulky, lossy component; it shows up where ripple specs are tight and board space allows it, such as linear audio amplifier supplies.

sections.heading: ESR and ESL: the capacitor isn't ideal
sections.body: A real capacitor behaves like an ideal capacitance in series with equivalent series resistance (ESR) and equivalent series inductance (ESL). Aluminum electrolytics pack high capacitance per dollar and per volume but carry meaningful ESR, often tens to hundreds of milliohms; polymer (conductive-polymer aluminum or tantalum) capacitors cost more but push ESR down to single-digit milliohms and tolerate far more ripple current for their size; ceramic (MLCC) capacitors have the lowest ESR and ESL of all but offer less capacitance per volume and lose much of their rated capacitance under DC bias. At switching frequencies, the ripple voltage a capacitor produces is often ESR times ripple current, not the classical I times dt / C charge term -- meaning swapping in a lower-ESR part can cut ripple more than adding capacitance.

sections.heading: Hold-up time: sizing bulk capacitance for a mains dropout
sections.body: Hold-up time is how long a supply must keep its output in spec after mains disappears -- commonly one line cycle or more, since a brief sag or a relay chattering on a nearby circuit can blink the AC input. The stored energy needed is E = 0.5 times C times (Vnom squared minus Vmin squared), where Vnom is the normal bus voltage and Vmin is the lowest bus voltage the downstream regulator can still work from. This equation, not a rule of thumb, is what sizes the bulk capacitor in any mains-fed supply expected to ride through a dropout.

sections.heading: Ripple-current ratings and the Arrhenius life rule
sections.body: Every electrolytic capacitor carries a rated RMS ripple current; exceeding it drives internal I-squared-R heating that raises the core temperature and shortens life. Capacitor life follows an Arrhenius-type thermal acceleration that vendors commonly summarize as a rule of thumb: life roughly halves for every 10 degC rise above the rated operating temperature. A capacitor rated for 2000 hours at 105 degC would be expected to last only about 1000 hours if run at 115 degC -- and, by the same rule, roughly 8000 hours if kept at 85 degC, which is why derating temperature is one of the cheapest reliability wins in a design meant to survive years of classroom use.

lessons.workedExample: A power supply's 380 V DC bus, downstream of a PFC boost stage, must ride through a 20 ms mains dropout (one full cycle at 50 Hz) while supplying 100 W, and the downstream converter can tolerate the bus sagging no lower than 300 V. Required hold-up energy is E = P times t = 100 W times 0.020 s = 2 J. Solving 2 J = 0.5 times C times (380 squared - 300 squared) = 0.5 times C times 54,400 gives C = 4 / 54,400 = 73.5 uF -- meaning a single 100 uF, 450 V bulk capacitor comfortably covers the requirement, while a 47 uF capacitor would not.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe hold-up sizing because 'I used a big capacitor' isn't an engineering answer -- '0.5 C (Vnom^2 - Vmin^2) equals the energy I need for 20 ms at 100 W, which gave me 73.5 uF minimum, so I used 100 uF' is. A strong answer also connects ESR to ripple voltage rather than treating capacitance as the only lever, and can state a concrete temperature-derating decision (why the design keeps capacitors away from a hot heatsink) rather than a vague 'capacitors don't like heat.' A weak answer picks a capacitor value from a reference design without being able to derive it.

questions.prompt: A 100 W supply needs 20 ms of hold-up on a 380 V bus that may sag to 300 V. Using E = 0.5 C (Vnom^2 - Vmin^2), what is the minimum bulk capacitance required?

options.text: About 7.4 uF
About 73.5 uF
About 735 uF
About 20 uF

explanations.a: This is off by a factor of ten from the correct value; check the exponent on the voltage-squared term.
explanations.b: Correct -- required energy is 100 W times 0.020 s = 2 J, and solving 2 = 0.5 C (380^2 - 300^2) = 0.5 C (54,400) gives C = 4/54,400 = 73.5 uF.
explanations.c: This is ten times too large for the given energy requirement.
explanations.d: 20 uF doesn't follow from the hold-up energy equation with these numbers.

questions.prompt: At switching frequencies, why can a capacitor's ripple voltage be dominated by ESR times ripple current rather than the classical I dt / C charge term?

options.text: Because ESR only matters at DC, not at switching frequency
Because real capacitors have non-zero equivalent series resistance, and the voltage drop across that resistance can exceed the capacitive charge-related ripple
Because ceramic capacitors have no capacitance at all above 1 kHz
Because ESR decreases as switching frequency increases, cancelling the charge term

explanations.a: ESR's effect is most significant at higher (switching) frequencies where ripple current is largest and fastest, not only at DC.
explanations.b: Correct -- the ESR times ripple-current voltage drop is an additional ripple term on top of the capacitive charge term, and it frequently dominates in real electrolytics at switching frequencies.
explanations.c: Ceramic capacitors retain significant capacitance well above 1 kHz; their issue is DC-bias derating, not disappearing capacitance.
explanations.d: ESR doesn't generally decrease with frequency in a way that cancels the charge term; the two ripple contributions simply add.

questions.prompt: Match each capacitor type to its characteristic tradeoff.

right.text: High capacitance per dollar/volume, but tens to hundreds of milliohms of ESR
Low single-digit-milliohm ESR and strong ripple-current handling, at higher cost
Lowest ESR/ESL overall, but loses rated capacitance under DC bias and offers less capacitance per volume

questions.explanation: Aluminum electrolytics are cheap and dense but carry high ESR; polymer capacitors trade higher cost for much lower ESR and better ripple handling; ceramics have the lowest ESR/ESL of the three but suffer DC-bias capacitance loss and lower volumetric density.

questions.prompt: A capacitor is rated for 2000 hours of life at 105 degC. Using the rule that life roughly halves per 10 degC rise, about how long would it be expected to last if operated continuously at 85 degC?

options.text: About 500 hours
About 1000 hours
About 2000 hours
About 8000 hours

explanations.a: 500 hours would result from operating well above the rated temperature, not 20 degC below it.
explanations.b: 1000 hours corresponds to running 10 degC above rating (115 degC), the opposite direction from this question.
explanations.c: 2000 hours is the rated life at 105 degC itself, not at a lower operating temperature.
explanations.d: Correct -- 85 degC is two 10 degC steps below the 105 degC rating, and life roughly doubles per step down: 2000 to 4000 to 8000 hours.

lessons.label: The Ideal Switch, Duty Cycle, and PWM

sections.heading: Two states, one number: duty cycle
sections.body: Every switch-mode converter reduces to a switch that is fully ON for a fraction D of each switching period Ts, and fully OFF for the remaining (1-D) times Ts, repeating at fsw = 1/Ts. D, the duty cycle, is the single control variable the rest of the converter reacts to. In a buck converter, for example, the averaged output relationship Vout = D times Vin holds as long as fsw is much higher than the LC output filter's corner frequency -- fast enough that the inductor and capacitor effectively integrate the chopped pulses into a smooth average rather than passing the individual switching edges through to the load.

sections.heading: State-space averaging: why the averaged model is trustworthy
sections.body: That averaging shortcut isn't an approximation engineers just hope works -- it was formalized by R. D. Middlebrook and Slobodan Cuk at Caltech, whose 1976 paper on a unified state-space averaging approach to modeling switching converters gave the field a rigorous way to replace a switch's fast, discontinuous behavior with a smooth, continuous average model valid whenever switching is fast relative to the filter dynamics. That's the theoretical backbone behind every 'Vout = D times Vin'-style equation used to design converters today.

sections.heading: Generating PWM: comparator plus ramp
sections.body: The classic way to turn a slowly varying control voltage into a duty-cycle-modulated switch drive is to compare it against a fast sawtooth or triangle ramp running at fsw: wherever the control voltage sits above the ramp, the comparator output is high (switch ON); wherever the ramp exceeds it, the output goes low (switch OFF). Raising the control voltage widens the ON interval and raises D; this comparator-plus-ramp scheme is the core of classic analog PWM controller families such as the SG3525 and UC3823.

sections.heading: The frequency tradeoff
sections.body: Raising fsw shrinks the inductor and capacitor needed for a given ripple target, since ripple current in an inductor scales roughly as 1/fsw for fixed L -- smaller, lighter, cheaper passives. But it isn't free: switching loss grows roughly as Psw is proportional to V times I times (tr+tf) times fsw, gate-drive loss grows as Pgate = Qg times Vgs times fsw, and magnetic core loss grows with frequency following something like the Steinmetz relation. Every converter design sits at a frequency chosen by balancing smaller passives against these three rising loss terms, which is why wide-bandgap GaN and SiC devices -- with much lower switching loss per transition -- have pushed practical switching frequencies far higher than silicon MOSFETs allowed.

lessons.workedExample: A buck converter drops 12 V to 5 V, so D = Vout/Vin = 5/12 = 0.417, independent of switching frequency. The MOSFET's gate charge is Qg = 10 nC and its gate drive swings Vgs = 10 V. At fsw = 500 kHz, gate-drive loss is Pgate = Qg times Vgs times fsw = 10e-9 times 10 times 500e3 = 0.05 W. Pushing to fsw = 5 MHz to shrink the inductor by roughly 10x raises gate-drive loss to 0.5 W -- a tenfold increase, before even counting the rise in switching-transition and core losses. That's the frequency tradeoff in one calculation: smaller magnetics against directly proportional loss growth.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe the frequency choice because a lot of student designs simply copy the default frequency from a reference design or eval board without knowing why. A strong answer states the duty-cycle relationship for their topology, explains that raising fsw shrinks L and C but raises gate, switching, and core loss roughly in proportion to fsw, and can point to at least one loss term (like Pgate = Qg Vgs fsw) with actual numbers. A weak answer says 'higher frequency is more efficient' or 'higher frequency is better for smaller parts' without acknowledging the tradeoff runs in both directions at once.

questions.prompt: A buck converter with Vin = 12 V produces Vout = 5 V. What duty cycle does the averaged model predict?

options.text: D depends only on the switching frequency, not on Vin or Vout

explanations.a: Correct -- for a buck converter, Vout = D times Vin, so D = Vout/Vin = 5/12 = 0.417.
explanations.b: D must be between 0 and 1 by definition; 2.4 is not a valid duty cycle.
explanations.c: 0.7 doesn't match 5/12; it would correspond to a different Vout/Vin ratio.
explanations.d: D is set by the Vout/Vin ratio in the averaged buck relationship; switching frequency affects ripple and loss, not the steady-state duty cycle itself.

questions.prompt: In the comparator-plus-ramp method of generating PWM, what happens when the control voltage rises?

options.text: The switching frequency automatically increases
The ON interval widens because the control voltage stays above the ramp for a larger fraction of the period, raising D
The ramp amplitude decreases to compensate
The comparator output goes permanently high, disabling switching

explanations.a: The ramp's own frequency, not the control voltage, sets fsw in this scheme; raising the control voltage doesn't change fsw.
explanations.b: Correct -- a higher control voltage stays above the rising ramp for longer within each period, widening the ON interval and increasing D.
explanations.c: The ramp amplitude is set by the oscillator circuit, not adjusted in response to the control voltage.
explanations.d: The comparator output still toggles every period as the ramp resets and rises again; it doesn't latch high.

questions.prompt: Match each consequence to the design choice that raising switching frequency causes.

right.text: Shrinks, roughly as 1/fsw for a fixed ripple target
Grows roughly proportional to V, I, transition time, and fsw
Grows proportional to Qg, Vgs, and fsw
Grows with frequency following a Steinmetz-type relation

questions.explanation: Raising fsw shrinks the required inductance/capacitance for a given ripple target, but raises switching-transition loss, gate-drive loss, and magnetic core loss -- the tradeoff every converter frequency choice balances.

questions.prompt: Order the events within one switching period generated by a comparator-plus-ramp PWM scheme.

items.text: The ramp voltage resets to zero at the start of the switching period
The ramp rises linearly while the control voltage stays comparatively constant
The comparator output is high, holding the switch ON, while the ramp remains below the control voltage
The ramp crosses above the control voltage, and the comparator output goes low, turning the switch OFF for the rest of the period

questions.explanation: Each switching period begins with the ramp resetting to zero; as it rises, the switch stays ON as long as the ramp is below the control voltage, and turns OFF the moment the rising ramp crosses above the control voltage, until the next period resets it.

lessons.label: Building It Safely: Isolation, Grounding, and Inrush

sections.heading: Why mains is a different hazard class than bench DC
sections.body: A bench DC supply is usually current-limited and can't push a dangerous amount through a body even at high voltage; the mains line (120 Vac or 230 Vac) is backed by a whole utility grid and a 15-20 A breaker, meaning it can drive tens of milliamps across the chest -- enough to cause cardiac fibrillation -- with essentially no current limiting of its own. Safety standards like IEC 62368-1 (the modern successor to IEC 60950-1) formally treat any circuit above roughly 60 V DC or 42.4 V peak AC as a hazardous voltage requiring protective measures, which is the line a student project crosses the moment it plugs into the wall instead of a wall-wart brick.

sections.heading: Creepage, clearance, and isolation class
sections.body: Creepage is the shortest path along a surface between two conductors; clearance is the shortest path through air. IEC 60664-1 sets minimum creepage and clearance distances that scale with working voltage and pollution degree -- several millimeters at typical mains working voltages -- and a board that routes primary (mains-connected) and secondary (low-voltage) traces too close together fails this regardless of how well it otherwise works. Functional isolation just lets the circuit operate and offers no shock protection; basic isolation gives one protective layer; reinforced isolation is a single insulation system equivalent to two independent layers, and it's what a double-insulated (Class II) design needs when there's no separate protective-earth path to fall back on.

sections.heading: Y-capacitors and leakage current
sections.body: Y-capacitors bridge from the primary side to the secondary or chassis to shunt high-frequency EMI noise to ground, but every Y-capacitor also leaks a small line-frequency current continuously, I = 2 pi f C V. Safety standards cap the total touch/earth leakage current a piece of equipment may present (tighter for handheld and medical equipment than for fixed appliances), so the Y-capacitor's value is chosen as much for staying under that leakage limit as for EMI performance -- oversizing it for 'better filtering' can silently push a design out of compliance.

sections.heading: Inrush limiting, fusing, bleeders, and the one-hand rule
sections.body: A discharged bulk capacitor looks like a near-short at power-up, and unlimited inrush current can run 10-100 times the steady-state current for one line cycle, stressing diodes, switch contacts, and fuses. An NTC thermistor (high resistance cold, low resistance once self-heated) or a relay-bypassed resistor tames that surge, and a slow-blow fuse sized for the inrush profile protects against real faults without nuisance-tripping on normal startup. A bleeder resistor across the bulk capacitor discharges stored energy to a safe level within seconds of power-off, since that capacitor can otherwise sit at a lethal voltage for minutes. When live measurement is unavoidable, the one-hand rule -- keeping the other hand out of the circuit, ideally in a pocket -- keeps any accidental current path off a route across the chest.

lessons.workedExample: A student builds a 400 V DC bus (from a boosted PFC stage) around a 100 uF bulk capacitor. Powered off, that capacitor still holds E = 0.5 times 100 uF times 400 V squared = 8 J -- enough for a painful shock. Adding a 15 k-ohm bleeder resistor across the bus gives a discharge time constant RC = 15,000 times 0.0001 = 1.5 s, so the voltage falls from 400 V to a much safer 60 V in about 1.9 time constants (roughly 3 seconds) after unplugging, at a continuous drain of 400 squared / 15,000 = about 10.7 W while the bus stays powered -- calling for a resistor rated well above that, such as a 15-20 W part, not the 5 W a first guess might reach for. The same board's first layout also measured only 4 mm of primary-to-secondary creepage; cutting a slot through the PCB lengthened the surface path to about 8 mm, comfortably clearing IEC 60664-1's basic-isolation creepage requirement at that working voltage.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe mains safety hard because a project that plugs into the wall without a documented isolation, leakage, inrush, or discharge plan is a real hazard, not a hypothetical one -- and because 'I was careful' isn't evidence. A strong answer states an actual creepage measurement and fix, a Y-capacitor leakage estimate, the inrush-limiting component used, and the bleeder resistor's time constant with a discharge time. A weak answer gestures at 'safety precautions' without a single number, or reveals the board was tested live with both hands on it and no verification that the bus had discharged.

questions.prompt: Why does a Y-capacitor's value matter for regulatory leakage-current limits, not just for EMI filtering?

options.text: Y-capacitors have no effect on leakage current, only on noise
Every Y-capacitor conducts a continuous line-frequency leakage current, I = 2 pi f C V, so a larger value raises leakage as well as filtering
Y-capacitors only leak current when the equipment is powered off
Leakage current limits apply only to Class I appliances with a ground pin

explanations.a: Y-capacitors do conduct a real, continuous leakage current in normal operation, not just noise current.
explanations.b: Correct -- the same capacitance that filters EMI also passes a line-frequency leakage current given by I = 2 pi f C V, so oversizing it for EMI can push a design over the allowed leakage limit.
explanations.c: The leakage current flows during normal powered operation, driven by the line-frequency voltage across the capacitor, not only when the equipment is off.
explanations.d: Leakage limits apply broadly across equipment classes, including double-insulated Class II designs, though the specific limits vary by category.

questions.prompt: What problem does an NTC thermistor at power-up specifically address?

options.text: It reduces steady-state switching loss in the converter
It limits the high inrush current that a discharged bulk capacitor would otherwise draw at the moment of power-up
It filters high-frequency EMI conducted back onto the mains
It discharges the bulk capacitor after power-off

explanations.a: Steady-state switching loss is unrelated to the NTC's role; the NTC is a startup-only inrush limiter.
explanations.b: Correct -- a discharged bulk capacitor looks like a near-short at turn-on, and the NTC's high cold resistance limits that surge before it self-heats to a low resistance for efficient normal operation.
explanations.c: EMI filtering is handled by dedicated EMI filter components (including Y-capacitors), not by the inrush-limiting NTC.
explanations.d: Discharging the capacitor after power-off is the bleeder resistor's job, not the NTC's.

questions.prompt: Match each mains-safety term to its definition.

right.text: Shortest path along a surface between two conductors
Shortest path through air between two conductors
Isolation that only makes the circuit work, with no shock protection
A single insulation system providing protection equivalent to two independent layers

questions.explanation: Creepage measures the surface path and clearance the through-air path between conductors; functional isolation provides no shock protection at all, while reinforced isolation delivers protection equivalent to two independent insulation layers in a single system.

questions.prompt: Order the safety steps for handling a mains-connected prototype after unplugging it, through to a live measurement if one is unavoidable.

items.text: Unplug the board and wait several bleeder time constants for the bulk capacitor to discharge
Verify with a meter that the bus voltage has actually dropped below a safe threshold before touching anything
If a live measurement is unavoidable, keep the other hand out of the circuit (in a pocket) so current has no path across the chest
Probe the board with the meter's ground clip clipped in place rather than held in the free hand

questions.explanation: Safe handling starts with unplugging and letting the bleeder resistor discharge the bulk capacitor, then verifying with a meter rather than assuming; when a live measurement can't be avoided, the one-hand rule keeps a stray current path off the chest, and clipping the meter's ground lead down instead of holding it removes one more way to become part of the circuit.

units.label: Switching Converter Topologies

lessons.label: The Buck Converter from First Principles

sections.heading: Volt-second balance sets the gain
sections.body: A buck converter is a switch, an inductor, a diode (or a second switch), and an output capacitor. When the top switch closes, the inductor sees Vin minus Vout across it and its current ramps up; when the switch opens, the diode freewheels and the inductor sees minus Vout, so current ramps down. In steady state the inductor current at the start and end of a switching period must be identical, otherwise it would ramp forever and nothing would settle. That forces the average voltage across the inductor over one cycle to be exactly zero: D(Vin-Vout) + (1-D)(-Vout) = 0, which reduces to Vout = D*Vin. This is the entire buck transfer function, derived without touching a transfer-function textbook, and it is the same volt-second argument every other switching topology in this unit reuses.

sections.heading: Ripple: the two knobs a designer actually turns
sections.body: The inductor ripple current is dI = (Vin-Vout)*D/(L*fsw), equivalently Vout*(1-D)/(L*fsw) — doubling either L or fsw halves the ripple. That ripple current then charges and discharges the output capacitor each cycle; a charge-balance argument on the cap gives an ideal ripple voltage of roughly dI/(8*fsw*C), plus a second term dI*ESR from the capacitor's equivalent series resistance. For electrolytic output caps, ESR usually dominates the ripple budget outright, which is why designers spec low-ESR or ceramic caps once ripple gets tight rather than just adding more capacitance. There is a second, separate constraint that the ripple-voltage budget alone does not capture: the same ripple current dI flows through the capacitor's ESR every cycle, dissipating I_rms^2*ESR as heat inside the part. Electrolytic caps are frequently life-limited by this self-heating rather than by ripple voltage — the datasheet gives a maximum RMS ripple-current rating, and exceeding it accelerates electrolyte dry-out and shortens the capacitor's service life even if the ripple-voltage number still looks acceptable on paper. A design that only checks dI/(8*fsw*C) against a voltage budget can pass that check and still cook its output cap; both the voltage-ripple and the current-rating constraints need to be checked independently.

sections.heading: Diode vs synchronous rectification
sections.body: A plain diode freewheels the inductor current during the off-time but drops its forward voltage Vf the whole time it conducts, burning Vf*Iout*(1-D) as fixed conduction loss regardless of how small Vout is. On a 3.3V rail, a 0.4V Schottky drop is over 10% of the output right there. Replacing the diode with a second MOSFET (synchronous rectification) turns that fixed-voltage loss into a resistive one, I^2*Rds(on)*(1-D), which for a few-milliohm FET is a fraction of a percent at the same current. That difference is exactly why every sub-2V core-voltage rail on a modern board is a synchronous buck and never a diode-rectified one.

lessons.workedExample: A 12V-to-3.3V buck runs at fsw=500kHz with L=4.7uH and Iout=5A. D=3.3/12=0.275, so dI=(12-3.3)*0.275/(4.7e-6*5e5)=2.3925/2.35≈1.02A, about 20% of load current — a normal ripple ratio. With Cout=22uF and ESR=5mOhm, Vripple≈dI*ESR+dI/(8*fsw*C)=5mV+11.4mV≈16mV. Rectification choice matters far more than ripple here: a 0.4V Schottky diode wastes 0.4*5*(1-0.275)=1.45W (about 9% of the 16.5W output), while an 8mOhm sync FET wastes only 5^2*0.008*0.725≈0.15W (under 1%).
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing the buck stage wants to see whether a student can derive Vout=D*Vin from volt-second balance rather than just quote it, and whether they know ripple is a designed quantity (set by L and fsw) rather than an unavoidable defect. The sharpest follow-up is rectification: a strong answer explains why a low-voltage rail needs a synchronous FET using the Vf*(1-D) vs I^2*Rds(on)*(1-D) comparison with real numbers; a weak answer says 'synchronous is more efficient' without being able to say why the gap gets worse as Vout drops.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of the volt-second balance derivation for Vout = D*Vin.

items.text: During Ton, the inductor voltage equals Vin - Vout.
During Toff, the inductor voltage equals -Vout.
Steady state requires the average inductor voltage over one period to equal zero.
Solving D(Vin-Vout) + (1-D)(-Vout) = 0 gives Vout = D*Vin.

questions.explanation: The two per-interval voltages are identified first, then the steady-state zero-average-volt-second condition is applied, and only then is the algebra solved for the gain.

questions.prompt: Holding Vin, Vout, and D fixed, what happens to inductor ripple current dI if switching frequency fsw is doubled?

options.text: It doubles
It is halved
It is unchanged
It quadruples

explanations.a: dI is inversely proportional to fsw in dI=(Vin-Vout)*D/(L*fsw), so doubling fsw cannot increase ripple.
explanations.b: Correct — fsw sits in the denominator alongside L, so doubling it halves dI, exactly like doubling L would.
explanations.c: fsw appears explicitly in the ripple formula's denominator, so ripple does change with it.
explanations.d: Quadrupling would require fsw to appear squared in the denominator; it appears only to the first power.

questions.prompt: Match each buck converter component to its role.

right.text: Connects Vin to the switch node during Ton
Stores and releases energy, keeping output current continuous
Carries current during Toff when the top switch is open
Absorbs the inductor ripple current, setting output ripple voltage

questions.explanation: The top switch gates energy from Vin, the inductor smooths that chopped input into continuous output current, the freewheeling device carries current when the switch is open, and the output cap absorbs whatever ripple current the inductor still has.

questions.prompt: In the worked example (12V to 3.3V, 5A), why does a synchronous FET lose roughly 10x less power than a diode in the freewheel path?

options.text: Because the diode loss is a fixed Vf*I term while the FET loss is resistive (I^2*Rds(on)) and small at this current
Because the FET switches faster than the diode
Because the diode only conducts during Ton, not Toff
Because synchronous rectification changes the duty cycle

explanations.a: Correct — the worked example shows 1.45W for a 0.4V diode versus about 0.15W for an 8mOhm FET, because one loss scales with a fixed voltage drop and the other with current squared times a tiny resistance.
explanations.b: Switching speed affects transition losses, not the conduction-loss comparison being made here.
explanations.c: It is the opposite: the freewheeling device (diode or sync FET) conducts during Toff, which is exactly the interval being compared.
explanations.d: Duty cycle is set by Vin, Vout, and volt-second balance; rectification choice does not change D.

lessons.label: Boost and Buck-Boost

sections.heading: The same argument, an inverted topology
sections.body: A boost converter puts the inductor in series with the input, a switch to ground, and a diode to the output. During Ton the switch grounds the switch node, so the inductor sees the full Vin across it; during Toff the diode conducts and the inductor sees Vin-Vout. Zero-average-volt-second balance gives D*Vin + (1-D)*(Vin-Vout) = 0, which simplifies to Vout = Vin/(1-D). A buck-boost swaps the diode's target from ground to a floating negative output: the inductor sees Vin during Ton and -Vout during Toff, giving D*Vin + (1-D)*(-Vout) = 0, or Vout = -D/(1-D)*Vin — same magnitude as boost's denominator, but inverted and referenced to a different rail.

sections.heading: Why D toward 1 is a mirage
sections.body: The ideal formulas climb without bound as D approaches 1, but real inductors have DCR, real switches have Rds(on), and real diodes have a forward drop, all sitting in the same current path as the inductor. Input current scales roughly as Iout/(1-D), so I^2*R losses in those parasitics grow faster than the ideal gain does. Past some duty cycle — commonly cited as around D=0.8-0.9 depending on the parasitics — added duty cycle produces more loss than more gain, and the achievable Vout actually peaks and then falls even as D is pushed higher. Practical boost designs are rarely pushed past that zone; a large step-up is better handled by a transformer-isolated topology or a multi-phase/multi-stage approach than by chasing D toward 1 on a single boost stage.

sections.heading: Where the ripple lives, and what that means for capacitor placement
sections.body: In a boost converter the inductor sits directly in the input path and carries current continuously regardless of switch state, so the current drawn from the source is smooth — a real advantage for EMI filtering and for sources like batteries that dislike being pulsed. The output side is the opposite: the diode only delivers current to the output capacitor during Toff, so the output cap alone supplies the load during Ton and gets recharged in pulses during Toff, meaning boost output current is pulsating and needs a low-ESR, adequately sized output cap. A buck converter is the mirror image: continuous current at the output (through the inductor into the load) but pulsating current at the input, which is why buck designs need the bulk of their capacitive ripple-current rating on the input side instead.

lessons.workedExample: A boost stage takes a single Li-ion cell (nominal 3.7V) up to a 5V USB rail. At nominal charge, D=1-Vin/Vout=1-3.7/5=0.26, comfortably inside the efficient zone. Near end of discharge the cell droops to 2.7V, pushing D to 1-2.7/5=0.46 — still fine. If the same cell instead had to reach 12V directly, D=1-3.7/12=0.69, edging toward the region where I^2*R losses in the inductor's DCR and the switch's Rds(on) start eating into the theoretical gain, which is why a single-cell-to-12V boost is a stretch better handled with a different topology or an extra stage.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about D approaching 1 specifically to separate students who memorized Vout=Vin/(1-D) from students who understand it is an idealization. A strong answer explains that real current scales with 1/(1-D) too, so parasitic I^2*R losses eventually outrun the ideal gain and the achievable Vout saturates and falls — a weak answer just says 'efficiency drops' without naming why the current itself is the culprit. The capacitor-placement question checks whether a student can trace which side of a given topology actually pulses, rather than assuming ripple is symmetric.

questions.prompt: A boost converter's inductor sees Vin during Ton and Vin-Vout during Toff. Applying zero-average-volt-second balance, what is Vout?

options.text: Vout = D*Vin
Vout = Vin/(1-D)
Vout = Vin*(1-D)
Vout = -D/(1-D)*Vin

explanations.a: That is the buck relation, derived from a different pair of per-interval inductor voltages.
explanations.b: Correct — solving D*Vin + (1-D)*(Vin-Vout) = 0 for Vout gives Vin = (1-D)*Vout, or Vout = Vin/(1-D).
explanations.c: This inverts the correct relationship; it would predict Vout falling as D rises, the opposite of boost behavior.
explanations.d: This is the buck-boost (inverting) relation, not the boost relation — boost is non-inverting.

questions.prompt: Why does a real boost converter's achievable Vout eventually peak and fall as D is pushed toward 1, even though the ideal formula Vin/(1-D) keeps climbing?

options.text: Input current scales roughly as Iout/(1-D), so I^2*R losses in real parasitics grow faster than the ideal gain
The switching frequency automatically drops as D increases
The diode stops conducting entirely once D exceeds 0.5
The output capacitor saturates magnetically at high duty cycle

explanations.a: Correct — as D climbs, the current the parasitics must carry rises faster than the ideal voltage gain, so I^2*R loss eventually dominates and pulls achievable Vout back down.
explanations.b: Switching frequency is set by the controller, not by duty cycle, and does not automatically change with D.
explanations.c: The diode's conduction window shrinks as D rises but it does not stop conducting at D=0.5; that threshold has no special significance here.
explanations.d: Capacitors do not saturate magnetically; that describes a core material effect in inductors and transformers.

questions.prompt: Using the worked example's single-cell boost (3.7V nominal to 5V), what duty cycle is needed as the cell droops to 2.7V near end of discharge?

explanations.a: 0.26 is the duty cycle at nominal 3.7V, not at the drooped 2.7V condition.
explanations.b: Correct — D=1-Vin/Vout=1-2.7/5=0.46, as stated for the drooped-cell case in the worked example.
explanations.c: 0.69 is the duty cycle the worked example computes for a hypothetical 3.7V-to-12V boost, a different case.
explanations.d: 0.85 is not computed anywhere in this lesson for this converter; it is not supported by the given numbers.

questions.prompt: Match each port, in each topology, to the current character it actually sees.

right.text: Continuous (smooth)
Pulsating (chopped)

questions.explanation: The inductor sits between the switch node and whichever port it directly feeds continuously; in a buck that is the output, so the input pulses and the output is smooth, while in a boost the inductor is on the input side, so the input is smooth and the diode chops current to the output.

lessons.label: CCM, DCM, and the Boundary Between Them

sections.heading: The boundary condition, mechanically
sections.body: In continuous conduction mode (CCM), inductor current ramps up during Ton and down during Toff but never reaches zero, so the rectifying device is still conducting when the next cycle starts. As load current drops, the average inductor current drops with it while the ripple amplitude — fixed by Vin, Vout, L, and fsw — stays the same, so eventually the down-ramp reaches exactly zero right at the end of the period. That boundary defines a critical inductance: for a buck, L_crit = (1-D)*R/(2*fsw), where R=Vout/Iout. Any inductor smaller than L_crit at a given load current pushes the converter into discontinuous conduction mode (DCM) at that operating point.

sections.heading: DCM breaks the clean D-only formula
sections.body: In CCM, Vout/Vin depends only on D. In DCM a third interval appears: after inductor current reaches zero, both the switch and the diode are off until the next cycle begins. Because that idle interval's length depends on how much load current is actually being drawn, the conversion ratio in DCM becomes a function of D, load, L, and fsw together, not D alone — a control loop tuned assuming CCM behavior can produce the wrong Vout, typically higher than D*Vin would predict, if it slips into DCM at light load without accounting for it.

sections.heading: The ringing signature and light-load coping strategies
sections.body: During the DCM idle interval, the switch node is no longer clamped by inductor current, so it is free to resonate between the inductor L and the switch's parasitic drain capacitance Coss, producing a damped ringing plateau visible on a scope — a signature that immediately tells an engineer the converter has entered DCM. Because per-cycle switching loss stays roughly fixed regardless of load while conduction loss falls with it, efficiency collapses at very light load if the converter keeps switching at full fsw. Real controllers respond with pulse-skipping or burst/PFM mode: below a load threshold they skip or bundle switching pulses, trading larger low-frequency output ripple for a much lower average switching rate and far better light-load efficiency. A synchronous buck has a second option that a diode-rectified one does not: because the low-side device is a FET rather than a diode, it can conduct inductor current backward (from output toward ground) instead of shutting off when current would otherwise reach zero. A controller can exploit this to hold the converter in forced CCM even at light load — deliberately letting current reverse each cycle rather than let the inductor current hit zero and ring — which avoids the DCM ringing and variable-frequency PFM behavior entirely at the cost of circulating current that is drawn from the output and dumped back through the low-side FET, a real conduction-loss penalty traded for a fixed switching frequency and simpler downstream filtering. This is the same diode-vs-synchronous-FET choice as the rectifying device covered earlier in this unit, now showing up as a light-load control-mode tradeoff rather than a conduction-loss-at-full-load one.

lessons.workedExample: A buck converts 12V to 5V (D=0.417) at fsw=300kHz with L=10uH. The critical load resistance is R=2*fsw*L/(1-D)=2*300e3*10e-6/0.583≈10.3 ohm, so Iout_crit=Vout/R=5/10.3≈0.49A. Below roughly half an amp this specific design enters DCM. At a 50mA load — ten times lighter — a controller with no light-load mode would keep switching at the full 300kHz doing almost no useful conduction work, losing most of its input power to switching and gate-drive loss; a controller with burst/PFM mode instead switches in bursts equivalent to a much lower effective frequency, recovering efficiency at the cost of larger low-frequency ripple on the 5V rail.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about DCM to see whether a student understands it as a qualitatively different conduction mode with load-dependent gain, not just 'low current.' A strong answer can compute or reason about the critical inductance/resistance boundary, name the L-Coss ringing plateau as the scope evidence of DCM, and explain pulse-skipping as a deliberate efficiency-vs-ripple tradeoff rather than a defect. A weak answer says only 'DCM happens at light load' without being able to say what changes about the conversion ratio or why the controller responds the way it does.

questions.prompt: What precisely defines the CCM/DCM boundary for a given inductor and load?

options.text: The inductor current ramps down and reaches exactly zero right at the end of the switching period
The output capacitor fully discharges each cycle
The switch stops turning on entirely
The duty cycle exceeds 0.5

explanations.a: Correct — the boundary is defined by the down-ramping inductor current just touching zero at the moment the next cycle begins; any lighter load pushes it into DCM.
explanations.b: The output capacitor's discharge behavior is a consequence of the load and ripple, not the definition of the CCM/DCM boundary.
explanations.c: The switch keeps operating normally in both CCM and DCM; only the inductor current's behavior between switch and diode conduction changes.
explanations.d: Duty cycle of 0.5 has no special relationship to the CCM/DCM boundary, which depends on L, R, and fsw instead.

questions.prompt: In the worked example (12V to 5V, fsw=300kHz, L=10uH), what is the critical load resistance below which the converter enters DCM?

options.text: ≈2 ohm
≈5 ohm
≈20 ohm

explanations.a: 2 ohm is well below the computed value and would correspond to a much heavier load, still in CCM.
explanations.b: 5 ohm is also below the boundary value computed in the worked example.
explanations.c: Correct — R=2*fsw*L/(1-D)=2*300e3*10e-6/0.583≈10.3 ohm, as computed in the worked example.
explanations.d: 20 ohm overstates the boundary resistance computed for this specific design.

questions.prompt: The ringing plateau seen on a scope during a DCM idle interval is produced by resonance between which two elements?

options.text: The inductor L and the switch's parasitic drain capacitance Coss
The inductor L and the output capacitor Cout
The switch's Rds(on) and the load resistance
The output capacitor's ESR and the diode's forward resistance

explanations.a: Correct — once both switch and diode are off, the inductor is left resonating with the small parasitic Coss at the switch node, producing the characteristic damped ringing.
explanations.b: Cout is decoupled from the switch node by the rectifying device during this interval and is not part of the resonant loop.
explanations.c: Rds(on) and load resistance are dissipative elements, not the reactive pair that produces a ringing (oscillatory) waveform.
explanations.d: ESR and diode resistance are also dissipative, not the resonant LC pair responsible for the ringing plateau.

questions.prompt: Why do many buck ICs deliberately skip switching pulses (burst/PFM mode) at very light load?

options.text: To cut the fixed per-cycle switching and gate-drive loss that would otherwise dominate when conduction current is tiny
To reduce electromagnetic interference at all load levels
To force the converter to stay in CCM permanently
To increase output ripple current through the inductor

explanations.a: Correct — switching loss is roughly fixed per cycle regardless of load, so at light load it can dominate; skipping pulses lowers the effective switching rate and restores efficiency at the cost of larger output ripple.
explanations.b: Burst mode is a light-load-specific technique, not a general EMI-reduction strategy applied at all loads.
explanations.c: Burst/PFM mode is used precisely because the converter would otherwise be deep in DCM at light load; it does not force CCM.
explanations.d: Burst mode trades switching frequency for larger low-frequency output ripple, not for higher inductor ripple current specifically.

lessons.label: Isolated Topologies I: The Flyback

sections.heading: A transformer that is really a coupled inductor
sections.body: In a flyback, the primary switch closing ramps up magnetizing current in the primary winding while the secondary diode stays reverse biased, so no energy reaches the secondary yet — energy is being stored as 0.5*Lp*Ipk^2 in the core. When the switch opens, the winding voltages flip sense, the secondary diode forward-biases, and that stored energy discharges into the output capacitor and load as the current ramps back down. Because energy is stored and then released rather than passed through instantaneously, this 'transformer' behaves as a two-winding inductor — which is exactly why flyback is best understood as a buck-boost converter with its single inductor split into a coupled primary/secondary pair to add isolation.

sections.heading: Turns ratio sets both the gain and the switch's punishment
sections.body: Turns ratio N=Ns/Np does two jobs at once. It sets the CCM voltage gain, roughly N*D/(1-D). It also sets how hard the primary switch gets hit: when the switch opens, the output voltage reflects back across the windings in proportion to Np/Ns, i.e. Vout/N, so the switch must block Vin plus that reflected voltage. Pick N too small (a low step-down winding ratio) and the reflected voltage spikes the switch's required voltage rating; pick it too large and the secondary diode and duty cycle become awkward. This single number is the central design compromise in every flyback.

sections.heading: Leakage inductance, snubbing, and cross-regulation
sections.body: Not all primary flux couples to the secondary. The uncoupled leakage inductance has nowhere to dump its energy when the switch snaps open, producing a fast voltage spike on the drain on top of the reflected voltage — left unclamped, it can exceed the switch's rating within nanoseconds. The traditional fix is an RCD snubber (resistor-capacitor-diode clamp across the primary) that simply burns the leakage energy as heat: cheap and lossy, and worse as power scales up. An active clamp replaces the resistor with a second switch that recycles the leakage energy back into the conversion instead of dissipating it, at the cost of a second gate driver. Separately, a flyback with multiple secondary windings regulates only one tightly via feedback; the others free-run and drift with load because leakage inductance and winding resistance differ per winding — this cross-regulation error, plus the simplicity of a single switch, single transformer, and no output inductor, is why flyback dominates roughly below the 100-150W range and loses ground to through-transfer topologies above it.

lessons.workedExample: An isolated 12V-to-5V bias supply uses a flyback with Np:Ns giving N=0.5, Lp=22uH, fsw=250kHz, and Ipk=1.2A. Energy stored per cycle is 0.5*22e-6*1.2^2≈15.8uJ, delivering 15.8uJ*250e3≈4W — consistent with a 5V/0.8A bias rail. The reflected voltage is Vout/N=5/0.5=10V, so the primary switch must block Vin+Vout/N=12+10=22V before accounting for the leakage spike; an unclamped leakage spike could push well past that within nanoseconds, which is why the design needs an RCD snubber (or active clamp) sized to keep the switch inside a 30V-rated part's now-tighter margin.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about the flyback because it is the isolated topology most students reach for without understanding it is energy-storage-based, not through-transfer. A strong answer explains that the secondary diode is reverse biased during Ton (so it is not a real transformer in the instantaneous-transfer sense), states what the RCD snubber is actually protecting against (the leakage-inductance turn-off spike, not general noise), and can reason about turns-ratio as a voltage-stress tradeoff. A weak answer says 'flyback equals isolated buck-boost' as a memorized label without being able to explain either mechanism.

questions.prompt: Why does the flyback secondary diode stay reverse biased while the primary switch is on?

options.text: Because during Ton the core is storing energy from the primary, not transferring it, and the winding polarity keeps the secondary diode blocked until the switch opens
Because the secondary winding has no current path at all
Because the output capacitor is disconnected during Ton
Because the turns ratio is always less than one

explanations.a: Correct — the flyback stores energy in the core during Ton and only releases it to the secondary once the switch opens and winding polarity flips to forward-bias the diode.
explanations.b: The secondary winding has a path (through the diode) but the diode is reverse biased by polarity during Ton, not because the path is missing.
explanations.c: The output capacitor stays connected the whole time; it simply supplies the load alone during Ton since the diode is not conducting.
explanations.d: Turns ratio can be greater than, equal to, or less than one; it does not determine whether the diode is reverse biased during Ton.

questions.prompt: In the worked example, if Lp were doubled to 44uH while Ipk stayed at 1.2A, what happens to the energy stored per cycle?

options.text: It roughly doubles, from about 15.8uJ to about 31.7uJ
It stays the same
It is halved
It quadruples

explanations.a: Correct — energy per cycle is 0.5*Lp*Ipk^2, which is linear in Lp, so doubling Lp with Ipk fixed doubles the stored energy.
explanations.b: Energy stored is directly proportional to Lp in this formula, so it cannot stay unchanged when Lp doubles.
explanations.c: Halving would require an inverse relationship with Lp; the formula shows a direct proportional relationship instead.
explanations.d: Quadrupling would require Lp to appear squared in the formula; only Ipk is squared, not Lp.

questions.prompt: Using N=0.5 and Vout=5V from the worked example, what voltage must the primary switch block due to reflected voltage alone, ignoring the leakage spike?

explanations.a: 12V is just Vin; it omits the reflected voltage contribution entirely.
explanations.b: 14.5V would come from mistakenly reflecting with N*Vout instead of Vout/N; the reflected voltage runs the other way across the turns ratio.
explanations.c: 17V would require a turns ratio around 1, not the N=0.5 used in the worked example.
explanations.d: Correct — Vin + Vout/N = 12 + 5/0.5 = 22V, exactly as computed in the worked example.

questions.prompt: Match each flyback component or technique to its job.

right.text: Dissipates the leakage-inductance turn-off spike as heat
Recycles leakage energy via a second switch instead of dissipating it
Sets the reflected voltage and thus the primary switch's voltage stress
Subject to cross-regulation error under asymmetric load, since only one winding is directly regulated

questions.explanation: The RCD snubber clamps the leakage spike by burning the energy resistively; the active clamp recovers that same energy instead; turns ratio directly sets the reflected-voltage switch stress; and any secondary winding beyond the one in the feedback loop drifts with load imbalance due to cross-regulation.

lessons.label: Isolated Topologies II: Forward, Push-Pull, and Bridges

sections.heading: Through-transfer needs a way back to zero flux
sections.body: Unlike a flyback's energy-storage transformer, a forward converter's transformer is a true through-transfer device: while the switch is on, power flows straight from primary to secondary in real time, with the secondary rectifier conducting during Ton and an output inductor smoothing the result — closer in behavior to a buck's continuous output current than to flyback's pulsed delivery. The catch is that a single-switch forward drives the core in only one flux direction, so every Ton pushes flux upward and something must actively bring it back before the next cycle or the core walks into saturation. The classic fix is a third reset winding, roughly matched in turns to the primary, that dumps the magnetizing current back to the input rail once the switch opens — which forces D<0.5 so there is always time left in the period for flux to reset. A two-switch forward instead resets by turning both switches off together and letting the magnetizing current freewheel through two clamping diodes back to the input rail, removing the D<0.5 restriction and roughly halving the voltage each switch must block versus the single-switch version.

sections.heading: Push-pull: alternating drive, and the failure mode that comes with it
sections.body: Push-pull drives a center-tapped primary with two switches alternating, each driving the core in an opposite flux direction on alternating half-cycles, doubling the usable flux swing versus a single-ended forward on the same core. The catch is that any tiny asymmetry between the two half-cycles — mismatched switch on-times, unequal winding resistance, unequal switch drops — fails to cancel exactly, so the net DC flux does not return to zero every cycle. That residual bias accumulates cycle after cycle, walking the core up the B-H curve in a staircase until it saturates, at which point the primary looks like a near short circuit and switch current spikes. This is why practical push-pull designs favor current-mode control, which corrects volt-second imbalance cycle by cycle, over simple voltage-mode control.

sections.heading: Where each topology earns its keep
sections.body: The single-switch forward converter's simplicity and D<0.5 headroom suit roughly the 100-500W band. Beyond that, per-switch current gets large enough that a half-bridge (two switches, each blocking only Vin, splitting the primary drive across a capacitive midpoint) or full-bridge (four switches driving the full primary swing) becomes the better fit, and full-bridge designs routinely run from several hundred watts into the multi-kilowatt range — at the cost of roughly double, then quadruple, the switch count and gate-drive complexity of a single-switch forward.

lessons.workedExample: A single-switch forward converter runs off a 170V rectified-mains bulk rail with a 1:1 reset winding, targeting D≈0.4 to deliver an isolated 24V, 300W output (about 12.5A). At 300W this sits comfortably in forward's zone. If the same 24V rail instead needed 1.5kW, primary current would scale roughly with power at fixed Vin, so the single 170V switch would carry about 5x the current, and a single-switch forward's device also has to block roughly 2*170V=340V during Toff (the reflected reset voltage stacked on Vin) — a combination of current and voltage stress a single device cannot survive at this power. A full-bridge fixes the voltage half of that problem directly: each of its four switches blocks only Vin≈170V, since the other side of the primary is always clamped to a rail rather than floating up to 2Vin. The switches still conduct in diagonal pairs, so each conducting device carries close to the same order of primary current a single-switch design would — the win at 1.5kW comes from roughly halving the per-switch voltage stress and better utilizing the core with bipolar (rather than reset-limited) drive, not from dividing current four ways.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing this lesson wants to know whether a student can explain why a forward converter needs D<0.5 (core reset via the reset winding), not just state the constraint, and whether they can justify a power-level topology choice with a mechanism — switch voltage and current per device — rather than a memorized wattage number. A strong answer walks from the reset winding's job to the D<0.5 constraint to why a two-switch or bridge design removes it; a weak answer names 'forward' or 'bridge' correctly by pattern-matching power level without explaining the switch-stress reasoning behind it.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of the reset winding in a single-switch forward converter?

options.text: To return the core's magnetizing flux to (near) zero before the next Ton, preventing saturation
To regulate the output voltage directly
To provide isolated feedback to the controller
To filter output ripple current

explanations.a: Correct — the reset winding dumps magnetizing current back to the input rail after the switch opens, resetting flux so the next Ton starts from the same point instead of walking toward saturation.
explanations.b: Output regulation is handled by the feedback loop adjusting duty cycle, not by the reset winding.
explanations.c: Isolated feedback (if used) typically comes from an optocoupler or a bias winding sensed separately, not the reset winding's function.
explanations.d: Output ripple filtering is the job of the output inductor and capacitor on the secondary side, not the primary-side reset winding.

questions.prompt: Why does a two-switch forward converter not need the D<0.5 restriction that a single-switch forward has?

options.text: It resets via clamping diodes that return magnetizing current to Vin whenever both switches turn off together, regardless of duty cycle
It uses a larger core that never saturates
It runs at a much lower switching frequency
It eliminates the need for core reset entirely

explanations.a: Correct — both switches opening together lets the magnetizing current freewheel through two clamping diodes back to the input, resetting the core without the timing constraint a single reset winding imposes.
explanations.b: Core size affects flux swing headroom but does not by itself remove the need for reset or the D<0.5 constraint that comes from a single reset winding's timing.
explanations.c: Switching frequency is a separate design choice; it is not what removes the D<0.5 constraint.
explanations.d: Core reset is still required in a two-switch forward; it just happens through clamping diodes instead of a reset winding, not eliminated altogether.

questions.prompt: What is the root cause of push-pull's staircase-saturation failure mode?

options.text: Volt-second imbalance between the two alternating half-cycles accumulates a net DC flux bias cycle after cycle
The switching frequency is set too high for the core material
Leakage inductance is too large
The output capacitor's ESR is too high

explanations.a: Correct — any small asymmetry between the two half-cycles fails to cancel exactly, so a residual DC flux bias accumulates cycle by cycle until the core saturates.
explanations.b: Switching frequency choice affects core loss and size but is not the mechanism behind staircase saturation, which is about volt-second imbalance between half-cycles.
explanations.c: Leakage inductance causes voltage spikes and snubbing concerns, not the DC flux walk that defines staircase saturation.
explanations.d: Output capacitor ESR affects ripple voltage on the secondary side, unrelated to primary-side flux balance.

questions.prompt: In the worked example, if the same 24V rail needed to scale from 300W to 1.5kW, which topology better survives the resulting stress, and why?

options.text: Full-bridge, because each of its four switches blocks only Vin instead of the ~2Vin a single-switch forward's device sees, even though per-switch current stays roughly the same order as the single-switch design
The original single-switch forward, because its reset winding scales automatically with power
A flyback, because it has no output inductor to size for higher current
Neither; power level does not affect topology choice

explanations.a: Correct — as stated in the worked example, a full-bridge halves the per-switch voltage stress to Vin (instead of the ~2Vin a single-switch forward's reset winding produces), which is the mechanism that lets it survive thermally at 1.5kW; it does not divide current four ways, since diagonal switch pairs still each carry roughly the full primary current.
explanations.b: The reset winding's timing constraint (D<0.5) does not change with power, and the single switch would still have to carry the full scaled-up current alone.
explanations.c: Flyback is well suited to low power (roughly under 100-150W per the earlier lesson), not to a 1.5kW isolated rail.
explanations.d: Power level directly drives per-switch current and voltage stress, which is exactly what determines which topology is thermally and electrically viable.

questions.prompt: Order the core-flux states of a single-switch forward converter over one switching period.

items.text: Switch closes; flux ramps up while the primary drives the secondary directly
Switch opens
Reset winding conducts, returning magnetizing current to Vin while flux ramps back down
Flux returns to (near) zero before the next switch closure

questions.explanation: Power transfer and flux buildup happen while the switch is closed; once it opens, the reset winding must actively bring the flux back down to zero before the cycle can safely repeat.

lessons.label: Cuk, SEPIC, and Charge Pumps

sections.heading: Cuk: moving energy through a capacitor, not a gap in an inductor
sections.body: Slobodan Cuk, whose 1977 Caltech dissertation on modeling and design of switching converters introduced the topology that bears his name, built a converter with two inductors — one on the input side, one on the output side — linked by a series coupling capacitor that does the actual work of transferring energy between them; a switch and diode alternate connecting that capacitor between the two inductor loops. The gain works out to the same buck-boost magnitude, Vout=-D/(1-D)*Vin, inverting like buck-boost, but because both inductors sit directly in series with their own port, the Cuk converter gets continuous, low-ripple current at both the input and the output simultaneously — something none of buck, boost, or buck-boost alone achieves. That combination suited applications where both low input ripple (source protection, EMI) and low output ripple mattered, at the cost of two inductors, a capacitor sized for the full transferred power's ripple current, and a polarity inversion to design around.

sections.heading: SEPIC: the same trick, no inversion
sections.body: SEPIC (single-ended primary-inductor converter) rearranges the same coupling-capacitor idea but repositions the output diode and inductor so the output is non-inverted, and critically, Vout is reachable whether Vin sits above or below it — duty cycle simply crosses D=0.5 at the point where Vin equals Vout, with no change in topology. That makes SEPIC the standard choice for a battery rail that straddles the output, such as a single Li-ion cell (roughly 4.2V full to 3.0V empty) feeding a fixed 3.3V rail: a plain buck fails once the cell droops below 3.3V, and a plain boost fails while the cell still sits above 3.3V near full charge, but a SEPIC just slides its duty cycle across 0.5 as the cell discharges and keeps regulating the whole way.

sections.heading: Charge pumps: no inductor at all
sections.body: The Dickson charge pump, published by J. F. Dickson in the IEEE Journal of Solid-State Circuits in 1976, does DC-DC conversion with only capacitors and diodes or switches, no magnetics, by shuttling charge between a cascade of pump capacitors on alternating clock phases; each stage bumps the voltage up by roughly one input voltage, so an N-stage pump ideally multiplies Vin by about N. With no inductor to enforce current flow, output voltage sags under load in a way that behaves like a fixed output resistance — roughly 1/(fsw*Cpump) per stage — even though no physical resistor exists; the pump simply cannot move charge fast enough at high current draw. That makes charge pumps a good fit only for light, well-defined loads such as bias or gate-drive rails and small voltage doublers, inductorless and cheap but sharply load-limited.

lessons.workedExample: A 3.7V-nominal Li-ion cell (4.2V full to 3.0V near-empty) feeds a fixed 3.3V rail. A plain buck works at 4.2V (D=3.3/4.2=0.786) but cannot reach 3.3V once Vin drops below it; a SEPIC handles the whole range instead, with D=Vout/(Vout+Vin) sliding from 3.3/(3.3+4.2)≈0.44 at full charge to 3.3/(3.3+3.0)≈0.52 near empty, never leaving regulation. Separately, a 3-stage Dickson charge pump generating a small 3.3V-to-~9V gate-bias rail at 2mA, with Cpump=100nF and fsw=1MHz, has an effective resistance of about 1/(1e6*100e-9)=10 ohm per stage, or roughly 30 ohm across 3 stages — at 2mA that is only about 60mV of sag, fine for a bias rail, but the same pump asked for 200mA would sag around 6V, making it useless at that current.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks why a student chose SEPIC over a plain buck or boost for a battery application specifically to check whether the student names the mechanism: the input range straddling the output voltage, with duty cycle crossing 0.5 at the crossover point. A strong answer can state roughly where D sits at each end of the battery's range; a weak answer just says 'SEPIC is more flexible.'
