For charge pumps, a strong answer recognizes the effective output resistance as the real limiting factor rather than treating the pump as a magic voltage multiplier with no current limit.

questions.prompt: What allows a Cuk converter to have continuous, low-ripple current at both its input and output ports simultaneously?

options.text: Two inductors, one in series with each port, with a coupling capacitor doing the energy transfer between them
A single large inductor shared between input and output
Two capacitors in place of both inductors
A transformer providing galvanic isolation

explanations.a: Correct — each port has its own inductor directly in series with it, so both input and output current stay continuous, while the coupling capacitor between the two inductor loops does the actual energy transfer.
explanations.b: A single shared inductor is characteristic of buck, boost, and buck-boost, not Cuk, and would not give continuous current at both ports independently.
explanations.c: Cuk uses inductors at both ports plus one coupling capacitor, not two capacitors replacing the inductors entirely.
explanations.d: Cuk is a non-isolated topology; it has no transformer providing galvanic isolation.

questions.prompt: Why is SEPIC specifically well suited to a Li-ion cell (3.0V to 4.2V) feeding a fixed 3.3V rail?

options.text: Because Vin straddles Vout across the discharge curve, and SEPIC's duty cycle simply crosses 0.5 at the point where Vin=Vout without changing topology
Because SEPIC always has higher efficiency than a buck or boost
Because SEPIC does not require an inductor
Because SEPIC inverts the output polarity, which the battery needs

explanations.a: Correct — as the worked example shows, D moves from about 0.44 to about 0.52 across the cell's full range, staying in regulation the whole time, which neither a plain buck nor a plain boost can do alone.
explanations.b: Efficiency is not universally higher for SEPIC; it is chosen here for its input-range flexibility, not a general efficiency advantage.
explanations.c: SEPIC uses two inductors (or a coupled equivalent), not zero; charge pumps are the inductorless option in this lesson.
explanations.d: SEPIC is non-inverting, unlike Cuk; polarity is not the reason it is chosen here.

questions.prompt: What fundamentally limits how much current a Dickson charge pump can supply before its output sags badly?

options.text: Its effective output resistance, set by how much charge the pump capacitors can move per switching cycle
Inductor core saturation
Zener breakdown of the pump capacitors
Thermal runaway of the diodes at any load

explanations.a: Correct — with no inductor to enforce current, the pump's finite per-cycle charge transfer behaves like a fixed output resistance, roughly 1/(fsw*Cpump) per stage, that determines how much the output sags under load.
explanations.b: Charge pumps contain no inductors, so core saturation does not apply to them.
explanations.c: Pump capacitors are not being driven toward Zener-type breakdown; the limiting behavior is resistive sag, not breakdown.
explanations.d: Thermal runaway is not the described mechanism; the limitation described is the effective output resistance from finite charge transfer.

questions.prompt: Match each topology to its defining energy-transfer mechanism.

right.text: Capacitive energy transfer between two port-side inductors, inverting output
Capacitive-coupled transfer, non-inverting, spans Vin above and below Vout
Cascaded pump capacitors clocked on alternating phases, no magnetics
Single inductor storing and releasing energy each cycle, inverting output

questions.explanation: Cuk transfers energy through a capacitor between two inductors and inverts; SEPIC uses the same capacitive-coupling idea but stays non-inverting and spans Vin on either side of Vout; the Dickson pump uses only clocked capacitors and diodes; and buck-boost, the baseline these all extend, stores energy in a single inductor and inverts.

questions.prompt: Order the events of one pump-capacitor stage in a Dickson charge pump across its two clock phases.

items.text: Clock phase low: the stage capacitor charges toward Vin through its diode or switch
Clock phase flips high: the capacitor's top plate is bootstrapped up by roughly one Vin
The boosted charge passes through the next diode or switch into the following stage's capacitor
The process cascades stage to stage, each adding roughly one Vin to the running total

questions.explanation: Each stage first charges toward the input voltage, then gets bootstrapped up by the clock transition, then hands that boosted charge to the next stage, and the cascade of identical stages is what produces the overall N-times multiplication.

lessons.label: Choosing a Topology on Purpose

sections.heading: The four questions that actually narrow it down
sections.body: Before touching a datasheet, four questions eliminate most of the topology space. Does Vin sit only above Vout, only below, or does it straddle Vout across the operating range? Does the application need galvanic isolation — mains-connected equipment, patient-touch circuits, or anything bridging two grounds that must never fault together? What power level, since that sets how many switches and windings the design can afford thermally and in part count? And what is the cost and part-count budget, given that a single-inductor non-isolated design is always cheaper than a transformer-isolated one for the same power when isolation is not required? Answering these four, in this order, prunes the field before a single efficiency number gets computed.

sections.heading: Case one, worked in full: 12V to 3.3V at 5A
sections.body: Vin sits always above Vout, no isolation is required, and the load is 16.5W — squarely a non-isolated buck, D=3.3/12=0.275. Rectification choice matters more than topology choice here: a 0.4V Schottky diode would waste 0.4*5*(1-0.275)=1.45W, about 9% of the 16.5W output, while an 8mOhm synchronous FET wastes only 5^2*0.008*0.725≈0.15W, under 1% — a roughly 10x difference that alone justifies the extra sync-FET and driver part count at this power level. A sync-buck IC in the 500kHz-1MHz range with a few-uH inductor comfortably clears 90%+ efficiency here, which is why sync-buck ICs for exactly this conversion are a commodity product category.

sections.heading: Case two and case three: isolation and a straddling range
sections.body: A 5V-to-400V isolated bias supply for something like an image-sensor or PMT bias needs isolation and an 80x step-up at very low power — comfortably under the flyback zone of roughly 100-150W, likely under 1W here. A forward or push-pull would need an extreme turns ratio and still fight core-reset or staircase-saturation constraints at this ratio and power; a flyback handles a large step-up at low power far more simply, at the cost of the cross-regulation and snubber design already covered. Sizing the flyback concretely: at D≈0.5 the CCM gain relation N*D/(1-D)≈80 needs N=Ns/Np≈80, and the reflected voltage that stresses the primary switch is Vout/N≈400/80=5V, giving a modest Vin+Vout/N≈5+5=10V switch-blocking requirement before the leakage spike — so the turns ratio, not the switch voltage rating, is the part of this design that is actually extreme, since winding an 80:1 transformer with low leakage inductance and acceptable interwinding capacitance at 400V isolation is the real engineering fight. Separately, a 2-cell battery pack (about 6.0V near-empty to 8.4V full charge, non-isolated — two Li-ion cells in series at 3.0V and 4.2V per cell) holding a fixed 6.0V rail straddles the output across its discharge curve exactly like a single Li-ion cell straddling 3.3V: no single-direction converter covers that range without dropping regulation near one end, so among the topologies this course covers, a SEPIC (or a four-switch non-inverting buck-boost) is needed — a single-direction buck or boost alone cannot cover the range.

lessons.workedExample: Walking the 12V-to-3.3V/5A case end to end: D=3.3/12=0.275. Diode-rectified conduction loss is 0.4V*5A*(1-0.275)=1.45W (about 9% of the 16.5W output); an 8mOhm synchronous FET instead loses I^2*Rds(on)*(1-D)=25*0.008*0.725≈0.145W (under 1%). That roughly 10x conduction-loss gap, not a general reputation for being 'more efficient,' is the actual number that justifies paying for the extra FET and gate driver at this power level — exactly the kind of stress equation that should back up a topology and rectification choice on a fair-project poster.
lessons.judgeFraming: This is the integration lesson, so the judge probes whether a student can walk from application requirements — voltage range, isolation, power level — to a specific topology and back that choice with a real number, rather than pattern-matching a circuit they have seen before. A weak answer names 'buck' or 'flyback' correctly but cannot say why the alternative fails; a strong answer eliminates alternatives with a specific figure, such as the diode-versus-sync-FET loss fraction, the turns-ratio-driven switch stress, or the duty-cycle range a straddling battery actually requires.

questions.prompt: For a 12V-to-3.3V, 5A, non-isolated conversion, which topology and rectification choice is justified, and by what number?

options.text: A synchronous buck, justified by roughly a 10x reduction in conduction loss versus a diode-rectified buck
A flyback, justified by the need for galvanic isolation
A SEPIC, justified by the input range straddling the output
A diode-rectified buck, justified by lower part count

explanations.a: Correct — the worked example shows about 1.45W lost with a diode versus about 0.145W with a synchronous FET, roughly a 10x difference that justifies the extra part count.
explanations.b: This case has no isolation requirement (Vin and Vout share a ground reference), so flyback's isolation is unnecessary complexity here.
explanations.c: Vin (12V) is always above Vout (3.3V) in this case; the input range does not straddle the output, so SEPIC's key advantage is not needed.
explanations.d: Lower part count is real, but at 3.3V the diode's fixed drop costs about 9% of output power, which the worked example shows a synchronous FET avoids for a small added cost.

questions.prompt: Why does a 5V-to-400V isolated low-power bias supply favor a flyback over a forward or push-pull converter?

options.text: A flyback handles a large step-up ratio at low power without the core-reset or staircase-saturation constraints that an extreme turns ratio would aggravate in forward or push-pull
Forward and push-pull converters cannot provide galvanic isolation
Flyback always has lower switch voltage stress than forward converters
400V outputs require a charge pump, not a transformer-based topology

explanations.a: Correct — at very low power (well under the flyback zone), the simplicity of flyback's single switch and transformer outweighs the core-reset and staircase concerns an 80x turns ratio would sharpen in forward or push-pull.
explanations.b: Forward and push-pull are both isolated, through-transfer topologies; isolation is not the differentiator here, power level and turns-ratio extremity are.
explanations.c: Flyback's reflected-voltage stress depends on turns ratio and Vout just as forward's does; it is not universally lower.
explanations.d: A charge pump is inductorless and load-limited (from an earlier lesson); it is not the tool for an isolated, transformer-based 400V bias rail.

questions.prompt: For a 2-cell battery pack (about 6.0V to 8.4V) holding a fixed 6.0V rail, why does neither a plain buck nor a plain boost work alone?

options.text: Vin straddles Vout across the discharge curve, so a buck fails once Vin drops below 6.0V and a boost fails while Vin is still above 6.0V
Neither topology can be built without a transformer
6.0V is too low a voltage for any switching converter to regulate
The battery's internal resistance is too high for any inductor-based converter

explanations.a: Correct — this is the same straddling problem as a Li-ion cell around 3.3V: a buck alone cannot reach 6.0V once Vin dips below it, and a boost alone cannot regulate down to 6.0V while Vin is still above it.
explanations.b: Both buck and boost are non-isolated, transformer-free topologies; a transformer is not the missing ingredient.
explanations.c: 6.0V is a perfectly ordinary regulation target for switching converters; voltage level is not the obstacle here.
explanations.d: Battery internal resistance affects available current, not whether a single-direction converter can straddle the output voltage.

questions.prompt: Order the four questions used to narrow down a topology before computing any efficiency numbers.

items.text: Does Vin sit only above Vout, only below, or does it straddle Vout?
Is galvanic isolation required?
What is the power level?
What is the cost and part-count budget?

questions.explanation: This order moves from the constraint that rules topologies in or out entirely (voltage-range relationship), through isolation and power level which set the topology family and switch count, and ends with cost and part count, which is the final tiebreaker once the family is already narrowed.

questions.prompt: Match each case study to the topology chosen for it.

left.text: 2-cell battery pack (about 6.0V to 8.4V) holding a fixed 6.0V rail

right.text: Synchronous buck
Flyback
SEPIC

questions.explanation: Case one is a simple non-isolated step-down where synchronous rectification pays for itself; case two needs isolation and a large step-up at low power, which flyback handles simply; case three straddles its output voltage across the battery's discharge range, which a single-direction buck or boost cannot cover without dropping regulation — SEPIC (or a four-switch buck-boost) is needed.

units.label: Switching Devices, Losses, and Thermal Design

lessons.label: Power MOSFETs and Their Datasheet

sections.heading: Rds(on): a resistance that climbs with heat
sections.body: A power MOSFET's on-resistance, Rds(on), is the number most students reach for first, but a single 25 C value is misleading. Rds(on) has a strongly positive temperature coefficient: as the silicon warms, carrier mobility drops and resistance rises, typically 1.7-2x from 25 C to a 125 C junction on a modern trench or superjunction part. This matters twice over. First, it means conduction loss is a moving target across a design's thermal cycle, so a loss budget built only on the datasheet's 25 C table under-predicts real losses. Second, the positive coefficient is a safety feature: if one die in a paralleled pair runs hotter and draws more current, its resistance rises and pushes current back to the cooler die, giving passive current sharing that a negative-coefficient device would not.

sections.heading: Gate charge, Coss, and the body diode
sections.body: Total gate charge Qg (and the Miller portion Qgd, the charge needed to slew the drain while the gate voltage plateaus) sets how much current a driver must source to switch the device in a given time, and Qg*fsw sets gate-drive power. Output capacitance Coss stores energy on every switching cycle regardless of load current; that energy is dissipated once per cycle and scales with fsw, so it becomes a real loss term above a few hundred kHz. Every MOSFET's body diode is a parasitic PN junction with a forward drop around 0.7-1.3 V, far worse than the channel, and when it has been conducting and is forced to turn off, it must sweep out stored minority carriers, a process characterized by reverse recovery charge Qrr. In synchronous rectifiers that Qrr shows up as a current spike through both devices at every turn-on edge.

sections.heading: Avalanche rating and the Rds(on)*Qg figure of merit
sections.body: The avalanche energy rating (often EAS, unclamped inductive switching energy) tells you how much energy the device can absorb when its drain voltage is driven briefly above breakdown by an inductive kick, a real event in switching converters with parasitic leakage inductance. It is a single-pulse rating, not a continuous one. Finally, because low Rds(on) and low Qg trade against each other within a given silicon process (a bigger die lowers resistance but raises capacitance and charge), engineers compare parts across vendors and process generations using the figure of merit Rds(on) x Qg: lower is better, and it is the standard way to say one part is genuinely a better switch rather than just a bigger one.

lessons.workedExample: A designer compares two 30 V MOSFETs for a 500 kHz synchronous buck: Part A has Rds(on) = 5 mOhm and Qg = 40 nC (FOM = 200); Part B has Rds(on) = 8 mOhm and Qg = 18 nC (FOM = 144). At 3 A rms, Part A's conduction loss is lower (45 mW vs 72 mW), but Part B's lower Qg cuts gate-drive and switching loss enough that its total loss at 500 kHz is smaller. At 100 kHz, the ranking flips and Part A wins because conduction dominates. The datasheet 25 C Rds(on) also needs correcting: at a 100 C junction, Part A's resistance is closer to 8.5 mOhm than 5 mOhm, changing the comparison again.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about Rds(on) and Qg to find out whether a student picked a MOSFET by browsing a distributor's cheapest-per-amp filter or actually reasoned about their switching frequency. A strong answer names the figure of merit, explains why it changes rank with frequency, and corrects Rds(on) for the expected junction temperature rather than quoting the 25 C datasheet number as if it were fixed. A weak answer treats Rds(on) as a single constant and cannot explain why a lower-resistance part might lose to a higher-resistance one in a high-frequency design.

questions.prompt: Roughly how much does a typical power MOSFET's Rds(on) increase from a 25 C to a 125 C junction?

options.text: It stays essentially constant
About 1.7-2x
About 10x
It decreases as the device warms

explanations.a: Rds(on) has a strong positive temperature coefficient in silicon MOSFETs; it does not stay flat.
explanations.b: Correct — carrier mobility falls as temperature rises, roughly doubling on-resistance between 25 C and a 125 C junction on typical parts.
explanations.c: A 10x rise would be extreme; real devices land in the 1.7-2x range over that temperature span.
explanations.d: It rises, not falls, with temperature — this is the opposite of the real behavior.

questions.prompt: Why does a MOSFET's positive Rds(on) temperature coefficient help when several devices are paralleled?

options.text: It has no effect on current sharing
A hotter die's rising resistance pushes current toward cooler, lower-resistance dies, balancing current
It cools the hottest die directly
It increases Qg on the hottest die so it switches faster

explanations.a: It has a direct, useful effect: it self-balances current across paralleled devices.
explanations.b: Correct — a die that runs hotter develops higher resistance, so it carries less current relative to cooler dies, a passive negative-feedback effect.
explanations.c: The coefficient affects electrical resistance, not thermal conduction directly.
explanations.d: Temperature affects Rds(on), not Qg, and this describes an unrelated mechanism.

questions.prompt: Match each MOSFET parameter to what it primarily determines.

right.text: Conduction loss at a given rms current
How long the drain voltage takes to slew during switching
Energy stored and dissipated once per switching cycle
Current spike through both devices at synchronous-rectifier turn-on

questions.explanation: Rds(on) sets I^2R conduction loss; Qgd is the charge that must be delivered while the drain voltage slews (the Miller plateau); Coss stores and releases energy each switching cycle; Qrr is the stored charge that produces a current spike when a conducting body diode is forced to turn off.

questions.prompt: What does the figure of merit Rds(on) x Qg let an engineer compare?

options.text: Only the raw die cost of two parts
How well a part balances conduction loss against switching-related loss, independent of die size
The avalanche energy rating of a part
The body-diode forward voltage

explanations.a: The FOM is an electrical performance metric, not a cost metric.
explanations.b: Correct — since a bigger die lowers Rds(on) but raises Qg, multiplying them gives a size-independent way to compare how well different process generations or vendors trade the two off.
explanations.c: Avalanche energy is a separate, unrelated rating (EAS).
explanations.d: Body-diode forward voltage is a separate parasitic-diode parameter, not part of this figure of merit.

lessons.label: Diodes, IGBTs, and Wide-Bandgap Devices

sections.heading: Schottky vs ultrafast silicon: a voltage ceiling problem
sections.body: A Schottky diode is a metal-semiconductor junction, a majority-carrier device with no stored minority charge, so it has essentially no reverse recovery and a low forward drop, roughly 0.3-0.5 V. Its catch is leakage current, which rises sharply with both reverse voltage and temperature, and a practical silicon Schottky voltage ceiling around 150-200 V, past which leakage and reverse-bias power loss become unacceptable. Above that ceiling, designers switch to ultrafast silicon PN diodes: minority-carrier devices with a higher forward drop (around 1-1.5 V) but engineered for a short, controlled reverse-recovery time (tens of nanoseconds) so the Qrr penalty at turn-off stays manageable at the higher voltages Schottky diodes cannot reach.

sections.heading: IGBTs and the tail current
sections.body: An insulated-gate bipolar transistor combines a MOSFET gate with a bipolar output stage, giving low conduction loss at high voltage because the bipolar junction supports voltage without needing the thick, resistive drift region a high-voltage MOSFET would need. The cost is a tail current: when the gate turns off, the minority carriers flooding the drift region cannot be swept out instantly and must instead recombine, so collector current decays over a tail lasting hundreds of nanoseconds to microseconds, dissipating real energy on every turn-off. This tail is largely frequency-independent in duration, so its loss scales directly with switching frequency, which is why IGBTs dominate above roughly 600 V at low switching frequencies (motor drives, welders, a few kHz to a few tens of kHz) where their low conduction loss wins, while MOSFETs win at high frequency because they have no tail at all.

sections.heading: Wide-bandgap devices change the trade
sections.body: Silicon carbide has a critical electric field roughly 10x that of silicon (about 2-3 MV/cm vs 0.2-0.3 MV/cm), which lets a SiC MOSFET support the same blocking voltage with a much thinner, less resistive drift region, giving dramatically lower Rds(on) per unit voltage than a comparable silicon device. SiC MOSFETs today are the mainstream choice in the 650-1700 V range, in EV traction inverters and solar strings. Gallium nitride HEMTs are lateral, majority-carrier devices with essentially no body diode and no reverse recovery at all, dominant from about 40-650 V, prized in fast chargers and compact power supplies where switching frequency and size matter most. Both remain more expensive per amp than silicon, though the gap has been closing steadily as fab volume grows.

lessons.workedExample: A 400 V, 20 kHz motor-drive inverter and a 400 V, 300 kHz DC-DC converter both need a switch rated above the silicon-MOSFET comfort zone. For the 20 kHz drive, an IGBT is the natural pick: its tail current fires only 20,000 times per second, so total tail-related loss stays small next to its low Vce(sat) conduction loss. For the 300 kHz converter, the same IGBT would pay its tail-current penalty 300,000 times per second, ballooning switching loss — a SiC MOSFET (or, if voltage allowed, a GaN HEMT) is the better choice because it has no tail current at all and its low-Rds(on)-for-the-voltage-class construction keeps conduction loss competitive.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask why a project chose an IGBT over a MOSFET, or a SiC part over silicon, to see whether the student understands the actual physical trade-off rather than repeating 'IGBTs are for high power.' A strong answer names the tail current explicitly, ties it to switching frequency, and can state roughly where the crossover sits (around 600 V, low tens of kHz). A weak answer says IGBTs are simply 'better for high voltage' with no mechanism, or cannot explain why a wide-bandgap device costs more but might still be worth it.

questions.prompt: Why does a silicon Schottky diode have essentially no reverse-recovery loss?

options.text: It is a majority-carrier device with no significant stored minority charge to sweep out
It has an unusually thick drift region
Its forward voltage is higher than a PN diode's
It operates only at low frequency

explanations.a: Correct — the metal-semiconductor junction conducts via majority carriers only, so there is no stored minority charge to remove at turn-off.
explanations.b: Drift region thickness relates to voltage rating, not the reverse-recovery mechanism.
explanations.c: Schottky forward voltage (0.3-0.5 V) is actually lower than a PN diode's, and this is unrelated to recovery behavior.
explanations.d: Its fast recovery is exactly what makes it well-suited to high frequency, not a limitation to low frequency.

questions.prompt: What physically causes an IGBT's tail current at turn-off?

options.text: Gate charge Qgd being unusually large
Minority carriers flooding the drift region that must recombine rather than being swept out instantly
Output capacitance Coss discharging
Avalanche breakdown at the drain

explanations.a: Gate charge affects switching speed generally but is not the source of the tail current itself.
explanations.b: Correct — the bipolar output stage relies on injected minority carriers to support current; when the gate turns off, those carriers can only leave by recombination, producing a decaying tail.
explanations.c: Coss is a MOSFET/capacitive parameter and is not the mechanism behind bipolar tail current.
explanations.d: Avalanche breakdown is an overvoltage failure mode, unrelated to normal turn-off tail behavior.

questions.prompt: Match each device to the voltage/frequency niche where it is typically the strongest choice.

right.text: Below about 150-200 V, any frequency
Above about 600 V, low switching frequency (few kHz-tens of kHz)
About 650-1700 V, high switching frequency
About 40-650 V, very high switching frequency, compact designs

questions.explanation: Silicon Schottky diodes are limited to roughly 150-200 V by leakage; IGBTs win above ~600 V at low frequency because their tail-current loss stays small; SiC MOSFETs cover 650-1700 V at high frequency with low Rds(on) for the voltage class; GaN HEMTs dominate 40-650 V where switching frequency and size matter most.

questions.prompt: SiC's critical electric field is roughly how many times that of silicon, and what design benefit does that give a SiC MOSFET?

options.text: About 10x higher, allowing a thinner drift region and lower Rds(on) at a given blocking voltage
About 10x lower, requiring a thicker drift region
Roughly equal to silicon, so the benefit is purely thermal
About 10x higher, but this only affects switching speed, not resistance

explanations.a: Correct — a critical field roughly 10x silicon's (about 2-3 MV/cm vs 0.2-0.3 MV/cm) lets the drift region be much thinner for the same blocking voltage, cutting its resistance.
explanations.b: SiC's critical field is higher, not lower, than silicon's — this reverses the real relationship.
explanations.c: The critical field difference is substantial, not negligible, and it drives an electrical benefit, not merely a thermal one.
explanations.d: The thinner drift region directly lowers Rds(on); it is not limited to a speed effect alone.

lessons.label: Where the Watts Go: Loss Accounting

sections.heading: Six loss terms live on the switch pair
sections.body: A synchronous buck's semiconductor losses split into six terms with independent physics. Conduction loss is Irms^2 x Rds(on), the ordinary resistive loss while a channel is on, and it depends on rms current, not average — for a high-side switch with duty cycle D, Irms is roughly Iout x sqrt(D). Switching loss is approximately 0.5 x Vds x Id x (tr + tf) x fsw, the overlap energy of voltage and current during the finite rise and fall time, paid every time the switch transitions and therefore proportional to frequency. Gate-drive loss is Qg x Vgs x fsw, the energy the driver dumps into charging and discharging the gate capacitance each cycle. Output-capacitance loss is 0.5 x Coss x V^2 x fsw, energy stored on Coss and dissipated resistively every cycle regardless of load. Whichever switch's body diode conducts during the dead time between one FET's turn-off and the other's turn-on pays Vf x Id x t_deadtime x fsw, using the body diode's much higher forward drop instead of the channel resistance. A sixth term rides along with that dead-time conduction: once the opposite switch turns back on, it forces the conducting body diode to recover, sweeping out its stored reverse-recovery charge Qrr and adding P_rr = Qrr x Vin x fsw — a term set by the diode's recovery charge and the input voltage rather than by Rds(on) or gate charge, and one that grows with frequency just like switching and Coss loss.

sections.heading: The inductor is not free either
sections.body: The output inductor adds two more terms: DCR loss, Irms^2 x DCR from the winding's copper resistance including ripple current, and core loss, the hysteresis and eddy-current dissipation the switching ripple's flux swing drives in the magnetic core. Core loss is not just a chart lookup — it follows the same Steinmetz relationship this unit's magnetics lesson introduces, P = k x f^a x B^b, where k, a, and b are material constants fit to the manufacturer's loss curves (a typically around 1.5-2.7, b around 2-3). Because b outruns a, core loss grows faster with peak flux swing than with switching frequency, which is why a first-pass estimate still starts from the datasheet curve rather than a guessed constant, but can then be extrapolated to a nearby operating point instead of re-read off the chart every time.

sections.heading: Building the full budget
sections.body: Building a full loss budget means summing all eight terms for a specific operating point — input voltage, output voltage, load current, and switching frequency — because none of them scale together: conduction loss and DCR loss fall as Rds(on) and winding resistance drop, but switching, Coss, gate-drive, reverse-recovery, and core loss all rise with frequency, so the design that minimizes one component's loss is rarely the one that minimizes total loss. In practice this means computing every term at the same operating point, ranking them by size, and re-checking that ranking whenever frequency, input voltage, or load changes: a term that is negligible at 100 kHz, like Coss or reverse-recovery loss, can become one of the two or three largest contributors once frequency triples, while a term that dominates at heavy load, like conduction loss, can fall behind the frequency-driven terms at light load.

lessons.workedExample: A 12 V to 5 V, 3 A synchronous buck at 500 kHz, duty cycle D = 5/12 = 0.417. High-side FET (Rds(on) = 30 mOhm, tr+tf = 20 ns): Irms = 3 x sqrt(0.417) = 1.94 A, conduction = 1.94^2 x 0.03 = 0.11 W; switching = 0.5 x 12 x 3 x 20e-9 x 500e3 = 0.18 W. Low-side FET (Rds(on) = 15 mOhm): Irms = 3 x sqrt(0.583) = 2.29 A, conduction = 2.29^2 x 0.015 = 0.08 W. Gate loss for both FETs (Qg = 10 nC and 15 nC, Vgs = 5 V): 25e-9 x 5 x 500e3 = 0.06 W. Coss loss (200 pF combined, 12 V): 0.5 x 200e-12 x 144 x 500e3 = 0.007 W. Dead-time diode conduction (20 ns x 2 edges, Vf = 0.7 V): 0.04 W. Reverse-recovery loss (Qrr = 5 nC on the low-side body diode): 5e-9 x 12 x 500e3 = 0.03 W. Inductor DCR loss (DCR = 20 mOhm): 3^2 x 0.02 = 0.18 W. Inductor core loss from the Steinmetz curve (k, a=1.9, b=2.3 fit to the datasheet, at this flux swing and frequency): about 0.05 W. Total loss = 0.11+0.18+0.08+0.06+0.007+0.04+0.03+0.18+0.05 = 0.74 W, giving efficiency = 15 W / 15.74 W = about 95%.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'where does your converter's lost power actually go' is testing whether efficiency is a measured, decomposed number or a single figure copied from a simulator. A strong answer breaks the loss into named terms — conduction, switching, gate, Coss, dead-time diode, reverse-recovery, inductor DCR and core — and can say which term dominates at their specific operating point. A weak answer states one overall efficiency percentage with no ability to say whether conduction or switching loss is bigger, or confuses average current with rms current in the conduction-loss formula.

questions.prompt: In the buck converter worked example, what is the approximate high-side MOSFET's rms current, given Iout = 3 A and D = 0.417?

options.text: 3.0 A, the same as the output current

explanations.a: The high-side switch only conducts during the on-time fraction D, so its rms current is less than the full output current.
explanations.b: Correct — Irms = Iout x sqrt(D) = 3 x sqrt(0.417) is approximately 1.94 A.
explanations.c: This does not match sqrt(0.417) x 3; it appears to use the wrong scaling.
explanations.d: This is just D itself, not the rms-current formula applied to the output current.

questions.prompt: Order these loss terms by the physical quantity they depend on, from a term that exists even with zero load current, to one that scales with rms current squared.

items.text: Coss loss: 0.5 x Coss x V^2 x fsw
Gate-drive loss: Qg x Vgs x fsw
Dead-time diode conduction: Vf x Id x t_deadtime x fsw
Conduction loss: Irms^2 x Rds(on)

questions.explanation: Coss and gate-drive losses depend only on voltage/charge and frequency, not load current, so they persist near zero load. Dead-time diode conduction scales linearly with load current. Conduction loss scales with the square of rms current, making it the most current-dependent term.

questions.prompt: Why does dead-time diode conduction use Vf (body-diode forward drop) instead of Rds(on) in its loss formula?

options.text: During dead time neither MOSFET channel is on, so current flows through the body diode's PN junction instead
Rds(on) is undefined during dead time
It is a typo and Rds(on) should be used instead
The body diode replaces the channel permanently after the first dead-time event

explanations.a: Correct — with both gate drives off during dead time, the inductor current has nowhere to go but through whichever body diode is forward-biased, and that junction drops Vf rather than an Rds(on)-scaled voltage.
explanations.b: Rds(on) is a device property that exists regardless; the issue is that the channel simply is not conducting, not that the parameter is undefined.
explanations.c: This is the correct, standard physics, not an error — dead-time conduction genuinely goes through the diode.
explanations.d: The channel resumes conducting normally as soon as the gate turns back on; there is no permanent diode takeover.

questions.prompt: In the worked example's full loss budget, roughly what efficiency does the 0.74 W total loss imply at 15 W output power?

options.text: About 95%
About 99.9%
About 80%
About 50%

explanations.a: Correct — 15 W / (15 W + 0.74 W) is approximately 95%, matching the worked example's stated result.
explanations.b: 0.74 W of loss on 15 W output is far too large a fraction to reach 99.9% efficiency.
explanations.c: 80% would require roughly 3.75 W of loss, more than five times what was budgeted here.
explanations.d: 50% would require loss equal to output power, wildly larger than the 0.74 W computed.

lessons.label: Gate Drivers, Dead Time, and Shoot-Through

sections.heading: Getting drive to a floating high side
sections.body: In a half-bridge, the high-side MOSFET's source sits on the switching node, not ground, so its gate drive must float with it. The cheap, common answer is a bootstrap circuit: a small capacitor charges toward the driver's supply through a diode whenever the low-side switch is on and the switching node is near ground, then that charged capacitor becomes the floating supply for the high-side driver on the next cycle. It is simple and low-cost but has a duty-cycle limit — if the high side stays on too long without a refresh window, the bootstrap capacitor droops and drive weakens. When duty cycle must approach 100 percent, or true galvanic isolation is required, designers instead use an isolated supply, typically a small transformer-coupled or isolated DC-DC converter dedicated to the high-side driver, which has no refresh requirement.

sections.heading: The Miller plateau and false turn-on
sections.body: During a MOSFET's turn-on or turn-off, gate voltage does not rise smoothly; it pauses at a plateau while the driver's current is entirely consumed charging the drain-to-gate (Miller) capacitance Cgd as the drain voltage slews. This plateau is the danger window: if the complementary switch on the same leg turns on while this device is off, the switching node's fast dV/dt drives current through this device's Cgd onto its gate node. If the driver's off-state pulldown impedance is too high, that induced current can push the gate above threshold and turn the device on when it should be off — false turn-on — momentarily shorting the bridge. The fix is a driver with a low, strong pulldown impedance (or a negative off-state gate bias) so induced Miller current is shunted away rather than raising gate voltage.

sections.heading: Gate resistance, dead time, and shoot-through
sections.body: Gate resistance Rg is a direct trade: smaller Rg delivers gate current faster, cutting tr, tf, and switching loss, but the resulting higher dV/dt and di/dt drive more ringing and EMI, and can worsen Miller-coupled false turn-on. Dead time, the deliberate gap where both switches are held off during a transition, must also be tuned: too short risks the two devices overlapping (shoot-through), while too long forces current through a body diode at its high Vf for longer than necessary, adding avoidable conduction loss — some drivers implement adaptive dead-time control that shortens the gap based on sensed switch-node voltage. Shoot-through itself, both devices conducting simultaneously, creates a near-short across the supply rail and is a destructive failure mode: without external current limiting it can destroy both devices in microseconds.

lessons.workedExample: A half-bridge driver with weak 10-ohm off-state pulldown drives a low-side MOSFET with Cgd = 80 pF next to a high-side switch turning on at dV/dt = 5 V/ns. The induced Miller current is roughly Cgd x dV/dt = 80e-12 x 5e9 = 0.4 A, which through the 10-ohm pulldown produces a 4 V bump on the gate node — enough to exceed a 2-3 V threshold and cause false turn-on. Swapping to a driver with a 1-ohm strong pulldown drops the induced bump to 0.4 V, safely below threshold, eliminating the shoot-through path without touching dead time at all.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe dead time and gate drivers because shoot-through is the classic 'it worked on the bench and then died' failure, and asking about it separates a student who only tuned for efficiency from one who understands the failure mode they were guarding against. A strong answer explains the Miller-coupling mechanism by name and states a specific fix (pulldown impedance, gate resistance, or dead-time value) rather than a vague 'we added dead time.' A weak answer cannot explain why false turn-on happens at all, or treats dead time as an arbitrary safety margin with no cost.

questions.prompt: Why does a bootstrap high-side gate supply have a duty-cycle limitation that an isolated supply does not?

options.text: The bootstrap capacitor can only recharge while the low-side switch is on, pulling the switching node near ground
Bootstrap circuits cannot deliver enough peak current at any duty cycle
Isolated supplies are actually slower to respond
Bootstrap diodes fail above 50 percent duty cycle by design

explanations.a: Correct — the bootstrap capacitor only refreshes during the low-side on-time; if the high side stays on continuously with little or no low-side time, the capacitor droops and cannot sustain drive.
explanations.b: Peak current capability is a separate driver-sizing question, not the source of the duty-cycle limitation.
explanations.c: Isolated supplies are not inherently slower; their advantage here is having no refresh requirement at all.
explanations.d: There is no fixed 50 percent threshold; the real constraint is how long the capacitor goes without a recharge window relative to its droop rate.

questions.prompt: What causes 'false turn-on' of an off-state MOSFET during its complementary switch's fast dV/dt transition?

options.text: Excess Qrr in the body diode
Current through Cgd, induced by the dV/dt, raising the gate above threshold through a too-high off-state pulldown impedance
The bootstrap capacitor discharging too quickly
Core loss in the output inductor

explanations.a: Qrr relates to reverse-recovery loss during diode turn-off, not to gate-voltage disturbance from a neighboring switch's transition.
explanations.b: Correct — the fast dV/dt at the switching node couples current through Cgd onto the off device's gate, and a weak pulldown lets that current raise gate voltage past threshold.
explanations.c: Bootstrap droop affects high-side drive strength over many cycles, not the fast single-transition coupling event described here.
explanations.d: Core loss is a magnetics phenomenon unrelated to gate-node voltage disturbances.

questions.prompt: What is the trade-off of choosing a smaller gate resistance Rg?

options.text: Faster switching and lower switching loss, but more ringing, EMI, and risk of Miller-coupled false turn-on
Slower switching with no other effect
Lower conduction loss only
No trade-off; smaller Rg is strictly better

explanations.a: Correct — smaller Rg speeds the gate charge/discharge, cutting switching loss, but the resulting higher dV/dt and di/dt increase ringing, EMI, and the risk of Miller-induced false turn-on elsewhere on the leg.
explanations.b: Smaller Rg speeds switching; it does not slow it.
explanations.c: Rg does not directly set Rds(on)-driven conduction loss; its main effect is on switching behavior.
explanations.d: There is a real trade-off — faster is not free, which is exactly why Rg is a tunable design choice.

questions.prompt: Match each dead-time choice or gate-drive symptom to its consequence.

right.text: Increased risk of shoot-through overlap
Extra body-diode conduction loss
Higher susceptibility to Miller-induced false turn-on
Near-short across the supply rail that can destroy devices in microseconds

questions.explanation: Too-short dead time risks the two switches overlapping; too-long dead time wastes energy in body-diode conduction; a weak pulldown lets Miller current falsely turn on the off device; and actual shoot-through creates a destructive low-impedance path across the rail.

lessons.label: Magnetics: Saturation, Core Loss, and Winding Loss

sections.heading: Flux, saturation, and why cores differ
sections.body: An inductor's core flux density follows directly from Faraday's law rearranged: B = (integral of V dt) / (N x Ae), the applied volt-seconds divided by turns and core cross-sectional area. Every core material has a saturation flux density Bsat past which permeability collapses and inductance drops sharply, letting current spike uncontrolled. Ferrite, the common choice in switch-mode converters, has a relatively low Bsat around 0.3-0.5 T with a hard knee: permeability holds steady, then falls off a cliff right at saturation, so a ferrite design needs real margin below Bsat. Powdered iron (iron-powder) cores behave differently: distributed air gaps built into the powder structure give a soft saturation, permeability rolls off gradually well before the material's higher Bsat near 1 T, which makes powdered iron more forgiving of transient overcurrent but generally lossier at a given flux swing.

sections.heading: Core loss follows the Steinmetz equation
sections.body: Core loss per unit volume is commonly modeled with the empirical Steinmetz equation, P = k x f^a x B^b, where k, a, and b are material constants fit to a manufacturer's loss curves, a typically in the range of about 1.5-2.7 and b around 2-3 depending on the ferrite grade. The practical use is comparative: doubling switching frequency raises core loss roughly by 2^a, while a modest increase in peak flux swing raises it much faster because of the exponent b, which is why designers push ripple current down (larger inductance, smaller flux swing) even when it costs a slightly bigger core.

sections.heading: Skin, proximity, and litz wire
sections.body: At high frequency, winding loss is not simply Irms^2 x DCR. Skin effect crowds current toward a conductor's surface, with skin depth delta = sqrt(rho / (pi x f x mu)) shrinking as frequency rises, so a wire's effective cross-section for AC current shrinks and its effective resistance climbs above the DC value. Proximity effect compounds this: the alternating magnetic field from neighboring turns induces eddy currents inside each conductor, crowding current into thin regions facing away from neighbors, sometimes dominating over plain skin effect in a tightly wound coil. Litz wire is the standard fix — many thin, individually insulated strands bundled and transposed so each strand spends equal time at every position in the bundle, averaging out the proximity-induced crowding and keeping effective AC resistance close to DC resistance well into the hundreds of kHz. The upshot for rating an inductor is that no single 'rated current' number captures its real limit; the true constraint is the winding and core temperature rise that current and flux swing together produce, which is why datasheets increasingly specify both a saturation current and a separate, lower heating current.

lessons.workedExample: A 10 uH ferrite inductor (Ae = 30 mm^2, N = 8 turns, Bsat = 0.4 T) in a 500 kHz buck sees 12 V applied for 0.83 us during the on-time. Flux swing: delta-B = (12 x 0.83e-6) / (8 x 30e-6) = 0.0415 T, well under the 0.4 T ceiling, so DC bias plus this ripple swing stays safely below saturation with margin for a fault transient. At 500 kHz, skin depth in copper is about 93 microns — only about a third of a 24 AWG wire's roughly 255-micron radius, so a single solid 24 AWG strand is already several skin depths thick and suffers real AC resistance rise; switching to a litz bundle of many 40 AWG strands (each strand's radius on the order of the skin depth itself) keeps effective resistance close to the DC value and keeps winding temperature rise, not the datasheet's saturation-current number, as the binding constraint on how much current the inductor can actually carry continuously.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about core selection or 'why litz wire' to check whether a student picked a magnetic component by copying a reference design or actually computed flux swing against Bsat. A strong answer walks through B = Vdt/(N x Ae), states which saturation limit (hard ferrite knee vs soft powdered-iron roll-off) applies to their part, and explains that the real current rating is set by temperature rise rather than a single saturation-current number. A weak answer cannot compute flux density at all, or claims an inductor's 'rated current' is a hard, single limit rather than a thermal one.

questions.prompt: In the worked example, what is the approximate flux swing delta-B for the 10 uH ferrite inductor?

options.text: About 0.0415 T
About 0.4 T, right at the saturation limit
About 4.15 T
About 0.83 T

explanations.a: Correct — (12 V x 0.83 us) / (8 turns x 30 mm^2) works out to about 0.0415 T, well below the 0.4 T Bsat.
explanations.b: 0.4 T is the core's saturation ceiling, not the computed operating flux swing — this design has margin, not zero margin.
explanations.c: This is off by two orders of magnitude from the correct calculation.
explanations.d: 0.83 T would exceed saturation entirely; the on-time in microseconds is not the flux density.

questions.prompt: How does ferrite's saturation behavior differ from powdered iron's?

options.text: Ferrite saturates softly at high Bsat; powdered iron saturates hard at low Bsat
Ferrite has a hard knee at a relatively low Bsat (about 0.3-0.5 T); powdered iron rolls off softly with a higher Bsat near 1 T
Both saturate identically; the only difference is cost
Powdered iron cannot saturate at all

explanations.a: This reverses the actual behavior — ferrite is the hard-knee, lower-Bsat material.
explanations.b: Correct — ferrite's permeability holds steady then drops sharply near a 0.3-0.5 T ceiling, while powdered iron's built-in distributed gaps give a gradual roll-off toward a higher ceiling near 1 T.
explanations.c: The two materials differ meaningfully in both saturation character and typical core loss, not just price.
explanations.d: All practical magnetic core materials saturate eventually; powdered iron just does so more gradually.

questions.prompt: What problem does litz wire specifically solve?

options.text: Core saturation
Skin and proximity effects raising effective AC resistance above the DC value
Steinmetz core loss
Bootstrap capacitor droop

explanations.a: Saturation is a core-material property; litz wire is a conductor construction and does not affect it.
explanations.b: Correct — transposed, individually insulated strands average out the current crowding from skin and proximity effects, keeping AC resistance close to DC resistance.
explanations.c: Steinmetz loss is a core-material phenomenon; litz wire addresses winding, not core, loss.
explanations.d: Bootstrap droop is a gate-drive supply issue, unrelated to winding construction.

questions.prompt: Why is 'temperature rise' the true limit on an inductor's current rating rather than a single fixed current number?

options.text: Because current itself has no physical effect on an inductor

Because both core loss (rising with flux swing and frequency) and winding loss (rising with rms current and AC resistance) jointly determine how hot the part gets, and that heat is the actual failure limit
Because manufacturers do not test inductors for current handling
Because saturation current and heating current are always the same number

explanations.a: Current drives both resistive winding loss and, through flux, core loss — it has a direct physical effect.
explanations.b: Correct — core loss and winding loss combine to set the part's temperature rise, and that thermal limit, not a single saturation number, is what a datasheet's separate heating-current rating is meant to capture.
explanations.c: Manufacturers do test for this, which is exactly why many datasheets list separate saturation and heating current ratings.
explanations.d: These are often different numbers precisely because saturation and thermal limits are governed by different physics.

lessons.label: Thermal Design and the Heat Path

sections.heading: A series chain of thermal resistances
sections.body: Heat generated at a device's silicon junction has to cross several interfaces before reaching ambient air, and each interface behaves like a resistor in a series chain: Rth(j-c) from junction to case, Rth(c-s) from case to heatsink (usually through a thermal interface material), and Rth(s-a) from heatsink to ambient. Because they are in series, the total is their sum, and steady-state junction temperature follows directly: Tj = Ta + P x Rth(j-a), ambient temperature plus dissipated power times the total path resistance. The practical use is diagnostic: if a design runs hotter than predicted, checking which stage of the chain dominates (a poorly applied thermal pad at the c-s interface is a common, fixable offender) tells you where to intervene rather than guessing.

sections.heading: SOA, derating, and the copper-as-heatsink trick
sections.body: A device's safe operating area (SOA) is a plot of allowable simultaneous voltage and current, bounded not just by a simple power limit but by thermal limits, avalanche capability, and secondary breakdown at high voltage with high current together, so a part can fail well below its steady-state power rating if the V-I combination strays outside the SOA curve. Datasheets also give derating curves showing how much power a device may dissipate as case or ambient temperature climbs, typically linear above some reference temperature, falling to zero at the maximum rated junction temperature. In today's surface-mount designs, many power parts (DPAK, QFN, and similar packages with an exposed thermal pad) rely on the PCB itself as the heatsink: a generous copper pour on multiple layers, connected through an array of thermal vias beneath the pad, spreads heat into the board's copper and out to ambient air, often the single biggest lever a student has for lowering Rth(j-a) without buying a discrete heatsink.

sections.heading: Pulsed loads need transient impedance, not steady-state resistance
sections.body: Steady-state Rth(j-a) assumes power has been applied long enough for the whole thermal chain to reach equilibrium, which overstates junction temperature rise for a short pulse — the silicon's own thermal mass absorbs a brief pulse before that heat has time to propagate through the case, interface, and heatsink. Transient thermal impedance Zth(t) captures this: a curve (or family of curves at different duty cycles) showing that a single short pulse produces far less temperature rise than the same power applied continuously, which lets a design running short, infrequent high-current pulses (a solenoid driver, a motor-start surge) survive peaks that would violate the steady-state rating. Turning any of this into a design margin means picking a junction-temperature target with headroom below the datasheet's absolute maximum (commonly 150 or 175 C) — for example designing to keep Tj under 125 C — to absorb tolerance stack-up, aging, and worst-case ambient rather than running right up to the rated limit.

lessons.workedExample: A TO-220 MOSFET with Rth(j-c) = 1.0 C/W, Rth(c-s) = 0.5 C/W (thermal pad), and a heatsink rated Rth(s-a) = 8 C/W dissipates 3 W in a 40 C ambient enclosure. Total Rth(j-a) = 1.0 + 0.5 + 8 = 9.5 C/W, so Tj = 40 + 3 x 9.5 = 68.5 C, comfortably under a 150 C rated maximum and even under a conservative 125 C design target. If the same part instead relies on PCB copper alone at Rth(j-a) = 40 C/W (no discrete heatsink), Tj rises to 40 + 3 x 40 = 160 C, exceeding the rating — showing directly why the heatsink stage of the chain is not optional at that power level.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'what junction temperature does your part actually run at' to check whether a claimed power rating was verified or just assumed from a datasheet's headline number. A strong answer walks the series Rth chain, states an actual Tj estimate with a stated ambient and margin below the rated maximum, and can distinguish steady-state from pulsed behavior if the load is intermittent. A weak answer quotes the device's absolute maximum junction temperature as if it were the operating temperature, or cannot explain why a heatsink's Rth(s-a) matters as much as the chip's own Rth(j-c).

questions.prompt: In the worked example, what is the junction temperature with the discrete heatsink in place?

explanations.a: Correct — Tj = 40 + 3 x 9.5 = 68.5 C, using the full series Rth(j-a) of 9.5 C/W.
explanations.b: 40 C is just the ambient temperature, before adding the temperature rise from dissipated power.
explanations.c: 160 C is the result for the no-heatsink case (Rth(j-a) = 40 C/W), not the heatsinked case.
explanations.d: 9.5 C/W is the total thermal resistance, not a temperature.

questions.prompt: Order the thermal path a watt of heat crosses, from where it is generated to where it is finally dissipated.

items.text: Silicon junction
Device case
Heatsink (through thermal interface material)
Ambient air

questions.explanation: Heat is generated at the junction, crosses Rth(j-c) to the case, crosses Rth(c-s) through the interface material to the heatsink, then crosses Rth(s-a) to reach ambient air — the same order the three series resistances are named in.

questions.prompt: Why can a device survive a short, high-power pulse that would violate its steady-state power rating?

options.text: The device's SOA rating does not apply to pulses
The silicon's own thermal mass absorbs the pulse before heat has time to propagate through the whole Rth(j-a) chain, so transient impedance Zth(t) is much lower than steady-state Rth(j-a)
Pulsed current does not generate heat
Rth(j-c) becomes negative during a pulse

explanations.a: SOA still applies to pulses — it is specifically defined with pulse-width-dependent curves for exactly this reason.
explanations.b: Correct — a brief pulse's heat is largely absorbed by the die's own thermal mass before it can propagate through case, interface, and heatsink, so transient thermal impedance for short pulses is well below the steady-state value.
explanations.c: Pulsed current dissipates power just as continuous current does; the difference is how much of that heat reaches the outer stages of the thermal path in the available time.
explanations.d: Thermal resistance does not go negative; the transient behavior is captured by Zth(t), a different (lower) quantity than steady-state Rth.

questions.prompt: In a surface-mount design with an exposed-pad power device and no discrete heatsink, what commonly serves as the heatsink?

options.text: The gate driver IC
PCB copper pour and thermal vias beneath the exposed pad
The output inductor's core
The bootstrap capacitor

explanations.a: The gate driver has no thermal role in dissipating the power device's heat.
explanations.b: Correct — copper pour on multiple PCB layers, connected via thermal vias under the exposed pad, spreads heat into the board and out to ambient, acting as the heatsink in many SMT designs.
explanations.c: The inductor core is a magnetics component unrelated to the power device's own thermal path.
explanations.d: The bootstrap capacitor is part of the gate-drive supply, not the thermal path.

lessons.label: Layout and Parasitics as Components

sections.heading: The hot loop and why its area matters
sections.body: Every switching converter has a 'hot loop': the path carrying pulsed, high-di/dt current, typically the input capacitor, the high-side switch, and the synchronous FET (or freewheeling diode) back to the capacitor's return. This loop is not a schematic abstraction — its physical trace geometry has real inductance, and every trace and via in it forms an unavoidable parasitic inductor. The loop's enclosed area sets that inductance directly, so a hot loop routed with the input cap far from the switches, or with the return path taking a long detour, can easily carry tens of nanohenries that a schematic shows as nothing at all.

sections.heading: Loop inductance turns switching edges into ringing
sections.body: That parasitic loop inductance obeys the same law as any inductor: V = L x di/dt. A MOSFET switching several amps in tens of nanoseconds produces a di/dt in the hundreds of millions of amps per second, and even a modest 5-10 nH of loop inductance then produces a voltage spike of several volts to tens of volts on top of the intended switching waveform, appearing as overshoot and ringing at turn-off. Beyond eating into voltage margin (or exceeding a device's rated Vds outright), this ringing radiates as EMI. The fix search usually starts with shrinking the physical loop before reaching for any add-on component, because less parasitic inductance is strictly better than damping a bigger one after the fact.

sections.heading: Snubbers, grounding, and why schematics alone are not enough
sections.body: When loop inductance cannot be shrunk further, an RC or RCD snubber tames the ringing by adding controlled damping. The ring-frequency method sizes it practically: observe the ringing frequency on a scope, add a known small capacitor across the ringing node and observe how much the frequency drops, which lets you solve for the existing parasitic capacitance and, from the original ring frequency and that capacitance, back out the parasitic loop inductance; a snubber resistor is then chosen to critically damp that L-C tank, with the snubber capacitor sized to shift the ring frequency down without adding excessive dissipation. Layout also determines whether control and analog signals stay clean: routing a single-point power ground (all high-current, high-di/dt returns converging at one location) separated from a dedicated analog/control return prevents the switching loop's ground bounce from corrupting the feedback reference. A converter can be entirely correct on the schematic and still fail — oscillate, overshoot, radiate excess EMI, or destroy a switch — purely because the physical layout gave its parasitics a shape the schematic never captured.

lessons.workedExample: A buck converter rings at 80 MHz at the switch-node turn-off edge. Adding a known 100 pF capacitor across the node drops the ring frequency to 40 MHz. Since f is proportional to 1/sqrt(LC), halving the frequency means the total capacitance quadrupled, so the original parasitic capacitance was about 100 pF / 3 = 33 pF. Using f = 1/(2*pi*sqrt(LC)) with f = 80 MHz and C = 33 pF gives a parasitic loop inductance of roughly 120 nH, a sign of a loosely routed hot loop that a tighter layout should shrink well below 10 nH. A snubber R is then chosen near sqrt(L/C) to critically damp that specific L-C tank, and the snubber C is picked a few times the parasitic C so it dominates the ring frequency without adding excessive turn-off dissipation.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'why does your board ring, and how did you fix it' is checking whether a student treats PCB layout as a real circuit element or as an afterthought. A strong answer names the hot loop specifically (which components form it), states that loop area sets parasitic inductance, and can walk through the ring-frequency method for sizing a snubber rather than picking snubber values by guesswork. A weak answer blames 'noise' generically or cannot explain why a schematic that simulates cleanly might still ring badly on a real board.

questions.prompt: Which three elements typically form a synchronous buck's 'hot loop'?

options.text: The output capacitor, the inductor, and the load
The input capacitor, the high-side switch, and the synchronous FET (or diode)
The gate driver, the feedback divider, and the compensation network
The bootstrap capacitor, the control IC, and ground plane

explanations.a: This is the low-di/dt output-side path; the pulsed, high-di/dt loop is on the input side with the switches.
explanations.b: Correct — the input capacitor, high-side switch, and synchronous FET (or freewheeling diode) carry the pulsed current and form the loop whose area sets parasitic inductance.
explanations.c: These are control-signal elements, not part of the high-current switching loop.
explanations.d: The bootstrap capacitor supplies gate drive; it is not part of the main power hot loop.

questions.prompt: Why does shrinking the hot loop's physical area reduce switching-edge ringing?

options.text: Smaller loop area directly reduces parasitic inductance, which lowers the V = L x di/dt overshoot at each switching edge
It has no effect on inductance, only on resistance
It increases Rds(on), damping the ring
It changes the MOSFET's Qg

explanations.a: Correct — loop inductance scales with the enclosed loop area, so a smaller loop means less L and less V = L x di/dt overshoot for the same switching di/dt.
explanations.b: Loop area is precisely what sets parasitic inductance; its effect on plain trace resistance is a secondary concern.
explanations.c: Layout changes do not alter a device's intrinsic Rds(on); that is a silicon property.
explanations.d: Gate charge Qg is a device parameter unrelated to loop layout.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of the ring-frequency method for sizing a snubber.

items.text: Observe the switch-node ringing frequency on a scope
Add a known capacitor across the ringing node and note the new, lower frequency
Solve for the original parasitic C and L from the frequency shift
Choose snubber R (near sqrt(L/C)) and snubber C to damp the ring

questions.explanation: You first measure the existing ring frequency, then perturb it with a known added capacitor to get a second data point, use the frequency shift to back out the unknown parasitic C and L, and finally pick snubber component values sized to damp that specific L-C tank.

questions.prompt: Why route a single-point power ground separated from a dedicated analog/control return?

options.text: To reduce the MOSFET's Rds(on)
To prevent high-di/dt switching-loop ground bounce from corrupting the analog feedback reference
To increase the snubber's damping resistance
Because it lowers the core loss in the inductor

explanations.a: Rds(on) is a device property set in silicon, not something layout grounding scheme changes.
explanations.b: Correct — the switching loop's high di/dt causes voltage drops (ground bounce) across shared ground impedance; separating that return from the sensitive analog/control reference keeps the feedback signal clean.
explanations.c: Snubber damping resistance is chosen from the L-C tank characteristics, not from grounding scheme.
explanations.d: Core loss is a magnetics-material phenomenon, unrelated to ground routing choices.

units.label: Measuring and Interpreting Converter Behavior

lessons.label: Measuring Efficiency Honestly

sections.heading: Two-wire measurement lies at high current
sections.body: Efficiency is just Pout / Pin, but getting Pout and Pin right is harder than it sounds. If you measure output voltage with the same two wires that carry the load current, the meter reads the voltage at the far end of those wires, not at the converter's output pins. A 1 m run of 22 AWG copper has roughly 0.05 ohms of resistance; at 3 A that is a 150 mV drop, which is 3% of a 5 V rail — enough to turn a real 95% efficiency into a reported 92% or 98% depending on which way the drop points. Four-wire Kelvin sensing fixes this by routing separate, near-zero-current sense leads to the converter's actual output (and input) terminals, so the voltage reading reflects the device under test, not the wiring.

sections.heading: Efficiency has a shape, not a number
sections.body: A single efficiency number at one load point hides more than it reveals; a proper characterization sweeps load from near-zero to full rated current and plots efficiency against it. The curve is not flat. At light load, fixed losses — controller quiescent current, gate-drive charge times switching frequency, core loss — are roughly constant in watts, so they are a large fraction of a small Pout and efficiency is low. As load rises, those fixed losses shrink relative to Pout and efficiency climbs, typically peaking somewhere between 20% and 50% of rated load. Past the peak, conduction losses (I^2R in MOSFET Rds(on), inductor DCR, and trace resistance) grow with the square of current and start to dominate, so efficiency rolls back down toward full load. A single number without the curve cannot tell a judge whether a converter was designed for a light standby load or a heavy continuous one.

sections.heading: A percentage without an uncertainty is a guess
sections.body: Every instrument in the measurement chain has a stated accuracy, and it has to be carried through to the final number. A bench DMM might specify 0.5% of reading on a DC voltage range; a precision power analyzer might specify closer to 0.1%. Because efficiency is a ratio of two independently measured powers, the relative uncertainties combine (added in quadrature for a reasonable estimate, or added directly for a conservative bound) rather than canceling out. A claimed 96.2% efficiency measured with instruments each good to about 0.3% should be reported as roughly 96.2% ± 0.5%, not as a bare four-significant-figure number that implies precision the equipment never delivered.

lessons.workedExample: A student measures a 12 V-to-5 V buck converter at 3 A output using a multimeter clipped to the same banana leads that carry the load current, both at the input and output. They report 97.4% efficiency. Redone with four-wire Kelvin sensing — separate 30 AWG sense leads soldered directly to the output capacitor pads and to the input connector, carrying negligible current — the true output voltage is 140 mV lower than the two-wire reading, and recomputed efficiency comes out to 94.7%. The 2.7-point gap is entirely wiring drop, not converter performance, and it only shows up once the sense and power paths are separated.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who sees "96% efficient" on a poster will almost always ask how it was measured, because this single number is the easiest one in a power-electronics project to fake by accident through sloppy probing. A weak answer is "I used a multimeter at full load" — one point, two-wire, no stated error. A strong answer names the sensing method (four-wire, sense leads at the DUT terminals), states that the converter was allowed to reach thermal steady state before the reading was taken, shows an efficiency-versus-load sweep rather than one point, and gives the number with an uncertainty band derived from the instruments' datasheet accuracy. That last step — turning 96.2% into 96.2% ± 0.5% — is the single strongest signal of measurement literacy a student can put on a board.

questions.prompt: Why does two-wire voltage sensing at high current understate or overstate a converter's true efficiency?

options.text: The multimeter's internal resistance draws extra current from the circuit
The measured voltage includes the IR drop across the current-carrying leads, not just the converter terminal voltage
Two-wire meters cannot measure DC voltages above 5 V accurately
The meter averages voltage over too long a time window

explanations.a: A voltmeter's high input impedance draws negligible current; that is not the source of the error here.
explanations.b: Correct — when the same leads carry load current and are used to sense voltage, the reading includes the resistive drop along those leads, shifting the apparent terminal voltage away from the true value at the converter.
explanations.c: Two-wire meters measure voltages in this range fine; the problem is what point in the circuit they are actually reading, not a range limitation.
explanations.d: Averaging window affects noise rejection, not this systematic lead-drop error.

questions.prompt: A converter's efficiency-versus-load curve typically dips at light load. What causes this dip?

options.text: I^2R conduction losses dominate when current is small
Fixed losses like quiescent current and switching losses are a large fraction of a small output power
The output capacitor cannot filter ripple properly below a minimum current
Meters lose accuracy when measuring small currents

explanations.a: I^2R losses scale with the square of current, so they are smallest, not largest, at light load.
explanations.b: Correct — quiescent current, gate-drive losses, and switching losses are roughly constant in watts regardless of load, so at low Pout they consume a disproportionate share of input power.
explanations.c: Capacitor filtering is not the mechanism behind the efficiency-versus-load shape described here.
explanations.d: This is about the converter's physical loss mechanisms, not instrument measurement error.

questions.prompt: Two instruments used to compute efficiency are each accurate to about 0.3% of reading. What is the most defensible way to report a measured 96.2% efficiency?

options.text: 96.2% exactly, since both instruments were calibrated
96.2% ± roughly 0.5%, reflecting the combined instrument uncertainty
96% flat, rounding away the decimal to be safe
There is no way to state efficiency without a reference-grade power analyzer

explanations.a: Calibration reduces bias but does not eliminate the stated accuracy tolerance; reporting no uncertainty overstates precision.
explanations.b: Correct — combining two independent ~0.3% relative uncertainties (roughly in quadrature or added conservatively) gives an uncertainty band near 0.5%, which should accompany the reported number.
explanations.c: Rounding to a whole percent discards real information without doing the actual uncertainty calculation.
explanations.d: A stated uncertainty can be computed with any instrument once its datasheet accuracy is known; a lab-grade analyzer just shrinks the band.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for producing a defensible efficiency measurement, from first to last.

items.text: Connect four-wire Kelvin sense leads at the converter's input and output terminals
Apply the target load and wait for the converter to reach thermal steady state
Record voltage and current at multiple load points to build an efficiency-versus-load curve
Combine instrument datasheet accuracies to state an uncertainty alongside each efficiency value

questions.explanation: Sensing must be wired correctly before anything is trustworthy, the circuit must settle thermally before a reading is meaningful, the sweep across load points reveals the real efficiency shape, and only after data exists can a supportable uncertainty be attached to it.

lessons.label: Probing Ripple Without Fooling Yourself

sections.heading: Bandwidth limiting: hiding noise or inventing it
sections.body: Output ripple specs on converter datasheets are almost always measured with the oscilloscope's bandwidth limited to 20 MHz, and this is not a shortcut — it matches what the spec is actually trying to characterize. A switching converter's output has a genuine low-frequency ripple component near the switching frequency (tens of kHz to a few MHz) riding on top of very fast, very local edge transients from the switch node coupling into the measurement. Viewed at full oscilloscope bandwidth (100 MHz to several GHz), those fast edges appear as sharp spikes that can be several times taller than the real ripple, dominated by probe-loop pickup rather than anything a downstream load actually experiences. Limiting to 20 MHz removes that high-frequency artifact and reveals the ripple waveform a datasheet comparison expects; but bandwidth-limiting can also mask a genuine fast glitch (a body-diode recovery spike, for instance) that matters for a different question, like EMI or device stress. The two views answer different questions, and a measurement is only honest when it states which one was used.

sections.heading: The ground lead is usually the biggest antenna on the bench
sections.body: The stock probe accessory — a spring clip on a 6-inch ground wire — forms a loop with the probe tip that is large enough to pick up magnetic field radiated from the converter's own switch node and inductor, and that pickup adds directly to whatever the probe reports. Replacing the ground lead with a ground-spring tip (a short metal spring that clips directly around the probe barrel and touches ground right next to the tip) shrinks that loop from centimeters to millimeters, cutting the induced noise dramatically. A tip-and-barrel technique — pressing the probe tip and its grounded barrel directly onto adjacent test points — achieves the same result without even needing the spring.

sections.heading: AC coupling and offset to see millivolts on volts
sections.body: Resolving 20-50 mV of ripple on a 5 V rail directly in DC coupling wastes most of the screen on the DC level. AC coupling removes the DC component so the scope's vertical gain can be set to resolve just the ripple, while an offset (or AC coupling combined with a DC offset on scopes that support it) recenters the trace. The risk is that a large abrupt event — a load step — can exceed the AC-coupling capacitor's ability to track and produce a settling transient that looks like ringing but is a coupling artifact, so any surprising feature seen in AC coupling should be cross-checked in DC coupling before it is trusted.

lessons.workedExample: A student probes a 5 V buck output with the stock spring-and-6-inch-ground-clip accessory, full 500 MHz bandwidth, DC coupled, and reports 400 mV of ripple — nearly 8% of the rail, which would fail any reasonable spec. Switching to a ground-spring tip barely changes the picture, but switching to 20 MHz bandwidth limiting collapses the trace to 35 mV of genuine low-frequency ripple; the remaining 365 mV was high-frequency loop pickup from the adjacent inductor, invisible to the load but dominating the unfiltered view. AC coupling at 20 mV/div then resolves the 35 mV waveform clearly enough to read its peak-to-peak value and its shape.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe ripple measurements because the number is trivially inflated by bad probing technique, and a student who reports 400 mV without noticing it is implausible for a 5 V rail is showing they never questioned their own setup. A weak answer treats whatever the scope displayed as ground truth. A strong answer states the bandwidth limit used and why (matching the datasheet convention), describes the grounding method (spring tip over the long clip lead), and can explain what changed and why when asked to compare a full-bandwidth trace to a 20 MHz-limited one — showing they understand the measurement is shaping the result, not just reading a number off a screen.

questions.prompt: Why do datasheet ripple specifications almost always state a 20 MHz oscilloscope bandwidth limit?

options.text: Because oscilloscopes below 20 MHz bandwidth are more accurate
To exclude high-frequency probe-loop pickup that inflates the reading beyond the genuine low-frequency ripple
Because switching converters cannot generate any signal content above 20 MHz
To make the converter appear to have lower ripple than it truly does

explanations.a: Bandwidth-limiting does not make a scope more accurate in general; it changes what frequency content is displayed.
explanations.b: Correct — the fast edges picked up by the probe loop can be far larger than the actual ripple a load would see, and 20 MHz limiting removes that artifact while preserving the genuine switching-frequency ripple.
explanations.c: Switch-node edges do contain energy well above 20 MHz; the limit is a deliberate choice about what to characterize, not a claim that nothing exists above it.
explanations.d: The convention exists to standardize and clarify the measurement, not to flatter the result — a full-bandwidth trace still exists and is meaningful for other questions like EMI.

questions.prompt: Why does replacing a 6-inch spring-clip ground lead with a ground-spring tip reduce apparent noise on a ripple measurement?

options.text: It increases the probe's input impedance
It shrinks the probe-to-ground loop area, reducing magnetic pickup from nearby switching currents
It filters out frequencies above 20 MHz automatically
It lowers the DC resistance of the ground connection

explanations.a: Input impedance is set by the probe's internal design, not by the length of the ground lead.
explanations.b: Correct — a long ground lead plus the probe tip forms a loop that acts as an antenna for the converter's own switching magnetic field; shrinking the loop shrinks the induced voltage error.
explanations.c: Bandwidth filtering is a scope setting, unrelated to ground-lead geometry.
