explanations.d: DC resistance of a short spring clip versus a longer wire is negligible either way; the mechanism is loop area, not resistance.

questions.prompt: While viewing ripple in AC-coupled mode, a large sudden ringing transient appears right after a load step. What should the student do before reporting it as real?

options.text: Report it immediately, since AC coupling always shows the true signal
Re-check the same event in DC coupling, since AC-coupling capacitors can produce settling artifacts after large abrupt steps
Increase the bandwidth limit to confirm the transient is real
Ignore it, since AC coupling cannot show load-step events at all

explanations.a: AC coupling can itself introduce coupling-capacitor settling behavior after a large step, so it is not automatically trustworthy for transient events.
explanations.b: Correct — cross-checking in DC coupling distinguishes a genuine circuit transient from an artifact of the AC-coupling capacitor recovering from a large step.
explanations.c: Bandwidth has no direct bearing on whether a feature is an AC-coupling artifact versus a real signal.
explanations.d: AC coupling does display transient events; the issue is that its own coupling network can distort large ones, not that it hides them.

questions.prompt: Match each ripple-measurement technique to the problem it primarily addresses.

left.text: Ground-spring tip instead of long clip lead

right.text: Resolving small millivolt-scale ripple on a several-volt DC rail
Removing high-frequency probe-loop pickup so the display matches the datasheet convention
Reducing magnetic-field pickup from nearby switching currents by shrinking the sense loop

questions.explanation: Bandwidth limiting removes fast edge content so the trace matches the standard ripple convention; a ground-spring tip shrinks the physical loop that picks up radiated switching noise; AC coupling with offset strips the DC level so the scope's gain can resolve a small ripple signal riding on a large rail voltage.

lessons.label: Reading a Switch-Node Trace

sections.heading: Duty cycle and switching frequency from the waveform
sections.body: The switch node — the junction between the high-side and low-side switches in a buck, boost, or similar converter — is the single most informative point to probe on a switching converter, because nearly every operating parameter leaves a fingerprint there. The basic reading is straightforward: the period between two rising edges gives the switching period Tsw, and its reciprocal gives the switching frequency fsw; the fraction of that period spent high (near the input rail) versus low (near ground) gives the duty cycle D. For an ideal continuous-conduction buck, D should sit close to the ratio Vout/Vin, so a quick duty-cycle read is a sanity check on the whole converter before any other measurement is trusted.

sections.heading: Ringing reveals parasitic inductance and capacitance
sections.body: Every switch-node edge is followed by a damped ring — a fast oscillation that decays over a handful of cycles — because the transition excites an LC tank formed by the parasitic loop inductance of the switching path (traces, pins, vias) resonating against the switch node's total capacitance, dominated by the MOSFET's output capacitance Coss. That ring is not just cosmetic noise; its frequency f_ring = 1/(2*pi*sqrt(L*C)) can be measured directly off the scope, and if Coss is known from the MOSFET datasheet, the parasitic loop inductance L can be solved for algebraically. A ring in the hundreds of MHz on a small SMPS points to a tight, well-laid-out loop; a ring down in the tens of MHz points to excess trace length or a large loop area, which also correlates with higher voltage overshoot and worse EMI.

sections.heading: Dead-time dips, DCM plateaus, and load-dependent signatures
sections.body: During the brief dead time between the high-side switch turning off and the low-side (or synchronous rectifier) turning on, neither switch conducts, so the inductor current forces the low-side MOSFET's body diode to conduct instead, clamping the switch node to roughly a diode drop below ground for that interval — a small, sharp negative dip just before the low-side gate turns on. If the load is light enough that inductor current reaches zero before the next cycle starts, the converter enters discontinuous conduction mode (DCM), and the switch node instead of holding a flat rail rings freely at the LC tank frequency and settles to a plateau partway between ground and Vin — a visually distinctive signature of DCM versus the sharp clean edges of continuous conduction. At very light load some controllers skip pulses outright (irregular, widely spaced edges) to hold regulation efficiently; under an overcurrent fault, current-limit foldback shows up as duty cycle or frequency visibly collapsing compared to normal operation; and a controller stuck in hiccup mode shows long stretches with no switching at all between retry attempts.

lessons.workedExample: A student probes the switch node of a 12 V-to-5 V buck at 500 kHz nominal and measures a period of 2.05 microseconds (fsw about 488 kHz, close enough to nominal) with the high portion lasting 850 ns, giving D = 0.41 — close to the ideal 5/12 = 0.417, confirming the converter is behaving as expected. Zooming into the turn-off edge, they measure a ring at 62 MHz; the MOSFET datasheet lists Coss around 150 pF at the operating voltage, so solving f = 1/(2*pi*sqrt(L*Coss)) for L gives roughly 44 nH of parasitic loop inductance — enough to explain the 2 V overshoot spike they see riding on top of the 12 V rail.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks a student to zoom into their own switch-node screenshot is testing whether the trace is decoration or data. A weak answer says "that's just switching noise." A strong answer reads duty cycle and frequency off the trace and checks them against the expected Vout/Vin ratio, identifies the post-edge ring and connects its frequency to parasitic loop inductance and MOSFET Coss, and can point to the small negative dip during dead time and explain it as body-diode conduction rather than dismiss it as an artifact. Being able to say "this ringing plateau means we're in discontinuous conduction at this load" from the shape of the trace alone is the clearest evidence a student actually understands the switch, not just the datasheet block diagram of it.

questions.prompt: A buck converter's switch node shows a small, sharp negative voltage dip just before the low-side switch turns on. What causes it?

options.text: The low-side MOSFET's body diode conducting during dead time
The output capacitor discharging through the load
Electromagnetic interference from a nearby digital circuit
The controller entering current-limit foldback

explanations.a: Correct — during dead time neither switch is actively conducting, so inductor current forces the low-side body diode to conduct, clamping the node about a diode drop below ground until the synchronous switch turns on.
explanations.b: Output capacitor discharge affects the output rail, not the switch node's brief sub-ground dip during dead time.
explanations.c: External EMI would not produce a consistent, repeatable dip timed precisely to the dead-time interval.
explanations.d: Current-limit foldback changes duty cycle or frequency over many cycles under fault conditions, not a single edge's dead-time behavior.

questions.prompt: The switch node rings at 62 MHz after each turn-off edge, and the MOSFET's Coss is known from its datasheet. What can be calculated from this?

options.text: The converter's efficiency at full load
The parasitic loop inductance in the switching path
The exact output voltage ripple
The controller's dead-time setting

explanations.a: Efficiency requires power measurements at input and output, not the ring frequency of a single edge.
explanations.b: Correct — the ring frequency and a known Coss let you solve f = 1/(2*pi*sqrt(L*C)) for the parasitic loop inductance L that forms the resonant tank with Coss.
explanations.c: Output ripple is a separate measurement at the output filter, not derivable from switch-node ring frequency alone.
explanations.d: Dead-time setting is a controller parameter read from timing between edges, not from the ring frequency itself.

questions.prompt: At light load, the switch node stops showing sharp clean edges and instead rings freely, settling to a plateau partway between ground and Vin before the next cycle. What operating mode does this indicate?

options.text: Continuous conduction mode (CCM)
Discontinuous conduction mode (DCM), where inductor current reaches zero before the next cycle
A short circuit on the output
Current-limit foldback

explanations.a: CCM shows sharp, clean transitions because current never reaches zero, which is the opposite of the free-ringing plateau described.
explanations.b: Correct — once inductor current hits zero before the next switching cycle begins, the node is no longer clamped by continuous current flow and free-rings at the LC tank frequency, settling to a plateau — the classic DCM signature.
explanations.c: A short circuit would pull the node toward ground continuously rather than produce a ringing plateau tied to the switching period.
explanations.d: Foldback is a fault response affecting duty cycle or frequency over many cycles, not the single-cycle ringing behavior tied to zero inductor current.

questions.prompt: Match each switch-node observation to what it indicates about converter operation.

left.text: Irregular, widely spaced switching edges at very light load
Duty cycle and frequency visibly collapsing under a fault condition
Long stretches with no switching activity, then a burst of pulses, repeating

right.text: Pulse-skipping to maintain regulation efficiently at light load
Current-limit foldback protecting against overcurrent
Hiccup-mode fault protection retrying periodically

questions.explanation: Irregular sparse pulses at light load are the pulse-skipping (PFM-like) behavior many controllers use for light-load efficiency; a collapsing duty cycle or frequency under fault is current-limit foldback; alternating dead periods and switching bursts is the hiccup-mode signature of repeated fault-retry cycles.

lessons.label: Measuring Current in a Switching Circuit

sections.heading: Four ways to see current, and none of them do everything
sections.body: A shunt resistor with a differential amplifier is the simplest option: a small, precise resistance (often milliohms) is placed in the current path, and a differential amplifier reads the voltage across it since neither terminal sits at ground. It is DC-capable and has bandwidth limited mainly by the amplifier, but it inserts real resistance into the circuit and its output is a small signal riding on a large common-mode voltage, which the amplifier must reject cleanly. A current transformer (CT) senses current inductively, is AC-coupled only — it cannot see a DC component at all — but offers very wide bandwidth and near-zero insertion loss, at the cost of needing a reset mechanism when duty cycle is high. A Hall-effect current probe senses the magnetic field around a conductor directly, so it can measure both DC and AC, clamps on non-invasively, but typically has lower bandwidth than a CT (tens of MHz at the high end) and is bulkier. A Rogowski coil, a flexible air-core coil that senses di/dt and requires an integrator, is AC-only like a CT but offers excellent bandwidth and can wrap around awkward high-current conductors without breaking the circuit.

sections.heading: Getting a clamp probe onto a PCB trace
sections.body: Hall and Rogowski clamp probes need a conductor to close around, which a flat PCB trace does not offer. The standard fix is to cut the trace and insert a small wire loop — just large enough for the probe's jaw to clamp — sized to keep the added loop inductance small, since an oversized loop can measurably distort high-di/dt switching waveforms and even show up in the switch-node ringing discussed elsewhere in this unit.

sections.heading: Reading the inductor current triangle, and its saturation hook
sections.body: In continuous conduction mode, inductor current is a clean triangle wave: it ramps up while the high-side switch is on (slope roughly (Vin - Vout)/L) and ramps down while it is off (slope roughly -Vout/L), riding on a DC average equal to the load current for a buck topology. Peak-to-peak ripple and DC offset are both read directly off this triangle. A healthy triangle has straight, constant-slope ramps because inductance is constant. If the core begins to saturate near the peak of the on-time ramp, inductance collapses as flux density approaches the material's saturation limit, so di/dt = V/L rises sharply and the ramp curves upward into a concave, accelerating "hook" instead of staying straight — a clear, recognizable warning that the inductor is undersized or being driven past its rated current for the operating conditions.

lessons.workedExample: A student wants to verify the inductor ripple current in a 12 V-to-5 V buck at 2 A load, switching at 500 kHz with a 10 uH inductor. They cut the inductor's PCB trace and insert a 5 mm wire loop, clamping a Rogowski probe around it. The captured waveform is a clean triangle centered at 2 A with about 0.58 A peak-to-peak ripple, matching the hand calculation (Vin-Vout)/L * D/fsw = 7/10uH * 0.417/500kHz ≈ 0.58 A. Pushing the load to 4 A, the top of each ramp visibly curves upward into a hook rather than staying straight — the inductor's core is saturating well before the datasheet's rated saturation current, revealing an underspecified part rather than a measurement error.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking "how do you know your inductor isn't saturating" is checking whether a student has actually looked at the current waveform rather than trusting a datasheet number. A weak answer cites the inductor's rated saturation current from a datasheet and stops there. A strong answer describes measuring the actual inductor current — naming the sensor used and why (a shunt for simplicity, or a clamp probe to avoid breaking the DC path) — and can describe or show the triangle waveform, reading off its ripple and DC level, and explain that an upward-curving hook near the peak would be direct evidence of saturation that a datasheet spec alone cannot rule out under real operating conditions.

questions.prompt: Why can a current transformer (CT) not be used to measure a converter's steady DC bus current?

options.text: CTs are only rated for currents below 1 A
CTs sense current inductively and are inherently AC-coupled, so they cannot respond to a constant DC level
CTs require the circuit to be powered off during measurement
CTs have too much bandwidth to resolve DC accurately

explanations.a: Current rating is a design choice of the specific CT, not the reason DC cannot be sensed.
explanations.b: Correct — a CT works by transformer action, which requires a changing flux; a constant DC current produces no changing flux and therefore no output, so CTs are fundamentally AC-only.
explanations.c: CTs are used on live circuits; measurement does not require powering down.
explanations.d: Bandwidth and DC response are unrelated properties; high bandwidth does not prevent or cause a DC blind spot.

questions.prompt: A student needs to clamp a Hall-effect current probe around a trace on a PCB. What is the standard way to make this possible?

options.text: Solder the probe jaws directly to the copper pour
Cut the trace and insert a small wire loop sized just large enough for the probe to clamp around
Increase the trace width until the probe jaw fits around the board edge
Replace the Hall probe with a shunt resistor, since Hall probes cannot be used on PCBs

explanations.a: Hall probes clamp around a conductor rather than being soldered on; soldering the jaws is not how these probes are used.
explanations.b: Correct — cutting the trace and inserting a small loop gives the clamp jaw something to close around, and keeping the loop small limits added parasitic inductance.
explanations.c: Widening a trace does not create a conductor a clamp jaw can physically close around.
explanations.d: Hall probes can be used on PCBs via an inserted loop; a shunt is a different, also valid, sensing method but not a forced substitute.

questions.prompt: An inductor current triangle waveform, normally straight-sided, starts curving upward into a concave hook near the top of each ramp as load increases. What does this indicate?

options.text: The current sensor's bandwidth is too low to capture the waveform
The inductor's core is approaching saturation, causing inductance to drop and di/dt to increase
The converter has entered discontinuous conduction mode
The switching frequency has increased

explanations.a: A bandwidth-limited sensor would round off or attenuate sharp features, not produce a smooth accelerating curve tied to current level.
explanations.b: Correct — as flux density approaches the core's saturation limit, inductance collapses, so di/dt = V/L rises and the normally straight ramp curves upward into a hook.
explanations.c: Discontinuous conduction shows current returning to zero and the switch node ringing, not a curved ramp at high load.
explanations.d: A frequency change would alter the period of the triangle, not bend an individual ramp's shape.

questions.prompt: Match each current-sensing method to its key DC/bandwidth property.

right.text: DC-capable, bandwidth limited mainly by the amplifier, adds series resistance
AC-only, wide bandwidth, needs a reset mechanism at high duty cycle
DC- and AC-capable via magnetic field sensing, moderate bandwidth, non-invasive clamp
AC-only via di/dt sensing plus an integrator, flexible, very wide bandwidth

questions.explanation: A shunt with a differential amplifier reads DC and AC but inserts resistance; a CT is AC-only and needs reset circuitry at high duty cycle; a Hall probe senses magnetic field directly so it covers DC and AC non-invasively but with moderate bandwidth; a Rogowski coil senses di/dt (so it is AC-only, needing an integrator) but delivers very wide bandwidth in a flexible form factor.

lessons.label: Load Transients and Loop Response

sections.heading: Building a controlled step-load fixture
sections.body: A load transient test needs a current step with a known, repeatable slew rate — not just a switch slamming a resistor on. A simple fixture uses a power MOSFET in series with a resistor, both in parallel with the existing load, with the MOSFET's gate driven by a function generator through a gate resistor so the turn-on and turn-off edges have a controlled slew rate, commonly around 1 A per microsecond for a typical low-power test. Controlling the slew rate matters because an unrealistically fast, near-instantaneous step mostly exercises the output capacitor's ESR and ESL rather than the feedback loop's actual response, while too slow a step never stresses the loop's bandwidth at all — the goal is a step fast enough to be a meaningful stimulus for the control loop being characterized, not for the physics of a hypothetical short circuit.

sections.heading: Undershoot, recovery time, and ringing as loop evidence
sections.body: When load current steps up, the output capacitor alone supplies the extra current until the feedback loop reacts and duty cycle increases, so the output voltage dips — the undershoot. The depth of that dip and the time it takes to return within the regulation band are direct, readable evidence of loop bandwidth and output capacitance: a faster loop reacts sooner and produces a shallower, shorter dip for the same step size and capacitor. If the recovery is not a clean single dip back to the setpoint but instead rings — overshoots past the setpoint, dips again, and settles in a decaying oscillation — that ringing is the classic signature of low phase margin, an underdamped closed loop that is stable but too close to the edge, and it is exactly the kind of behavior a bench transient test is designed to expose before it becomes a field failure.

sections.heading: Measuring loop gain directly by injection
sections.body: A transient response shows symptoms; a loop-gain measurement shows the cause directly. The standard technique breaks the feedback loop at a point where a small series resistor (typically 10 to 50 ohms) can be inserted without disturbing DC operation — usually in the feedback divider path — and an injection transformer couples a small swept-frequency AC signal across that resistor. A frequency response analyzer measures the signal on both sides of the injection point and computes their ratio as gain and phase versus frequency, producing a Bode plot of the actual loop gain. The crossover frequency is where the gain trace crosses 0 dB, and the phase margin is read as the distance between the measured phase at that frequency and the -180 degree instability threshold — giving numbers that can be compared directly against the qualitative undershoot and ringing observations from the transient test.

lessons.workedExample: A student builds a MOSFET step-load fixture on a 5 V, 2 A buck, stepping the load from 0.5 A to 2 A at roughly 1 A/us. The first design shows a 180 mV undershoot (3.6% of the rail) that rings twice before settling in about 40 microseconds — a sign of low phase margin. After increasing the feedback compensation capacitor, the same step produces a clean 90 mV undershoot with a single smooth recovery in 15 microseconds and no ringing. A follow-up injection sweep with a 20 ohm break resistor in the feedback divider confirms the diagnosis directly: crossover frequency rose from about 8 kHz to 22 kHz and phase margin improved from roughly 28 degrees to 58 degrees, matching the transient-domain improvement with a frequency-domain number.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who watches a transient screenshot ring twice before settling is looking for the student to connect that shape to loop stability rather than shrug it off as "a little noise." A weak answer describes the undershoot number alone with no mention of ringing or recovery time. A strong answer reads undershoot depth, recovery time, and any post-transient ringing as evidence of bandwidth and phase margin, and — if pushed further — can describe or show a direct loop-gain measurement using series injection across a break resistor, naming the crossover frequency and phase margin in degrees. Being able to move from "it rang twice" to "phase margin was around 28 degrees" is the difference between describing a symptom and diagnosing it.

questions.prompt: Why is the slew rate of a step-load fixture deliberately controlled rather than made as fast as physically possible?

options.text: An uncontrolled, near-instantaneous step mostly exercises the output capacitor's ESR/ESL rather than the feedback loop's actual bandwidth
MOSFETs cannot switch faster than 1 A per microsecond
Fast steps damage the converter's output capacitor permanently
Oscilloscopes cannot capture edges faster than 1 A per microsecond

explanations.a: Correct — a step far faster than the loop can possibly respond to mostly reveals capacitor ESR/ESL behavior in the first instants, which is a different question from characterizing the feedback loop's own bandwidth and stability.
explanations.b: MOSFETs can switch far faster than 1 A/us; the limit here is a deliberate test-fixture choice, not a device limitation.
explanations.c: A well-designed test does not damage the capacitor; the concern is measurement relevance, not component safety.
explanations.d: Modern oscilloscopes easily capture edges much faster than this; capture speed is not the limiting factor.

questions.prompt: After a load step, the output voltage overshoots past the setpoint, dips again, and settles in a decaying oscillation before stabilizing. What does this ringing indicate?

options.text: The output capacitor value is too large
Low phase margin — an underdamped closed loop that is stable but close to the instability edge
The load step slew rate was set too slow
The converter has entered discontinuous conduction mode

explanations.a: A larger output capacitor generally reduces undershoot depth rather than causing oscillatory ringing.
explanations.b: Correct — decaying oscillation after a transient is the textbook signature of an underdamped, low-phase-margin loop: stable, but with less design margin than a cleanly recovering response.
explanations.c: A too-slow slew rate would understate loop stress, not create ringing; ringing is a property of the loop's response, not the stimulus speed.
explanations.d: DCM is an inductor-current operating mode visible at the switch node, unrelated to closed-loop transient ringing on the output.

questions.prompt: In a series-injection loop-gain measurement, what does the crossover frequency represent on the resulting Bode plot?

options.text: The switching frequency of the converter
The frequency at which the measured loop gain crosses 0 dB
The frequency at which the output capacitor's impedance is minimum
The frequency at which the injection transformer saturates

explanations.a: Switching frequency is a separate parameter measured at the switch node; it is not generally the same as the loop's gain crossover frequency.
explanations.b: Correct — crossover frequency is defined as the frequency where the measured loop gain magnitude equals 0 dB (gain of one), and it marks roughly the bandwidth of the feedback loop.
explanations.c: Capacitor impedance minimum (its ESR frequency) is a component property, not the definition of loop crossover.
explanations.d: Transformer saturation is a fixture-limitation concern, not what the crossover point on the Bode plot represents.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for making a direct loop-gain measurement by series injection.

items.text: Identify a point in the feedback path where a small series resistor (10-50 ohms) can be inserted without disturbing DC operation
Couple a small swept-frequency AC signal across that resistor using an injection transformer
Measure the signal on both sides of the injection point across the frequency sweep
Compute the ratio of the two measurements to plot loop gain and phase versus frequency

questions.explanation: The break point must be chosen first so the injection does not disturb normal operation, then the injection transformer couples the stimulus across it, then both sides of the break are measured across the sweep, and only then can their ratio be computed to produce the loop gain and phase Bode plot.

lessons.label: Thermal and EMI Bench Checks

sections.heading: Three ways to read temperature, and what each actually measures
sections.body: An IR camera reads a surface's infrared emission and converts it to temperature across a whole field of view, which is excellent for finding the single hottest component on a board at a glance, but it only sees the outer surface — it can be fooled by low or unknown emissivity on shiny metal cans and reads the case, not the junction inside. A thermocouple, glued or taped directly to a package, gives a single accurate point reading with better absolute accuracy on that spot, at the cost of thermal lag (the thermocouple's own mass takes time to equilibrate) and needing contact that can disturb small components. For the part that usually matters most in a converter, the switching MOSFET, there is a third option: using Rds(on) itself as an on-die thermometer, since silicon Rds(on) has a strong positive temperature coefficient — commonly rising by roughly 0.4 to 1% per degree Celsius, meaning it can nearly double from 25 degrees C to 125 degrees C — so measuring the drain-source voltage drop at a known current and comparing it to the datasheet's Rds(on)-versus-temperature curve gives a junction-adjacent reading no external sensor can match.

sections.heading: Steady state takes minutes, not seconds
sections.body: Thermal mass means temperature readings taken seconds after power-up or a load change are still climbing, sometimes for several minutes, before the board reaches equilibrium with its enclosure and ambient air. A hot-spot number recorded too early understates the real operating temperature and can hide a part that will fail hours into continuous use, so a defensible thermal check holds the load steady and watches the peak temperature until it stops rising, not until it looks stable for a moment.

sections.heading: Pre-compliance conducted EMI: LISN, spectrum analyzer, and the Class B shape
sections.body: A Line Impedance Stabilization Network (LISN) sits between the mains supply and the converter under test, presenting a standardized impedance to the device while coupling its conducted noise current out to a spectrum analyzer and blocking noise already present on the mains from contaminating the reading. Sweeping the analyzer from 150 kHz to 30 MHz and overlaying the result against the CISPR 32 / EN 55032 Class B conducted-emissions limit gives a pre-compliance check before a formal lab test. That limit line has a recognizable shape rather than a flat ceiling: roughly 66 dBuV quasi-peak at 150 kHz, declining to about 56 dBuV by 500 kHz, holding close to that level up to 5 MHz, then stepping up to around 60 dBuV quasi-peak through 30 MHz. A converter with spread-spectrum frequency dithering — deliberately wobbling the switching frequency instead of holding it fixed — spreads its harmonic energy across a wider band, so a narrow-resolution-bandwidth analyzer reads a lower peak at any single frequency even though the total radiated and conducted energy is unchanged; this can be enough to pass a peak or quasi-peak limit without actually reducing the noise a listener (or a nearby radio) experiences.

lessons.workedExample: A student measures their buck converter's MOSFET with an IR camera immediately after switching to full load and reads 68 degrees C on the case. Ten minutes later, still at full load, the IR reading has crept up to 81 degrees C and stopped climbing — the true steady-state temperature was 13 degrees higher than the early reading suggested. Cross-checking with the Rds(on) method — measuring 41 mV across the MOSFET at a known 8 A test pulse and comparing to the datasheet's Rds(on)-vs-temperature curve — corroborates a junction temperature consistent with the settled IR reading, giving two independent methods that agree once steady state is actually reached.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks "how hot does this actually get" is testing whether a thermal claim was taken at steady state or grabbed the moment the camera came out. A weak answer gives one IR snapshot taken right after power-up with no mention of how long the board ran. A strong answer states how long the load was held before the reading was recorded, ideally cross-checks a surface method (IR or thermocouple) against a more direct one like Rds(on)-based sensing on the hottest device, and — for a project that discusses EMI at all — can describe a LISN-based pre-compliance conducted scan against the Class B limit rather than only claiming "it doesn't cause radio interference" with no measurement behind it.

questions.prompt: Why can using a MOSFET's own Rds(on) as an on-die thermometer give a better estimate of junction temperature than an IR camera aimed at the package?

options.text: Rds(on) is unaffected by current, so it gives a cleaner reading
Rds(on) has a strong positive temperature coefficient tied to the silicon itself, while an IR camera only sees the outer case surface and can be thrown off by emissivity
IR cameras cannot detect temperatures above 60 degrees C
Rds(on) measurement requires no test equipment at all

explanations.a: Rds(on) measurement specifically depends on driving a known test current; it is not current-independent.
explanations.b: Correct — Rds(on) tracks the actual silicon temperature closely via its positive temperature coefficient, while an IR camera reads surface infrared emission, which depends on emissivity and lags the internal junction.
explanations.c: IR cameras used for electronics routinely read well above 60 degrees C; this is not a real limitation.
explanations.d: Measuring Rds(on) accurately requires a known test current source and a precision voltage measurement, not zero equipment.

questions.prompt: A student records a hot-spot temperature 10 seconds after applying full load and reports it as the converter's operating temperature. What is the main problem with this?

options.text: 10 seconds is too long, so the reading captures unnecessary noise
The board has not yet reached thermal steady state, so the true peak temperature is understated
IR cameras require at least a minute of warm-up before any reading is valid
Full load current changes too quickly to be measured at all

explanations.a: The problem is not measurement noise from timing; it is that the physical system has not finished heating up.
explanations.b: Correct — thermal mass means components keep heating for minutes after a load step, so an early reading is lower than the true steady-state peak.
explanations.c: Camera warm-up is a separate, minor consideration and not the core issue with a 10-second post-load reading.
explanations.d: Load current itself can be applied essentially instantly; the slow part is the thermal response of the components, not the electrical step.

questions.prompt: A converter uses spread-spectrum frequency dithering. How does this typically affect a conducted-emissions scan against the CISPR 32 / EN 55032 Class B limit?

options.text: It reduces the total radiated and conducted energy the converter produces
It spreads harmonic energy across a wider band, lowering the peak reading at any single frequency without reducing total energy
It has no effect on the measured spectrum at all
It shifts the switching frequency below 150 kHz, removing it from the measurement range

explanations.a: Total emitted energy is unchanged by dithering; only its distribution across frequency changes.
explanations.b: Correct — dithering spreads the same total harmonic energy across a wider frequency band, so a narrow-resolution-bandwidth analyzer reads a lower peak at each frequency even though nothing about the total noise energy has decreased.
explanations.c: Dithering measurably changes the spectral shape on a scan, visibly broadening and lowering individual harmonic peaks.
explanations.d: Dithering wobbles the switching frequency around its nominal value; it does not relocate the fundamental below the 150 kHz measurement floor.

questions.prompt: Match each thermal or EMI measurement tool to its primary role.

right.text: Single-point contact temperature reading with good absolute accuracy but thermal lag
Whole-board surface temperature mapping to locate hot spots, limited by emissivity
Presents standardized impedance and couples conducted noise current to a spectrum analyzer for an EMI scan

questions.explanation: An IR camera maps surface temperature across the whole board to find hot spots but depends on emissivity; a thermocouple gives an accurate single-point contact reading but reacts slowly due to its own thermal mass; a LISN standardizes the mains impedance seen by the converter while routing its conducted noise to a spectrum analyzer for a pre-compliance EMI scan.

units.label: Landmark Work and Open Debates

lessons.label: From Mercury-Arc to Thyristor: How the Field Began

sections.heading: Before silicon: arcs and metal oxides
sections.body: For the first half of the twentieth century, converting AC to DC at real power levels meant either rotating machines or the mercury-arc rectifier: a sealed glass or steel tank where an arc struck between a pool of liquid mercury (the cathode) and graphite anodes conducted current in one direction only, valve-like. Mercury-arc rectifiers electrified early subway systems and HVDC links but were bulky, needed warm-up time, and could misfire ('arc-back'), damaging equipment. Selenium and copper-oxide rectifiers, dry metal-oxide stacks patented in the 1920s-30s, replaced mercury arcs in lower-power roles like battery chargers and radio supplies, but their forward drop was high and they degraded with heat and age.

sections.heading: Silicon replaces the arc
sections.body: The shift to silicon followed the silicon transistor work at Bell Labs in the mid-1950s, which proved silicon p-n junctions could be made reliably at scale. Bell Labs researchers, including William Shockley's group, described the four-layer p-n-p-n switching structure theoretically, but it was General Electric that turned it into a practical controllable power device. At GE's Clyde, New York plant, Gordon Hall built a working p-n-p-n silicon controlled rectifier (SCR) in 1956-57 on a shoestring budget; applications engineer Frank W. 'Bill' Gutzwiller took the first prototype and demonstrated it controlling the speed of an electric drill, the first solid-state motor speed control. GE commercialized the SCR in early 1958, with Gutzwiller driving the technical literature and promotion that taught engineers how to use it.

sections.heading: Naming the discipline
sections.body: The SCR (and later the triac and gate turn-off thyristor) gave designers a rugged, cheap way to switch large currents with a small control signal, but for over a decade the resulting work had no unified identity: it was scattered across power engineering, electronics, and control journals. William E. Newell, at Westinghouse, argued in his widely cited 1973 IEEE paper 'Power Electronics: Emerging from Limbo' that this fragmentation was holding the field back. He proposed that power electronics was interstitial to three parent disciplines, power, electronics, and control, illustrating it as three overlapping circles (often remembered as a cube of interacting axes). Newell's framing gave the field a name and a boundary, and the community he was addressing coalesced into the IEEE Power Electronics Society (PELS), chartered as its own technical society in 1988 after growing out of the IEEE Power Electronics Specialists Conference (PESC) lineage that had begun in 1970; Newell's three-circle definition is still the reference point for defining what counts as power electronics.

lessons.workedExample: A 1958 industrial catalog lists a GE SCR rated 16 A average, 200 V blocking, controllable by a few milliamps at the gate, replacing a mercury-arc tube the size of a fire extinguisher plus its vacuum pump and warm-up timer. A modern student rebuilding this history with a TO-220 SCR (e.g., a 2N6397-class device) on a breadboard can reproduce Gutzwiller's drill demo: firing the gate later in each AC half-cycle chops more of the sine wave, lowering the drill's average voltage and RPM, the same phase-control principle now used in lamp dimmers and small motor controls.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe the mercury-arc-to-silicon transition to see whether a student understands that power electronics is a materials and packaging story as much as a circuits one: silicon didn't just make devices smaller, it removed warm-up time, arc-back failures, and the need for a technician to babysit a vacuum tank. A strong answer names Hall's SCR, Gutzwiller's application push, and explains WHY silicon beat mercury-arc (reliability, size, instant-on) rather than just asserting 'semiconductors are better.' A weak answer treats the thyristor as always having existed and cannot say what problem it solved.

questions.prompt: What was the primary practical drawback of mercury-arc rectifiers that silicon thyristors solved?

options.text: Mercury-arc rectifiers could not carry any current at all
They required warm-up time, could misfire (arc-back), and were bulky
They only worked on DC input
They could not be used in HVDC transmission

explanations.a: Mercury-arc rectifiers carried substantial current; that was their whole purpose in early HVDC and subway systems.
explanations.b: Correct — warm-up time, arc-back misfires, and bulk (glass/steel tank, vacuum pump) were the practical costs silicon devices eliminated.
explanations.c: Mercury-arc rectifiers converted AC to DC; they operated on AC input, not DC.
explanations.d: Mercury-arc rectifiers were in fact used for early HVDC links; that was one of their main applications.

questions.prompt: Match each person to their contribution in the SCR's development.

right.text: Built the first working SCR device at GE in 1956-57
Demonstrated the SCR controlling a drill's speed and led applications engineering
Named and bounded power electronics as a discipline in a 1973 paper

questions.explanation: Hall built the device, Gutzwiller demonstrated and promoted its use, and Newell, at Westinghouse, later defined power electronics as the overlap of power, electronics, and control disciplines.

questions.prompt: According to Newell's 1973 argument, why had power electronics failed to develop as a coherent field before then?

options.text: No semiconductor devices existed yet capable of high-power switching
Work was scattered across power, electronics, and control specialties that did not communicate
Governments had banned commercial thyristor use
Mercury-arc rectifiers were considered good enough and research funding stopped

explanations.a: By 1973 the SCR had existed commercially for over a decade; devices were not the barrier Newell identified.
explanations.b: Correct — Newell's central claim was that parochialism among power, electronics, and control specialists stifled communication and prevented the field from being recognized as its own discipline.
explanations.c: There was no such ban; SCRs were widely sold commercially from 1958 onward.
explanations.d: Newell's concern was disciplinary fragmentation, not that research had stalled due to satisfaction with mercury-arc technology.

questions.prompt: Order these events chronologically.

items.text: Mercury-arc rectifiers power early subway and HVDC systems
Bell Labs silicon transistor work proves silicon junctions can be mass-produced
Gordon Hall builds the first working GE SCR
Newell publishes 'Power Electronics: Emerging from Limbo'

questions.explanation: Mercury-arc technology came first (early 1900s), then Bell Labs' silicon transistor work in the mid-1950s enabled reliable silicon devices, then Hall's 1956-57 SCR, and finally Newell's 1973 paper named the resulting field.

lessons.label: Middlebrook, Cuk, and State-Space Averaging

sections.heading: A converter that changes topology every microsecond
sections.body: A buck, boost, or flyback converter is not one linear circuit; it is two (or more) different circuits that the switch alternates between every switching period. Before the mid-1970s, designers handled this largely by building a prototype, measuring its loop response on a network analyzer, and tweaking compensation by feel, because there was no general accepted way to write a small-signal transfer function for a circuit that changes its own topology twice a cycle. The first real crack in that gap was G. W. Wester and R. D. Middlebrook's 1973 paper 'Low-Frequency Characterization of Switched dc-dc Converters,' which averaged buck, boost, and buck-boost power stages into approximate continuous models, but it was restricted to those specific topologies rather than offering a general method. At Caltech, Middlebrook's power electronics group kept pushing to make converter design a predictive, computable discipline rather than a bench craft.

sections.heading: The 1976 PESC paper
sections.body: Middlebrook and his student Slobodan Cuk published 'A General Unified Approach to Modelling Switching-Converter Power Stages' at the 1976 IEEE Power Electronics Specialists Conference in Cleveland. Their method, state-space averaging, writes the state equations for each switch position, then averages them weighted by duty ratio D over one switching period, producing a single continuous, time-invariant state-space model whose small-signal linearization yields a standard transfer function. From that same paper came a canonical circuit model, an equivalent circuit with an ideal transformer and controlled sources, that let any PWM converter's control-to-output and line-to-output transfer functions be read off directly, including the right-half-plane zero that boost and flyback converters exhibit. The same research thread produced the Cuk converter itself, a topology using a capacitor rather than an inductor as the primary energy-transfer element, giving continuous, non-pulsating current at both input and output.

sections.heading: What averaging assumes, and where it stops working
sections.body: State-space averaging rests on two assumptions: the switching ripple on inductor currents and capacitor voltages is small relative to their DC values (the small-ripple approximation), and the control loop's bandwidth is well below the switching frequency, typically by a factor of five to ten, so the averaged model, which throws away all information at and above the switching frequency, remains valid where the loop actually operates. When designers push crossover frequency too close to fsw, or when a converter runs in discontinuous conduction with large ripple, or when fast phenomena like peak-current-mode sampling matter, the averaged model quietly stops predicting reality, which is exactly the gap that later current-mode modeling work had to close.

lessons.workedExample: Consider a buck converter switching at 100 kHz with duty ratio D = 0.4, built from ideal switch and diode states. Writing the inductor and capacitor state equations separately for the switch-on and switch-off intervals, then averaging them as D times the on-state equations plus (1-D) times the off-state equations, collapses two linear circuits into one averaged model. Linearizing around the DC operating point gives a control-to-output transfer function with a double pole at the LC corner frequency, roughly 1/(2*pi*sqrt(LC)), that a designer can hand to a compensator design tool, no bench iteration required, as long as the intended loop crossover stays well under 100 kHz/10, about 10 kHz.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who sees state-space averaging invoked wants to know the student understands it as an approximation with named validity conditions, not a magic transfer-function generator. The strong answer states the small-ripple and bandwidth-separation assumptions explicitly and can say what breaks (DCM, high-bandwidth loops, fast current-mode dynamics) when they are violated. The weak answer cites 'Middlebrook's model' as a black box that always applies, which is precisely the overreach that got exposed a decade later by current-mode instability nobody's averaged model predicted.

questions.prompt: Why couldn't a switching converter be analyzed with ordinary linear small-signal circuit theory before state-space averaging?

options.text: Switching converters don't have inductors or capacitors
The circuit's topology itself changes every switching period, so no single fixed linear circuit describes it
Linear circuit theory cannot handle DC voltages
Transfer functions cannot be computed for any circuit with a diode

explanations.a: Switching converters are built almost entirely from inductors, capacitors, switches, and diodes; that's not the obstacle.
explanations.b: Correct — a converter alternates between distinct circuit topologies (switch on vs. off) each cycle, so it isn't a fixed linear system in the way ordinary small-signal analysis assumes.
explanations.c: Linear circuit theory handles DC operating points routinely; that isn't the barrier state-space averaging addressed.
explanations.d: Diodes appear throughout linear and nonlinear circuit analysis; the issue is the changing topology, not the presence of a diode.

questions.prompt: What does state-space averaging assume in order to be valid?

options.text: Switching ripple is small and loop bandwidth is well below the switching frequency
The converter operates only at duty ratio D = 0.5
The output capacitor has zero equivalent series resistance
The converter never enters steady state

explanations.a: Correct — the small-ripple approximation and a loop bandwidth well below fsw (roughly 5-10x separation) are the two conditions the 1976 Middlebrook-Cuk method relies on.
explanations.b: State-space averaging works across the full range of duty ratios from 0 to 1, not just D = 0.5.
explanations.c: ESR is a real-world parasitic that can be included in the model; it is not a validity requirement of the averaging method.
explanations.d: The method models both the DC steady-state operating point and small-signal dynamics around it; it does not require the converter to never settle.

questions.prompt: Match each item to what it is known for.

right.text: Led the Caltech power electronics group that produced state-space averaging
Co-authored the 1976 PESC paper as Middlebrook's student
A topology using a capacitor as the primary energy-transfer element

questions.explanation: Middlebrook led the Caltech group, Cuk was his co-author on the 1976 paper, and the Cuk converter that resulted from the same research line transfers energy through a capacitor rather than an inductor.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of the state-space averaging method.

items.text: Write separate state equations for each switch position (on-state, off-state)
Average the state equations, weighted by duty ratio D, over one switching period
Find the DC operating point of the resulting averaged model
Linearize around that operating point to get a small-signal transfer function

questions.explanation: The method starts from per-topology state equations, averages them by duty cycle into one continuous model, solves for the DC operating point, then linearizes for small-signal analysis.

lessons.label: The Extra Element Theorem and the Input-Filter Trap

sections.heading: A working supply that fails when you protect it
sections.body: A regulated DC-DC converter often needs an LC input filter to keep its switching noise off the source bus and to smooth the source's own ripple. A well-meaning engineer designs a well-damped filter, bench-tests it alone, confirms the converter alone is stable, connects the two, and finds the whole system oscillates or fails outright. This is not a rare mistake; it was common enough by the mid-1970s that R. D. Middlebrook wrote it up as a general design criterion rather than a one-off bug.

sections.heading: Negative incremental input resistance
sections.body: The root cause is a property of every regulated converter: because a feedback loop holds output voltage (and hence output power) constant against line variations, the input power Pin = Vin * Iin is also held roughly constant across small perturbations. If Pin is constant, then Iin must fall when Vin rises, so the converter's incremental (small-signal) input resistance, dVin/dIin, is negative, even though its DC or large-signal input resistance is positive. An LC filter, meanwhile, has an output impedance that peaks near its own resonant frequency. Middlebrook's input-filter design criterion states that if the filter's output impedance magnitude approaches or exceeds the converter's input impedance magnitude near that resonance, the negative-resistance behavior can drive the combined system unstable, degrading phase margin or causing outright oscillation, even though each half was stable alone.

sections.heading: The Extra Element Theorem as the general tool
sections.body: The input-filter criterion is a specific case of a broader technique Middlebrook formalized: the Extra Element Theorem (EET), laid out in his widely cited 1989 IEEE Transactions on Education paper 'Null Double Injection and the Extra Element Theorem.' The EET lets a designer find how any circuit's transfer function changes when one additional element, an inductor, a filter, a parasitic capacitance, is added, by computing only two auxiliary quantities from the original circuit (the impedance the extra element sees, under two limiting conditions) rather than re-deriving the whole network from scratch. Applied to the input-filter problem, the EET shows directly that the filter modifies the converter's loop gain by a correction factor that stays near unity, and therefore harmless, only when the filter's output impedance is kept well below the converter's input impedance across the relevant frequency range, giving designers a design-time inequality to check instead of a post-hoc bench failure to debug.

lessons.workedExample: A 28 V, 5 A regulated buck module has a measured incremental input impedance of about 15 ohms at its control loop's crossover region. An engineer adds an LC filter (a few hundred microhenries with a film capacitor) sized only to meet a conducted-EMI spec, without checking its output impedance against that 15 ohms. The filter's output impedance peaks at roughly 20 ohms near its resonant frequency, above the converter's input impedance there, and the assembled system rings and eventually latches into oscillation on power-up. The documented fix is to add a damping resistor (with a series blocking capacitor to avoid efficiency loss) across the filter's output, pulling its peak impedance safely below the converter's input impedance, restoring the phase margin the converter had on the bench alone.
lessons.judgeFraming: This is one of the sharpest counterintuitive results in power electronics, so judges ask about it specifically to see if a student has internalized why 'both parts work alone, so the system works' is false here. A strong answer explains negative incremental input resistance from Pin = constant, states Middlebrook's criterion (filter Zout must stay well below converter Zin), and can name a fix (damping the filter). A weak answer says 'the filter interfered with the converter' without being able to say what interfered, which is exactly the vague diagnosis this criterion exists to replace.

questions.prompt: Why does a regulated DC-DC converter exhibit negative incremental input resistance?

options.text: Because its feedback loop holds output power roughly constant, so input current rises as input voltage falls
Because the converter's diodes conduct in the reverse direction
Because all inductors have negative resistance at high frequency
Because the converter is unregulated and draws whatever current the source allows

explanations.a: Correct — with Pin held roughly constant by the regulation loop, Iin must increase when Vin decreases (and vice versa), giving dVin/dIin < 0 in the small-signal sense.
explanations.b: Diode conduction direction is unrelated to this small-signal input-impedance property; it is a consequence of closed-loop power regulation.
explanations.c: Real inductors have positive resistance (their winding resistance); this has nothing to do with the converter-level effect described.
explanations.d: The effect specifically requires regulation (constant output power); an unregulated converter would not show this property in the same way.

questions.prompt: According to Middlebrook's input-filter design criterion, when does adding an LC input filter risk destabilizing an otherwise-stable converter?

options.text: Whenever any filter at all is added, regardless of its impedance
When the filter's output impedance approaches or exceeds the converter's input impedance near the filter's resonance
Only when the filter uses an electrolytic capacitor
Only if the converter is unregulated

explanations.a: The criterion is quantitative, not absolute; filters with sufficiently low output impedance relative to the converter's input impedance do not destabilize the system.
explanations.b: Correct — instability risk arises specifically when filter output impedance is not kept well below the converter's (negative) input impedance across the relevant frequency band.
explanations.c: Capacitor chemistry (electrolytic vs. film) affects ESR and losses but is not the criterion itself; the criterion is about impedance magnitudes.
explanations.d: The negative-input-resistance behavior driving this instability specifically requires closed-loop regulation; an unregulated converter would not exhibit it.

questions.prompt: What does the Extra Element Theorem let a designer compute?

options.text: How a circuit's transfer function changes when one additional element is added, using only two auxiliary impedances from the original circuit
The exact junction temperature of a power semiconductor
The total harmonic distortion of an AC power line
The switching frequency that minimizes EMI

explanations.a: Correct — the EET expresses the change in a network's transfer function due to one added element as a correction factor derived from two impedances computed in the original (unmodified) circuit, avoiding a full re-derivation.
explanations.b: Junction temperature is a thermal calculation involving power dissipation and thermal resistance, unrelated to the EET.
explanations.c: THD is a power-quality metric computed from harmonic content, not something the EET addresses.
explanations.d: EMI-optimal switching frequency involves filter and loss tradeoffs; it is not what the EET computes.

questions.prompt: Order the events in the classic input-filter failure scenario.

items.text: Converter alone is bench-tested and found stable
LC filter alone is designed to meet an EMI spec
Filter and converter are connected together
The combined system oscillates because filter output impedance exceeds converter input impedance near resonance

questions.explanation: Each subsystem is verified stable in isolation, then connecting them exposes the negative-incremental-input-resistance interaction that Middlebrook's criterion predicts and a bench test of either part alone cannot reveal.

lessons.label: Current-Mode Control and the Subharmonic Oscillation Dispute

sections.heading: A control scheme that goes unstable on its own
sections.body: Peak current-mode control regulates a converter by comparing the sensed inductor current, ramping up during the switch-on interval, against a control voltage each cycle; when the current hits that threshold, the switch turns off. Designers liked it because it gives inherent cycle-by-cycle overcurrent protection and simplifies the outer voltage loop to a single-pole response. But by the late 1970s, engineers found that at duty ratios above 0.5, the current waveform could become unstable on its own, oscillating between a high and low peak every other cycle, a subharmonic oscillation at half the switching frequency, regardless of how well the voltage loop was compensated. The known fix, adding a fixed-slope compensating ramp to the sensed current signal (slope compensation), damps the effect, but for years the field lacked an agreed model for exactly how much compensation was needed and why the instability appeared specifically at D > 0.5.

sections.heading: The modeling fight
sections.body: Early attempts folded current-mode control into Middlebrook and Cuk's state-space-averaged framework using an averaged three-terminal model of the switch, treating the inductor current loop as if it were just another feedback path. These averaged models could not predict the subharmonic instability at all, because averaging discards exactly the cycle-to-cycle, near-switching-frequency information the effect depends on. Vatché Vorperian's PWM switch model, published in 1990, offered a more general small-signal building block for the switch network itself but still needed extension to fully capture current-mode's discrete, sampled nature. The decisive move came from Raymond Ridley, whose Virginia Tech PhD dissertation (November 1990) and 1991 journal paper treated the inductor current sensing as a genuinely sampled-data process, valid up to half the switching frequency, and derived a model that predicted the subharmonic oscillation and the exact amount of slope compensation needed to prevent it, without requiring a full discrete z-transform treatment.

sections.heading: Where the lineage sits today
sections.body: Ridley's sampled-data model became the standard reference for peak-current-mode design and is still cited in current IC datasheets and application notes. It also clarified the design space around peak current mode: average-current-mode control (which regulates the average, not peak, inductor current, avoiding the need for slope compensation but with slower dynamics), valley current-mode and hysteretic control (switching on measured minimum or a current window, common in fast point-of-load converters), and constant-on-time control (fixing the on-time and letting frequency vary, popular in modern low-duty-ratio buck regulators) all trace back to this same subharmonic-instability problem, each trading away peak current mode's simplicity for a different stability or transient-response property.

lessons.workedExample: A synchronous buck converter runs at 300 kHz with Vin = 12 V and Vout = 7.2 V, giving D = 0.6, above the 0.5 threshold. Without slope compensation, a small perturbation in the inductor current at turn-on grows each cycle rather than decaying, because the down-slope of the current (proportional to Vout/L) is smaller than what stability requires relative to the up-slope (proportional to (Vin-Vout)/L) at this duty ratio, producing visible current-waveform doubling on an oscilloscope every other switching cycle. Adding a compensating ramp with a slope at least half the inductor's down-slope, injected into the current-sense comparator, restores single-cycle convergence, which is exactly the quantity Ridley's model lets a designer calculate directly rather than find by trial and error on the bench.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe current-mode instability because it's a rare case where a control loop can be unstable even with a textbook-perfect voltage-loop compensator, so it tests whether a student understands that stability sometimes lives inside the modulator, not just the feedback path. A strong answer names the D > 0.5 threshold, explains slope compensation as adding a ramp to counter runaway current perturbations, and can say why averaged models missed it (they discard switching-frequency-scale information) while Ridley's sampled-data model caught it. A weak answer says 'current mode needs compensation' without being able to say what specifically goes unstable or why duty ratio is the trigger.

questions.prompt: At what condition does peak current-mode control become inherently unstable without slope compensation?

options.text: Duty ratio D greater than 0.5
Switching frequency below 10 kHz
Output capacitance above 100 microfarads
Input voltage below 5 V

explanations.a: Correct — for duty ratios above 0.5, current perturbations grow cycle-to-cycle rather than decay, producing subharmonic oscillation unless slope compensation is added.
explanations.b: Switching frequency alone does not trigger the instability; it is the duty ratio (the up-slope/down-slope relationship) that determines it.
explanations.c: Output capacitance affects voltage-loop dynamics and ripple but is not the trigger for peak-current-mode's inherent subharmonic instability.
explanations.d: Input voltage magnitude alone doesn't determine the instability; what matters is the resulting duty ratio relative to the 0.5 threshold.

questions.prompt: Why couldn't averaged (state-space) models of the era predict current-mode subharmonic oscillation?

options.text: Averaging discards the near-switching-frequency, cycle-to-cycle information the instability depends on
Averaged models only work for boost converters
Averaged models assume infinite switching frequency
Current-mode control had not been invented when averaged models were developed

explanations.a: Correct — averaging smooths out behavior within a switching period, exactly where subharmonic oscillation lives, so it structurally cannot capture the effect.
explanations.b: Averaged models apply to buck, boost, and other topologies alike; the limitation is about frequency content, not topology.
explanations.c: Averaged models assume switching is fast relative to the loop bandwidth, not literally infinite; but the assumption still discards switching-rate detail.
explanations.d: Current-mode control predates Ridley's sampled-data model by over a decade; averaged models simply failed to capture its instability, not because it didn't yet exist.

questions.prompt: Match each researcher or model to its contribution.

right.text: Published a small-signal PWM switch model as a general building block
Developed a sampled-data current-mode model predicting subharmonic oscillation and required compensation
Adds a fixed-slope ramp to the sensed current signal to damp the instability

questions.explanation: Vorperian's PWM switch model provided a general small-signal building block; Ridley's dissertation and 1991 paper treated current sensing as sampled data and predicted the instability and needed compensation; slope compensation is the practical fix of adding a ramp to the current signal.

questions.prompt: Which control variant regulates the average, rather than peak, inductor current, avoiding the need for slope compensation?

options.text: Average-current-mode control
Peak current-mode control
Voltage-mode control with no current sensing
Open-loop PWM with fixed duty ratio

explanations.a: Correct — average-current-mode control regulates the average inductor current rather than its instantaneous peak, sidestepping the peak-sampling mechanism that causes subharmonic oscillation, at the cost of slower loop dynamics.
explanations.b: Peak current-mode control is exactly the scheme that requires slope compensation above D = 0.5; it does not avoid the issue.
explanations.c: Voltage-mode control doesn't sense current at all, so it is a different control family, not a variant that solves the current-mode subharmonic problem.
explanations.d: Open-loop fixed-duty PWM has no feedback and no current-mode instability question to solve in the first place; it isn't a current-mode variant.

lessons.label: Soft Switching and the Resonant School

sections.heading: The cost of switching fast
sections.body: A hard-switched converter turns its transistor on or off while it still carries significant voltage and current simultaneously, dissipating energy proportional to switching frequency in every transition and radiating EMI as fast dV/dt and dI/dt edges. Through the 1970s this capped practical switching frequencies at tens of kilohertz for anything but small loads, keeping magnetics (and therefore converters) physically large. Fred C. Lee's group at Virginia Tech, first as VPEC (Virginia Power Electronics Center) and later expanded into CPES (Center for Power Electronics Systems), spent the 1980s building a research program specifically around making the switch transition itself lossless.

sections.heading: Quasi-resonant and ZVS/ZCS families
sections.body: The VPEC approach added a small resonant LC tank around the switch so that its voltage or current is forced to zero before the transition happens: zero-voltage switching (ZVS) turns the device on only after its voltage has rung down to zero, and zero-current switching (ZCS) turns it off only after current has rung down to zero. Lee and collaborators, including work such as Tabisz and Lee's 1987 multiresonant switch papers, published a family of quasi-resonant and multiresonant converter topologies through the 1980s that let switching frequencies climb into the megahertz range with sharply reduced switching loss and EMI, at the price of extra resonant components, wider component stress variation across load and line, and harder small-signal modeling than a plain PWM converter.

sections.heading: LLC's takeover and the standing argument
sections.body: Of the resonant topologies this program produced, the LLC resonant converter, using two inductors and a capacitor to achieve ZVS on the primary switches and near-ZCS on the secondary rectifiers across a wide load range, eventually became the dominant choice for the DC-DC stage in high-efficiency AC-DC power supplies (server PSUs, chargers, LED drivers), largely displacing simpler resonant and hard-switched designs for that role by the 2000s. But the underlying question the VPEC program raised was never fully settled. Even inside VPEC, work such as Lotfi, Vorperian, and Lee's 1988 PESC paper 'Comparison of Stresses in Quasi-Resonant and Pulse-Width-Modulated Converters' documented that resonant topologies traded lower switching loss for higher peak voltage and current stress on the same devices, a tradeoff still at the center of the argument: resonant designers argue the added complexity buys real efficiency and EMI headroom that hard switching cannot match at a given frequency. Hard-switching advocates counter that wide-bandgap devices (silicon carbide, gallium nitride) with much lower switching loss per transition let hard-switched designs reach comparable frequencies and efficiencies with a simpler, more analyzable topology and fewer resonant-tolerance headaches, an argument that is still actively made on both sides today.

lessons.workedExample: A 65 W USB-C laptop charger built as an LLC resonant converter switches its primary FETs at roughly 100-150 kHz (varying with load, since LLC is frequency-modulated rather than duty-cycle modulated) while achieving ZVS turn-on across most of the load range, letting the design hit around 94% efficiency in a shirt-pocket-sized enclosure. A hard-switched flyback of the same power rating, built with silicon MOSFETs, would need to switch at a similar or lower frequency to keep switching losses tolerable, or use GaN devices to switch faster with acceptable loss, illustrating concretely why the resonant-vs-wide-bandgap-hard-switching argument is really an argument about which lever, topology or device physics, is the cheaper way to buy high frequency.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge raises soft switching to see if a student can explain WHY resonant topologies help (removing the voltage-current overlap during transition, not just 'it's more efficient') and can locate the live tradeoff rather than declaring one approach simply obsolete. A strong answer names ZVS or ZCS specifically, ties it to reduced switching loss and EMI, and can articulate both sides of the resonant-vs-wide-bandgap-hard-switching argument. A weak answer treats 'resonant' as a synonym for 'better' without saying what physically changes at the switch transition.

questions.prompt: What physically happens during a zero-voltage-switching (ZVS) turn-on that reduces switching loss?

options.text: The switch voltage has already rung down to zero before the device turns on, eliminating the voltage-current overlap
The switch is turned on twice as fast as in hard switching
The input voltage is halved by a transformer before reaching the switch
The gate drive current is increased to force a faster transition

explanations.a: Correct — ZVS uses a resonant tank to bring the switch's voltage to zero before turn-on, so there is no simultaneous high voltage and rising current during the transition, which is what dissipates energy in hard switching.
explanations.b: Switching speed alone (dV/dt, dI/dt) is a separate factor from ZVS; ZVS specifically addresses the voltage-current overlap, not just speed.
explanations.c: Voltage halving via a transformer doesn't address the switching-transition loss mechanism ZVS targets.
explanations.d: Increasing gate drive current changes switching speed but doesn't eliminate the voltage-current overlap; that requires the resonant zero-crossing timing ZVS relies on.

questions.prompt: Which topology, emerging from the resonant-converter research line, became the dominant DC-DC stage choice in high-efficiency AC-DC power supplies?

options.text: The Cuk converter
The LLC resonant converter
The basic buck converter
The mercury-arc rectifier

explanations.a: The Cuk converter came from Middlebrook and Cuk's state-space-averaging research line, a different lineage focused on modeling, not resonant soft switching.
explanations.b: Correct — the LLC resonant converter, using two inductors and a capacitor for ZVS/near-ZCS across a wide load range, became the dominant choice for high-efficiency AC-DC DC-DC stages.
explanations.c: A basic hard-switched buck converter does not provide the soft-switching benefits that made resonant topologies attractive for this role.
explanations.d: Mercury-arc rectifiers are a pre-silicon technology unrelated to the 1980s resonant-converter research program.

questions.prompt: Match each institution/program to its role in soft-switching history.

right.text: 1980s program that developed quasi-resonant and multiresonant converter families
Later expanded successor program at Virginia Tech
Researcher who led both programs and co-authored key multiresonant-switch papers

questions.explanation: VPEC was the 1980s Virginia Tech program that produced the quasi-resonant and multiresonant converter work; CPES was its later expanded successor; Fred C. Lee led both and co-authored foundational multiresonant-switch papers such as the 1987 Tabisz and Lee work.

questions.prompt: What is the core argument wide-bandgap hard-switching advocates make against resonant designs?

options.text: That devices like SiC and GaN have low enough switching loss per transition to reach comparable frequency and efficiency with a simpler, more analyzable topology
That resonant converters cannot achieve any efficiency gain over hard switching
That LLC converters are incapable of megahertz-range operation
That silicon devices always outperform wide-bandgap devices in switching loss

explanations.a: Correct — the argument is that wide-bandgap devices reduce per-transition switching loss enough that hard switching becomes competitive without resonant topology's added complexity and tolerance sensitivity.
explanations.b: The debate is about which approach is the more cost-effective path to a given frequency/efficiency target, not a claim that resonant designs offer zero benefit.
explanations.c: LLC converters can and do operate into the hundreds of kHz and beyond; this isn't the hard-switching camp's claim.
explanations.d: The wide-bandgap argument is the opposite: that SiC/GaN devices have lower switching loss than silicon, which is what makes hard switching at high frequency viable.

lessons.label: Wide-Bandgap: GaN vs SiC vs Silicon

sections.heading: The figure of merit behind the hype
sections.body: B. Jayant Baliga, working at GE in the early 1980s, formalized why a wider semiconductor bandgap makes a better power switch: a material's critical electric field for avalanche breakdown scales strongly with bandgap, and a device's specific on-resistance (Ron times active area) for a given breakdown voltage scales inversely with roughly the cube of that critical field. This relationship, now called Baliga's figure of merit, predicts that silicon carbide (bandgap about 3.3 eV) and gallium nitride (about 3.4 eV) can in principle achieve on-resistance per unit area one to two orders of magnitude lower than silicon (1.1 eV) at the same blocking voltage, meaning smaller, cooler, faster-switching devices for the same job.

sections.heading: Two wide-bandgap camps, one silicon holdout
sections.body: The two materials split into different commercial niches shaped by their physics and manufacturing history. GaN devices are typically lateral, built on silicon or SiC substrates using high-electron-mobility transistor (HEMT) structures, and dominate lower-voltage, high-frequency roles (under about 650 V) such as fast chargers and data-center power, led commercially by companies including EPC (Efficient Power Conversion), Navitas Semiconductor, and GaN Systems. SiC devices are vertical, more like a conventional MOSFET, and dominate higher-voltage roles (900 V to several kV) such as EV traction inverters and solar string inverters, a market Wolfspeed (formerly Cree) pioneered and still leads. Silicon has not stood still either: superjunction MOSFETs, which use alternating p and n columns to spread the depletion region and beat silicon's own theoretical on-resistance limit, remain the cost leader in many mid-voltage roles, so the live commercial argument is really cost-per-watt and per-application, not a simple 'wide bandgap always wins.'

sections.heading: The Little Box Challenge test
sections.body: In 2014 Google and the IEEE Power Electronics Society launched the Little Box Challenge, offering a $1 million prize for the highest power-density DC-AC inverter meeting a 2 kW, 120/240 Vac split-phase output specification, with a minimum acceptable density of 50 W per cubic inch. After testing at the National Renewable Energy Laboratory in late 2015, the winner, announced in 2016, was CE+T Power's team Red Electrical Devils from Belgium, which used gallium nitride switches (with support from GaN Systems) to reach roughly 143 W per cubic inch, about 14 cubic inches total volume, nearly triple the minimum requirement. Critics noted the contest optimized for volume above nearly everything else, so entries used exotic, expensive cooling and control tricks unlikely to be cost-competitive in mass production; it demonstrated what GaN made physically possible for power density, not what wide-bandgap devices cost per watt in a commodity product, which remains the actual battleground today.

lessons.workedExample: Comparing two 650 V-rated switches for a 300 W USB-C charger: a silicon superjunction MOSFET might have Ron of roughly 0.3 ohm in a standard TO-220-sized package, while a GaN HEMT rated for the same voltage and current can hit a similar or lower Ron in a package a fraction of the size, with far lower gate charge and output capacitance, letting the charger switch at 1-2 MHz instead of ~100 kHz. That higher frequency shrinks the magnetics enough to fit the whole charger in a case barely larger than a standard wall plug, which is exactly the design tradeoff (device cost premium vs. magnetics and enclosure savings) that determines whether GaN wins a given product.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask about GaN vs SiC vs silicon because it's a live, ongoing commercial and physical debate, not settled science, so the strong answer names the actual tradeoff axis (voltage range and cost-per-watt, not 'GaN is just better') and can cite Baliga's figure of merit as the physical reason wide-bandgap materials win on Ron per area. A strong answer also treats the Little Box Challenge as evidence of a physical ceiling raised, not proof of commercial viability, and can say why (exotic cooling, non-mass-producible techniques). A weak answer picks a favorite material and cannot say what voltage or frequency regime the claim applies to.

questions.prompt: According to Baliga's figure of merit, why do SiC and GaN allow lower specific on-resistance than silicon at the same breakdown voltage?

options.text: Their higher critical electric field for breakdown lets the same blocking voltage be achieved with a thinner, less resistive drift region
They conduct heat better, which directly lowers electrical resistance
They are always doped more heavily than silicon by manufacturing convention
Their bandgap has no relationship to on-resistance; the advantage comes only from smaller die size

explanations.a: Correct — a wider bandgap raises the critical electric field for avalanche breakdown, letting a given breakdown voltage be reached with a thinner, more lightly resistive drift region, which is the physical basis of Baliga's figure of merit.
