explanations.b: Thermal conductivity is a separate, real advantage of SiC in particular, but it is not the mechanism behind the on-resistance relationship in Baliga's figure of merit.
explanations.c: Doping level is a design choice within each material's constraints, not an inherent difference guaranteed by manufacturing convention.
explanations.d: Bandgap is directly related to the critical field and hence to specific on-resistance; this is the entire basis of the figure of merit.

questions.prompt: Match each company or device type to its wide-bandgap niche.

right.text: GaN devices for lower-voltage, high-frequency roles like fast chargers
SiC devices for higher-voltage roles like EV traction inverters
Silicon technology remaining the cost leader in many mid-voltage applications

questions.explanation: GaN companies target lower-voltage, high-frequency applications; Wolfspeed pioneered and leads SiC for higher-voltage roles; silicon superjunction MOSFETs remain the cost-effective choice in many mid-voltage roles where wide-bandgap's premium isn't justified.

questions.prompt: What did CE+T Power's Red Electrical Devils achieve in the Little Box Challenge?

options.text: A 2 kW, 120/240 Vac inverter at roughly 143 W per cubic inch in about 14 cubic inches, using GaN switches
A 2 kW, 120/240 Vac inverter using only silicon superjunction MOSFETs at the minimum required density
A 500 W inverter that failed to meet the minimum density requirement
A mercury-arc-based inverter that won on cost alone

explanations.a: Correct — the winning entry used GaN switches to reach about 143 W/in^3 in roughly 14 cubic inches total, well above the 50 W/in^3 minimum, for a 2 kW, 120/240 Vac output.
explanations.b: The winning entry used GaN devices, not silicon superjunction MOSFETs, and exceeded the minimum density by nearly threefold rather than just meeting it.
explanations.c: The challenge specification was 2 kW, not 500 W, and the winning entry comfortably exceeded the minimum density requirement.
explanations.d: Mercury-arc technology is obsolete pre-silicon technology entirely unrelated to this 2014-2016 contest.

questions.prompt: What did critics say the Little Box Challenge results did NOT prove?

options.text: That GaN-based designs would be cost-competitive per watt in mass-produced commodity products
That GaN switches physically permit higher power density than silicon
That silicon devices exist
That inverters can be built at all

explanations.a: Correct — critics pointed out the contest optimized for volume using exotic, expensive cooling and control techniques, demonstrating a physical ceiling rather than mass-production cost-competitiveness.
explanations.b: The contest results did demonstrate this; the higher power density achieved with GaN was the real, uncontested outcome.
explanations.c: This was never in question and isn't the subject of the criticism.
explanations.d: This is trivially true and unrelated to the specific critique of the contest's rules and incentives.

lessons.label: Open Questions and Contested Standards

sections.heading: Efficiency regulation and its critics
sections.body: Power supply efficiency is now regulated, not just marketed. The voluntary 80 PLUS program certifies desktop and server power supplies at tiers from Standard through Bronze, Silver, Gold, Platinum, and Titanium, each requiring a minimum AC-DC conversion efficiency at set load points, 20%, 50%, and 100% of rated load for the lower tiers, with Titanium adding a 10% load point since it is meant to reward supplies that stay efficient even lightly loaded. Separately, the US Department of Energy's Level VI standard and the EU's Code of Conduct for external power supplies set mandatory minimum efficiency and no-load power limits for the wall-wart adapters that charge phones and laptops. Critics of both regimes make the same core complaint: the certification load points are a handful of snapshots, not a real usage profile, so a supply tuned to ace 50% and 100% load can be mediocre at the 5-15% loads where many always-on devices (routers, chargers left plugged in) actually spend most of their life, meaning the badge can overstate real-world energy savings.

sections.heading: Two component-level fights: electrolytics vs. film, and GaN reliability
sections.body: Inside long-life converters (server PSUs, LED drivers, EV chargers rated for 10+ years), the standing reliability debate is electrolytic versus film capacitors for the DC bus. Aluminum electrolytics are cheap and offer high capacitance per dollar, but their electrolyte slowly dries out, an Arrhenius-type process that roughly doubles wear-out life for every 10 C drop in operating temperature, making them a common first-failure component. Film capacitors avoid electrolyte-dry-out failure but cost more per microfarad and are physically larger, so the argument over which to specify is really an argument about where in the design a project should pay for lifetime. A newer, unresolved fight concerns GaN transistors specifically: their dynamic on-resistance, Rds(on) measured shortly after a high-voltage turn-off, can be measurably higher than its DC-tested value due to charge trapping at the device's surface, and vendors and independent labs still disagree on how much this affects long-term efficiency and reliability claims in real applications.

sections.heading: Two open systems questions
sections.body: Two broader questions remain genuinely unsettled. First, analog versus digital control: digital controllers (running a compensator in firmware) offer flexibility, telemetry, and adaptive tuning that analog compensators cannot match, but add latency, quantization error, and firmware complexity that analog loyalists argue aren't justified for a fixed-point, high-volume design. Second, and largest in scope, does ever-higher switching frequency actually shrink a finished system? Raising frequency shrinks the magnetics, the classic promise of wide-bandgap devices, but it also raises dV/dt and dI/dt, demanding a larger, more elaborate EMI filter and, if switching losses aren't fully controlled, a bigger heatsink, so whether the net system, filter and thermal management included, actually gets smaller is a live, application-specific argument rather than a settled rule.

lessons.workedExample: A server power supply advertised as 80 PLUS Titanium tests at 96% efficiency at 50% load, exactly meeting its certification point, but a field audit finds the same unit running at 8% load (typical for an idle rack server) manages only about 88% efficiency, well below its badge's implied performance, because the certification's load points don't include anything below 10%. A design team debating whether to switch that supply's primary-side bus capacitors from aluminum electrolytic to film faces the concrete tradeoff directly: film capacitors would remove electrolyte dry-out as the dominant wear-out mechanism and could extend rated life from roughly 5-7 years to well past 10, but would raise bill-of-materials cost enough to matter at server-fleet volumes.
lessons.judgeFraming: This unit tests whether a student can hold a standard's stated purpose and its real gap side by side, rather than treating a certification badge as proof of real-world performance. A strong answer names a specific standard (80 PLUS, DOE Level VI, or EU CoC), states what load points it actually tests, and can say concretely where that leaves a blind spot (light-load efficiency, or no-load power). A strong answer on the component-level debates cites the actual physical mechanism (electrolyte dry-out, GaN charge trapping) rather than just saying 'reliability is a concern.' A weak answer treats any of these as settled facts rather than open, application-dependent tradeoffs.

questions.prompt: What is the main criticism of efficiency certification programs like 80 PLUS?

options.text: They test efficiency at only a few load points, which may not represent how the supply is actually used, such as at very light load
They only test at 100% load and ignore all other conditions
They measure output voltage ripple instead of efficiency
They are mandatory and prevent any product from being sold without certification

explanations.a: Correct — the criticism is that certification snapshots at set load points (like 20/50/100%, or 10/20/50/100% for Titanium) can miss real-world usage that sits at very light load, overstating typical energy performance.
explanations.b: 80 PLUS explicitly tests multiple load points, not just 100%; that is part of what the certification measures.
explanations.c: 80 PLUS certifies AC-DC conversion efficiency, not output ripple; ripple is a separate specification entirely.
explanations.d: 80 PLUS is a voluntary certification program, not a mandatory requirement to sell a power supply.

questions.prompt: What is the dominant wear-out mechanism that makes aluminum electrolytic capacitors a common first-failure point in long-life converters?

options.text: Gradual electrolyte dry-out, an Arrhenius-type process accelerated by temperature
Sudden dielectric breakdown at any voltage below their rating
Magnetic saturation of the capacitor's core
Corrosion caused specifically by GaN switching harmonics

explanations.a: Correct — electrolyte dry-out is a slow, temperature-accelerated (Arrhenius) process, with wear-out life roughly doubling for every 10 C reduction in operating temperature, making it the classic electrolytic-capacitor failure mode.
explanations.b: Electrolytic capacitors are typically rated to operate well below breakdown voltage in normal use; dry-out, not sudden breakdown, is the characteristic long-term failure mechanism.
explanations.c: Capacitors don't have a magnetic core to saturate; that concept applies to inductors and transformers, not capacitors.
explanations.d: Electrolyte dry-out is a general thermal aging mechanism unrelated specifically to GaN devices or their switching harmonics.

questions.prompt: What causes GaN transistors' dynamic Rds(on) to differ from their DC-tested on-resistance?

options.text: Charge trapping at the device surface following a high-voltage turn-off
The device physically changes size when switching at high frequency
GaN devices have no on-resistance at all in normal operation
Dynamic Rds(on) is purely a measurement artifact with no real physical cause

explanations.a: Correct — charge trapping at the GaN device's surface after a high-voltage blocking state can transiently raise Rds(on) above its DC-measured value, a real and still-debated effect on efficiency and reliability claims.
explanations.b: GaN devices do not physically change size with switching; the effect is electrical (charge trapping), not mechanical.
explanations.c: GaN devices, like all real transistors, have nonzero on-resistance; dynamic Rds(on) refers to that resistance being elevated after switching, not to its absence.
explanations.d: Dynamic Rds(on) is a real, physically grounded effect from charge trapping, not merely a measurement artifact, though the extent of its practical impact is genuinely debated.

questions.prompt: Order these from lowest to highest minimum efficiency tier in the 80 PLUS program.

items.text: 80 PLUS Standard
80 PLUS Bronze
80 PLUS Gold
80 PLUS Titanium

questions.explanation: The 80 PLUS tiers rise from Standard through Bronze, Silver, Gold, Platinum, to Titanium, each requiring progressively higher minimum efficiency at its tested load points, with Titanium adding the strictest requirements including a 10% load point.

questions.prompt: Why is 'higher switching frequency always makes the system smaller' considered an open question rather than a settled rule?

options.text: Higher frequency shrinks magnetics but can require a larger EMI filter and heatsink, so net system size is application-dependent
Switching frequency has no measurable effect on magnetics size
Higher switching frequency always increases efficiency with no downside
EMI filtering requirements decrease as switching frequency increases

explanations.a: Correct — while higher frequency does shrink magnetics, it raises dV/dt and dI/dt, which can demand a larger EMI filter and, if switching losses aren't controlled, more thermal management, so the net effect on overall system size is genuinely application-dependent.
explanations.b: Higher switching frequency directly reduces required magnetics size, per standard transformer/inductor design (volt-second) relationships; that effect is well established, not the disputed part.
explanations.c: Higher frequency can increase switching losses if not managed with fast, low-loss devices, so it is not an unconditional efficiency win.
explanations.d: Higher switching frequency typically increases EMI filtering demands due to faster edges, the opposite of decreasing them.

units.label: Control, Feedback, and Advanced Conversion

lessons.label: Small-Signal Models of a Switching Converter

sections.heading: Why a switch needs to be averaged before it can be analyzed
sections.body: A buck converter's switch node slams between 0 V and Vin tens of thousands of times a second, so classical linear circuit theory cannot touch it directly. Middlebrook and Ćuk (1976) solved this with state-space averaging: replace the switch and diode with their duty-cycle-weighted average over one switching period, producing a continuous nonlinear model. The next step, perturbation and linearization, is what actually turns that averaged model into something a transfer function can describe: write every quantity as a DC operating point plus a small AC wiggle around it — duty cycle d = D + d̂, output voltage v = V + v̂, inductor current i = I + î — substitute those into the averaged equations, and discard every product of two hatted (AC) terms since those are second-order and tiny compared to the first-order ones. What survives is a set of linear equations in the hatted variables alone, and Gvd(s) = v̂(s)/d̂(s) — the control-to-output transfer function this whole unit builds on — falls straight out of that linear system. Vorpérian (1990) repackaged the same physics as the PWM switch model, a three-terminal averaged element that drops into standard circuit simulators as if it were a transistor, which is why SPICE decks for power stages usually contain a block literally called 'PWM switch' rather than an actual MOSFET.

sections.heading: The buck: a clean double pole and one real-world zero
sections.body: For a voltage-mode buck converter, the control-to-output transfer function (duty cycle to output voltage) is dominated by the output LC filter, giving a double pole at f0 = 1/(2π√(LC)) where the phase drops 180 degrees over roughly a decade — a sharp, resonant-looking feature that a compensator must tame. The output capacitor's equivalent series resistance (ESR) adds a zero at fz = 1/(2π·C·ESR), which restores 90 degrees of phase above fz. With an old aluminum electrolytic (high ESR) that zero sits low enough to help compensation; with a low-ESR ceramic bank the zero moves far out and the double pole's phase lag has to be fought with compensator zeros instead.

sections.heading: Boost and buck-boost: the zero that lies to you
sections.body: Boost and buck-boost converters add a right-half-plane (RHP) zero, at fRHPZ = R(1−D)^2/(2πL) for a boost stage, that behaves unlike any zero a student has met before: it adds gain (like a normal zero) but subtracts phase (like an extra pole), because increasing duty cycle to raise output voltage first forces the inductor current up, briefly starving the output before the higher current catches up. A compensator cannot simply cancel it with a pole the way it would a left-half-plane zero. The accepted design rule is to keep the loop's crossover frequency at roughly one-third to one-fifth of fRHPZ, sacrificing bandwidth (and transient speed) for stability margin.

lessons.workedExample: A boost converter steps 12 V to 48 V (D ≈ 0.75) into a 5 A load (R = 9.6 Ω) through L = 22 µH. fRHPZ = R(1−D)^2/(2πL) = 9.6 × 0.0625 / (2π × 22e-6) ≈ 4.34 kHz. A designer targeting the usual 1/5 rule sets crossover near 870 Hz — an order of magnitude slower than a comparable buck at the same power level, which is precisely why boost-derived topologies feel sluggish under fast load steps. Note that current-mode control does not fix this: it collapses the LC double pole into a single pole (Lesson 03), but fRHPZ is a topological feature of the boost/buck-boost power stage itself and shows up in the current-command-to-output transfer function just as it does in the duty-cycle-to-output one — the real remedies are shrinking L, running at higher load current, or moving to a two-stage architecture.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who sees a boost or buck-boost converter on a board asks 'how did you set your loop bandwidth?' specifically to check whether the student knows the RHP zero exists, because it is the single most common reason a student's boost converter oscillates or rings badly under load transients despite a Bode plot that 'looked fine' in simulation with an idealized model. A strong answer names fRHPZ, computes it from L, D, and R, and explains the phase-lag mechanism (current has to rise before voltage can follow); a weak answer just says 'I added compensation until it looked stable' with no numeric target tied to the topology's own physics.

questions.prompt: In a buck converter's control-to-output transfer function, what creates the double pole at f0 = 1/(2π√(LC))?

options.text: The output LC filter
The MOSFET's gate capacitance
The output capacitor's ESR
The PWM comparator's propagation delay

explanations.a: Correct — the inductor and output capacitor together form a second-order LC filter, and its resonance produces the double pole.
explanations.b: Gate capacitance affects switching speed and drive loss, not the control-to-output small-signal transfer function's dominant poles.
explanations.c: ESR produces a zero (fz), not the double pole; the pole comes from the reactive LC pair, not the resistive parasitic.
explanations.d: Comparator delay is a high-frequency, usually negligible effect and is not what creates the dominant double pole.

questions.prompt: Why can't a compensator simply cancel a right-half-plane zero the way it cancels an ordinary (left-half-plane) zero?

options.text: RHP zeros only exist in simulation, never in real hardware
An RHP zero adds gain like a normal zero but subtracts phase like a pole, so pole-zero cancellation would require an unstable compensator pole
RHP zeros only appear at DC and never affect the AC loop
Compensators cannot have any zeros at all

explanations.a: RHP zeros are a real, measurable feature of boost and buck-boost converters, not a simulation artifact.
explanations.b: Correct — the RHP zero's magnitude response looks like a zero but its phase response looks like a pole, so canceling it would need a compensator pole placed in the unstable right half-plane.
explanations.c: The RHP zero acts across a band of frequencies near fRHPZ, not just at DC; it directly shapes the AC loop response.
explanations.d: Compensators routinely use zeros (that is the whole point of type II/III networks); the issue is specific to canceling an RHP zero.

questions.prompt: Match each small-signal modeling concept to its description.

right.text: Middlebrook and Ćuk's (1976) method of duty-cycle-averaging the switch/diode pair before linearizing
Vorpérian's (1990) three-terminal averaged element usable directly in circuit simulators
Frequency where output capacitor parasitic resistance restores 90 degrees of phase
Feature unique to boost/buck-boost that adds gain but removes phase

questions.explanation: State-space averaging is Middlebrook and Ćuk's foundational method; the PWM switch model is Vorpérian's simulator-friendly repackaging of it; the ESR zero comes from the output capacitor's parasitic resistance; the RHP zero is the boost/buck-boost-specific feature that adds gain while subtracting phase.

questions.prompt: A boost converter has fRHPZ = 4.34 kHz. Following the standard 1/5 design rule, roughly where should the loop crossover frequency be set?

options.text: Around 870 Hz
Around 4.34 kHz, exactly at fRHPZ
Around 21.7 kHz, above fRHPZ
It should be set as high as the switching frequency allows, ignoring fRHPZ

explanations.a: Correct — 4.34 kHz / 5 ≈ 870 Hz, keeping crossover well below the RHP zero's destabilizing phase loss.
explanations.b: Crossing over right at fRHPZ leaves essentially no phase margin, since the RHP zero's phase lag is already severe near its own frequency.
explanations.c: Crossing over above fRHPZ means fighting a topology that is actively losing phase and gaining gain at that frequency — the opposite of the stability rule.
explanations.d: Ignoring fRHPZ and crossing over near the switching frequency is exactly the mistake the 1/3-to-1/5 rule exists to prevent.

lessons.label: Designing the Compensator

sections.heading: The error amplifier and the divider that sets the target
sections.body: A voltage-mode loop compares a scaled sample of the output (through a resistive feedback divider) against a fixed reference at an error amplifier, and the compensation network wrapped around that amplifier is what actually shapes loop stability. The divider only sets the DC operating point (Vref × (R1+R2)/R2); all the interesting frequency-domain work happens in the feedback impedance around the amplifier, which is why two converters with identical dividers can have wildly different transient behavior depending on the network chosen.

sections.heading: Type II versus type III, and where their poles and zeros go
sections.body: A type II network gives one pole at the origin (for infinite DC gain and zero steady-state error), one zero, and one high-frequency pole; it supplies roughly 90 degrees of phase boost and suits plants that already have a favorable phase, such as a current-mode buck or a voltage-mode buck whose high-ESR electrolytic output cap already places its ESR zero at low frequency, doing much of the phase-boost work already. Built around a feedback resistor R1, a top resistor R2, a compensation capacitor C1 in series with R2, and a smaller capacitor C2 across R2, its zero sits at fz1 = 1/(2πR2C1) and its high-frequency pole at fp1 = 1/(2πR1C2) — the designer places fz1 near the plant's double pole to cancel its phase loss and fp1 out near or above crossover to roll off gain before switching noise. A type III network adds a second zero-pole pair, delivering up to nearly 180 degrees of boost, and is what a voltage-mode buck with a high-Q double pole and a distant ceramic-capacitor ESR zero needs to survive the double pole's 180-degree phase cliff. The design target across both is 45 to 60 degrees of phase margin, more than 10 dB of gain margin, and a crossover frequency placed around fsw/5 to fsw/10 so the compensator has settled well before switching artifacts and sampling effects corrupt the model.

sections.heading: The isolated case: an optocoupler in the loop
sections.body: In an isolated flyback or forward converter, the feedback path must cross the isolation boundary, almost always with a TL431 shunt regulator on the secondary driving an optocoupler LED, whose phototransistor sits on the primary side. This adds an extra pole from the optocoupler's junction capacitance and pull-up resistor, typically in the low kHz to tens-of-kHz range, that eats into the available phase budget and must be accounted for separately from the TL431's own compensation network. Worse, current transfer ratio (CTR) varies enormously — commonly quoted with a 2:1 or wider spread across parts even within one bin, and it degrades with temperature and over the optocoupler's lifetime (LED light output decays with aging current), so a loop tuned tightly around nominal CTR can lose margin as the part ages.

lessons.workedExample: A 200 kHz voltage-mode buck with a ceramic output cap (ESR zero pushed out past 100 kHz) shows a double pole at 3 kHz with phase collapsing to -180 degrees by roughly 10 kHz. A designer picks a type III network, placing its two zeros just below the double pole (around 2-2.5 kHz) to cancel its phase loss and its two high-frequency poles near the ESR-zero region to roll off gain before switching noise. Crossover lands at 25 kHz (fsw/8), and bench measurement with a network analyzer shows 52 degrees of phase margin — inside the 45-60 degree target and confirming the hand calculation rather than trusting the simulation alone.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes compensator choice because 'I used a type III because it worked' versus 'I used a type III because my double pole needed 180 degrees of phase boost and a type II only gives 90' is the clearest signal of whether a student understands why the network topology follows from the plant, not from a datasheet template. For isolated designs, a strong answer volunteers the optocoupler pole and CTR spread unprompted as a design risk; a weak answer treats the optocoupler as a wire and is caught flat when asked why the loop behaves differently at low temperature or after months of operation.

questions.prompt: Why does a type III compensator have two zero-pole pairs instead of the single pair in a type II network?

options.text: To supply nearly 180 degrees of phase boost for plants with a high-Q double pole
To increase the DC output voltage set point
Because isolated converters legally require an extra pole-zero pair
To eliminate the need for a feedback divider

explanations.a: Correct — a single pole-zero pair (type II) only supplies about 90 degrees of phase boost, which is not enough to counter the roughly 180 degrees a double pole can strip away.
explanations.b: The DC set point is fixed by the feedback divider ratio against the reference, not by the compensator's pole-zero count.
explanations.c: There is no such legal requirement; the extra pair is chosen for phase-boost reasons tied to the plant's own dynamics.
explanations.d: The feedback divider is still required in a type III network; it sets the DC operating point independently of compensator order.

questions.prompt: An optocoupler's current transfer ratio (CTR) commonly varies 2:1 or more across parts and degrades with age. What is the main design consequence?

options.text: The loop's DC gain through the optocoupler stage shifts, so margin tuned tightly to nominal CTR can erode over time and temperature
CTR variation only affects switching frequency, not loop gain
CTR variation has no measurable effect on an isolated feedback loop
CTR variation only matters for non-isolated converters

explanations.a: Correct — CTR sets how much LED current becomes phototransistor current, directly scaling loop gain through that stage, so wide part-to-part and aging variation is a real margin risk.
explanations.b: CTR is a current-gain property of the optocoupler stage; it affects loop gain, not switching frequency, which is set by the PWM controller.
explanations.c: CTR spread is a well-documented, measurable design concern in isolated flyback/forward feedback loops.
explanations.d: Optocouplers and CTR only appear in isolated topologies in the first place; non-isolated converters don't use them at all.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of a typical voltage-mode compensator design process, from first to last.

items.text: Characterize the power stage's control-to-output transfer function (poles, zeros)
Choose type II or type III based on how much phase boost the plant needs
Place compensator zeros and poles to hit target crossover, phase margin, and gain margin
Verify on the bench with a network analyzer or frequency-response measurement

questions.explanation: You must know the plant's dynamics before choosing a network type, choose the network type before placing specific poles/zeros, and only after placing them can you verify the real, built loop meets its targets — simulation and hand calculation are not a substitute for bench confirmation.

questions.prompt: Where is crossover frequency typically targeted relative to switching frequency (fsw), and why?

options.text: fsw/5 to fsw/10, so the loop settles before switching-frequency artifacts and sampling effects corrupt the averaged model
Exactly at fsw, to maximize transient response
Above fsw, since higher crossover always means a faster loop
There is no relationship between crossover and switching frequency

explanations.a: Correct — the averaged small-signal model breaks down as frequency approaches fsw, so crossover is kept well below it, typically fsw/5 to fsw/10.
explanations.b: Crossing over at fsw would push the loop into a region where the averaged model no longer holds and switching noise dominates.
explanations.c: Higher crossover is not always better; above fsw the averaged model is invalid and stability cannot be reliably guaranteed.
explanations.d: The averaging assumption underlying the whole small-signal model directly ties valid crossover range to switching frequency.

lessons.label: Current-Mode Control in Practice

sections.heading: Three flavors of an inner current loop
sections.body: Current-mode control wraps a fast inner loop around the inductor current, then lets a slower outer voltage loop set that current's target. Peak current mode, the most common variant since the UC3842-family controllers popularized it in the 1980s, compares a sensed rising inductor current against a control voltage and terminates the switch's on-time the instant it hits that level. Valley current mode instead triggers turn-on at a current valley, useful in some buck regulators for its natural pairing with fixed off-time or constant-on-time schemes. Average current mode senses and closes the loop on the average, not peak or valley, inductor current, which costs an extra amplifier and compensation stage but avoids the peak-to-average error that plagues peak current mode in continuous-conduction power-factor-correction stages carrying large ripple.

sections.heading: Why the inner loop collapses the double pole into one pole
sections.body: Ridley (1991) formalized what designers had observed empirically: because the current loop forces inductor current to track the control signal almost instantaneously, the inductor stops behaving like an independent energy-storage state from the voltage loop's point of view. The result is that the LC double pole of voltage-mode control collapses into a single dominant pole set by the output capacitor and load resistance, plus a much higher-frequency sampling pole related to switching frequency. A single pole needs far less phase boost to compensate — often just a type II network suffices where voltage mode would demand a type III — which is the main reason current-mode control is the default choice in commercial PWM ICs.

sections.heading: Slope compensation, current limiting, and blanking the turn-on spike
sections.body: Peak current mode has a well-known instability: at duty cycles above 50%, any small perturbation in inductor current grows every switching cycle instead of decaying, producing subharmonic oscillation at half the switching frequency. The fix is slope compensation, an artificial ramp added to the sensed current (or subtracted from the control voltage) with a slope of at least half the inductor's current downslope, which damps the perturbation back to zero rather than letting it grow. Because the loop already terminates on-time based on measured current, peak current mode gets cycle-by-cycle current limiting essentially for free — no separate limiter circuit is needed, the loop simply refuses to let current exceed its programmed ceiling on any given switching cycle. That same current sense signal, however, sees a large spurious spike the instant the switch turns on (from diode reverse recovery and node capacitance discharge), so practical controllers blank the sense signal for a short leading-edge blanking interval, typically on the order of 100 ns, to avoid tripping on that spike instead of real inductor current.

lessons.workedExample: A peak current-mode buck runs at 500 kHz (2 µs period) with an inductor whose current falls at m2 = 0.4 A/µs during the off-time. The duty cycle sits at 0.6, above the 50% threshold where subharmonic oscillation becomes possible without compensation. The designer adds a slope-compensation ramp with slope Se = 0.25 A/µs, satisfying the rule Se ≥ 0.5 × m2 (0.5 × 0.4 = 0.2 A/µs), and confirms on the bench that a deliberately injected current-loop disturbance decays within two switching cycles instead of growing — direct evidence the compensation ramp is doing its job rather than just being present on the schematic.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about slope compensation specifically at duty cycles above 50% because it is the fastest way to tell whether a student copied a reference design or understands why current-mode control needs it at all; a student who can state the Se ≥ 0.5×m2 rule and explain subharmonic oscillation as a per-cycle perturbation that either grows or decays has done real analysis, while one who says 'the datasheet had a compensation resistor so I used it' has not engaged with the mechanism. The same distinction applies to leading-edge blanking: a strong answer connects the blanking window to the specific turn-on spike it exists to suppress, not just 'noise.'

questions.prompt: Match each current-mode control variant to its defining feature.

right.text: Terminates on-time when sensed current hits a rising threshold; most common variant
Triggers turn-on at a current minimum, pairs naturally with constant-on-time schemes
Closes the loop on mean inductor current, avoiding peak-to-average error in high-ripple PFC stages

questions.explanation: Peak current mode terminates on the rising current peak, valley current mode triggers on the current valley, and average current mode senses and regulates the mean current directly, at the cost of an extra amplifier stage.

questions.prompt: Why does adding an inner current loop simplify voltage-loop compensation compared to voltage-mode control?

options.text: It collapses the LC double pole into a single dominant pole, requiring less phase boost from the outer compensator
It eliminates the need for a feedback divider entirely
It removes the output capacitor from the circuit
It increases switching frequency automatically

explanations.a: Correct — per Ridley (1991), the fast current loop makes the inductor track its control signal almost instantly, so from the voltage loop's perspective the plant behaves as a single pole rather than a resonant LC pair.
explanations.b: A feedback divider is still needed in current-mode control to set the DC output voltage against the reference.
explanations.c: The output capacitor remains in the circuit and still sets the dominant pole's location along with the load resistance.
explanations.d: Current-mode control doesn't change the switching frequency, which is set by the oscillator or clock, not by the control method.

questions.prompt: A peak current-mode buck operates at D = 0.6 with an inductor current downslope m2 = 0.4 A/µs and no slope compensation. What happens?

options.text: The loop is prone to subharmonic oscillation at half the switching frequency, since D > 0.5
Nothing — slope compensation is only needed when D < 0.5
The converter's switching frequency doubles automatically to compensate
The output capacitor's ESR zero disappears

explanations.a: Correct — above 50% duty cycle, peak current-mode control without adequate slope compensation lets small current perturbations grow cycle over cycle, producing subharmonic oscillation.
explanations.b: The instability risk is specifically at D > 0.5, not D < 0.5; below 50% the natural loop dynamics are stable without added ramp.
explanations.c: Switching frequency is set by the oscillator, not adjusted automatically in response to loop instability.
explanations.d: The ESR zero is a property of the output capacitor's parasitic resistance and is unrelated to slope compensation or subharmonic oscillation.

questions.prompt: What is leading-edge blanking, and why is it needed in peak current-mode control?

options.text: A brief window after turn-on where the sensed current signal is ignored, to avoid false-tripping on the turn-on spike from diode reverse recovery and node capacitance discharge
A delay before the switching converter is allowed to start up at all
The time the error amplifier takes to settle after a load step
A filter that removes the switching ripple from the output voltage

explanations.a: Correct — the current sense signal sees a large spurious spike right at turn-on, so controllers blank (ignore) that signal for a short interval, typically around 100 ns, to avoid mistaking it for real inductor current.
explanations.b: Leading-edge blanking happens every switching cycle during normal operation, not just once at converter startup.
explanations.c: Error amplifier settling time is a voltage-loop compensation concept, unrelated to the current-sense blanking window.
explanations.d: Output ripple filtering is a separate output-filter design issue, not what leading-edge blanking addresses.

lessons.label: Multiphase and Interleaving

sections.heading: Ripple cancellation and its nulls
sections.body: An N-phase converter splits the total load current across N parallel power stages, each switching at the same frequency fsw but phase-shifted by 360/N degrees from its neighbors, so their individual triangular inductor-current ripples partially cancel when summed at the shared output node. The cancellation is not uniform across duty cycle: total ripple drops to exactly zero at N discrete duty-cycle points, D = k/N for k = 1 to N−1. A two-phase converter nulls at D = 0.5; a three-phase converter nulls at D = 1/3 and D = 2/3. Away from a null, ripple is still reduced compared to a single phase carrying the full current, but the reduction is duty-cycle-dependent, which is why datasheets for multiphase controllers publish ripple-versus-duty-cycle curves rather than a single number.

sections.heading: Current sharing and how it fails
sections.body: Interleaving only delivers its ripple and thermal benefits if each phase actually carries an equal share of the load current. Real phases mismatch because of inductor DCR tolerance, current-sense offset, and layout-driven trace resistance differences, and without active current-sharing control one phase can 'hog' current, running hotter and aging faster while its neighbors coast — a failure mode that gets worse under positive thermal feedback, since a hotter phase's MOSFET RDS(on) rises further with temperature. Multiphase controllers correct this by comparing each phase's sensed current against the average (or against a master phase) and trimming individual duty cycles to converge on equal sharing, typically within a few percent.

sections.heading: Faster transients, and why VRMs have no alternative
sections.body: Interleaving multiplies the effective output ripple frequency seen by the output capacitor to N×fsw, since the phases' ripple currents overlap and partially cancel in time as well as amplitude. A higher effective ripple frequency means a smaller output capacitor can hold the same ripple voltage, and it means the converter's overall response to a load transient is effectively N times faster in the sense that phases can be added or shed within a fraction of one native switching period. Coupled inductors — magnetically linking adjacent phases on a shared core, an approach pushed into mainstream VRM design in the 2000s — further shrink ripple and improve transient response beyond what discrete inductors achieve, at the cost of a more complex magnetic design. This combination is why modern CPU and GPU voltage regulator modules, delivering 100+ amps at core voltages under 1.2 V with millivolt-level droop (load-line) specifications, are built exclusively as multiphase designs: no single-phase converter can deliver that current with acceptable ripple, transient response, and thermal distribution in the available board space.

lessons.workedExample: A four-phase VRM feeds a CPU core at 1.0 V, 120 A total, with each phase's controller trimming duty cycle so all four channels sit within 3% of the 30 A average — verified by clamping a current probe on each phase's inductor during a full-load burn-in rather than trusting the controller's internal telemetry alone. At the operating duty cycle of D = 0.083 (1.0 V from a 12 V bus), the four-phase ripple-null condition (D = 0.25, 0.5, 0.75) is not met, so residual ripple remains, but it appears at 4 × 300 kHz = 1.2 MHz rather than 300 kHz, letting the design use roughly a quarter of the bulk output capacitance a single-phase converter would need for the same ripple voltage.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge examining any multiphase board asks how current sharing is verified, because a design that assumes equal sharing without measuring it is a design that has likely never been tested under real thermal stress — an unmonitored hogging phase can run substantially hotter than its neighbors and fail first. A strong answer describes probing each phase's inductor current individually and states the sharing tolerance achieved; a weak answer points to a controller datasheet claim without any bench verification. Naming the specific ripple-null duty cycles (D = k/N) also separates a student who derived the interleaving benefit from one who just cited 'less ripple' as received wisdom.

questions.prompt: At what duty cycle does a three-phase interleaved converter achieve a full ripple-cancellation null (other than D=0 or D=1)?

options.text: D = 0.5 only
There is no duty cycle where a three-phase converter reaches full cancellation

explanations.a: Correct — the general rule D = k/N for k = 1 to N−1 gives D = 1/3 and D = 2/3 for a three-phase (N=3) design.
explanations.b: D = 0.5 is the null point for a two-phase (N=2) converter, not a three-phase one.
explanations.c: D = 1/4 and D = 3/4 are the null points for a four-phase (N=4) converter.
explanations.d: Three-phase interleaving does reach full cancellation, at two specific duty-cycle points given by k/N.

questions.prompt: Without active current-sharing control, what typically causes one phase in a multiphase converter to 'hog' more current than its neighbors?

options.text: Mismatches in inductor DCR, current-sense offset, or trace resistance between phases
Each phase switches at a different frequency by design
The output capacitor selectively favors one phase
Current hogging cannot occur if all phases use the same controller IC

explanations.a: Correct — real-world component and layout tolerances (inductor DCR, sense offsets, trace resistance) create small mismatches that, left uncorrected, let one phase carry disproportionate current.
explanations.b: All phases in an interleaved design switch at the same frequency, staggered in phase timing, not frequency.
explanations.c: The shared output capacitor sums current from all phases; it does not selectively favor any single phase.
explanations.d: Using the same controller IC per phase does not eliminate component-level tolerances that cause sharing mismatch; active correction is still needed.

questions.prompt: Why do CPU/GPU voltage regulator modules delivering 100+ A with millivolt-level droop specs rely exclusively on multiphase designs?

options.text: A single phase cannot deliver that current with acceptable ripple, transient response, and thermal distribution in the available board space
Single-phase converters are always cheaper, so multiphase is used purely for marketing
Multiphase designs are required by USB-C charging standards
A single phase would produce zero ripple, which is undesirable for CPU stability

explanations.a: Correct — at 100+ A with tight droop tolerances, splitting current across phases is necessary for thermal distribution, transient speed (effective N×fsw response), and output capacitance sizing.
explanations.b: Multiphase designs are typically more expensive and complex than single-phase; they are chosen for capability, not cost savings.
explanations.c: VRM phase count is an engineering choice tied to current and transient requirements, not a USB-C or any charging standard.
explanations.d: Zero ripple is not the goal, nor would a single phase actually produce it; the concern is current capacity and transient response, not ripple elimination.

questions.prompt: Match each multiphase design feature to what it improves.

left.text: Coupled inductors on a shared core

right.text: Raises effective ripple frequency to N×fsw, shrinking required output capacitance
Further reduces ripple and improves transient response beyond discrete inductors
Prevents one phase from running hotter and aging faster than its neighbors

questions.explanation: Phase-shifted switching itself raises the effective ripple frequency seen by the output capacitor; coupled inductors add a further ripple/transient improvement on top of that; active current-sharing control is what prevents thermal imbalance from an unequally loaded phase.

lessons.label: Soft Switching: ZVS, ZCS, and the LLC

sections.heading: Where hard-switching loss actually comes from
sections.body: Every MOSFET carries an output capacitance, Coss, that stores energy ½·Coss·V² across the drain-source junction. In a hard-switched converter, that energy is dumped and dissipated inside the device itself every time it turns on into a charged Coss, and the loss scales linearly with switching frequency (½·Coss·V²·fsw), which is exactly why hard-switched designs hit a frequency ceiling before magnetics can shrink further. Soft switching does not eliminate this stored energy — it redirects it. In zero-voltage switching (ZVS), the circuit's own inductive energy discharges Coss to near zero before the device turns on, so the ½CV² energy becomes circulating reactive energy shuttled around the resonant tank instead of heat dissipated in the switch. Zero-current switching (ZCS) achieves the analogous result for turn-off, timing commutation so current has already fallen to zero.

sections.heading: ZVS in the phase-shifted full bridge, and where it disappears
sections.body: A phase-shifted full bridge achieves ZVS by using the transformer's leakage inductance (plus, often, an added external inductor) as an energy reservoir: during the dead time between one leg's switches turning off and the other turning on, that stored inductive energy resonantly discharges the outgoing switch's Coss, letting the incoming switch turn on into zero volts. The mechanism has a hard floor, though — at light load, the leakage inductance carries too little current to hold enough stored energy (½·L·I²) to fully discharge Coss within the fixed dead time, so ZVS is lost precisely where efficiency matters most for standby and light-load operation, forcing designers to add extra light-load ZVS-assist circuitry or accept hard-switching losses at low power.

sections.heading: The LLC resonant converter's gain curve
sections.body: The LLC converter (named for its two inductors and one capacitor: series resonant inductor Lr, magnetizing inductance Lm, and resonant capacitor Cr) is prized because its voltage gain is a function of switching frequency relative to the resonant frequency fr = 1/(2π√(Lr·Cr)). Below resonance (fs < fr), the gain curve rises above unity, boosting output voltage as frequency drops; above resonance (fs > fr), gain falls below unity, bucking output voltage as frequency rises. Operating near fr gives near-unity gain with primary-side ZVS across the full load range and secondary-side rectifier currents that fall naturally to zero (ZCS-like behavior), eliminating diode reverse-recovery losses that plague hard-switched rectifiers. The tradeoffs are real: variable-frequency operation complicates EMI filter design because energy spreads and shifts across a frequency band rather than sitting at one fixed switching harmonic; light-load regulation requires pushing frequency far above fr, which the gain curve resists (it flattens), often forcing burst-mode operation instead; and start-up must sweep frequency down carefully from a high initial value to avoid large inrush circulating currents and voltage overshoot in the resonant tank.

lessons.workedExample: An LLC converter designed for fr = 100 kHz targets nominal operation at 95 kHz (just below resonance) to get slight voltage boost while retaining ZVS. At full load, primary current is high enough that ZVS holds cleanly across the switching leg. At 5% load, the controller must push frequency up toward 160 kHz to buck the gain down to the lighter regulation point, but the LLC gain curve above resonance flattens with decreasing load, so the controller instead switches to burst mode — running bursts of full-frequency switching separated by idle periods — to hold regulation without chasing an increasingly steep and noise-sensitive frequency excursion.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'does your converter lose ZVS at light load?' because it is the question that separates a student who measured switch-node voltage on an oscilloscope across the full load range from one who only verified ZVS at the single full-load point where it is easiest to achieve. A strong answer describes the leakage-inductance energy argument (½LI² must exceed the Coss discharge energy) and states where ZVS was lost on their own board; a weak answer asserts 'soft switching' as a blanket property of the topology without acknowledging it is load-dependent.

questions.prompt: In zero-voltage switching, what happens to the energy stored in a MOSFET's output capacitance (Coss) before turn-on, compared to hard switching?

options.text: It is discharged resonantly by circuit inductive energy and becomes circulating reactive energy rather than being dissipated as heat in the switch
It is permanently removed from the circuit and never returns
It increases the switch's turn-on loss compared to hard switching
Coss energy is irrelevant to switching loss in any topology

explanations.a: Correct — ZVS redirects the ½Coss V² energy into the resonant tank as circulating energy instead of dissipating it in the switch at turn-on.
explanations.b: The energy is not removed from the system; it circulates within the resonant tank rather than being destroyed.
explanations.c: ZVS reduces turn-on loss compared to hard switching by avoiding dissipating the Coss energy in the device.
explanations.d: Coss energy dissipation (½Coss V² per cycle, scaling with fsw) is precisely the mechanism soft switching is designed to address.

questions.prompt: Why does a phase-shifted full bridge tend to lose ZVS at light load?

options.text: The leakage inductance carries too little current to store enough energy (½LI²) to fully discharge Coss within the dead time
Light load increases the transformer's leakage inductance, which should improve ZVS instead
ZVS is unaffected by load current in a phase-shifted full bridge
The dead time automatically lengthens at light load to compensate

explanations.a: Correct — the stored inductive energy scales with the square of current, so at light load there simply isn't enough energy in the leakage inductance to swing Coss fully before the fixed dead time ends.
explanations.b: Leakage inductance is a fixed physical property of the transformer construction; it doesn't change with load current.
explanations.c: ZVS is directly load-dependent in a phase-shifted full bridge precisely because the energy source (inductive current) scales with load.
explanations.d: Dead time is typically a fixed or narrowly adaptive timing parameter, not something that automatically compensates for insufficient stored energy at light load.

questions.prompt: In the LLC converter's gain-vs-frequency curve, what happens to voltage gain as switching frequency rises above the resonant frequency fr?

options.text: Gain falls below unity (bucking behavior)
Gain rises further above unity
Gain stays exactly at unity regardless of frequency
Gain becomes undefined above resonance

explanations.a: Correct — above resonance (fs > fr), the LLC gain curve drops below unity, so raising frequency further bucks the output voltage down.
explanations.b: Gain rising above unity is the below-resonance (fs < fr) behavior, not the above-resonance region.
explanations.c: Gain equals roughly unity only near fr itself; it is not constant across the whole frequency range.
explanations.d: The gain curve is well-defined and continuous above resonance; it simply trends below unity and flattens at light load.

questions.prompt: Order these events in a phase-shifted full bridge achieving ZVS on a given leg, from first to last.

items.text: Outgoing switch turns off, leaving leakage inductance current flowing
Leakage inductance current resonantly discharges the incoming switch's Coss during dead time
Incoming switch's drain-source voltage reaches near zero
Incoming switch turns on with near-zero voltage across it

questions.explanation: ZVS requires the outgoing switch to turn off first (preserving inductive current), that current then resonantly discharges the incoming switch's Coss during the dead-time interval, bringing its voltage to near zero, and only then does the incoming switch turn on — into a near-zero voltage rather than the full bus voltage.

lessons.label: Digital Control and Nonlinear Loops

sections.heading: Two resolutions that must agree, or the loop hunts forever
sections.body: A digital PID controller samples the output through an ADC, computes a correction, and applies it through a digital PWM (DPWM), but both stages are quantized, and their resolutions interact in a way analog control never has to worry about. Peterchev and Sanders (2003) formalized the failure mode: if the smallest voltage step the DPWM can produce (its LSB, referred to the output) is coarser than the ADC's LSB, the controller can never settle onto a single duty-cycle code that produces zero error — it perpetually overshoots one DPWM step, sees a nonzero error, corrects, overshoots the other way, and repeats, producing a persistent limit-cycle oscillation even though the loop is nominally 'stable.' The fix is architectural, not tunable: DPWM resolution must be made finer than the effective ADC resolution, typically by adding sub-bit dithering to the PWM output or extending the counter clock, so the actuator can always find a code that produces less voltage error than the sensor itself can distinguish.

sections.heading: Why digital control earns its keep: telemetry and reconfigurability
sections.body: Beyond avoiding limit cycling, digital controllers such as Texas Instruments' UCD9000-family parts expose PMBus, a standardized I2C-based protocol (from the System Management Interface Forum) for reading back output voltage, current, temperature, and fault status, and for writing compensator coefficients, sequencing delays, and voltage margins without touching hardware. This is the feature that justifies digital control's cost in server and telecom power: a rack of point-of-load converters can be remotely monitored, retuned, and fault-logged over the same bus that reports their health, something no fixed analog compensator network can do.

sections.heading: Nonlinear control for the fastest transients
sections.body: Hysteretic and constant-on-time (COT) control abandon the linear compensator model entirely, comparing output voltage (or ripple) directly against a band or threshold and switching the instant a boundary is crossed, giving single-cycle response to a load step because there is no error-amplifier delay to wait out. This is why low-power point-of-load converters (TI's D-CAP and D-CAP2 modes, for instance) favor it for fast-transient applications. The cost is a variable switching frequency that shifts with input voltage, load, and output ripple, spreading EMI energy across a band rather than concentrating it at fixed harmonics — good for average EMI but harder to filter and to characterize for conducted-emissions testing. Adaptive dead-time control, adjusted in real time from measured switch-node timing rather than a fixed datasheet value, and auto-tuning, which injects a test perturbation and measures the loop's own frequency response to compute compensator coefficients on power-up, are further nonlinear-adjacent features unique to the digital domain. None of this is free: digital control costs more silicon area, more power for the ADC and DSP core, and more design complexity than a two-op-amp analog compensator, so it earns its place specifically where telemetry, multi-rail sequencing, or adaptive retuning under changing conditions matter — not in a simple single-output wall adapter.

lessons.workedExample: A digital buck controller uses a 10-bit ADC sampling a 1.0 V rail, giving an ADC LSB of roughly 1 mV, but drives a DPWM with only 7 effective bits over its duty-cycle range at a 500 kHz switching frequency, giving a DPWM output LSB of about 4 mV — coarser than the ADC can resolve. The loop limit-cycles, visible on a scope as a persistent low-frequency ripple riding on top of the switching ripple. The fix is dithering the DPWM output between two adjacent duty-cycle codes on alternating cycles, synthesizing an effective sub-LSB step finer than the ADC's 1 mV resolution, which eliminates the limit cycle without touching the PID coefficients at all.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who spots unexplained low-frequency ripple on a digitally controlled board's output asks about ADC and PWM resolution specifically, because limit-cycle oscillation is the signature bug of digital power control and naming Peterchev and Sanders' resolution-matching condition versus just retuning PID gains (which cannot fix a resolution mismatch) is the clearest test of whether a student understands digital control's quantization-specific failure mode rather than treating a DSP as a drop-in replacement for an analog error amplifier.

questions.prompt: Per Peterchev and Sanders (2003), what condition on ADC and DPWM resolution avoids limit-cycle oscillation in a digital power converter?

options.text: The DPWM's output-referred voltage LSB must be finer than the ADC's LSB
The ADC and DPWM must sample at exactly the same clock frequency
The DPWM's LSB must be coarser than the ADC's LSB
Limit cycling cannot be avoided in any digital controller

explanations.a: Correct — if the actuator (DPWM) can always produce a smaller voltage step than the sensor (ADC) can distinguish, the loop can settle onto a code with zero perceived error instead of oscillating between adjacent codes forever.
explanations.b: Clock frequency matching between ADC and DPWM is not the relevant condition; it's the relative fineness of their respective LSBs.
explanations.c: This is backwards — a coarser DPWM than ADC is exactly the condition that causes limit-cycle oscillation.
explanations.d: Limit cycling is avoidable through the specific resolution-matching condition (or added dithering), not an inherent, unavoidable property of digital control.

questions.prompt: Why can't retuning the PID coefficients alone fix a limit-cycle oscillation caused by a coarse DPWM relative to the ADC?

options.text: The oscillation is a quantization/resolution mismatch, a structural property of the actuator and sensor, not a gain or phase margin problem the PID coefficients control
PID coefficients have no effect on any aspect of loop behavior in digital controllers
Retuning PID coefficients always fixes limit cycling immediately
Limit cycling only occurs in analog controllers, never digital ones

explanations.a: Correct — because the DPWM simply cannot produce a fine enough step to match what the ADC can measure, no choice of PID gains changes the fact that the actuator's minimum step is too coarse.
explanations.b: PID coefficients do shape loop dynamics generally; the point is specifically that they cannot fix a resolution mismatch, not that they're irrelevant to everything.
explanations.c: Retuning gains does not resolve a structural quantization mismatch; the fix requires finer DPWM resolution (e.g., dithering), not different gains.
explanations.d: Limit-cycle oscillation from resolution mismatch is a digital-control-specific phenomenon; it doesn't have a direct analog-control equivalent since analog signals aren't quantized this way.

questions.prompt: What is the main tradeoff of hysteretic or constant-on-time (COT) control compared to fixed-frequency linear compensation?

options.text: Faster single-cycle transient response, at the cost of a variable switching frequency that spreads EMI across a band
Slower transient response but perfectly fixed switching frequency
No difference in transient response or EMI behavior
COT control eliminates the need for an output capacitor

explanations.a: Correct — by reacting directly to voltage/ripple crossing a threshold rather than through an error-amplifier's delay, COT and hysteretic control respond within a switching cycle, but their frequency shifts with operating conditions, complicating EMI filtering.
explanations.b: COT control is chosen specifically for its fast transient response; fixed frequency is what it trades away, not what it gains.
explanations.c: There is a real, well-documented tradeoff between transient speed and frequency-domain EMI predictability between these control methods.
explanations.d: An output capacitor is still required for filtering and stability in COT designs; the control method doesn't remove that need.

questions.prompt: According to the lesson, when does digital control's added cost and complexity (versus a simple analog compensator) actually pay off?

options.text: When telemetry, multi-rail sequencing, or adaptive retuning under changing conditions are needed, as in server/telecom power via PMBus
In every application, since digital control is always strictly better than analog
Only in single-output wall adapters with no monitoring requirements
Digital control never provides any advantage over analog compensation

explanations.a: Correct — the lesson ties digital control's value specifically to PMBus telemetry, remote reconfigurability, and adaptive features, which matter in server/telecom racks with multiple monitored rails, not in cost-sensitive simple designs.
explanations.b: The lesson explicitly notes digital control costs more silicon, power, and design complexity, so it is not universally the better choice.
explanations.c: This is the opposite of the lesson's point — a simple single-output wall adapter is exactly where digital control's extra cost is least justified.
explanations.d: Digital control's advantages (telemetry, reconfigurability, auto-tuning) are real and specifically named; the lesson does not claim it is useless.

units.label: Motor Drives, Grid Interfaces, and Case Studies

lessons.label: H-Bridges and DC Motor Drives

sections.heading: Four-Quadrant Operation and PWM Schemes
sections.body: An H-bridge is four switches arranged so a DC motor's two terminals can each be tied to either supply rail, giving four-quadrant operation: forward-motoring, forward-braking, reverse-motoring, and reverse-braking — the bridge can drive current in either polarity and can also absorb current flowing backward out of the motor when it spins faster than commanded. How the bridge is PWMed shapes the current waveform. In sign-magnitude PWM, only one diagonal pair chops while the opposite-side switches stay fixed to set direction, so the motor sees 0V or +V, never -V; average voltage runs 0 to +V and ripple stays confined to one leg. In locked-antiphase (bipolar) PWM, both legs switch every cycle and the motor sees +V or -V on every pulse — duty cycle above 50% gives net forward voltage, below 50% net reverse. Bipolar switching is more linear near zero speed but forces the full supply swing across the motor every cycle, roughly doubling ripple current and switching losses.

sections.heading: Freewheeling: Slow Decay vs Fast Decay
sections.body: When a PWM switch turns off mid-cycle, the motor's inductance keeps current flowing and it must freewheel somewhere. Slow decay (synchronous or diagonal freewheeling) routes that current through a low-side switch pair, or its body diode, back to the same rail, so loop voltage is near zero and current decays gradually — low ripple, quiet operation, but sluggish current-loop response. Fast decay forces current back through the diagonally opposite switches into the supply, so the full rail voltage opposes it; current collapses quickly, giving crisp torque control at low speed but higher ripple current, more switching loss, and more electromagnetic noise. Many modern driver ICs let firmware choose per-cycle or blend the two as mixed decay.

sections.heading: Regenerative Braking, Dead Time, and Driver-IC Reality
sections.body: Two more mechanisms matter. First, dead time: before flipping a leg's active switch, the driver holds both switches off for tens to a few hundred nanoseconds so outgoing and incoming devices never conduct together and short the rail (shoot-through). During dead time the leg's voltage is set by whichever body diode conducts, not the intended command, so near the zero-crossing of duty cycle the actual output deviates from commanded — a documented source of torque ripple and audible motor noise. Second, braking turns the motor into a generator; if the electronics can't sink that current, the supply rail bus-pumps upward, and a brake resistor or a sized bulk capacitor must absorb it. Device choice matters too: the classic L298 is a bipolar dual H-bridge rated near 2A per channel continuously with roughly a 2V drop per switch, so it runs hot; modern MOSFET-based parts like the DRV8871 use roughly 565 mΩ combined high-side-plus-low-side on-resistance — still far lower conduction loss than the L298's BJT drop — for far higher efficiency and current density in a fraction of the board area.

lessons.workedExample: A robotics team drives two 12V gearmotors (2.5A stall) through an L298N breakout at 20kHz PWM. The board runs hot within minutes and occasionally browns out mid-turn: the L298's BJT outputs drop nearly 2V per switch (4V across the bridge) at 2.5A, dissipating 10W with no heatsink, and its 2A continuous rating is already exceeded at stall. Swapping to a DRV8871 module (MOSFET, ~565 mΩ RDS(on) combined HS+LS, 3.6A peak) cuts conduction loss to roughly 3.5W per motor (I²R ≈ 2.5² × 0.565Ω) — still well under the L298's 10W. The team also notices the 12V rail spikes to 15V whenever the robot brakes going downhill — regenerated current with nowhere to go — so they add a 470µF bulk capacitor across the supply near the drivers to absorb the transient instead of letting it trip the driver's overvoltage protection.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks why the team picked fast decay instead of slow decay for their speed loop is testing whether the student understands the driver as a control system, not a black box that 'makes the motor go.' A weak answer says 'it worked better'; a strong one names the tradeoff — fast decay collapses inductor current quickly against the rail voltage for tighter current-loop bandwidth, at the cost of ripple and EMI, while slow decay is quieter but sluggish. The same probe works on dead time: a student who explains that dead time, not friction, is why their motor stutters near zero PWM duty has diagnosed a real electrical phenomenon rather than shrugged at a symptom.

questions.prompt: Which PWM scheme drives the full supply voltage (+V or -V) across the motor on every switching cycle, giving smoother linearity near zero speed at the cost of higher current ripple?

options.text: Sign-magnitude PWM
Locked-antiphase (bipolar) PWM
Fast decay
Sensorless commutation

explanations.a: Sign-magnitude only chops one leg and keeps the motor between 0V and +V, not the full ±V swing.
explanations.b: Correct — locked-antiphase switches both legs every cycle, so the motor sees +V or -V on every pulse.
explanations.c: Fast decay describes how current recirculates when a switch turns off, not the steady-state PWM voltage pattern.
explanations.d: Sensorless commutation is a BLDC concept unrelated to DC H-bridge PWM style.

questions.prompt: In an H-bridge, what specifically causes torque ripple right around the zero-crossing of commanded duty cycle, even with well-matched switches?

options.text: Motor bearing friction
Dead time between switching one leg's high side and low side
The size of the flyback diode
Insufficient PWM frequency

explanations.a: Friction is roughly constant torque loss and doesn't specifically spike at the zero-crossing.
explanations.b: Correct — during dead time the leg voltage is set by whichever body diode conducts, deviating from the commanded value right where duty cycle crosses its symmetric point.
explanations.c: Diode sizing affects loss and heat, not the timing error at the zero-crossing.
explanations.d: Raising PWM frequency changes ripple frequency but does not remove the dead-time-caused distortion itself.

questions.prompt: Match each freewheeling (decay) mode to its characteristic behavior.

right.text: Current recirculates through same-side switches near 0V loop voltage; low ripple, quiet, slower current response
Current forced back through diagonal switches against full rail voltage; fast collapse, higher ripple and EMI
Both legs switch every cycle regardless of commanded direction

questions.explanation: Slow decay routes current through low-side switches back to the same rail for a near-zero loop voltage, giving low ripple but sluggish response; fast decay forces current against the full rail voltage through the diagonal switches, collapsing it quickly at the cost of ripple and noise.

questions.prompt: Order the events in one leg's dead-time-protected switching transition, from high-side conducting to low-side conducting.

items.text: High-side switch turns off
Both switches held off for the dead-time interval (current freewheels through a body diode)
Low-side switch turns on

questions.explanation: Dead time is inserted between turning the outgoing switch off and the incoming switch on to guarantee they never overlap and short the supply rail; during that gap current freewheels through whichever body diode is forward-biased.

questions.prompt: A team's L298-based driver runs hot at 2.5A per channel while a DRV8871-based driver stays cool at the same current. What's the main reason?

options.text: The DRV8871 uses a much higher PWM frequency
The L298's BJT outputs have much higher voltage drop (~2V per switch) than the DRV8871's low-RDS(on) MOSFETs
The DRV8871 has a built-in cooling fan
The L298 lacks flyback diodes entirely

explanations.a: Switching frequency affects ripple and switching loss, not the dominant conduction-loss gap between BJT and MOSFET outputs described here.
explanations.b: Correct — the L298's bipolar outputs drop roughly 2V per switch at rated current, while the DRV8871's MOSFETs drop a small fraction of that.
explanations.c: Neither part has a built-in fan; the DRV8871 stays cool because it dissipates far less power, not because of active cooling.
explanations.d: The L298 does need external flyback diodes in many designs, but that omission isn't why it runs hot — conduction loss is.

lessons.label: BLDC, Stepper, and Three-Phase Drives

sections.heading: Trapezoidal Six-Step Commutation: Sensored and Sensorless
sections.body: A brushless DC (BLDC) motor is really a three-phase AC synchronous motor with trapezoidal back-EMF, driven by a three-phase bridge that energizes only two of three windings at a time while the third floats — six distinct switch states per electrical revolution, each spanning 60°, hence six-step or trapezoidal commutation. Sensored designs read three Hall-effect sensors spaced 120° apart to know exactly when to advance to the next state. Sensorless designs instead watch the floating phase: its back-EMF crosses zero roughly at the midpoint between commutation events, and the controller times the next switch 30 electrical degrees after that crossing. The catch is that back-EMF amplitude scales with speed (BEMF = kω), so near zero or low RPM the signal is too small relative to switching noise to detect reliably — sensorless controllers must start blind, forcing an open-loop ramp before handing off to zero-crossing detection, and they generally can't hold true zero-speed torque the way a sensored or FOC drive can.

sections.heading: Field-Oriented Control: Turning Three AC Phases into Two DC Knobs
sections.body: Field-oriented control (FOC) reframes the same three-phase problem the way a separately excited DC motor already works: one current knob for flux, one for torque, both DC quantities a simple PI loop can regulate. The Clarke transform first collapses the three phase currents (Ia, Ib, Ic) into two orthogonal stationary-frame currents (Iα, Iβ); the Park transform then rotates that frame to align with the rotor's measured or estimated angle, producing Id (flux-producing) and Iq (torque-producing) as steady DC values at constant load. Driving sinusoidal rather than trapezoidal current removes the torque dips six-step commutation produces at each 60° switch point, cuts audible noise, and — by trimming Id for field weakening — extends usable speed range past the motor's base speed. The cost is a rotor-angle sensor or observer and meaningfully more compute than six-step's simple state machine.

sections.heading: Steppers: Microstepping via Chopper Regulation, and the Shared Power Stage
sections.body: Stepper motors get smooth, high-resolution motion the same way: instead of full-stepping (typically 1.8° per step, 200 steps/rev) or half-stepping, microstepping drives the two phase windings with sine- and cosine-weighted current levels so the rotor's equilibrium position lands between full-step poles. That current shaping is enforced by chopper regulation — driver ICs like the A4988 or DRV8825 sense actual coil current through a sense resistor and rapidly switch the phase on and off, using fixed-off-time or fixed-frequency hysteresis, to track a per-microstep reference regardless of supply voltage or motor back-EMF. Worth recognizing: the six-switch three-phase bridge under a BLDC or FOC drive is the identical power stage used in a grid-tie solar inverter or a motor-drive VFD — same MOSFETs, same half-bridge legs — the only difference is whether the control algorithm outputs six-step commutation states or a continuously modulated sine wave.

lessons.workedExample: A hobbyist upgrades a quadcopter's BLDC motors from a sensored six-step ESC to a sensorless FOC-class ESC. At full throttle in flight, the sensorless design works fine — back-EMF is large and clean at 20,000+ RPM. But on the bench, spinning up from a dead stop under load (simulating a heavy prop), the motor stutters and sometimes fails to start: back-EMF is proportional to speed, so near 0 RPM there's no usable signal, and the controller must run an open-loop startup ramp, guessing commutation timing until speed builds enough for zero-crossing detection to lock on. Switching to an FOC controller with a magnetic encoder eliminates the stutter because rotor angle is measured directly rather than inferred from back-EMF, giving full torque control from a standstill.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe sensorless BLDC's low-speed behavior because it exposes whether a student understands back-EMF as the actual sensing mechanism rather than treating 'sensorless' as a magic feature. A weak answer says the motor 'just needs calibration'; a strong one explains that back-EMF scales with speed, so the signal genuinely vanishes near zero RPM, forcing an open-loop startup — a real physical limitation, not a bug to code around. The same test applies to FOC: a student who can name the Clarke and Park transforms and explain why turning three AC phases into two DC currents enables smooth torque has engaged with the control theory, not just cited a buzzword from a datasheet.

questions.prompt: Why does sensorless back-EMF zero-crossing commutation fail near zero motor speed?

options.text: The Hall sensors overheat
Back-EMF amplitude is proportional to speed, so it's too small to detect reliably at low RPM
The chopper driver runs out of PWM resolution
The Clarke transform becomes undefined at zero speed

explanations.a: Sensorless designs have no Hall sensors present to overheat.
explanations.b: Correct — since BEMF = kω, the signal genuinely shrinks toward zero as speed drops, not just becomes harder to filter.
explanations.c: Chopper/PWM resolution is a stepper-driver concept, not the cause of sensorless BLDC's low-speed limitation.
explanations.d: The Clarke transform is well-defined at any speed including zero; it's an FOC concept, not what causes sensorless commutation to fail.

questions.prompt: Match each term to what it actually does in a three-phase or stepper drive.

right.text: Converts three phase currents into two orthogonal stationary-frame currents (Iα, Iβ)
Rotates the stationary frame into the rotor-aligned d-q frame, producing steady Id/Iq
Switches stepper coil current on and off against a sensed reference to hold a target microstep current
Give three 120°-spaced digital signals marking six commutation states per electrical revolution

questions.explanation: Clarke turns three-phase currents into a two-axis stationary frame; Park rotates that into the rotor-synchronous d-q frame where FOC's PI loops run; chopper regulation is how stepper drivers enforce a precise microstep current independent of supply voltage; Hall sensors are the direct-measurement alternative to back-EMF sensing for six-step commutation.

questions.prompt: What does field-oriented control specifically gain by regulating Id and Iq instead of driving trapezoidal six-step current?

options.text: It eliminates the need for a three-phase bridge
Smoother torque and less audible noise, since sinusoidal drive removes the torque dips at each 60° commutation step
It automatically doubles the motor's top speed
It removes the need for any rotor position information

explanations.a: FOC uses the exact same three-phase bridge hardware as six-step commutation; only the switching pattern changes.
explanations.b: Correct — sinusoidal Id/Iq control removes the torque dips six-step's discrete 60° steps produce.
explanations.c: Field weakening can extend speed range, but it doesn't automatically double it, and that isn't the primary gain from Id/Iq control itself.
explanations.d: FOC needs rotor angle even more precisely than six-step does — it's central to the Park transform.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of a stepper driver's chopper current-regulation cycle.

items.text: Driver compares sensed coil current (via sense resistor) to the current microstep's target reference
If sensed current is below the reference, the driver turns the phase switch on to build current
Once sensed current reaches the reference, the driver turns the switch off for a fixed interval, letting current decay
The cycle repeats at high frequency, holding average coil current at the sine/cosine-weighted microstep level

questions.explanation: Chopper regulation is a closed loop: sense current, compare to the target, switch on to raise it or off to let it decay, repeating fast enough that the average current tracks the commanded sine/cosine microstep level.

lessons.label: Battery Charging and Energy-Storage Interfaces

sections.heading: The CC-CV Charge Profile and Why Overcharge Is Dangerous
