explanations.a: An open circuit (ZL → ∞) gives Γ = +1, full reflection with no phase inversion.
explanations.b: Correct — a short circuit sets ZL = 0, giving Γ = (0 − Z0)/(0 + Z0) = −1: full reflection with a 180° phase flip.
explanations.c: A matched load gives Γ = 0, since the numerator (ZL − Z0) is zero.
explanations.d: ZL = 2Z0 gives Γ = (2Z0 − Z0)/(2Z0 + Z0) = 1/3 ≈ 0.333, a partial, non-inverted reflection.

questions.prompt: A 100 Ω load on a 50 Ω line gives Γ = 0.333. What fraction of the incident power reflects?

explanations.a: 33.3% is the fraction of incident voltage that reflects (|Γ|), not power.
explanations.b: Correct — reflected power fraction is |Γ|² = 0.333² ≈ 0.111, or 11.1%.
explanations.c: 50% would require |Γ| ≈ 0.707, far more mismatch than a 100-on-50 Ω case produces.
explanations.d: 66.7% is simply 1 − 0.333, mixing up the voltage reflection fraction with power delivered; it isn't a meaningful power quantity here.

questions.prompt: Match each load condition to its reflection coefficient Γ.

left.text: ZL = 100 Ω on a 50 Ω line

questions.explanation: Open gives Γ=+1, short gives Γ=−1, a matched load gives Γ=0, and 100 Ω on a 50 Ω line gives Γ=(100−50)/(100+50)=0.333.

questions.prompt: One port shows a return loss of 6 dB and another shows 20 dB. Which is better matched, and why?

options.text: The 6 dB port, because lower numbers mean less power is lost
The 20 dB port, because a higher return loss in dB means less power reflects
They are equally matched, since return loss doesn't depend on Γ
The 6 dB port, because return loss is inverted for complex loads

explanations.a: This has the relationship backwards — return loss in dB grows as reflection shrinks, so a lower dB number means a worse match.
explanations.b: Correct — RL = −20 log10|Γ|, so a larger RL means a smaller |Γ|; 20 dB corresponds to |Γ| ≈ 0.1 (1% power reflected) versus 6 dB's |Γ| ≈ 0.5 (25% reflected).
explanations.c: Return loss is defined directly in terms of |Γ|; it isn't independent of it.
explanations.d: Return loss's sign convention doesn't invert for complex loads — |Γ| is used either way, and the same formula applies.

lessons.label: Standing Waves, VSWR, and What It Actually Costs You

sections.heading: Two Waves, One Pattern
sections.body: Whenever a line isn't perfectly matched, a reflected wave travels backward and superposes with the forward wave already traveling toward the load. The sum doesn't move — it's a standing wave, a fixed spatial pattern of voltage maxima and minima that doesn't propagate, even though both component waves do. Where the forward and reflected waves arrive in phase, voltage adds constructively to a maximum (an antinode); a quarter-wavelength away, the round-trip phase shift has flipped by 180°, and the waves cancel toward a minimum (a node). Because that phase relationship repeats every half wavelength of travel, adjacent maxima — and adjacent minima — are spaced λ/2 apart along the line, a pattern historically read directly off a slotted line with a sliding probe before modern network analyzers existed.

sections.heading: VSWR: One Number for the Whole Pattern
sections.body: The voltage standing wave ratio compresses that pattern into a single number, VSWR = Vmax/Vmin = (1 + |Γ|)/(1 − |Γ|). A perfectly matched line has |Γ| = 0 and VSWR = 1:1 (a flat line, no standing wave at all); a total mismatch (open or short) drives VSWR to infinity. Working the earlier 100-on-50-Ω example, |Γ| = 0.333 gives VSWR = 1.333/0.667 = 2.0, so '2:1 VSWR' and 'Γ = 0.333' describe the identical physical mismatch. That 2:1 case reflects 11% of the power and costs a mismatch loss of −10 log10(1 − |Γ|²) = −10 log10(0.889) ≈ 0.5 dB — small enough that most receivers or antennas wouldn't notice it by ear or by signal report.

sections.heading: Why 1.5:1 Is a Spec, and What VSWR Actually Endangers
sections.body: If 2:1 only costs half a decibel, why do amateur-radio and commercial specs commonly demand 1.5:1 or better (|Γ| ≈ 0.2, about 4% reflected)? Not primarily to save power — it's to protect the transmitter. A standing wave produces voltage antinodes that can run well above the forward-wave voltage alone, and the reflected power flows back into the final amplifier stage, where it can raise dissipation, unbalance push-pull output transistors, or in tube gear exceed the plate voltage rating. Solid-state PAs commonly include VSWR foldback circuits that automatically cut output power once reflected power crosses a threshold, precisely because a sustained high-VSWR fault (a disconnected antenna reading as an open, VSWR = ∞) can destroy output devices in seconds, even though the wasted power itself is a small fraction of the total.

lessons.workedExample: On a slotted line, a student measures the standing-wave envelope on a 50 Ω line feeding an unknown antenna: the voltage probe reads 3.0 V at the maxima and 1.0 V at the minima. VSWR = Vmax/Vmin = 3.0/1.0 = 3:1. Solving VSWR = (1+|Γ|)/(1−|Γ|) for |Γ| gives |Γ| = (VSWR−1)/(VSWR+1) = 2/4 = 0.5, so 25% of the forward power (|Γ|² = 0.25) is reflecting back toward the transmitter — a mismatch loss of about 1.25 dB, but more importantly a load the transmitter's foldback circuit would likely flag before the student ever gets a chance to read the meter.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges reach for VSWR because it's a favorite target for the misconception that 'high VSWR means mostly wasted power.' A weak answer says a 2:1 VSWR reading is bad because 'half the power gets lost.' A strong answer does the arithmetic — 2:1 is only |Γ| = 0.333, 11% reflected, half a decibel of loss — and instead explains that the real hazard is the standing wave's voltage antinodes and the reflected power hitting the transmitter's final stage, which is why manufacturers spec foldback protection and why operators chase 1.5:1 for equipment safety, not for the fraction of a dB it saves.

questions.prompt: A load produces Γ = 0.333. What is the resulting VSWR?

explanations.a: 1.33 is just 1+|Γ|, the numerator of the VSWR formula alone — the denominator (1−|Γ|) still needs to be divided in.
explanations.c: 3:1 would require a larger |Γ| (about 0.5), not 0.333.
explanations.d: VSWR is always ≥ 1 by definition (Vmax ≥ Vmin), so a value below 1 is not physically possible.

questions.prompt: What is the primary danger of sustained high VSWR to a transmitter, as opposed to simple power waste?

options.text: It roughly halves the transmitted power at any VSWR above 1.2:1
Voltage antinodes and reflected power reaching the final amplifier stage can overstress or destroy output devices
It permanently changes the transmitter's operating frequency
It has no real risk below a VSWR of 10:1

explanations.a: Even a fairly high VSWR like 2:1 wastes only about 11% of the power — nowhere near half — so this overstates the loss.
explanations.b: Correct — elevated voltage at antinodes and reflected power flowing back into the PA can raise dissipation, unbalance output transistors, or exceed voltage ratings, which is why foldback protection exists.
explanations.c: VSWR affects impedance matching and power handling, not the oscillator frequency itself.
explanations.d: Moderate VSWR (well below 10:1) can already stress a PA enough to trigger foldback protection or, in unprotected gear, cause damage over time.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for measuring VSWR with a slotted line and probe.

items.text: Slide the probe along the slotted line, sampling voltage at each position
Record the maximum voltage reading, Vmax, and the minimum voltage reading, Vmin
Compute VSWR = Vmax / Vmin
If needed, convert VSWR to |Γ| using |Γ| = (VSWR−1)/(VSWR+1)

questions.explanation: You must scan the line to find the extremes before you can record Vmax and Vmin, then divide to get VSWR, and only then convert to Γ if the reflection coefficient itself is needed.

questions.prompt: Along a line with a standing wave, how far apart are adjacent voltage maxima?

options.text: λ
2λ

explanations.a: λ/4 is the spacing between an adjacent maximum and minimum, not between two maxima.
explanations.b: Correct — the forward/reflected phase relationship that produces a maximum repeats every half wavelength of travel, so maxima (and minima) recur every λ/2.
explanations.c: A full wavelength would place two maxima and two minima in between, not adjacent maxima.
explanations.d: 2λ is far larger than the actual repeat distance of the standing-wave pattern.

lessons.label: Impedance Along the Line and the Quarter-Wave Transformer

sections.heading: The Input Impedance Looking Into a Line
sections.body: A transmission line doesn't just carry a load's impedance unchanged back to the source — it transforms it. For a lossless line of characteristic impedance Z0 and length l terminated in ZL, the impedance looking into the line is Zin(l) = Z0 (ZL + jZ0 tan(βl)) / (Z0 + jZL tan(βl)), derived by solving the telegrapher's equations for the forward and reflected waves and dividing total voltage by total current at the input. Because tan(βl) is periodic with period π, Zin repeats every time βl advances by π — that is, every half wavelength (l = λ/2). A line exactly half a wavelength long reproduces the load impedance unchanged regardless of Z0, a useful fact when a feedline length doesn't need to hit an exact match.

sections.heading: The Quarter-Wave Inversion
sections.body: At l = λ/4, βl = π/2 and tan(βl) → ∞, and the formula collapses to Zin = Z0²/ZL — the line inverts the load impedance, scaled by Z0². This is the basis of the quarter-wave transformer: to match a real load ZL to a source impedance Z0,src with no reactive components, insert a quarter-wavelength section of a different characteristic impedance Z0,T = √(Z0,src × ZL). Choosing Z0,T that way, and only that way, makes the transformed impedance at the input exactly Z0,T²/ZL = Z0,src — a perfect match, but only at the design frequency, since the λ/4 condition depends on frequency and the match narrows quickly off-band. How narrow depends on how far βl drifts from its design value of π/2: move off f0 and βl no longer equals π/2, the cancellation in the Zin formula stops being exact, and the input VSWR climbs as frequency departs from center. A commonly cited rule of thumb for a single quarter-wave section is on the order of 10% fractional bandwidth for a target VSWR around 1.5:1 — workable for a single-band antenna feed but too narrow for a radio that has to cover several bands. Cascading multiple quarter-wave sections, with each section's characteristic impedance chosen from a Chebyshev or binomial polynomial instead of a single geometric mean, widens that bandwidth substantially, trading extra sections — and extra board or coax length — for a flatter match across a wider frequency range.

sections.heading: Stubs: Turning Line Length Into a Reactance
sections.body: Terminating a short line in a short or open circuit instead of a resistive load turns Zin into a pure reactance you can set just by choosing length. A shorted stub (ZL = 0) gives Zin = jZ0 tan(βl) — inductive for any length under λ/4. An open stub (ZL → ∞) gives Zin = −jZ0 cot(βl) — capacitive under λ/4. At exactly λ/4, a shorted stub's tan(βl) diverges, presenting an open circuit, while an open stub's cot(βl) goes to zero, presenting a short. Because a length of line can synthesize an L or a C without an actual inductor or capacitor (and without their parasitic losses at high frequency), open and shorted stubs are the standard building block of microwave matching networks, printed directly onto a PCB or milled into a coax fixture.

lessons.workedExample: An antenna presents a clean, resistive 100 Ω at 300 MHz, and the feed system is standard 50 Ω coax. A quarter-wave transformer needs a section with Z0,T = √(50 × 100) = √5000 ≈ 70.7 Ω — close to commercially available 75 Ω line, though a purpose-built 70.7 Ω section (an air-spaced or semi-rigid line) gives an exact match. At 300 MHz in free space λ = 1.0 m, so a quarter wavelength is 0.25 m; in a coax with velocity factor 0.66 the physical length shrinks to 0.66 × 0.25 ≈ 0.165 m ≈ 16.5 cm. Cut and inserted between the 50 Ω feed and the 100 Ω antenna, that 16.5 cm of 70.7 Ω line presents Zin = 70.7²/100 ≈ 50 Ω back to the transmitter.
lessons.judgeFraming: This is where judges separate students who memorized 'Zin = Z0²/ZL at a quarter wave' from students who understand it's a narrowband trick with a specific derivation. A weak answer states the quarter-wave formula without knowing why tan(βl) diverges at l = λ/4. A strong answer connects the periodicity of Zin to the tangent function, explains why the transformer's own Z0 must be the geometric mean of source and load, and volunteers the limitation: it only matches a purely resistive load at one design frequency, which is why real antenna feeds often need an additional reactive matching stage alongside it.

questions.prompt: For a lossless line, what does Zin become at exactly l = λ/4?

options.text: Zin = ZL, unchanged from the load
Zin = Z0²/ZL
Zin = Z0 + ZL
Zin = 0, regardless of ZL

explanations.a: Zin = ZL happens at l = λ/2 (or any multiple of λ/2), not at a quarter wavelength.
explanations.b: Correct — at l = λ/4, tan(βl) → ∞ and the general Zin formula collapses to Zin = Z0²/ZL, the quarter-wave inversion.
explanations.c: Simple addition isn't how transmission-line impedance transformation works; the relationship is the ratio Z0²/ZL.
explanations.d: Zin only goes to zero at λ/4 if ZL itself is infinite (an open load); for a finite ZL it's Z0²/ZL, a finite value.

questions.prompt: To match a 50 Ω source to a purely resistive 100 Ω load with a quarter-wave transformer, what characteristic impedance should the transformer section have?

explanations.a: Using the source's own impedance for the transformer section would not perform any impedance transformation.
explanations.b: Using the load's impedance for the transformer would also fail to transform anything — it needs to be between the two.
explanations.c: Correct — Z0,T = √(Z0,src × ZL) = √(50 × 100) = √5000 ≈ 70.7 Ω, the geometric mean of source and load impedances.
explanations.d: 150 Ω is the simple sum of 50 and 100, not the geometric mean the quarter-wave formula requires.

questions.prompt: Match each stub condition to the reactance it presents.

right.text: Inductive reactance
Capacitive reactance
Looks like an open circuit
Looks like a short circuit

questions.explanation: A short stub under λ/4 gives Zin = jZ0 tan(βl), inductive; an open stub under λ/4 gives Zin = −jZ0 cot(βl), capacitive. At exactly λ/4, a shorted stub's tan(βl) diverges to present an open, while an open stub's cot(βl) goes to zero to present a short.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for designing a quarter-wave transformer to match a source to a load.

items.text: Confirm the load is purely resistive at the design frequency
Compute the transformer's characteristic impedance, Z0,T = √(Z0,source × ZL)
Compute the physical length using the operating wavelength and the transformer line's velocity factor
Fabricate and insert the transformer section between the source and the load

questions.explanation: The quarter-wave formula only cancels reactance for a resistive load, so that must be confirmed first; then the geometric-mean impedance is computed; then that abstract quarter wavelength is converted into a real physical length using the transformer line's own velocity factor; only then is it built and installed.

lessons.label: The Time-Domain View: TDR and Signal Integrity

sections.heading: Reading a Line's Impedance in Time, Not Frequency
sections.body: Time-domain reflectometry sends a fast voltage step down a line and watches what comes back on an oscilloscope, rather than sweeping frequency the way a network analyzer does. Every place the line's impedance changes — a connector, a via, a kink in a cable, the load itself — reflects part of the step, and the local reflection coefficient at that point is read directly from the amplitude of the returning bump relative to the incident step, using the same Γ = (Z − Z0)/(Z + Z0) from the frequency-domain picture. Because the reflection takes a finite round-trip time to return, and that time multiplied by the line's propagation velocity (c × velocity factor) gives twice the distance to the discontinuity, a single TDR trace locates every impedance bump along a cable or PCB trace and shows whether it's higher or lower than Z0 from the sign of the bump.

sections.heading: Terminating the Line: Series vs. Parallel
sections.body: Two termination strategies prevent reflections from ever becoming a problem. Series (source) termination places a resistor at the driver so that Rsource + Rseries ≈ Z0; the driver launches a half-amplitude step, which reflects fully off an open/high-impedance receiver, doubles to full amplitude at the far end, and is then absorbed on the way back at the matched source — the receiver sees one clean, full-swing edge. Parallel (load) termination instead places a resistor equal to Z0 directly at the receiver, absorbing the wave the instant it arrives with no reflection at all, at the cost of a continuous DC current draw through that resistor whenever the line is driven high.

sections.heading: Why a Fast Edge Turns a Short Trace Into an RF Problem
sections.body: A widely used rule of thumb, from Howard Johnson and Martin Graham's 1993 textbook High-Speed Digital Design, treats a trace as a transmission line once its length exceeds about one-sixth of the distance the edge travels during its rise time — a critical length Lcrit ≈ v × Tr / 6. A typical FR4 PCB trace propagates at roughly 15 cm/ns. With a 1 ns edge, Lcrit ≈ 15/6 ≈ 2.5 cm — so a 15 cm trace, six times past that threshold, needs real termination even though the circuit around it is otherwise 'just DC' digital logic. Left unterminated, that stub rings and overshoots: the reflected wave arrives back at the driver out of sync with the next transition, superposing into overshoot, undershoot, and damped oscillation that can false-trigger a receiver's input threshold.

lessons.workedExample: A TDR test on a 50 Ω coax pushes a step in at t = 0 and sees a small positive bump return at t = 4 ns. With a velocity factor of 0.66 (v = 0.66 × 3×10⁸ ≈ 1.98×10⁸ m/s), the round-trip distance is v × t = 1.98×10⁸ × 4×10⁻⁹ ≈ 0.79 m, so the discontinuity sits at half that: d ≈ 0.40 m down the cable. The bump's amplitude is 5% of the incident step (Γ ≈ 0.05), positive, so the local impedance is higher than 50 Ω: Z = Z0(1+Γ)/(1−Γ) = 50 × 1.05/0.95 ≈ 55 Ω — consistent with a slightly undersized connector pin at that point, not a full break.
lessons.judgeFraming: TDR questions test whether a student can connect a picture on an oscilloscope to a physical fault location and cause. A weak answer says 'the bump means there's a problem' without extracting distance or impedance from it. A strong answer reads the bump's timing to get distance (using the cable's actual velocity factor, not the speed of light), reads its sign and size to get the local impedance and its direction of mismatch, and can explain, using the rise-time rule of thumb, why their specific trace or cable length crossed into transmission-line territory in the first place rather than asserting it by intuition.

questions.prompt: A TDR trace shows a reflection returning at t = 4 ns on a cable with velocity factor 0.66. Roughly how far away is the discontinuity?

options.text: About 1.2 m
About 0.40 m
About 0.79 m from the source to a point beyond the discontinuity
About 2 m

explanations.a: 1.2 m overstates the distance; it doesn't account for halving the round-trip travel to get one-way distance.
explanations.b: Correct — v × t ≈ 1.98×10⁸ × 4×10⁻⁹ ≈ 0.79 m is the round-trip distance, so the discontinuity itself is at half that, about 0.40 m.
explanations.c: 0.79 m is the round-trip distance the wave traveled, not the one-way distance to the discontinuity.
explanations.d: 2 m greatly overstates the distance for a 4 ns round trip at this velocity.

questions.prompt: Which termination style draws continuous DC current through its resistor whenever the line is driven high?

options.text: Series (source) termination
Parallel (load) termination
Neither style draws continuous current
Both draw identical continuous current

explanations.a: Series termination places its resistor at the driver and only briefly passes current during the edge transition; it doesn't draw steady current in the high state.
explanations.b: Correct — a parallel resistor at the receiver, sized to Z0, sits across the line and draws continuous current whenever the driven voltage is nonzero.
explanations.c: Parallel termination specifically does draw continuous current in the high state, since the resistor is a steady DC path to the termination voltage.
explanations.d: The two styles behave differently; series termination avoids the steady current draw that parallel termination has.

questions.prompt: A TDR bump has a negative amplitude relative to the incident step. What does that indicate about the local impedance at that point?

options.text: It is higher than Z0
It is lower than Z0
It is exactly equal to Z0
The line has broken completely at that point

explanations.a: A higher local impedance produces a positive bump (Γ = (Z−Z0)/(Z+Z0) is positive when Z > Z0), the opposite of this case.
explanations.b: Correct — Γ is negative when Z < Z0, since (Z − Z0) is negative, producing a downward (negative) bump on the TDR trace.
explanations.c: An impedance equal to Z0 gives Γ = 0, producing no visible bump at all.
explanations.d: A complete break (open circuit at that point) would give Γ = +1, a large positive bump, not a negative one.

questions.prompt: Match each termination or line condition to its defining characteristic.

right.text: Resistor near the driver absorbs the reflection on its return trip
Resistor at the far end absorbs the wave immediately, at the cost of continuous DC current
Multiple reflections bounce back and forth, producing ringing and overshoot
Produces no visible bump on a TDR trace

questions.explanation: Series termination absorbs the reflection back at the source; parallel termination absorbs it immediately at the load but draws steady current; an unterminated stub reflects repeatedly, causing ringing; a matched load reflects nothing, so it produces no TDR bump.

questions.prompt: Order what happens on a series-terminated line driving a high-impedance (unterminated) receiver.

items.text: The driver launches a half-amplitude step, since Rsource + Rseries ≈ Z0 forms a voltage divider
The half-amplitude wave travels down the line toward the receiver
The wave reflects fully off the high-impedance receiver, doubling to full amplitude
The receiver sees one clean, full-swing edge
The reflected wave travels back down the line and is absorbed at the matched source

questions.explanation: Series termination relies on a half-swing launch, a full reflection at the open receiver that restores full swing there, and a final absorption of the returning wave back at the source so no further reflections occur.

lessons.label: Real Lines: Coax, Microstrip, CPW, and Waveguide

sections.heading: Coax: The Default for Flexible, Shielded Runs
sections.body: Coaxial cable's characteristic impedance follows directly from its geometry: Z0 = (138/√εr) × log10(D/d), where D is the inner diameter of the outer shield, d is the diameter of the center conductor, and εr is the dielectric's relative permittivity. RG-58's polyethylene dielectric (εr ≈ 2.3) and its standard D/d ratio work out to Z0 ≈ 50 Ω, the near-universal choice for RF test equipment and amateur radio because it balances power-handling capacity against attenuation (75 Ω coax, common in cable-TV distribution, instead minimizes loss for a fixed outer diameter). Coax is fully shielded and flexible, but at millimeter-wave frequencies its loss climbs fast and small connectorized coax becomes expensive and mechanically delicate.

sections.heading: Microstrip: Cheap, Dense, and On Every PCB
sections.body: Microstrip runs a copper trace over a grounded dielectric substrate with no top shielding, making it the default RF structure on a printed circuit board. Its impedance depends on trace width W, substrate height h, and an effective permittivity εeff that blends the substrate's εr with the air above the trace, roughly εeff ≈ (εr+1)/2 + (εr−1)/2 × 1/√(1+12h/W). On standard 1.6 mm FR4 (εr ≈ 4.3), hitting 50 Ω takes a trace about 2.9 mm wide — a number every PCB designer eventually memorizes. Microstrip is cheap and easy to route but radiates slightly and is dispersive, since εeff itself shifts with frequency.

sections.heading: Coplanar Waveguide: Grounding Without a Backside Via
sections.body: Grounded coplanar waveguide (GCPW) puts ground planes on the same layer as the signal trace, on either side with a defined gap, plus a solid ground layer underneath stitched to the top ground with vias. The gap width, not just the trace width, sets the impedance, which decouples the line's impedance from substrate thickness more than microstrip does — useful when a board's stack-up is fixed by other constraints. GCPW is the preferred structure for connectorized RF test boards and MMIC (monolithic microwave IC) launch pads because its ground reference sits right next to the signal, close to what an SMA edge launch expects.

sections.heading: Waveguide: No Center Conductor, No Loss Ceiling — Until Cutoff
sections.body: A hollow rectangular waveguide carries energy with no center conductor at all, guided by reflections off its metal walls, which makes it the lowest-loss, highest-power-handling option — but it only propagates above a cutoff frequency set by its cross-section, fc = c/(2a) for the dominant TE10 mode, where a is the guide's broad wall dimension. WR-90 waveguide (a = 22.86 mm) cuts off at 6.56 GHz and is used single-mode across the entire X-band, 8.2–12.4 GHz, staying safely above cutoff and below the next mode's onset. Waveguide is bulky, rigid, and expensive to machine, so it shows up only where coax and microstrip losses become unacceptable — radar transmitters, satellite feeds, and high-power test setups.

lessons.workedExample: A 50 Ω microstrip trace needs to be routed on standard 1.6 mm FR4 (εr ≈ 4.3). Starting from a trial width-to-height ratio W/h ≈ 1.8, a typical starting point for 50 Ω on this substrate, the effective permittivity works out to εeff ≈ (4.3+1)/2 + (4.3−1)/2 × 1/√(1+12/1.8) ≈ 3.0. With h = 1.6 mm and W/h ≈ 1.8, the trace width is W ≈ 1.8 × 1.6 mm ≈ 2.9 mm — matching the rule-of-thumb figure PCB designers reach for without re-deriving it every time. A designer who instead needed a connectorized coax jumper to the same board would reach for standard 50 Ω RG-58 or semi-rigid cable rather than trying to match 2.9 mm microstrip.
lessons.judgeFraming: This lesson tests whether a student sees transmission-line choice as an engineering tradeoff rather than a fixed recipe. A weak answer says 'I used microstrip because it's on the PCB' with no comparison. A strong answer can name why coax was or wasn't chosen (shielding vs. cost vs. flexibility), why microstrip's 2.9 mm width follows from the substrate they specified rather than an arbitrary choice, and — for a project running above a few GHz — whether waveguide's cutoff behavior was ever a live consideration, showing they understand that structure sets both impedance and a usable frequency floor or ceiling, not just a cosmetic difference in how the 'wire' looks.

questions.prompt: In the coax impedance formula Z0 = (138/√εr) × log10(D/d), what do D and d represent?

options.text: D is the outer jacket diameter and d is the shield's wall thickness
D is the inner diameter of the outer shield and d is the diameter of the center conductor
D is the dielectric's relative permittivity and d is the loss tangent
D and d are both measured in wavelengths, not physical length

explanations.a: Jacket diameter and shield thickness aren't the geometric quantities the formula uses; it's the dielectric's inner and outer conductor diameters that matter.
explanations.b: Correct — D is the shield's inner diameter and d is the center conductor's diameter; their ratio, combined with εr, sets Z0.
explanations.c: εr already appears separately in the formula as the dielectric constant; D and d are physical diameters, not electrical properties.
explanations.d: D and d are physical lengths (e.g., millimeters); the formula only needs their ratio, which is dimensionless, not a wavelength measure.

questions.prompt: Roughly what trace width gives 50 Ω microstrip on standard 1.6 mm FR4 (εr ≈ 4.3)?

options.text: About 0.5 mm
About 2.9 mm
About 8 mm
About 16 mm

explanations.a: 0.5 mm would be far too narrow for 50 Ω on this substrate thickness; a much thinner trace would push impedance well above 50 Ω.
explanations.b: Correct — on 1.6 mm FR4, a W/h ratio near 1.8 gives 50 Ω, meaning a trace width of about 2.9 mm.
explanations.c: 8 mm would push impedance well below 50 Ω, since wider traces relative to substrate height lower the impedance.
explanations.d: 16 mm — equal to ten times the substrate height — would give a very low impedance, nowhere near 50 Ω.

questions.prompt: Match each transmission-line type to its best-fit characteristic or use case.

right.text: Flexible, fully shielded cable runs
Cheap, dense routing directly on a PCB
Connectorized RF test boards and MMIC launch pads
Highest power handling and lowest loss, but only above a cutoff frequency

questions.explanation: Coax is the flexible shielded default; microstrip is the cheap PCB workhorse; GCPW suits connectorized test boards and IC launches because its ground sits beside the signal; waveguide offers the best loss and power figures but only propagates above its cutoff frequency.

questions.prompt: WR-90 waveguide cuts off at 6.56 GHz. Which band is it commonly used for, single-mode?

options.text: VHF, 30–300 MHz
X-band, 8.2–12.4 GHz
Exactly at its 6.56 GHz cutoff frequency
Below 6.56 GHz, where it still weakly propagates

explanations.a: VHF is far below WR-90's cutoff frequency; the waveguide simply would not propagate at all in that band.
explanations.b: Correct — WR-90 is the standard waveguide for X-band, 8.2–12.4 GHz, comfortably above its 6.56 GHz cutoff and below the onset of the next higher-order mode.
explanations.c: Operating right at cutoff gives near-infinite group delay and impractical loss; real systems operate well above it.
explanations.d: Below cutoff, a waveguide's dominant mode doesn't propagate as a traveling wave at all — the field decays exponentially instead.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for hand-computing a 50 Ω microstrip trace width on a given substrate.

items.text: Note the substrate height h and dielectric constant εr
Pick a trial width-to-height ratio, W/h
Compute the effective permittivity εeff from that trial ratio
Compute the resulting Z0 estimate and compare it to the 50 Ω target
Adjust W/h and repeat until Z0 converges on 50 Ω

questions.explanation: The substrate's fixed properties must be known first, then a trial geometry is guessed, effective permittivity is computed from that guess, the resulting impedance is checked against the 50 Ω target, and the ratio is refined iteratively until it converges.

units.label: The Smith Chart and Impedance Matching

lessons.label: How the Smith Chart Is Built

sections.heading: A map, not a picture
sections.body: The Smith chart looks like a decorative circle full of arcs, but it is a precise coordinate transformation. Start with a load impedance Z normalized to the line's characteristic impedance Z0: z = Z/Z0 = r + jx. The reflection coefficient at that load is Gamma = (z - 1)/(z + 1), a bilinear (Mobius) map. Bilinear maps have a defining property: they take circles and lines to circles and lines. Because the right half of the z-plane (all impedances with r >= 0, meaning passive, non-generating loads) has infinite extent, the map folds that entire half-plane into the interior of a single unit circle in the Gamma-plane. Every physically realizable passive impedance, from a dead short to an open circuit, lands somewhere inside or on that one circle.

sections.heading: Where the constant-r and constant-x lines go
sections.body: In the z-plane, lines of constant resistance r and constant reactance x are straight lines perpendicular to each other. Under the Gamma = (z-1)/(z+1) map, constant-r lines become circles that all pass through the point Gamma = +1 (the r = infinity, open-circuit point) and are tangent to each other there; constant-x lines become arcs that also pass through Gamma = +1. The r = 0 circle (zero resistance) is the outer boundary of the chart itself, and the r = 1 circle is the specific circle that passes through the exact center, Gamma = 0, which is the point z = 1 -- a perfectly matched load.

sections.heading: Landmarks: short, open, match, and the two hemispheres
sections.body: Four points orient every reading. Gamma = -1, the chart's left extreme, is z = 0: a short circuit. Gamma = +1, the right extreme, is z = infinity: an open circuit. Gamma = 0, dead center, is z = 1: the matched condition, the entire goal of the matching problem. The chart splits top-to-bottom along the real axis: the upper half holds every impedance with positive reactance (x > 0, inductive), the lower half holds every impedance with negative reactance (x < 0, capacitive). Phillip H. Smith first published this construction as 'Transmission Line Calculator' in Electronics magazine in January 1939, building it as a mechanical calculating aid before slide rules and calculators made point-by-point complex arithmetic tedious; a later, more detailed unit on the chart's history covers how the tool evolved.

lessons.workedExample: A load has Z = 25 + j50 ohms on a 50 ohm line. Normalize: z = 0.5 + j1.0. On the chart, find the r = 0.5 circle (a circle smaller than the r = 1 circle, sitting to the left of center) and the x = 1.0 arc (an arc in the upper, inductive half). Their intersection is the plotted point. Reading its position relative to the outer scale gives |Gamma| directly as a distance from center, and the angle of Gamma directly as rotation from the positive real axis -- both without computing (0.5 + j1.0 - 1)/(0.5 + j1.0 + 1) by hand.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'what is the Smith chart actually a plot of?' is testing whether a student memorized a picture or understands a coordinate transform. A weak answer says 'it shows impedance for matching.' A strong answer names the bilinear map Gamma = (z-1)/(z+1), explains why an infinite half-plane compresses into a finite disk, and can point to why r = 1 is not an arbitrary circle but the specific locus of every impedance whose real part already equals the line impedance. That distinction is what lets a student later explain, rather than just execute, every matching move built on top of the chart.

questions.prompt: What mathematical relationship maps normalized impedance z to the reflection coefficient plotted on the Smith chart?

options.text: Gamma = z - 1
Gamma = (z - 1)/(z + 1)
Gamma = z / (z + 1)
Gamma = 1/z

explanations.a: This is not a bilinear map and does not confine passive impedances to a finite region.
explanations.b: Correct -- this bilinear (Mobius) transform maps the entire right half of the z-plane into the unit disk of Gamma.
explanations.c: This resembles an admittance-style ratio but is not the reflection-coefficient definition used to build the chart.
explanations.d: This is the reciprocal used to move from impedance to admittance, not the impedance-to-Gamma mapping.

questions.prompt: A point lies in the lower half of the Smith chart. What does that tell you about the impedance there?

options.text: Its resistance is negative
Its reactance is capacitive (x < 0)
It represents an open circuit
Its reactance is inductive (x > 0)

explanations.a: Negative resistance would fall outside the chart entirely, not simply in the lower half.
explanations.b: Correct -- the lower hemisphere is defined by negative reactance, i.e. capacitive impedances.
explanations.c: The open circuit is a single point, Gamma = +1, on the right edge, not a whole hemisphere.
explanations.d: Inductive (positive) reactance is the upper hemisphere, the opposite of this point's location.

questions.prompt: Match each Smith chart landmark to the physical condition it represents.

right.text: Short circuit, z = 0
Open circuit, z = infinity
Perfect match, z = 1
Every impedance whose real part equals Z0

questions.explanation: The chart's extremes are the short and open, its center is the matched point, and the r = 1 circle is the locus of resistances exactly equal to the line's characteristic impedance -- the circle every matching network is trying to reach.

questions.prompt: Why does the entire right half of the z-plane (r >= 0, any x) compress into a finite disk on the Smith chart?

options.text: Because engineers chose to draw it that way for convenience
Because the bilinear map Gamma = (z-1)/(z+1) sends the infinite half-plane of passive impedances into the bounded unit circle
Because only impedances up to 50 ohms are physically realizable
Because reactance is always bounded to plus or minus 1

explanations.a: It is not an arbitrary drawing choice -- it is a direct mathematical consequence of the transform.
explanations.b: Correct -- the bilinear map is what compresses infinite r into a finite radius, which is precisely why the chart can be a single closed disk.
explanations.c: Impedances of any magnitude are physically realizable; 50 ohms is just a common normalization reference, not a hard limit.
explanations.d: Reactance is not restricted to plus or minus 1 in ohms; only the normalized reflection coefficient magnitude is bounded to 1.

lessons.label: Reading Impedance, Admittance, and Motion on the Chart

sections.heading: One chart, two readings: the immittance overlay
sections.body: A single impedance point z has a matching admittance y = 1/z, and on the Smith chart that admittance point sits exactly 180 degrees around the same |Gamma| circle -- flipping through the center. This is not a coincidence of the geometry; it falls straight out of the algebra. Substituting y = 1/z into Gamma_z = (z-1)/(z+1) gives Gamma_y = (1/y-1)/(1/y+1) = (1-y)/(1+y) = -(y-1)/(y+1) = -Gamma_z, so the admittance point's reflection coefficient is exactly the negative of the impedance point's -- the same magnitude, rotated by precisely 180 degrees. Rather than redraw a whole new chart, engineers overlay the impedance grid (r and x circles) with an admittance grid (g and b circles, identical in shape but rotated 180 degrees) to get what is called the immittance or ZY chart. This single overlay is what makes real matching-network design practical: you never leave the chart to convert between series and shunt element math, you just read the same point off a different grid.

sections.heading: Why the overlay matters: series moves on r-circles, shunt moves on g-circles
sections.body: Adding a series reactance to a load changes x but leaves r untouched, so on the impedance grid that move slides the point along its constant-r circle. Adding a shunt susceptance changes b but leaves g untouched, so on the admittance grid that move slides the point along its constant-g circle. A matching network is built by alternating these two motions: read the point's r-circle for a series step, flip to the admittance grid via the 180-degree symmetry to read its g-circle for a shunt step, and repeat until the point lands on the center. This is the mechanical core of every L-network, stub, and multi-section design covered in the rest of this unit.

sections.heading: Motion along the line: rotation, VSWR circles, and Q
sections.body: Moving along a lossless transmission line toward the generator changes Gamma's phase but not its magnitude, since Gamma(l) = Gamma(0) e^{-j2*beta*l}. On the chart this is a clockwise rotation around the center at constant radius; because the phase term repeats every beta*l = pi, one full 360-degree trip around the chart corresponds to exactly lambda/2 of physical line, not a full wavelength. The chart's outer rim carries a 'wavelengths toward generator' (WTG) scale so this rotation can be read directly in fractions of a wavelength rather than degrees. A second scale runs the opposite way around the same rim: 'wavelengths toward load' (WTL), which counts counterclockwise instead of clockwise. WTL is just the mirror of WTG -- reading toward the load instead of toward the generator is useful when a design works backward from a known match point to figure out how far back down the line a given impedance sits. Because |Gamma| stays fixed while sliding along a line, every such circle is simultaneously a constant-VSWR circle: VSWR = (1+|Gamma|)/(1-|Gamma|). A different family of arcs, constant-Q arcs (Q = |x|/r or |b|/g), are sometimes overlaid to bound how much reactive buildup -- and therefore how narrow a bandwidth -- a matching path is allowed to accumulate.

lessons.workedExample: A load reads z = 0.5 - j0.5 on the impedance grid. Flipping 180 degrees around the center on the same |Gamma| circle lands on the admittance grid at y = 1 + j1 (the reciprocal). From here, adding a shunt inductor (negative susceptance) slides the point down along the g = 1 arc toward y = 1 + j0, the matched admittance point -- a move that would be far messier to find by algebra alone, since it requires computing 1/(0.5 - j0.5) and then solving for the exact susceptance that cancels +j1, all of which the chart shows as a single readable arc.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe chart 'motion' questions because they reveal whether a student can use the Smith chart as a design tool rather than just a lookup picture. A weak answer treats every matching step as a fresh algebra problem with the chart as decoration. A strong answer says, unprompted, 'series elements move me along a constant-r circle, shunt elements move me along a constant-g circle after I flip to admittance, and moving down the feedline just rotates me at constant radius' -- because that sentence is the entire logic of L-network and stub design in one breath.

questions.prompt: On the impedance (z) grid, adding a series reactance to a load moves its point along which curve?

options.text: A constant-conductance (g) circle
A constant-resistance (r) circle
A constant-VSWR circle only if the load is matched
The outer rim of the chart

explanations.a: Constant-g circles are the admittance-grid analog for shunt elements, not series elements on the impedance grid.
explanations.b: Correct -- a series reactance changes only x, so r stays fixed and the point slides along its constant-r circle.
explanations.c: VSWR circles are centered on the chart's center and track |Gamma|, unrelated to which grid a series element moves along.
explanations.d: The outer rim is the r = 0 circle; a series reactance does not push an arbitrary point out to the rim.

questions.prompt: How much physical transmission-line length corresponds to one full 360-degree rotation around the Smith chart?

options.text: One full wavelength, lambda
One quarter wavelength, lambda/4
Half a wavelength, lambda/2
It depends on the load impedance

explanations.a: A full wavelength would be two full trips around the chart, since Gamma repeats every lambda/2.
explanations.b: A quarter wavelength is only a 180-degree rotation -- halfway around, not all the way.
explanations.c: Correct -- because Gamma(l) depends on e^{-j2*beta*l}, the phase repeats every beta*l = pi, i.e. every lambda/2 of line.
explanations.d: The rotation-per-length relationship comes from the line's electrical length only; it does not depend on the terminating load.

questions.prompt: Why do engineers overlay an admittance grid on the impedance grid to form the immittance (ZY) chart, rather than using two separate charts?

options.text: Because admittance and impedance points are unrelated and must be looked up independently anyway
Because a given point's admittance is exactly its impedance point rotated 180 degrees on the same |Gamma| circle, so one overlay reads both
Because the admittance grid only applies to lossless lines
Because it removes the need to track reflection coefficient magnitude

explanations.a: They are directly related by y = 1/z, which is exactly why the overlay works -- they are not independent lookups.
explanations.b: Correct -- the 180-degree symmetry means one plotted point already carries both readings, avoiding a redraw or a manual reciprocal calculation.
explanations.c: The admittance relationship y = 1/z holds generally; the overlay is not restricted to lossless lines.
explanations.d: Reflection coefficient magnitude is unaffected by which grid you read -- the overlay doesn't touch that quantity at all.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to use the immittance chart for a series-then-shunt matching move, starting from a plotted load point.

items.text: Plot the load's impedance point on the z-grid
Slide along the constant-r circle to add a series reactance
Read the same point's position on the overlaid admittance grid
Slide along the constant-g circle to add a shunt susceptance

questions.explanation: You start by plotting the load, apply the series element first (moving along its r-circle on the impedance grid), then switch readings to the admittance grid to apply the shunt element (moving along its g-circle) -- the order matters because each element type only makes sense on its matching grid.

lessons.label: L-Networks: Two Components, One Match

sections.heading: Four topologies, one branching rule
sections.body: An L-network is the simplest possible impedance matcher: one series element and one shunt element, arranged as an upside-down L. There are four versions -- series-then-shunt or shunt-then-series, and each element can be an inductor or a capacitor -- but which family applies is decided by a single geometric fact: whether the load's normalized resistance r sits inside or outside the r = 1 circle on the Smith chart. If r_L < Z0 (the point is inside the r = 1 circle), the correct topology places the series element next to the load first, walking the point out along its constant-r circle until it crosses the g = 1 circle, then a shunt element finishes the job along that g = 1 arc into the center. If r_L > Z0 (outside the r = 1 circle), the order flips: shunt first to reach r = 1, then series to finish. Getting the order backward simply fails to reach the center -- the two arcs will not intersect the way the design needs.

sections.heading: Q is not optional -- it is baked into the two resistances
sections.body: Once the two resistances are fixed (the load and the line or source impedance), the L-network's loaded Q is not a free design choice; it falls straight out as Q = sqrt(R_high/R_low - 1), where R_high and R_low are simply the larger and smaller of the two resistances being matched. This single number sets the network's bandwidth: a larger resistance ratio forces a higher Q, which means a narrower usable frequency range around the design frequency. Once Q is known, it fixes both component reactances directly: the element next to R_low needs X_s = Q * R_low, and the element next to R_high needs X_p = R_high / Q -- no chart or trial-and-error is needed once the two resistances are known. Each of those two reactances is free to be either sign, though, so every L-network position actually admits two valid component choices, not one: X_s (or X_p) can be built as an inductor or as a capacitor, since either one supplies a reactance of the required magnitude. That leaves a genuine low-pass-versus-high-pass design choice layered on top of the forced topology and Q -- picking the inductor-first or capacitor-first combination decides whether the network additionally rolls off harmonics above the design frequency or below it, which matters when the load also has to reject out-of-band energy. An L-network therefore trades matching two specific resistances for zero control over bandwidth -- if the ratio is large, the match is inherently narrowband, and no component choice within the L topology changes that.

lessons.workedExample: Match a 10 ohm resistive load to a 50 ohm line at 100 MHz. Since r_L = 10 < Z0 = 50, use the series-first topology: series X_s, then shunt X_p. The forced Q is sqrt(50/10 - 1) = sqrt(4) = 2. Series reactance X_s = Q * R_low = 2 * 10 = 20 ohms; choosing the inductive solution, at 100 MHz that is L = X_s/(2*pi*f) = 20/(6.283e8) approximately 31.8 nH. Adding that series L to the 10 ohm load gives 10 + j20 ohms, whose admittance is 0.02 - j0.04 S -- the 0.02 S real part already equals 1/50, confirming the g = 1 circle was reached. A shunt capacitor supplying +j0.04 S cancels the remainder: C = 0.04/(2*pi*f) approximately 63.7 pF. On the chart this is one arc-and-arc path from z = 0.2 to the center; algebraically it is the same two numbers. Its narrowband limitation: with Q = 2, the network's usable bandwidth is only on the order of f0/Q, roughly 50 MHz around the 100 MHz design point, well short of a broadband match.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking 'why did you pick that L-network orientation?' is checking whether a student understands that topology is not a style choice -- it is forced by where the load sits relative to the r = 1 (or g = 1) circle. A weak answer tries every combination until simulation software says it works. A strong answer states the r_L versus Z0 comparison up front, states the resulting Q from the two resistances, and volunteers the bandwidth consequence before being asked -- showing they know the L-network bought a match at the cost of frequency range, not a free lunch.

questions.prompt: A 10 ohm load is being matched to a 50 ohm line. Which L-network topology is correct, and why?

options.text: Shunt element first, because 10 ohms is a low resistance
Series element first, because the load's normalized resistance (0.2) is inside the r = 1 circle
Either order works equally well for any resistive load
Series element first, because 50 ohms is the standard system impedance

explanations.a: Low resistance alone doesn't determine order -- it's specifically whether the normalized value is inside or outside the r = 1 circle that decides topology.
explanations.b: Correct -- since r_L = 10/50 = 0.2 is less than 1, the point sits inside the r = 1 circle, so the series element must be added first to reach the r = 1 circle before the shunt element can finish the match.
explanations.c: The two orders are not interchangeable; the wrong order fails to intersect the needed circle and cannot reach the center.
explanations.d: 50 ohms being the 'standard' system impedance is not the reason -- the deciding factor is the ratio r_L versus Z0 relative to 1, which happens to be true here but for a different reason than stated.

questions.prompt: For the 10 ohm to 50 ohm L-network match, what is the network's forced Q?

explanations.a: 5 is the raw ratio R_high/R_low (50/10), not the Q value -- the formula requires subtracting 1 before the square root.
explanations.b: Correct -- Q = sqrt(R_high/R_low - 1) = sqrt(50/10 - 1) = sqrt(4) = 2.
explanations.c: This inverts the ratio direction; Q uses R_high over R_low, not the reciprocal.
explanations.d: 4 is the value under the square root (50/10 - 1); the Q itself is the square root of that, which is 2.

questions.prompt: What does a higher L-network Q imply about the resulting match?

options.text: A wider, more broadband match
A narrower bandwidth around the design frequency
No effect on bandwidth, only on component cost
A lower reflection coefficient at all frequencies

explanations.a: Higher Q is the opposite of broadband behavior in a matching network -- it concentrates the match around one frequency.
explanations.b: Correct -- Q sets the loaded bandwidth roughly as f0/Q, so a larger Q (driven by a larger resistance ratio) means a narrower usable range.
explanations.c: Q directly governs bandwidth, not just cost; it is not a cosmetic parameter.
explanations.d: A higher Q worsens the match away from the design frequency even though it can still be exact at that single frequency.

questions.prompt: Match each load condition to the correct first move in an L-network match.

right.text: Add the series element first
Add the shunt element first

questions.explanation: A load inside the r = 1 circle needs a series step first to walk its resistance up to the r = 1 circle; a load outside it needs a shunt step first to walk its resistance down to that same circle -- either way, the second element then finishes the trip to the center.

lessons.label: Stub and Distributed Matching

sections.heading: Single-stub tuning: a line length plus one shunt stub
sections.body: A single-stub tuner replaces the L-network's lumped shunt element with a short length of open- or short-circuited transmission line (a stub), which is a pure reactance at any frequency where it has no length-dependent loss. The design has two steps on the chart: first choose a series line length d that rotates the load's admittance (moving clockwise, at constant |Gamma|, along the wavelengths-toward-generator scale) until it lands exactly on the g = 1 circle; second, choose a stub length l whose input susceptance exactly cancels whatever remaining susceptance sits at that point, reading the stub's own susceptance off the chart's rim (a stub is just a line terminated in a short or open, so its input impedance is read the same way as any other line length). A double-stub tuner swaps the adjustable line length for a second fixed-spacing stub -- useful when the physical distance to the load cannot be changed, only the two stub lengths can be tuned, typically at a fixed spacing such as an eighth or three-eighths of a wavelength between the stubs.

sections.heading: Open or shorted -- a fabrication choice, not a physics one
sections.body: Either stub type provides the same reactance range, but the practical choice depends on the transmission medium. In coax and open two-wire construction, shorted stubs are usually preferred: a short is a solid, low-loss termination, while an open stub can radiate slightly and its exact 'electrical open' shifts with fringing capacitance at the cut end. In microstrip and other planar circuit board media, the preference often flips: an open stub avoids the extra via-to-ground needed for a short, and that via adds parasitic inductance that complicates the design at higher frequencies, so many microstrip designs favor open stubs despite the fringing-capacitance correction they require.

sections.heading: When copper beats components: the distributed crossover
sections.body: Quarter-wave transformers (a single line section with Z1 = sqrt(Z0 * R_L) matching a real load R_L to Z0) and stub tuners are both distributed techniques: they use line length and characteristic impedance instead of discrete inductors and capacitors. Below roughly 1-2 GHz, lumped L and C parts are usually the practical choice -- smaller, cheaper, and not requiring inconveniently short physical line lengths. Above that range, real inductors and capacitors start running into their self-resonant frequency, the point where a part's own parasitic capacitance or inductance cancels its intended reactance and its behavior stops matching its printed value. A short length of well-controlled circuit-board copper, by contrast, behaves predictably to much higher frequencies, so distributed matching becomes the more repeatable choice as frequency climbs.

lessons.workedExample: A load admittance, after normalizing, sits at y = 0.5 - j0.3 S. A single-stub tuner design first finds how far to move the line: rotating clockwise from that point along its constant-|Gamma| circle, the design reads off the WTG scale that a line length of roughly 0.215 wavelengths brings the point onto the g = 1 circle, landing near y = 1 + j0.82. A shorted stub is then chosen (say, on coax) whose length gives an input susceptance of -j0.82 S, canceling the remainder and leaving y = 1 + j0 -- a perfect match. Reading the stub's required length uses the same chart, starting from the short-circuit point (Gamma = -1) and rotating until the susceptance scale reads -0.82.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask about stub choice (open versus shorted, lumped versus distributed) because it tests whether a student's design decisions track real fabrication constraints rather than textbook defaults. A weak answer picks a stub type arbitrarily or claims lumped parts 'just don't work' at high frequency without saying why. A strong answer names self-resonant frequency as the specific failure mode of lumped parts at high frequency, and explains the open-versus-shorted tradeoff in terms of via inductance on a board versus radiation and fringing on coax -- showing the choice was made for the physical medium in front of them, not copied from a diagram.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of a single-stub matching design on the Smith chart.

items.text: Plot the normalized load admittance
Rotate clockwise along the constant-|Gamma| circle to find the line length that reaches the g = 1 circle
Read the remaining susceptance at that point on the g = 1 circle
Choose a stub length that supplies the exact canceling susceptance

questions.explanation: The load is plotted first, then a series line length rotates it onto the g = 1 circle, then the leftover susceptance at that point is read, then a stub of the right length is chosen to cancel it -- each step depends on the one before it.

questions.prompt: Above roughly 1-2 GHz, why do many designers switch from lumped L/C matching networks to distributed (stub or line-length) matching?

options.text: Lumped components become more expensive than copper traces at any frequency
Lumped components approach their self-resonant frequency, where parasitics dominate and their behavior no longer matches the printed value
Distributed matching requires fewer design steps on the Smith chart
Stubs eliminate the need for a characteristic impedance reference

explanations.a: Cost is not the driving reason for the crossover; the underlying issue is physical, not economic.
explanations.b: Correct -- near a part's self-resonant frequency, its parasitic reactance cancels or overwhelms the intended reactance, so the part stops behaving like its nominal value.
explanations.c: Distributed designs are not fewer steps; they use the same chart methodology as lumped designs, just with different building blocks.
explanations.d: Distributed elements are still defined relative to a characteristic impedance Z0; they don't remove that reference.

questions.prompt: In a microstrip (printed circuit board) design, why might an open stub be preferred over a shorted stub?

options.text: Open stubs have zero fringing capacitance, unlike shorted stubs
A shorted stub requires a via to ground, which adds parasitic inductance that complicates high-frequency design
Open stubs provide a different susceptance range than shorted stubs
Shorted stubs cannot be fabricated in microstrip at all

explanations.a: Open stubs actually have fringing capacitance at the cut end that must be corrected for -- they are not free of parasitics.
explanations.b: Correct -- a via-to-ground adds its own inductance to the intended short, which is harder to control as frequency rises, so many board designs favor open stubs instead.
explanations.c: Both stub types can reach the same range of susceptance values; the choice is about fabrication practicality, not available range.
explanations.d: Shorted stubs can be fabricated in microstrip using a via; they are simply less convenient at higher frequencies, not impossible.

questions.prompt: What characteristic impedance does a quarter-wave transformer need to match a real load R_L to a line impedance Z0?

options.text: Z1 = sqrt(Z0 * R_L)
Z1 = Z0 * R_L
Z1 = Z0 - R_L

explanations.a: A simple average does not produce the impedance transformation a quarter-wave line performs; that relationship is not derived from transmission-line theory.
explanations.b: Correct -- a quarter-wavelength line transforms Zin = Z1^2/R_L, so setting Zin = Z0 gives Z1 = sqrt(Z0 * R_L).
explanations.c: A direct product without the square root would give units of ohms-squared, not an impedance.
explanations.d: A subtraction does not reflect how a quarter-wave line's impedance transformation actually works.

lessons.label: Broadband Matching and Its Hard Limit

sections.heading: Stacking sections to widen the band
sections.body: A single L-network or single quarter-wave transformer matches well at one frequency and degrades quickly on either side, because its Q is fixed by the resistance ratio it has to cover. The fix is to split one big jump into several smaller ones: a multi-section transformer chains a handful of quarter-wave (or shorter) line sections, each with its own characteristic impedance, so no single section carries the full mismatch. R. E. Collin's 1955 paper on multisection quarter-wave transformers formalized two design families still used today. A binomial (maximally flat) transformer spreads the section impedances using binomial-coefficient ratios so the reflection coefficient stays as flat as mathematically possible near the design frequency, trading some bandwidth for a very smooth, ripple-free passband. A Chebyshev (equal-ripple) transformer instead allows the reflection coefficient to oscillate between a fixed small ripple bound across the whole band, which for the same number of sections yields a wider usable bandwidth than the binomial design -- the classic flatness-versus-bandwidth tradeoff. Tapered lines take this to its continuous limit, smoothly varying the impedance along the line's length instead of stepping it, which further suppresses discrete reflections at the cost of needing physically longer lines.

sections.heading: The wall you cannot design around
sections.body: No matter how many sections are added, a reactive load imposes a hard mathematical ceiling on how good and how wide a match can simultaneously be. Hendrik Bode derived the gain-bandwidth limit for RC networks in 1945, and Robert Fano generalized it in 1950 into what is now called the Bode-Fano criterion. For a simple load modeled as a resistor R in parallel with a capacitor C, the criterion states that the integral of ln(1/|Gamma(w)|) over all frequency is bounded: the integral cannot exceed pi/(R*C). That single inequality is a conservation law -- it says the load's own stored energy (via C) sets a fixed 'budget' of matching quality, and every matching network, no matter how clever, spends from that same budget. A very deep, narrowband match spends the budget fast over a small frequency range; a shallower, wider match spreads the same budget thin across a larger range. The two cannot both be maximized.

sections.heading: What this means in practice
sections.body: The direct, practical reading of Bode-Fano is that a perfect match (|Gamma| = 0) across all frequencies for a reactive load is not merely difficult with current techniques -- it is physically impossible, because achieving it would require the integral of ln(1/0) to be finite, which diverges. Any real matching design, no matter how many sections, is choosing a point on the same tradeoff curve the load's own capacitance or inductance already fixed. This is why antenna and amplifier matching specs always state a bandwidth alongside a return-loss target, never one without the other; asking for a perfect match over an unlimited band is asking for something the theory rules out before a single component is chosen.

lessons.workedExample: An antenna's feed point behaves like R = 50 ohms in parallel with C = 2 pF near its operating frequency. The Bode-Fano bound gives an integral limit of pi/(R*C) = pi/(50 * 2e-12) approximately 3.14e10 (in units of radians/second, since the integral is over angular frequency). A designer choosing to hold |Gamma| <= 0.1 (about -20 dB return loss, ln(1/0.1) = 2.303) across a bandwidth Delta-f can use the bound to estimate roughly how wide Delta-f can be before the budget runs out, and immediately see that pushing for -30 dB (ln(1/0.032) approximately 3.47) over the same width is not free -- it eats a larger share of the same fixed integral, so something else, usually bandwidth, must shrink to pay for it.
lessons.judgeFraming: This is one of the places a judge can separate a student who read a datasheet from one who understands the physics. A weak answer says a wider-bandwidth match 'just needs more components' or 'a better filter.' A strong answer names Bode-Fano directly, states that the limit comes from the load's own reactive element (its C or L), and concludes that a perfect match over an unlimited band is impossible in principle -- not an engineering shortfall to be solved with a fancier network. Being able to say why more sections help (spreading, not escaping, the same budget) versus what more sections cannot do is the exact line between a working intuition and a memorized term.

questions.prompt: According to the Bode-Fano criterion for a load modeled as R in parallel with C, what quantity bounds the integral of ln(1/|Gamma(w)|) over all frequency?

options.text: pi/(R*C)
R*C
pi*R*C

explanations.a: Correct -- for a parallel R-C load, the integral of ln(1/|Gamma(w)|) over all angular frequency cannot exceed pi/(R*C).
explanations.b: R*C alone is a time constant, not the bound value; the bound is pi divided by that product, not the product itself.
explanations.c: This inverts the relationship -- multiplying by R*C instead of dividing gives the wrong direction entirely.
explanations.d: R and C do not combine by simple addition in this relationship, and this form doesn't match the derived criterion.

questions.prompt: What does the Bode-Fano criterion imply about achieving a perfect match (|Gamma| = 0) across all frequencies for a reactive load?

options.text: It is achievable with enough matching-network sections
It is physically impossible, since it would require the bounded integral to diverge to infinity
It is possible only above 1 GHz
It is possible only for purely resistive loads, which this criterion does not apply to

explanations.a: No number of sections escapes the bound -- more sections redistribute the same fixed budget, they do not increase it.
explanations.b: Correct -- ln(1/0) is infinite, so a perfect match at every frequency would violate the finite pi/(R*C) bound, making it impossible in principle.
explanations.c: The impossibility is not frequency-dependent in this way; it follows from the load's reactive element regardless of operating band.
explanations.d: Purely resistive loads have no reactive energy storage and are a different case; the criterion as stated concerns reactive (RC or RL) loads specifically.

questions.prompt: Match each broadband matching technique to its defining characteristic.

right.text: Reflection coefficient oscillates within a fixed small bound across the band, giving wider bandwidth for the same section count
Reflection coefficient is as smooth and ripple-free as possible near the design frequency
Impedance varies continuously along the line instead of stepping between discrete sections

questions.explanation: Binomial design maximizes flatness at the cost of some bandwidth, Chebyshev design accepts ripple in exchange for wider bandwidth at a given section count, and a tapered line is the continuous limit of stepping impedance in ever-smaller increments.

questions.prompt: Who generalized Bode's 1945 gain-bandwidth limit into the broader matching-network bound now called the Bode-Fano criterion, and when?

options.text: Robert Fano, in 1950
Phillip Smith, in 1944
R. E. Collin, in 1955
Sergei Schelkunoff, in 1938

explanations.a: Correct -- Robert Fano generalized Bode's 1945 RC gain-bandwidth result into the broader matching-network limit in 1950.
explanations.b: Phillip Smith is credited with the Smith chart itself, a different (though related) contribution to RF engineering, not the Bode-Fano limit.
explanations.c: Collin's 1955 work covered multisection transformer theory (binomial and Chebyshev designs), not the Bode-Fano bound itself.
explanations.d: Schelkunoff made foundational contributions to antenna and waveguide theory but is not the source of this particular bandwidth-matching limit.

lessons.label: Matching for Noise vs Matching for Power

sections.heading: Two different 'best' points on the same chart
sections.body: Every matching problem up to this point has aimed at one target: the center of the chart, zero reflection, maximum power transfer via a conjugate match (Zin = Zs*). An amplifier's input stage has a second, competing goal -- minimum added noise -- and the source reflection coefficient that minimizes noise, called Gamma_opt, is generally a different point on the chart than the conjugate-match point. A transistor is characterized by four noise parameters that fix where Gamma_opt sits and how sharply noise rises away from it: Fmin (the lowest possible noise figure, achieved only when the source impedance is exactly Gamma_opt), Rn (an equivalent noise resistance describing how fast noise figure degrades as the source moves away from Gamma_opt), and Gamma_opt itself, specified by both a magnitude and a phase. Plugging these into the transistor's noise-figure equation produces circles of constant noise figure on the Smith chart, concentric around Gamma_opt, the same way constant-gain circles are concentric around the conjugate-match point -- and the two families of circles do not share a common center.

sections.heading: Choosing a compromise, and why the front end gets priority
sections.body: A designer overlays the constant-noise-figure circles and constant-available-gain circles on one chart and picks a source impedance in the region where an acceptable noise-figure circle and an acceptable gain circle overlap -- accepting a noise figure slightly above Fmin in exchange for gain closer to the amplifier's maximum, or vice versa. This tradeoff matters most at the very first stage of a receiver chain. The Friis noise formula shows that the total system noise figure is dominated by the first stage's noise figure, with each subsequent stage's contribution divided down by the gain of everything before it -- so the first low-noise amplifier (LNA) stage is deliberately matched toward Gamma_opt for minimum noise, even at some cost to its own gain, while later stages (whose noise contribution is already suppressed by that preceding gain) are matched instead toward the conjugate-match point for maximum power transfer and gain.

sections.heading: A precondition the chart doesn't show by itself
sections.body: Simultaneous conjugate matching -- picking source and load impedances that conjugate-match each other through the active device at the same time -- is only a valid design target if the transistor is unconditionally stable at that frequency, meaning it will not oscillate regardless of what impedance is presented to it. This is checked with the Rollett stability factor K and the auxiliary determinant Delta: the device is unconditionally stable only when K > 1 and |Delta| < 1. If those conditions fail, the calculated 'simultaneous conjugate match' impedances may not even exist as physically realizable (passive) points, or realizing them can drive the amplifier into oscillation, so this stability check has to happen before any noise or gain circle is trusted.

lessons.workedExample: An LNA transistor's datasheet lists Fmin = 0.8 dB, Rn = 4 ohms, and Gamma_opt = 0.5 at 60 degrees, all measured at 2 GHz. Its conjugate-match source impedance for maximum gain, computed separately from S-parameters, works out to a different point, roughly Gamma = 0.3 at 20 degrees. A designer draws a 1.0 dB noise-figure circle around Gamma_opt and a constant-gain circle (say, 1 dB below maximum available gain) around the conjugate-match point; the two circles overlap in a small region. Picking a source impedance from inside that overlap gives a noise figure within 0.2 dB of the transistor's floor while sacrificing only about 1 dB of available gain -- a compromise neither the pure-noise nor pure-power design point would offer alone.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'why not just conjugate-match the input for max gain?' is testing whether a student understands that RF front-end design is not one optimization problem but two competing ones. A weak answer treats maximum power transfer as the only goal an amplifier could have. A strong answer names Gamma_opt as a distinct point from the conjugate match, explains that the first stage is prioritized for noise because of Friis's formula (later-stage noise gets divided down by earlier gain), and -- if pushed -- mentions that none of this is meaningful unless the stage is first confirmed unconditionally stable via K and Delta.

questions.prompt: What is Gamma_opt, and how does it relate to the conjugate-match point for maximum power transfer?

options.text: It is the same point as the conjugate match, just under a different name
It is the source reflection coefficient that minimizes noise figure, and it is generally a different point than the conjugate-match point
It is the load-side reflection coefficient that maximizes bandwidth
It only applies to passive matching networks, not active devices

explanations.a: They are generally distinct points on the chart -- that distinction is the entire reason noise matching and power matching are treated as separate design problems.
explanations.b: Correct -- Gamma_opt is the source impedance that achieves the transistor's minimum noise figure Fmin, and it does not usually coincide with the conjugate-match impedance for maximum gain.
explanations.c: Gamma_opt is a noise-related, source-side parameter, not a bandwidth or load-side quantity.
explanations.d: Gamma_opt is a property of the active device (transistor) itself, characterized by its noise parameters, not a passive-network-only concept.

questions.prompt: Per the Friis noise formula, why is the first stage of a receiver chain matched for minimum noise while later stages are matched for maximum power/gain?

options.text: Later stages have no noise contribution at all
The first stage's noise figure dominates the total system noise figure, while later stages' noise contributions are divided down by the gain preceding them
Later stages are always built with lower-noise transistors
The first stage cannot be conjugate-matched due to stability constraints

explanations.a: Later stages do contribute noise; their contribution is just reduced, not eliminated, by the gain ahead of them.
explanations.b: Correct -- Friis's formula divides each successive stage's noise contribution by the cumulative gain before it, so the first stage's noise figure sets the floor for the whole chain.
explanations.c: Component choice isn't the reason; the formula's structure itself explains why the first stage matters most regardless of part selection.
explanations.d: Stability constraints apply to any stage, not specifically the first, and are not the reason for this noise-versus-power priority.

questions.prompt: Match each noise parameter to what it describes.

right.text: The lowest achievable noise figure for the device
An equivalent resistance describing how quickly noise figure degrades away from the optimum source impedance
The specific source reflection coefficient (magnitude and phase) that achieves minimum noise

questions.explanation: Fmin is the noise floor itself, Rn describes the sensitivity/steepness of noise-figure degradation moving away from that floor, and Gamma_opt is the exact source impedance location where the floor is achieved.

questions.prompt: What precondition must be verified before treating a calculated simultaneous conjugate match as a valid design target?

options.text: The device must have Fmin = 0 dB
The device must be unconditionally stable, i.e. Rollett factor K > 1 and |Delta| < 1
The load impedance must equal exactly 50 ohms
The amplifier must operate below 1 GHz

explanations.a: Fmin = 0 dB is not physically achievable for a real device and is not the stability precondition in question.
explanations.b: Correct -- unconditional stability (K > 1 and |Delta| < 1) must hold, or the computed conjugate-match impedances may not be realizable or safe to use.
explanations.c: 50 ohms is a common reference impedance but not a requirement for a valid simultaneous conjugate match.
explanations.d: Stability must be checked at whatever frequency the amplifier operates; there is no such frequency restriction on when the check applies.

lessons.label: Baluns, Transformers, and Practical Matching Hardware

sections.heading: Why unbalanced-to-balanced conversion is its own problem
sections.body: Coaxial cable is unbalanced: its outer conductor is grounded and carries the return current asymmetrically. Many antennas, most famously the dipole, are balanced: they expect two feed points driven with equal-and-opposite currents relative to ground. Feeding a balanced antenna straight from unbalanced coax lets stray current flow on the outside of the coax shield itself, turning the feedline into part of the antenna -- distorting the radiation pattern and pulling RF into equipment the antenna was never meant to couple to. A balun (balanced-unbalanced) transformer exists specifically to force that equality. A current balun (also called a choke or sleeve balun) works by presenting a high impedance to common-mode current on the shield, actively forcing the two output currents equal regardless of how unequal the two load halves are; a voltage balun instead just transforms voltage and assumes the load is roughly symmetric, so it can pass significant common-mode current if the load is not well balanced -- current baluns are generally the more robust choice.

sections.heading: Two ways to build a transmission-line transformer
sections.body: The common 4:1 and 9:1 impedance-ratio baluns used at HF and VHF are usually one of two topologies. Guanella's 1944 design uses one or more transmission-line sections connected in series on the output and parallel on the input (or vice versa), so the lines genuinely operate in their transmission-line mode across a wide band -- this gives excellent low-frequency performance because the design does not rely on core inductance alone. Ruthroff's 1959 design instead wires the transmission line more like an autotransformer, which is simpler and uses less wire for the same ratio, but its low-frequency limit is set by the core's inductance (not transmission-line action), so it typically has a narrower usable bandwidth at the low end than an equivalent Guanella design.

sections.heading: Core material and the tuner-is-not-a-fix caution
sections.body: The ferrite core material matters as much as the winding topology. Type 43 mix is the traditional choice for HF and low-VHF baluns, commonly recommended from roughly the high end of the HF band up through the low VHF range; type 61 mix, a lower-loss material at higher frequency, is generally preferred as the design moves further up into VHF. Finally, an antenna tuner at the transmitter end is often misunderstood: it matches the transmitter to whatever impedance the feedline presents at that end, which lets the radio operate happily and protects its output stage -- but it does nothing to the actual standing-wave pattern on the line itself.
