lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe digital sensor use because it is easy to treat an I2C or SPI reading as raw physical truth when it is actually the output of several vendor-controlled processing steps. A strong answer can name the specific compensation the chip performs (or explicitly checked the datasheet for internal filtering, like an IIR setting) and states what that means for the resolution or response time they are claiming. A weak answer reports the chip's number without acknowledging that any conditioning happened between the physical world and the bus transaction.

questions.prompt: A design needs to read six low-rate environmental sensors with a microcontroller that has very few spare pins. Which bus is the better fit, and why?

options.text: SPI, because it always runs faster than I2C regardless of sensor count
I2C, because its shared two-wire, addressed bus lets many devices share the same pins, at the cost of some arbitration overhead
SPI, because it requires no chip-select lines at all
Neither is suitable; only an external multiplexed ADC can serve six sensors

explanations.a: SPI's higher speed comes at the cost of a dedicated chip-select line per device, which works against a pin-limited design with many sensors.
explanations.b: Correct -- I2C's two shared, addressed wires let many low-rate sensors coexist on the same pins, which is exactly the pin-limited, many-sensor, low-speed scenario I2C is suited for.
explanations.c: SPI requires a separate chip-select line per device (in the common single-master, multi-slave topology), which is the opposite of pin-efficient for many devices.
explanations.d: Digital sensors with I2C or SPI interfaces are specifically designed to avoid needing an external ADC; that is the point of the digital interface.

questions.prompt: Why does a digital sensor like the BME280 store factory calibration coefficients on-chip rather than shipping every unit with an identical, generic conversion formula?

options.text: To increase the sensor's price without any technical benefit
Because each individual die has manufacturing variation, and per-unit coefficients measured at the factory correct for that specific chip's behavior
Because a generic formula would require more computation than the host can perform
To prevent the sensor from being used with any microcontroller other than the manufacturer's own

explanations.a: Per-unit calibration exists for accuracy, not as an arbitrary cost driver.
explanations.b: Correct -- individual dies vary slightly due to manufacturing tolerances, so factory-measured, unit-specific coefficients correct for that specific chip far more accurately than one shared formula could for every unit.
explanations.c: The compensation formula is a straightforward polynomial evaluation well within the capability of nearly any host microcontroller; computational load is not the reason.
explanations.d: TEDS-style calibration data and I2C/SPI compensation formulas are documented and usable by any compliant host, not locked to a specific manufacturer's controller.

questions.prompt: Order the steps a host performs to get a compensated physical reading from a factory-calibrated digital sensor like the BME280.

items.text: At startup, read the sensor's factory calibration coefficients from its NVM registers
Trigger a measurement and read the resulting raw ADC counts over the bus
Apply the vendor's published compensation polynomial using the stored coefficients
Report the result as a temperature, pressure, or humidity value in physical units

questions.explanation: The host first reads the sensor's unique factory calibration coefficients once at startup, then triggers measurements and reads back raw ADC counts, applies the vendor's compensation formula using the stored coefficients to those raw counts, and finally reports the compensated value in physical units.

questions.prompt: Match each term to what it describes.

right.text: Two-wire, addressed, shared bus favoring many low-rate devices on limited pins
Chip-select-per-device bus favoring fewer, higher-speed devices
On-sensor data block with manufacturer ID, calibration date, and transfer-function coefficients enabling self-description
Timing skew between sequential reads on a shared bus that can be mistaken for a real physical discrepancy in fusion algorithms

questions.explanation: I2C is the shared, addressed, pin-efficient bus; SPI trades pins for speed with per-device chip select; TEDS under IEEE 1451 lets a sensor describe itself to a host automatically; and sample jitter is the timing skew introduced by sequential reads on a shared bus, which matters most for algorithms assuming simultaneous samples.

lessons.label: Sensor Fusion and Estimating What You Cannot Measure Directly

sections.heading: Two sensors, two complementary flaws
sections.body: No single low-cost sensor gives a clean, drift-free estimate of orientation. A gyroscope reports angular rate directly and has low short-term noise, but any orientation estimate built by integrating that rate accumulates the gyro's small constant bias error over time -- a bias of even 0.1 degree per second integrates to 6 degrees of drift in one minute. An accelerometer measures the direction of gravity (plus any linear acceleration) and never drifts over time, since it makes no reference to the past, but it is noisy sample-to-sample and gives a wrong tilt estimate whenever the sensor is actually accelerating rather than sitting still. The two error profiles are complementary: the gyro is trustworthy at high frequency (fast changes) and untrustworthy at low frequency (long-term drift); the accelerometer is the reverse.

sections.heading: Complementary and Kalman filtering
sections.body: A complementary filter exploits this directly: high-pass the gyro-integrated angle and low-pass the accelerometer-derived angle, then add the two, with a time constant (often around 1 second) setting the crossover frequency between them. A Kalman filter, from Kalman's (1960) formulation of the optimal linear estimator, does the same job more rigorously: it maintains a state estimate and its uncertainty (covariance), predicts forward using a process model (gyro integration), then corrects using each new measurement (the accelerometer), weighting the correction by a gain computed from the ratio of process noise Q (how much the prediction is trusted) to measurement noise R (how much the sensor reading is trusted). A large Q relative to R makes the filter trust new measurements heavily; a small Q relative to R makes it trust its own model and drift-prone prediction more. Tuning Q and R is largely empirical, matched to each sensor's real noise characteristics -- underestimating R makes the filter overreact to accelerometer noise from vibration.

sections.heading: Redundancy catches faults fusion alone cannot
sections.body: A single fused estimate cannot tell you whether one of its input sensors has failed outright -- a stuck gyro axis or a saturated accelerometer still produces plausible-looking numbers that a filter will happily blend in. Redundant sensors (a second IMU, or cross-checking gyro-derived orientation against a magnetometer's heading) let a system compare independent estimates and flag one that diverges beyond an expected tolerance, a technique used in aircraft and spacecraft attitude systems where an undetected single-sensor fault is unacceptable.

sections.heading: What fusion cannot do: fix a biased sensor
sections.body: Neither a complementary filter nor a standard Kalman filter removes a sensor's systematic bias unless that bias is explicitly modeled as part of the state being estimated. If a gyro carries an uncalibrated fixed offset, an unmodified fusion filter treats every biased reading as ground truth input and the fused estimate drifts at a rate set by that bias, just as an unfused integration would -- fusion does not average away a systematic error, it propagates it. Addressing this requires either calibrating the gyro's bias beforehand or extending the filter to estimate bias as an additional state, which is why many practical implementations (including popular alternatives like Madgwick's (2010) orientation filter) explicitly track a bias term rather than assuming the raw sensor is correct.

lessons.workedExample: A student building a self-balancing robot fuses a 6-axis IMU's gyro and accelerometer with a complementary filter, alpha = 0.98 on the gyro-integrated angle and 0.02 on the accelerometer angle, giving roughly a 1-second crossover time constant. The robot balances well during normal operation. But the gyro was never calibrated for its resting bias, which measures 0.4 degrees per second; because the filter has no bias state, the fused angle estimate slowly leans in one direction over several minutes even while the robot is level, exactly the drift the fusion was supposed to eliminate -- the fix is a 5-second stationary calibration at startup to measure and subtract the gyro's bias before it ever enters the filter.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe sensor fusion because 'we used a Kalman filter' is often stated as if the filter itself guarantees accuracy, when in fact an uncalibrated sensor feeding a perfectly-tuned filter still produces a biased result. A strong answer explains specifically how the gyro was calibrated (or how bias was estimated as a state) before fusion, and can state what Q and R represent in their own tuning. A weak answer cannot explain why the filter was chosen over the alternative, or assumes fusion is a general-purpose fix for any sensor imperfection.

questions.prompt: Why are a gyroscope and an accelerometer considered complementary sensors for orientation estimation?

options.text: The gyro is accurate at high frequency but drifts over time from integrated bias; the accelerometer is drift-free over time but noisy sample-to-sample and disturbed by real acceleration
Both sensors measure exactly the same physical quantity, so combining them simply averages out random noise
The gyro never has any error, while the accelerometer is the only source of drift
The accelerometer measures angular rate directly, while the gyro measures gravity direction

explanations.a: Correct -- the gyro's integration turns a small constant bias into growing long-term drift, while the accelerometer has no time-integration step so it does not drift, but is noisy at any instant and corrupted whenever the sensor is truly accelerating.
explanations.b: They measure different physical quantities (angular rate versus gravity/acceleration direction); fusion is not simple averaging of redundant identical measurements.
explanations.c: Both sensors have real error sources; the gyro drifts over time from bias integration and the accelerometer is noisy and acceleration-sensitive.
explanations.d: This reverses the two sensors' actual physical quantities.

questions.prompt: In a Kalman filter, what does a large process noise Q relative to measurement noise R cause the filter to do?

options.text: Trust its own prediction model heavily and largely ignore new sensor measurements
Trust new sensor measurements heavily, correcting its estimate more strongly toward each new reading
Disable the prediction step entirely and output raw sensor data
Automatically detect and remove any sensor bias present

explanations.a: This describes the opposite case -- large Q relative to R means the prediction is trusted less, not more.
explanations.b: Correct -- a large Q signals that the process model's prediction is uncertain, so the Kalman gain increases and the filter weights new measurements more heavily in the update step.
explanations.c: The prediction step still runs every cycle; a large Q changes how much the update step trusts it, not whether it runs.
explanations.d: Q and R govern the weighting between prediction and measurement; they do not model or remove systematic sensor bias unless bias is explicitly added as a state.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of one Kalman filter predict-update cycle.

items.text: Predict the new state estimate using the process model (e.g., integrating gyro rate)
Predict the updated covariance (uncertainty) of that estimate
Compute the Kalman gain from the ratio of process noise Q to measurement noise R
Correct the state estimate using the new measurement (e.g., accelerometer reading), weighted by the gain

questions.explanation: Each cycle first predicts the new state from the process model, then propagates the uncertainty (covariance) of that prediction, computes the Kalman gain from the relative trust in the prediction versus the new measurement (Q versus R), and finally uses that gain to correct the predicted state with the new measurement.

questions.prompt: Match each fusion-related concept to what it addresses.

left.text: Process noise Q vs measurement noise R

right.text: Sets the frequency below which the accelerometer is trusted and above which the gyro is trusted
Lets a system flag a sensor whose independent reading diverges from another sensor, catching faults fusion math alone cannot detect
Propagates unchanged through any standard fusion filter, causing continued drift, unless explicitly estimated as an added state
Sets the relative weight a Kalman filter gives its own prediction versus each new sensor measurement

questions.explanation: The complementary filter's time constant sets the crossover between trusting the gyro and the accelerometer; redundancy allows cross-checking sensors to catch faults; an unmodeled bias passes through fusion unchanged and keeps causing drift; and Q versus R sets how a Kalman filter balances its own prediction against incoming measurements.

lessons.label: Case Studies: Environment, Structure, and Body

sections.heading: An environmental node: PM2.5 and CO2 with humidity in the way
sections.body: A low-cost PM2.5 sensor (the Plantower PMS5003 is a common example) pulls air through a chamber with a small fan, shines a laser diode across it, and infers particle mass from the intensity and rate of light scattered off individual particles onto a photodetector. The forced conditioning choice is a humidity correction: airborne particles are hygroscopic and swell as they absorb water, so above roughly 70-80% relative humidity the sensor scatters light as if there were far more particulate mass than is truly present, and vendors publish empirical correction curves against a co-located humidity sensor to compensate. A companion CO2 sensor typically uses non-dispersive infrared (NDIR): an IR source, a gas cell, and a narrowband detector tuned to CO2's roughly 4.26 micrometer absorption line, with concentration following the Beer-Lambert law. NDIR modules commonly self-calibrate with an automatic baseline correction (ABC) algorithm that assumes the sensor sees outdoor-level (about 400 ppm) air at some point each day; the dominant error term in continuously-occupied, poorly-ventilated spaces is exactly this assumption failing, since the baseline slowly walks upward toward whatever the room's minimum CO2 actually is.

sections.heading: A structural load cell: bridge geometry does the temperature compensation
sections.body: A strain-gauge load cell or structural-health sensor uses a full Wheatstone bridge with four active gauges bonded to the structure, oriented so mechanical strain changes opposite pairs of arms in opposite directions while thermal expansion changes all four arms identically. Because the bridge output depends on the difference between arms, the common thermal effect cancels and only the differential mechanical signal survives -- this bridge geometry is the conditioning choice that makes the sensor usable outdoors at all. The dominant residual error term is imperfect thermal matching between gauges (differing self-temperature-compensation coefficients or slightly different bonding), which leaves a small apparent-strain-with-temperature term that a full calibration sweep over the expected temperature range must characterize and subtract.

sections.heading: A biopotential front end: fighting impedance and mains at once
sections.body: An ECG or EMG front end faces electrode-skin impedance that can range from roughly 1 kilohm with conductive gel and skin prep to over 1 megohm with dry electrodes, demanding a very high input-impedance instrumentation amplifier so this variable impedance does not itself become a signal-dependent gain error. The forced conditioning choice against 50/60 Hz mains interference is a driven-right-leg circuit, following the design Winter and Webster (1983) published: rather than grounding the patient, an auxiliary amplifier senses the common-mode voltage on the body and actively drives it back in antiphase through a third electrode, which suppresses common-mode interference far more than passive grounding or common-mode rejection ratio alone can achieve. Even with that circuit, the dominant remaining error term is motion artifact: any change in electrode-skin contact or cable movement injects a transient far larger than the millivolt-scale biopotential itself.

lessons.workedExample: A student's ECG front end uses an AD8232-class instrumentation amplifier with two chest electrodes and a driven-right-leg circuit built around Winter and Webster's (1983) topology: a summing amplifier senses common-mode voltage from the two sensing electrodes and drives a third electrode in antiphase to cancel it, reducing 60 Hz interference visible on the trace from several millivolts (unusable) down to tens of microvolts. During a validation test the student intentionally loosens one electrode; the trace immediately shows a slow baseline wander far larger than the residual 60 Hz ripple, demonstrating that even with the driven-right-leg circuit working correctly, motion/contact artifact remains the dominant error source, not mains pickup.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe case-study instrumentation chains by asking 'what's the biggest source of error in your measurement, specifically?' because that question filters out students who built a working circuit without understanding its own limitations. A strong answer names the actual dominant term for their application -- humidity-driven PM2.5 overestimation, NDIR baseline drift, residual thermal mismatch in a bridge, or motion artifact in a biopotential trace -- and explains why the conditioning choice they made (humidity correction curve, bridge geometry, driven-right-leg circuit) does not fully eliminate it. A weak answer says 'noise' without identifying which specific error dominates.

questions.prompt: Why does a low-cost optical PM2.5 sensor tend to overestimate particulate mass at high relative humidity?

options.text: The laser diode's wavelength shifts with humidity, changing the scattering calibration entirely
Airborne particles absorb water and swell (hygroscopic growth), scattering more light, which the sensor cannot distinguish from a genuine increase in particulate mass
High humidity causes the sensor's fan to slow down, reducing airflow and undercounting particles
Water vapor itself is counted directly as particulate matter by the photodetector

explanations.a: Humidity does not shift the laser diode's emission wavelength in a way that drives this error; the mechanism is particle swelling, not source drift.
explanations.b: Correct -- hygroscopic particles absorb ambient moisture and grow larger, scattering more light per particle, and the optical measurement has no way to separate that swelling from an actual increase in dry particulate mass, which is why vendors apply an empirical humidity correction curve.
explanations.c: The described error is an overestimation from increased scattering, not an airflow-related undercounting effect.
explanations.d: Water vapor molecules are far too small individually to register as discrete scattering events the way particulate matter does; the error comes from swelling of existing particles, not vapor being miscounted as particles.

questions.prompt: An NDIR CO2 sensor's automatic baseline correction (ABC) algorithm assumes the sensor periodically sees fresh outdoor-level air (about 400 ppm) to reset its zero point. Why does this assumption specifically fail in a continuously-occupied, poorly-ventilated room?

options.text: Because NDIR sensors cannot measure CO2 concentrations above 1000 ppm at all
Because the room's minimum CO2 level never actually drops to outdoor levels, so the algorithm's baseline slowly walks upward toward whatever the room's true minimum is, not 400 ppm
Because the infrared source degrades faster in occupied rooms due to higher humidity
Because occupied rooms have too much ambient light for the NDIR detector to function

explanations.a: NDIR sensors are commonly rated well beyond 1000 ppm; the described error is a calibration drift issue, not a range limitation.
explanations.b: Correct -- ABC assumes the lowest reading over some window represents outdoor-level fresh air; in a space that is never adequately ventilated, that lowest reading is still elevated, so the algorithm mistakenly treats an elevated level as the new zero, walking the baseline upward over time.
explanations.c: NDIR performance can be affected by environmental factors, but the specific ABC failure described is about the baseline assumption, not source degradation from humidity.
explanations.d: NDIR sensing uses an internal IR source and a narrowband detector at a specific absorption wavelength; ambient visible light is not the mechanism here.

questions.prompt: Why does a full four-arm Wheatstone bridge in a load cell cancel thermal expansion but not real mechanical strain?

options.text: Because thermal expansion changes all four bridge arms identically (a common-mode effect that cancels in the differential output), while mechanical strain changes opposite arm pairs in opposite directions (a differential effect that survives)
Because the bridge is only sensitive to temperature, not strain, by design
Because mechanical strain and thermal expansion are physically the same effect and cannot be distinguished by any bridge configuration
Because the bridge excitation voltage is temperature-compensated internally, unrelated to the gauge arrangement

explanations.a: Correct -- the bridge's differential output rejects any change common to all four arms, such as uniform thermal expansion, while preserving the opposite-sign changes that true bending or loading strain produces across gauge pairs oriented for this purpose.
explanations.b: The bridge is sensitive to both effects; the geometry is specifically what separates them by rejecting the common-mode thermal component.
explanations.c: They are distinct physical effects with different signatures across the bridge arms, which is precisely what allows the geometry to separate them.
explanations.d: Thermal compensation here comes from the mechanical/electrical arrangement of the gauges on the bridge, not from the excitation voltage source.

questions.prompt: Match each instrumentation chain to its dominant residual error term.

left.text: ECG front end with driven-right-leg circuit

right.text: Humidity-driven hygroscopic particle growth causing overestimated mass at high RH
Baseline drift when the assumed fresh-air reference point is never actually reached
Residual apparent strain from imperfect thermal matching between the four gauges
Motion or contact artifact, which persists even after mains interference is actively suppressed

questions.explanation: Each application's forced conditioning choice addresses one major error source but leaves a distinct dominant residual: humidity correction for PM2.5 does not fully capture nonlinear hygroscopic growth; ABC calibration for CO2 fails when the fresh-air assumption is never met; bridge geometry cancels ideal thermal expansion but not gauge-to-gauge mismatch; and the driven-right-leg circuit suppresses mains interference but leaves motion artifact as the largest remaining error.

lessons.label: Designing an Instrumentation Project for the Fair

sections.heading: Start from a written spec, not from parts
sections.body: Every instrumentation project should begin with a short written specification derived from the measurand itself, before any sensor is chosen: the expected range (minimum and maximum values the physical quantity can take), the resolution needed to distinguish a meaningful change (the smallest difference that would change the conclusion), the bandwidth (how fast the signal changes, which sets the minimum sample rate by the Nyquist criterion), and an uncertainty target (how tight an error bound the hypothesis actually requires). A student who cannot state these four numbers before touching a breadboard has not yet defined the experiment, only picked a topic.

sections.heading: Build the chain, then compute a noise budget before soldering anything
sections.body: With a spec in hand, sensor, excitation, amplifier gain, filter cutoff, and ADC configuration are each chosen to meet it: sensor range and sensitivity matched to the expected signal, amplifier gain set so the full expected signal range fills the ADC's input span without clipping, an anti-aliasing filter cutoff set below half the chosen sample rate, and ADC resolution and data rate chosen with the earlier lesson's noise-free-bits table, not its raw bit count. Before building, every noise source in the chain -- sensor noise, amplifier input-referred noise, and ADC effective noise at the chosen data rate -- should be converted to the same physical unit and summed into a single noise budget, then compared against the uncertainty target from the spec. If the budget does not meet the target, the design changes now (a lower-noise amplifier, a longer lock-in time constant, a slower and higher-resolution ADC setting) rather than after a working circuit produces disappointing numbers.

sections.heading: Calibration and validation are part of the deliverable
sections.body: Calibration data means the sensor's response measured against a known reference standard across the full expected range, not at a single convenient point -- documenting the residuals (how far each calibration point deviates from a best-fit line) shows both accuracy and linearity, and repeating the same reference measurement multiple times documents repeatability. Validation data goes one step further: an independent check, ideally with a different method or reference, that the fully assembled system produces a result consistent with a known truth under real operating conditions, not just under bench calibration.

sections.heading: The three failure modes judges look for first
sections.body: Unstated uncertainty -- a result reported as a bare number with no error bars or repeatability data -- is the single most common gap, because it makes the result impossible to evaluate against the hypothesis. Uncalibrated sensors -- raw ADC counts or a factory-nominal transfer function reported as if they were verified physical units -- is the second, since it assumes accuracy that was never demonstrated. Resolution claimed from digits -- treating a 16-bit or 24-bit ADC word width as if it equaled 16 or 24 real bits of resolution, ignoring the noise floor -- is the third, and it is the fastest way to lose credibility with a judge who knows to ask for the noise-free-bits figure instead.

lessons.workedExample: A student studying an exothermic reaction needs water temperature to +-0.1 degrees C over a 15-40 degree C range, sampled once per second. Working backward from that spec, they select a thermistor with a factory tolerance of +-0.2 degrees C -- already larger than the target -- so before building anything they plan a calibration against a NIST-traceable reference thermometer at five points spanning the full range, fitting their own Steinhart-Hart coefficients rather than using the datasheet's nominal ones. Their noise budget sums the thermistor's post-calibration residual (+-0.03 degrees C), the amplifier's input-referred noise converted to temperature units (+-0.02 degrees C), and the ADC's noise-free-bits-limited resolution at 1 SPS (+-0.01 degrees C), totaling well under the +-0.1 degree C target -- computed before any board was populated.
lessons.judgeFraming: The question 'what is your measurement's uncertainty, and how did you get that number?' is the single most reliable way judges separate a real instrumentation project from a wired-together demo. A strong answer walks through a noise budget computed before the build and calibration data collected across the full range with documented residuals. A weak answer reports a bare result, cannot say whether the sensor was calibrated against anything, and defends its precision by citing the ADC's bit count rather than its actual noise-limited resolution -- exactly the three failure modes this lesson names.

questions.prompt: Order the stages of designing an instrumentation project, from first to last.

items.text: Define the measurand's range, required resolution, bandwidth, and uncertainty target in writing
Select a sensor and excitation scheme matched to that spec
Choose amplifier gain, filter cutoff, and ADC settings, then compute a noise budget against the uncertainty target
Build the circuit and calibrate it against a known reference standard across the full range
Collect independent validation data confirming the assembled system matches a known truth

questions.explanation: A sound instrumentation design starts by writing the measurement spec, then selects a sensor to match it, then computes a noise budget for the rest of the signal chain before building anything, then builds and calibrates against a reference standard, and finally validates the assembled system independently.

questions.prompt: What is a noise budget, and when should it be computed?

options.text: A tally of every noise source in the signal chain converted to a common unit and summed, computed before the circuit is built so the design can be adjusted if it does not meet the uncertainty target
A record of how much money was spent on low-noise components, tallied after the project is finished
The ADC's rated bit count, which alone determines whether the design will meet its uncertainty target
A single measurement taken after calibration to confirm the sensor works

explanations.a: Correct -- a noise budget sums sensor, amplifier, and ADC noise (converted to the same physical unit) and compares the total to the uncertainty target before hardware is built, so the design can still be changed if the budget falls short.
explanations.b: A noise budget is about noise sources and their magnitudes, not project spending.
explanations.c: Raw ADC bit count overstates real resolution once noise is accounted for; the noise budget uses the noise-limited figure instead, and combines it with other chain elements.
explanations.d: A noise budget is a design-time calculation across the whole chain, not a single post-hoc measurement.

questions.prompt: Why is claiming resolution directly from an ADC's bit count (e.g., '24-bit means 24 bits of resolution') a red flag to a science-fair judge?

options.text: Because it ignores the noise floor -- real usable resolution is set by the noise-limited effective bits at the chosen data rate, which is typically far fewer than the raw word width
Because ADCs never actually have as many bits as advertised on the datasheet
Because bit count is irrelevant to resolution entirely and should never be mentioned
Because judges prefer analog measurement systems over any digital ones

explanations.a: Correct -- as covered in the sigma-delta ADC lesson, the digital word width is not the same as the noise-limited effective resolution, which depends on data rate and the specific noise-free-bits figure for that configuration.
explanations.b: The advertised bit count is real as a digital word width; the issue is that noise, not dishonesty about word width, limits how many of those bits carry real information.
explanations.c: Bit count is relevant as an upper bound on resolution; the problem is treating it as the actual achieved resolution without accounting for noise.
explanations.d: The concern is about accurately stated resolution, not a general preference for analog over digital systems.

questions.prompt: Match each common failure mode to what a strong project provides to avoid it.

left.text: Uncalibrated sensor reported as physical units

right.text: Repeated measurements and computed error bars accompanying the reported result
Documented calibration residuals against a known reference standard across the full expected range
A noise-budget-derived effective resolution figure instead of the raw bit-width number

questions.explanation: Unstated uncertainty is answered with repeatability data and error bars; an uncalibrated sensor is answered with documented calibration residuals against a traceable reference across the full range; and resolution claimed from digits is answered with a noise-budget-based effective resolution rather than the ADC's nominal word width.
